The results show that the best setup depends on the task, and they give engineers measured guidance for multi-card training.
arxiv-2505-23305:
Yunkee Chae and Kyogu Lee built a single music model in 2025 that both creates songs and pulls them apart. Older tools either generate a full mix or split a mix into fixed instrument tracks, like drums or vocals only. Their system, MGE-LDM, learns full mixes, partial mixes, and single stems together inside one compact diffusion model.

At run time the same model can invent a whole track, fill in a missing part, or extract any source named in a text request. Splitting and filling are both treated as filling gaps in a hidden sound space. Training mixed several multi-track datasets without fixed instrument labels, which keeps the tool flexible for new sounds.
arxiv-2505-23905:
Shashank Dattathri and co-authors explain a wobble that can shift galaxy centers in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. Some galaxies look lopsided, with their dense core sitting off center. The authors study round, self-gravitating star systems with a sharp change between inner and outer density slopes.

Such systems break a classic stability rule, and simulations show a rotating dipole mode then grows. The mode torques the core loose, and it sloshes around the center on a slow, oval path for a long time. Trapped stars drain energy from the feature that drove the growth, which slowly erases it. The authors link the process to lopsided galaxies and off-center nuclei.
arxiv-2505-24305:
Mingxu Zhang and co-authors present SR3D in this 2025 paper, a training-free method that lets robots grasp glass and shiny objects. Depth cameras fail on transparent and glossy surfaces, so grasp planners get bad maps. Prior fixes need complex setups or waste the little data a single view gives. SR3D starts from one color photo plus a flawed depth view.

Outside vision models first rebuild the object's 3D mesh from the photo. The hard step is placing that mesh back into the real scene at the right spot and size. View matching and keypoint matching use meaning and shape cues from both the photo and the depth data. The result is a repaired depth map that supports grasp detection. Tests in simulation and the real world back the approach.
arxiv-2506-00905:
Maryam Hadipour and Soroush Haseli present a 2025 physics paper on extracting work from quantum states with help from noise. In quantum thermodynamics, a demon-like helper that measures a system and feeds back the result can pull out extra work. This gain, called daemonic ergotropy, usually needs quantum correlations to begin with.

The authors start with merely classically correlated states, which should give no gain. They show that a damping channel, a common noise type, can create the needed quantum correlations on the way through. If the channel has memory, past events shape later noise and preserve the system-helper link. The gain then grows further. Noise, in this setting, becomes a resource rather than a nuisance.
arxiv-2506-01005:
He Song and co-authors chart the excited states of a hypothetical heavy particle in a 2025 paper. The particle is a pentaquark, a bundle of five quarks, here made only of heavy charm and bottom quarks and their antimatter partners. They picture it as a diquark paired with a triquark, two clusters inside one particle.

Regge trajectories are curves that link a particle's mass to its spin or excitation level. The authors build four series of such curves for this pentaquark, from two kinds of internal motion. They give rough mass estimates for the excited states in each series. Three of the curves have long, heavy full forms, since a pentaquark has inner structure that a plain meson lacks. Simple fitted curves match those forms well. All four series rise with a shared two-thirds power pattern.
arxiv-2506-01205:
Antonia Karamolegkou and four co-authors tested whether language models can spot double meanings, in a paper published in 2025. A word or line can be read two ways, and spotting that helps with jokes, traps in text, and readings of doubt. Their test set holds sound, word, and structure twists, plus altered foils: word swaps, synonym swaps, and random changes.

Asked directly, models failed to flag the twists with any strength. But thin probes trained on the models' own internal states read the twists with high accuracy, at times over nine in ten. The relevant code lives in set layers of the network. The authors release the data and code. They say the gap shows that prompts miss what models in fact know, a fact that test design must face.
arxiv-2506-02205:
Yuliang Gu and co-authors upgrade a trajectory optimizer used in model-based robot learning, in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. The base optimizer samples many candidate paths and keeps the best, but its single-peak sampling settles too early in multi-peak terrain. Their version runs a team of samplers in parallel.

A weighted center, built with a flexible distance rule, pools what the team learns. The weakest samplers are then respawned near that center inside a trust zone. The add-on is light and drops into standard pipelines. Tests on toy problems, cluttered navigation, and full learning pipelines improved both speed and quality.
arxiv-2506-02405:
Zhiya Tan, Xin Zhang, and Joey Tianyi Zhou tackle a new task: tracing which image models edited a picture, and in what order, in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. Real fakes pass through many hands and tools, yet past work handled only one edit stage. Later edits often erase the marks of earlier ones.

The team built a data set by running three image models in sequence on the same faces. Over eighty thousand images resulted. Their model learns each tool's own editing style rather than blended fingerprints. Tests, including part-removal checks, showed the method works well on tangled edit chains.
arxiv-2506-04505:
Oskolkov, Zhang, Makarov, Yudin, and Panov teach robots to navigate using three dimensional scene graphs in twenty twenty-five. A scene graph maps how objects relate in space. That map helps a robot guess where a target object likely sits. Their framework learns the graph representation with open vocabulary labels.

Training mixes three methods to speed and stabilise learning. Imitation learning lets the agent copy demonstrations. Curriculum learning raises task difficulty step by step. Experiments ran in the Isaac Sim simulator. Scene graphs raised success rates most in hard navigation cases. The code is openly released for other researchers. The authors target mapless navigation in partly unknown spaces.
arxiv-2506-04605:
Ava Morrissey, George Zhou, Chelsea X. Huang, and six colleagues report a search for an escaping atmosphere in this two thousand twenty-five astronomy paper. Their target is HIP94235b, a sub-Neptune planet about one hundred twenty million years old. Atmospheric loss is thought to shape the observed split in the small-planet population. Escaping gas can be traced through excess absorption in hydrogen and metastable helium lines.

Using the CRIRES+ spectrograph on the Very Large Telescope, the team observed two transits and found no escaping helium. One-dimensional Parker wind models turn that null result into an upper limit on the mass loss rate. A search for water features in the transmission spectrum also came up empty. The authors conclude the planet likely lacks a large hydrogen-helium envelope, matching photoevaporation expectations for its age.
arxiv-2506-05205:
Jackson Petty and co-authors built a test of complex reasoning for language models in two thousand twenty-five. The test, called RELIC, gives a model a grammar in its prompt and asks if a string fits the language that grammar defines. Grammar size and string length can be raised to make the task harder.

Even top reasoning models did poorly as tasks grew harder. They did not spend more effort to keep up; they spent less, using fewer reasoning tokens. Their style also shifted from working out a step-by-step method to guessing. The authors call that shift a form of quiet quitting on hard tasks, which would stay hidden if only final answers were checked.
arxiv-2506-07005:
Sebin Sebastian, Kolay, Abhidev, Ding, Furukawa, and Nath wrote this paper in two thousand twenty-five, with some given names shown as initials in the byline. It probes a triangular lattice antiferromagnet built on ytterbium ions.

Lab tests of pull, heat, and magnetization, plus crystal field sums, pin the ground state as a Kramers doublet with an effective spin of one half. The spins link only weakly, and nuclear resonance checks find no long-range order down to low heat, though spin waves stay lively. Field scaling of the spin-lattice rate shows strong paramagnetic swings. The clean, disorder-free crystal looks apt for hunting quantum spin-liquid physics.
arxiv-2506-07305:
Jorge Bellorin writes out, in a 2025 paper, the full motion equations of quadratic gravity in their energy-based form, a bookkeeping task the theory's fans had long deferred. Quadratic gravity is a leading attempt to fix gravity's quantum behavior, built from squares of curvature. Its energy-based form is algebraically heavy, so the work runs through a symbolic algebra system.

Bellorin then simplifies the equations around flat space and splits the ripples into parts along and across their travel. Matched against the standard field equations, the simplified form holds exactly when the space ripples are traceless, a condition a free function in the formalism can impose at will. As a check, the equations are set loose on uniform expanding universes and solved outright. The paper is offered as groundwork for anyone working this theory.
arxiv-2506-09205:
Haiyan Wang introduces, in a 2025 paper, a hybrid design method for quantum neural networks that keeps circuits small enough for today's noisy machines. The framework pairs a transformer, which squeezes rich classical data down to a form a few qubits can hold, with a shallow quantum circuit whose layout is tuned by a genetic algorithm.

The genetic search, NSGA-II, trades two goals against each other: higher accuracy and fewer basic gates. On four benchmarks, from iris flowers to heart disease data, the method matched or beat leading quantum models while using far fewer gates in most cases. A curvature analysis showed the trained networks sit far from the flat zones that stall quantum training. The author presents the design as a good fit for current quantum hardware.
arxiv-2506-10105:
Mathew Thomas Arun, Shyam M, and Ritik Pal study rare processes that change baryon number in a 2025 particle physics study. Interest grew after a large detector reported possible candidate events for neutron to antineutron change. Such processes would be described by operators built from six quarks.

The authors track how those operators change as energy scales shift, running from everyday scales up to very high ones. They consider whether new physics at middle energies, not yet ruled out by collider searches, alters that running. Two scenarios are compared, one with only known particles in between. The work helps connect low-energy searches with high-energy theories.
arxiv-2506-11005:
Mouna Dhaouadi, Bentley Oakes, and Michalis Famelis extract developer rationale from open source software in two thousand twenty-five. New helpers must grasp a project's history to choose well. Past reasons hide across many changes, and reading them all takes huge effort. No past tool laid out clashes among those reasons on its own.

Their build rests on Kantara, a past frame for rationale care. Pretrained models and large language models pull out decision lines. Structure checks flag clashes and slow design rot. A Linux kernel module served as the first test case. Five more active projects tested how far the method spreads.
arxiv-2506-12405:
Emmanuel Deruty and co-authors show that single synthetic tones in electronic pop can carry several pitches at once, and that artists use the effect on purpose, in work from twenty twenty-five. A harmonic tone usually reads as one pitch. Studio made tones can break that rule.

Listening tests had people count pitches in single tones and transcribe tone sequences by ear. Synthetic tones from tracks by the artist Vitalic and others conveyed more pitches than natural counterparts. Answers varied a lot between listeners. Strong upper partials and certain echo profiles in the signal tracked the ambiguity. The authors conclude that perceived pitch sets depend on both the listener and the listening setup.
arxiv-2506-13805:
Bonam Mingole, Aditya Majumdar, Firdaus Ahmed Choudhury, and a wider team wrote this research paper, published in 2025. It puts chatbots in the clinic's waiting room: real people posed their everyday health worries to four public language models, and nine physicians graded the answers for benefit and harm.

Earlier studies used exam questions or expert-written cases, nothing like the messy queries users actually type. A week-long university competition crowdsourced 212 real or imagined concerns from thirty-four participants. The models' replies were scored by board-certified doctors. On average, most responses leaned helpful, but the grading exposed failures a benchmark would miss. Self-diagnosis and triage are exactly where a confident wrong answer hurts most. The authors argue evaluation must go in the wild, with real questions and clinician judges, before these tools are trusted with health.
arxiv-2506-14405:
Jarkko Kotaniemi and co-workers tuned vibration-canceling commands for a bendy robot arm from gauged data in a 2025 paper. Input shaping convolves a command with a timed impulse train so the arm's own induced waves cancel its natural ringing. The right impulse timing depends on the arm's changing pose and stuff. Instead of building all that in, the team gauged residual vibration across the workspace once. Then interpolates shaper settings for any new pose from the recorded map.

Tests on a three-dimensionally printed arm built from several stuff showed large drops in leftover vibration after moves. The appeal is useful: a simple, robust classic technique becomes self-tuning with one calibration sweep, no fragile model needed.
arxiv-2506-15205:
Lizardo Valencia Palomo tests whether event generators can reproduce quarkonia born inside jets at the Large Hadron Collider. The paper from twenty twenty-five starts from an embarrassment: PYTHIA 8 predicts prompt J/ψ mesons mostly isolated, against LHCb and CMS data showing them embedded. Color reconnection tweaks do not rescue the mismatch. The new quarkonia parton shower inside a recent PYTHIA release does.

With the shower on, simulation meets data, and reconnection settings start to separate measurably. A prediction for the heavier Υ(1S) meson says experiments should raise their jet momentum cuts to tell the variants apart. Quarkonium production theory, long unsettled, gains a discriminator it can actually run.
arxiv-2506-20405:
The Casimir effect is a faint attraction between uncharged plates, born of quantum fluctuations in empty space. Tian-Ming Zhao and Rong-Xin Miao study it on networks: graphs of edges joined at nodes, a setting that broadens interface conformal field theory. They propose a new rule for what happens at a node and show it respects energy conservation, since the energy flowing into a node sums to zero.

With that rule in place, a striking result follows. The Casimir force on one edge of a network can flip from attractive to repulsive when the lengths of the other edges are adjusted. What is usually fixed by geometry becomes tunable. The authors build the case from a simple network of free massless scalars in one space dimension, then extend it to richer networks and higher dimensions. They close with open questions for the field.
arxiv-2506-20505:
Ball, Bromley, and Kenyon hunted for symbiotic stars in the Gaia space survey's third data release in twenty twenty-five. A symbiotic star pairs a cool giant with a hot compact companion fed by the giant's wind. Only a few hundred are confirmed, though the galaxy should hold far more.

Starting from known systems, the team characterized their brightness, colors, and low-resolution spectra, which show hydrogen emission from the interaction. They then searched the full archive for bright red giant-like sources whose spectra matched a template built from the known stars. A machine learning algorithm trained on confirmed systems produced a catalog of one thousand six hundred seventy-four candidates. Cross-matches with infrared and X-ray surveys singled out twenty-five especially compelling candidates for follow-up.
arxiv-2506-20705:
Kin Kwan Leung, Rasa Hosseinzadeh, and Gabriel Loaiza-Ganem link convolutions, intrinsic dimension, and diffusion models in two thousand twenty-five. The manifold view says real data lie on thin sheets in big spaces. Diffusion models add noise by convolution, then learn to undo it. A past estimator reads local dimension from how density shifts with noise.

That estimator, FLIPD, was proved only for flat sheet data. The team proves it under far more real assumptions. A twin result holds when uniform noise swaps in for Gaussian noise. Local dimension gauges data complexity and flags outliers and fakes. The proof firms up a tool in wide use.
arxiv-2506-21705:
Mhatre and colleagues find that galaxies with heavier central black holes sit closer to their neighbors. Their paper appeared in two thousand twenty-five. The environments of active galactic nuclei reveal how supermassive black holes grow. Earlier clustering studies hinted that massive black holes favor dense regions. The signal was weak, and accretion rate showed little link. The team brings a sharper statistic to the question.

They use kth-nearest-neighbor counts, which capture finer clustering detail than pair counts. The sample is an unbiased set of nearby active nuclei from the Swift/BAT survey. Distances are measured to galaxies from the 2MASS catalog. Nearest neighbors lie closer around the heaviest black holes. The result firms up the case that setting shapes black hole growth.
arxiv-2506-22505:
Hassan Baker, Matthew Emigh, and Austin Brockmeier segment objects with only image-level labels. Their twenty twenty-five computer vision paper avoids costly pixel masks. Special fields like sonar and medical imaging lack large labelled sets. Knowing whether an object is present is far cheaper to label.

Their method pastes cut-out objects onto fresh background images. Those rebuilt scenes create counterfactual training examples. Backgrounds are clustered so swaps target a chosen background type. Training pushes rebuilt scenes to match real scenes from that cluster. A second loss term guides the masking network further. The approach learns object shapes without ever seeing a hand-drawn mask.
arxiv-2506-22705:
Md Abdullah-Al Kaiser and three colleagues wrote a 2025 paper on a computer chip that uses light to do math. AI workloads now flood data centers with data, and classic chips waste time and power shuttling data between memory and processor. Light-based in-memory chips promise to break that bottleneck.

Their design centers on a photonic tensor core built from light-based SRAM cells. A new electro-optic converter turns results back to signals with little waste. The mixed-signal layout aims for high speed at low energy. Tests judge how the core handles the dense math of neural networks. Such chips could shrink the power bill of large AI models.
arxiv-2506-22905:
Xiang Yuan, Loic Halbert, Lucas Visscher, and Andre Severo Pereira Gomes weigh two fast-spin quantum chem ways side by side. The work came out in 2025. Both work out how bits of stuff reply twice to charge and pull fields. Twice-reply traits rule how light bends in glass-like goods. Heavy bits call for fast-spin math.

The team built a fast-spin linked-group twice-reply code. It came next to their past move-based form of the same code. Both codes run with fast-spin frames of two or four parts. They run with plain frames. They treat still fields and fields that swing back and forth. Test cases reach first bend traits of gas pairs down the salt-form row. They also work out Verdet marks for heavy rare gases and picked pairs. Those marks gauge how pull turns light as it flies.
arxiv-2506-23305:
Rachit Saluja and co-authors release an MRI data set of newborn lungs in a 2025 paper. Bronchopulmonary dysplasia is a common lung complication in preterm babies, usually judged by portable X-ray. MRI could give richer detail without radiation or sedation, but data to train segmentation tools has been missing.

The set holds free-breathing 3D MRI scans from forty newborns, most with the disease, each paired with expert outlines of the lungs and trachea. Rich clinical data come with the scans. The team also provides baseline segmentation models checked against clinical judgment. The resource is meant to spur image tools that can help clinicians sort out the causes of the disease in each baby.
arxiv-2507-02505:
Suri Deekshita, Sanjay, Saravana Veni, Conrad Tabi, and Timoléon Kofané simulate vortex droplets in two-part Bose-Einstein condensates lit by photonic spin-orbit coupling. Their paper from twenty twenty-five solves the Gross-Pitaevskii equation in two space dimensions plus time. Coupling stretches the droplets, and each part grows its own vortex cluster. Quantum fluctuation terms, of Lee-Huang-Yang type, push back against the spread.

At low coupling and weak interaction terms, droplet shapes hold. As coupling rises, vortices take over the pattern. Stronger interactions then melt the vortices back into droplets. The dance shows how two knobs trade control of the texture. The authors note small-atom-count droplets as a next, lab-friendly target. The work serves cold-atom and condensed matter readers alike.
arxiv-2507-04305:
Ali Bagci and Philip Hoggan examine the math tools used to compute atom energies, in a 2025 paper. Quantum chemists build electron clouds from sets of standard shapes called orbitals. The authors study full, well-behaved sets of these shapes whose main quantum number need not be a whole number.

They show how to build accurate and fast sets from such shapes. They also warn that treating the fractional numbers as free knobs can produce sets that look valid but are not, since some shapes may collapse into copies of others. Tests on two families of atoms gave lower ground-state energies than earlier published sets. The paper helps users of a classic atom method choose safer building blocks.
arxiv-2507-05605:
Six researchers wrote a paper in two thousand twenty-five on a classroom feedback tool that talks to the teacher's wrist. Student response systems help in lectures, but all of them show feedback on a screen the teacher must watch. Their prototype, Hapster, sends live class feedback to an Apple Watch as both visuals and vibration patterns.

Six instructors and one hundred fifty-five students at a United States university tried the system. Participants found it effective for live feedback and engagement. Teachers, though, struggled to tell the vibration patterns apart mid-lecture. The authors weigh flexibility against misuse and point to accessibility and moderation questions.
arxiv-2507-06505:
Yun Ling and Heping Wang compute typical size ratios for random polynomials on curved spaces. Their paper appeared in two thousand twenty-five. A Nikolskii factor compares one norm of a polynomial against another. Worst-case bounds grow fast with degree. Random choices behave far better, usually. The setting is diffusion polynomials on closed Riemannian manifolds. Coefficients are independent Gaussian noise.

The authors find the exact order of the average factor. For finite target norms, the average stays constant as degree grows. For the supremum norm, it grows only like a root of a logarithm. Both crush the worst-case rates. The proof works through eigenpairs of the Laplace-Beltrami operator. Approximation theory gains sharp expectations for random expansions.
arxiv-2507-07105:
Yushen Zuo and a large team build 4KAgent, a system of smart agents that can raise any image to a very sharp, large form. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-five.

The system can take a small, badly worn image and turn it into a clear, true-to-life large one, and can be run more than once for still larger results. It has three core parts. One shapes the work to the use case. One, the sight agent, reads the image with sight-language models and quality experts, then plans the fix. One, the repair agent, then does the work. The aim is one tool that can clean and grow all kinds of images.
arxiv-2507-07705:
Jie Jiang and Zebin Zhang wrote a 2025 paper on what drives the Sun's eleven-year activity cycle in one leading model. The model is the distributed-shear Babcock-Leighton dynamo, which builds the Sun's magnetic field inside its convection zone, the churning outer layer. A slow pole-to-equator flow below the surface has long been seen as a key driver in older models.

In older flux transport models, that flow sets the sunspot pattern and the length of the cycle. Jiang and Zhang tested several flow patterns in the newer model, including deep and shallow single cells. Their title gives the answer: the subsurface flow plays only a minimal role here. The finding redirects attention to other parts of the dynamo.
arxiv-2507-09905:
Zijian Guo, Zhenyu Wang, Yifan Hu, and Francis Bach develop statistical theory for a robust learning framework in a 2025 study. Data pooled from several sources differ in distribution, and a model must still work on a target domain where only unlabeled data exist. Their conditional group framework hedges against the worst plausible shift within groups, using the standard cross-entropy loss for classification.

The authors supply the inference side: how estimates from such training behave and how uncertain they are. Guarantees matter because robust training is often adopted on faith. Theory for domain adaptation helps practitioners know when the hedge is worth its cost.
arxiv-2507-10205:
Friedemann Kemm works on a 2025 improvement to a two-dimensional model of traffic flow. Such models treat cars on a road network much like a fluid, and they help planners test how jams form and clear. Kemm takes a model published not long before and shows how it can be made both simpler and cheaper to run.

The main gains come from how time steps are chosen and how traffic at the edges of the area is handled. He gives a method to work out the time step limits the model needs. He also adds a sub-step scheme for inflow and outflow at the borders. Together, these changes cut computing cost a great deal on large areas with coarse grids, such as a whole region rather than one town.
arxiv-2507-10505:
Jia-Xin Lin and three co-authors hunted for signs of odd baryon states in pair data. Their paper, from twenty twenty-five, deals with resonances known as Xi star states. In their view, these states form as loose bound pairs from channel mixing. The mixing joins a set of meson and baryon pairs. The team built the force kernel from a gauge based frame and tied the channels with a mixed smoothing scheme.

Their scan found two states whose traits match known listed states of this class. They then worked out pair link curves at tiny scale to see if labs could spot them. Readers in hadron physics get testable signs for states whose nature is still in doubt.
arxiv-2507-11805:
Shijie Qin and Shijun Liao simulate turbulent flow with extreme care in a 2025 paper. Standard simulations of turbulence are known to be polluted by numerical noise, because turbulent paths react sharply to tiny disturbances. Their clean method cuts both kinds of numerical error to any level required, keeping noise negligible over long spans. They apply it to a three-dimensional flow for the first time.

Compared against the clean benchmark, the standard result drifted off quickly. Its flow patterns lost the right symmetry, its energy cascade shifted, and even its long-run statistics diverged. The authors argue their benchmark should be used to judge what standard turbulence simulations can really claim.
arxiv-2507-12305:
Ma'sum and five co-authors build a way for models to learn from a stream with no saved old data in this twenty twenty-five paper. Stream learning sees each batch once, so old skills can fade fast as new ones land. Saved old samples fix the fade but break strict data rules in some fields.

Inside, their method leans on short prompt cues fed to a fixed pre-trained model. One light cue maker holds broad skill, while small shift tools hold task-tuned skill. A mixed update rule keeps old cues safe while new cues are learned. Tests on four image sets beat top rival methods with fewer parts and fair speed.
arxiv-2507-14205:
Pavel Malinovskiy wrote a 2025 paper proposing a network design that serves both crowded cities and remote villages. The catalog title carries a long citation note, but the paper itself joins three tools: software-run wireless mesh networks, direct broadcasts to phones, and cloud streaming. Cities suffer overload while rural areas lack coverage, and one design tackles both.

Tests in Bangkok, Mumbai, and rural Finland cut delay by over a third and shifted forty percent of traffic off the main links, he reports. Rural coverage rose by about twenty-eight percent, and fairness of access improved. The system recovered from faults in under ten seconds. The author also urges spectrum and subsidy policies to help such designs spread.
arxiv-2507-14705:
Sai Wang and co-authors present Neo, a 2025 framework for testing language-model agents at scale. Such agents act differently from turn to turn, so fixed test sets and hand testing go stale fast. Neo automates the work with two agents of its own: one writes questions and one grades the answers, sharing a common context store.

Test chats are drawn from a chance model spanning dialogue flow, user intent, and emotional tone, so talks stay varied and human-like. Tried on a live seller finance chatbot, Neo found edge-case faults in five attack classes at close to the rate of expert human testers, while producing tests ten times faster. The authors release the tool for wider use.
arxiv-2507-15205:
Xinran Li, Xiujuan Xu, and Jiaqi Qiao read emotions in conversation in 2025 with a graph model that looks both near and far. A line's feeling depends on nearby replies and on the talk's longer arc. Their network builds two graphs: one over distant lines, one over close ones.

A regularizer keeps the two views distinct, while a bridging module lets them inform each other. Training follows a curriculum that starts with easy examples. A difficulty score pays special attention to shifts between similar emotions, which models often confuse. On two standard conversation datasets the system beat existing benchmarks. The authors say the long-short split is the source of the gain.
arxiv-2507-16405:
Stassa Patsantzis, a solo author, asks whether a logic-learning system can teach itself from a handful of positive examples alone, in a 2025 paper. Inductive logic programming learns readable rules from examples, and its strongest methods can invent new concepts and handle recursion. The catch is that they need a hand-built background theory and carefully chosen negative examples, which take expert effort.

Patsantzis sets up a self-supervised version of the task and builds a system, Poker, that grows its own examples as it learns. It makes fresh cases, labels them positive or negative, and learns from the enlarged set. A general template scheme replaces the hand-tailored background theory. In tests on grammar learning, Poker's accuracy rose as it generated more of its own examples. A rival system, given no negatives, guessed too broadly.
arxiv-2507-16505:
Camillo Imbimbo and Ludovico Porro give one unified account of anomalies in four-dimensional theories with strong symmetry, in a paper from twenty twenty-five. Anomalies are quantum effects that break a symmetry the classical theory promised to keep. They are tightly constrained, and cataloguing them guides model building.

A classic recipe handles gauge anomalies through special polynomials in curvature. Superconformal theories, though, host two kinds of anomaly at once, one of each famous type. The authors widen the recipe using an ideal of constraint polynomials that mixes curvatures with connections. Anomalies then fall out of a cohomology computation at a set degree. The richer ideal explains naturally why both anomaly types coexist.
arxiv-2507-18705:
M. Messa and co-authors proved the great distance of a gravitationally magnified galaxy in 2025 using the James Webb Space Telescope. The Cosmic Gems arc is a young galaxy stretched into an arc by a foreground group's gravity, and photometry had suggested it sits in the universe's first few hundred million years. Photometric redshifts can deceive, so the team took a six-hour spectrum with the telescope's near-infrared spectrograph, the first direct spectroscopic test.

The spectrum showed the sharp Lyman-alpha continuum break, the fingerprint of neutral hydrogen absorbing ultraviolet light. At the expected wavelength, along with faint hydrogen and oxygen release lines from the spectrum's far end. Those lines fix the redshift exactly, at just over nine point six, proving the arc's antiquity. A weak Balmer break and an extremely blue ultraviolet slope complete a portrait of a very young, hot stellar group.
arxiv-2507-19105:
Sokolovski and Matzkin revisit the tunneling time problem in a 2025 paper. Quantum theory seems unable to say how long a particle spends inside a barrier, so workers often infer time from where a wave packet ends up. The authors swap the barrier for a tunable interferometer with two arms. In that setup, the outgoing packet can be advanced or delayed at will.

They argue the uncertainty principle blocks adding up the times spent in each arm when both are used. Nor is there cause to claim faster-than-light or negative times, since one arm alone can place the packet at the same spot, even more strongly. Tunneling, they say, works the same way.
arxiv-2507-21305:
Cooperman, Iyer, Rowan, and Son build flows that mix at an exponential rate yet let a trace fade slowly, in work from twenty twenty-five. A trace that rides a flow, with a hint of its own spread, should fade fast when the flow mixes well. Smooth flows that mix exponentially give fade times with bounds set by the square of a log term. The team asks if rough flows break that speed-up.

Their flows are rough, just continuous, yet mix exponentially, the same at each level of spread. Fade time stays of the order of one over diffusivity, which means no speed-up at all. The team finds sharper bounds tied to the mix rate, with spelled-out constants. Rates that change with time are let in too, which suits flows built by chance. How smooth the flow is decides the speed-up.
arxiv-2507-21505:
Conan Gillis measures a runaway growth function in group theory in a 2025 paper. The Baumslag-Gersten group is famous among algebraists for extreme behavior packed into a simple definition. Its conjugator length function asks how long a word must be to witness that two elements are conjugate, and it grows astonishingly fast.

Gillis shows the function matches a tower of exponentials whose height itself grows with the input, about the base-two logarithm of n. That beats any fixed-height tower. He asks whether any one-relator group could grow faster still. Along the way he computes the same function for iterated Baumslag-Solitar groups, where it matches an iterated exponential of matching depth.
arxiv-2507-21905:
Viacheslav Pirogov and Maksim Artemev test deepfake detectors on wild, real-world style data in two thousand twenty-five. Fake faces threaten ID checks and trust in media. Many detectors shine in the lab yet have never faced messy field data.

The team built a set of over half a million high-grade fakes with top current generators and ran modern detectors on it. Fewer than half scored above sixty percent on a standard ranking score, and the worst sat at chance. Plain edits hurt a lot: JPEG squeezes and image touch-ups cut scores sharply. Code and data are public. The verdict is blunt: spotting fakes in the wild stays hard, and lab scores flatter the tools.
arxiv-2508-00005:
Tilman Hinnerichs and co-authors use syntax rules to fence the search space of program synthesis, in this 2025 paper. A synthesizer hunts a huge space of candidate programs, and constraint solvers are the usual hounds. Those solvers usually encode what a program must do, not what it may look like. Rules about shape can be checked and spread without ever running the program, which makes them cheap and general.

The team builds BART, a solver that propagates such shape rules to model whole program spaces, marking not just valid programs but likely useful ones. On enumeration tasks the rules cut away up to ninety-nine percent of the space. Search then finished far faster. The authors call this a shift from checking solutions to sculpting the haystack.
arxiv-2508-00605:
Farhana Haque, Abdur Rahman, and Sumon Ahmed (2025) present a topic modeling method built for Bengali, a language short on research tools. Topic models find the hidden themes in large text collections. English dominates the field, while Bengali work lacks modern methods and shared benchmarks. Their model, GHTM, blends three views of each document. Word statistics, word meaning vectors, and a graph network over the text combine into one representation. Matrix factorization then extracts the topics.

Across three Bengali data sets, the hybrid beat both classic and recent rivals on topic quality and diversity. It stayed light to run, unlike heavy neural systems. It even beat established graph models on the English 20 Newsgroups benchmark. The team also releases NCTBText, a set of 8,650 Bengali textbook documents, to widen the field beyond newspapers. The authors frame both contributions as infrastructure for a language the field has skipped.
arxiv-2508-01005:
Yiqun Chen and co-authors let a planner agent assemble a custom retrieval workflow for each question, balancing answer quality against cost, in work from twenty twenty-five. Retrieval augmented generation grounds language models in fetched documents. Fixed pipelines waste effort on easy questions and skimp on hard ones.

Executor agents handle steps like query rewriting, document picking, and drafting. A planner agent, trained by reinforcement learning, picks and orders the steps per question across several turns. Rewards track answer score, with a penalty for cost. On multiple question sets, the adaptive setup kept quality high while holding cost and delay in check. Code was released in public.
arxiv-2508-01105:
Md Sultanul Islam Ovi and co-authors build a learning system that flags student stress early, in work from 2025. Stress harms student health and grades, while surveys and spot checks react too late. Their system sorts stress from two survey data sets that cover mind, school, setting, and social factors.

A six-stage pipeline cleans the data, picks key traits, trims size, and trains six base models. Voting and stacking blends then lift the scores. The best blends hit high marks on both sets, past prior records. The authors frame context-aware data tools as a real aid for campus well-being teams.
arxiv-2508-02205:
Milorad Bežanić and co-authors compare two ways to build gravity on a noncommutative spacetime. In such spaces, coordinates fail to commute, bending the rules of geometry. Star-product methods host several rival gravity models. Some rest on twisted symmetry, others on a braided form of it.

The two models here yield different gravity actions on paper. Yet in set cases their physical fallout matches exactly. They share the same three-graviton vertex, a basic scattering building block. Simple vacuum solutions also coincide between the pair. The overlap maps how the crowded model landscape fits together.
arxiv-2508-06805:
Aarav Mehta, Priya Deshmukh, Vikram Singh, Siddharth Malhotra, Krishnan Menon Iyer, and Tanvi Iyer draw crisp organ boundaries for medical scans with a top-down refinement edge detector. Their paper from twenty twenty-five notes that convolutional networks ace natural-image edges yet blur the millimeter precision medicine demands. Their design upsamples and fuses deep semantic features with fine low-level cues along a backward pathway. Sub-pixel upsampling sharpens the final trace.

Anisotropic volumes get slice-wise refinement plus light three-dimensional context, keeping costs sane. On CT and MRI organ sets, boundary scores and Hausdorff distances beat baselines and rival medical contour methods clearly. Plugged downstream, the crisp maps lift segmentation accuracy, registration, and lesion outlining near organ borders.
arxiv-2508-07705:
Falla, Roberti, Limongi, and Chieffi show rotation explains the observed ratio of two gamma-ray isotopes from massive stars, in a paper from twenty twenty-five. Aluminum twenty-six and iron sixty are ejected by massive stars. A satellite measures their galactic flux ratio near zero point two four. Stellar models are computed with and without rotation.

Non-rotating models predict a ratio near zero point zero six, far too low. Including rotation reproduces the observed value successfully. Added models refine the spread of starting spin rates. Yields rest on an established published model grid. Rotation is essential physics for chemical evolution models.
arxiv-2508-09205:
Yoni Schirris and four co-authors argue that explanation tools for medical AI produce measurements, not explanations, and propose a way to actually test explanations. A heat map like GradCAM shows which features sway a classifier, but the claim it suggests might be false. In pathology, a wrong explanation can hide reliance on spurious features that harm some patients.

Their proof of concept pairs an AI-integrated slide viewer with vision-language models. Sliding-window experiments on the slide test an explanation's claims directly, while the models quantify how predictive the explanation is. Competing explanations could be distinguished both qualitatively and numerically. The authors frame the system as a step from explainable AI toward genuinely explained AI.
arxiv-2508-09305:
Jamie Kimble, Bruce Sagan, and Avery St. Dizier carry a K-theoretic promotion operator from tableaux to labelings of general partially ordered sets. Promotion, invented by Schutzenberger, cycles labels through a diagram and anchors a field called dynamical algebraic combinatorics. Pechenik had defined its K-theory cousin for packed labelings of tableaux. Writing in twenty twenty-five, the team applies that operator to posets broadly and to rooted trees in particular, where the combinatorics can be fully unraveled.

Under stated conditions, orbit sizes and the operator's order obey clean divisibility rules. For several named tree families, extended stars, combs, zippers, and a three-leaved type, the authors determine orbit sizes completely for certain packing parameters. The paper extends a circle of results showing promotion's hidden regularity survives far beyond its original tableau home.
arxiv-2508-10205:
Dario Bosch, Georgiy Solomakha, Felix Glang, Martin Freudensprung, Nikolai Avdievich, and Klaus Scheffler wrote this paper in two thousand twenty-five. It builds an MRI antenna array whose transmit pattern can switch mid-pulse, to even out the flip angle at ultrahigh field.

Eight coaxial dipoles carry PIN diodes and inductors that reshape the current along each stick. That shifts the field between the top and base of the brain by a fair step in models. Fired fast during a pulse, the switch can more than double flip angle evenness in one scheme. A built array shows the effect too, though weaker than the models. The trick adds a new knob without more costly transmit channels.
arxiv-2508-12205: Zikang Dong, Zhonghua Li, Yutong Song, and Shengbo Zhao study how large the values of quadratic Dirichlet L-functions can become near the central point. Working conditionally, they examine the functions at points close to one half within a suitable range. Their result shows the values there can reach the same order of magnitude as the large values at the central point itself.
arxiv-2508-13005:
Jiawen Xu and Odej Kao test whether richer internal features help models spot new classes and learn over time, in a paper from 2025. Two hard tasks frame the study. One asks a model to flag inputs from classes it never saw in training. The other asks it to add new classes without forgetting old ones.

Many past methods try to boost feature diversity as a side trick, but few tested its role directly. Xu and Kao run controlled tests of that one factor. More diverse features improved the spotting of unseen classes. They also helped the model keep old knowledge while taking in new classes in the lifelong learning task. The authors hope the clear evidence will guide both new methods and new theory.
arxiv-2508-13605:
Andrea Lachmann's paper from 2025 works in algebraic geometry, on rings that blend two kinds of counts for spaces tied to symmetry groups. The spaces in question are classifying spaces, which stand in for all bundles of a given group. Lachmann takes up the group of roots of unity and the multiplicative group, alone and in pairs.

The method builds on a plan set out by di Lorenzo and Mantovani in 2023 for the even case. Lachmann works out the full Chow-Witt rings for these spaces and their products, plus a tower of related counts. The same treatment covers pairs of projective spaces and a product of two classifying spaces for the multiplicative group.
arxiv-2508-14105:
Jahid Chowdhury Choton, John Woods, and William Hsu build a customizable training ground for teams of robots that must navigate together. Guiding many robots through continuous space in uncertain settings remains an open problem. Deep reinforcement learning is popular for it, but training is slow and sample-hungry, and most setups offer no formal guarantees about the task.

Their environment asks robots to visit a set of target regions by the shortest paths, framed formally as a Markov decision process. The team relates the navigation task to finding the best policy for that process. They crafted several variants of the world and benchmarked six learning methods, both gradient-based and not. A learned policy was then run inside a 3D simulator of an agricultural field with uncertainties to test robustness. The authors offer the environment as guidance for building training worlds that transfer to real machines on limited budgets.
arxiv-2508-15005:
Ovidiu Racorean wrote this gravity paper in 2025 on the BTZ black hole, a tidy model hole in three dimensions. He reworks its inner region by swapping the roles of space and time in the metric, then stretches that inner geometry to its full extent. The stretched inner form turns out to mirror the outer solution's shape.

That mirror lets him assign a paired quantum state, a thermofield double, to the inner build, apart from the one long tied to the outer build. Counting both states as dual to the whole hole, he works out the bulk's partition function. The count describes a spacetime that cannot be oriented, like a strip with a twist. He also builds a paired state that links zones where space and time point in opposed senses.
arxiv-2508-15705:
Anton Ni, Adam Rettig, and Joonho Lee present a method for grand canonical density functional theory in two thousand twenty-five. The method is tuned for solid state systems and uses Gaussian type basis sets. In this grand form, the count of electrons can change, as at a charged surface. The team cuts the free energy direct, with the density matrix as the sole free object.

The electron count updates on its own as the solve proceeds. A model of solvent is built in for real cell like settings, at modest extra cost. Tests on rust at silver faces match past work well. The code sits in a known quantum chemistry package.
arxiv-2508-16705:
Pimenta, Schlippe, and Schaaff probe consciousness-like behavior in language models with a maze navigation test. Models must move through mazes from a first-person view. The test taps spatial sense, perspective taking, goal focus, and step order at once. The team distilled consciousness theories into 13 traits to check. Twelve leading models were run with zero, one, or a few example shots. Reasoning-tuned models beat their standard twins across the board.

Gemini 2 Pro led on full path accuracy at about 53 percent. DeepSeek-R1 led on partial paths at about 81 percent. The wide gap between those scores shows models lose a steady self-model mid-task. Genuine, lasting self-awareness remains out of reach.
arxiv-2508-16805:
Victoria DiTomasso and co-authors announce, in a 2025 paper, a two-planet system around the bright nearby star HD 60779. The star is much like the Sun and close enough for close study. Two dips in its light, caught by the TESS telescope and confirmed later, mark a sub-Neptune planet on a thirty-day orbit, about three and a quarter times Earth's width.

Nearly three hundred precise velocity measures then weighed that planet at about fifteen Earth masses and revealed a second, heavier world farther out. The outer planet takes about 104 days per orbit and weighs at least twenty-eight Earth masses; whether it crosses the star is unknown. Both orbits look round, hinting at a calm past. The system's fast motion through space keeps its ultraviolet light clear of gas absorption, which suits studies of air escaping from the inner planet.
arxiv-2508-17005:
Thi-Nhung Nguyen, Hoang Ngo, Dinh Phung, and two colleagues use long-term planning by language models to answer hard questions over tables, in a paper published in two thousand twenty-five. Table questions often need several operations in sequence: filter, sort, compute, compare. Popular chain-of-thought methods improvise step by step and often drop constraints hidden in the question.

The authors instead have the model lay out an explicit long-term plan first. The steps are tightly linked and all serve the final goal. Execution then follows the plan rather than wandering. This structure also trims stray detail from the reasoning trace. The approach targets table question answering and fact verification, where one missed condition flips the answer. Planning ahead, the authors argue, is what separates a lucky chain of thoughts from a reliable procedure. Their method leans on planning abilities that large models already show.
arxiv-2508-17605:
Jonathan Crall and four co-authors present HotSpotter, a fast tool that picks out single animals from their coat patterns. The tool is not tied to one species. Their work came out in twenty twenty-five.

HotSpotter pulls key spots from a photo and matches them to a labeled photo bank. One method checks a new photo against each bank photo in turn and ranks the scores. A second method uses fast near neighbor search with a scoring rule drawn from recent work on grouping photos. Trials on banks of more than a thousand photos covered zebras, giraffes, leopards, and lionfish. Matches were more exact than past methods and took just a few seconds each.
arxiv-2508-19905:
Imad Ali Shah and seven co-authors review, in a 2025 paper, whether hyperspectral cameras can help self-driving cars see the road. Such cameras split light into many thin bands, which lets them tell materials apart, not just shapes. That skill could sort road surfaces, spot pedestrians, and read bad weather scenes where ordinary cameras fail.

The team analyzed 216 commercially available cameras and graded them by automotive needs: frame rate, spatial resolution, spectral band count, and compliance with temperature standards. A stark gap showed. Only four cameras met the performance bars for speed and detail, and none met the automotive temperature grade. Past datasets for this technology are also thin, with few bands and few scene types. The authors map where the field stands and list the work needed to bring such cameras into real cars.
arxiv-2508-21005:
Satyam Tyagi and a co-author published this cybersecurity paper in 2025. Ransomware does its worst damage by spreading sideways through a network from one compromised machine to many. The authors build a graph model of that spread: machines are points, and reachable services such as remote desktop form the connecting edges. Each service gets a pivot potential, a score for how easily an attacker can hop onward through it.

Repeatedly applying the model yields a matrix of compromise chances between every pair of machines within a set number of hops. From it come two headline scores: an overall susceptibility rating and an estimate of the blast radius, the share of assets an average attack would reach. On real enterprise snapshots, cutting the highest-risk service links shrank both scores the most. The authors pitch the framework for judging segmentation and ranking defenses.
arxiv-2509-00105:
Shaoting Feng leads a team with ten co-authors who present AdaptCache in 2025, a storage system that speeds up language model serving. Chat tools often reuse past context, such as chat history and documents. Serving systems store the key-value cache for that context, a set of saved inner values, so it need not be recomputed. At scale those caches outgrow fast memory and spill to slower drives.

Most hits then come from the slow tier, which adds delay. AdaptCache squeezes caches with loss, which drops some detail, and picks the method, rate, and tier for each entry. The aim is more hits in fast memory and less loading delay, with quality kept high. Smarter cache tiers could cut the cost of busy chat services.
arxiv-2509-00305:
Ghassen Baklouti, Maxime Zanella, and Ismail Ben Ayed present LIMO in 2025, a loss for transductive few-shot learning with the CLIP vision-language model. Few-shot learning adapts a model from a handful of labeled examples. Transductive methods also use the unlabeled test batch at hand, which can sharpen those few labels, but work on foundation models is still young.

Their loss joins three terms: mutual information between images and text class descriptions, a penalty for drifting from text-driven zero-shot predictions, and a standard cross-entropy term on the labeled shots. Parameter-efficient fine-tuning keeps the update light. The mix targets strong accuracy while staying close to the base model's knowledge.
arxiv-2509-00605:
Rishiraj Acharya, writing alone, proposes Gated Associative Memory, or GAM. GAM is a new design for sequence modeling. Such tasks process ordered data, like text, step by step. The Transformer is the current standard design. It relies on self-attention, whose cost grows with the square of length. Long inputs thus become very costly to process.

The GAM block runs in linear time instead. It replaces attention with two paths that run in parallel. A causal convolution path captures local context near each token. A memory retrieval path captures global, content-based patterns. A gating step blends the two paths for each token. Acharya built GAM from scratch for the tests. He compares it with a Transformer and with Mamba. The tests use the WikiText-2 and TinyStories datasets.
arxiv-2509-01205:
Neutrinos are ghostly particles whose tiny masses and mixing still test particle theory, and dark matter adds a second puzzle. Bhabana Kumar and Mrinal Kumar Das build a model that aims to explain both at once, without supersymmetry. Their setup pairs left and right sectors and uses a modular symmetry group to shape how particles couple.

In the model, neutrino masses arise through a type II seesaw route, where heavy partners make the known neutrinos light. Fits favor a normal ordering of neutrino masses and a lower range for one mixing angle. The predicted effective Majorana mass falls in a span future tests can probe. The lightest sterile neutrino also serves as a dark matter candidate, with a mass range that matches the observed cosmic abundance.
arxiv-2509-01305:
Most star-forming galaxies link their mass tightly to how much dust dims their light, but a strange group breaks that pattern. Laura Bisigello, with seven co-authors, studies HELM galaxies, low-mass systems with very high dust extinction, first flagged by the James Webb Space Telescope. They may change how astronomers think dust is made in young galaxies.

To learn their dust content, far-infrared views over wide areas are needed. The team forecasts what PRIMAger, a planned far-infrared camera, would see for candidate HELM galaxies in a deep thousand-hour survey of one square degree. They expect tens of thousands of detections, with a third of sources seen in at least four filters. Those data would allow detailed fits of dust emission and estimates of dust traits across cosmic time.
arxiv-2509-01805:
Helen E Read leads four co-authors in showing that bent elastic strips can lock into patterns like driven systems do. In driven systems, certain drive strengths cause a lock-in where the response turns unstable in a regular beat. The team finds the same lock-in in a purely static setup with no motion over time. Their strips rest on a base whose height varies in a wavy pattern.

Under pressure, the strips switch between near regular and fully regular buckling shapes. Both computer models and lab tests show the alternation clearly. The match between static buckling and dynamic instability was not known before. Even simple elastic parts can thus show rich pattern behavior worth study by engineers.
arxiv-2509-02305:
Nuria Alabau-Bosque and six co-authors wrote a 2025 study that tests the vision model CLIP, which links images and text, by having it play the board game Hues and Cues. Players in that game give and follow colour clues, so it probes colour naming and perception.

The authors compare CLIP choices with human answers across game situations. Overall the model matched people fairly well. Still, play exposed cultural biases and uneven behaviour when colours were described at different levels of detail. Those flaws stayed hidden under standard benchmarks. The paper argues that game-based tests can reveal weaknesses in AI models that usual scores miss, and it offers a fresh route for checking how human-like a model really is.
arxiv-2509-02505:
Evan M. Wilson, Joseph A. Prescott, and Jason T. Haraldsen wrote a 2025 condensed matter paper on a magnetic interaction called Dzyaloshinskii-Moriya, which twists neighbouring spins in tiny clusters. Such effects matter for nanoscale magnetism and spintronics devices.

The authors derive a general structure factor formula for a pair of spin-half particles, a dimer. That formula shows how the interaction's strength ratio and phase control an energy gap and the intensity of a key transition. Exact diagonalisation of a spin Hamiltonian, including outside magnetic and electric fields, supports the analysis. The interaction splits energy levels and pushes them apart. Heat capacity anomalies line up with spin selection rules, linking measurable thermodynamics to microscopic rules.
arxiv-2509-03405:
Daniela Gottesman and 6 co-authors released LMEnt in 2025, a suite for tracing how language models turn training text into knowledge. Models increasingly answer questions about the world. Yet the path from pretraining data to internal beliefs is poorly understood. Controlled resources are needed, because ordinary web corpora cannot be fully annotated or replayed.

LMEnt bundles three parts. First comes a knowledge-rich pretraining corpus, with every entity mention annotated from Wikipedia. Second comes an entity-based retrieval tool over that data. It beats existing tools by large margins. Third come a dozen small pretrained models, saved at thousands of checkpoints during training. Case studies show that how often entities appear together, and in what forms, shapes learning trends. As models bind entities more tightly, their facts resist in-context editing. Inconsistent predictions during training, by contrast, flag facts that edit easily.
arxiv-2509-03605:
Christian Northe sets out to split entanglement by fermion parity in a Majorana fermion theory in a 2025 physics paper. Entanglement measures how strongly two parts of a quantum system are linked. Majorana fermions are unusual particles that act as their own antiparticles, described here by a conformal field theory.

Northe studies the vacuum, a fermion state, and states built from conformal interfaces, which join distinct theory regions. Splitting space into intervals can be done two ways, giving distinct entanglement spectra set by spin structures. Plain entropies cannot tell those structures apart, but symmetry-resolved entanglement can. Fermion parity, whether the fermion count is even or odd, becomes the label that resolves them. With an unpaired Majorana zero mode present, the parity-resolved entropies share energy equally at all orders. Without one, the imbalance is measured by special Ramond-sector data. Links to symmetry-protected topological phases are sketched.
arxiv-2509-03705:
Zohar Amitay and one co-author's 2025 research paper is about controlling high harmonic generation by placing an atom inside a quantum cavity. High harmonic generation shines intense light on atoms to produce much higher-frequency light, useful for attosecond pulses lasting billionths of a billionth of a second. Normally the atom sits in open space under a continuous laser field.

Using non-Hermitian Floquet theory, which handles repeating light fields in open systems, they find a single cavity photon can already change the process. Coupling the cavity wisely to light-driven atomic states creates polaritonic Floquet states, hybrids of atom, light field, and cavity. Those hybrids emit side harmonics around the usual odd harmonics. Different cavity setups give different spectra, and chains of cavities widen the options further. The resulting pulse sequences differ from cavity-free ones, opening a control route for other strong-field processes.
arxiv-2509-03805:
Saki Imai and three co-authors' 2025 research paper focuses on measuring how vision-language models build common ground during conversation, not just whether they succeed. Grounding is the gradual process by which partners develop shared understanding through interaction. Most benchmarks test these models in single turns or question answering, missing that interactive core entirely.

Their suite scores four things: grounding efficiency, how well content aligns, lexical adaptation, and how human-like the dialogue feels. One hundred fifty self-play sessions of referential games are run between three proprietary models, then compared against human pairs playing the same games. Each model departs from human patterns on three metrics or more, with GPT-4o mini coming closest overall. Two lessons stand out for benchmark design. Task success scores alone do not show successful grounding happened. Strong alignment between image and utterance also fails to predict task success reliably.
arxiv-2509-03905:
Shinya Kanemura and one co-author describe a surprising cancellation in leptogenesis, a leading explanation for the universe's matter-antimatter imbalance, in a 2025 theoretical physics paper. In leptogenesis, a heavy particle decays out of equilibrium and creates a net lepton asymmetry, later converted into the baryon asymmetry we observe. Intuition says changing that particle's mass or couplings should change the final asymmetry a lot, especially when washout is weak.

The authors demonstrate the opposite for a general class of decay scenarios. Varying mass and couplings barely moves the lepton asymmetry at all. The reason is a cancellation: the effects largely offset each other through the decaying particle's own evolution. Once leptogenesis works at one benchmark point, a much broader parameter space opens around it. The flip side is practical too. Tuning mass and couplings to boost the asymmetry will be challenging, since the mechanism resists that kind of adjustment.
arxiv-2509-04105:
Min Gi Park and two co-authors revisit a classic theory of the early universe in light of fresh telescope data in a 2025 physics paper. The Starobinsky model describes inflation, a burst of rapid expansion just after the Big Bang. New combined observations, labeled P-ACT-LB-BK18, sit slightly at odds with what the original model predicts. That mild mismatch motivates the team's update.

Small extra terms are added to the model's gravity equations, built from higher powers of a quantity called the Ricci scalar. Even modest changes of that kind pull predictions closer to the new data. The changes also limit how the universe could have reheated after inflation ended. Older cosmology models thus face sharper tests.
arxiv-2509-04205:
M Atzori Corona and five co-authors forecast what next-generation neutrino detectors could measure in a 2025 physics paper. The COHERENT experiment watches neutrinos, nearly massless particles, bounce off whole atomic nuclei. Two planned detectors anchor the study: a cold cesium iodide crystal and a ton-scale tank of liquid argon. Precise bounce counts can pin down the weak mixing angle, a basic constant of particle physics, at low energies.

The same data should reveal how neutrons spread inside nuclei. Limits on the neutrino's tiny electric charge and magnetic traits could match or beat today's combined world results. Sensitivity to hypothetical new carrier particles is also mapped. Neutrino physics gains a sharper low-energy tool.
arxiv-2509-04405:
Meagan Herbold and two co-authors forge fake quasar spectra that behave like the real cosmic forest in a 2025 astrophysics paper. Light from distant quasars passes through hydrogen clouds, leaving a thicket of absorption lines called the Lyman-alpha forest. Its one-dimensional power pattern probes the early universe's structure, heat history, and even neutrino mass. Instrument quirks can fool that probe, so trustworthy synthetic spectra are essential for checking analysis pipelines in giant surveys like DESI.

Their lognormal mock method tunes random fields to copy the real flux evolution and power shape across cosmic time. Matches reach sub-percent accuracy for average flux and percent level for the power pattern. Extensions could add contaminants and instrument effects.
arxiv-2509-04705:
Three large language models are compared as helpers in apparel design by Nusrat Jahan Lamia and one co-author in a 2025 study. The models, from OpenAI, Gemini, and DeepSeek, were tested across stages of textile work. Those stages include sustainable choices, cost effectiveness, and production planning.

The authors checked how well models replicate garment design from parameters such as fabric construction, shade, weave, and silhouette. They also compared performance across body types and purposes such as fashionwear and sportswear. A custom dataset supported fabric image generation and classification. In their tests, OpenAI tools performed best on fabric construction and classification tasks.
arxiv-2509-04905:
Large artificial intelligence models promise help with circuit design, but whether they can beat established tools is contested. Qiang Xu, lead author with five co-authors, frame that debate in a 2025 paper written for a conference panel on circuit design automation. Experts from universities and industry give their views.

The paper examines what large language models and large circuit models can do in practice. It also covers their basic limits and future prospects. Reliability, scale, and clarity form the core arguments. The authors weigh whether such models can beat or complement traditional design methods. Their overview covers a fast-moving and disputed technology trend.
arxiv-2509-05005:
Inferring the dipole amplitude from deep inelastic scattering data can be framed as a scan-like reconstruction problem. Henri Hänninen, lead author with two co-authors, develop that framing in a 2025 particle physics paper. They write the inference as a discrete linear inverse problem, analogous to computed tomography.

Standard inverse problem methods then reconstruct known dipole amplitudes from simulated cross section data at realistic precision. Unlike earlier work, no fit parametrisation is assumed. That freedom also lets them quantify uncertainty in the inferred amplitude more generally. The authors aim at bias-free analysis of data from past and future electron colliders.
arxiv-2509-05105:
Some topological spaces let every real-valued function into a huge product factor through a small, well-behaved space. Anton Lipin, lead author with two co-authors, characterise such spaces in a 2025 topology paper. Their factorisability notion uses the product of uncountably many real lines as the target.

They prove an equivalence linking factorisability to an embedding property of Stone-Čech compactifications. Factorisability is hereditary and countably multiplicative, and such spaces are hereditarily Lindelöf and separable. Strikingly, whether nonmetrisable examples exist depends on set theory: under one standard extra assumption all examples are second-countable, while under another a classic fan space qualifies.
arxiv-2509-05305:
Predicting how the brain folds as it grows is tackled with borrowed physics by Yingjie Zhao and three co-authors in a 2025 paper. Brain shape reflects genes and mechanics and links to development and disease, but its folded, uneven geometry makes measurement hard.

Their physics-transfer method first solves growth on simple shapes like spheres and oval solids, where elastic instability is well understood. A neural network carries that physics into detailed brain models, trained on a library of high-grade simulations built to fill a data gap. The approach characterises features and forecasts folding well, showing local deformation matters more than background shape. Checks against medical images support its use as a digital twin.
arxiv-2509-05405:
A public home for data on fleeting cosmic events debuts with stars torn apart by black holes, in a 2025 paper by Noah Franz and twelve co-authors. Studying transients across many wavelengths is essential, but published measurements are scattered across papers and formats.

Their repository, OTTER, stores event information and brightness measurements from radio to X-ray in a schema built for multi-source data. Open software, an access interface, and a web app let users view and analyse the collection. The first release holds the largest photometric archive yet of tidal disruption candidates, with well over a hundred thousand observations of hundreds of candidates. Four example studies show the archive at work, and users can contribute new data.
arxiv-2509-05505:
Answering medical questions from the research literature is the job of a system built by Mansi Garg and five co-authors in a 2025 paper. Ordinary health search lags behind published evidence, while biomedical papers are hard for the public to use directly.

Their system pairs retrieval with generation: articles from PubMed, curated question sets, and medical encyclopaedias are searched by meaning using compact embeddings and a fast vector index. A fine-tuned open language model then writes concise, context-aware answers, trained cheaply with a low-rank adapter method. On breast cancer literature, focused retrieval lifted scores for factual consistency and relevance over baselines. Future work targets more languages, privacy, and personalisation.
arxiv-2509-05805: Jürgen Müller answers a pointed question in pure group theory in this short 2025 paper. It asks whether the projective cover of the trivial module for the sporadic simple group J4, taken in characteristic eleven, is a permutation module. A projective cover is the largest indecomposable building block sitting over a module, and permutation modules come from group actions on sets. Müller determines the ordinary character of that cover, and the character settles the title question.
arxiv-2509-05905:
Some interstellar visitors may not leave the solar system at all, argue Rainer Marquardt-Demen and two co-authors in a 2025 paper. Most objects arriving from other stars pass through once and escape, but gravity, especially near Jupiter, can trap a small share. The authors predict where those captured objects should now be found.

Their framework joins an analytic model of the incoming flux near Jupiter with N-body simulations that follow capture and long-term wandering. Captures happen roughly once every couple of centuries, and survival favors steep, highly inclined orbits that rarely meet planets. The predicted steady population clusters at high inclinations, far out near the inner Oort cloud, where it hides among native long-period comets. Over a hundred known objects already sit inside the model's densest region.
arxiv-2509-06005:
Choosing how strongly each place influences its neighbors is a modeler's dilemma in spatial econometrics, and Xin Miao and three co-authors address it in a 2025 paper. Their setting is the multivariate spatial autoregressive model, where each location's outcome depends on others through a weights matrix. Often several candidate matrices exist, and the true one may not be among them.

The authors propose a selection method whose estimator is asymptotically optimal for squared loss even then, and consistent when the true matrix is a candidate. A model averaging estimator that blends candidates shares the optimality. Simulations confirm strong finite-sample performance, and an application to Sina Weibo data shows how a user's posting is shaped by the accounts they follow.
arxiv-2509-06305:
Reconstructing the state of light itself, mode by mode, gets faster convex optimization tools in a 2025 paper led by Shengyong Li with nine co-authors. Bosonic states, encoded in electromagnetic fields, serve quantum sensing, communication, and error correction, but their tomography faces dense measurement bases and huge Hilbert spaces. The team attacks the scaling problem on three fronts.

Efficient displacement operator computation, Hilbert space truncation, and stochastic convex optimization each remove a bottleneck. On top, a sample-based maximum-likelihood method is tailored to flying modes, light in transit. Simulations of four-mode and nine-mode problems show accurate, practical reconstruction. The authors offer the package as reliable tooling for high-dimensional, multi-mode state characterization.
arxiv-2509-06705:
Building a three-dimensional skeleton from one flat image is the task set by Mohamed Zayaan S in a solo 2025 computer vision paper. The system, Cortex-Synth, must recover both the skeleton's geometry and its topology, meaning how the joints connect. Guessing depth and structure from a single view is inherently ambiguous.

Three ideas drive the design. A hierarchical graph attention mechanism refines the skeleton at several scales, a spectral method using Laplacian eigenvalues adjusts the topology in a differentiable way, and adversarial training keeps the pose structure consistent. Four modules generate a pseudo three-dimensional point cloud, encode it, decode joint positions, and build the graph. On ShapeNet the method improved joint position accuracy and graph similarity over earlier work and cut topological errors sharply. Uses range from robot handling to medical imaging and character rigging.
arxiv-2509-06805:
Galaxy clusters found by the Euclid space telescope are matched against known clusters in a 2025 validation paper by the Euclid Collaboration. Euclid will detect huge numbers of optically selected clusters across a vast survey area, reaching far beyond redshift one. Many low-redshift clusters are already known from other surveys, and recognizing those matches is a key validation step.

The authors assembled catalogues and meta-catalogues of known clusters for the matching, enriching Euclid entries with external measurements where counterparts exist. To show the method, they used the Dark Energy Survey's first-year RedMaPPer cluster catalogue in place of the future Euclid catalogue. The exercise also produced an updated version of that catalogue with multi-wavelength counterparts attached. Careful cross-matching protects the final Euclid cluster catalogue from double counting and missed identifications.
arxiv-2509-06905:
Memory networks that can store hugely many patterns get a new variant from Linda Albanese and three co-authors in a 2025 neural networks paper. Hopfield models are linked memories: store patterns, then fetch them back from partial cues. A recent exponential family raised storage capacity a lot, and this paper proposes another member built differently.

The cost function is built from exponentials of plain quadratic losses, which naturally favors setups that recall a stored pattern perfectly. The model is not a mean-field system, yet its dynamics and retrieval traits remain open to analysis and match the first exponential model. A signal-to-noise argument shows stored patterns stay stable fixed points of the zero-temperature dynamics up to hugely many patterns. Wider basins of attraction shrink the load somewhat, but capacity keeps its exponential scaling, and a separate derivation confirms the prefactors.
arxiv-2509-07005:
Qimao Yang and Jing Guo work on using a variational quantum linear solver for quantum transport in tiny semiconductor devices, in a 2025 paper. Earlier work with this solver in device studies mostly tackled the Poisson equation. There the matrix behind the linear system is real and symmetric, a comparatively friendly case.

Transport problems are harder, because their matrices are complex and lack symmetry. The pair propose new cost functions that handle such systems and run faster. They also give cheaper ways to evaluate those functions, cutting circuit complexity and making results less sensitive to noise. Their tests use the non-equilibrium Green's function method for the transport equation. The quantum route matters because classical computing struggles as device grids grow in size.
arxiv-2509-07105:
Galaxies that form stars glow in both infrared light and radio waves, and the link between the two is tested here for a full galaxy sample. M. E. Moloko and 7 co-authors present the work in 2025. They use new observations from the MeerKAT radio telescope, plus data from the Very Large Array, for galaxies in the IRAS Revised Bright Galaxy Sample.

The team sorts galaxies by their main energy source and by whether they are merging with a neighbor. Isolated galaxies show a tighter and slightly higher ratio of infrared to radio output than merging ones. Merging galaxies also form stars faster and look redder in some infrared colors. The ratio also falls as radio power and galaxy mass rise. These patterns help show how collisions change the way galaxies shine.
arxiv-2509-07205:
Jussi Behrndt and 4 co-authors work out sesquilinear forms for a class of Sturm-Liouville operators in 2025. Sturm-Liouville operators are differential operators that govern vibrations, heat flow, and quantum states on an interval. The singular, lower semibounded cases are the hard ones, where endpoints can behave badly but energies stay bounded below. Each self-adjoint version of such an operator carries one matching sesquilinear form, a function of two inputs that is linear in one and conjugate-linear in the other.
