The authors characterize that form using principal and nonprincipal solutions, the two basic solution types near an endpoint, through generalized boundary values. They write the forms in full for every endpoint case: both ends limit circle, one end limit circle, or both ends limit point. The catalogue closes a gap for analysts who need the form behind a given operator, for instance in spectral theory.
arxiv-2509-07405:
Rihab Ben Belgacem and 1 co-author study a heat-like equation with mixed diffusion in a 2025 paper. The equation mixes ordinary local diffusion with a nonlocal kind, where each point feels distant points directly, plus a Hardy-Hénon source term that grows near a singular weight. A time weight that varies in a regular, controlled way multiplies the source. Such equations model spread processes where both nearby and far-away influence matter.

The authors ask the Fujita question: for which powers do all solutions blow up in finite time, and for which do small solutions last forever? They sharpen the dividing line for the unforced case, then prove no global weak solutions exist under growth conditions in the forced case. Small starting data and forcing, by contrast, guarantee solutions that last for all time. The work is presented as the first on blow-up for this mixture class.
arxiv-2509-07605:
Ali Nawaz and 2 co-authors benchmark binary classifiers under class imbalance in 2025, with no rebalancing applied. Imbalance, where one class is rare, plagues fields like medical diagnosis and anomaly detection. Most studies jump straight to fixes such as oversampling. A basic question stays open: how well do classifiers do as-is when the rare class shrinks?

A diverse set of classifiers is tested on real and synthetic datasets. The rare class is cut down step by step, in one-shot and few-shot regimes. Synthetic decision boundaries of varied complexity mimic real-world difficulty. Undersampling, oversampling, and one-class methods are also run for comparison. The results confirm that classification degrades as imbalance grows. That gives practitioners an honest baseline before they reach for remedies. Knowing the untreated failure level helps judge whether a fix truly helps.
arxiv-2509-07705:
Spin waves can carry information at very high frequencies without wasting energy as heat, but launching short ones is hard. Mathieu Moalic and 3 co-authors propose a hybrid magnetic nanostructure in a 2025 research paper. One part is a small rim magnetized in the plane of the film. It acts as a cavity. The rim couples to a second region magnetized out of the plane.

Micromagnetic simulations show a uniform microwave field excites the rim's basic mode. Its second harmonic, at twice the frequency, then launches into the second region as a traveling spin wave. The design works in strip shapes for flat waves and disks for radial waves. Efficiency grows with drive strength, and the output frequency tunes with the magnetic field or cavity width. The authors suggest compact on-chip spin-wave sources for future neural network hardware.
arxiv-2509-07905:
Biomedical knowledge graphs map genes, diseases, and drugs, but machine learning needs them as numbers, not diagrams. Hamid Ahmad, Heiko Paulheim, and Rita T. Sousa present Bio-KGvec2go in a 2025 research paper. The service generates and serves ready-made embeddings, numerical versions of graph knowledge, for widely used biomedical ontologies. It extends an existing web service called KGvec2go.

Pre-trained embeddings spare each research group the cost of retraining models on the same data. Biomedical ontologies change often, though, so stale embeddings mislead. Bio-KGvec2go updates its embeddings in step with new ontology releases. Users can fetch current embeddings with minimal computing effort of their own. The authors frame the service as support for efficient, timely biomedical research, and for more sustainable computing overall.
arxiv-2509-08105:
Complex reasoning in low-resource languages gets a boost from a 2025 paper by Kosei Uemura and 5 co-authors. Large language models reason well in English but lag where training data is scarce. Earlier encoder-plus-decoder approaches improved mid and high-resource languages while leaving low-resource ones far behind, widening the gap the methods meant to close.

Their framework, MERLIN, stacks models in two stages with a curriculum that moves from general bilingual text to task-specific data, adapting only a small set of extra weights. On an African maths benchmark it beats a strong prior method by a wide margin and outperforms a commercial mini model. Gains extend to other multilingual reasoning tests, suggesting curriculum alignment transfers broadly.
arxiv-2509-08205:
Tiny hot targets in infrared images get a lighter, tougher detector from Jingjing Liu and 4 co-authors in a 2025 image processing paper. Deep unfolding networks perform well at this task because they unroll a classical algorithm into a learnable network, keeping interpretability. Existing versions, though, carry too many parameters and falter under noise.

The proposed network rebuilds robust principal component analysis, which separates a scene into background and sparse targets, with a hierarchical bottleneck that squeezes channel dimensions to cut weight. Infrared small target detection supports surveillance, rescue, and guidance systems where the target may be a few pixels. A detector that runs on modest hardware and survives noisy sensors widens where it can be deployed.
arxiv-2509-08605:
Solar prominences, cool clouds of gas held above the Sun, are the subject of a 2025 paper by F. Matković and 7 co-authors. The team models their brightness at millimeter wavelengths using single-dish observations from ALMA, a large radio telescope array in Chile.

Measured brightness sits below that of the quiet Sun, matching prominences seen in absorption against the disk. The modeled gas is far denser and far cooler than quiet Sun material. A non-hydrostatic assumption, meaning pressure alone does not hold the gas up, gives a more consistent picture. Magnetic support and heat radiation by free electrons best explain the signal.
arxiv-2509-08705:
Shalima Binta Manir and 1 co-author build a context-gated graph learner that recreates human biases in a 2025 paper. Their Theory of Mind framework follows dual-process ideas from cognitive science. One system is fast and habitual, the other is slower and context sensitive.

A graph convolutional network acts as the fast system, while meta-learning drives the slower system. A learned gate balances the two for each case. Tests use classic false-belief tasks, where a person must track what another believes. The model mirrors anchoring, framing, priming, and fatigue effects. It also generalizes to new contexts, linking AI design with human reasoning research.
arxiv-2509-08805:
Matthieu Vilain and 3 co-authors handle multiple hypotheses in dense image matching in a 2025 paper. Dense matching finds a partner in a second image for every pixel of the first. Standard methods keep only one guess per location at each scale.

At depth edges or strong zoom, neighbors can spread widely, so one guess often fails. Their BEAMER architecture keeps several hypotheses and carries them across scales with beam search and attention. That design proves far more robust than prior methods in hard cases. The gain is largest at depth discontinuities and strong zoom. The work rethinks a basic choice in matching pipelines.
arxiv-2509-09205:
Daniel Lozano-Gómez and 1 co-author find a fragmented spin liquid phase in pyrochlore spin systems in a 2025 paper. Pyrochlore crystals have a lattice of corner sharing tetrahedra, a shape that frustrates simple magnetic order. Their spins carry both dipole and octupole traits.

In a field along one crystal axis, a mixed phase shows up before full saturation. It holds a spin liquid on kagome planes, a broken Z2 symmetry, and partial spin alignment at once. The dipolar parts can form a liquid driven by the octupolar one, even with no dipole forces. In scattering tests, this shows as faint shadow pinch points under strong peaks. Real candidate materials are named.
arxiv-2509-09305:
Gas giant planets may form when a young disk tears itself apart, but textbooks say that only happens far from the star. Hans Lee, Sergei Nayakshin, and Richard A. Booth revisit that boundary in a 2025 research paper. Standard arguments require very massive disks and place fragmentation beyond about fifty astronomical units. The missing ingredient, they argue, is dust growth, which changes how the disk cools.

Using opacity that depends on temperature and maximum grain size, they re-evaluate a critically fragmenting disk analytically. Dust growth lets fragmentation begin considerably closer in. Critical disk masses and accretion rates both drop. The initial fragments land in the gas giant mass range rather than the brown dwarf range. The authors caution that full numerical models must still test effects like grain mobility. If the result holds, giant planet formation by fragmentation becomes a likelier story.
arxiv-2509-09505:
Haoran Wu and 17 co-authors present PLENA in 2025, a hardware and software system built for long-context inference by AI agents. Agent workloads differ from chatbots: they swallow whole web page structures or long tool-call histories, so context grows huge. Moving that data off chip then hits two walls, limited bandwidth and limited capacity, leaving compute units idle.

PLENA attacks both walls through three pathways: a flattened systolic array, an asymmetric quantisation scheme inside efficient compute and memory units, and built-in support for FlashAttention. A custom instruction set, compiler, simulator, and design search flow complete the stack. Tests report throughput well above an A100 graphics processor on the studied workloads.
arxiv-2509-09705:
Claudio Pinhanez and 4 co-authors test whether small language models give the same answer twice in a 2025 reliability study. They asked open models with two to eight billion parameters each question ten times, using items from the MMLU-Redux and MedQA multiple-choice benchmarks. Settings varied from sampling temperature to model size, and fine-tuned versions were compared against their base forms.

Questions answered the same way every time typically covered only half to four fifths of a test for small models at low temperature. Accuracy among those steady answers tracked overall accuracy fairly well. Medium models, at fifty to eighty billion parameters, looked far steadier. New charts and measures in the paper help readers weigh raw accuracy against repeatability when picking a model.
arxiv-2509-09805:
Francisco M. López and 4 co-authors upgrade a simulated infant in 2025 so the model can grow up in silico. Babies change fast: bodies enlarge, muscles strengthen, and senses sharpen month by month. Most developmental robots freeze one age, which hides exactly those shifting limits. The new MIMo version spans birth to twenty-four months with a body that grows and gains actuation strength as it ages.

Vision is foveated, with sharpness that improves over time, and signals between brain and body travel with realistic delays. Refreshed links to common simulation and learning libraries round out the release, together with a module for inverse kinematics and a generator of random environments. Researchers can now watch sensorimotor development unfold inside one continuous, openly shared model.
arxiv-2509-10405:
Nicholas Carlotti, Mirko Nava, and Alessandro Giusti teach a robot to judge where another robot is, using only a single camera and no pose labels, in this 2025 robotics paper. Their trick is light: the observed robot carries several LEDs whose on-off states are known during training, along with rough viewing directions and one calibration photo at a known distance.

Two robots wander randomly to gather training data, no infrastructure or human labeling needed. The model learns by predicting each LED's state from an image, and in doing so it picks up the other robot's position, distance, and bearing. At run time the LED states can be anything and do not matter. The approach rivals supervised methods that need pose labels or a CAD model, transfers to new settings, and handles several robots at once.
arxiv-2509-10505:
Gravitational waves hide in detector noise. Jericho Cain hunts them without templates in this solo-authored 2025 study. Standard searches match data against banks of predicted waveforms. That struggles with unusual signal shapes and shifting noise. Cain trains an unsupervised autoencoder to spot anomalies instead. A continuous wavelet transform comes first. It tracks chirps in time and frequency.

Training on LIGO data surfaced a trap. Data from several observing runs were mixed at first. Reconstruction errors then clustered by run, not by astrophysics. The cause was calibration differences between data releases. Retraining on the single O4 run removed the effect. The final model reached about ninety-seven percent precision. Recall reached about ninety-six percent on O4 tests. That rivals supervised methods. The run-mixing lesson now guides machine learning work on multi-epoch gravitational wave data.
arxiv-2509-10605:
Ravneet Bedi and four co-authors explore what a future muon collider could discover about heavy axions in this 2025 particle physics paper. Axions were invented to solve the strong CP problem, a fine-tuning puzzle in quantum chromodynamics. Heavy versions, with masses in the tera-electron-volt range, arise in several consistent scenarios that also fix the axion quality problem.

Unlike typical axion-like particles, these heavy QCD axions interact mainly through an anomalous coupling to gluons, so they would appear at a collider as a bump in pairs of jets. The authors analyze three- and ten-TeV muon collider designs in detail. Their projections show such a machine could extend the discovery reach for heavy axions well beyond existing experiments, deep into the multi-TeV mass range.
arxiv-2509-10805:
Long Meng and Dexuan Zhou tame the Schrödinger equation for many-electron systems in this 2025 numerical analysis paper. Following N interacting particles over time is computationally brutal, because the wavefunction lives in a space whose dimension grows with every particle. Their lever is regularity: they prove the wavefunctions possess mixed regularity, smoothness that acts separately in each variable.

That structure licenses sparse grid approximations, which sample the space on a clever skeleton rather than everywhere. The authors build a sparse grid scheme using Gaussian-type orbitals, the standard building blocks of electronic structure. Tests on the helium atom and the hydrogen molecule show the sparse approach offers an efficient alternative to full grid discretization. For quantum chemistry, results like this chip at the exponential wall standing between small molecules and larger ones.
arxiv-2509-11105:
Itay Horin, Arik Kreisel, and Or Alon introduce FANG in this 2025 computational physics paper. FANG is a Monte Carlo event generator, a program that simulates particle collisions or decays, built for cases where only some outgoing directions matter.

Most generators scatter simulated particles over every possible direction and throw away the rest, which wastes effort. FANG instead generates events with chosen particles already aimed at fixed directions or narrow angular windows in the lab frame, while keeping the underlying physics correct. Checked against exact results and older generators, it agrees well and cuts the computing cost by several orders of magnitude. The tool targets particle, nuclear, and detector physics studies.
arxiv-2509-11305:
N. Zimmermann and twenty-three co-authors report follow-up work on distant galaxy clusters in this 2025 astronomy paper. Candidates came from the eROSITA X-ray telescope's first all-sky survey. The picks were systems with very high estimated redshifts.

The team gathered near-infrared J-band images. Telescopes at Calar Alto and Wendelstein took them. Survey photometry was combined with the new images. The goal was a radial excess of same-colored galaxies. That excess is the fingerprint of a real cluster. Nine of eighteen candidates were confirmed. Each received a photometric redshift estimate. The J-band data roughly doubled color precision. The misses matter too. A notable share of distant catalog entries look spurious.
arxiv-2509-11605:
Seoik Jung and four co-authors rethink how video anomaly detectors are tested. This 2025 computer vision paper treats footage from surveillance cameras. Finding odd events matters for public safety. Past test sets judge models frame by frame or by whole video. Never both. That hides how well a system generalizes.

The team designs a sampling plan first. It steers frames toward anomaly-dense stretches. Full coverage of each video is kept. Two companion test sets follow. One scores frame-level reasoning from chosen stills. The other uses time-marked segments and adds an oddness scoring task. On the UCF-Crime set, results rose at both levels. Anomaly-focused sampling beat uniform and random picks in controlled checks.
arxiv-2509-11905:
A poset built from parabolic cosets inside a finite Coxeter group is the object of a 2025 paper by Theo Douvropoulos and one co-author. The project grows out of parallels with the Coxeter complex on one side and parking functions on the other.

The authors prove the poset is Cohen-Macaulay, a strong structural property. They also derive an explicit formula for the character of its single nonzero homology group. The formula uses the Möbius function of the intersection lattice. Twisting that character by the sign character turns it into a positive element of the parabolic Burnside ring. Its coefficients turn out to encode the colored h-vector of a related chamber complex, with the sign twist mirroring the standard move from f-vectors to h-vectors.
arxiv-2509-12205:
Factory managers must keep production, stock, and quality inside safe bounds today while steering toward long-term targets. Achraf Bouhmady and two co-authors frame that balancing act as a viability problem in 2025, with price, quality spending, and advertising as the levers a manager controls.

The framework uses Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman theory to carve out the set of starting states from which the plant can stay viable and reach its target, without assuming the system is fully controllable. Numerical studies of the equation turn the theory into simulation tools. The goal is decisions that protect daily operations while serving durability aims.
arxiv-2509-12305:
Two-dimensional gauge theories are simple enough to solve yet rich enough to surprise. Rishi Mouland and two co-authors chart the phase structure of Abelian examples in 2025, including a theory coupling a scalar and a fermion and the two-flavor Schwinger model with unequal charges.

As masses vary, the phase diagrams show critical lines and points of two different central charges, a richer landscape than the small setting suggests. The study builds toward chiral gauge theories in two dimensions. Those theories matter because they allow symmetric mass generation, where fermions gain mass while their symmetries stay intact, a trick forbidden in ordinary settings.
arxiv-2509-12405:
Grading a medical answer is harder than grading a math answer, because several phrasings can all be right and errors can harm. Wen-wai Yim and five co-authors build MORQA in 2025, a multilingual benchmark for judging the judges: automatic metrics that score open-ended medical question answering in English and Chinese.

Each question carries several gold answers written by medical professionals, plus expert ratings of system outputs. Classic metrics based on word overlap correlate poorly with those experts. Evaluators built on large language models track expert judgment far better, thanks to sensitivity to meaning and tolerance for varied correct phrasings.
arxiv-2509-12505:
Nathan Walker and 3 co-authors model the light from a short gamma-ray burst emerging from a neutron star merger in a 2025 paper. The joint detection of a burst and gravitational waves in 2017 sparked nearly a decade of work on such mergers. What mechanism produces the burst's emission remains an open question.

The team injected a relativistic jet into ejecta from a realistic three-dimensional merger simulation using a hydrodynamics code. They then modeled the photospheric emission, light escaping from the jet's surface, with a radiative transfer code. Spectra peaked around one megaelectronvolt for viewers looking along the jet and fell off noticeably off-axis. Distinct non-thermal tails appeared at low and high energies. The study is presented as the first of its kind with a realistic merger treatment.
arxiv-2509-13105:
Guan-Ru Qiao, Bing Bai and seven co-authors put a quantum random number chip into real-time use in 2025. True random bits from quantum rules serve secure talk and codes. Small size is key for wide use.

Vacuum noise is the entropy source, held in a hybrid light chip. Parts sit in a compact ceramic pack. A small controller reads raw bits and sends clean bits via a serial port. Output holds steady across the full plant heat range. Speed tops five megabits per second. The chip fits comms and crypto gear as built.
arxiv-2509-13305:
Kuan Li, Zhongwang Zhang and 15 co-authors train open web agents in 2025 to rival closed DeepResearch systems with WebSailor-V2. Closed agents show superhuman search skill on hard benchmarks. Open models lack a pattern for cutting extreme doubt in vast data.

Novel high-doubt tasks are built by structured sampling and masking. A cold start plus a duplicate-sampling learner instills the pattern. The full pipeline lifts open agents past all open rivals on hard search tasks. Scores match closed agents, closing the gap. Doubt-cutting, not scale alone, is named as the missing skill.
arxiv-2509-13405:
Carla Ferradini, Martin Sandfuchs and two co-authors define in 2025 what the security parameter means for quantum key distribution. Quantum keys carry an explicit failure bound under stated physics assumptions. Computational schemes give only asymptotic claims with no explicit bound at set sizes.

An axiomatic path reads the parameter as the maximum chance of security failure. That read is defended step by step. Past criticisms of the definition are reviewed and answered in turn. Clear meaning matters since keys guard real traffic. The note gives users a firm grip on what a bound promises and what it does not.
arxiv-2509-13805:
Florian Wiesner, Zoë Gray, Matthias Wessling, and Stephen Baek present the General Physics Transformer in a 2025 paper. It is a step toward a physics foundation model. Language models train once and adapt everywhere. Physics machine learning still builds a fresh solver per system. A single model that infers the governing dynamics from context alone would change that.

Their transformer trained on a large, diverse body of simulation data. It simulates fluid-solid interaction, shock waves, thermal convection, and multi-phase flow. It does so without being told the underlying equations. It beat specialized designs by wide margins across domains. It also generalized plausibly to entirely unseen systems through in-context learning. And it stayed more stable over long prediction rollouts. One model, it seems, can absorb general physical principles.
arxiv-2509-14005:
The ATLAS Collaboration searches for a distinctive Higgs boson signature in a 2025 collider paper. It uses proton-proton collision data from the Large Hadron Collider. The target events pair a Higgs boson with one high-energy photon. The Higgs decays to a bottom quark and antiquark. Production runs mainly through vector-boson fusion. Requiring the photon slashes the multijet background that usually swamps this decay.

Sensitivity gains came from better background modeling, a neural-network classifier, and a direct binned-likelihood fit. The fit ran on that classifier's output. The measured Higgs signal strength came out well below the standard model prediction, but with a large uncertainty. The observed significance was only a fraction of a standard deviation, against an expected one and a half. In plain terms, the data show no convincing signal in this channel yet.
arxiv-2509-14105:
Shan Jiang and five co-authors publish a comment in 2025 on thermal Hall measurements in the cuprate La2CuO4. A recent paper by Hu and co-workers reported resolving no thermal Hall signal in that material with high-resolution measurements, setting a tight upper bound. The comment argues two relevant points escaped that team's attention.

First, thermal Hall signals far below that resolution bound have in fact been detected in disordered perovskite insulators, so a null result at that sensitivity does not close the question. Second, the commented sample's ordinary thermal conductivity is markedly lower than that of the sample which did show a Hall signal. Drawing on strontium titanate data, the authors note a pattern across insulator families: more disorder, weaker thermal Hall response, an anti-correlation the original interpretation missed.
arxiv-2509-14205:
Eric C.-Y. Yuan and Teresa Head-Gordon address a stability problem in computer models of molecules in their 2025 study. Models learned from data can predict forces well on familiar cases, yet their simulations can break down when molecules move into new shapes that the training data never covered.

Their fix is to pre-train the model on cheap, low quality force field data for single molecules, which the authors call teaching the irrelevant parts. Fine tuning on a small set of costlier, more exact labels then teaches how molecules interact and react. With that order, simulations of gas molecules, liquid water and hydrogen burning stayed stable and accurate, unlike models trained from scratch.
arxiv-2509-14305:
Marko Lela, writing alone in 2025, works on lower bounds for small depth circuits, a core topic in computing theory. He introduces a cost measure for classifiers that obey resource limits. The style follows minimum description length, where shorter accounts cost less.

Lela proves a stable reduction lemma for maps that preserve data distributions between problems. He then applies it to random 3XOR problems, which ask whether parity conditions hold, on a balanced data spread. A clean translation turns each XOR condition into clauses of 3SAT, a classic satisfiability problem, with no loss on the image. The lower bound for the circuit class then transfers to 3SAT. Code and checks are supplied with full match in verification, supporting the stated bound.
arxiv-2509-15005:
Facundo Domínguez and Arnaud Spiwack argue that automated theorem solvers belong in everyday programming, in a 2025 programming languages paper. SMT solvers, which check logical formulas automatically, are usually reserved for formal verification specialists. The authors claim that wiring them into a compiler's static checks makes ordinary type checkers far more capable.

Their vehicle is refinement types as realized in Liquid Haskell, where types carry logical conditions that the solver verifies. A case study on handling binder scopes in compilers shows the style at work on a mundane, error-prone task. As a side contribution, they built a prototype theory of finite maps for the Liquid Haskell solver to support the study. The vision is programming that feels simpler because the checker proves more.
arxiv-2509-15105:
Liran Nochumsohn, Raz Marshanski, Hedi Zisling, and Omri Azencot forecast time series with a mixture of simple linear experts in a 2025 machine learning paper. Big pre-trained forecasters post strong zero-shot results but cost heavily to run. Super-Linear asks how far deliberately simple components can go instead.

Each expert is a linear model specialized to one frequency regime, trained on data resampled to match that regime. A light spectral gating mechanism picks which experts deserve trust for a given series. The mixture stays cheap, scales gracefully, and remains interpretable, since each expert's role is visible. Across benchmarks the model performs strongly while improving efficiency and robustness to sampling-rate changes. The design is a reminder that frequency structure, handled plainly, carries much of what time series forecasting needs.
arxiv-2509-15405:
Nicholas Luber leads a team that caught a small galaxy losing its gas in open space. The galaxy, AGC 727130, is light, rich in atomic gas, and makes few new stars. Radio maps show its gas stretched far out on one side, while the other side looks calm. Two nearby dwarf galaxies sit close, but the team find they are not the cause.

A search of large scale maps puts the galaxy where several cosmic web strands cross. Such places may hold hot, thin gas. The team argue the galaxy is plowing through that gas, which strips its own gas away like wind. This process could explain why some lone small galaxies stop forming stars.
arxiv-2509-15505:
Ji Liu leads a large team that builds a compiler for catching errors in quantum programs. Full error correction is heavy, so many groups use error detection instead: spot bad runs and throw them away. Adding detection by hand is slow work. It needs extra qubits, checks placed by hand, and tuning for each machine.

Their compiler, QuantEM, takes a quantum circuit, a chosen detection code, and a map of the target machine. Three parts then do the work: one rewrites the program with checks, one fits it to the hardware, and one handles results and resource counts. The design is modular, so new codes and machines can be added. The tool aims to make detection routine.
arxiv-2509-15705:
Marco Mordacci leads a team that teaches quantum circuits to place like data far apart. Their classifiers run on quantum states held in a space where distance matters. If states with the same label cluster tightly, sorting gets easier. Hard data, like medical images, need an encoding that builds those clusters on purpose.

The encoding circuit learns from a loss borrowed from face recognition, which pulls same label states close and pushes others away. Gaps between the averaged states of each class gauge the success. On handwriting and medical image tasks, the encoding beats a standard one with the same classifier. It also needs a much shallower circuit.
arxiv-2509-15805:
Tianyang Wang leads a team that sharpens active learning with a student model. Active learning picks the most useful unlabeled items to label next, based on doubt. Past doubt gauges need complex side models that are hard to train, above all in niche fields like cell imaging. The team use knowledge transfer instead.

The main task model acts as teacher, and a plain side model learns from it as student. Both train together in each round. The gap between their outputs on an item gauges doubt. The student needs no special training tricks and fits many tasks. The team also show doubt ties to a bound on the task loss, not its raw value. Tests span vision and cell tasks.
arxiv-2509-15905:
David Calhas and Arlindo Oliveira propose neural networks that feed their own high level views back in. Most networks pass data one way, from input to output. Their Deep Feedback Models mix the input with inner summaries over time. That loop lets the network refine its state step by step, like a mind settling on a choice.

They model the loop as a differential equation solved by a recurrent network. A decay term keeps the state from blowing up, so it settles. Tests cover object recognition and image cutting. The feedback models beat one way rivals, above all with little data or heavy noise. They also carry over to medical images and resist varied noise types. Code is public.
arxiv-2509-16005:
Matrix models in physics hide their key patterns in the spread of their eigenvalues, the core numbers of a matrix. Samuel Kováčik and Katarína Magdolenová show how to rebuild that spread from bootstrap results, a method that bounds values with math rules. From the rebuilt spread they can compute free energy, a value that picks the best physical solution.

The pair first check their method on a well-known quartic model, where the answer is known. They then use it on a newer, uneven multi-trace model with many candidate solutions. Free energy picks the right one each time, which makes the tool vital for hard model studies.
arxiv-2509-16405:
Family trees of species sometimes tangle, where branches merge as well as split, and those merges mark key events like hybridization. Alexey Markin and Tavis K. Anderson study a new code that writes a tree as a short list of numbers by noting where each leaf attaches. They tie that code to a classic problem of splitting several trees into merge-free parts.

A corrected distance between codes turns out to equal the size of the best such split, given a good leaf order. The split itself can be rebuilt from the codes. Extensions cover trees with multi-way splits, and date-ordered microbial data may make event spotting fast.
arxiv-2509-16605:
J. Terasaki and O. Civitarese address a long-standing spread in nuclear predictions in a 2025 physics paper. Some nuclei may decay by a rare path that gives off no neutrinos. The rate of that decay hinges on a nuclear quantity that models peg at quite different values. That spread clouds what experiments can say about neutrino mass.

The pair offer a way to pin that quantity down with less model bias. Their results suggest the target mass range has not yet been reached. That verdict assumes the lightest neutrino is very light. They also compute values for a palladium isotope. Clearer values would let costly experiments aim with more care.
arxiv-2509-16705:
Shuubham Ojha, Felix Gervits, and Carol Espy-Wilson build a small speech cleaner for edge devices in a 2025 paper. Phones and hearing aids have little power to spare. A cleaner must run fast and still lift speech out of noise. Their model uses a compact design with a twist they call reverse attention.

Tests score both sound quality and how well words survive. Their model beat similar-sized rivals on both counts. Word errors fell by a clear margin over raw, noisy speech. Sound quality scores rose as well. A light model that runs on the device itself could help calls and captions without sending audio to the cloud.
arxiv-2509-16805:
Md. Atabuzzaman, Ali Asgarov, and Chris Thomas study a bias in vision-language models in a 2025 paper. On multiple-choice questions about images, models may favor a letter or a slot, like always picking A. That bias can mask true visual skill. The team benchmark how strong the bias is across models.

They also offer a fix that makes models more robust. Their work gives fresh insight into where these models fail on fine visual tasks. Data and code are shared in public. Test makers can use the benchmark to check a model before trusting its scores. Fairer tests matter as such models enter schools and workplaces.
arxiv-2509-17305:
Jiarui Li, Zixiang Yin, Zhengming Ding, Samuel J. Landry, and Ramgopal R. Mettu wrote a 2025 arXiv paper on predicting how T cell receptors bind their targets. That binding drives adaptive immunity and sits at the heart of T cell therapies. Past transformer models predict it well, but their designs often rest on habit rather than evidence.

The team first built a post-hoc explanation tool, then used what it revealed to shape a new encoder-decoder transformer. The tool showed which mixes of receptor and peptide inputs carry the most signal, which guided the cross-attention design. Extra training goals and an early-stop rule based on explanation quality round out the design. The final model set the best scores so far while also reading more clearly. It held up on new data, and its explanations shed light on how sequence patterns drive binding.
arxiv-2509-17705:
G Kavya Keerthana, S Ananya, and Ranganatha D prove number patterns for a kind of split count of whole numbers. Their 2025 paper works on overpartition tuples, where parts may be marked in more than one way. An old guess by Saikia set out rules for these counts modulo small numbers.

The team shows those rules hold for all counts, not just prime or odd ones. They also prove new rules for tuples that use odd parts only. Some of those rules had been guessed by Sarma and by Das with co-workers. Plain checks modulo two and three drive the proofs.
arxiv-2509-17905:
Zongqian Wu and 5 co-authors fix a bias in how language models pick paths to a solution. Their 2025 paper deals with test-time scaling, where a model tries many reasoning paths and pools them. Models tend to favour one style, such as algebra for a maths task, and skip other valid styles like shape-based paths.

Their frame, TTS-Uniform, first lists the styles on offer for a task. It then splits the try budget evenly across those styles. Shaky styles are cut before the pool step. Tests across models and bench sets show the even split makes scaling work far better.
arxiv-2509-18105:
Nachiket N Naik and 4 co-authors test when built-in structure helps forecast a supply chain bulge. Their 2025 study deals with the bullwhip effect, where small demand swings grow as orders move up a chain. Two model styles face off on a one-stage test bed.

One style learns the whole flow law with a neural equation. The other keeps stock and order rules fixed and learns just a small policy tweak. Under steady and plain random demand, the structured style forecast far better. Under wild, heavy shocks, the free style won. Training on more of the path did not change that split.
arxiv-2509-18205:
HongZheng Liu, YiNuo Tian, and Zhiyue Wu set a fair-cost floor for how complex a quantum circuit must be. Their 2025 paper notes that circuit cost counts shift with the reference state and the rules used. Reset steps, for one, carry an entropy cost that tallies often leave out.

Their frame fixes the reference, the build tools, and the atomic costs in advance. In that fixed frame, they prove a lower bound tied to how far a target state sits from a max-entropy start. Fixed final measures let a third party check the bound. That makes cost claims open to audit.
arxiv-2509-18305:
What wake forms behind a square block that rises through still water? Intesaaf Ashraf, Stephane Dorbolo, and Neetu Tiwari study that flow in lab tests. Their 2025 paper tracks a square cylinder moving upward at speeds summed up by the Froude number, a ratio that compares motion with wave effects. They film the water flow to map speed and swirl behind the block.

The films show the wake is ruled by a steady pair of counter-turning swirls, not by swirls shed one after another. As speed rises, the swirl strength grows fast at first, then levels off near a clear threshold. The swirl area stays about the same size while the spin inside gets stronger. The results help explain how rising bodies pull water along with them. That matters for ship and offshore design.
arxiv-2509-18705:
The planet holds hundreds of thousands of plant species, but photos for training AI cover only a small share. Hervé Goëau, Pierre Bonnet, and Alexis Joly overview the PlantCLEF 2019 challenge in this paper. The challenge tested automated identification on the flora of data-poor tropical regions. Its data set held ten thousand species, centered on the Guiana Shield and the northern Amazon.

That region ranks among the richest on Earth for plant and animal diversity. As in the prior edition, the organizers compared the best systems against top tropical flora experts. The paper presents the challenge resources and scoring rules. It summarizes the approaches of the competing research groups. It then analyzes the main outcomes. The edition is a companion to the 2021 challenge overview by the same team. Both probe how far AI can go where training data is scarce.
arxiv-2509-19005:
Renáta Rusnáková and two co-authors automate a fiddly step in quantum annealing, a method that uses quantum hardware to search for good solutions. Their test problem is minimum bisection: split a graph into two equal halves while cutting as few edges as possible. On the annealer, a penalty term forces the halves to stay balanced, and its strength must be set well or answers suffer.

The team first derives a starting penalty from the graph itself. Two gradient boosting models then predict a good range for a multiplier on that start, using the graph's size, density, and the starting value. Trained on hundreds of random graphs, the method gave balanced splits on every test case. It also beat the classic Metis tool on cut size in every test.
arxiv-2509-19205:
Silicon can be doped in sheets a single atom thick, and Quinn T. Campbell and three co-authors compute what happens when two such sheets of opposite type interact. One sheet uses phosphorus, which donates electrons. The other uses boron or aluminum, which accept them. Using density functional theory, the team varies the distance between the sheets and calculates the electronic structure at each gap.

At separations of a nanometer or less, the two dopant potentials overlap and largely cancel, leaving behavior much like pure silicon. Beyond that distance the sheets act independently, like a p-n diode with a plain silicon layer between them. Charge can still tunnel across at larger gaps, and the tunneling chance exceeds that of a standard silicon barrier. Interacting atomic layers of this kind could form the basis of ultra-small devices.
arxiv-2509-19505:
Guiding a heat-like process to zero in finite time is the heart of null controllability. Juan Límaco and three co-authors study a diffusion equation whose spread rate fades at the boundary and depends on the whole state at once. They use a game-like strategy: one leader control acts first, and two follower controls settle into a Nash balance for paired goals.

The hard step is proving the linearized system can be steered, which rests on weighted estimates of Carleman type. A fixed-point style theorem then lifts the result to the full nonlinear system. The nonlocal term couples the equations in ways that complicate the optimality conditions. Such results matter where diffusion weakens, as in some population and materials models. The paper adds a hierarchical twist: control with leaders and followers, not a single hand.
arxiv-2509-19605:
Storms in space can damage satellites and power grids, yet the best physics simulations run too slowly for live forecasts. Daniel Holmberg and seven co-authors train a neural stand-in on data from Vlasiator, a detailed near-Earth plasma simulation. Their model treats space as a graph and steps conditions forward on its own. Solar wind readings upstream drive the forecast.

The stand-in gives fast single forecasts of near-Earth conditions. A generative twist yields ensembles, many forecasts at once, which show how unsure the outlook is. That honesty about doubt is what forecasters need to warn operators in time. The authors frame the tool as an add-on to current systems, not a swap. It could bring physics-grade space weather within reach of real-time use.
arxiv-2509-19705:
Choosing a spine operation means weighing patient traits, surgical routes, and risks that vary by person. J. Ben Tamo and eight co-authors build a causal learning framework that estimates effects for each patient. Each decision, such as front versus back approach or surgery versus none, is treated as its own task. Shared layers let the tasks teach each other.

A weighting scheme strengthens the causal reading of the observational data. The team tests on a public fusion set of about a thousand patients and a private scoliosis set. Standard statistics strain under such mixed, uneven data. Estimates tuned to the individual could help surgeons and families weigh options with clearer eyes. The work stays careful: it supports decisions rather than making them.
arxiv-2509-19805:
Amateur telescope photos of stars are blurry, and standard image translators often warp the stars they try to sharpen. Shantanusinh Parmar and Silas Janke build StrCGAN, a generative model for restoring stellar images. It extends the CycleGAN design with two additions. Multi-spectral fusion aligns optical and near-infrared views, and astrophysical regularizers guard star shapes.

Reference images from all-sky surveys across several missions guide the training. Reconstructions must stay consistent across wavelength bands, not just look sharp in one. The target data comes from small telescopes with limited quality. Better restoration lets modest gear contribute cleaner sky records. The authors stress fidelity over prettiness: a sharpened star that changed shape is a scientific error, not an improvement.
arxiv-2509-20005:
Droplets filled with swimming microbes can move, wobble, and act almost alive. L. Malik and seven co-authors trap tens of mesoscale swimmers inside droplets resting on a water-repelling surface. With few swimmers, the droplet rings at its natural resonance, like a struck bell. Crowding changes the tune: confinement bends the motion away from the classical pattern.

Scaling laws built by the team describe the crowded regime well. Swimming strokes in packed three-dimensional droplets differ from those in flat, quasi-two-dimensional films. The findings reveal how living cargo can actuate a droplet from inside. Bio-inspired droplet motors could serve micro-robotics, fluid handling, and sensing. The work blends soft matter physics with the mechanics of life at the mesoscale.
arxiv-2509-20105:
Venkat Margapuri, Garik Kazanjian, and Naren Kosaraju wrote this 2025 arXiv paper on how language models reason. Long chains of thought often lose their thread, most of all when a task needs strict step-by-step logic. The team tries to fix this with a reward drawn from a quantum physics tool called Projected Entangled Pair States.

The reward scores how well a chain of thought sticks to a clear target shape. It is added to a well-known training method for reinforcement learning. No teacher marks each step; the score guides learning by shape alone. Tests used math word problems and two other reasoning sets, GSM8K, StrategyQA, and EntailmentBank. Scores for coherence rose above those of supervised, contrastive, and plain pretrained baselines. The team presents this quantum-inspired score as a sound base for chains of thought that hold together.
arxiv-2509-20305:
Small systems change phase too, and Michael Bachmann shows how to spot those changes in a 2025 arXiv paper. Physicists read phase changes from energy histograms, charts built during computer runs. Bachmann gives a direct way to pull key values from such a chart. Those values feed a new inflection-point method that sorts phase changes by type.

The method works for systems of any size. Bachmann tests it on a small peptide, a chain of seven building blocks, as it clumps together. For that case, the method laid out the full chain of phase changes in order. The test shows how much a single chart can tell. The paper is short and aimed at method users. It offers a cheap route to map phase changes in small systems.
arxiv-2509-20405:
Detectors that flag synthetic speech work well in the lab and falter in the wild, according to Visar Berisha, Prad Kadambi, and Isabella Lenz in a 2025 arXiv paper. Real calls arrive through shifting devices, codecs, sample rates, and rooms. Every new condition multiplies the old ones, creating blind spots the authors call coverage debt. Attackers can aim straight at those gaps.

Reanalyzing a recent cross-testing framework, the authors find two patterns. Newer synthesizers erase the artifacts that detectors learned to rely on. Conversational domains like teleconferences, interviews, and social media are consistently the hardest to protect. Since worst-case behavior governs security, average benchmark scores mislead. The authors advise treating detection as one auxiliary signal inside layered defenses. Provenance checks, personhood credentials, and policy safeguards should carry the real weight.
arxiv-2509-20705:
Design models of a building go stale as soon as work starts on site. Reza Akhavian and four co-authors propose BIM2RDT, a 2025 framework that turns static building information models into live, robot-ready digital twins. Safety during execution is the stated first priority.

The agentic AI framework joins three streams of data. Building models supply geometry and meaning. Internet-of-things sensors supply activity data from the site. Robots add visual and spatial data as they move through the area. Together these streams keep the twin current enough for autonomous field work. The authors present the system as a bridge between office design data and real-time jobsite intelligence for construction management.
arxiv-2509-21205:
Iñigo Alonso and 3 co-authors built a large data set in 2025 for table understanding from images. Many past sets use fake tables drawn by a program. Real tables are messier, with varied layouts and styles. Models need to read both the cells and the look of the page. The new set aims to close that gap.

The set is called TABLET. It holds millions of cases across many tasks, built from millions of real tables. Most tables keep their first visual form. The authors also add VisualTableQA, a test that needs both sight and table reading. Training two known vision models on TABLET raised their scores on seen and new tasks. It also made them stronger on real world tables.
arxiv-2509-21405:
Identifying flying objects whose dynamics are already known is the task in a 2025 paper by Nyi Nyi Aung and 2 co-authors. Learning and sorting are combined in one system. The setting is unmanned aerial vehicles, where motion equations are well understood. Physics informed learning uses those equations inside the network. The result promises faster training with high hit rate.

Their physics informed residual neural network maps states and predicts state derivatives. A softmax layer then gives multi class confidence estimates. Three vehicle types serve as case studies: quadcopter, fixed wing, and helicopter craft. Results show high sorting hit rate with reduced training time. The authors present the approach as promising for system identification where underlying dynamics are known.
arxiv-2509-21605:
Operator learning offers fast stand-ins for partial differential equations, but error ranges are essential. Tian Yu Yen and 2 co-authors present a generative approach in a 2025 paper. Likelihood based methods infer parameter distributions from noisy data. Stochastic operators may yield actions where a likelihood is hard or impossible to construct. Their method, GenUQ, avoids constructing a likelihood at all.

A generative hyper network makes distributions that fit the observed data. The approach rests on measure theory. Operator models map between functions, replacing expensive numerical integration with fast scoring. Uses in sea ice, combustion, and atmospheric physics motivate the work. Tests show predictive error ranges for operator learning without that machinery. The point is trust in the map: a fast model is of use just when its doubt is known and small.
arxiv-2509-22005: Mingjin Li and Jianren Long work in complex analysis. Their topic is the radial weighted Bergman spaces of functions over the unit disc. Their 2025 paper studies Carleson embeddings. These are maps that carry those function spaces into measure spaces. The paper asks when such a map is r-summing. That property is a strengthening of compactness, defined through sums of norms. They characterize the r-summing Carleson embeddings. They also give conditions that ensure the property. The results cover all positive ranges of the two integrability exponents involved.
arxiv-2509-22305:
Emanuele Cristoforoni and Federico Villone study the spectrum of an elliptic operator on a domain wrapped in a thin reinforcing layer. The setup models a body surrounded by a coating whose thickness varies along the boundary and whose stiffness is scaled by a small parameter. The operator carries a Robin boundary condition, which mixes the function's values and its outward slope. Their 2025 paper asks what happens to the eigenvalues, the operator's natural frequencies, as that small parameter tends to zero.

They prove the spectrum converges to the spectrum of a simpler elliptic operator posed on the inner domain alone, with no layer. Beyond the limit itself, they compute a first-order asymptotic expansion, which describes how the eigenvalues approach their limits at leading order. Such expansions matter for reinforced materials and coated structures, where a thin layer is used to tune behavior.
arxiv-2509-22405:
Shayne Wadle and Karthikeyan Sankaralingam propose many small, specialized cores to speed up single-thread work. Single threads still matter, but bigger, wider cores give less and less gain. The team studied hardware counter data and found sixteen distinct behavior states in running programs. Each state needs a different mix of core features.

Their design, SAHM, pairs each state with a core built for it. Threads move to the best core as behavior shifts. Tests found speed gains of about one sixth in realistic runs. The gains held up even when moving a thread cost a lot, dropping by less than one point.
arxiv-2509-22605:
Wings Zhang leads a large team that found over a hundred fast-moving objects in a northern sky survey. Using the third data release of the UKIRT Hemisphere Survey, the team hunted for high proper motion sources not known before. They found 127 new objects moving fast across the sky. Many with Gaia matches look like distant, low-mass stars. Their high speeds and colors suggest low metal content, marking them as M-type subdwarfs.

Spectra confirmed low mass and low metals for two of the stars. For sources without Gaia data, colors suggest late-M, L-type, and possible T-type dwarfs. Follow-up spectra are still needed to pin down the types of the full set.
arxiv-2509-22705:
Nicholas Bermingham, David White, and Nathan Willey track Ohio's overdose epidemic with a topological lens. Topological data analysis captures spatial structure in complex data, but its use on data that moves through time is still rare. The team applies the Mapper algorithm to overdose data from 2007 to 2024. Mapper builds a graph that summarizes a data set's shape through overlapping cover sets.

Their new cover method respects geography and highlights time-dependent variables. A Mapper view of regional demographics shows how those factors relate to overdose deaths. The approach reveals temporal trends, hotspots, and lagged patterns tied to both place and community traits. It extends earlier topological studies of disease spread.
arxiv-2509-22805:
Manuel Goimil-García and Irene Tamborra find the steady flavor state of neutrinos streaming through uneven matter. When neutrinos cross a medium whose density varies, flavor conversion gains new physics from the streaming term. That term cascades flavor waves toward ever finer spatial and angular scales. Over time, large-wavenumber perturbations damp out, smearing the flavor pattern.

The pair give a simple recipe to forecast the final steady flavor mix without solving the full kinetic equations. Flavor equipartition on one side of the spectrum, often proposed as the generic outcome, turns out to be a special case. It depends on how asymmetric the neutrino and antineutrino populations are. The scheme aids supernova and merger simulations.
arxiv-2509-23305:
Attacking a live industrial control system to test defenses can be dangerous, so simulation has to stand in. Jaxson Brown and 5 co-authors built ICS-SimLab, a containerized suite for that work. Docker containers let researchers spin up varied control systems fast. Most prior testbeds cover one architecture, which biases security tools. This suite targets many architectures under the Purdue reference model.

Three demos show the range: a solar smart grid, a bottle filling plant, and an intelligent device system. The team ran cyber attacks on the simulations to prove the setup. Configurable builds support intrusion detection research across systems.
arxiv-2509-23405:
Diffusion language models sample along planned paths, but they train as if paths were random. Fred Zhangzhi Peng and 7 co-authors prove that mismatch matters and fix it. Planners pick smarter spots to denoise at each step. The standard training bound, they show, misdescribes a planner-guided denoiser. A new planned bound folds the planner's reverse dynamics into training.

Their scheme, PAPL, is a small change to the masked diffusion loss. Gains show across domains. Protein sequences improved by about forty percent in relative terms. Text and code generation also rose clearly. Training and inference finally assume the same path style.
arxiv-2509-24405:
Asking a database questions in plain language works well in English and far worse in other tongues. Khanh Trinh Pham and 4 co-authors built MultiSpider 2.0, a text-to-SQL benchmark in eight languages, from German and French to Japanese and Vietnamese. It keeps the structural difficulty of its source benchmark while adding linguistic and dialect variation.

Leading models scored near zero on execution accuracy with raw reasoning, far below their marks on the earlier multilingual version. A baseline of collaborating language agents that refine queries in rounds lifted accuracy several-fold, yet a wide gap remained. The results expose how much multilingual database access still lags.
arxiv-2509-24705:
Andreia Carrillo and four co-authors traced how the chemical slope of a swallowed galaxy blurred as it fell into ours, in a paper published in 2025. The galaxy, called the Sausage, built a slope: its core stars ran rich in metals, and its rim ran poor. In eight simulated twins of the fall, each had such a slope at entry, by both span and flight force.

By today the span slope had worn to a tenth or less of its first grade. The force slope wore less, and large donors kept it best. At a set span now, poor stars came from the rim of the donor. At a set metal wealth, far stars came from the rim too. The wear grade tied to donor mass and fall time. Pin those down, the authors say, and the first slope can be read.
arxiv-2509-25205:
Daksh Pandey wrote a 2025 paper on learning from graph data without exposing it. The catalog gives the author as Pandey D, while the head gives the full name. Graphs model networks like citations and friendships. A strong self-teaching method for graphs uses steps that clash with homomorphic encryption, the math that lets computers work on locked data.

Pandey's framework rebuilds both the network and its training loss using only polynomial steps, which encryption can handle. Tests on three standard citation sets matched the unlocked method's accuracy and beat it on one. Private training on graphs could serve hospitals and banks, whose networks are valuable and sensitive at once.
arxiv-2510-00005:
Bambozzi and Lazda publish a correction with teeth, withdrawing a claimed theorem from the first author's earlier paper on dagger quasi-Stein spaces. The non-Archimedean analogues of Stein spaces in complex geometry. The earlier work claimed dagger versions of Cartan's Theorems A and B, including the vanishing of higher cohomology for coherent sheaves. But the authors now show Theorem B fails for perhaps the main nontrivial example of such a space.

Their counterexample is the product of the dagger open unit disc with the dagger closed unit disc. Where they prove the first cohomology group of the structure sheaf does not vanish, contradicting the claimed theorem directly. The proof writes the space as an increasing union of affinoid domains and shows a derived inverse limit of the section rings is nonzero. Using a general criterion for inverse systems of vector spaces.
arxiv-2510-00105:
Noah Vowell and a large team of co-authors published this 2025 astronomy paper in the OATMEAL survey series. The survey measures how the orbits of heavy planets and brown dwarfs line up with their stars' spin. This entry studies HIP 33609 b, a brown dwarf far heavier than Jupiter. It circles a hot, young star once every 39 days on a stretched orbit.

The team watched the brown dwarf cross its star using a spectrograph on the Magellan telescope in Chile. They found its orbit tilted only slightly from the star's spin axis. That near-alignment, paired with the stretched orbit, points to a calm migration path inward. The authors argue the dwarf likely formed by fragmentation, much like a small star. Its behavior closely matches that of warm giant planets, hinting at a shared history.
arxiv-2510-00705:
Kim and four co-authors show that a multimodal model's own uncertainty can steer its attention in this 2025 arXiv paper. Multimodal large language models miss fine details, such as small objects in huge images or key moments in long videos. Fixes usually mean task-specific fine-tuning or bolt-on detectors, which cost effort and generalize poorly. The team's insight is simple: the model's output entropy drops when it sees the visual input that actually matters.

Their Uncertainty Guidance framework scores candidate crops, frames, or segments by that entropy and feeds the model the most informative pieces first. No training is involved, and the same mechanism serves three tasks: visual search, long video understanding, and temporal grounding. Off-the-shelf models using the method performed competitively with specialized fine-tuned systems in their experiments. The result suggests intrinsic uncertainty is a general, cheap signal for fine-grained perception.
arxiv-2510-00805:
Zhu and five co-authors at the University of Science and Technology of China speed up Generative Flow Networks in this 2025 arXiv paper, presenting MG2FlowNet. GFlowNets learn to sample objects, such as molecules, with probability proportional to a reward, which balances quality against diversity. In search spaces with rare high-reward pockets, GFlowNet sampling overexplores and finds candidates slowly. The authors graft Monte Carlo Tree Search into the loop to steer generation.

Tree search evaluates trajectories and guides sampling toward promising branches, while a polynomial upper-confidence rule keeps exploration honest. A dial controls how greedy that guidance becomes, users can trade diversity for reward. Experiments showed the method discovering high-reward regions faster than baselines and continuing to produce high-reward samples. Diversity of the distribution was preserved throughout. Tests used action spaces and rewards, which the authors note as the scope limit.
arxiv-2510-01105:
Andriopoulos, Dong, Adhikari, and Ross study the geometry of neural regression in this 2025 arXiv paper. Regression networks output vectors for control, robotics, and finance, yet the shape of what they learn is poorly understood. In classification, networks show collapse, and collapse helps them generalize. The team asked whether that holds when the outputs are numbers, not labels. They measured the dimension of the last-layer features and compared it with that of the targets.

Across control tasks and datasets, collapse in regression hurt performance instead. Collapsed models squeezed their features below the target dimension, and that squeeze threw away information the outputs needed. Healthy models kept feature dimension at or above the target dimension. The authors split into over-compressed and under-compressed regimes, with fixes: widen features in the first, narrow them when data are scarce and noisy. Intrinsic dimension thus works as a check.
arxiv-2510-01205:
Bauman and co-authors match each stage of a demanding quantum chemistry workflow to the hardware that suits it best. High-accuracy electronic structure methods strain memory and compute in very different proportions per stage. Their workflow couples a memory-hungry downfolding step with a lighter simulation step.

Prototype memory expansion hardware absorbed the downfolding phase's appetite. A cloud quantum platform then ran the many smaller simulations quickly and elastically. A shared allocator improved performance further in multi-machine runs. The study offers a template for deploying advanced chemistry codes across today's fragmented hardware landscape. Downfolded Hamiltonians compress the chemistry before the heavy simulation begins. Capacity, not speed, is the bottleneck CXL memory relieves. ExaChem runs on the prototype systems supplied the second testbed. Pacific Northwest National Laboratory anchors the author team. Heterogeneous hardware is the new normal for supercomputing centers everywhere.
arxiv-2510-01805:
Kielak surveys a deep question about the shape of spaces in this 2025 mathematics paper. A manifold fibres over a circle when it can be built by sweeping one smaller shape around a loop. Asking whether some finite cover of the space fibres is the virtual fibring question. Thurston's famous conjecture on the three-dimensional case was bold, and it turned out to be true.

The survey explains how the problem becomes algebra through the fundamental group. Finiteness properties of certain subgroups then decide whether fibring can occur. Two obstructions dominate the story, the Euler characteristic and L-squared homology. Recent progress centers on RFRS groups, where Novikov rings and L-squared theory interact fruitfully. Applications include weaker fibring forms and tests for coherence failures. The final part offers conjectures for higher dimensions, with honest labels for how plausible each one seems.
arxiv-2510-02205:
Cossetto, Rodenfels, and Sartori chart how microbes split their energy losses between heat and chemistry in this 2025 paper. Living cells lose energy, a loss usually equated with the heat they release. Growing cells also export chemical entropy through the metabolites they swap. How the total splits between those channels was largely unexplored.

The authors mined a large database of microbial growth experiments. Aerobic respiration matched the textbook picture: little chemical entropy, with losses mainly as heat. Several anaerobic metabolisms broke that pattern fully. They produced as much chemical entropy as heat during growth. Stranger still, acetate-eating methanogenesis and sulfur respiration turned out endothermic, absorbing heat while growing. Microbes evidently exploit every mix of heat and chemical entropy that nets positive entropy production. Heat measures alone, the paper warns, undercount what anaerobic life loses.
arxiv-2510-02305:
Farghly and co-authors explain why diffusion models respect the hidden shape of data. Their 2025 statistics paper tests the manifold hypothesis. That idea says real data clusters near a low dimensional surface. Diffusion models seem to learn that surface remarkably well. The authors trace the effect to score matching training. Training smooths the learned score function in a log domain. They show this smoothing acts along the surface, not across it. Smoothing therefore behaves like a kernel adapted to the geometry. Enough samples make the match close.

Experiments confirmed the theoretical picture in practice. Different smoothing choices steered the learned surface itself. The team could control which manifold the model generalized along. Architecture habits may add further hidden biases. The result turns a folk belief into a mechanism. Builders gain a lever for shaping generated data. Geometry aware design starts from this insight.
arxiv-2510-02505:
Ridley rebuilds the meaning of probability inside the many worlds view of quantum theory. His 2025 philosophy of physics paper tackles two famous problems. Many worlds says every outcome happens in some branch. Probability then struggles to mean anything at all. That is the incoherence problem facing the view. The quantitative problem asks why branch weights follow the Born rule. Ridley argues that self-locating belief can solve the first problem. An observer spread across time extended worlds can be unsure where they sit. Belief shares should track the physical pattern of the wavefunction.

He surveys and rejects rival fixes for the weight problem. Simply postulating the Born rule explains nothing, he argues. His alternative reads the rule as a generic pattern in the wave. A time symmetric reformulation, the Fixed Point Formulation, supplies foundations. Retrocausal ideas enter through that time symmetry. Quantum probability gains a physical home.
arxiv-2510-03105:
Ghasemi and Marshall bound a polynomial from below on a product region. The region joins several hyperellipsoid blocks side by side. Each block constrains its own group of variables. Knowing a safe floor for a polynomial helps verify designs. Their algorithm rests on geometric programming, a fast convex method. Earlier work handled one ellipsoid or the open space. This paper merges those cases into the product setting.

Special cases fall out with no extra work. One block returns the earlier ellipsoid bound directly. Many single-variable blocks return a bound on a box. There, a plain formula sometimes does the whole job. Semidefinite programming can give sharper floors when it finishes. Often it cannot finish at all on large inputs. The new bound trades some sharpness for sheer computability. Engineers who need quick certified floors gain a tool. The authors compare both routes with care throughout.
arxiv-2510-03305:
Zheng and a team of climate and data science researchers present a 2025 arXiv paper on how machine learning projects in climate modeling are actually run. Climate work faces sparse data, huge scales, and strict physics demands. The authors argue that success turns less on the model itself than on the workflow around it. They study real projects from a United States science center that joins AI with Earth physics.

Across eight case studies, the team traces shared design patterns. The projects cover fast stand in models, learned physics parts, and inference drawn from simulations. Each workflow grounds its steps in physical knowledge and feeds on simulation data. The authors distill habits that keep such work rigorous: clear setup, honest checks, and steps others can repeat. Their guide lowers the barrier for climate scientists and data experts who must build models together.
arxiv-2510-03405:
Badhe presents a 2025 arXiv paper that simulates courtroom procedure with AI agents to hunt for loopholes. LegalSim treats legal rules as code inside a game like setting. Plaintiff and defendant agents pick moves such as discovery requests, motions, and sanction bids. A stochastic judge model rules on the moves with tuned grant rates and cost splits. Four strategy types compete, from reinforcement learning to a large language model policy and a hand written heuristic.

Scoring rewards more than winning; it also tracks how much cost and delay a side inflicts on the other. Across settings like bankruptcy stays and tax cases, agents discovered exploit chains that stay legal yet harm the system. One learning policy, PPO, won most often, while a bandit policy proved the most steady across rivals. The results argue for red teaming legal rule systems themselves, not just the models that use them.
arxiv-2510-03605:
Javanmard, Mirzasoleiman, and Mirrokni present a 2025 arXiv paper explaining when test time computation helps language models reason, based on what training data contained. They study transformers on an in context weight prediction task from linear regression. In that setting, chain of thought at test time acts like steps of a Newton solver. The analysis yields links among test time compute, context length, and the mix of training tasks. Experiments on nonlinear transformers, including GPT-2, confirm the picture.

Three findings stand out. At a fixed error level, more test time compute lets a model manage with fewer in context examples. If a skill is missing from training, extra compute can hurt. Task hardness, measured through the smallest eigenvalue of the feature covariance, predicts where scaling pays off. Training on diverse, relevant, and hard tasks gave the best test time scaling. Data curation, not just inference budgets, decides whether longer reasoning helps.
arxiv-2510-03905:
Sakai and colleagues wrote this 2025 arXiv paper tracing a century of gender stereotypes in Japanese writing. Surveys cannot reach back to 1900, but books and documents from each year survive. The team trained one word embedding per year, giving a hundred snapshots of word use. They then measured how strongly words leaned toward female or male associations over time.

Three domains told a layered story: home, work, and politics. Work and politics flipped from male-leaning to female-leaning by the 1970s, tracking women's real entry into jobs and public life. Yet home also grew more female-leaning instead of fading. Women were written about as homemakers and workers at once, rather than one role replacing the other. Occupation stereotypes also tracked the actual share of women in each job. The findings show language records social change slowly, with new roles added before old expectations loosen.
arxiv-2510-04105:
Deshmukh presents this 2025 arXiv paper extending a cornerstone theorem of harmonic analysis to a setting based on Hausdorff capacities. Capacities measure the size of sets too irregular for ordinary volume, which makes them natural in nonlinear potential theory. Rubio de Francia's extrapolation theorem classically says that an inequality proven for one exponent, with suitable weights, transfers to all exponents. Analysts rely on it to avoid reproving estimates case by case.

The paper proves the analogue of that theorem where Hausdorff capacities replace measures. The argument follows the classical strategy but leans on the recently developed theory of capacitary Muckenhoupt weights. Those weights supply the control needed to move estimates between exponents in the capacitary world. Establishing extrapolation there unlocks a workhorse tool for capacitary inequalities. The result should let researchers transfer known single-exponent estimates across the full exponent range in this nonlinear setting.
arxiv-2510-04305:
Jacob and colleagues present this 2025 arXiv paper on mixing two separated kinds of passive particles using a tiny team of learned active particles. Active matter systems consume energy locally and generate collective motion, but steering them toward a specified task is difficult. Here only about two percent of the particles are active, and a neural network agent directs their behavior. The goal is mixing of two initially segregated passive species.

Conventional run-and-tumble particles already stir the system, yet the trained smart particles mixed faster and more efficiently. The learned strategy surprised the authors: spreading the active particles everywhere was not optimal. Instead, they confined their motion to an off-center zone of activity. That eccentric stirring drove a global rotation of the passive particles around the system center. The work links reinforcement learning with active matter design for microfluidic transport and adaptive materials.
arxiv-2510-04405:
Shoulong Li, Liang Liang, and Liang Ma wrote this 2025 paper on black holes in a modified theory of gravity. The theory adds a vector field that breaks Lorentz symmetry on its own, an effect called bumblebee gravity. The team first built an exact black hole solution that carries both electric and magnetic charge. They then studied how the black hole stores heat and energy.

Using the Wald formalism, the authors computed the mass and entropy of the new black hole. Those values obey the first law of black hole thermodynamics, a key consistency check. The team then extended the solution to the Taub NUT case, a black hole type with a twist like charge. Last, they generalized the charged solution to spaces with more than four dimensions. The work gives theorists exact models for testing how broken Lorentz symmetry might show up near black holes.
arxiv-2510-04505:
Gábor Benedek and Tibor Krisztin wrote this 2025 paper on delay equations whose present rate depends on a past value. Such equations model blood cell production, lasers, and other systems with a lag. The feedback here is unimodal: it rises, peaks, and then falls. The authors map the unstable sets that flow out of steady states and periodic orbits. Those sets are made of connecting orbits that link one object to another.

A model case in the Mackey Glass line has three steady states when the feedback gain is high. The unstable curve from the middle steady state splits into two branches. One branch always runs down to the zero state. The other branch switches its target at a threshold value of the gain. Below the threshold it also ends at zero, and above it it lands on a complex invariant set. Under conditions that set is a periodic orbit.
arxiv-2510-04605:
Jingyao Zhang and four coauthors wrote this 2025 paper on diffusion language models for software work. Most code models write one token at a time from left to right, which hides code structure and runs slowly. Diffusion models instead refine a whole draft in steps, reading context from both sides. The team ran a test of such models across the software life cycle. Tasks covered code generation, defect detection, and program repair.

The benchmark held fifty three thousand tasks drawn from software work. A seven billion diffusion model beat autoregressive rivals by about thirty percent on average accuracy. The gain on repair across files was larger still, with accuracy more than doubling. The diffusion models ran with lower delay than their autoregressive peers. Reading structure from both directions seems to suit code, which depends on far apart lines. The authors present diffusion as the stronger base pattern for software engineering tools.
arxiv-2510-04805:
Daniel Le, Bao Le Hung, and Heejong Lee wrote this 2025 mathematics paper proving a case of Serre weight conjectures. The conjectures link Galois representations, which encode symmetry, to modular forms. For representations valued in the group GSp4, work predicted which weights occur. Two teams had stated versions with conditions at primes above p. A proof needed a genericity assumption that nobody could check.

The authors remove weakness. They prove the weight part of the conjecture for tamely ramified representations with explicit genericity conditions. The proof leans on bounds for patched modules and on deformation rings they compute. As a payoff, they prove a modularity lifting theorem for the group. Theorems say that a representation that looks modular in a sense is modular in full. Lifting theorems power results like the proof of Fermat’s last theorem. The work strengthens the bridge between Galois theory and automorphic forms.
arxiv-2510-04905:
Tao, Qin, and Liu wrote this 2025 survey paper on code generation that looks things up before writing. Language models now write working functions, but software lives in whole repositories. Code there must respect files, shared names, and project conventions. Retrieval augmented generation fetches relevant code and docs into the model context first. This survey maps the literature on that idea, with weight on the repository level.

The authors sort prior work along axes. Generation strategies, retrieval modes, model designs, training styles, and evaluation habits each get a taxonomy. They gather the data sets and benchmarks the field uses. Gaps get named plainly: retrieval misses cross file links, and context limits still bite.
