The results identify a neural mechanism devoted to detecting what is not there.
arxiv-2511-21805:
Kwak and colleagues simulate how spiral arms form in a Milky Way-like galaxy disk sitting inside a halo of dark matter. Instead of stirring the disk by hand, they let structure grow alone and study how resolution, disk stability, and a live halo change what appears. They track spiral patterns labelled m equals 1 through 6, which count how many arms each pattern has.

In well-resolved runs with a live halo, spirals appear in a cascade: many-armed patterns form and fade first, then fewer-armed patterns follow, with the action drifting inward. Raising the particle count tenfold delayed visible spirals by about 0.5 billion years and bar formation by about 1.9 billion years, but did not change the overall path. The three-armed pattern marked when inner-disk angular momentum transport began, ahead of bar formation, while fixed halos produced strong early spirals but no coherent cascade.
arxiv-2511-21905:
Radevych and colleagues connect two major materials-simulation programs. VASP is a widely used first-principles code with a rich library of functionals and pseudopotentials, while EPW specializes in electron-phonon interactions. That coupling between electrons and lattice vibrations governs superconductivity, heat flow, and carrier mobility. Their interface computes interaction matrix elements with VASP's supercell method, then interpolates them inside EPW.

They demonstrate the link on two textbook problems. For magnesium diboride, solving the anisotropic Migdal-Eliashberg equations gave superconducting gap closing temperatures of about 36 kelvin with one functional. The temperatures were 38 kelvin with VASP's PBE and 46 kelvin with a newer functional, bracketing the experimental value of 39 kelvin quoted in the study. For cubic boron nitride they computed carrier mobility with the ab initio Boltzmann transport equation. The result is a route to temperature-dependent properties with VASP's full library.
arxiv-2511-22305:
Fenoglio, Li, Barbiero, and colleagues keep federated learning accurate when every client's data drifts in a different way. Federated training pools many devices' data without centralizing it. A single global model degrades badly when clients' distributions differ, and clustered variants usually must know the shift types and cluster count in advance. Their Flux framework computes privacy-preserving descriptors on each client, clusters clients by descriptor similarity, trains one model per cluster. Even assigns brand-new, unlabeled clients to the right cluster model at test time.

Across four benchmarks, two real-world datasets, and ten baselines, Flux improves accuracy by up to 23 percentage points over the baseline under all four shift types, with overhead comparable to FedAvg. Ablations credit the descriptors themselves: swapping test-time assignment for random clusters costs up to 53 points of accuracy on MNIST in their tables.
arxiv-2511-22705:
St-Onge and colleagues build a floor robot that transfers patients and trains them to stand. Regaining the sit-to-stand motion is key to functional mobility and avoiding rehospitalization. Yet devices split into passive raising aids, moving patients on trajectories without engaging them, and rehabilitation systems, supporting partial bodyweight but unable to adapt training to mobility levels or work outside rooms. The team's two-degrees-of-freedom floor robot adjusts impedance and vertical and forward forces.

Experiments with healthy adults showed the device barely impacts natural sit-to-stand kinematics and delivers precise weight unloading at the centre of mass, up to 61 kilograms at the reported speed. It can add a forward virtual spring helping shift bodyweight onto the feet at seat-off. In transfer mode it lifts patients up to 200 kilograms, retaining raising-aid capability. One limitation surfaced: constrained seating lowered peak velocity, traced to actuator stroke.
arxiv-2511-23205:
Tang and colleagues merge two separate steps of data analysis, dimension reduction and regression, into a single method for problems with many correlated predictors. Their PLS-Lasso builds the partial least squares idea, compressing predictors into latent directions chosen for their link to the response, directly into the Lasso penalty. It comes in two versions, one blending the two goals with a tuning knob and one without it.

Both versions ship with algorithms the authors prove converge to global optima, a guarantee plain Lasso-style methods do not always offer for such blended objectives. Tested against ordinary Lasso on financial index tracking, the task of mimicking an index with few assets, both variants showed promise. Version one proved unstable, winning when the required portfolio was very sparse but fading as the allowed sparsity decreased in their experiments.
arxiv-2512-00105:
Finding interesting patterns in large numerical databases can overwhelm analysts with far too many results. Djawad Bekkoucha and co-authors present a sampling approach for interval patterns in a 2025 journal article. Instead of listing everything, sampling draws a manageable subset at random, weighted by an interestingness measure.

Measures such as frequency or hyper-volume decide which patterns are more likely to be drawn. The authors describe their method as the first sampling approach built for interval patterns in numerical data. It offers data miners a practical way to explore huge pattern spaces without drowning in output. Interval patterns describe ranges rather than single values, which suits sensor and financial data.
arxiv-2512-00605:
Combinatorial bandit problems force repeated choices under constraints, balancing learning with earning. Aurélien Delage and Romaric Gaudel study matroid bandit linear optimization in 2025, exploiting unimodality to gain efficiency. Recent approaches already achieve optimal regret, matching the known lower bound.

Time complexity remains the problem, especially for large matroids or costly membership oracles, as in recommendation systems that must ensure diversity. Unimodality, a single-peaked structure in the problem, can be leveraged to cut computation. The result aims at bandit algorithms that stay optimal in regret while finally running fast enough for real platforms. Matroids generalize independence, covering scheduling, spanning trees, and diversity constraints alike. Unimodality gives the search a peak to climb instead of a plateau to wander.
arxiv-2512-00705:
Seongyeon Park and five coauthors present FlexiWalker, a 2025 computer systems paper on random walks over graphs. Random walks hop from node to node and support many graph analysis tasks. Dynamic walks change their hop chances as the graph evolves, which makes them flexible but hard to speed up.

Most fast CPU and GPU designs rely on precomputed data, which dynamic walks break. Users are left with slow frameworks or hand-tuned code that fits one workload only. FlexiWalker is a GPU framework that adapts at runtime to varied workloads. Its goal is fast dynamic walks without rewriting kernels for each new job.
arxiv-2512-01305:
Jianru Duan studies a torsion invariant for three-dimensional shapes. The invariant is built from L2 methods, which use square-summable data. Sutured decomposition cuts a shape into simpler parts. Duan asks what the invariant can tell about a shape's fibers.

He proves it detects whether a given class is fibered. That means it can tell if the shape is built from a surface swept along a loop. One case is set aside, for closed graph shapes with no curved metric of the right type. Such tests help sort shapes that look alike at first glance.
arxiv-2512-01605:
Anurag and co-authors count the cost of VQE for small molecules. VQE is a hybrid quantum-classic method to find ground-state energies. Those energies drive drug and materials design. Noise and small quantum hardware cap its use today.

The team gauges resources under distinct fermion mappings and Hamiltonian cuts. Each choice shifts qubit counts and circuit depth. Clear counts show which choices save most. That guides chemists to spend scarce quantum time on the setups most likely to yield sound energies. Small molecules are the test bed where quantum chemistry hopes to beat classic methods first, so honest costs there set the field's pace.
arxiv-2512-01805:
Caroline Piaulet-Ghorayeb and co-authors find a window for water-hydrogen demixing on warm sub-Neptunes. Sub-Neptunes are the most common planet type found. Their bulk makeup is still poorly known. Old views said only very cold planets could split volatiles into layers.

Warm, metal-rich sub-Neptunes may split as well, the team argues. Envelopes once thought fully mixed could stratify. Layering changes how heat and chemistry move inside the planet. That shift alters how observers should read spectra of the most common planets known. Metal-rich envelopes are common in the sub-Neptune census, so a demixing window there reshapes population models, not just single planet stories.
arxiv-2512-02105:
An anomaly is an obstruction: a symmetry of a quantum system that cannot be gauged or realized by a trivial state. Alexander Czajka, Roman Geiko, and Ryan Thorngren build in 2025 a rigorous topological theory of such anomalies for systems living on a lattice.

They also construct spectra of invertible states and quantum cellular automata, mathematical objects that organize these phases. With those spectra, both anomalies and symmetry-protected topological phases can be classified up to a blending equivalence. The classification tells physicists which exotic states of matter can exist on a lattice and which are forbidden in principle.
arxiv-2512-02205:
The Integrable Optics Test Accelerator at Fermilab is a small ring built to test bold plans for strong particle beams. Four authors, Banerjee, Romanov, Stancari, and Wallbank, report in 2025 on the traits and motion of proton beams in that ring.

The ring lets staff study how space charge, beam load effects, and bent optics act on each other in storage rings. These effects cap how bright a beam can be. The proton cases worked out here guide tests that could unlock brighter beams for the next machines. Such groundwork must come first, before the new optics can leave theory and run in steel.
arxiv-2512-02905:
F. Andreatta and three co-authors build technical tools for computing p-adic maps that link geometry and number theory. Their ongoing work targets explicit reciprocity laws for the group GSp4. Tools of this kind compute Abel-Jacobi maps in p-adic étale settings.

The authors define syntomic polynomial cohomology for filtered Frobenius log isocrystals. The setting covers proper, semistable schemes over a local field's integers, with smooth generic fiber and horizontal divisors. Solid foundations here underpin some of the deepest current work on L-functions and motives. Base tools earn their keep in the work they let peers skip. This set is built to be that kind of base for a hard line of proofs.
arxiv-2512-03005:
Dawei Li and six co-authors test whether language models can mediate online flame wars instead of fueling them. Models increasingly sit inside everyday communication, drafting and smoothing messages. Their potential to foster empathy and constructive dialogue is an important frontier for responsible AI, the authors argue.

A mediator model would step into heated threads and cool them toward resolution. The study asks whether current models can serve that role at all. Evidence here guides platforms weighing AI moderation that aims higher than deletion, toward actually repairing conversations between angry users. Cool heads are scarce in a flame war. A calm third voice that both sides can hear may do what bans and blocks can not do at all.
arxiv-2512-03505:
Quantum systems can show nonclassical traits in phase space. Kyu-Won Park and Jongin Jeong develop a complex entropy framework for those traits in this 2025 work. They apply it to avoided crossings in an oval quantum billiard.

For a real Wigner function, the Gibbs-Shannon functional becomes complex. Its imaginary part, tied to the Wigner-negative volume, serves as an entropy-like measure of nonclassicality. The authors add Fisher control of that negativity. Such measures help track how quantum behavior fades into classical motion. Negativity measures mark where classical pictures fail inside the billiard's phase space.
arxiv-2512-03605:
Eduardo Espindola and Yu Tang steer quadrotors straight from raw sensor readings, skipping the state estimator most controllers depend on. Cheap inertial units and GPS feed their 2025 perception-feedback design directly. Gyroscope bias, a classic poison for such schemes, is corrected inside the loop.

Lyapunov analysis proves the tracking error stays practically stable under outside disturbances, and becomes exponentially stable when disturbances vanish. Simulations under noisy measurements and uncertain parameters backed the theory. The appeal is simplicity: fewer estimation layers between sensing and action on small drones. Their controller held its line in silico against the messiness that breaks fragile designs.
arxiv-2512-04105:
Legal help exists online in abundance, yet citizens still stall on legal websites full of jargon and complicated forms. Jinzhe Tan and Karim Benyekhlef introduce LegalWebAgent in a 2025 preprint, a framework sending a language-model agent onto the web on the user's behalf. The target is access to justice in Québec's civil law system.

The agent works in three stages. An Ask module interprets the user's need in natural language. A Browse module then navigates pages on its own, reading both page structure and screenshots, filling in forms and calendars as needed. An Act module assembles what was found, or completes the action directly. The authors built a benchmark of fifteen realistic legal tasks. Across models tested, success rates averaged in the mid-eighties percent, which they take as evidence of real autonomy on messy websites.
arxiv-2512-04505:
Koichi Saito, Tsuyoshi Miyatsu, and Myung-Ki Cheoun merge two models of nuclear matter into one that spans from thin gas to the dense cores of neutron stars. At extreme density, nucleons overlap so much that quarks start to roam across the whole system, a state called quarkyonic matter. Separate models handled the low and high ends. Their 2025 arXiv paper joins the dual quarkyonic model to the quark-meson coupling model, forming the QQMC model.

Inside QQMC, each nucleon keeps a relativistic cloud of quarks with a Gaussian shape. A first pass with a plain Fermi gas gave jumps and blow-ups at the density where the quarkyonic phase starts. An infrared regulator smooths those flaws away. The joined model then yields energy, pressure, and sound speed across the full density range. A smooth span matters for neutron star structure, where each density shell must match the next.
arxiv-2512-05005:
Luke Peters and a large team of co-authors report the first millimetre-wave frequency comb drawn directly from an optical microcomb. A frequency comb is a ruler of evenly spaced tones, and versions reaching into the sub-terahertz range are wanted for faster wireless links, sharp sensing, and precise positioning. Tiny ring-shaped optical devices had already set records for quiet single tones, but none had produced a whole comb at these wavelengths.

The team's filtered microcomb feeds light-sensing antennas that convert the optical comb straight down to millimetre waves, with no amplifier needed. The source is steady enough for time-domain spectroscopy without lining up pulses, and it held up over a long test path even while running freely. Running several light patterns at once also lets the team reshape the output spectrum simply by choosing among the patterns.
arxiv-2512-05205:
Sören Wilkening, Timo Ziegler, and Maximilian Hess extend a quantum search heuristic to handle combinatorial problems with constraints. Many practical tasks — scheduling, routing, allocating — amount to choosing the best option among astronomically many, subject to rules. Their earlier method built on Grover's quantum search; this work generalizes it to problems whose constraints are linear, the most common kind in practice.

The authors frame the method as a platform rather than a single algorithm: circuit optimizations and machine learning techniques can be plugged in to push performance further. They compare the approach against leading classical solvers to gauge its standing. The results, they argue, show the algorithm could deliver a genuine speed advantage once suitable quantum hardware exists. The paper is a step toward quantum optimization that respects the constraints real problems impose, rather than assuming them away.
arxiv-2512-05405:
Adam Mantz and six co-authors set out a strategy for squeezing the most from X-ray observations of faint objects like galaxy clusters. The data from telescopes such as Chandra and XMM-Newton mix the target's glow with foreground emission from our Galaxy, the X-ray background, and particle noise inside the instruments. Rather than subtracting these contaminants, the authors forward-model all of them together with the source.

Forward modelling is the cleaner path: it needs no binning of the data and lets systematic uncertainties be averaged over. Applying the methods to several clusters at intermediate and high redshift, with masses and shapes, they find modest gains even for bright clusters. The advantages grow larger for the faint, distant, low-surface-brightness cases where every photon counts. The paper documents a time-dependent miscalibration of Chandra's detectors found in archival data, and supplies a correction for it.
arxiv-2512-05605:
Shun Xu writes on vertex operator algebras, the algebraic structures that encode two dimensional conformal field theory. When such an algebra has a symmetry of finite order, earlier work built an associative algebra from it, due to Dong, Li, and Mason. A second construction, by Dong and Jiang, built modules that link two of these algebras. Each construction was known to match certain pieces of a larger enveloping algebra, but the two facts were proved apart.

The 2025 paper gives a single, shorter proof that covers both matches at once. Xu shows that the twisted associative algebra and the twisted bimodule both arise as the same kind of subquotient of the universal enveloping algebra of the twisted algebra. It makes plain that two tools built for different jobs spring from one source. It also helps later work on twisted representations.
arxiv-2512-05705: Nihat Gökhan Göğüş, Rewayat Khan, Eungil Ko, and Ji Eun Lee study block Toeplitz operators whose symbols are matrices with a circulant pattern. Toeplitz operators are a test bed in operator theory. The paper asks when such block operators are binormal, a relaxed form of the normal case. It also examines certain dilations of these operators. A dilation views an operator as part of a larger one. Finally, it analyzes which subspaces stay invariant under them. The results show how the circulant symbol structure shapes behavior.
arxiv-2512-05805:
Parinya Karndumri, writing alone, finds a large family of Janus solutions in five dimensional supergravity. Janus solutions are interfaces: spacetime regions where two different vacuum states meet along a wall, each side settling into its own anti-de Sitter geometry. The theory carries strong supersymmetry, five vector multiplets, and a product gauge group. It admits four vacua, differing in how much symmetry they keep.

Working first in a smaller truncation with three vector multiplets, Karndumri finds interfaces joining the two vacua of that theory, plus flow interfaces between the two symmetry patterns. Repeating the search in the full theory yields Janus solutions between the four vacua. There are even multi-Janus examples, chains of interfaces stacked together. Such solutions matter to holography, where a gravity interface describes a field theory defect. The catalogue gives builders concrete geometries for defects where two symmetry patterns share a border.
arxiv-2512-06905:
Zijian Zhou and co-authors tackle a hard trick for video generation: making a new clip that follows a written prompt while keeping a person or object looking exactly like a reference image. Existing methods learn from costly bundles that tie a reference, a finished video, and a caption together. Gathering such bundles at scale is slow and expensive, which caps how good the models can get.

Their system, Saber, drops the bundles entirely. It trains only on ordinary video and text pairs, using a masked training scheme and a tailored attention design to learn what makes a subject stay itself across frames. Extra mask tricks fight the copy-paste look that plagues this kind of generation. Saber handled varying numbers of reference images well, and on a public benchmark it beat methods that had used the expensive bundled data. Clever training, it seems, can replace pricey data.
arxiv-2512-07205:
Eunjung Lee, Hee-Suk Cho, and Chang-Hwan Lee measure a hidden error that creeps into gravitational-wave astronomy when merging neutron stars travel on oval rather than circular paths. If analysts fit such a signal with circular-orbit waveforms, the inferred properties shift systematically. An earlier study quantified that bias without spin; this one adds the stars' spin, the realistic case, for binaries heard by today's detectors.

Using a fast analytic method, checked against full Bayesian sampling, the authors generate ten thousand random binaries spanning plausible masses. Spins, and small orbital eccentricities, then compute the bias in chirp mass, mass ratio, effective spin, and tidal softness. The first three biases trace narrow bands that bend gently with eccentricity. The tidal bias, by contrast, scatters widely depending on mass and spin.
arxiv-2512-07305:
Tobias Abraham Haider reruns a published experiment to see whether its conclusions survive a change of scenery. The original work tested a pre-trained Google image model, Inception-ResNet-v2, on camera trap photos of European wild mammals. Haider rebuilds the study from scratch with open resources and a fresh data set of nine hundred images spanning ninety species, applying only minimal preparation before classification.

The overall accuracy landed in the low sixty percent range, close to the seventy-one percent the original reported despite the different pictures. Per-species performance, though, swung wildly, and the averaged F-score was low, exposing how uneven the model is across animals. A recurring cause is misalignment: wildlife categories do not map neatly onto the everyday classes the model was trained to name. Haider's verdict is double.
arxiv-2512-07705:
Saroj Gopali, Bipin Chhetri, Deepika Giri, Sima Siami-Namini, and Akbar Siami Namin wrote this 2025 paper on forecasting time series. Classic tools and deep networks both predict such data. Foundation models raise a fresh question: can they beat the specialists?

The team tests large language models through in-context learning. Zero-shot and few-shot styles are both put to work on forecasting. Two commercial chat models join Google's TimesFM, a transformer built for time series. Two deep learning rivals, a temporal convolutional network and an LSTM, complete the field.  TimesFM posts the best overall showing, with the lowest error score. Its running time stays competitive with the rest of the field. One chat model also performs well in the pure zero-shot setting. Pretrained foundation models, the authors conclude, suit real-time forecasting. They deploy with little adaptation.
arxiv-2512-08005:
Stepan Vanecek, Matthew Turner, Manisha Gajbe, Matthew Wolf, and Martin Schulz, computer scientists who work on high performance computing, posted a study on arXiv in December 2025. Their topic is CXL memory, a technology that lets several computers share one pool of attached memory. They ask whether such shared memory could replace message passing between nodes in large scientific programs.

The team presents a toolchain and an extended performance model for message based communication. It traces how MPI programs touch memory, both inside one node and across nodes, then predicts which transfers would speed up through direct shared memory. They validate the model on a heat transfer mini app and the HPCG benchmark. The fine grained results point programmers to the exact calls worth optimizing first.
arxiv-2512-08105:
Francisco Sequeira Murillo, Viviana Rosero, Joshua Marvil, and colleagues, astronomers, posted a survey paper on arXiv in December 2025. It is the third radio paper from the SOFIA Massive star formation survey, covering twelve intermediate mass protostars seen with the Very Large Array. The team studied source shapes, hidden companions, and how radio emission varies with frequency.

Across the target regions they resolved many compact sources and reported eight new detections, four never seen at any wavelength. Seven sources show jet like shapes and radio behavior consistent with ionized jets. With earlier survey papers, the sample grows to twenty nine protostars across a wide brightness range. Intermediate mass objects emit less radio light than a simple scaling from low mass protostars would predict. That shortfall matches theory, where swollen young stars ionize less gas. The enlarged sample sharpens tests of how massive stars are born.
arxiv-2512-08205:
Xiushan Jiang, Dong Wang, Weihai Zhang, Daniel W C Ho, and Yuanqing Wu, control theorists, posted a study on arXiv in December 2025. Their subject is the linear quadratic regulator for a mean field stochastic system, a setting where many interacting agents act under randomness. They design a controller that learns from data while keeping one foot in classical control theory.

The team first reframes the design task as a static constrained optimization problem that keeps the same solutions. Solving a generalized Lyapunov equation then gives the matching dual problem, and they prove the two sides have no gap. From the optimality conditions they build a primal dual learning algorithm. Crucially, they give a partly model free version that connects directly to the classic policy iteration method. A high dimensional example confirms the methods work. The paper adds theory that could make learning based controllers more efficient and safer to trust.
arxiv-2512-08605:
Anton Babaev, an accelerator physicist in Russia, posted a short letter on arXiv in December 2025. It concerns the van der Meer method, the standard way colliders calibrate their luminosity, the number that turns detector counts into physics rates. The method assumes the two beams profiles factorize neatly, but at the NICA collider now being commissioned, an hourglass effect distorts the particle density near the collision point by design.

Babaev revises the formalism for exactly that distorted case. The hourglass effect matters significantly for calibration at NICA, so ignoring it would bias the numbers. More generally, he proposes an approach for estimating the bias of the method whenever beams are non factorizable, not just at his own facility. Short calibration notes rarely make headlines, but every cross section a collider publishes rests on them.
arxiv-2512-08905:
Kaizhi Zheng and coauthors present EvoScene, a framework that builds textured three dimensional scenes from a single image without extra training. Creating full scenes from one view is a long standing challenge in vision and graphics. Recent generators recover decent geometry for single objects, but they generalize poorly to large, complex scenes with faithful structure and texture.

EvoScene combines two strengths: geometric reasoning from three dimensional generation models and visual knowledge from video generation models. It works in three repeating stages. A spatial prior starts the scene, then a mesh is generated under visual guidance, and then new views are generated under spatial guidance. By alternating between two and three dimensional domains, the system improves structure and appearance step by step. Experiments on diverse scenes show better geometric stability, more consistent textures, and better completion of unseen regions than strong baselines.
arxiv-2512-09105:
Adi Manor and coauthors study how a robot attentiveness and competence jointly shape human cognitive trust in the robot. Cognitive trust, the belief that a robot can perform its task accurately, is central to good human robot interaction. Competence and reliability are known to shape that trust, but recent work suggests attentiveness also plays a role.

Participants performed a search task with a robotic dog in a design that varied competence and attentiveness independently, each at high or low levels. High attentiveness compensated for low competence in a striking way. People who worked with a highly attentive but poorly performing robot reported trust close to those with a highly competent robot. When attentiveness was absent, low competence caused a sharp drop in trust. The findings reveal an affective compensatory mechanism that sits beside classic competence based accounts. Trust building, the authors argue, involves emotional processes that designers often overlook.
arxiv-2512-09305:
Somnath Mondal and Lakshmi Kanta Patra study how to estimate the scale parameters of a statistical model used for lifetimes and reliability data. The model mixes two exponential distributions at different scales, making it flexible for survival analysis, medical studies, and finance. The authors focus on the case where the two scale parameters are known to be ordered.

They judge estimators under two loss functions, Stein loss and symmetric loss. Under stated conditions they prove the standard affine equivariant estimator can always be beaten. They then build a class of improved estimators that uniformly dominate the best one of that standard type. The boundary member of their class turns out to be a generalized Bayes estimator. They apply the results to the multivariate Lomax and exponential inverse Gaussian distributions, compare risks in simulations, and illustrate the methods on two real datasets.
arxiv-2512-09405:
Wenbo Luo and colleagues study how to couple light into optical fibers at wide angles, a need for probes that collect light from broad areas. Tiny structures patterned on the fiber's end face can boost that coupling, but earlier theories mostly described bare waveguides and ignored how the added structures change the behavior.

The authors introduce a power-in-bucket model, an analytical way to predict coupling for structure-modified waveguides. They test it on two standard illumination cases, a Gaussian beam and a plane wave. The model's predicted improvements agree well with experiments, especially for multimode fibers under large-angle light. Using the model to tune the beam and fiber parameters, they show that identical ring gratings can raise the coupling efficiency substantially at a steep incidence angle. They offer the model as a design tool for structure-enhanced probes for wide-angle, broadband light collection.
arxiv-2512-10005:
Parvinder Solanki, Igor Lesanovsky, and Gabriele Perfetto show that randomly resetting a quantum system can make it settle down faster. Relaxation toward a stationary state can be painfully slow, especially near a first order phase transition, where the relaxation time can diverge. Their protocol interrupts the dynamics only during an initial window. At random times inside that window, the system is reset to a chosen state. After the window closes, it evolves freely to its steady state.

The speedup appears in few body open systems and in a hard many body case alike. Sometimes the acceleration is exponential, echoing the Mpemba effect, where hot water can freeze faster than cold. The protocol is universal in a practical sense: designing it needs only a few macroscopic facts about the target state, such as the order parameter of the transition. No fine tuning of the starting state is required.
arxiv-2512-10105:
A team led by Soorya Ram Shimgekar maps the hidden structure of conspiracy talk in Singapore based Telegram groups. Their first finding corrects the usual picture: conspiratorial messages are woven into everyday discussion, not confined to echo chambers. The approach has two stages. A fine tuned language model classifies messages as conspiratorial or not, trained on a few thousand expert labeled examples. Then a signed belief graph links messages, with edge signs marking agreement or disagreement in belief, weighted by textual similarity. A graph neural network with a special loss learns embeddings that separate ideological alignment from writing style.

Clustering those embeddings across more than half a million messages revealed seven story archetypes: legal topics, medical concerns, media discussion, finance, distrust of officials, group moderation, and general chat. Conspiratorial content appeared inside routine finance, law, and daily life clusters, not only in distrust focused ones.
arxiv-2512-10505:
Martin Rivas examines a classical picture of the Dirac particle. This is an electron-like object whose mass and spin size must never change under any interaction. The reason is the atomic principle: an elementary particle has no excited states. He studies one such particle inside an external electromagnetic field as a closed system, where total energy, momentum, and angular momentum must be conserved.

The particle has two distinguished points, a centre of charge and a centre of mass. And the field does work along different paths for each. When those two works differ, the excess energy must leave as radiation. So an accelerated Dirac particle radiates while a spinless one does not. Keeping the spin's size fixed then forces new terms into the equations. A reaction force along the momentum and a reaction torque, read as momentum and angular momentum carried away by the radiation.
arxiv-2512-11005:
P. Batista and a large team of co-authors set out what astronomers could learn if stars could be imaged at far finer detail than today. Many expected surface features cannot be drawn from spectra alone. They range from brightness patterns caused by spin or tides to spots, pulsations, passing exoplanets, and sudden flares.

Current optical interferometers link telescopes across a few hundred metres and can resolve only the nearest large stars. Planned kilometre scale arrays could measure even a nearby white dwarf's radius. The white paper imagines still larger arrays spanning many kilometres, which would reveal white dwarf surfaces at the detail now possible only for supergiants. It was written for a European Southern Observatory call about science in the 2040s.
arxiv-2512-11405:
B. Candelpergher presents new polynomial expansions for two of the most studied functions in mathematics, the Dirichlet eta function and the Riemann zeta function. The zeta function encodes the spread of prime numbers, and formulas valid inside its key strip, the region where its deepest secrets live, are especially valuable. Convergent expansions there are hard to come by.

The building introduces a family of hypergeometric polynomials whose roots all lie exactly on the key line. These polynomials connect to a standard family named for Meixner and Pollaczek. From them, Candelpergher builds expansions for both functions that converge throughout the strip, plus orthonormal expansions for their restriction to the key line itself. The expansion coefficients are given explicitly using rational combinations of a few famous constants and zeta values at whole numbers. Such formulas give analysts new handles on functions that resist direct computation.
arxiv-2512-11505:
Priyam Basu, Yunfeng Zhang, and Vipul Raheja introduce BAID, a benchmark for auditing the detectors that claim to spot AI generated text. Schools and workplaces increasingly use such detectors, and scattered reports already showed bias against people learning English. No systematic audit across wider social and language factors existed.

BAID contains over two hundred thousand samples spanning seven bias categories: demographics, age, school grade level, dialect, formality, political leaning, and topic. Each sample also has a synthetic twin rewritten to preserve content while reflecting a subgroup's writing style. Testing four leading open source detectors revealed consistent disparities, with notably low recall for texts from underrepresented groups, meaning their genuine writing is misclassified more often. The authors argue detectors should pass bias audits like this before public deployment.
arxiv-2512-12005:
Marcus Kasdorf and co-authors release MemNNetSim, a shared simulator for nanowire networks whose junctions act as memristors, resistors with memory. Random nanowire webs are promising for brain like computing, but each research group models the junctions its own way, so results are hard to compare.

The Python framework runs static and dynamic network studies under any junction model in one place. Users can swap models and watch the same web behave under each. The team shows it probing reservoir computing, where the web itself does part of the thinking. A unified bench should speed the search for designs that learn well, and make claims across papers easier to check.
arxiv-2512-13105:
Antoine El-Hayek, Monika Henzinger, and Jason Li present an algorithm that keeps track of the minimum cut of a graph as edges change over time. A minimum cut is the cheapest set of edges whose removal splits the graph. The algorithm must be exact, deterministic, and fast after each update.

Their method updates in subpolynomial time as long as the cut is not too large, a far wider range than the prior best allowed. Paired with graph sparsification, it also yields the first near-exact dynamic minimum cut algorithm for weighted graphs with fast randomized updates. The key new piece is a deterministic local minimum cut method.
arxiv-2512-13205:
P. I. Hurtado, J. J. del Pozo, and P. L. Garrido find scaling laws for steady fluid flows described by the Navier-Stokes-Fourier equations. Hydrodynamics claims to capture the collective behavior of many systems using only symmetries and conservation laws. Testing that claim far from equilibrium is the paper's aim.

They show that steady density and temperature fields are set by pressure and one kinetic field that measures excess motion. That field obeys its own spatial scaling law, which the other fields inherit. Large molecular dynamics simulations of model fluids confirmed the predictions through clean data collapses. The laws held up even with strong finite-size effects at molecular scales.
arxiv-2512-13705:
Siqi Wang and co-authors study learning rate annealing in large language model training and whether good settings transfer across models. The learning rate schedule shapes final model quality, but searching for the best one is costly at large scale. They work with the Warmup-Steady-Decay scheduler.

Their refined framework folds in training steps, maximum learning rate, and annealing behavior to predict good schedules. Tests on dense and Mixture-of-Experts models show optimal annealing ratios follow consistent patterns. Those patterns transfer across training setups, so smaller models can act as reliable proxies for larger ones. The result offers practical guidance for picking schedules without exhaustive hyperparameter searches, and was accepted to AAAI 2026.
arxiv-2512-14005:
Bitao Shen and co-authors show a fully integrated hybrid oscillator that sustains microcomb lasing on a chip. Microcombs are compact coherent light sources with uses in metrology, data links, and sensing. Hybrid cavities place gain and Kerr nonlinearity together, so the lasing mode resonates in the nonlinear cavity itself.

Past versions were only partly built or needed an outside drive, making the system harder and raising power use. Their design folds the pump laser, nonlinear resonator, and feedback into a two-element chip cavity: a high-Q microresonator plus a reflective semiconductor optical amplifier. Operation is self-starting and stable with no active feedback. The microcomb reached linewidths below 1 kHz at base, integrated linewidths near 100 kHz, and over 24 hours of self-sustained running.
arxiv-2512-14605:
Hyperelliptic functions generalize the classical elliptic functions and come with a rich algebraic structure. Direct proofs are given here for two theorems about explicit polynomial vector fields, defined in infinitely many variables, that are tied to differentiating these functions of any genus.

One result shows the operators that define the fields commute, so the order in which they act does not matter. The other shows each operator annihilates certain polynomials built from generating functions. Commuting operators are prized in integrable systems and mathematical physics, where they often signal hidden order. The paper supplies careful proofs where the theory needs them.
arxiv-2512-14705:
Economic networks link firms, banks, and sectors, and the survival of each node depends partly on pressure from its neighbors. The graph-embedded hazard model, GEHM, is a framework for survival dynamics on such weighted economic networks.

The model couples a graph-based p-Laplacian diffusion operator, which spreads stress across links, with a stochastic structural drift, while an aggregate complexity factor evolves as an Itô process. The resulting system mixes partial differential and stochastic differential equations. It aims to capture how node-level survival reacts to nonlinear diffusion pressure in a changing economy, giving network risk modelers a new tool.
arxiv-2512-14805:
Ellie Y. Cheng and three coauthors study a new style of coding that mixes plain language prompts with normal programs. In this style, a prompt tells a large language model what to do, much like a line of code. The hard part is letting prompts and program code share the same data without tedious hand copying.

Their answer is shared program state, built into a system called Nightjar for Python. Prompts inside a Nightjar program can read variables, work with objects, and steer the flow of the code. In tests, Nightjar programs matched or beat hand written ones, gaining 4 to 19 percent in accuracy. They also cut code length by 39.6 percent on average, though they could run slower than hand written code.
arxiv-2512-14905:
N. Reyes leads a team of 29 authors describing AMKID, a huge camera for the APEX telescope in Chile. The camera senses faint heat light at submillimeter wavelengths, which carries clues about planet forming disks and distant galaxies. Mapping that faint glow from the ground, fast, has been a technical challenge for decades.

AMKID sits on the 12 meter APEX dish at 5100 meters altitude and watches two bands at once, near 350 and 850 gigahertz. Its field of view spans 15.3 by 15.3 arcminutes, with 13,952 detectors in the high band and 3,520 in the low band, the most of any such camera. Tests of the low frequency array matched the design, with beams at the diffraction limit. Under good skies it can map a square degree in an hour to a depth of 25 millijansky, opening new science for APEX.
arxiv-2512-15505:
Rohit Jena, Pratik Chaudhari, and James Gee independently recheck strong zero shot claims from the LUMIR challenge in a 2025 paper. The challenge tests methods that align brain MRI scans, and its leaders were said to generalize well to unseen image contrasts and resolutions. That claim sits uneasily with known domain shift problems in deep learning.

The recheck finds deep methods match classic iterative methods on standard T1 weighted images and even on macaque scans. Performance drops sharply on other contrasts, though, with effect sizes from 0.7 to 1.5. Deep methods also fail on 0.6 millimeter images and react strongly to preprocessing choices. The authors urge evaluation that mirrors real clinical work.
arxiv-2512-16405:
Marco Cappa and three co-authors theorize about sticky polymers in a 2025 paper posted to arXiv. Associative polymers carry attractive stickers that bind and unbind reversibly. In dilute solution a single chain folds onto its own stickers, forming a single-chain nanoparticle, a soft construct used in materials design and drug delivery.

Simulations show the number of sticker types changes everything: one type gives a smooth thickening into a network as concentration rises, while several types trigger an abrupt, first-order jump. The authors build a mean-field theory using the nanoparticle fluid as a reference. It prices the free energy cost of moving a bond from inside one chain to between two chains, exposing how sticker order along the chain shapes phase behavior. Loop statistics and chain excluded volume emerge as the key microscopic ingredients.
arxiv-2512-16805:
Klaus Jansen, Tobias Mömke, and Björn Schumacher study how hard it is to reoptimize SetCover, the classic task of covering a set with few chosen subsets. In reoptimization, a solved case changes slightly, and the solver may reuse the old answer.

Four changes are covered: adding or removing a set, and adding or removing an element. Some cases were known to be easier than plain SetCover. The team shows the rest are just as hard to approximate as the classic problem. For two cases with a known PTAS, a scheme whose error can be made tiny, they prove no faster EPTAS exists under standard hardness beliefs, via a new proof blend.
arxiv-2512-17005:
Neville Francis, Peter Reinhard Hansen, and Chen Tong reframe identification in structural dynamic models as an optimization task. Instead of leaning only on imposed limits, they pick the rotation of shocks that best lines up with chosen target variables.

Their OASIS scheme is invariant to shock order and scale, and plain Cholesky identification turns out to be a constrained case of the same goal. OASIS closes about twice the gap to perfect correlation that recursive orderings do. The same frame gives a principled route for proxy VAR models with many proxies and leakage. Revisiting 22 published studies, they find proxy uses where leakage shifts the headline findings.
arxiv-2512-17205:
Sanjay Mallick and Ripan Saha take up a question raised by Yi about when two functions must in fact be the same function. They study an L-function, a special function built from a number sequence, next to a general meromorphic function, one that is smooth except at isolated poles. The goal is a single broad test for uniqueness.

Their main result gives general conditions under which sharing enough values forces the two functions to match. The authors say the test improves and extends all earlier results of this kind to the widest setting so far. A large set of worked examples backs the claims and shows where the test can be applied.
arxiv-2512-17305:
Edgar Ribeiro João, Manuel Parra-Royón, and Julián Garrido plan how the world's largest radio telescope array will share its flood of data. The Square Kilometre Array will pour out more data than any single site can hold. A global network of regional centres, called SRCNet, will store and process that stream for astronomers everywhere.

The team writes a semantic model, in a web format called JSON-LD, that names every node, resource, link, and workflow in the network. Clear shared names let centres work together and let a future broker ask, in real time, which centre is free to run a job. The model fits both central and spread-out layouts, and query tests checked its internal consistency.
arxiv-2512-17705:
Joshua Issa and Falk Herwig argue that a dying star can forge its most famous radioactive ash before it ever explodes. Titanium-44 glows in supernova wreckage for decades, and textbooks credit the explosion itself for making it. In some massive stars, though, the oxygen and carbon shells merge and burn while the star still lives, and that merger also cooks titanium.

Simulating a 15-solar-mass star with mixing rules drawn from 3D fluid models, the pair finds the merger's titanium output swings wildly with the mixing style, over four orders of magnitude. In strong cases it out-produces the explosion and matches what telescopes see, while leaving nickel-56 untouched. Reading supernova remains now means asking what the star made in its final days, not just its final second.
arxiv-2512-17805:
Ben Adcock, Gregor Maier, and Rahul Parhi ask a basic question about operator learning. How well can any method recover an unknown map between function spaces from a limited set of noisy examples? Their theory sets hard limits, called minimax bounds, on the best error any learner could reach.

For smooth Lipschitz operators, the team proves matching upper and lower bounds under two kinds of noise and two sampling designs. One result is stark. The error cannot shrink at any steady power rate as samples grow. Even assuming extra smoothness does not help. Knowing these limits tells builders when more data alone will not fix a learning problem.
arxiv-2512-18205:
Amna Ejaz, Sarah Dodson-Robinson, and Charlotte Haley help planet hunters tell true rhythms from red noise. Star light often flickers with slow, rolling patterns called red noise, which can fake a planet's tidy beat. Charts of rhythm strength are judged against a false alarm line, yet that line is often drawn as if the noise were plain white static.

Their method first flattens the roll with a fitted trend, then sets the alarm line from a quick likelihood shortcut, now stretched to uneven sampling. On Kepler star data, the red noise line kept only true spin signals, while the white noise line blessed fakes. Tests on three stars and fake data agree, and the code is public.
arxiv-2512-18305:
Remo Marini and Riccardo Arpe score cyber risk with a math form that quantum machines can chew. Old risk grades lean on static, word based scales that miss how a flaw in one corner of a network can echo across the whole web. Their model casts risk as a QUBO puzzle, a yes or no grid that both classic and quantum solvers can attack.

On a lifelike 255 node setup, risk spread in patterns no one could spot by eye. Trials grew to 1,000 nodes across classic, quantum, and mixed solvers. Pure quantum runs matched classic answers but paid a steep cost in mapping the dense puzzle onto sparse hardware. Mixed solvers skipped that cost and look the most promising at scale.
arxiv-2512-18405:
El Kindi Rezig leads a six author team building Buckaroo, a visual tool for cleaning messy data by direct touch. Data prep is a known choke point in analysis, and scripts hide how a fix in one corner ripples elsewhere. Buckaroo instead groups records on its own and flags flaws like gaps, outliers, and wrong types inside and across those groups.

Scale is the hard part: drawing every row is impossible, yet a plain sample can hide rare but grave errors. Their answer samples with an eye for errors and folds data into layers that support smooth pan and zoom. A link to the Hopara viewing engine shows the idea at work, and expert reviewers found the fit strong.
arxiv-2512-18505:
Vagrant Gautam describes a seminar built around a habit that troubles natural language processing: researchers use big words like interpretability, bias, reasoning, and stereotypes without defining them. Each subfield quietly shares an understanding of such terms, and real choices rest on it, from which datasets get built to which metrics get trusted. His paper, posted to arXiv in December 2025, lays out the course he created.

The seminar asks students what these concepts mean, what they should mean, and how they ought to be measured. It draws on an interdisciplinary reading list and leans on discussion and critique rather than lectures. The paper serves as a teaching blueprint for anyone training NLP students to question the concepts behind their measurements before accepting the numbers those measurements produce.
arxiv-2512-18605:
Qinglin Zeng, Jing Yang, and Keze Wang teach language models to fix their own reasoning mid-stream. A popular efficiency trick watches a model's confidence and kills off low-confidence attempts early, as DeepConf does. But stopping throws away partly built reasoning. Their paper, posted to arXiv in December 2025, turns the low-confidence signal into a trigger for reflection instead.

When confidence dips below a threshold, the model writes a reflection prompt, reviews its current state, names likely errors, and continues along a corrected path. On math reasoning benchmarks including AIME 2025, this reflective confidence approach beats strong early-stopping baselines on accuracy at similar computing cost. The lesson is general: a doubtful draft is often worth repairing rather than discarding, especially when the repair is guided by the model's own signals.
arxiv-2512-18805:
Ronaldo Laishram and eight co-authors watch galaxies die from the inside out in the Spiderweb Protocluster, a crowded city of young galaxies seen as it was about 11 billion years ago. Using deep images from the James Webb and Hubble space telescopes, they fit every pixel's spectrum to map stellar mass and star formation across each galaxy. Their paper, posted to arXiv in December 2025 and accepted by The Astrophysical Journal, targets quenching, the shutdown of star birth.

Massive quiet galaxies, above ten to the power 10.5 solar masses, show clear inside-out quenching: their centers form stars at roughly a tenth the rate of their outskirts. Smaller star-forming galaxies show flat profiles instead. Central activity also drops as the bulge grows more dominant. The patterns match feedback from active galactic nuclei, showing quenching machinery was already running at redshift two.
arxiv-2512-18905:
Chunmei Wang and Shangyou Zhang design a numerical method for interface problems, where a physical property jumps across a boundary inside the domain, as heat flow through layered materials. Their weak Galerkin finite element method, posted to arXiv in December 2025, is built for nonconvex polygonal partitions, the awkward meshes real geometries produce.

The method carries a built-in stabilizer and keeps a simple, symmetric and positive definite structure, properties that make large systems solvable. The authors derive, with full rigor, an error estimate of optimal order in the discrete H1 norm, so accuracy improves at the best possible rate as the mesh refines. Numerical experiments confirm the theory and show the method staying robust on hard cases. For engineers simulating composites, fluids with interfaces, or living tissue, that mix of flexibility and guarantees is the point.
arxiv-2512-19105:
Arpan Sur, Sudipta Saha, Chih-Yu Lee, and Ichiro Takeuchi design a photonic switch from a new phase-change alloy, Ge4Sb6Te7. Phase-change materials flip between glassy and crystalline states and hold the state without power. That makes them attractive as tiny, non-volatile parts for light-based neural networks.

The team measured the alloy's optical constants in both states, then shaped a segmented switch on a silicon-on-insulator platform for telecom light. Simulations show segmentation lifts the on-off contrast more than sevenfold over a plain design, with low loss. Laser heating switches the device with less than a nanojoule, and the alloy supports dozens of distinct light levels for weights.
arxiv-2512-19305:
Javier Vela-Tambo, Jorge Gracia, and Fernando Dominguez-Castro built CienaLLM, a tool that pulls structured facts about climate harm out of news text. Tracking the social and economic damage of hazards means reading huge piles of mixed articles by hand. Their framework uses open-weight language models to extract the facts with no task training.

Prompts and output schemas are configurable, and pipelines can run in steps, in the cloud or on site. A large factorial study varied model family, size, precision, and prompt style. Parsing fixes nearly erased format errors, bigger models proved steadiest, and quantization saved much compute for a small accuracy cost.
arxiv-2512-19505: Alexander Lubotzky and Matthew Stover answer a question raised by Belolipetsky and Lubotzky about which groups can act as the full symmetry group of a complex hyperbolic surface. For every finite group, they prove, there are infinitely many distinct compact complex hyperbolic two-manifolds whose automorphism group is exactly that group. The result is stated in one stroke: no finite group is excluded, and each occurs in endless variety. It closes the existence question for automorphism groups of such surfaces in full generality.
arxiv-2512-19605:
Eric Zimmermann, Harley Wiltzer, Justin Szeto, David Alvarez-Melis, and Lester Mackey introduce KerJEPA, a family of self-supervised learning methods for vision. The family grows out of joint-embedding predictive architectures, where shaping learned representations toward a round Gaussian form is known to steady training and improve later performance. KerJEPA replaces the usual regularizer with kernel-based measures of how far representations sit from a chosen prior.

One member of the family recovers the existing SIGReg regularizer, which approximates a sliced maximum mean discrepancy with a Gaussian prior and kernel. By widening the menu of kernels and priors and computing the high-dimensional limit of sliced discrepancies in closed form, the authors gain design flexibility and stability. They use those tools to train strong vision models at scale.
arxiv-2512-19705:
Jian Xue, Qian Zhang, and Wu Zhu ask what happened to financial analysts when generative AI landed on their desks. They exploit the 2023 integration of generative AI into the FactSet platform as a natural experiment in AI access. Reports from FactSet-associated analysts form the treatment group, with other data vendors supplying placebo comparisons.

After integration, those reports grew markedly richer: more distinct information sources, broader topical coverage, and more analytical methods, delivered faster. Yet relative forecast accuracy fell precisely where information-processing demands were greatest. A machine-learning benchmark fed the same inputs showed no such decline, pointing at human attention, not worse information, as the bottleneck. The study concludes that generative AI loosens the constraint on gathering information while tightening the one on processing it.
arxiv-2512-19805:
Deepit Sapru writes a practitioner's playbook for aiming marketing offers with causal evidence rather than hunches. The framework starts by estimating conditional average treatment effects with uplift learners, which identify which customers an offer actually changes, not merely who was likely to buy anyway. It then solves a constrained allocation problem to pick targets and offers.

Business guardrails sit inside the optimization from the start: budget limits, revenue protection, and customer-experience constraints bound what the algorithm may do. Supported decisions include retention messaging, event rewards, and spend-threshold assignments. Offline simulations and online A/B tests both showed the approach beating propensity-based and static targeting baselines, and the paper packages the method as a reusable routine for causal targeting at scale.
arxiv-2512-19905:
Indranil Halder and Cengiz Pehlevan build a solvable toy model of a fashionable practice: letting a language model judge its own multiple attempts. Inference-time scaling spends compute at answer time by sampling many candidates and selecting with a reward, here supplied by a judge model. The principles behind when that helps remain murky, so the authors study Bayesian linear regression with a reward-weighted sampler as an analytically tractable stand-in.

In the high-dimensional regime they derive closed forms for the predictive mean and variance, then track generalization error as samples accumulate. With a well-matched reward, error falls monotonically, and in the best-of-k teacher-reward limit it decays quadratically in the number of samples. A badly misspecified reward instead creates a finite optimal sample count beyond which more sampling hurts, and task difficulty erodes the whole advantage.
arxiv-2512-20105:
Haiyun Wei leads a nine-author team making synthetic LiDAR scans for self-driving work, from almost any start material. Realistic, controllable point clouds are prized fuel for simulation. Past generators traded quality against breadth of control. LiDAR data are complex, while control signals are simple. LiDARDraft bridges that gap with a middle step. It uses a three-dimensional layout, cheap to get from text, images, or sketches.

All inputs are turned into such layouts. The layouts are then rendered into semantic and depth control signals. A range-map ControlNet uses those aligned signals to steer cloud generation with care. The result is controllable, high-quality LiDAR synthesis. Whole driving scenes can be built from scratch. A text sketch of a street can become a full scan.
arxiv-2512-20305:
Mebin Jose, Jisha Francis, and Sudheesh Kumar Kattumannil extend accelerated failure time models, a workhorse of survival analysis. These models describe how covariates speed up or slow down time to an event. Classic versions force that effect into a linear formula, which misses curved relationships common in clinical data.

Their approach, KAN-AFT, lets the regression function be an unknown smooth function written through a Kolmogorov-Arnold representation. The classic linear model survives as a special case. Estimation handles right-censoring through several adjusted losses, while pruning and symbolic approximation keep the fitted functions readable. Simulations show the method recovering linear structure when present and bending when needed. Clinical data sets confirm competitive prediction with transparent covariate effects.
arxiv-2512-20605:
Seijin Kobayashi and a large team find hierarchical skills hiding inside large autoregressive models. Reinforcement learning on token-by-token generation explores clumsily, especially when rewards are sparse. Their idea is to let a second, higher-order sequence model steer the base model's internal activations instead of its tokens.

The higher-order model compresses long stretches of behaviour into internal controllers. Each controller executes a meaningful action sequence over a long timescale and carries its own learned termination condition, so controllers can be composed. Directly reinforcing these controllers, a process the authors call internal reinforcement learning, solves grid-world and MuJoCo tasks with hierarchical structure where ordinary fine-tuning fails on sparse rewards. Latent actions, it turns out, were inside the model all along.
arxiv-2512-20805:
Jack Lee Jennings and four co-authors aim to freeze living cells with less damage. Cryopreservation depends on cooling speed, thawing, protective chemicals, and the cells themselves. Labs still design slow-cooling schedules mostly by trial and error, adjusting temperatures by rule of thumb rather than by principle.

The team derive a mathematical method from first principles that shapes the cooling curve to lower injury risk. The method produces concrete predictions for how temperature should fall over time. They check those predictions against published data and fresh experiments of their own. The result is a general computational recipe for better slow-cooling profiles for cells held in suspension.
arxiv-2512-21005:
Edwin Fong, Lancelot James, and Juho Lee tackle epidemic forecasting where the data is mostly zeros. Regions that have never reported a case still need outbreak predictions, and relative-rate methods wobble badly around zero counts. Their framework, the Poisson Hierarchical Indian Buffet Process, is built on absolute abundance and had already proven itself on sparse microbiome and ecological counts. Applied to infectious disease, it borrows statistical strength from related regions instead of treating each silent region as a blank.

Experiments on disease data produce coherent forecasts even for areas with no cases so far, and the setup supports diversity contrasts that ecologists know well. For public-health modelers, the chapter supplies both the computing tools and evidence that sound borrowing across neighbors beats patching zeros.
arxiv-2512-21205:
Gargi Mukherjee, Helen Zhang, and Ying Zhong sharpen the mathematics of counting ways to write a number as a sum of distinct parts. The distinct partition function grows ferociously, and its asymptotic expansion, a formula that approximates the count for large inputs, is only as useful as its error bounds. The authors supply explicit bounds for the shifted version of the function, where the argument is raised by any fixed nonnegative shift, making the approximation rigorous rather than suggestive.

With a trustworthy formula in hand, they settle a family of inequality questions completely, computing the exact threshold sizes beyond which each inequality holds permanently. The families come from invariants of the quartic binary form, from double Turan inequalities, and from Laguerre inequalities, together with their companion variants. Partition theorists gain a template: precise asymptotics first, then exact finite thresholds instead of eventual, unverified claims.
arxiv-2512-21305:
Cohomology rings encode a space's shape algebraically, and Manas Mandal and Divya Setia ask how freely those rings can be reshuffled for certain homogeneous spaces. With extra classes imported from spaces whose cup products vanish, they find rigidity: the automorphisms are tightly constrained. Their test case is a sphere times a complex Grassmannian, whose graded ring maps they classify.

The same circle of ideas feeds coincidence theory, the study of points where two maps agree. Mandal and Setia derive necessary conditions for generalized Dold spaces to have the coincidence property, the fixed-point property included. From those conditions they extract usable sufficient criteria guaranteeing a coincidence point for pairs of continuous maps on such spaces.
arxiv-2512-21405:
Fiana Jacobzon studies a family of classes of analytic functions built from one special function, the Gauss hypergeometric function, which in this case equals a simple logarithmic expression. Each class imposes prescribed constraints on the derivatives of its functions. Jacobzon asks what geometric properties these classes have and how they fit together.

She pins down the classes' geometry, including sharp estimates on their coefficients, meaning bounds that cannot be improved. The family also turns out to form a filtration of infinitesimal generators, the objects that generate one-parameter semigroups of functions. Jacobzon also studies how the semigroups evolve. A further finding is that the filtration links naturally to the Ma-Minda starlike functions, a well-known family in geometric function theory.
arxiv-2512-22105:
Momir Adžemović presents TDLP, a method for multi-object tracking, where software must keep each object's identity straight across video frames. Tracking-by-detection systems are fast but usually match detections to tracks with hand-built rules. Fully learned systems avoid the rules but cost far more computation. TDLP aims to keep the speed while learning the matching from data.

TDLP treats each frame's matching as link prediction: it predicts the correct continuation of every track among the new detections. It works mainly from box geometry, with optional pose and appearance cues, and stays modular. On multiple benchmarks it beats leading systems of both kinds, and a detailed comparison shows link prediction outperforms metric-learning matching, mainly with mixed feature types.
arxiv-2512-22305:
Sultan Amed, Chan Yu Hang, and Sayantan Banerjee present PDx, a system that keeps credit risk models fresh after deployment. Lenders forecast each borrower's probability of default, but models trained once quietly decay as borrower behavior shifts, and many institutions struggle to move models into production and maintain them. PDx wraps the model in a full machine learning operations pipeline with continuous monitoring, retraining, and validation.

A champion-challenger scheme regularly recalibrates candidate models on the latest data and promotes the best by out-of-time validation. Across peer-to-peer, business, and auto loan datasets, tree-based groups classified defaulters best but needed frequent updates, while linear models and neural networks degraded faster. The authors target short-term, small-ticket digital lending, where behavior changes fastest.
arxiv-2512-22705:
Ahmed Abdullah, Sana Fatima, and Haroon Mahmood present GHaLIB, a multilingual system for detecting hope speech, the encouraging counterpart of hate speech that natural language processing has mostly ignored. Research concentrates on English, leaving low-resource languages like Urdu without tools for fostering positive online discussion. The authors focus on Urdu while testing whether proven transformer architectures transfer to this kinder classification task.

They fine-tuned pretrained multilingual models, XLM-RoBERTa, mBERT, EuroBERT, and UrduBERT, with simple preprocessing. On the PolyHope-M 2025 benchmark, the system reached an F1 score above ninety-five percent for Urdu binary classification and about sixty-five percent for the harder multi-class version. Spanish, German, and English results were similarly competitive, suggesting current multilingual models can serve low-resource communities for hope speech detection.
arxiv-2512-22905:
Kai Liu and a large team introduce JavisGPT, a multimodal language model that both understands and creates videos with sound. Earlier systems handled silent video or treated audio as an afterthought, so keeping speech, effects, and picture in step was hard. JavisGPT links an encoder, a large language model, and a pretrained audio-video diffusion generator through a fusion module designed around synchronization.

Training proceeds in three stages, moving from general multimodal pretraining through audio-video fine-tuning to large-scale instruction tuning. For the last stage the team built JavisInst-Omni, a dataset of more than two hundred thousand dialogues about audio-video content, curated with GPT-4o. On benchmarks for joint audio-video understanding and generation, JavisGPT outperformed existing multimodal models, with the clearest gains in complex scenes where sound and image must stay tightly synchronized over time.
arxiv-2512-23305:
Yongbin Du and Xiangdong Zhang compute how acoustic black holes respond to being disturbed. Acoustic black holes are fluid systems where sound cannot escape a region, mimicking event horizons in the laboratory. Their tidal response is summarized by Love numbers, borrowed from gravitational physics. The authors study static perturbations carried by a scalar field and by a Dirac field, in both four-dimensional and three-dimensional versions of the geometry.

Demanding regularity at the horizon and matching to large-distance behavior, they extract the mode ratio defining the Love number. In the four-dimensional case the scalar Love number is nonzero, while the fermionic ones collapse into a clean universal power law. In three dimensions the scalar field develops logarithms that make its Love number vanish for even modes but not odd ones. The contrast between integer and half-integer spin responses is the main lesson for analogue gravity.
arxiv-2512-23405:
Nathan Buskulic and three co-authors build theory for learning to solve blind inverse problems, where signal and measurement process are partly unknown. Blindness creates identifiability traps and symmetric duplicate solutions that break methods designed for known operators, yet data-driven solvers perform well in practice with little theory and little clarity. In imaging, blindness often means tuning the device, so guarantees matter. The authors work inside the framework of linear minimum mean square estimators.

Within that framework they derive closed forms for the optimal estimators and extend classical recovery results to the blind setting. They show matches with tailored Tikhonov regularization whose structure reflects the distributions of signal, noise, and operator. Error is shown to vanish as noise and operator randomness shrink under a source condition. Finite-sample bounds quantify how learned estimators depend on noise, conditioning, and sample count. Experiments confirm the predictions.
arxiv-2512-23805:
Lars van der Laan and Nathan Kallus fix a quiet flaw in fitted Q-evaluation, a standard way to judge a decision policy from logged data. The method repeatedly regresses Bellman targets onto a function class, but under distribution shift that process can fail to converge even when the true value function is representable. The authors trace the instability to geometry: ordinary regression measures error in the norm of the data-gathering distribution, which need not preserve the Bellman operator's contraction.

Their repair changes only the regression weights, weighting by the target policy's discounted occupancy ratio so the projection norm matches the target dynamics. Exact weighting restores contraction and removes the usual need for Bellman completeness. They derive finite-sample guarantees with estimated weights and misspecified classes, and pair the method with fitted occupancy-ratio evaluation for an end-to-end guarantee under coverage assumptions.
arxiv-2512-24005:
Brijesh Kumar Jha, Subhra Sankar Dhar, and Akash Ashirbad Panda study a hard estimation problem. The setting is random equations driven by Lévy noise. Such noise includes sudden jumps. Only sparse sample paths are observed. Dense recordings are not available.

Given a set of sparsely seen curves, they build least squares estimates. Three unknown parts of the model are estimated. They are the drift term and the diffusion term. The jump term is the third. The authors derive how fast these estimates converge. Extra material adds two checks on the theory. One applies the method to a benchmark dataset of curves. The other is a small simulation study. The work serves readers who model jumpy processes from rare observations.
arxiv-2512-24305: R D Hazeltine constructs a coordinate system fitted to a magnetic mirror field. The field is given in advance and is cylindrically symmetric. Rather than forcing standard coordinates onto that geometry, the coordinates are built to match the field itself. The note is very brief and purely constructive: it presents the coordinate system and its fit to the symmetric mirror geometry.
arxiv-2512-24705:
Monika Schleier-Smith offers lecture notes on joining atomic spins to light inside optical cavities for quantum measurement, simulation, and computing. Many atoms coupled to one spread-out light mode form the central system. The notes build from basics: light imprints information on atoms, and atoms imprint information back on light.

That two-way link enables quantum non-demolition measurements, engineered nonclassical states, and photon-mediated interactions between distant atoms. Collective spin models come first, with entanglement-enhanced measurement, then richer many-body physics using space-time control or several cavity modes. Students and researchers get a guided path into cavity quantum electrodynamics and its uses.
arxiv-2601-00105:
Muhammad U Nasir, Yuchen Li, Steven James, and Julian Togelius present Mortar, a system that invents game mechanics on its own. Their 2026 study notes that mechanics, the rules governing play, are normally crafted slowly by expert designers. Mortar pairs a quality-diversity search algorithm with a large language model to propose many varied mechanics, then builds complete games mixing new mechanics with archived ones through tree search.

Each mechanic is scored by how much it helps a game preserve skill ordering, meaning stronger players reliably beat weaker ones. The authors report the resulting games look diverse and playable, and that evolved mechanics raise the skill-ordering score. Ablation tests check what each component contributes, and a user study gathers human judgments of the games. For automatic game design, Mortar shows a workable loop where invented rules are judged not by novelty alone but by whether they make skill matter.
arxiv-2601-00405:
Dmitri E Kharzeev presents a set of lectures arguing that quantum entanglement is a unifying base for both statistical physics and high-energy physics. The lectures were given at a 2025 summer school in the Tatra mountains of Poland. His central notion is a maximal entanglement limit, reached at long times or high energies, in which the phases of quantum states can no longer be observed.

In that limit, reduced descriptions of a system take a thermal form, and probability-based accounts appear without assuming randomness. Kharzeev draws out results for the parton picture of matter, for how confining strings break up, and for collisions at high energy. The small-x behavior of structure functions also follows, in his account, from entanglement and Hilbert space geometry.
arxiv-2601-00505:
Mario de Lucio, Pavlos Vlachos, and Hector Gomez model how electric charge affects the fate of antibody drugs injected under the skin. Monoclonal antibodies are large protein medicines, and after a subcutaneous injection they must travel through tissue, bind their targets, and enter circulation. Charge shapes each of those steps, yet it is hard to observe directly.

The authors build a mathematical and computational model grounded in the Nernst-Planck equations and porous media flow, following two antibodies with different electric properties. They vary buffer acidity, body mass index, injection depth, and drug concentration, then compare the simulations with published experimental data. The study maps how formulation and patient factors steer short-term transport and longer-term binding and absorption.
arxiv-2601-00905:
Eliot Park, Abhi Kumar, and Pranav Rajpurkar test whether vision-language models can decide what is recyclable, a judgment the public routinely gets wrong. Sorting an item correctly depends on context: what it is made of, whether it is dirty or damaged, and what the local rules allow. The study evaluates three leading commercial models on a curated image dataset.

Models had to match items to appropriate bins, including judging whether an item would physically fit. Harder scenarios adjusted the location's guidelines, added contamination or structural damage, and used objects made of several materials. The findings map where image-based reasoning already handles everyday recycling decisions well and where contextual intelligence still falls short, a practical audit of AI assistants for household sustainability questions.
arxiv-2601-01205:
Ziwen Fu, Qu-Zhi Li, and Jun Wang compute how pions and kaons, two light particles, scatter off each other at low energy. They use lattice quantum chromodynamics, which simulates the strong force on a grid of points in space and time. Their setup uses three flavors of quarks at their true masses, on a fine grid, and measures the pair's energy levels in one still frame and six moving frames.

From those levels, standard formulas give the scattering phase shifts, which sum up how the particles deflect each other. The team extracts the scattering length, the effective range, and a shape parameter for the gentlest wave pattern. The numbers match their own analytic predictions from chiral perturbation theory, as well as experiments and earlier studies.
