The result abstracts a classic extremal-length minimization method of Weber and Wolf. Such frames help geometers build surfaces with tightly controlled analytic data.
arxiv-2603-02005:
Wendi Wang, Jiaxi Yang, Yongkang Du, and Lu Lin debias generated graphs by asking a counterfactual question. Their 2026 work targets graph diffusion models, which can inherit and amplify topology bias from traits like gender or region. Fair generators so far need full labels or joint updates of structure and attributes, which limits general use.

Their model, FairGDiff, asks whether the graph would change if a sensitive trait were different. A causal model links sensitive traits, biased link formation, and the generated structure. The counterfactual answer yields an unbiased treatment estimate folded into both diffusion directions. Generated graphs then stand independent of sensitive traits while keeping structural integrity. Wide tests on real data show a better fairness-utility trade-off than prior fair generators, with scalability intact.
arxiv-2603-02105:
Dhrumil Bhatt, Anakha Kurup, and R. C. Mala present a routing protocol that keeps smart grid sensor networks alive under jamming. Their 2026 protocol, DAMCR, targets reliability, adaptability, and energy efficiency across grid and industrial networks. Radios must hop technologies while attackers try to block the spectrum.

Chaotic frequency hopping spreads signals to resist jamming and add physical-layer security. Link-adaptive power control tunes transmission power to live link quality and remaining node energy. Priority-aware classification separates routine monitoring traffic from urgent fault and protection messages. Simulations mix LoRa, Wi-Fi, and dual-radio nodes under several fading models in a standard tool. Delivery stays near perfect across scenarios, with low latency held even under controlled jamming attacks, beating static single-radio rivals.
arxiv-2603-02305:
Bharath Sambasivam, Kyle Sherbert, Karunya Shirali, and colleagues present a quantum algorithm for time evolution in this 2026 paper. Simulating how a quantum system changes over time is a core task for quantum computers. Their method, TIMES-ADAPT, works inside a small low-energy corner of the full system. A trained unitary first untangles the system's energy states within that corner.

Fixed-depth circuits then carry out the time evolution, with time as a simple dial setting. Two versions cover starting states given in energy terms or in raw qubit terms. Tests use variants of a standard spin model, the Heisenberg XXZ chain. Uses include wave packet motion and energy transport in spin systems. Fixed depth at any time point could ease near-term hardware limits.
arxiv-2603-02405:
Philipp Schröer and Joost-Pieter Katoen present one approach for many goals on random programs in this 2026 paper. Probabilistic programs mix code with chance, and analysts ask varied questions about them. Each question, or objective, once needed its own reasoning machinery. Their trick adds a single reward statement to the language.

A program transformation then applies a chosen function to the total reward. The transformation works from step-by-step differences in reward, keeping it incremental. Moments, threshold chances, budget overruns, and generating functions all become expressible. Every objective reduces to one existing reasoning method for weakest preconditions. The team automated the check in a deductive verifier. Example programs show the single approach handling many objectives cleanly.
arxiv-2603-02605:
Yun-Wen Mao and Roman Krems optimize molecules with very little data in this 2026 paper. Chemical space is vast and discrete, so finding molecules with target properties is hard. Standard machine learning optimizers need large data sets to model that space. Their Bayesian framework works inside a subspace of well over a hundred thousand molecules.

Fewer than two thousand training points suffice for precise optimization. The key is a low-dimensional descriptor that encodes real physics of each molecule. A reliable inverse map turns optimized descriptor points back into valid molecules. On a standard benchmark, entropy targets were hit every time in their tests. Most runs needed under a thousand evaluations to succeed. Zero-point energy targets also scored high success for larger molecules.
arxiv-2603-03205:
Aradhye Agarwal, Gurdit Siyan, Yash Pandya, and colleagues teach tool-using agents to pause, check, and sometimes refuse. A chat model's worst slip is a bad sentence, but an agent's single misstep, opening files or typing credentials, can cause irreversible harm. Their 2026 framework, MOSAIC, makes the safety decision an explicit, learnable step.

Inference follows a loop: plan, check, then act or refuse and replan. Training uses preference comparisons between whole trajectories, avoiding the need for labeled steps and catching safety contrasts that single scores miss. Across three model families and fresh benchmarks covering harmful tasks, prompt injection, and privacy leaks, harmful behavior fell by up to half. Refusals of injected attacks rose, leakage dropped, and benign task performance held or improved.
arxiv-2603-03405:
Shion Matsumoto and three colleagues introduce a new free-energy functional for learning and inference. Two classic objectives, forward and reverse KL divergence, push models in opposite directions, and averages alone cannot explain why. Their 2026 construction, the Surprisal-Rényi Free Energy, is built from log-moments of the likelihood ratio and sits outside the usual family of divergences.

Both KL divergences return as singular endpoint limits of the new functional. Expansions near those limits expose the variance of the log-likelihood ratio as a first-order correction, revealing an explicit mean-variance trade-off. The functional is also the unique minimizer of a weighted sum of KL terms, a Gibbs-style characterization. Finally, it directly controls large deviations of excess code length, giving a precise minimum description length reading. The results clarify the geometry behind the two KL regimes.
arxiv-2603-03505:
Shang Wu and eight colleagues teach a system to rewrite video prompts so the physics comes out right. Leading text-to-video generators make gorgeous clips that break physical law. The authors show the fault lies in thin prompts, not the generators: hand-added physics detail reliably fixes the output, but hand-writing does not scale. Their 2026 framework, PhyPrompt, automates that expert rewriting with reinforcement learning.

Stage one fine-tunes a language model on physics-focused reasoning examples, teaching it to weave in motion and force detail while keeping user intent. Stage two applies group-based policy optimization under a shifting reward: meaning fidelity first, physical commonsense increasingly later. The seven-billion-parameter system beat far larger commercial models on joint success, improving physics and meaning together rather than trading one for the other. Gains also transferred, untouched, to three other video architectures.
arxiv-2603-04005: Wang and others propose a training-free diffusion method for traversing the rate-distortion-perception tradeoff. The tradeoff captures lossy compression limits across bitrate, fidelity, and quality, yet neural methods usually sit at fixed points needing retraining. The method combines reverse channel coding with a score-scaled flow decoder built on pretrained diffusion models. Theory proves the decoder optimal for distortion-perception under white Gaussian noise, and the full method optimal in the Gaussian case. Experiments confirm flexible navigation of the tradeoff, offering a real route to adaptive compression.
arxiv-2603-04205: Zhou and others present Real5-OmniDocBench, a full-scale real reconstruction benchmark for robust document parsing. While vision-language models score near-perfectly on digital document benchmarks like OmniDocBench, yet their results in the unpredictable real world stays largely unknown without managed yet realistic evaluations. They present the first benchmark performing a full-scale one-to-one real recreation of the entire OmniDocBench v1.5 with 1,355 images across five real-world scenarios: Scanning, Skew, Warping, Screen-Photography, and Illumination.
arxiv-2603-04505: Parente and colleagues explain why cosmic dust warms with redshift. Far infrared galaxy emission hints dust temperature rises with redshift, though sparse sampling limits high redshift constraints. A semi-analytic galaxy model with dust, post-processed by radiative transfer, predicts the same rise, matching observations broadly. Feature analysis names star formation surface density and dust to gas ratio as main drivers, tracing radiation intensity and warm cloud depth. Galaxies with dense star formation and low dust to gas ratios run warmer, while grain size and chemistry matter little.
arxiv-2603-04705: He and colleagues guide object search with language and gesture. Robots helping humans in open-world settings must parse vague orders to locate objects. Base models excel at multi-mode grounding but lack doubt handling for long-horizon tasks. POMDPs offer planning under uncertainty but support limited modes. LEGS-POMDP joins language, gesture, and views, tracking doubt over target ID and place. In tests, multi-mode fusion beats rivals at 89 percent success. Real-world tests on a four-legged robot prove robust sensing and doubt cuts under vague orders.
arxiv-2603-05305: Kang Luo and team offer Fusion4CA, built on BEVFusion to exploit visual input for bird's-eye-view finding from LiDAR and RGB. Current methods over-rely on LiDAR with insufficient RGB exploration. Fusion4CA aligns image features against 3D shape contrastively and adds a camera branch mining RGB information. An off-the-shelf mind adapter exploits pretrained weights, and coordinate attention boosts fusion. On nuScenes it reaches 69.7% mean average precision in only 6 training epochs with few added parameters, beating a 20-epoch baseline. Simulated lunar tests validate effectiveness and generalization.
arxiv-2603-05805: Chaudhari and team compare mixture-of-experts and dense models using cross-codes, a sparse auto-encoder version for several firing spaces jointly. Five-layer dense and expert models with equal active settings train on 1 billion tokens of code, science, and stories. BatchTopK cross-codes with set shared features explain about 87 percent of fraction spread and expose org gaps. Expert models learn much fewer unique traits than dense models. Expert traits fire more thickly than shared ones, while dense traits fire less thickly, so experts focus where dense models spread.
arxiv-2603-06005: Xu finds all delta bi-derivs for Witt, Virasoro, and W(a,b) systems, plus their all central spreads with a tilde. Finding the complete set of such bi-derivs across these systems gives a full sorting for each member of the family. The paper then gives some uses of these findings, showing how the sorting results can be used beyond the finding itself.
arxiv-2603-06405: Ali and colleagues formalize tag allocation by an influence provider for sellers with budgets and influence requirements. Their outdoor-advertising regret problem seeks allocations meeting demand within budget at low total regret. They prove it NP-hard and inapproximable within any constant factor, with a regret model that is neither monotone nor submodular, so plain greedy allocation fails. A fairness-aware round-robin greedy method balances advertisers while cutting regret, aided by randomized greedy and local search variants. Real trajectory and billboard tests support the methods.
arxiv-2603-06605: Lee and team restore time and variable priors in the STAR Set Transformer for digital health records. For uneven time series, input layout matters as models split events, not slicing time. STAR adds soft attention biases: a temporal nearness penalty with timescales and a field-type affinity from a feature-fit matrix, tested across fusion schedules. On three intensive care prediction tasks, STAR-Set beats prior set baselines and regular-grid and event-time grid approaches.
arxiv-2603-06705: Stiefenhofer recasts Constructal evolution as a nonsmooth system that changes over time, not a static design choice. Flow layouts become states of a Filippov frame on a compact set, where one-way limits create switch lines. A loss rule acts as a check for steadiness, and a tightening rule yields one rest point. Every path converges to it fast, and the classic area-to-point ladder appears as sliding sets.
arxiv-2603-07105: Bavuma and colleagues extend the Peter-Weyl theorem to a wider class of groups. They start from classical representation theory for compact groups, then focus on locally compact groups that hold large nontrivial compact open subgroups. For such groups, they show functions can be approximated by others that locally match the classic representative functions. The result widens a core tool of harmonic analysis to settings where compactness holds only in part.
arxiv-2603-07205: Yu and colleagues present a general nonperturbative Hamiltonian framework linking finite-volume lattice QCD spectra to experimental scattering observables. To demonstrate it, they extract omega meson resonance parameters by jointly analyzing isoscalar three-pion and isovector two-pion systems. The Hamiltonian unifies single-particle omega, two-particle rho-pion, and three-particle pion dynamics in one unitary formalism. Fitting leading lattice spectra at pion masses of 208 and 305 MeV, they describe the lattice spectra accurately and obtain robust rho and omega pole positions.
arxiv-2603-07305: Sun and colleagues propose a crop-yield forecaster built to hold up across wide regions and many years. A new backbone tracks both daily growth rhythms and year-to-year dependencies, while a retrieval step adapts the model to new places. Retrieved past cases are then corrected for cross-year bias that the inputs cannot explain. On county-level corn data the framework beats varied baselines and proves sturdier under spatial variation.
arxiv-2603-07705: Thoma, Piliouras and Marris propose differentiable equilibrium blocks for deep incentive design across economics and computer science. Designing multi-agent dealings with good outcomes is hard due to hard math, many answers and wobble. Their game-free blocks plug into a smooth framework, and one neural network trained per task with a unified pipeline solves full instance ranges. Three tasks validate the approach: inverse equilibrium problems, contract design and machine scheduling.
arxiv-2603-07805: Wu and colleagues benchmark three formula-based frameworks, MODNet, CrabNet, and a Magpie random forest, for battery traits from the Battery Explorer dataset. They test accuracy, plot numerical features with 2D maps, and score results. CrabNet beats the other models across all tests, checked by bootstrap retests and two cross-check plans against a baseline on unseen data. Blind grouping with t-SNE and DBSCAN shows tidy groupings without labels, and the final model beats controls as an oracle for electrode formula screening.
arxiv-2603-08205: Mirian presents a design study for a Transverse Deflecting Structure for longitudinal beam checks at the DALI facility. The structure gives the electron bunch a time-varying sideways kick, enabling direct measurement of the bunch profile along its length. With a dispersive spectrometer section, it also rebuilds the phase space along the bunch. The report reviews how RF deflecting cavities work, covering the sideways kick, time-to-space mapping, and how bunch length relates to cavity settings.
arxiv-2603-08805: Tiyasa Kar and colleagues build a general background-field recipe for deep inelastic dijet production. Feynman propagators become path-ordered exponentials that spread onto any contours of many pieces to yield gauge-covariant operators. The recipe gives the dijet cross section for any kinematics, recovers known back-to-back results, and links the eikonal and back-to-back regimes with a numeric map.
arxiv-2603-09205: Benjamin Reichman and colleagues study emotion as a hidden factor that shapes how language models attend to and reason over text. Prior work mostly treated emotion as a label to predict, as in sentiment tasks. They show attention measures such as locality and entropy shift with emotional tone and track question-answering scores. Their AURA-QA dataset gives balanced, human-written passages for controlled tests, and a training regularizer that limits emotion-linked drift improves reading scores.
arxiv-2603-09605: Xufeng Yang and colleagues propose Nemo, a flash cache design that cuts write amplification for tiny-object workloads on log-structured devices. Even on advanced zoned or flexible-placement SSDs, application-level amplification dominates over device-level costs. Nemo raises the hash collision probability in a set-associative cache to improve set fill rates. A bloom filter based index keeps memory overhead low, and hybrid hotness tracking holds the miss ratio down, hitting low amplification, high memory efficiency, and low misses together.
arxiv-2603-09805: Qing-Bo Ma and a large team ask how a galaxy's past star forming bursts shape the 21-cm signal from the epoch of reionisation. Most models smooth that history out, even though mergers and feedback cause bursts and quiet spells. Feeding a detailed galaxy model into their pipeline yields slightly larger, warmer ionised zones than a steady rate gives. Older stellar mixes make smaller zones at fixed mass.
arxiv-2603-09905: Ethan Pinarski and coauthors check how cleanly the ODIN survey picks out Lyman alpha emitting galaxies at three redshifts. ODIN images wide sky areas through narrow band filters tuned to thin cosmic slices. Long DESI spectra confirm most bright candidates, with high success at each target redshift. The main impostors are active galactic nuclei and lower redshift line emitters, while oxygen emitters are almost fully removed.
arxiv-2603-10205: Rick Oerder and Jan Hamaekers introduce Flexible Cutoff Learning for machine learning interatomic potentials whose cutoff radii can change after training. Standard potentials fix the cutoff during training, locking in one accuracy cost balance. Their models train with cutoffs sampled randomly per atom, so deployment can tune each atom's radius to the task. On molecular crystals, optimised cutoffs cut compute cost by over half with almost no rise in force error.
arxiv-2603-10305: Savannah L Ferretti and co-authors add structure to machine learning of nonlocal climate processes, so what the model learns stays readable. Their data-driven integration kernels first gather each field over space, height, or time with learnable weighting functions, and only then apply a local nonlinear map. Each kernel can be read as a pattern showing which places, levels, and past times matter most. On South Asian monsoon rain, kernel models nearly match baseline skill with far fewer trained weights, curbing overfitting risk.
arxiv-2603-10405: Lin Li, Tuo Lin, Yiwen Chen, and Xin M Tu study exposure time effects in stepped wedge trials where a delayed outcome is cut off by administrative censoring. Late-crossing clusters face the heaviest censoring, yet only they show long exposure times, so the design couples the two problems. Using an always recorded short term surrogate, each effect is identified through a bridge relation. They derive an efficiency bound that doubles as a design criterion, then give a cross fitted estimator with proven asymptotic normality.
arxiv-2603-10505: Hyungjoo Chae, Jungsoo Park, and Alan Ritter present VeriEnv, a framework that clones real websites into synthetic training grounds for web agents. Real sites are risky to explore, rarely reset cleanly, and seldom give checkable feedback, which holds back agent learning. VeriEnv uses language models as environment builders, making fully working copies with controlled internal access through a Python SDK. Agents can then invent their own tasks with rewards that code can verify, no heuristic judges needed. Agents trained this way generalized to unseen sites and improved as environments multiplied.
arxiv-2603-10705: Yuyao Ge and co-authors propose PRISM-Delta, a method for prompt highlighting that steers a large language model toward marked spans. Older key-editing methods often extract directions that capture shared structure, not the difference between relevant and irrelevant context. Their method decomposes the gap between positive and negative cross-covariance matrices, keeping discriminative energy and dropping shared directions. Each attention head gets a soft importance weight, and the approach extends to value representations. Tests on four benchmarks and five models matched or beat the best prior method.
arxiv-2603-11205: Lin Zhang and coauthors ask whether a language model trained purely on text can help find the fake words hidden inside partially doctored speech, where only specific words were edited. They build a speech language model that localizes fake words by next-token prediction and test it on two partially fake speech datasets. The model often leans on editing-style patterns learned in training, especially word-level polarity swaps. This helps in-domain but leaves open how to generalize to editing styles it has never seen.
arxiv-2603-11505: Azimi and co-authors present Gen-Fab, a model that predicts how photonic designs come out of fabrication. Etch errors and corner rounding vary by feature size and shape, so outcomes vary too. A conditional GAN on Pix2Pix, it takes a design layout and paints varied SEM-like images, with a noise vector enabling the one-to-many spread. Against three U-Net baselines on unseen structures, it wins on accuracy and uncertainty. Its IoU reaches 89.8 percent, and its outputs track the real outcome spread best.
arxiv-2603-11805: Elmakais and Glickman ask whether Israel's 255 municipalities split into cantons that vote alike. They group neighbouring towns to maximize shared political lean, testing four clustering algorithms, four feature sets, three distance metrics, and six values of K: 264 setups in all. BlocShares with agglomerative clustering scores highest on silhouette, at 0.987 with cosine distance. An NMF and Louvain pairing balances sameness, quality, and readability best, with stable borders across five elections. Its five-canton map shows a mixed center-right core around Tel Aviv and a right-wing belt from Jerusalem southward.
arxiv-2603-12205: Koliesnikova and Ramière speed up iterative solvers for frictionless contact problems, free of parameter limits. Their frame splits each step in two: solve displacement for given contact forces, then update the forces. Only standard stiffness systems appear, so no saddle-point matrices need special handling. Uzawa and penalty splitting schemes both fall out of the same frame. A crossed-secant acceleration then lifts the slow fixed-point rate sharply. Tests on 3D academic and industrial cases show the practical gains clearly.
arxiv-2603-12905: Joana Reuss and co-authors extend Dirichlet Prior Augmentation for few-shot crop-type classification under real label skew. Farm data are scarce and long-tailed, while few-shot training sets are often balanced by hand. That mismatch shifts the prior and hurts generalization in the field. DirPA simulates varied priors during training to blunt the skew. This study widens the test scope to several European Union countries. DirPA held up across regions, stabilized training, and lifted per-class scores.
arxiv-2603-13005: Timothée Dao and co-authors demonstrate a quantum extreme learning machine that resists concentration effects on real hardware. Quantum reservoir methods promise rich features, yet noise and concentration can erase input distinctions at scale. Their system ran on IBM Quantum machines with up to 124 qubits and over 5,000 two-qubit gates. A tuning strategy tracks observable spread, capacity, and task scores to find robust settings. Local eigentask analysis then picks features cheaply. Scores rivaled top classical baselines on forecasting and image tasks.
arxiv-2603-13105: Zhicheng Zhu and Adrien Busnot Laurent introduce aromatic and clumped multi-indices for the study of volume-preserving methods. Butcher forests grow into aromatic and clumped forms that matter for such methods. The new objects cut the problem down to one dimension while keeping much structure. Standard multi-indices lose that structure by contrast. The authors give the algebraic frame: pre-Lie-Rinehart, Hopf algebroid, and Hopf algebra forms. A Hopf embedding to the BCK algebra is also generalized.
arxiv-2603-13505: Fernando Delbianco tests the exclusion restriction with a single instrument when a latent factor confounds the data. With one instrument, the restriction cannot be tested from second moments, and naive tests fail. If the hidden common cause has non-Gaussian parts, fourth-order cumulants make the test possible, he shows. His scalar is zero when exclusion holds and non-zero when it does not. A companion statistic grades how strong identification is. Simulations show correct size, where the naive OLS test always rejects.
arxiv-2603-13605: Rana Shahout, Hayder Tirmazi, Minlan Yu, and Michael Mitzenmacher introduce Orla, a library for serving LLM-based multi-agent systems. Agentic applications combine many LLM inference steps, tool calls, and heterogeneous infrastructure. Developers now compose orchestration code, serving engines, and tool logic by hand. Orla separates request execution from workflow-level policy as a serving layer above existing inference engines. A stage mapper assigns stages to models and backends, an orchestrator schedules them, and a memory manager handles KV cache state. A customer support workflow demonstrates the system.
arxiv-2603-14105: Wu and Arias build a first-principles theory of vacuum Wannier functions for scattering and photoemission at solid surfaces. The theory unites tight-binding and nearly-free-electron views across the solid-vacuum boundary. Analytic results for standard Wannier functions in any dimension guide a 3D close-packing rule, checked in numerics. That rule lets them build full Born-series scattering states on a dense k-space grid. Tests on graphene and hexagonal boron nitride show fixes beyond the first-Born approximation, with no fitted vacuum potentials.
arxiv-2603-14405: Lee, Kim, and Hwang merge single-modality biology models into one multimodal model with ES-Merging. Standard merging picks blend weights from parameter-space rules that ignore what each model knows. Their method reads signals from the embedding space instead. Coarse signals set layer-wise blend weights, and fine signals set element-wise ones. The two combine for a fuller estimate. Tests show better cross-modal reasoning and better retention of single-modal knowledge than prior merging methods.
arxiv-2603-14805: Bakal frames AI Skills as the base unit for enterprise knowledge in agentic software work. Firms hold key know-how in documents written for human eyes. Agents and new hires then guess, err and tax senior staff. Knowledge Activation packs skills into Atomic Knowledge Units with governance built in. Each unit states what to act on, which tools to use and what limits bind. Units link into a graph that agents can walk. Engineers get grounded guidance without rebuilding context each time, Bakal argues.
arxiv-2603-14905: Avdizhiyan, Razdolski and Bykov steer light-matter effects in tiny metal cavities with hot electrons. Laser pulses inject fast hot electrons at the metal surface. That flow shifts how the cavity traps and boosts light. Strong laser sources often damage samples before such effects show. Their setup dodges lasting damage by design. Simulations match a simple model of the time-linked response. Heat-driven shifts map across a wide range of settings. Fast control of quantum emitters gains a path, they argue.
arxiv-2603-15005: Znotins pretrains a suite of encoder models built just for Latvian, a language with little training text. The suite covers RoBERTa, DeBERTaV3, and ModernBERT designs, plus long-context variants. He tests them on a broad set of Latvian language benchmarks. The best model, lv-deberta-base, has 111 million parameters. It beats larger multilingual models and earlier Latvian encoders. All models and test resources are released for public use.
arxiv-2603-15105: Salman and co-authors present DD-SAF, a sparse adaptive filter that uses error memory to spot active coefficients early. Zero-attracting filters penalize small coefficients, but young active ones also start small and get punished. Their filter tracks how often each coefficient feeds the error over time. A coefficient that keeps appearing is likely active, so its penalty lifts. Theory shows the same stability as standard least-mean-square filtering with better steady-state error. Simulations confirm faster convergence and lower deviation than rival methods.
arxiv-2603-15205: Balfagon examines what a possible 20 GeV gamma-ray excess would imply for CET Omega, an informational extension of quantum field theory and cosmology. The theory adds a small, state-dependent correction to early-Universe radiation density. The correction is negligible at nucleosynthesis and recombination but matters at WIMP freeze-out. Numerical solutions show percent-level shifts in relic abundance and smaller changes to the gamma-ray flux shape. A wide parameter range stays consistent with Planck, BBN, and BAO data while predicting signs that future missions could see.
arxiv-2603-15505: Da Hora and Simas test whether oscillons still trace back to Q-balls when the field has non-canonical kinematics. Their model uses one real scalar field with a generalized kinetic term. A renormalization group perturbation expansion, carried to third order, says the link survives the odd kinematics. Three test cases match numerical runs well at small and moderate amplitudes. At larger amplitudes, a two-Q-ball seed captures the modulated profile. A phi-sixth case lands in a different universality class, explored at fifth order.
arxiv-2603-15905: Bogdan recovers synthesizer settings from recorded sound with evolution search. Note tools capture pitch but drop the timbre that names an instrument. His Instrumental system couples a 28-parameter subtractive synth to CMA-ES. A blended perceptual loss guides the search without gradients. Terms track mel spectra, spectral centroid, and MFCC distance. Matching loss hit 2.09 on real recorded audio. Eight improvement hypotheses faced systematic tests. Only parametric EQ boosting helped in a clear way. More parameters alone did not help matching.
arxiv-2603-16005: Gonzalez-Sanz and Avella Medina extend a breakdown result for optimal transport maps. Breakdown asks how much bad data can wreck a transport map. Recent work tied the map's breakdown point to Tukey depth. That tie was shown for the squared Euclidean cost alone. Their note covers general convex cost functions instead. The cost choice leaves the breakdown point unchanged, they prove. All transport-based quantiles then share the same strong breakdown trait. The result closes the characterization for wide cost classes.
arxiv-2603-16105: Monaco and co-authors pick compression calibration data by word frequency shape. Pruning and quantization lean on the calibration set they train against. Model-based pickers cost too much for huge models and data. Their ZipCal strategy chases lexical diversity under Zipf patterns. The method reads data traits only, never model signals. Uniform random sampling loses to ZipCal across pruning tests. A top perplexity-based picker only ties ZipCal on task scores. ZipCal runs about 240 times faster on average. Linear cost keeps the curation step cheap at scale.
arxiv-2603-16205: Monter and co-authors study how to move trapped colloidal particles with the least energy. The particles interact, and each sits in its own optical trap. For quiet systems with conservative forces, the best paths are straight lines at steady speed. The shape of the force does not change this. Strong noise or nonconservative forces break the rule. With hydrodynamic coupling, curved paths won in tests. They exploit flows the particles make together.
arxiv-2603-16305: Majumder, Dutta, and Nandi study time lags tied to slow oscillations in a black hole binary. The system is GRS 1915+105, watched by AstroSat for 441 ks over three years. The team found the oscillations in four variability classes. Classes switched within a few hours as the flow changed shape. Frequencies ran from 1.38 to 7.38 Hz, and soft lags of 1.59 to 13.49 ms appeared at all frequencies. No sign flip showed near 2 Hz, unlike older RXTE results.
arxiv-2603-16405: Zhang and co-authors revisit backdoor attacks on image segmentation models. Segmentation guides self-driving cars, yet its backdoor risks were understudied. Older work borrowed threat models from image classification. The team maps four broad attack vectors plus two fine-grained ones. Their BADSEG framework tunes triggers and label tricks for each case. Attacks worked well across many architectures, including the Segment Anything Model. Six standard defenses failed to stop them reliably.
arxiv-2603-16505: Göß compares two ways to relax mixed-integer nonlinear programs. Relaxations swap a hard problem for an easier bound problem. Global parabolic relaxations use paraboloids as global bounds. Their one-shot computation can explode into an intractable model. Göß gives an iterative method that works where the old one failed. Tests then face PARA against piecewise linear relaxations. Piecewise wins when tolerance is loose. PARA wins as tolerance tightens. Sine constraints widen the PARA edge.
arxiv-2603-16805: Sun and co-authors ask whether each stem of a mixed audio track can carry its own watermark. Their setup embeds a distinct watermark in each stem, then mixes, separates, and decodes each output. A naive pairing of standard watermarking with off-the-shelf separation recovers bits poorly. Separation artifacts, it turns out, differ from generic distortions. The team therefore trains the watermarking with the separator inside the detection loop. On speech-plus-music and vocal-plus-accompaniment mixes, post-separation recovery improves a lot while sound quality holds up.
arxiv-2603-17105: Dumitru and Leustean apply proof mining to a viscosity type iteration in fixed point theory. Their target is the inexact generalized Halpern iteration, an extension of an iteration lately studied by Kanzow and Shehu. They obtain quantitative and qualitative results on asymptotic regularity and its T variant for this iteration. Special cases give matching results for the Kanzow-Shehu iteration and the sequential averaging method. For particular parameter choices, they compute explicit rates of regularity. In one case, the rates come out linear.
arxiv-2603-17205: Fang and co-authors present OPERA, a data pruning framework for adapting dense retrieval models to new domains. Not all training pairs help equally. Their static pruning keeps only high similarity query document pairs, which lifts ranking quality but can hurt recall. Their dynamic pruning instead adjusts sampling odds during training, favoring quality while keeping the full set reachable. Across eight datasets, dynamic pruning gave the best ranking and retrieval scores. It also reached standard fine tuning quality in under half the training time.
arxiv-2603-17505: Fathima and co-authors model light from double white-dwarf mergers that leave a neutron star. The flash comes from cooling ejecta plus spin-down power from the newborn star. Its strength hinges on the star's magnetic field and spin period. They simulate light curves in LSST bands across that parameter space. Reach runs from 30 to 820 megaparsecs in their estimates. Only high dipole factors stay visible once survey cadence counts.
arxiv-2603-17805: Damele proves a rigidity theorem for finite skew braces. A skew brace carries two group operations that interact through one shared rule. He looks at braces whose multiplicative group splits as a product of two non-abelian simple groups. In that case, the additive group can never be supersolvable, he shows. The result limits which group pairs a finite skew brace can join. Simple group structure on one side forces roughness on the other.
arxiv-2603-17905: Kamat and co-authors resolve a phase puzzle in the superconductor UTe2 with ultrasound. Two phase lines seemed to meet at a triple point, which thermodynamics forbids. Pulse-echo sound measures find a fresh boundary where order fades on cooling. The crossing point is thus tetracritical, not triple, they report. Past it, two order parameters merge into one multi-component state. Fierce rivalry between them explains the odd loss of order.
arxiv-2603-18005: Wischounig, Abdallah, and Jatowt survey negative sampling for dense information retrieval. They review 35 key papers and sort methods into random, mined, and synthetic groups. New LLM-driven ways to make negatives get full coverage, unlike past reviews. Each family is weighed on strength, compute cost, and ease of use. The survey ends with open problems and the promise of LLM-made synthetic data.
arxiv-2603-18105: Joshi and Bhand present an adaptive steganographic encryption framework for digital images. Fixed least-significant-bit embedding treats smooth and textured regions alike, raising distortion and detection risk. A Mamdani fuzzy system sets pixel-wise depth from one to three bits. Inputs are local entropy, edge strength, and payload pressure, computed to stay in sync after embedding. Argon2id and AES-256-GCM add payload secrecy and integrity on top.
arxiv-2603-18405: Ismailov, Silvestrov, and Al extend joint numerical radius results to the (f, delta) setting. Classical bounds for n-tuples of Hilbert space operators form the starting point. They derive new lower and upper bounds for this generalized joint radius. Sectorial operators receive special estimates in the new framework. The work adds diverse contributions to this branch of operator theory.
arxiv-2603-18605: Bizoń and Romańczukiewicz study how a soliton's internal mode slowly fades in a one-dimensional quadratic Klein-Gordon model. The soliton also carries an unstable mode. On a finely tuned set of starting data, that instability is suppressed. The internal mode then leaks energy into the continuum over long times. A cubic resonant approximation captures both the slow decay and the nonlinear frequency shift. The damping rate comes from a Fermi golden rule type coefficient, giving a precise account of the energy transfer.
arxiv-2603-18905: Moretto and co-authors give a steadier way to model faults and cracks in rock with mismatched grids. Their mortar method ties the two sides of a break with multiplier fields that stand for contact force. A simple choice for those fields breaks a key stability rule. They add a force-jump term whose scale is set by the method itself, with no user tuning. Tests show stable force profiles even when one side uses a much finer grid.
arxiv-2603-19005: Luo and co-authors benchmark AI agents and human-AI teams on field-specific data science tasks. Their AgentDS set holds seventeen challenges across six industries. They run an open contest with twenty-nine teams and eighty people. AI-only systems score below the top quarter of entrants. They lag most on domain reasoning, where field knowledge counts. The best entries come from people and AI working together. The team reads this as a case against full automation claims. Human skill stays central in such work, they argue.
arxiv-2603-19305: Bao and co-authors make humanoid robots move with agility while staying within physics limits. Motion models trained on human data often yield moves a robot cannot safely do. Their PhyGile system makes robot-native motion at test time, guided by physics-based prefixes. A tracking controller is first trained with a staged mix of experts. It is then tuned on the generated moves under those same prefixes. Tests off and on real robots show fast, stable motion. The loop cuts the gap between made and done moves.
arxiv-2603-19605: Kikuchi and co-authors study a sheared granular gas whose restitution depends on collision speed. The gas is made of hard spheres under steady shear. Using kinetic theory, they derive the shear viscosity of the gas. When restitution switches between two values with impact speed, viscosity traces an S-shaped curve. A jump in viscosity then appears between low- and high-shear regimes. Both regimes follow Bagnold-type scaling. The jump comes from kinetic effects alone, with no friction or jamming.
arxiv-2603-19905: Pichlmann and co-authors show that heat-flow curves can act as fingerprints for the strength of aluminum alloys. They aged four 6xxx alloys in varied ways, then ran calorimetry scans and tensile tests. Machine learning models trained on the scans predicted yield strength, tensile strength, and elongation well. The best model, Lasso, reached R squared values up to 0.93. On a fully unseen alloy, accuracy fell sharply. Adding just one or two anchor samples from that alloy largely restored it.
arxiv-2603-20005: Liu and co-authors present NEC-Diff, a diffusion system for filming motion in near darkness. Low light brings heavy noise and lost texture to normal cameras. Event cameras sense brightness changes and handle wide light ranges, so they can help. Past methods lean on events for texture but ignore noise in both signals. NEC-Diff joins RAW images with event data under a physics-based constraint. It estimates the signal quality of each source on the fly. Fusion then feeds only trusted cues into the diffusion process.
arxiv-2603-20105: Roy and co-authors give recursive language models a typed runtime based on lambda calculus. Long inputs strain the fixed context window of language models. Recursive models split the prompt and solve subproblems in pieces. Existing versions let the model write free control code in a read-eval-print loop. That freedom makes runs hard to verify or predict. The λ-RLM frame runs a small library of pre-verified combinators instead. Neural inference happens only on bounded leaf subproblems. It beat standard recursive models in 29 of 36 test comparisons.
arxiv-2603-20405: Baudart and co-authors report an experiment in AI-driven formal proof on Putnam problems. Claude Opus 4.6 worked with MCP tools built for the Rocq proof assistant. The tools follow a compile-first plan with interactive fallback. Running alone on an isolated machine, the agent proved 10 of 12 problems. It deployed 141 subagents over 17.7 hours of active compute. The run used about 1.9 billion tokens in total. All proofs from the experiment are publicly available.
arxiv-2603-20505: Habib and co-authors speed up counterfactual reasoning inside the ProbLog language. ProbLog handles uncertainty while staying declarative and interpretable. What-if reasoning, though, can be slow and unstable in accuracy. Their transformation builds Single World Intervention Programs from a ProbLog program. Clauses split into observed and fixed parts tied to the query. Counterfactuals then reduce to marginal inference over a simpler program. They prove correctness under weaker independence assumptions than before. Experiments show a 35% cut in inference time versus prior methods.
arxiv-2603-20605: Cui and Wu study a compound Poisson process that moves in jumps and drifts downward. They look at its finite trips away from zero. Each trip splits into a part above zero and a part below zero. The team asks how the lengths and heights of these parts relate. They prove both measures are strongly linked in the limit. The two parts also show a clear scale symmetry.
arxiv-2603-20805: Giannopoulos and co-authors present CollabORAN, a layered control design for open radio access networks. Control loops in O-RAN often run alone at one timescale each. Their design joins three app levels in one nested loop. The rApp sets traffic aware policy over minutes. The xApp assigns spectrum with a hypergraph coloring method each second. The dApp at the distributed unit enforces fairness in milliseconds. Simulations showed better fairness and less user starvation. Spectrum reuse stayed efficient in dense, shifting settings.
arxiv-2603-21005: Bates and co-authors study ties in prime races over function fields. The race compares counts of primes in distinct congruence classes modulo a polynomial. A tie means the counts are equal for infinitely many bounds. They give infinitely many examples where ties hold under congruence conditions on the bound. One proof uses the explicit formula with L-functions and a matrix form of Möbius inversion. Another uses an explicit bijection from a group action. The examples include characteristic two cases.
arxiv-2603-21205: Lopez-Rodriguez re-analyzes a claim that a PAH emission line in a nebula is polarized. These hydrocarbons trace star formation and gas content, and their polarization could probe magnetic fields. An earlier study reported about two percent polarization in the 11.3 micrometer line of the MWC 1080 nebula. Using the same CanariCam data, he measures a value consistent with zero. He shows the earlier result follows from oversubtracting a constant instrumental term. Current dust models agree with the null result.
arxiv-2603-21305: Zakariyya and co-authors present FedDP-STECAR, a privacy-preserving framework for federated video action recognition. Federated training avoids sharing raw video, but gradients can leak motion patterns, and full model syncs cost heavy bandwidth. Their method fine-tunes and perturbs only a small set of task relevant layers under differential privacy. Only those layers travel during aggregation, which cuts communication by over ninety nine percent. On UCF-101, federated training runs about forty eight percent faster while keeping strong accuracy.
arxiv-2603-21405: Nathwani and co-authors measure heat and charge flow in a thin film of NdNiO3, a perovskite oxide with a metal-insulator transition. Using frequency-domain thermoreflectance, they see a sharp change in out-of-plane thermal conductivity at the transition. A photoreflectance method shows a large change in carrier diffusivity too. Electrical resistance shows strong hysteresis, but the out-of-plane measures do not. They blame uneven percolation of nanoscale domains, and they propose both methods as probes of phase transitions.
arxiv-2603-21905: Ichihara and co-authors measure pressure waves inside a tiny droplet hit by an underwater shock. Such shocks matter for fuel combustion and gentle medical treatments, but they are hard to quantify. Their method adapts background-oriented schlieren imaging, with a new ray-tracing correction, sync gear, and a projected backdrop. They tracked shocks inside and outside a millimetric perfluorohexane drop in water. Sound speeds, the shock focus point, and peak pressure all matched simulations. The setup also caught a phase shift at focusing only guessed before.
arxiv-2603-22105: The VERITAS Collaboration reports a gamma-ray study of the microquasar SS 433. SS 433 sits inside the W50 remnant and fires relativistic jets. Such jets may feed cosmic rays up to the knee of the energy spectrum. The team uses over 150 hours of VERITAS observations above 100 GeV. They resolve extended emission from both the eastern and western jet lobes. No emission appears from the central binary. The lobe spectra favor a leptonic origin in this energy range.
arxiv-2603-22205: Boahen and co-authors build and test electron gas devices on strontium titanate surfaces. Hydrogen plasma treatment forms a patterned two-dimensional electron gas with high mobility. Mobility reaches up to 7400 in the usual units. They sweep electron density across the dome range. No superconducting transition appears, even near 10 millikelvin. The authors link this absence to confinement and orbital rearrangement. They also map how side gates tune the gas. Wider gate spacing tunes it more, against their first guess.
arxiv-2603-22505: Lozano and co-authors extend cotunneling theory to molecules with strong multireference character on surfaces. Scanning tunneling spectra of single molecules often show steps that are symmetric in bias. Standard theory explains those steps well. The authors show that when tip and substrate couple to the molecule unevenly, the step shapes can turn lopsided. Orbital-dependent coupling adds to the effect. Their result gives a fresh microscopic account of the lopsided peaks and dips often seen near the Fermi level.
arxiv-2603-22705: Shishido and co-authors look for odd eye movement patterns in adults with autism. Group averages can hide single-person traits, they note. The team recorded smooth pursuit eye movements in 18 autistic adults and 39 typical adults. Each person got an outlier score based on timing lag and spatial error. In the typical group, 5.1 percent counted as outliers. In the autism group, the rate was 38.9 percent. Mean scores were also far higher in the autism group. The authors say single-person analysis may help find clinical subtypes.
arxiv-2603-22805: Xiang and co-authors study the costs of switching fields at the start of a research career. They use PhD applications to all programs at one large university from 2013 to 2023. Applicants from outside a program's field have lower grades and test scores. Even after adjusting for those traits, they are less likely to be admitted. A letter from inside the target field shrinks that penalty. Enrolled switchers are also less likely to graduate. They show no edge in publication output, on average or at the top.
arxiv-2603-23005: Wei and co-authors extend an image steganography network to many users and keys. Steganography hides secret data inside normal-looking images. The base system, PUSNet, handles one user with one key pair. Their PUSNet-MK adds strict key isolation. A mismatched-key loss blocks decoding when the wrong key is used. Tests show high-quality stego images and accurate secret recovery for the right key. Cross-key leakage is prevented, they report. The code is released in public.
arxiv-2603-23505: Melo presents HyperFrog, an experimental post-quantum key encapsulation scheme with a topological secret. Most LWE designs draw the secret at random from a simple distribution. HyperFrog instead mines a 3D voxel grid for linked subgraphs of set complexity. That structure becomes a sparse binary secret with tight geometric shape. Shared keys come from noisy linear relations plus hashing, wrapped in a Fujisaki-Okamoto style transform. Melo ships a reference build with self-tests and speed checks. He flags the scheme as a research vehicle, not a product.
arxiv-2603-23605: Mangeolle and Knolle show how new quantum oscillation tones can arise with no order at all. Oscillation tones map the shape of a metal's Fermi surface. Density waves can add tones by folding that surface into new pockets. The pair study electrons scattered between hot spots by a wobbling boson mode. That scattering opens time-dependent tunneling paths, like magnetic breakdown in motion. The paths trace rebuilt surface areas, so tones appear. The tone strengths bend with heat in ways the standard Lifshitz-Kosevich form misses.
arxiv-2603-23905: Gunara studies how massive Maxwell fields decay on a charged black hole background. He works on subextremal Reissner-Nordström exteriors and splits the field by spherical harmonics. The even sector stays a coupled two-by-two system, but it splits cleanly far from the hole. Three channels carry shifted angular momenta, and these set the late-time thresholds. Gunara builds a spectral theory for the cut-off resolvent and rules out growing modes. The full field decays logarithmically on compact sets, with explicit polynomial tails for one part.
arxiv-2603-24205: Krauss and co-authors use quantum optimal control to suppress dynamic crosstalk between qubits. Dynamic crosstalk comes from the control fields themselves, so it is hard to spot and predict. Their method reads the perfect entangler spectrum, where peaks flag unwanted entanglement with spectator qubits. For parametric gates in tunable coupler systems, they derive pulse shapes that remove the crosstalk. Only small pulse changes are needed, even for the hardest-to-predict form. They present the spectrum test as a general control principle for quantum hardware.
arxiv-2603-24405: Technau revisits Shapiro's problem on polynomials with large partial sums of coefficients. For a polynomial bounded by one on the unit disk, how large can the sum of its first coefficients get? Newman gave an exact answer for one case in 1978, with little progress since. Technau finds exact answers for some related sums using Lagrange interpolation identities. For the original question, an asymptotic answer comes via a quantitative Eneström-Kakeya theorem, plus a general inequality for weighted coefficient sums.
arxiv-2603-24605: Liang and co-authors introduce bid-ask martingale optimal transport for pricing illiquid derivatives. Classical martingale transport forces model marginals to match the mid-prices of vanilla options exactly. In practice, firms fit bid and ask marginals instead. Their relaxed version only asks that model marginals sit between the bid and ask marginals. The result gives realistic price bounds and, by strong duality, equals the superhedging price when positions are priced at ask and bid. As spreads vanish, it converges to the classical problem at a quantified rate.
arxiv-2603-24705: Huch and Keane develop amortised inference for correlated discrete choice models using equivariant networks. Logit models dominate applied choice work for their closed forms, but they restrict how buyers switch between options. Their emulator approximates choice probabilities for general error laws, including correlated errors. The design respects the invariance properties of choice models, and an approximation proof backs it. Sobolev training makes the emulator learn probabilities and their derivatives too. Once trained, it gives fast likelihood and gradient values, and the estimators are consistent.
arxiv-2603-25005: Amin and co-authors test which part of a code-error classifier matters most. They pair eight fine-tuned language models with four sequence decoders, making 32 variants, and tune them on real Python error data. The best single run, CodeT5+ with a GRU, scores a weighted F1 of 0.8243. Careful ablations then show the encoder drives the gains, not the decoder. A plain linear head even beats the GRU hybrid on the same encoder, and it trains about 24 percent faster.
arxiv-2603-25305: Vallejo, Romano, and Gair measure the gap between gravity-wave and light distances without assuming a model. If gravity differs from Einstein's theory, waves and light from one merger can imply different distances. Their ratio tests that gap. The new method stays non-parametric, free of theory or shape assumptions. They apply it to black hole mergers in the GWTC-3 catalog. Cosmology and population traits are fit jointly. The results agree with general relativity and with older parametric checks.
arxiv-2603-25705: Dumitriu-I. and co-authors study the thermoelectric Hall response of two-dimensional Dirac fermions. The fermions are massive and interact, and the work is to first order in the interaction. They compute the Nernst response to a Luttinger-type gravitational potential. They also compute particle magnetization, which removes fake non-transport parts. For general interactions, the magnetization takes a strikingly simple form. Even after it is subtracted, the Hall coefficient does not vanish at zero temperature. The authors blame a breakdown of locality at the smallest scales.
arxiv-2603-25805: Kegel and Nonino study when cyclic branched covers pin down a transverse knot. Earlier work found distinct transverse knots whose covers all match as contact manifolds. The authors build more examples of such non-isotopic pairs. They then prove the converse for many other knots. For those knots, the contact type of the cyclic branched covers decides the transverse isotopy class. The note sharpens both sides of the question. It shows where covers fail as a full invariant and where they suffice.
arxiv-2603-26205: Ma and Xiong study neutron star structure with a Walecka-type model under Bayesian analysis. Their relativistic mean-field framework is fit to nuclear data and neutron star observations. Pure hadronic matter can still produce a peak in the sound speed, they find. The peak comes from mixing among the omega, rho, sigma, and a0 mesons. Such peaks are often read as signs of a phase transition. Their result gives the peak a plain hadronic origin instead. The model describes both medium and massive neutron stars well.
arxiv-2603-26505: Liu and co-authors propose a faster way to compute the second Chern number of four-dimensional topological systems. The number comes from an integral of Berry curvature over the Brillouin zone. Their method refines the mesh on its own, packing grid points where the curvature spikes. Against a lattice-gauge method and plain uniform grids, it reaches the same accuracy with far fewer diagonalisations. It also uses little memory and stays accurate near phase transitions, where standard methods often struggle.
arxiv-2603-27305: Sasatani and co-authors add hierarchical resonators to room-scale wireless power systems for targeted charging. Cavity resonators fill a room with a broad magnetic field. Small or tilted coils couple to that field too weakly to charge well. Their relay resonators wake on demand and re-emit a stronger local field nearby. Tests raised transfer by over a hundredfold. A 15 mm receiver drew up to 500 mW of DC power. Multiple relays could be picked and turned one by one. The demos target furniture-embedded charging.
arxiv-2603-27405: Bushnell presents DynamicLogLog, a faster way to count distinct items in a stream. The classic HyperLogLog tool has an error spike and uses six bits per bucket. His design shares one exponent across all buckets. Each bucket then needs just four bits. A quick mask rejects most items before any bucket check. That step makes it over ten times faster when bandwidth is tight. Tests show flat low error at about 1.83 percent. Variants push accuracy higher still.
arxiv-2603-27705: Mao and Chen segment medical scans from just a few examples. Their RAP framework needs no training at all. It retrieves look-alike support cases with DINOv3 features. Boundary cues then adapt the support mask to the query. That pre-mask becomes prompts for SAM 2. Voronoi sampling picks positive prompt points. Sector sampling picks negative ones. Tests across benchmarks beat prior few-shot methods.
arxiv-2603-27805: Zdziarski and co-authors explain PeV photons from the Cyg X-3 binary. LHAASO recently found orbit-modulated PeV light from the system. Helium nuclei accelerate in a compact magnetized jet zone. They drift downstream and escape the jet. There they strike starlight and the donor wind. Pion production then yields the photons. Most seen photons come from the counterjet side. Long sight lines through the wind explain that tilt. Phase peaks also match the model.
arxiv-2603-27905: Cruz presents ATLAS-RTC, a runtime guard for language model output. Structured output often drifts mid-generation. The system watches each decoding step for contract drift. Light signals flag trouble before errors land. Fixes include biasing, masking, and rollback moves. First-attempt success rises by twenty to thirty-eight points. Latency falls up to 88 percent in failure-heavy runs. Many failures trace to decoding artifacts alone.
arxiv-2603-28005: Zhang compares four ways for a language model judge to label whether an answer is supported by a reference. One design splits the answer into atomic claims; others use a holistic rubric, split the reference instead, or combine both. Labels come from TruthfulQA, ASQA, and QAMPARI. Splitting the reference proved 12-21 points more accurate on ASQA, at modest extra token cost. Splitting the answer helped mainly where labels hinge on false beliefs rather than completeness.
arxiv-2603-28405: Kodavanti and four co-authors shrink diffusion transformers so image generation can run on phones. EdgeDiT is tuned for mobile neural processors like Qualcomm's Hexagon and Apple's Neural Engine. A hardware-aware search prunes parts of the backbone that mobile data flows handle badly. The leaner models cut parameters by up to 30% and latency by 1.65 times, with quality intact. Benchmarks show a better speed-quality trade than mobile U-Nets and plain diffusion transformers.
arxiv-2603-28505: Dong, Panamaldeniya, and Mei report the first cold run of compact germanium ring-contact detectors built for rare-event hunts like LEGEND-1000. The ring-and-groove contact aims to keep point-contact sensitivity in bigger crystals, but its bumpy shape makes fabrication tricky. The team refined drilling, polishing, coating, and mounting, then cooled two prototypes to 77 K. Both biased stably and showed clear gamma peaks from americium and cesium sources. A lithium contact step comes next.
arxiv-2603-28605: Dinh and Jin present Unsafe2Safe, a pipeline that anonymizes images while keeping them useful for training. Large image datasets often hold identifiable or sensitive content. Their system uses a vision-language model to flag privacy risks. It writes paired private and public captions and turns the public one into neutral edit instructions. Diffusion editors then rewrite only the sensitive regions. Across three datasets, face and text similarity and demographic predictability fell a lot. Downstream accuracy stayed close to training on raw data.
arxiv-2603-28805: Bray-Ali proposes a laser spectroscopy measurement that would determine the gravitational constant G to 38 parts per billion. The setup uses a 3 milliwatt tunable laser at 2458 nanometres. Its beam passes through a 1 tesla magnetic field in a Mach-Zehnder interferometer. Photons converting into axions inside the field create a small modulation at the dark port. The peak of that modulation marks the axion Compton frequency. A relation linking that frequency to G and other constants gives the value, a claimed 600-fold gain.
arxiv-2603-29405: Suo and co-authors present HIRE, a method that edits vision-language models to cut hallucinations. These models sometimes state facts that clash with the image. Retraining fixes this at high cost, and contrastive decoding doubles inference work. HIRE instead finds the internal features tied to hallucination. It then edits those features on the fly to remove the false content. The added compute cost stays small. Benchmarks show top results, the authors report. The method also gives strong control over hallucinations.
arxiv-2603-29805: Hennick and Corlouer bring a quantum chemistry tool into deep learning: the two-datapoint reduced density matrix. Sudden jumps in model skill during training are hard to predict. Tracking this matrix over a sliding window gives two warning signals. One is a spectral heat capacity tied to critical slowing down. The other, a participation ratio, shows how broad the change is. Top eigenvectors stay easy to read. Tests cover grokking, induction heads, and emergent misalignment.
arxiv-2604-00005: Sun and team ask whether emotional signals can shape language models and agents, proposing E-STEER, a clear steering system. Existing studies mainly treat emotion as a style factor or perception target, missing its mechanistic role in tasks. E-STEER enables direct steering at hidden-state level, treating emotion as a set variable. With it, the team studies emotion's impact on reasoning, generation, safety, and multi-step work. Results reveal non-monotonic emotion-behavior links: specific emotions can enhance skill, improve safety, and shape multi-step agent work.
arxiv-2604-00305: Serry and two colleagues propose a framework for finding stabilization domains for input-limited discrete-time nonlinear systems, mapping each domain through value functions on metric spaces of compact sets. They establish their core traits and derive Bellman-type equations. A physics-informed neural network then learns them by building them into training. Two test examples show the method estimates these domains well and builds stabilizing controls from the learned functions.
arxiv-2604-00505: Lei and Xie develop generalisation bounds for overparameterised shallow neural networks that depend on initialisation and stay non-vacuous. Overparameterised networks often generalise well despite having more parameters than training examples, a benign overfitting puzzle. One promising explanation ties generalisation to the distance from initialisation, often far smaller than the parameter norm itself. Existing analyses measure that distance with the Frobenius norm and often yield vacuous bounds in practice. The new bounds use the path-norm of the initialisation distance for shallow networks with general Lipschitz activations.
arxiv-2604-00805: The Euclid Collaboration studies how redshift-distribution uncertainty affects the joint analysis of photometric galaxy clustering and weak gravitational lensing in data release 1. The key question is whether knowing the mean redshift per bin suffices, or whether higher-order moments matter for unbiased cosmology. They find the mean must be known to 0.004 times one plus the redshift to recover 80 percent of the constraining power. Width uncertainty proves negligible once the mean is pinned down.
arxiv-2604-00905: Novokreschenov and Kavokin study the origin of Kardar-Parisi-Zhang scaling in the phase motion of 1D and 2D light-matter clouds. They show the key cause behind the power laws seen in first-order links is shifts in Goldstone-mode numbers. Those numbers arise from natural breaking of U(1) symmetry. Computer runs and theory confirm the key powers of the KPZ class follow straight from Goldstone motion, linking tiny-scale cloud settings to the order of emitted light.
arxiv-2604-01505: Ahmed, Hasan and Rapakoulias compute angular phase-space integrals with three and four denominators via the Mellin-Barnes representation. The approach converts multifold Mellin-Barnes integrals into real parametric integrals in terms of Goncharov polylogarithms. For three denominators, results reach order epsilon squared and the single-massive case order epsilon. For four denominators, massless and single-massive cases are solved to epsilon zero. Integrals with multiple massive momenta follow from fraction decomposition to the single-massive case. Recursion relations relate integrals with higher denominator powers to master integrals.
arxiv-2604-01705: Yang and colleagues built EndoASR, a speech recognition system tuned for live use during gut endoscopy, where special terms and noisy rooms strain ordinary tools. A two-stage tuning method built on fake endoscopy reports sharpens its grasp of clinical language and its tolerance for noise. In tests across six endoscopists, its character error rate fell from 20.52 percent to 14.14 percent while medical term accuracy rose sharply. A trial across five centers showed the gains held in varied clinics, and the compact system runs fast on bedside devices.
arxiv-2604-02205: Blandino and colleagues test 5G base station sensing for drones, using a monostatic setup where one base station sends and receives. Following 3GPP urban macro aerial assumptions, they build an end to end chain for multi target detection and 3D location with a 5G downlink waveform and positioning signals. Detection tops 70 percent with false alarms under 5 percent, and location errors run to a few meters. They release the 5GNRad simulator so others can reproduce the baseline.
arxiv-2604-02305: Dewan characterizes Hölder continuity on rank one Riemannian symmetric spaces of compact type through Cesàro means. The result feeds approximation applications and a study of the Talbot effect from diffraction theory. For almost every fixed time, Dewan studies Hölder continuity and the fractal profile of Schrödinger propagation via decay of Littlewood Paley projections of the initial data. Expansions of zonal spherical functions near the origin and cut locus, useful in their own right, also emerge.
arxiv-2604-02405: Trippe and colleagues rank lunar sites for the Laser Interferometer Lunar Antenna, which would exploit the Moon seismic quietness to catch decihertz gravitational waves. Two concepts are weighed: a 1 km proof of concept antenna and a full observatory with arms at least 40 km long. The Moon changing orientation and orbital motion modulate sources for sky localization, so no unique lunar region is imposed by detector response. Line of sight limits deployment most. A coarse to fine search over lunar datasets passes 434 initial antenna seeds and 71 observatory centers from 4,050 global seeds.
arxiv-2604-02605: Selvakumar and five colleagues run the first mechanistic study of audio-visual language models, tracing how audio and visual features fuse layer by layer into text. Rich audio meaning appears in middle layers but rarely reaches the final output when audio conflicts with vision, because deeper fusion layers favor visual signals. The audio behavior closely matches the vision-language base model, pointing to limited extra training on audio supervision.
arxiv-2604-02905: Kim and seven colleagues present UniSpector, a system for universal open-set defect spotting in industrial inspection via spectral-contrastive visual prompting. Closed-set systems miss novel defects. Prompt methods suffer embedding collapse under high intra-class variance and subtle inter-class differences. UniSpector builds a meaning-structured prompt topology with orientation-invariant spectral-spatial codes and contrastive training. Prompt-guided query selection adds adaptive object queries aligned with the prompt. It beats baselines by about 20 and 16 percent on two benchmarks.
arxiv-2604-03005: Chen, Song, Ye and Wang probe quantum correlations in top quark-antiquark pairs produced through QCD. The top quark, the most massive Standard Model particle, decays so fast that its spin polarization survives intact, making it ideal for such probes. They measure quantum mutual information, relative entropy of coherence, complete complementarity relations, and the intrinsic relationship, tracing how each depends on kinematic variables. As the gluon mixing probability rises for quark and gluon initial mixing, the maximum of the intrinsic relation's left-hand side also rises.
arxiv-2604-03205: Jaiswal and colleagues build an intrusion detector for medical Internet-of-Things networks from Tsetlin Machines, a rule-based method that states attack patterns as logic. Tested on the CICIoMT-2024 dataset, it reaches 99.5 percent accuracy on binary decisions and about 91 percent on multi-class decisions, beating standard classifiers. Vote scores and clause heatmaps show which rules drive each decision, aiding trust.
arxiv-2604-03405: Lishkova and colleagues set out steering with backup plans: head for a target while keeping the ability to divert to a required count of other sites. Control Lyapunov functions build regions of pull, combined in a tuning filter, while backward reach-avoid sets extend the idea to finite spans. Both filters need only one more constraint than the number of sites, avoiding combined blow-up and allowing safe real-time switching.
arxiv-2604-04205: Zhou, Zhou and Sonner show that three fixed Hamiltonians can mimic fully random quantum dynamics. The Hamiltonians are sampled once and held steady, while only evolution times vary. A two-step version fails to produce general unitary designs. Adding a third quench imposes stricter matching conditions that remove the leftover freedom. The three-step version reaches a target accuracy faster even with imperfect time averaging, and the claim holds across symmetry classes and interaction ranges.
arxiv-2604-04705: Pekaric and six colleagues design the SAFT-GT toolchain tackling safety and security challenges in complex systems, especially self-adaptive systems. The paper describes the toolchain's architecture, including Attack-Fault Trees building and model combination. The toolchain integrates with existing systems, allowing safety checks without extensive changes. The approach faces threats, including known holes and new attack vectors. As a use case, the toolchain joins the feedback loop of self-adaptive systems. A user study with domain experts shows the toolchain's value and ease of use.
arxiv-2604-04905: Khan and five colleagues build ClickAIXR, a system that lets people in extended reality click a real object and ask about it in plain language. Unlike cloud-based tools or gaze-only selection, it runs a vision-language model on the device and uses controller pointing for precise choice. Once clicked, the object image is processed locally, and answers arrive as text and speech. Local inference cuts ambiguity, protects privacy, and lowers delay, and a user study compares the tool with gaze-based rivals.
arxiv-2604-05005: Bi and five co-authors present EduIllustrate, a benchmark for testing language models on mixed text-diagram lessons for K-12 STEM problems. Testing of school models has focused on Q and A and tutor work, leaving a gap for media teaching content that pairs accurate visuals with step-by-step reasoning. The benchmark holds 230 problems across five subjects and three grade levels, with a fixed protocol and stepwise links to enforce visual match across diagrams. An eight-part rubric grounded in media learning theory scores both text and visuals.
arxiv-2604-05105: Mucci and six co-authors demonstrate a circuit QED analog of an atomic micromaser, using an artificial, multi-level atom as the gain medium. The atom is pumped into a population-inverted state by a microwave tone. The flexibility of the circuit QED platform let the team precisely engineer the level structure, coupling, and dissipation of the micromaser components. The device shows rich physics and points to ways recent developments in microwave quantum circuits can probe maser physics, extending atomic physics tools into engineered quantum systems.
arxiv-2604-05405: Li and six colleagues make 3D object detection weather-aware by routing each sample among three parallel streams: pure LiDAR, pure 4D radar, and a gated fusion branch. A small router reads a condition token drawn from visual and semantic prompts and blends the streams per sample, while weather-supervised training keeps the branches distinct. On the K-Radar benchmark the method leads the field and exposes how reliance shifts between sensors as weather changes.
arxiv-2604-05505: Pehlivanoglu and three colleagues schedule hybrid quantum-classical jobs across cloud providers, where a seconds-long circuit can queue for a day. Their Qurator scheduler models jobs as dynamic graphs with quantum constraints like entanglement links and no-cloning rules, scoring fidelity from provider calibration data. On four months of real queue data it stays within 1 percent of the best-fidelity baseline at low load and cuts queue time by 30 to 75 percent at high load.
arxiv-2604-05705: Walker, Durie, and Umerski show an applied voltage can flip the sign of out-of-equilibrium interlayer exchange coupling in a magnetic trilayer. When a quantum-well state sits in the ferromagnet's hybridization gap, a small bias switches the lowest-energy state between parallel and antiparallel alignment. The bias response tracks system conductance across three barrier designs, with tightest confinement giving the lowest switching currents.
arxiv-2604-05905: Peñil and seven colleagues test the claimed 2.1-year X-ray period in blazar PG 1553+113 with two Swift monitoring campaigns. They find no firm sign that X-rays repeat on the same cycle, though high-emission states tentatively match gamma-ray predictions. The X-ray curve does follow the long-term linear trend seen in gamma-ray, optical, and radio bands, but stochastic variability limits firm period claims.
arxiv-2604-06005: In a 2026 paper, Avrahamy, Gur-Arieh, and Geva introduce ROTATE, a data-free way to untangle what neurons in a language model encode, working on weights alone with no forward passes. Neurons carrying one clear concept show high kurtosis, a peakedness measure, when projected onto the model's vocabulary. Rotating weights to maximize that peakedness recovers sparse readable directions the authors call vocabulary channels. Tests on two instruction-tuned models show the channels match neuron behaviour, and channel descriptions beat activation-based baselines by two to three times.
arxiv-2604-06305: Fernández-Ontiveros and ten colleagues study the post-starburst galaxy ESO 420-G13, host to a low-luminosity active nucleus, with JWST mid-infrared spectroscopy and ALMA carbon monoxide data. Despite faint radio and X-ray emission, massive molecular and ionized outflows drive powerful kinetic feedback. A previously undetected compact jet powers it. Interaction peaks about 370 parsecs north of the nucleus, where a fast ionized stream emerges perpendicular to the jet. About 5 percent of the central reservoir is already expelled, with the rest turbulent and warm, signaling ongoing feedback.
arxiv-2604-06405: Lopez, Liu, Koutras, and Freire demonstrate BDI-Kit, a toolkit for schema and value matching that eases data harmonization. It offers two interfaces: a Python API for developers to build flows programmatically, and an AI-aided chat interface for experts to harmonize data through dialogue. The demo shows users searching, checking, and tuning matches through auto matching, AI thought, and user tuning. Two cases appear: building parts, checking outputs, and reusing transformations through the Python API; and talking with the assistant to refine outputs from its tips.
arxiv-2604-06505: Weiyue Li and seven colleagues build MedConclusion, 5.7 million PubMed structured abstracts for conclusion generation. Each instance pairs other sections with the original conclusion, giving natural evidence-to-conclusion supervision. Journal data like category and SJR support subgroup analysis. Evaluating diverse models under conclusion and summary prompts, scored by gold metrics and LLM judges, finds three things. Conclusion writing differs sharply from summary writing. Strong models cluster closely under current automatic metrics. Judge identity substantially shifts absolute scores. It is a reusable resource for evidence-to-verdict reasoning.
arxiv-2604-06605: Liu and Wang derive sharp gradient estimates for a weighted p-Laplacian equation on a complete smooth metric measure space. The equation carries a logarithmic term, and the setting assumes a lower bound on the m-Bakry-Emery Ricci curvature, with two nonzero constants. Applying Nash-Moser iteration, they obtain the estimates and use them to prove Liouville theorems for the equation. The results bound how fast solutions can change across the space.
arxiv-2604-06905: In this paper, Jaiswal, Kow, and Sahoo study the spectral part Laplace with mixed Dirichlet edge data. They bring a Dirichlet-to-Neumann map for this tool and analyze a linked inverse problem. They also prove an extra density result for the spectral part Laplace, rounding out the paper's two main contributions.
arxiv-2604-07205: Lim and 20 colleagues report a cryogenic platform at 4 kelvin that traps atoms in large, defect-free arrays for quantum computing.
