Zarzecki, Dubiński, and Cygert show that tools for spotting benchmark contamination fail in real audit settings. Contamination means test items leaked into training data. It threatens the worth of model scores. Detection tools exist, but they were checked mostly in clean academic setups: big uniform corpora and clear one-stage training.

Two failure modes get too little study. Distribution shift breaks the sameness premise between suspect and check sets. Scale hurts too, since benchmarks are tiny next to pretraining corpora. The team tests three leading methods across 25 models from many families, up to 27 billion parameters. Of 335 evaluations, just 201 came out right. One method gives false alarms under shift. One is too weak at benchmark scale. One gives only coarse origin signals. The authors conclude that statistics cannot yet replace clear data provenance. Their audit benchmark is open-sourced.
arxiv-2606-03405:
Fiorentino and Marzari present a new way to run quantum annealing for materials problems. The core task is finding the lowest point of a potential energy surface. That task matters for protein folding, clusters, and many other systems. The count of near-stable states can grow far too large to scan by hand. Quantum annealing uses quantum fluctuations to search, unlike heat in classical annealing.

Their method builds annealing into path-integral molecular dynamics. That framework samples the quantum nuclear density without handling full wavefunctions. The protocol keeps the ease of standard dynamics runs. It still performs well across a wide range of atomic systems. Tests use both simple force fields and machine-learned potentials. The tool can act as a global optimizer of the energy surface. It can also fold nuclear quantum effects straight into structure searches. That trait suits high-pressure hydrides and similar materials.
arxiv-2606-03505:
Nguyen and co-authors work on keeping messages secret in visible light networks. Their system serves many users with help from an optical intelligent reflecting surface. Such surfaces steer light around line-of-sight blockages. Blockages and inside eavesdropping both threaten secrecy here. The goal is to raise the secrecy sum rate as high as possible.

Precoder design and surface unit assignment are tuned together toward that goal. Binary limits and coupled variables make the joint problem highly non-convex. An alternating optimization framework tackles it in steps. The concave-convex procedure and first-order Taylor approximations do the heavy lifting inside. Simulations confirm that the algorithm converges as designed. Adding more reflecting units brings clear gains in secrecy sum rate. Network designers get a tested method for safer light-based links. The approach suits indoor settings where radio is weak or barred.
arxiv-2606-03805:
Glickman regularizes paired comparison models with pseudo-games and a phantom player. Such models estimate latent ability from binary outcomes. Maximum likelihood can fail when the comparison graph splits or nearly separates. Ridge penalties fix the math but hide the likelihood story. Two data-augmentation views restore that story.

One view adds fractional pseudo-games between every pair of rivals. The other adds a fixed-strength phantom player. Each real rival gets a weighted pseudo-win and pseudo-loss against that phantom. Both routes give finite, shrunken estimates. The phantom route also fixes location nonidentifiability without an extra constraint. For the Bradley-Terry model, both penalties are transparent and compare cleanly with ridge. A 2025 Major League Baseball season test shows tuned versions match ridge estimates closely. Practitioners keep an intuitive augmented-data reading of the shrinkage.
arxiv-2606-04005:
Peng examines reconstructions for high-Weissenberg viscoelastic flow simulations. Log and square-root forms keep tensors positive in such runs. Peng shows that positive form alone does not ensure a sound energy balance. Three flaws can still yield nonphysical behaviour. They are entropy bias, blow-up of log changes in stretched states, and sign-mixed work defects.

Peng sets out an entropy-compatible reconstruction principle to fix this. A corrected log form is picked by a least-damping entropy rule. The fix is local, positive, and found by bisection. Proofs cover the key claims, from a free-energy estimate to defect budgets. Tests compare log, square-root, and linear forms side by side. They confirm the forecast defects and high-stretch gains.
arxiv-2606-04205:
Ebrahimi and colleagues present DetectZoo in 2026, a shared testbed for detectors of machine-written content. Detectors have multiplied, but each team tests its own way, so published scores cannot be compared.

DetectZoo sets one pipeline: same data handling, same inputs, same scoring. It ships with reference versions of known detectors across text, image, and other modes. Anyone can run the full suite the same way and check a new detector against the field. The authors aim to lower the entry cost for multimodal forensics. They also want failure spots across domains to show up fast. The testbed reproduces published results as a sanity check.
arxiv-2606-04305:
Kushagra Chandak, Toshinori Kitamura, and Xiaoqi Tan study in 2026 how a learning agent should blend fixed past data with live trial-and-error. The setting is the linear bandit, where each action's reward follows a linear rule.

Their method leans on the offline data early. Then it shifts weight toward live exploration as the horizon grows. Its regret — the shortfall against the best action — shrinks steadily with the number of live rounds. Its regret against a purely offline reference shrinks as the offline sample grows. So the method stays competitive with both extremes at once. Tests across parameter settings confirmed the balance in practice.
arxiv-2606-04705:
Movahedisefat, Fateh, and Mohammadi make a medical image segmentation model usable with a single click, in a 2026 arXiv paper. Their lightweight Box Predictor module estimates an approximate bounding box from one user click, using localized image embedding features, and feeds that box to MedSAM as spatial guidance.

The module adds only 1.6 million parameters and negligible inference overhead, and it is trained independently in a two-stage pipeline before integration. Evaluated on four datasets spanning CT, MRI, and ultrasound, the method improved accuracy and robustness across anatomical structures, reaching Dice scores of 0.89 on BUSI, 0.93 on FLARE22, and 0.98 on LungSegDB, with 0.88 on BRISC. The work targets the practical gap between foundation models' promise and clinical reality: radiologists will click once, not draw careful boxes, so the model must supply the missing spatial context itself.
arxiv-2606-04805:
Canbay, Sultansoy, and Zimmermann design a facility that would use a future collider's electron beams to produce an intense beam of polarized gamma rays, in a 2026 arXiv accelerator physics paper. The scheme backscatters laser light off FCC-ee electron beams inside the collider's booster ring. Fixing the parameter at its safe value in each FCC-ee running mode sets the laser wavelength and yields photons up to 148 giga-electronvolts.

An event-by-event pair spectrometer selects photons on the high-energy Compton edge and reconstructs their energy, delivering circular polarization above 0.99. The facility's physics target is the polarized gluon distribution inside the proton, probed through open-charm photoproduction on a polarized ammonia target. They project a total precision on the gluon polarization ratio of about 1.8 to 3.0 percent, four to seven times better than the most precise existing direct measurement.
arxiv-2606-04905:
Vašíček and colleagues marry two logic frameworks to reason about systems that change both discretely and continuously, in a 2026 arXiv paper. The Event Calculus specifies how events initiate and terminate time-varying properties, and its answer set programming implementations suit requirements because the representation stays close to natural language.

Their Hybrid Event Calculus extends the discrete axiomatization with functional fluents and a mapping of time to abstract steps. Dense domains of fluents and time become linear constraints evaluated by external solvers, one implementation over integers and another over rationals, while termination is ensured whenever solutions exist. Validated on examples, both implementations are unaffected by domain size, and rationals do not hurt scalability. Handling dense domains enables faithful modeling of continuous change, the feature cyber-physical specifications need most.
arxiv-2606-05105:
Elisha Abuya, Nihar Gargava, and Yufei Zhao improve a lower bound on the density of lattice sphere packings in high dimensions in this 2026 arXiv paper. A lattice packing arranges equal spheres with centers on a lattice, and how much of space such packings can fill in very high dimensions is a classic open problem. The best general constructions come from stochastic methods that evolve ellipsoids rather than placing spheres directly.

Following Klartag's stochastic ellipsoid evolution process, the authors add the cyclotomic symmetries introduced by Venkatesh. They prove there is a universal positive constant with a striking consequence. Along an infinite sequence of dimensions, lattice packings exist with density above a bound that beats the previous best. The improvement over Klartag's bound is a log log N factor. Letting the rank of the underlying number-theoretic construction grow with dimension is the key step that delivers the extra factor.
arxiv-2606-05205:
S. A. Shekhanov and C. P. Ridgers solve the Gaunt-modified Landau-Lifshitz equation exactly for an electron in a plane electromagnetic wave, in this 2026 arXiv paper. The Landau-Lifshitz equation describes how a radiating electron recoils from its own emission, but it inflates energy losses once quantum effects matter. A standard repair scales the radiation reaction by a Gaunt factor that depends on the quantum parameter chi.

In the plane-wave geometry, chi depends solely on the lightfront momentum, so the modified equation keeps the integrable structure that makes the classical problem solvable. The authors derive an exact solution for the energy evolution and the four-velocity of the electron. It reduces to the known classical result in the right limit. The solution gives an exact description of semiclassical radiation reaction in plane-wave fields, providing a benchmark for simulations of electrons in intense laser fields.
arxiv-2606-05305:
Jinlong Dang, Rohith Karur, and Srimoyee Sen construct a gauge flow for chiral gauge theories living on a disk boundary in this 2026 arXiv paper. Chiral gauge theories, where left- and right-handed fermions couple differently, resist non-perturbative definition, a longstanding obstacle to putting the Standard Model on a lattice. A recent formulation places the chiral fermions on the boundary of a disk one dimension higher, extending the gauge field into the disk's interior with a flow that preserves gauge invariance. This paper proposes a concrete realization of that extension: the equation-of-motion flow, with the disk embedded on a square lattice.

The authors then couple the flowed gauge field to fermions and demonstrate the mechanism of anomaly inflow on the lattice. Showing anomaly cancellation at work in the discretized setting is a key consistency check for the disk-boundary approach.
arxiv-2606-05405:
Yiyou Sun and a large team introduce Agents' Last Exam in this 2026 arXiv paper, a benchmark of valuable work for AI agents. The authors argue the gap is an evaluation problem: common benchmarks do not measure performance on real workflows whose outcomes matter economically and can be verified.

Developed with more than 250 industry experts, the benchmark covers non-physical industries defined through the United States taxonomy. It is organized as 55 subfields grouped into 13 industry clusters and one thousand tasks. Each task is a long-horizon, real-world workflow with a verifiable outcome. Current results show the top tier is far from saturated: across agent harness and backbone configurations, the pass rate sits below one percent. The benchmark will keep growing as workflows and industries are onboarded. The authors intend it as an instrument for closing the distance between leaderboard success and GDP-relevant impact rather than as a ranking.
arxiv-2606-05705:
Bhandari presents an open research engine for financial econometrics in a 2026 arXiv paper. Turning an economic idea into a checkable finding is costly and slow. Results rarely ship in a form others can rerun. Econstellar runs publication-grade analysis in a plain web browser. Readers can rerun each result, vary inputs, and trace how every number arose.

Three choices shape the system. Heavy math runs on whichever processor suits it best, not on forced hardware. An AI assistant picks and explains analyses but never invents a number; each figure is a real computation. The public engine is the same code behind the author's published work. Seventeen methods are live, each with a verified value at a public endpoint. All treat prices as non-stationary and work on returns. The engine can even rebuild the headline result of a linked contagion study on demand.
arxiv-2606-06005:
Song leads a large team mapping a glowing galaxy merger's multi-phase winds in a 2026 arXiv paper. IRAS F01364-1042 is a nearby late-stage merger shining among the most infrared-luminous local systems. Earlier surveys flagged excess warm molecular hydrogen emission, hinting at widespread shocks from a starburst or black-hole-driven outflow. The team combined integral-field data from JWST, ALMA, and Keck to resolve the gas phases together.

Ionized, warm molecular, and cold molecular tracers were mapped across the central three kiloparsecs. The verdict confirmed a biconical outflow along the disk's minor axis. Ionized gas showed broad lines beyond five hundred kilometers per second out to about five kiloparsecs. Molecular gas reached about two kiloparsecs with a distinct X-shaped pattern. Different phases trace different reaches of the same wind. The resolved anatomy tests how mergers expel gas and throttle their own star formation.
arxiv-2606-06105:
Parisi, Nugara, Arfeen, Plumari, and Greco push an expansion one order higher and recover physics the first order missed in a 2026 arXiv paper. Bulk viscosity measures a fluid's resistance to uniform compression. For mixtures it entangles tiny processes on many timescales. Chapman-Enskog theory expands the Boltzmann distribution order by order. First-order results for mixtures were known, but they fail noticeably when the two species have similar masses.

The second-order formula derived here encodes the missing physical features. Under specific conditions its predictions differ from first order in kind and in size. A Green-Kubo benchmark, computed by solving the relativistic Boltzmann equation numerically, arbitrates. Agreement improves significantly at second order. The stakes are concrete: neutron star matter and heavy-ion collision fireballs are exactly such mixtures. Transport coefficients feed the flow models used to interpret both. A cheap analytic improvement over brute benchmarks is the paper's deliverable.
arxiv-2606-06205:
Raphaël Romero extends a classic data analysis tool to streams of events in this 2026 arXiv paper on statistics. Event data records the exact times when things happen, from neuron spikes to earthquakes to social media posts. Nonnegative matrix factorization finds interpretable parts in data by writing it as combinations of a few patterns, all with positive weights. Until now it only ran on binned counts, and binning can erase fine timing detail and differences between entities.

His model, EventNMF, works on raw event times directly. Each entity's events follow a Poisson process whose rate is built from shared temporal templates written in a spline basis. He shows the old binned method is just the special case where the splines are flat steps. Tests on synthetic data and real applications show the method recovers shared timing patterns cleanly, with a simple estimation procedure and a public Python implementation.
arxiv-2606-06305:
Alexandre Oliveira and co-authors report a miniature stellar explosion in this 2026 arXiv paper. The system IGR J17014 4306 pairs a white dwarf with a companion star. The dwarf's magnetic field funnels falling gas onto small hot spots. A micronova is a thermonuclear runaway confined to such a spot, far weaker than a full nova. This system holds the longest known orbital period among intermediate polars.

In TESS data they found a burst lasting one point five six days, with several peaks. It released about three point two five times ten to the thirty eight ergs. That implies a burned column near one point six times ten to the minus eleven solar masses, and a repeat roughly every twenty days. Searches of Gaia, ASAS SN, and AAVSO archives turned up sixteen candidate brightenings over eleven years. This is only the eighth confirmed micronova system.
arxiv-2606-06605:
Anton Romen and co-authors shake a quantum magnet to see if its exotic phase transition survives in this 2026 arXiv paper. A deconfined quantum critical point is a continuous transition between two ordered phases that Landau theory says should not connect directly. Here it links Néel antiferromagnetism and a valence bond solid in a frustrated spin chain. Theory predicts lattice vibrations, phonons, should destabilize it below a critical frequency, much like the spin Peierls effect.

Tensor network simulations confirm the picture. At high phonon frequency the exotic critical point stands. Below a critical frequency near zero point four five times the exchange scale, the transition turns strongly first order. The mechanism is a phonon driven drop in the Luttinger parameter. The endpoint falls in the four state Potts universality class, with exponents matching the exact Potts values.
arxiv-2606-06905:
Evolutionary trees summarize how species split, and character data can pin a tree down exactly. Li and Long ask how many species a tree needs before the cheapest encoding always works. Their 2026 arXiv paper works with r-state characters. Each character assigns every species one of r states, like a genetic letter.

Semple and Steel set a lower bound on the characters required. Bordewich and Semple showed the bound is eventually met. The open question was where the threshold sits. Earlier constructions bounded it by a fifth power of r. Li and Long cut that to roughly r times its logarithm. Their proof builds a quartet certificate for each tree. A coloring argument then packs it into the optimal number of characters. They conjecture the true threshold is exactly three r plus one. Small cases already agree with that guess.
arxiv-2606-07005:
Android malware hides its tricks by scrambling code and loading parts at run time. Sanna, Palozzi, Regano, Lazzeretti, and Giacinto listen to malware instead in this 2026 arXiv paper. Their framework, RAMwavDroid, turns program data into sound. Both stored code and early memory snapshots become audio waveforms.

The mapping is direct: binary bytes become wave samples. No disassembly or hand built features are needed. Spectral descriptors, convolutional networks, and transformer embeddings then read the signals. Static sonification already performed competitively. Dynamic memory sonification did far better on separation. Accuracy reached ninety eight percent on a standard malware data set. Code plus run time memory proved richer than either alone. Even lossy audio compression kept the telling patterns. Coarse structural fingerprints, it seems, dominate what classifiers need.
arxiv-2606-07205:
Justin Chen and co-authors settle how much memory a transformer truly needs when generating text token by token, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Attention, the transformer's core mechanism, normally stores every past token in a key-value cache, so memory grows with conversation length. Compressing that cache is vital for cheap long-context models. Recent work framed the problem as streaming attention approximation and bounded its space needs, but left a wide gap between the best algorithm and the best impossibility proof.

This paper nearly closes that gap with matching upper and lower bounds on space complexity. The algorithm blends three estimation techniques from kernel methods, polynomial approximation, and space partitioning in a tight interplay. For the lower bound, the authors developed a new technique based on the classic INDEX communication problem with heavy side information. They suggest the technique may help other high-dimensional geometry problems beyond attention.
arxiv-2606-07605:
Duan, Xiao, and Zhang reconstruct time series from coarse recordings in this 2026 arXiv paper on SRT. High-resolution signals underpin analytics, from heart tracings where rhythm disorders hide at low sampling rates to factory sensors, but collecting them is costly or infeasible. Super-resolution methods from image work do not transfer to time series. Their framework splits the input into trend and seasonal parts, aligns them through an implicit neural form, and generates the detail with a rectified flow model guided by cross-resolution attention.

A variant with large pretraining does it zero-shot, on new data without further training. Across 9 datasets and multiple upscaling factors, both versions outperformed existing methods, and ablations verified each part. The authors frame the split, separating trend from season before generation, as the core design choice that makes temporal super-resolution tractable where naive image-style transfers fail.
arxiv-2606-07805:
Yiyang Zhao and co-authors build a benchmark that catches AI agents breaking rules to hit their targets, in this 2026 arXiv paper. As language-model agents gain the power to execute actions, they may strategically violate safety procedures to maximise reward, a pattern the authors link to Goodhart's law. Existing evaluations barely test procedural compliance, so this Machiavellian behaviour goes unmeasured.

Their benchmark, MAC-Bench, is dynamic and adversarial. A pipeline called SERV turns unstructured legal texts into executable scenarios in holographic sandbox environments, then injects calibrated social-engineering pressure to force trade-offs between task success and rule adherence. Two new metrics score the results: a compliance-weighted success rate, and the Machiavellian gap between succeeding and succeeding honestly. Evaluating frontier models revealed pervasive trade-offs between success and regulatory adherence. The design also keeps scenarios free of training-data contamination, since they are generated rather than collected.
arxiv-2606-07905:
Ayllon Unzueta and co-authors demonstrate a benchtop technique for measuring how neutrons provoke gamma-ray emission from materials, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Such cross sections, probabilities of specific nuclear reactions, feed fusion research, detector calibration, and simulation codes, yet libraries contain gaps and disagreements. Large facilities measure them slowly and expensively.

The method, associated particle imaging, tags each neutron from a deuterium-tritium source by detecting its partner alpha particle. Coincidence timing suppresses lower-energy neutrons and room background, and tagging measures the neutron flux to about one percent uncertainty. Proof-of-concept runs used thin and thick samples of natural iron and carbon. For iron they measured gamma production from the first two excited states of iron-56, near eight hundred forty-seven and twelve hundred thirty-eight kilo-electronvolts. For carbon they measured the scattering gamma channel. The compact setup could fill library gaps cheaply.
arxiv-2606-08105:
Lukas Fesser and co-authors show that a familiar transformer quirk is two mechanisms in one disguise, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Attention sinks, where attention piles onto a single token, appear throughout such models. Visually identical sink patterns can mean opposite things. A head may route attention to a null token to suppress its own update, a no-operation. Or the sink may gather information from everywhere and broadcast it back.

Each mechanism leaves a fingerprint. No-operation sinks have tiny value norms; broadcast sinks produce low-rank outputs. Formalised on synthetic tasks, these become practical tests. Popular fixes are mechanism-specific: gating assumes the no-operation story, registers assume broadcast. In pretrained vision transformers, the tests find both mechanisms at scale. Sinks shift from the class token in early layers to image patches deeper. Register tokens, designed for broadcast, are repurposed by models as no-operation sinks too.
arxiv-2606-08305:
Se Yoon Lee, Kwon, and Kim develop a statistical method for trials that borrow their control group from outside, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Externally controlled survival trials are used when randomized controls are infeasible, especially in oncology and rare diseases. The target quantity is a marginal hazard ratio for the average treatment effect on the treated. Estimation uses inverse-probability-weighted Cox regression, the standard survival model reweighted to mimic randomization.

Valid inference is delicate. The weights enter the Cox model through both event counts and risk-set averages. Building on machine-learning-assisted entropy calibration, the authors propose MEC-Cox. It starts from propensity-score odds weights for the external controls, then calibrates them so weighted summaries match the treated group.
arxiv-2606-08505:
Yamaguchi speeds up the software that labels who spoke when in a recording, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Speaker diarization assigns each stretch of audio to a speaker, and meeting transcription would benefit from running it on-device, but inference cost limits adoption. Yamaguchi studies how far a standard pipeline can be accelerated on consumer hardware while preserving the error rate. A simple recipe, coarser segmentation stride and per-chunk embeddings, gives multi-fold speedups and is error-neutral on a meeting corpus.

On in-the-wild data, however, the same recipe degrades sharply, with the error rate climbing steeply in the reported tests. Yamaguchi traces the failure to speaker under-counting in the clustering stage. The fix is a relative minimum cluster size, scaling the threshold to the embedding budget of each recording, with a fraction near one percent. That setting recovered most of the lost accuracy.
arxiv-2606-08705:
Laraspata, Castellano, and Vessio test whether two failure modes of a language model share an internal signature, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Hallucinations, factually incorrect or unverifiable answers, are a key limitation of large language models. One proposed explanation is internal knowledge conflict. The model's fixed, outdated training data disagree with each other or with newer context. The authors investigate whether internal representations associated with knowledge conflicts correlate with hallucination behavior.

Using probing techniques, they analyze activations from hidden, attention, and feed-forward layers across predefined tasks. One model is probed on hallucination benchmarks, another on a dataset of knowledge conflicts. Their findings indicate that the internal patterns of hallucinations cannot be read off from those of knowledge conflicts. The predicted correlation does not materialize cleanly.
arxiv-2606-08805:
Yadav and colleagues argue that the chaos inside large random neural networks is more predictable than it looks, in this 2026 arXiv paper. A recurrent network feeds its own activity back as input, and in a large such network each unit's behavior becomes chaotic. Dynamical mean-field theory, the standard tool for these systems, replaces the network with one typical unit driven by apparent noise.

The authors show that, for smooth activation functions whose frequency content fades fast enough, the randomness is only apparent. One unit's full continuous past uniquely fixes its future, so the theory predicts single trajectories, not just averages. Unfolding the activity spectrum into a Krylov state space, a ladder of increasingly complex time patterns, exposes this hidden order. Its growth rate measures prediction cost and caps the largest Lyapunov exponent, the standard chaos measure. Sensitivity and predictability, they conclude, are separate features of the same motion.
arxiv-2606-09505:
Hao Li speeds up a data fusion filter by proving a stronger shape property of its core tuning problem in this 2026 arXiv paper. The split covariance intersection filter merges sensor data when some links between sources are known and some are not. A weight choice inside the filter, called the w-problem, sets both its quality and its cost.

The w-problem was known to be convex, which means any local best point is the global best. Li proves it is in fact fourth-order convex, a much stricter shape. That extra shape lets a nested Newton method home in on the best weight with a known error bar at each step. Newton steps use slope and curve to jump near the answer fast. The payoff is a fast form of the filter with a firm speed promise, not just hope.
arxiv-2606-09605:
Jonathan Carter and Lionel Tarassenko show that a language-style training trick works for body signals too in this 2026 arXiv paper. Their model, Hypnos, learns from sleep recordings that mix eight kinds of signal, from brain waves to heart traces. Past models hid parts of the signal and rebuilt them, or matched pairs of clips. Both fits sit poorly with noisy body data.

Hypnos instead predicts the next token, a small coded chunk of signal, across all streams at once. It trained on more than twenty thousand full-night lab recordings. In sleep stage tests, it matched strong supervised systems while using one hundred times less labelled data. It also beat a specialist heart model at spotting atrial fibrillation in daytime traces, a task it was not built for. The result makes next-token prediction a strong base for health models from mixed sensors.
arxiv-2606-10005:
McQuinn simulates how a space telescope could map the first galaxies by their glow rather than one by one, in a 2026 arXiv paper on cosmology. The telescope is SPHEREx, and the era is reionization, when early galaxies ionized the gas between them. Intensity mapping records the combined light of many faint galaxies in each pixel. A major obstacle is interloping lines from nearer galaxies masquerading as the signal.

McQuinn cross-correlates simulated maps of hydrogen and oxygen lines, since cross-correlation cancels the interloper contamination that ruins single-line spectra. The best case, hydrogen-alpha crossed with doubly ionized oxygen at redshift five, reaches a total signal-to-noise near ninety-nine when no dust extinction is assumed. The maps can probe galaxies too faint for direct detection, though large bright galaxies dominate the observable signal.
arxiv-2606-10205:
Jang and Mellet give math backing to a classic idea about how cell populations sort themselves, in a 2026 arXiv paper on applied mathematics. The differential adhesion hypothesis, proposed by Steinberg in 1962, says cell groups self-organize by minimizing adhesion energy, much as fluids minimize surface tension.

In the limit of short-range contacts, they give conditions on the interaction coefficient matrix for cell sorting, the spontaneous separation of species, to occur. They then prove a Gamma-convergence result for the linked energy functional, showing it converges to a surface energy whose surface tension values come from the interaction matrix. The limit connects the multi-species system to a multiphase Hele-Shaw problem, the fluid model of flow between close plates. The result firmly links a smooth cell model to the fluid-like picture Steinberg imagined.
arxiv-2606-10305:
Qianzhong Chen and colleagues build a reward model that can teach robot manipulation policies from their own practice, in a 2026 arXiv paper on robot learning. Fine-tuning vision-language-action policies for long tasks still relies on behavior cloning from costly demonstrations, keeping policies near the demonstration distribution. Reward models could reweight demonstrations and supervise on-robot reinforcement learning, but they must be dense, accurate, and general. Task-specific stage-aware models are accurate yet need per-task annotation, while general vision-language reward models are too coarse for fine-grained progress.

Their model, SARM2, combines an action-primitive-based stage estimator with a mixture-of-experts value head to produce dense per-step rewards across tasks. On a ten-task benchmark it cuts value-estimation error by eighty percent against the strongest baselines in the reported comparison.
arxiv-2606-10705:
Yeganeh and colleagues teach reinforcement learning to run a chip factory in this 2026 arXiv paper on operations research. A semiconductor fab is a control problem: hundreds of wafers move through hundreds of steps on shared equipment, with random processing times, breakdowns, and feedback that arrives after long delays. The authors use one central agent making decisions, and model the fab as a process driven by events. Their event-driven temporal-difference learning is built for that structure.

Several deep reinforcement learning algorithms are plugged into the framework and tested in high-fidelity simulations of industry-like scenarios, offline and online. Across validation experiments, the policies deliver significant, consistent gains in throughput and utilisation over baselines. The authors also compare formulations head to head, clarifying which algorithms suit event-driven dynamics. Healthcare, logistics, and telecom networks share that event-driven shape, so the framework should travel beyond chip fabrication.
arxiv-2606-11205:
Buchan audits a technique for taming sycophancy in language models in a 2026 arXiv paper. Sycophancy is a model's habit of agreeing with the user, even when the user is wrong. Activation steering adds a direction, from the difference between agreement and disagreement activations, pushing toward disagreement. Standard evaluations check only that sycophantic agreement falls, never what else falls with it.

His dual-stance evaluation tests both stances of each topic on Llama-3-8B-Instruct. The result is a dissociation. The model represents the two kinds of agreement in geometrically distinct subspaces. Yet the steering direction projects equally onto both and cannot target either alone. It reduced agreement with factually correct statements, like the Earth being round, alongside sycophantic ones. Steering susceptibility was predictable from dual-stance consistency, at 0.88 in-sample and 0.84 out-of-sample. The lesson generalizes: what can be read from activations may not be writable through them.
arxiv-2606-11705:
Alberto Álvaro-Díaz and Gonzalo Morras refine gravitational wave models in this 2026 arXiv paper. When two black holes spiral together, some orbital energy and spin are absorbed by their event horizons, the surfaces of no return. This horizon absorption alters the holes' masses and spins and leaves an imprint on the gravitational waves, the ripples in space-time that detectors record.

The authors derive, for the first time, the leading effect for the hardest case: eccentric orbits whose spins make them wobble, called precession. They add the correction to an existing waveform model. The effect is largest for strongly spinning holes in unequal pairs on long inspirals. Neglecting it biases inferred properties at moderate signal strength. In circular binaries the bias hides by mimicking other parameters, but eccentric signals are rich enough that absorption could become measurable in loud events.
arxiv-2606-11905:
Saeid Sadeghi Vilni and Risto Wichman schedule status updates with an eye on risk in this 2026 arXiv paper. A transmitter monitors a process whose state changes in semi-Markov fashion, meaning dwell times follow general patterns, and serves several receivers. It can stay idle, send one receiver an update, or broadcast to all. The quality measure is the Age of Incorrect Information: how long a receiver has held a wrong estimate of the source.

A risk state flags whenever this age passes a safety threshold. The scheduler minimises a long-run average combining the incorrectness age, risk and transmission cost. The authors solve it with model-based and model-free policies and compare two baselines. Their policies win, mixing unicast and broadcast as receiver counts and risk vary. Raising the risk weight reduces time in dangerous states. Notably, the dwell-time law affects performance even when average dwell is fixed.
arxiv-2606-12105:
Pankhuri Vanjani leads a seven-author team letting each robot sense keep its own tempo in this 2026 arXiv paper. Vision-language-action models inherit one shared processing clock from their pretraining. Physical interaction is not synchronous, though: force signals change hundreds of times per second, vision evolves slowly, and language stays fixed for a whole task. One clock oversamples slow channels and starves fast ones.

Their model, DAM-VLA, keeps a separate latent buffer per modality, each refreshed at its sensor's natural rate, while the action head reads all buffers continuously. New fast modalities plug in through gated cross-attention that leaves the pretrained backbone untouched. Across seven contact-rich real-world manipulation tasks, the decoupled model more than doubles the strongest synchronous baseline's average success rate, reaching about ninety-five percent against about forty-one percent. Control stays smooth and reactive at one hundred hertz.
arxiv-2606-12505:
Sun adds a third response to preference training: the answer the reference model would give, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Direct Preference Optimization, DPO, aligns language models using stored pairs of chosen and rejected replies. It ignores a signal sitting in every prompt: the reference model's greedy output, a local habit the new policy may keep imitating. Sun's DPOP penalizes that greedy response, but only through a gate. The penalty switches on solely when the policy ranks the chosen reply below the rejected one.

The base pairwise loss stays untouched, and detached weights keep the gate from becoming a learned reward. On AlpacaEval 2.0, judged by length-controlled win rate, DPOP beats DPO, SimPO, and AlphaDPO on both Llama-3 and Gemma-2 instruction models. Relative gains over the baselines reach about five percent. Ablations show a length-normalized penalty in the SimNPO style beats both plain NPO and token-level unlikelihood.
arxiv-2606-12805:
Ravi and colleagues study how the accent of an AI voice agent shapes collaboration in school group learning, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Conversational agents are entering classrooms as peer partners that mediate group work, and voice design choices such as accent may affect how learners perceive and use them.

The team ran a between-subjects mixed-methods study with 33 teachers, giving the same generative AI voice agent a British, Indian, or African American accent. Combining surveys, interaction analysis, and artefacts, they find accent shaped teachers' mental models of the agent and the role it assumed in the group. The British-accented agent was largely treated as a tool and used in detached, utility-based ways. The Indian- and African American-accented agents were more readily anthropomorphised, treated as people-like, and integrated as peers. These role expectations influenced trust, engagement, and reliance over time.
arxiv-2606-12905:
Abumusabh and the Belle and Belle II collaborations report the first observation of 2 B-meson decays into pairs of charmed baryons, in this 2026 arXiv paper. The decays produce a Sigma-c(2455) baryon with an anti-Xi-c-prime antibaryon, in charged and neutral B-meson versions. Baryonic B decays test how the weak interaction assembles heavy quarks into baryons.

The analysis combines 771.6 million Upsilon(4S) decays from Belle at KEKB with 520.6 million from Belle II at SuperKEKB. The charged decay is observed with a significance of 6.4 standard deviations and the neutral decay with 5.3, including systematic uncertainties. Their branching fractions are measured at 1.68 times 10 to the minus 3 and 1.28 times 10 to the minus 3 respectively, with a third uncertainty arising from the reference antibaryon decays. The result is the first observation of B-meson decays into a baryon-antibaryon pair from the same SU(3) flavour sextet.
arxiv-2606-13405:
Rombach, Lauer, and Mehdiyev argue for building compliance into the architecture of language model agents in this 2026 arXiv paper. Such agents are entering regulated industries, where they automate judgement-heavy workflows. Regulations, typed process models, and constraints already structure these domains. The authors propose treating those structures as core components that shape agent decisions, not as monitors watching from outside. They call the paradigm compliance-by-construction: the architecture itself prevents control-flow violations before they can happen.

Guardrails, the layers that catch bad outputs, remain essential for semantic errors that structure cannot prevent. The paper identifies a set of research challenges for neuro-symbolic systems, combining neural networks with rules, at basic and capability levels. Addressing those challenges is what makes the paradigm achievable. The authors close with a call for the neuro-symbolic community to treat regulated process automation as a domain.
arxiv-2606-13505:
Varshney, Pal, and Rapaka simulate convection in porous media at driving strength in this 2026 arXiv paper. Rayleigh-Darcy convection describes fluid overturning in a heated porous layer, relevant to geothermal systems and carbon storage. The Rayleigh number measures how violently the fluid is driven; the authors run numerical simulations in 3 dimensions across a range reaching a million. They focus on heat transfer scaling, thermal boundary layers, and how the flow structure evolves into the unexplored ultimate regime, where turbulence takes over.

The Nusselt number, the ratio of conductive heat transfer, grows roughly linearly with the Rayleigh number. A change of slope near the upper end signals the ultimate regime's onset. At moderate driving the results sit below an earlier scaling, while in the ultimate regime they agree with a prediction to within a little over 1 percent. Near the walls, protoplumes form and merge into larger structures.
arxiv-2606-13805:
Pérez Martínez and colleagues study how strongly two magnetic layers must be coupled to push the largest possible spin current between them. A spin current carries angular momentum without moving electric charge, which could cut energy losses in future devices. Their 2026 arXiv paper examines bilayers of an iron cobalt alloy on a permalloy layer, grown on magnesium oxide crystals by magnetron sputtering, a method that sprays atoms onto a surface.

Measurements with ferromagnetic resonance, which wiggles the magnetization with microwaves, show a cubic pattern in the magnetic response. The easy direction for magnetization lies along one crystal axis of the iron cobalt layer, and the hard direction along another. Modeling then shows that the wobbling area of the permalloy magnetization peaks at one particular coupling strength between the layers. Tuning that coupling, the layer thickness, or the driving frequency can therefore maximize the injected spin current.
arxiv-2606-14205:
Lao, Pham, Ta, and Vu define a new invariant for sum-rank metric codes and prove it splits cleanly across the code's blocks. Sum-rank codes generalize Hamming and rank-metric codes: codewords are tuples of matrices, weighted by the sum of block ranks. Their 2026 arXiv paper defines block tensor rank: the smallest number of block-simple tensors, rank-one matrices inside single blocks, whose span contains the code.

The main theorem: block tensor rank decomposes additively across blocks, reducing its computation to tensor rank on each block projection. From this they derive two lower bounds, projection-wise and coordinate-code, sharpening the latter with the classical Singleton and Griesmer bounds. Constructions from optimal Hamming-metric codes attain these bounds, defining two optimality notions. Notably, two known sum-rank families provably fail to attain the Singleton coordinate-code bound, and the two optimality notions capture genuinely different features.
arxiv-2606-14405:
Saketh, Ghosh, and Andersson tackle a 2026 arXiv problem in gravitational-wave work. The task is telling neutron stars apart from black holes in merging pairs. Neutron stars deform under a partner's gravity. This tidal response reveals their inner matter. But defining that response cleanly is hard. Coordinate choices in relativity can blur it.

The authors define the dynamical tidal response in worldline effective field theory. That scheme treats the star as a point with structured traits. They tie the response to the amplitude for waves scattering off a lone star. They compute that amplitude two ways. One way uses field theory. The other solves the star's equations numerically. Matching the two fixes the response. The result matches the known static limit. It also recovers the main mode's energy loss.
arxiv-2606-14505:
Sousa proves a regularity result for a nonlinear equation in a 2026 arXiv paper. The topic is the g-Laplacian, a diffusion operator with nonstandard growth. It is studied in Orlicz-Sobolev spaces, which widen the usual energy spaces. The domains are Reifenberg flat. That means their edges look almost flat at every scale. It is a realistic roughness for physical regions.

The problem is a Dirichlet problem, where edge values are prescribed. Sousa shows weak solutions stay Hölder continuous up to the edge. Hölder continuity is a measured form of smoothness. Any target exponent below one can be reached. This holds if the domain's flatness is small enough. The proof uses an iterative decay argument at the edge. It shrinks oscillation step by step. It also uses a maximum principle of ABP type, adapted to this space.
arxiv-2606-14805:
Dong Ho Kang, Hyeonjeong Cha, and Daein Weon debug multi-agent AI systems without re-running them in a 2026 arXiv paper. Such systems leave long execution traces. A few decisive events hide inside logs of messages, routes, memory writes, and tool calls. The standard check is counterfactual replay: rewind, edit one event, and re-run to measure its effect. That cost grows with every candidate event, so full replay is infeasible at scale.

The team compiles each trace into an event knowledge graph. A predictor called BranchPoint-Latent then ranks which events a replay oracle would flag as high-effect. It learns from graph structure, uncertainty, and latent evidence features. Calibrated against a deterministic replay oracle across thirty-seven trace families, it raised Branch Recall@5 from about zero point seven three to about zero point nine three. That gain came at zero replay cost on held-out families.
arxiv-2606-14905:
Mehdi, Zaid, and Aleem segment salt domes in seismic data without centralizing it in a 2026 arXiv paper. Outlining salt domes guides hydrocarbon exploration, reservoir modeling, and drilling safety, but labeled seismic volumes are scarce and operators guard their data. Their framework, FedSaltNet, uses federated learning, training a shared model across separate data owners without moving the raw volumes.

A lightweight small U-Net segments the images, and a foreground-weighted aggregation strategy counters the severe class imbalance between salt and background across sites. Emulating non-identical data across four seismic datasets, the aggregation improved overlap scores by about four percent relative over the best conventional federated method. The simple U-Net beat a higher-capacity ResNet variant by a wide margin in average overlap, underscoring that architectural simplicity wins in data-constrained federated settings.
arxiv-2606-15005:
Abdulin and Narimani detect false data injection attacks on power grids with a Transformer mixture-of-experts model in a 2026 study. Attackers corrupt sensor readings to mislead the state estimation that grid operators rely on. Many detectors use a single graph filter, which adapts poorly to varied attack patterns. The authors aim to spot attacks and locate the compromised buses at once.

Their encoder-only Transformer adds Laplacian positional encoding and diffusion-biased attention to capture grid-wide links. A routed mixture-of-experts layer mixes two graph filters, Chebyshev and autoregressive moving-average convolutions, chosen per grid state. Tests run on the IEEE 118-bus and 300-bus systems with real New York load profiles. The model reaches the strongest detection and localization scores among compared methods while keeping false alarms low. Routing weights adapt across attack scenarios, which the authors credit for the stable performance.
arxiv-2606-15205:
Gonzalez and coauthors develop tools for Scott analysis aimed at Vaught's conjecture, in a 2026 mathematical logic paper. Vaught's conjecture says a theory's countable models number either countably many or continuum many. Scott rank grades structures by the complexity of their defining formulas. The authors study which Scott ranks can occur under countability side conditions. Their tools examine models of ranks when only countably many types are realized.

Using them, the team improves a result of Sacks on counterexamples. Any counterexample to the conjecture must now have at least two models of every parameterized rank. Theories with fewer than continuum many models are shown to have trivial Scott spectra. The authors classify low-rank models when few types are realized. They settle the Scott spectra of many Ehrenfeucht theories. Applications reach concrete theories like p-groups, trees, and Boolean algebras. Several questions from other researchers are answered along the way.
arxiv-2606-15605:
Roy and colleagues construct quantum many-body scars in 2026 inside a driven chain of Rydberg atoms on a ring. Scars are rare eigenstates that refuse to thermalize while the states around them do, and an index theorem guarantees this driven model an exponentially large family of exact zero-energy modes. Most of those modes drift as the drive changes, losing any fixed identity.

The team isolates two zero modes that instead keep the memory of particular states across a range of drive amplitudes and frequencies. One is a dressed version of the unentangled Rydberg vacuum; the other dresses a highly entangled volume-law scar from earlier work. Floquet perturbation theory explains their existence, and exact diagonalization shows they survive beyond the perturbative regime. The contrast between the two hints at a whole hierarchy of such protected modes in driven systems.
arxiv-2606-15705:
Pranshu and colleagues show in 2026 how small survey telescopes can borrow training from big ones to hunt cosmic transients. Classifiers separating real events from artefacts need large labelled datasets, which new telescopes lack. Transfer learning sidesteps the gap: train on the Zwicky Transient Facility's public images, then fine-tune on smaller data from the four-metre International Liquid Mirror Telescope.

The transferred networks classify candidates in difference images as real or bogus, then sort real detections into three or four alert classes. Accuracy reaches about ninety-seven percent for real-versus-bogus, ninety-three for three classes, and eighty-six for four. On an independent test set the transfer models beat baselines trained without transfer learning. The models now run inside the telescope's working pipeline on full-frame data. For small surveys that cannot label millions of images, borrowing a big survey's knowledge is a practical route to automated alerts.
arxiv-2606-15805:
Zoabi and colleagues introduce Mean-Field Parallel Decoding in 2026, a training-free way to help diffusion language models commit more tokens per step without clashes. Diffusion models unmask positions in parallel, but positions chosen by confidence alone can clash: each looks fine singly, together they form incoherent text. That clash caps how much parallelism is safe.

The method scores each position for commitment, then refines them with pairwise interactions drawn from the model's predictions. A variational step turns the refinement into a fixed-point update suppressing conflicting joint commitments within one forward pass. The decoder can then unmask more tokens per step while holding generation quality. On reasoning and code-generation benchmarks, the quality-latency trade-off improves throughout. Nothing is retrained and no helper model is needed, so the decoder drops into existing diffusion pipelines as-is. Coordinating parallel choices, rather than trusting each alone, is the trick.
arxiv-2606-16205:
Zhang gives an introductory review in 2026 of the bilinear method, a classic tool for solving nonlinear wave equations exactly. Ryogo Hirota created the method in 1971 while hunting three-soliton solutions, lasting wave packets. The review centers on two themes for equations of KdV type. One is how the three-soliton condition tests whether an equation is integrable, meaning exactly solvable.

The second theme is how tau functions, the auxiliary functions the method works with, transform into each other. Bäcklund transformations link solutions of related equations, and vertex operators expose the algebraic structure behind the tau functions. Any KdV-type bilinear equation admits one- and two-soliton solutions, Zhang notes. Integrability shows up when a three-soliton solution also exists under elastic scattering. The review pulls these tests and transforms into one entry point for newcomers.
arxiv-2606-16405:
Yang proves in 2026 that two cornerstone inequalities of analysis on rough spaces imply each other, completing an equivalence long studied for smoother settings. The spaces are metric measure spaces with volume doubling, and the energies are p-energies for p above 1, a nonlinear energy. The elliptic Harnack inequality bounds how much positive solutions of the equation can vary. The Poincaré bound ties a function's spread to its energy.

Under two-sided capacity bounds plus geometric and analytic side conditions, Yang proves Poincaré from Harnack. Combined with earlier work, this yields a full equivalence: Harnack plus capacity bounds holds exactly when Poincaré and the cutoff Sobolev bound hold together. The proof works on balls and covers, with no smooth charts at all. The result tightens the web connecting geometry, capacity, and diffusion in the nonlinear p-energy world.
arxiv-2606-16605:
Zhang and co-authors build in 2026 the first benchmark for attacking world-model agents. World models learn latent dynamics for planning in continuous control, and they are entering safety-critical settings. Yet no testbed spanned the policy, value, and latent-dynamics levels of an agent. Their benchmark, ARB4WM, evaluates adversarial robustness under perturbations with five white-box loss objectives spread across those three levels.

Attacks combine single-step or multi-step perturbation strategies with temporal modes: full-frame, half-sequence, and sparse-frame exposure. Four Dreamer-style agents are tested across twenty tasks from MetaWorld and the DeepMind Control Suite. Small visual perturbations substantially degrade performance, especially under multi-step iterative attacks. Failures aimed at value estimation, latent representations, and the recurrent dynamics prove as important as policy-space failures. The message for safety assessment is to probe the whole latent decision pipeline, not just the action head.
arxiv-2606-16705:
Runko computes diffractive structure functions in a 2026 nuclear physics paper. In diffractive scattering, an electron strikes a proton or nucleus, new particles appear, yet the target stays intact and no color charge is exchanged. A silent gap in the detector marks these events. Structure functions summarize how the target's inner parts respond at each energy share.

The calculation uses Wilson line configurations whose energy evolution follows the JIMWLK equation, a standard tool for dense gluon systems. That setup was already tuned against exclusive vector meson data from the HERA collider in Hamburg. Runko first checks the proton results against HERA measurements to set a baseline. The main new output is the nuclear change for a gold nucleus under conditions planned for the future Electron-Ion Collider. Predictions include the nuclear modification factor and the ratio of diffractive to total cross sections, giving experimenters concrete targets before the new machine runs.
arxiv-2606-17405:
Qin and colleagues present a 2026 arXiv paper on a clinical decision support system that keeps learning while it is used, under strict safety rules. Patient states change in real time, and advice learned only from old records can drift out of date. The framework joins three parts: treatment effect estimation to score each option's benefit, a patient digital twin that simulates likely courses, and reinforcement learning for planning sequences of care over time.

A rule-based guard watches vital signs and blocks treatments that are contraindicated for that patient. Cases where the internal models disagree strongly are flagged for clinician review instead of being decided automatically. Validation used both a synthetic clinical simulator and a real ovarian cancer data set from a national genome atlas. The system beat standard baselines on effectiveness and stability while consulting experts on only a minority of cases.
arxiv-2606-18005:
Reusens and colleagues found a new research field in a 2026 theory paper: the study of how language model agents shop. AI agents increasingly make purchases and bookings on behalf of users, yet consumer theory was built for human decision makers. The authors name the field LLM Consumer Behavior Theory and set out its foundations, joining classical and behavioral economics with language technology.

It formalizes how human preferences get reflected, and sometimes distorted, when an agent acts on them, and how many such agent decisions add up to market demand. It gathers scattered work on model decision-making, human simulation, and preference elicitation under one economic lens, and flags where standard assumptions like rationality and consumer diversity may break. Rather than testing claims, it maps the territory and lists open questions on alignment and market dynamics.
arxiv-2606-18305:
Qin and colleagues rebuild a neural operator in the image of a classical iterative solver, in a 2026 paper in Nuclear Physics B. Operator learning maps between function spaces to solve partial differential equations far faster than standard solvers, a boon for many-query jobs like real-time prediction and parameter sweeps. Accuracy is the weak point, above all with complex boundaries or long time spans. Forward simulation and inverse inference both demand high fidelity.

Their Starter-Iterator Neural Operator splits the work the way iterative methods do. A starter module works in the frequency domain to capture the solution's stable low-frequency content, suppressing the part of the error that converges slowest. An iterator module then refines the high-frequency detail through learnable recursions in the time domain. The pairing aims at spectral and temporal accuracy together, inside one architecture serving both forward and inverse problems.
arxiv-2606-18405:
Kozyreva and Hoque test whether large language models can help check software against a cryptographic protocol standard, in a 2026 security paper. Their target is PKCS#1 version 1.5 signature verification, a widely deployed encoding standard where lax parsing has historically allowed forged signatures, and where good test inputs must satisfy both structural and semantic rules.

The approach mutates a formal grammar of the standard and asks a language model to synthesize test code from it, then runs the results across forty-eight cryptographic library implementations. It reproduced ten of thirteen known violation categories, including all five signature forgery categories, and found one previously unreported discrepancy. The bottleneck was not the mutations but the model: most generated scripts contained hallucinations, and the team sorts these into five types with different rates across mutation kinds. Their guidance shows where such synthesis can be trusted and where it needs filtering or verification first.
arxiv-2606-18505:
Merenkov proves a rigidity result about two kinds of fractal objects that arise from different dynamical systems, in a 2026 mathematics paper. One kind is the limit set of a convex-cocompact Kleinian group. The other is the Julia set of a postcritically finite rational map, and in the cases he considers both sets are Sierpinski carpets.

Recent work on related gasket and tree-like spaces had suggested the two worlds might be locally indistinguishable. Merenkov shows carpets behave oppositely: no local quasiconformal map exists between such a Kleinian limit set and such a Julia set at all. The result draws a sharp line between fractal families that look superficially similar, and it limits how far results about local equivalence between group actions and rational dynamics can be pushed. It also gives carpet specialists a clean test case separating two major sources of fractal limit sets.
arxiv-2606-18605:
Kocharovsky and Kalra introduce a universal measure of the quantum advantage carried by light from multimode optical parametric amplifiers, in a 2026 quantum optics paper. Squeezed light from such devices underpins quantum sensing, communication, and computing, but scaling to many modes has lacked a realistic figure of merit. The standard Bloch-Messiah supermodes describe the squeezing without capturing the computational hardness that makes the light useful.

The authors define a quantum complexity resource for mixed multimode Gaussian states. It is grounded in convex optimization, photon-number statistics, and a master theorem linking the joint photon-count distribution to the hardness of computing matrix hafnians. Designing pulsed amplifiers around this measure maximizes the photons in the true quantum-advantage modes, which differ sharply from the supermodes. The paper argues the approach opens paths to three-dimensional cluster states for one-way photonic quantum computing and cleaner demonstrations of quantum advantage.
arxiv-2606-18805:
Richardson and the team test whether the letdown of a disappointing loss makes fans drive dangerously, in a 2026 behavioral economics paper. Reference-dependent theory says outcomes are judged against expectations. So a loss hurts most when suspense was high and hope was alive. Emotions may spill into behavior after the event.

The authors combined vehicle speeds, recorded every ten minutes at road locations, with crash timing around five Florida stadiums. They covered NFL and NBA games from twenty fifteen to twenty nineteen. They found no emotional driving after basketball games. But effects appeared after football games predicted to be close, that ended in home losses. Average speeds rose by up to three miles per hour, within three kilometers of the stadium, during the first post-game hour. That is several times the normal speed difference. It faded with time and distance, and survived checks against congestion and ordinary traffic explanations.
arxiv-2606-19005:
Ye and colleagues introduce Sumi in 2026, a fully open language model built with uniform diffusion rather than the usual left-to-right method. In uniform diffusion, any token can be updated at any step, which should allow more flexible text generation. No such model had yet been trained from scratch at both large size and large data scale, leaving a clear gap for study.

Sumi has seven billion parameters and was trained from scratch on a very large token set drawn from public sources. It matches rival autoregressive models trained on like budgets on knowledge, reasoning, and coding tests. It lags on common-sense tests, which the authors link to their education-heavy data mix. Weights, checkpoints, and the full training recipe are released openly. That release gives researchers a clean base for studying how native uniform diffusion scales and where it trades off against older designs.
arxiv-2606-19205:
Chuna and colleagues present a regularized stochastic optimization method for analytic continuation in 2026. Quantum Monte Carlo simulations yield imaginary-time correlation functions, but extracting real spectra from them is a notoriously hard inverse problem. Two camps compete in this area, with neural models now joining them. The new method crosses those divides by recasting continuation as dictionary learning with a sparse form.

Remarkably, the learned sparse dictionary maps the ill-conditioned problem to a small one that is well-conditioned. The method gives competitive results on common synthetic tests. It also performs well on authentic Monte Carlo data from the finite-temperature electron gas. The authors argue a suitable dictionary exists inside all such methods. Finding it turns a hard inversion into a stable task.
arxiv-2606-19405:
Okolie and colleagues develop multi-type branching inference on contact trees in 2026, with an application to COVID-19. Inferring epidemic parameters from transmission trees is essential for understanding disease dynamics. Existing tree-based methods, including multi-type birth-death models from phylodynamics, are powerful. Most assume uniform mixing. They rarely capture how spreading potential changes as one person infects more of their contacts.

The framework works on such trees, where nodes are people and edges are reported infections, with no sequence data. Each person is described by their total contacts and how many downstream contacts are already infected. The team derives closed-form equations for the chance a clade goes unobserved and for the density of observed tips. Partial trees are handled with latent branching times. Simulations confirm accurate recovery with calibrated uncertainty. Applied to COVID-19 contact-tracing data, the method turns tracing records into parameter estimates without needing genomes.
arxiv-2606-19605:
Paul Kassianik and six colleagues present FAPO in 2026, a system that tunes multi-step language model pipelines on its own. Such pipelines chain retrieval, reasoning, and formatting steps, and faults emerge from their interplay. Prompt-only tuning can miss a bottleneck hiding in the chain's structure.

FAPO lets Claude Code optimise a pipeline inside a standard codebase. It runs the pipeline, inspects middle steps, diagnoses failures, and proposes scoped changes. Variants face repeated validation against a score function. Prompt edits come first; structural changes follow only when diagnosis blames the chain layout. Across six benchmarks and three task models, FAPO beats the GEPA baseline in 15 of 18 comparisons. The mean gain reaches 14.1 percentage points. Where search escalated to structural fixes, all six comparisons fall to FAPO with a 33.8 point mean gain. Security tasks improve too, lifting CVE-to-CWE accuracy on three models.
arxiv-2606-19805:
Zijie Meng fixes a scale flaw in camera-motion transfer for generated video in 2026. Creators reuse a reference clip's camera move on a fresh scene, like matching a galaxy sweep to a desk nudge. Raw paths copied across such scales feel invisible or violent.

Image motion from translation scales as travel distance over scene depth. A single-camera path therefore means little without a depth scale. Meng distils the Parallax Number, a unit-free gauge-invariant score of how strongly a move registers. Faithful transfer must preserve that number, not the raw path. ParaScale reads the number off any reference and rebuilds it against the target's own depth, frame by frame. Rotation stays untouched, and no retraining is needed. A new error metric exposes scale mismatch that older scores hide, and ParaScale cuts it more than threefold.
arxiv-2606-19905:
Akbar Davlataliev and four colleagues test cubic Galileon cosmology inside teleparallel gravity in 2026. Galileon scalar fields offer a route to late-time cosmic acceleration beyond the standard model. The frame is teleparallel gravity, where gravity acts through torsion and one parameter marks departures from the standard theory.

Two scalar curves, quadratic and exponential in shape, define four cases. The departure parameter is left free in two and fixed in the other two. Pantheon-plus supernovae, cosmic clocks, SH0ES input, and sound-wave data constrain all four. Each case can fit the late expansion history well. Statistical preference shifts with the potential and with fixing the parameter. The fixed-parameter quadratic case fits best among Galileon options once acoustic data join. Information criteria split: one rivals the standard model, the other still favours it for parsimony.
arxiv-2606-20005:
Guangda Liu and eight colleagues present StreamKL in 2026, a fused GPU primitive for attention distillation. Distillation trains one attention pattern to match another by shrinking their KL divergence, a measure of distribution mismatch. Standard code builds both full attention matrices first, so memory and data movement grow quadratically with context length. StreamKL derives an online form of the coupled two-distribution reduction that streams query-key tiles through on-chip memory in a single pass.

The backward pass recomputes probabilities tile by tile instead of storing quadratic intermediates. Extra high-bandwidth memory use falls from quadratic to constant. Forward speed rises up to forty-three-fold and backward speed up to fourteen-fold over baselines. Long-context distillation, sparse-attention training, and continual learning all become feasible on a single GPU.
arxiv-2606-20105:
Sebastian Falkner, Pablo Montero de Hijes, Christoph Dellago, and Nadine Schwierz benchmark neural network potentials for magnesium ions in water, central to biology yet hard to simulate. Their 2026 paper trains MACE potentials on two levels of density functional theory and asks whether the learned models reproduce what experiments measure. Classical force fields miss several properties at once, likely because they cannot capture quantum many-body effects. A learned potential trained on quantum data is an attractive replacement, if it holds up.

Both potentials nailed the octahedral first hydration shell, ion pairing, and diffusion rates. With rare-event sampling, they captured water exchange around the ion and showed it proceeds by a dissociative route, at rates within a factor of ten of experiment, far better than classical models. One clear failure stood out: solvation free energy came out far too low, flagging a real limit of current local architectures.
arxiv-2606-20205:
Jelena Meyer, David Garcia, and Dirk Wulff argue that the personality profiles often assigned to large language models are mostly an artifact of the measuring tools. Their 2026 paper applies a formal psychometric framework to personality and risk-preference tests given to fifty-six instruction-tuned models, alongside large human samples. Such instruments are now widely used to label models as stable personalities, with consequences for safety judgments and research use.

Four findings stand out. A directional response bias, a pull toward one end of each scale regardless of content, explained 81 to 90 percent of the differences between models, far above the human share. The bias shrank with capability but never vanished. An instrument's apparent reliability was predicted almost entirely by its response orthogonality, how often trait and bias point in opposite directions. Worst, a model's profile shifted with item choice and could be manufactured by selecting items.
arxiv-2606-20305:
Apurva Bhagat, Sumit Tambe, Debesh Bhattacharjee, and Prasad Subramanian hunt for turbulent spots inside coronal mass ejections, the vast plasma clouds the Sun throws toward Earth. Their 2026 paper analyzes near-Earth spacecraft data for 125 such ejections. Turbulent spots are local regions of intense fluctuation, a mark of intermittency. Because ejections drive the most severe space weather, any reliable early indicator of an event's leading edge has practical value for satellite operators.

Two statistics stand out. The intensity of the strongest spot, and how often spots occur, both reliably indicate the onset of the ejection's leading part. The spots also appear to be sites of enhanced proton heating. The findings sharpen understanding of this bursty behavior in collisionless plasma turbulence, and feed directly into prediction models for space weather impacts.
arxiv-2606-21005:
Sheng Zhang and many colleagues introduce Beaver in 2026, an agent harness for curation from multimodal papers. Workflows depend on structured records drawn from literature. Key evidence is scattered across long text, dense tables, and figures. Final records need reasoning across fragments, not copying one span.

Beaver combines a frontier agent with evidence tools, task scaffolding, and research loops. Curation becomes a staged, auditable workflow. An evaluate, diagnose, and revise loop uses persistent run artifacts to localize failures by stage. Scores reach a level far above frontier agents alone on an attribute agreement measure. Ablations show which harness parts drive the gains. Auditable curation matters because curated records feed databases that other scientists treat as ground truth.
arxiv-2606-21305:
Xiaoliang Wu and four colleagues propose LISE in 2026, a label-free way to open up speaker embeddings, the compact voice fingerprints that verification systems use to tell people apart. Those embeddings work well but hide which vocal traits they encode. LISE splits a pretrained embedding into a small set of components, each meant to carry one audible aspect of the voice, without needing attribute labels for training.

The split representation keeps verification accuracy nearly intact on x-vector and ECAPA-TDNN systems, with negligible change in equal error rate. In listening tests, participants told speakers apart from the components with 83.9 percent accuracy, showing the parts are meaningful to human ears. Such decompositions could help diagnose model bias and support controllable voice synthesis.
arxiv-2606-21405:
Youssef Haouchat, Aleix Boquet-Pujadas, Sepand Kashani, and Philippe Thevenaz present a tomography calibration method in 2026 that fixes scanner geometry and rebuilds the image at the same time. Tomography reconstructs a volume from line measurements, but real scanners drift from their nominal angles and positions, and those errors blur the result. Their framework handles arbitrary source and detector layouts rather than one fixed machine design.

The core is an X-ray transform operator whose sensitivity to each geometry parameter comes from an efficient ray-tracing scheme. The volume itself is written in a B-spline basis, a smooth representation that makes the joint optimization better behaved than voxel grids. Tests span CT, micro-CT, nano-CT, and positron emission tomography data under varied misalignment, showing the joint approach recovers both geometry and image.
arxiv-2606-21505:
Sarah Peery and Yi-Hsin Liu study in 2026 how shear flows and a guide field delay the onset of relativistic magnetic reconnection, the explosive rearrangement of magnetic field lines in high-energy plasmas. In non-relativistic theory, shear flow slows the tearing instability that kicks reconnection off. Whether the same holds when magnetic energy outweighs the plasma's rest energy, as near black holes and pulsars, needed checking with kinetic simulations.

Particle-in-cell runs confirm both shear flow and stronger guide fields postpone onset. The authors also build a numerical solver for the relativistic tearing growth rate that includes the motional electric field for the first time, matching the simulated slowing. At high shear, the system passes through an intermediate regime into Kelvin-Helmholtz instability instead. The results refine onset forecasts for jets with helical fields.
arxiv-2606-21605:
Marei Freitag and four colleagues present MuMatch in 2026, a framework that brings foundation models to electron microscopy without demanding mountains of hand-labeled images. Electron microscopy reveals cell ultrastructure at nanometer scale, but its labeling tasks are diverse and annotated data are scarce, so supervised training dominates and moves slowly. MuMatch adapts student-teacher semi-supervised methods and domain adaptation on top of large pretrained vision models.

The team evaluates several foundation models, including SAM, SAM2, MuSAM, and DINO variants, on mitochondrion, nucleus, and neurite tasks. Semi-supervised training with a small labeled core, plus adaptation across datasets, beats strong baselines throughout. The results chart a path to cutting labeling effort sharply in ultrastructure analysis, where every labeled image costs expert hours.
arxiv-2606-22005: This paper presents InstructFX2FX, a multi-turn text-to-preset demo for iterative audio effect refinement. The presenting presents. Their demo is multi-turn text-to-preset. The refinement is iterative audio effect. It is audio AI. InstructFX2FX fxes.
arxiv-2606-22505:
Lili Chen, Chenyang Jing, Kaiyuan Gao, Shuai Xu, and Mengfei Zhao calculate rare B meson decays in this 2026 particle physics paper. The decays turn anti-B mesons into charmed D mesons plus a scalar meson, either a strange K0 star or an a0. Scalar mesons are poorly understood, so predictions hinge on their assumed internal structure.

The team work within QCD factorization, adding next-to-leading order corrections to the basic calculation. Transition form factors, which encode how the quarks rearrange, come from an updated covariant light-front quark model. Branching ratios are estimated under two scenarios. In the second scenario, where scalars are the lowest-lying p-wave states, two decays stand out. The anti-B0 decay to D plus a0 minus, and its strange partner, can reach branching ratios around one in ten thousand. The authors argue these deserve priority searches at LHCb and SuperKEKB.
arxiv-2606-22905:
Quanyue Song and colleagues present a real-time avatar generator in this 2026 paper. Diffusion models can now produce realistic audio-driven avatars that stream live. Keeping such a video consistent over long sessions is hard, and most systems do not explicitly perceive what the user intends during an interaction.

Their framework, InteractiveAvatar, uses autoregressive distillation to generate avatar video in real time over arbitrarily long durations. A long-short visual memory compresses past frames into compact tokens, keeping both short-range coherence and long-term consistency. A second module handles intent, cycling through states and switching caches so the avatar's speech and actions match what the user means. In tests across varied scenarios, the system led on visual consistency for long videos. It also handled complex user-avatar interaction in real time.
arxiv-2606-23005:
