Joining the agreeing families' sequences produced a fully resolved family tree. The topology also held up under tests built to exclude uneven evolution rates. Organismal history, they conclude, survives in most of the genome.
europmc-pmc2125105:
Richard M. Pearce and Max Minor Peet, of the University of Pennsylvania, returned in 1913 to dogs that had lived a year without their spleens, the seventh paper of the spleen series. Two marks of the spleenless state had been found early: red cells that resist breaking, and a weaker tendency to jaundice after hemolytic serum. Do they last?

They do. A year after the operation the red cells' increased resistance is as plain as at any earlier period, and the blunted jaundice response persists with it. One easy explanation fails: the resistance cannot be credited to more young, reticulated cells in the blood, since those are not increased. Readers get a long follow-up proving an organ's absence can reset the blood for good.
europmc-pmc2125305:
James W. Jobling, William Petersen, and A. A. Eggstein of Vanderbilt's pathology department in Nashville studied trypsin shock in 1915, the twenty-second of the ferment series. Trypsin injected into dogs' veins produces a shock much like anaphylactic and peptone shock. The blood's chemistry during it is their subject.

Serum protease and lipase rise markedly after the injection. The antiferment, the blood's guard against its own ferments, drops distinctly and recovers within four to twenty-four hours. Non-coagulable nitrogen barely moves and never by much. Heat-killed preparations mimic some of the symptoms. Route decides everything: under the skin or by stomach the ferment is practically without effect, while absorption from the intestine either raises serum protease quietly or triggers outright poisoning. The white cell curve follows no constant relation to the ferment levels. Readers get shock translated into a balance sheet of enzymes and their keeper.
europmc-pmc2126405:
Hideyo Noguchi opened his yellow fever etiology series with the clinical and pathological picture of the disease in Guayaquil. His 1919 Journal of Experimental Medicine paper draws on cases admitted to the Yellow Fever Hospital there, directed by Dr. Wenceslao Pareja. He analyzed one hundred seventy-two cases, describing general features and single symptoms separately.

Nothing in the Guayaquil cases departed from what earlier students of yellow fever had described elsewhere, in epidemics and in settled regions alike. The disease there was classic in all its aspects, in symptoms and in post-mortem findings alike. That sameness matters for the series: a cause found in Guayaquil material can be tested against a standard, well-known disease picture. The paper therefore serves as the fixed clinical ground for the laboratory papers that follow it.
europmc-pmc2128205:
John W. Churchman, of Cornell, returned to the behavior of bacteria toward the dye gentian violet. His paper appeared in the Journal of Experimental Medicine in 1921. Earlier work had sorted bacteria into dye-loving and dye-shunning kinds and tied that split to the Gram stain. Churchman's new experiments disturb that tidy picture in several ways.

From a pure culture of a dye-shunning organism he isolated a dye-loving variant, a strain within a strain. Some Gram-negative strains also proved dye-positive, which breaks the assumed link between the two reactions. The dye reaction, he argues, cannot rest on a special affinity for one part of the dye molecule. Dead bacterial bodies placed between living bacteria and the dye partly shielded the living ones and let them grow. Divided-plate tests then showed how many traps wait between laboratory dye studies and real chemotherapy.
europmc-pmc2131305:
Binger and Christie, at the Hospital of The Rockefeller Institute for Medical Research, opened an experimental study of diathermy in 1927. Diathermy passes high frequency currents through the body to heat deep tissue, and it was used in treatment. Part one asks a basic question: how hot do the lungs actually get, compared with the rest of the body?

The pair built special thermocouples to read deep temperatures in anesthetized dogs. In life, inner body temperatures could be raised only a little above rectal temperature. Lung temperature normally sat slightly below rectal temperature, but during treatment-strength currents it rose slightly above instead. Right after death, deep tissue between the electrodes heated up sharply, a warning that living blood flow limits the heating.
europmc-pmc2131505:
James Gamble and Monroe McIver, with the assistance of Pauline Marsh and Dorothy Sloan, followed body fluid losses in a 1928 paper. A pancreatic fistula drains the gland's juice out of the body instead of into the gut. That steady loss was already known to kill. The pair set out to explain, step by step, what the body loses and from where.

The core event is a growing shortage of sodium and chloride, the salts needed in large amounts to build pancreatic juice. Water is lost with them, drawn first from the fluid between cells and from blood plasma. For about two thirds of the survival time, plasma stays near normal at the expense of the tissue fluids, and body weight falls from the start. At last plasma volume itself drops, grave symptoms follow, and death comes unless salts and water are replaced.
europmc-pmc2140505:
Wallace Fenn published a theoretical paper in 1922 on how living cells meet solid bodies. Working from surface tension alone, he treats a model fluid cell touching flat and curved surfaces. The paper derives the resting position of such a cell on a flat surface. Three surface tensions fix it: cell to fluid, fluid to solid, and solid to cell.

The same resting state follows from the contact angle where cell meets solid. Fenn then computes the surface energy at each stage of a cell swallowing a particle a quarter of its own size. No particle, it turns out, will be ingested unless the tensions would also make the cell spread without limit on a flat surface of the same stuff. Blood cell stickiness is a pure surface tension effect, he argues, though protoplasm flow also counts in real cells.
europmc-pmc2140705:
Crozier and Federighi wrote part two of the Limax locomotion study in 1925, from Rutgers and the Carnegie Institution. Part one had fixed the temperature law of the slug's pedal waves. Here the slug climbs vertically with added loads hung on it, and the wave pattern is measured again to see whether load breaks the rules.

It does not. The straight proportionality between speed and wave frequency, and between speed and single-wave size, holds under load. At equal speeds of progression, those quantities are the same whatever mass is lifted. The pedal organ, though driven by central impulses from the animal, thus works essentially as an independent effector, a self-running machine.
europmc-pmc2140905:
Henry Murray, with the assistance of Yetta Porosowsky, wrote part eleven of his physiological ontogeny series in 1926, on the chemistry of chicken embryo tissues. Under his standard incubation conditions, he measured acidity, chloride, total carbon dioxide, and protein in the tissues across the whole incubation period, as functions of age.

Tissue acidity and chloride both fall with age, fastest between the tenth and thirteenth days. Total carbon dioxide rises with age, perhaps as shell calcium carbonate is taken up and laid down as bone. Protein concentration rises too, fastest a little later, in the middle of the second week. Electrolytes, protein, and fat each change fastest at their own age, an order Murray reads as biochemical development proceeding by molecular mobility, not as one balanced shift.
europmc-pmc2211305:
Cole and Vassar reviewed BACE1 in 2007, the enzyme that starts production of beta-amyloid in Alzheimer's disease. Amyloid plaques are a hallmark of the disease, and beta-amyloid likely plays an early, central role. Mice lacking BACE1 make no beta-amyloid. They are also free of neuronal loss and certain memory deficits seen in the disease. BACE1 levels are elevated in Alzheimer's brains, strengthening the case for blocking it.

The review covers the enzyme's discovery, its normal biology and its dysregulation in disease. New data warn that abolishing BACE1 completely may cause behavioural and physiological changes. Several other proteins that BACE1 cuts have now been identified. Failing to process those substrates may explain some abnormalities in deficient mice. The authors also link vascular disease, a key risk factor, to the harmful BACE1 changes.
europmc-pmc2213705:
Wei and co-workers mapped in 2008 the gene network behind lifespan extension by calorie restriction in yeast. Eating less is the only intervention, short of genetic change, known to slow ageing from yeast to mice. It is linked to quieting the Tor, Akt and Ras nutrient pathways. The team deleted candidate genes and measured chronological lifespan, how long non-dividing yeast cells survive, under restriction and pathway defects.

A kinase called Rim15 proved required for lifespan gains from restriction and from Ras2, Tor1 or Sch9 defects. Removing stress-resistance factors Gis1 and Msn2/4, both switched on by Rim15, largely reversed the benefit. Deleting both RAS2 and SCH9 plus restricting calories gave a remarkable ten-fold lifespan extension. Losing Rim15 only partly reversed that combined effect, so extra mediators exist.
europmc-pmc2596305:
Salliot, Dougados, and Gossec pooled randomised trials in 2009. They checked whether three newer biological drugs for rheumatoid arthritis raise the risk of serious infections. Those are infections that threaten life or need hospital care. Tumour necrosis factor blockers, the older biologics, are known to raise this risk. The team analysed twelve placebo-controlled trials of rituximab, abatacept, and anakinra found through systematic searching to October 2007.

Across 745 rituximab, 1,960 abatacept, and 2,062 anakinra patients, neither rituximab nor abatacept showed a significant rise in serious infections against placebo. High-dose anakinra, at 100 milligrams daily or more, looked different. Its odds ratio reached 3.40 against placebo, and 9.63 against the low dose. The authors flag those figures as a real concern, especially in patients with other illnesses. They call for large practice-based studies to confirm the profile.
europmc-pmc2627605:
Corbel reviewed brucellosis in 1997, a bacterial disease passed from animals to people that remains a major zoonosis worldwide. Many countries had eradicated the cattle species Brucella abortus. But Brucella melitensis, from sheep and goats, had become the principal cause of human disease. Brucella suis was newly infecting cattle too. Distinctive strains from marine mammals had extended the genus's known range.

The review covers the bacterium's biology, from the surface sugars and stress proteins behind its virulence to the immune responses that protect against it. Diagnosis still rested on culturing the organism and antibody tests, with enzyme immunoassay replacing older methods and PCR under evaluation. Treatment relied on tetracyclines combined with other antibiotics. No satisfactory human vaccine existed, though engineered weakened mutants looked promising.
europmc-pmc2633005:
Bursac, Gauss, Williams, and Hosmer automated a model-building strategy for logistic regression in 2008, the statistical workhorse for yes-or-no medical outcomes. Choosing which candidate variables belong in a model is the central problem, and mechanical selection algorithms have known limitations. Statisticians Hosmer and Lemeshow had described purposeful selection. There, the analyst judges each variable step by step. This paper turns that craft into an algorithm.

The team tested their macro against three standard procedures in SAS software, forward, backward, and stepwise selection, in simulations. The advantage appeared when the goal was risk factor modelling rather than pure prediction. Beyond clearly significant variables, the method keeps important confounding variables. Mechanical rules drop those. The result is a slightly richer model. They demonstrate it on the Worcester Heart Attack Study data.
europmc-pmc2717805:
Campeau and co-authors presented in 2009 a set of fifty-nine viral vectors, DNA carriers that use viruses to enter cells, for adding or silencing proteins in mammalian cells. Studying a protein often means raising or lowering its amount, but hard-to-transfect cells resist normal methods. Older viral systems needed separate backbones for each job and offered few drug-selection options.

Their Gateway-based system shuttles a gene, silencing hairpin, or microRNA from an entry clone into many destination vectors with very high success. Options cover steady or switchable expression, retroviruses and lentiviruses, and fusion proteins. Tests included arresting cell division by protein control and driving primary cells into senescence, a permanent rest state.
europmc-pmc2852405:
Igosheva and colleagues showed in 2010 that a mother's obesity can damage the energy systems of her eggs and earliest embryos. Obese women conceive more slowly and miscarry more often, and the egg stage was the prime suspect. Using mice made obese by diet before conception, the team filmed living eggs and fertilized zygotes with fluorescent probes and measured their mitochondria, the inherited power units that fuel development.

Eggs from obese mothers ran hotter mitochondria with more DNA copies and new construction. Yet they leaked more damaging oxygen byproducts while their protective glutathione ran low, a picture of oxidative stress. The strain showed in outcomes: significantly more eggs from obese mothers failed to reach the blastocyst stage, the first milestone of embryo growth.
europmc-pmc2858705:
Bouvet and colleagues rebuilt in a test tube in 2010 how the SARS coronavirus caps its messenger RNA, a disguise that helps the virus make proteins. A cap is a small chemical tag added to the start of an RNA strand. The virus uses its own enzymes, called methyltransferases, to build the tag in steps.

The team showed the steps run in a fixed order and need three viral proteins, not two. First one enzyme adds the first methyl group, making a simple cap. Then a second enzyme adds another methyl group, but only when a helper protein switches it on. A known antiviral chemical blocked both enzymes at low doses, which marks the capping steps as promising drug targets.
europmc-pmc2865505:
Stegle, Parts, Durbin, and Winn built in 2010 a statistical method that cleans gene activity data before hunting for genetic effects. Gene readings shift with cell state, lab conditions, and hidden factors that can drown out real genetic signals. Their method, called VBQTL, models the gene of interest and the confounders together inside one probability framework.

Tested on simulated data and on yeast, mouse, and human sets, the method gave sharper estimates of each confounder's share. In a whole-genome scan of an outbred human group, it found three times as many nearby genetic effects on gene activity as earlier scans had reported. About a quarter of the tested gene probes showed a clear genetic link once the noise was handled properly.
europmc-pmc2865805:
Mukherjee, Ray, and Thakur reviewed in 2009 solid lipid nanoparticles, tiny fat-based spheres built to carry drugs through the body. The particles sit at the front of nanotechnology, the science of very small structures, because their size lets them enter tissues larger carriers cannot reach. Loading a drug inside can aim it at a chosen site and release it slowly.

Their survey compares the plain solid particles with two cousins, mixed-lipid carriers and lipid-drug pairs, and explains how their structures differ. It weighs clear advantages, such as low toxicity and cheap scale-up, against limits like drug leakage during storage, and offers fixes for each. Production routes suited to large batches and the lab tests used to check particle quality round out the guide.
europmc-pmc2868005:
McLeay and Bailey set out in 2010 to unify a common gene-control test and check which version works best. The test, motif enrichment analysis, asks which DNA-binding proteins likely control a set of genes by spotting their binding patterns, called motifs, in gene control regions. Until then the methods demanded a hand-picked gene set and an arbitrary cutoff signal.

Their framework accepts every control region labeled with a measured signal, with no gene list needed upfront. Some of their methods still use a cutoff, some find the best cutoff from the data, and two need no cutoff at all. Testing all of them on protein-binding data from real experiments showed which approaches recover true regulators most reliably, giving biologists a firmer basis for choosing.
europmc-pmc2872605:
Heidorn and colleagues uncovered in 2010 a paradox in which blocking a cancer growth switch can speed tumors up instead of slowing them. The switch, a protein called BRAF, drives melanoma and other cancers when mutated. Drugs that block BRAF help many patients, but tumors with a second faulty switch, called RAS, react in the opposite way.

In those cells the blocked BRAF teams up with a sister protein, CRAF, and together they fire the growth pathway even harder. A working-dead form of BRAF copied the drug effect exactly, and pairing it with faulty RAS produced melanoma in mice. Blocking healthy BRAF alone did not cause the effect. Tumors should be gene-tested before treatment, the authors urge, to find who might be harmed.
europmc-pmc3016705:
Sur and Sinha gave an overview of event-related potentials, tiny brain voltages locked to specific events, in a 2009 article aimed at psychiatry readers. Recording scalp electricity in step with stimuli exposes both sensory and thinking processes without any invasion.

Distinct waveform bumps mark stages of processing. They run from early sensation to attention, memory updating, and error spotting. The review explains each major component, then tours findings across psychiatric conditions, where amplitudes and timings often shift with illness. Because the signals reflect summed brain activity tied to chemical messengers, they offer a window on faulty brain control.
europmc-pmc3040205:
Pena and a nationwide team measured in 2011 the genetic ancestry of Brazilians from four regions, testing whether skin color labels match ancestry. Brazil's population mixes European, African, and Native American roots, and medical studies had long treated regions as sharply different based on color counts. The team used forty ancestry informative DNA markers on more than nine hundred volunteers who labeled themselves white, brown, or black.

Ancestry varied a lot within every color label, and the same label meant different mixes in the north and the south. When the team weighted results by official census shares, a more uniform picture emerged. European ancestry led in every region, making up roughly three fifths to over three quarters of the total. The authors tie this to the large European immigration of the past two centuries, part of a stated whitening policy.
europmc-pmc3110205:
Charles Runckel and colleagues published a 2011 field study in PLoS ONE tracking germs in honey bees over a full season. Bees pollinate many food crops, yet colonies in several regions had been dying in an unexplained pattern. The team sampled a large migratory beekeeping operation often, using chip tests, targeted gene tests, and very deep sequencing.

Known bee viruses and a gut parasite peaked in summer, while a fungal parasite and one new virus peaked in midwinter. Deep sequencing also uncovered four viruses never described before, two of them present in huge amounts in the bees. The work gives a baseline of normal infection patterns, without which sick colonies cannot be judged fairly.
europmc-pmc3167805:
Florent Mouliere and colleagues reported that tumour DNA floating in blood is chopped far smaller than normal DNA in a 2011 paper in PLoS ONE. Such circulating DNA is a hoped-for cancer test, but past studies disagreed wildly on amounts, partly for lack of standard handling. The team measured fragment sizes carefully in mice carrying human colon tumours and in patients with metastatic bowel cancer.

Tumour-derived fragments clustered at short lengths, and both their amount and their fragmentation rose with tumour weight. Measurement worked best when targeting short stretches, which much past work had missed. Patients showed several-fold higher fragmentation than healthy volunteers. A size-aware blood test, the authors suggest, could separate tumour signal from background far better than raw quantity alone.
europmc-pmc3176805:
Xiao-Wei Song and colleagues released a free toolkit for analysing resting brain scans in a 2011 paper in PLoS ONE. Brain imaging at rest, with no task, had boomed for studying intrinsic networks, but no public, integrated, easy tool existed for processing the data. Their package runs inside a common scientific platform with a point-and-click window.

After standard preparation elsewhere, the toolkit computes linked activity between regions, local synchrony, and the strength of slow spontaneous fluctuations in two forms. Helper functions sort scanner files, strip trends, filter signals, extract time courses, remove nuisance effects, run statistics, and display corrected results. The open-source package aims to standardise resting-state analysis so results compare cleanly across labs.
europmc-pmc3199605:
Humberto Lara and colleagues reviewed silver nanoparticles as germ-killing compounds in this 2011 article in the Journal of Nanobiotechnology. Silver has a long history as an antimicrobial, and making it into particles a few nanometers wide opened new medical possibilities. The authors survey evidence that these particles can kill bacteria and also act against viruses.

Much of the antiviral evidence comes from HIV research, where the particles were shown to interfere with the virus and to block transmission in cultured human cervix tissue. The review explains how the particles are thought to attach to viral outer surfaces and prevent infection. The authors present the field as young and largely unexplored, with prevention and treatment uses still to be proven.
europmc-pmc3210605:
Sara Bordbar, Farooq Anwar, and Nazamid Saari reviewed the food and health value of sea cucumbers in this 2011 article in Marine Drugs. These marine animals, long eaten and used in folk medicine across Asia and the Middle East, are rich in vitamins and minerals. The authors gather what is known about their useful compounds.

Sea cucumbers contain a wide array of bioactive substances, including saponins, chondroitin sulfates, sulfated polysaccharides, peptides, and essential fatty acids. Studies have linked these compounds to effects ranging from antioxidant and anti-inflammatory action to blood-clot prevention and tumor inhibition. The review weighs that evidence to judge how sea cucumbers might serve as functional foods or nutraceutical ingredients, beyond their established place in regional cuisines.
europmc-pmc3222005:
Constantine Karvellas and colleagues pooled the evidence on when to start dialysis-like blood cleaning. Their patients were critically ill adults whose kidneys had failed suddenly. The review and meta-analysis appeared in Critical Care in 2011. Timing was controversial, and trials disagreed. The team searched major databases through mid-2010 for studies comparing early against late initiation.

Fifteen studies qualified, only two of them randomized trials, and overall quality was low. Pooling suggested early treatment was linked to clearly lower mortality at twenty-eight days, though the studies differed greatly from one another. Most studies also reported faster kidney recovery, shorter treatment, and shorter intensive care stays with early starts, but no clear difference in long-term dialysis dependence. The authors stress that better trials are needed before a firm recommendation.
europmc-pmc3226505:
C. Arden Pope and colleagues compared how fine-particle exposure drives two causes of death, in this 2011 study in Environmental Health Perspectives. Smoking, secondhand smoke, and polluted air all deliver tiny particles. Those particles raise the risk of lung cancer and cardiovascular death. But the shape of the risk curve at different doses was unclear. The team used a huge American Cancer Society cohort of well over a million adults.

For cardiovascular death, risk climbed steeply even at low exposure, then flattened at high doses. For lung cancer, risk kept rising in a nearly straight line, reaching very high levels in heavy smokers. The difference matters for policy: at low pollution levels cardiovascular deaths dominate the projected burden, while lung cancer grows in relative importance where exposure is high. Burden estimates that flatten both curves would understate lung cancer.
europmc-pmc3228705:
Ravi Subramanian and colleagues catalogued a family of fossil viruses embedded in the human genome, in this 2011 paper in Retrovirology. Long ago, retroviruses infected germ cells and became permanent, inherited DNA. The HERV-K HML-2 group is the most recently active of these families, and many copies still carry readable genes whose activity rises in several cancers and other disorders.

No previous study had characterized every HML-2 element, so the team produced the most complete catalog yet, covering full and partial proviruses plus the lone leftover promoter pieces. They corrected several annotation errors, including a mislabeled subgroup, and found these elements are preferentially kept on gene-rich chromosomes and near genes. The catalog lays groundwork for testing whether these ancient viruses contribute to disease.
europmc-pmc3286505:
Reintam Blaser led an international working group whose 2012 recommendations set shared language for gut problems in very sick patients. Specialists in intensive care had long used conflicting terms, which made studies hard to compare. The group, working under a European intensive care society, built its definitions from published evidence and expert judgment.

Their system names acute gut injury and grades it in four steps, from raised risk up to organ failure that threatens life at once. It also defines feeding intolerance and common symptoms such as vomiting, diarrhea, and stalled stomach emptying. Alongside the terms, the authors give practical advice on treatment and urge doctors and researchers to adopt the shared definitions.
europmc-pmc3294705:
Bakonyi and colleagues reported West Nile virus strains found in birds in central Europe, in a 2006 paper. The virus, spread by mosquitoes, is the most widespread member of its virus group and had been known in the region for decades without causing illness. Genetic family trees divide its strains into two main lineages, with the second long thought to live only in Africa.

The team describes illness in geese and a goshawk in Hungary caused by a lineage two strain, the first time such a strain was seen causing brain inflammation outside Africa. A lineage one strain also appeared in the region. Comparing the two lineages side by side helps scientists track how this virus moves and changes across continents.
europmc-pmc3306205:
McCormack and Shiell reviewed whether neighborhood design truly causes people to be more active, in a 2011 paper. Studies link walkable surroundings to more walking and exercise, but most are snapshots that cannot rule out a simple explanation. Active people may simply choose to live in active friendly places, a bias called self selection.

The review kept only studies that adjusted for that bias or that used natural experiments. Most links between surroundings and activity pointed the expected way or vanished. Mixed land use, connected streets, higher density, and overall design quality stood out as real influences. Surroundings mattered most for walking to get somewhere, rather than walking for leisure. A few studies saw links weaken once self selection was handled, and the authors call for more experiments.
europmc-pmc3406005:
Salathé and many colleagues introduced digital epidemiology in 2012, a field born from the flood of data people shed online and by phone. Health agencies have long gathered disease data through clinics and field staff. Digital traces, from searches to social posts, can now report illness faster and closer to real time.

Early wins include tracking flu activity almost live, spotting odd outbreaks in remote places, mapping crowd movement during epidemics, and gauging vaccine sentiment during pandemic planning. The authors stress the technical challenge of sifting meaning from the deluge. Done well, they argue, these streams complement traditional surveillance and cross borders that official systems cannot.
europmc-pmc3436805:
Rausch and co-workers released DELLY in 2012, a program that finds large structural changes in genomes from sequencing data at single-letter precision. Such rearrangements, from deletions to flips and swaps between chromosomes, drive both normal variation and cancer. Older tools caught only parts of the spectrum.

DELLY merges three kinds of evidence: oddly spaced read pairs, long-range mate pairs, and reads split across a breakpoint. That blend lets it catch deletions, tandem duplications, inversions, and balanced swaps, including tangled events. On simulated data it beat rival methods across many settings, and on real data from the 1000 Genomes Project and cancers it held up, with spot checks confirming high accuracy. The software is freely available.
europmc-pmc3441905:
Kellman, Wilson, Xue, Ugander, and Arai built an automated method in 2012 for mapping the water-and-matrix space between heart muscle cells, a measure that swells in scarring and edema. Standard contrast scans miss diffuse scarring spread evenly through the heart. Their method combines pre- and post-contrast relaxation maps, calibrated by a blood measure, into a pixel-by-pixel map.

Automation is the point: the program fixes breathing motion between scans and finds the blood pool itself, tasks that otherwise eat expert time. Across six hundred maps from several hundred patients, over four fifths rated good or excellent, and alignment fixes improved most maps. Healthy heart muscle values came out tight and consistent. The team says clinical workflow is now realistic.
europmc-pmc3458305:
Eggenhofer and co-workers tracked infused mesenchymal stem cells in mice in 2012 to learn where they go and how long they live. These cells are in trials for many disorders, and animal studies show lasting benefits, but the cells' own fate after infusion was murky. Donor cells were tagged with a glowing protein and a radioactive label, then hunted across organs by culture and counting.

An hour after infusion most label sat in the lungs, and living donor cells could be grown back only from lung, and only within the first day. By three days they were gone everywhere, and debris, not living cells, reached the liver. Even injuring the liver failed to lure viable cells there. Lasting benefits, the authors conclude, must work through other cells the infusion stirs up.
europmc-pmc3557905:
Martin Jinek and colleagues, including Jennifer Doudna, published a short methods paper in eLife in 2013 on editing genes in human cells with RNA guidance. Bacteria use a system called CRISPR, where a protein named Cas9 cuts foreign DNA at sites picked by a guide RNA. The authors tested whether that bacterial tool could be made to cut chosen sites in human DNA.

Inside human cells, Cas9 joined with hybrid guide RNAs and made double-strand breaks exactly where the RNA sequence pointed. Both the protein and correct RNA binding were required for cutting. Tests with cell extracts showed that making and loading the RNA was the step that limited how much cutting occurred. Adding length to one end of the RNA improved targeting. The paper presents RNA-guided editing as a simple route to planned changes in human cells.
europmc-pmc3561105:
Yu Zhang and colleagues published a genomics study in PLoS Genetics in 2013 on four related transcription factors in Arabidopsis seedlings. Seedlings grown in darkness follow a pale, elongated growth plan, and four proteins called PIFs keep that plan running. Light triggers destruction of the PIFs and switches the seedling to normal green growth. How the four factors divide their shared work was the open question.

Combining maps of where PIF3 binds DNA with gene activity data, the group listed its direct target genes. Tests in seedlings missing different PIF combinations then showed a patchwork: each gene answers to the four factors in its own mix of strength and direction. Since all four bind the same short DNA motifs, the pattern likely comes from sharing the same binding sites. The work explains how near-identical regulators still produce varied output.
europmc-pmc3564705:
Zachary Burningham, Mia Hashibe, Logan Spector, and Joshua Schiffman reviewed the epidemiology of sarcoma in Clinical Sarcoma Research in 2012. Sarcomas are cancers of bone and soft tissue. They make up over a fifth of solid cancers in children but under one percent in adults, and what raises a person's risk is still poorly mapped compared with common cancers.

Risks sort into three groups in the review: exposures, inherited susceptibility, and the two combined. Radiation from earlier cancer treatment is firmly tied to later sarcoma, with bone tumor risk climbing as dose rises. Certain jobs and chemicals, such as herbicides and chlorophenols, are suggested risks, and growth during puberty is linked to bone sarcoma in the young. Infections play a defined role for Kaposi sarcoma. Readers get one gathered account of a rare, scattered evidence base.
europmc-pmc3566605:
Gina Dillon, Rafat Hussain, Deborah Loxton, and Saifur Rahman reviewed the health toll of intimate partner violence against women in the International Journal of Family Medicine in 2013. Violence by a partner is a public health problem in rich and poor countries alike. Their review gathers what studies from 2006 to 2012 show about the mental and physical damage that follows such abuse.

Seventy-five papers, from Western and developing countries, paint a consistent picture despite rates varying by culture. Partner violence was tied to depression, post-traumatic stress, anxiety, self-harm, and broken sleep. Physical effects ran from chronic pain and lasting poor function to gynecological problems and raised risk of sexually transmitted infections, including HIV after sexual abuse. Most studies used validated measures, which strengthens the pattern. The authors close with what the findings mean for clinics and for better research design.
europmc-pmc3597605:
Luc Biedermann and colleagues tracked gut bacteria through smoking cessation in PLoS ONE in 2013. The gut community is tied to bowel inflammation and metabolic disease, and smoking shapes both, yet its effect on the microbes themselves was little studied. Ten healthy smokers gave stool samples across nine weeks of a controlled quit program, while five continuing smokers and five non-smokers served as comparisons.

Quitting reshaped the gut in clear strokes. Two large bacterial groups, Firmicutes and Actinobacteria, grew, while Bacteroidetes and Proteobacteria shrank, and overall variety rose. The new profile resembled the gut pattern reported in obesity rather than leanness. That echo raises a testable idea: the well-known weight gain after quitting may run partly through the microbes. The authors frame smoking as a genuine environmental force on the human gut community.
europmc-pmc3617005:
Paola Longati and colleagues grew pancreatic cancer in three dimensions in BMC Cancer in 2013. Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma kills nearly every patient it strikes, largely by shrugging off chemotherapy. Drugs that pass flat, two-dimensional cell culture tests then fail in people, raising the suspicion that flat culture itself lies. Their team grew human and mouse pancreatic cancer lines as floating balls called spheroids, using a simple additive to help them form, and profiled what changed.

Ball-grown cells poured out scaffolding proteins, switched their fuel use toward sugar fermentation, and raised a handful of marker genes and one microRNA sharply. Against a panel of new drug candidates benchmarked to the standard drug gemcitabine, nearly all drugs weakened in the ball model, matching the clinic's hard reality, while three compounds kept their punch. The system runs at screening scale, offering drug hunters a cheaper early warning than flat plates gave.
europmc-pmc3656905:
Melatonin helps sleep, but only a little, Ferracioli-Oda, Qawasmi and Bloch find in a 2013 meta-analysis in PLoS ONE. Melatonin is a body hormone sold as a sleep aid, tested against dummy pills for primary sleep disorders, where no other cause explains the poor sleep. The team searched a major data bank for such trials and pooled three outcomes: time to fall asleep, total sleep time and sleep quality.

Nineteen studies with 1,683 people made the pool. Melatonin cut the time to fall asleep by about seven minutes and added about eight minutes of sleep. Sleep quality scores rose by a small margin too. Longer trials and higher doses showed bigger gains on the two time measures. The gains are modest next to drug aids, but a mild side-effect record may still earn it a place in care.
europmc-pmc3657405:
Antioxidant pills can help or harm, and the dose of stress decides which, Poljsak, Šuput and Milisav argue in a 2013 review in Oxidative Medicine and Cellular Longevity. Reactive oxygen forms, short-lived chemicals made in daily body work, damage cells over time, yet some serve as signals cells need. Supplements that mop them up are hugely popular. Yet some trials found such pills did nothing, and a few found raised death rates.

Balance is the core claim: too much oxidative stress harms, and too little harms too, since the body needs some reactive forms for signalling. Cutting stress that is not there helps no one. The authors urge that a person's own stress level be measured well before supplements are prescribed. When synthetic antioxidants are used, timing and need should lead, not habit.
europmc-pmc3661305:
Telling a crystal's hand, left or right, can be done with finer tools, Parsons, Flack and Wagner show in a 2013 article in Acta Crystallographica Section B. Crystal builders refine a model against X-ray reflections, and pairs of reflections that mirror each other, called Friedel pairs in the text, carry the hand signal. For light-atom crystals the signal is faint, and plain methods leave the hand unsure.

The authors define two ways to use those pairs in refinement: gaps between pair members, and ratios of their strengths. Fed into the fit, these measures fix the hand with high precision. The gain holds even for light-atom crystals, where the hand signal is weakest. For chemists who must know which mirror form they hold, since drug action can turn on that hand, the method tightens a long-loose step.
europmc-pmc3708105:
Ma and Chan review type 2 diabetes in East Asian populations, where the disease is epidemic yet looks different from its European and American forms. East Asian patients typically develop diabetes at a lower body weight and younger age. They carry more fat around the organs at any given weight. They also show early failure of insulin-producing beta cells, on top of insulin resistance.

These patients face higher risks of kidney complications and a tilt toward stroke among cardiovascular outcomes, while cancer is emerging as a leading cause of death. Rising childhood and young-onset diabetes worries the authors most. They call for urgent awareness, earlier diagnosis, and prevention fitted to Asian populations.
europmc-pmc3715105:
Unjali Gujral, R Pradeepa, Mary Beth Weber, K. M. Venkat Narayan, and V. Mohan wrote a review in the Annals of the New York Academy of Sciences in 2013 on type 2 diabetes in South Asians. People with roots in India, Pakistan, and nearby countries face very high rates of the disease, both at home and abroad, and rates keep rising fast.

The review sets out the body traits and life conditions that raise that risk, and compares South Asians with white and other groups. Built-in susceptibility mixes with rapid shifts in diet, activity, and daily life. The authors call for prevention that starts early, acts strongly at both the personal and population level, and fits the culture of the people it serves.
europmc-pmc3717505:
Snorre Stuen, Erik Granquist, and Cornelia Silaghi wrote a review in Frontiers in Cellular and Infection Microbiology in 2013 on Anaplasma phagocytophilum, a bacterium spread by Ixodes ticks. It has long been known for causing tick-borne fever in farm animals in northern Europe. More recently it has been found across much of the northern half of the world, in many mammal hosts.

The review centers on the ecology and spread of the bacterium, and on the role of wildlife in keeping it going. Illness ranges from silent infection to fatal disease in animals and in people, and many cases are likely missed. Several genetic variants exist, but few full genomes are done, so how the variants differ in spread and harm is still unclear.
europmc-pmc3899005:
Elie Jami, Bryan A. White, and Itzhak Mizrahi link rumen microbes to milk traits in PLoS One, with the record dated 2014. Cows depend wholly on rumen bacteria to digest feed. The team ask whether the mix of those bacteria tracks with how much milk a cow gives and what is in it.

Deep gene reads charted the rumen community in a group of dairy cows alongside their yield and milk make-up. Several measures tied strongly to the levels of particular bacterial members. The ratio of two big bacterial phyla tracked milk fat output, echoing a pattern seen in human gut studies of body fat. Genus-level links added detail. The authors propose shaping the rumen mix to lift farm yield.
europmc-pmc3933205:
Brynmor Lloyd-Evans and colleagues review trials of peer support for people with severe mental illness in BMC Psychiatry in 2014. Peer support, where people with lived experience of mental illness support others, has spread into services worldwide on strong enthusiasm but thin proof. The team searched major databases to July 2013 for randomized trials of non-residential peer support.

Eighteen trials with 5,597 participants covered mutual support groups, peer support services, and services delivered by peers. Reporting was incomplete and bias risk high. The pooled results showed little or no effect on hospital use, overall symptoms, or satisfaction with services. There were some positive signs for hope, recovery, and empowerment, though they were inconsistent. The authors conclude that current trial evidence does not back mandating peer support in services.
europmc-pmc3988705:
Jhalka Kadariya, Tara C. Smith, and Dipendra Thapaliya review staphylococcal food-borne disease in BioMed Research International in 2014. The illness comes from food spoiled by toxins made ahead of time by Staphylococcus aureus. It ranks among the most common food-borne illnesses in the world and in the United States.

Symptoms include nausea, vomiting, and belly cramps, with or without loose stools. One toxin, called SEA, is heat stable and causes most cases worldwide. Poor food handling in shops explains most outbreaks, yet the germ also turns up in raw retail meat. Safe handling, a steady cold chain, clean tools, and care from farm to fork form the core advice. Gaps in research and in watch systems still need work.
europmc-pmc4009805:
Matthias Dodt, Johannes T. Roehr, Rina Ahmed, and Christoph Dieterich present a tool for cleaning DNA sequencing reads, in Biology in 2012. Modern sequencers yield millions of short reads at once. Reads often carry extra tags: adapter bits from the machine process, barcodes that mark which sample a read came from, or natural leader bits from the source organism.

Their software, FLEXBAR, spots such tags by exact overlap matching, then sorts or trims them with wide scope for tuning. It handles formats from all current platforms, keeps read pairs matched, and can process barcode reads on their own when asked. Fine settings let users set where to search and how strict the match must be. The tool runs on many threads, pairing speed with care. Tests cover read mapping, sorting pooled samples back apart, and spotting splice leader bits in worm data. One command can run a whole multi-step job.
europmc-pmc4010405:
Kasandra Burgos and a team of co-authors hunt for disease markers in body fluids from patients with Alzheimer's or Parkinson's disease, in PLoS ONE in 2014. Brain tissue cannot be sampled in life, which has slowed the search for clear markers. Tiny RNAs, called microRNAs, leave brain cells in small sacs and ride safely in blood and spinal fluid.

The team sequenced the small RNAs in spinal fluid and blood serum from people who had died with full brain checks after death. Groups held close to seventy Alzheimer's patients, a like number with Parkinson's, and somewhat more healthy controls. Thirteen new microRNAs turned up. Levels of many shifted with disease traits such as plaque and tangle counts, Lewy body spread, and stage of damage. Many shifts matched changes already reported in brain tissue. The results suggest fluid microRNA profiles mirror cell changes in the diseased brain.
europmc-pmc4069805:
Danny R. Youlden, Susanna M. Cramb, Cheng Har Yip, and Peter D. Baade reviewed breast cancer rates and deaths among women across the Asia-Pacific region. Their overview appeared in Cancer Biology and Medicine in 2014. They drew on public cancer registry and mortality databases, plus data requested from single registries.

Breast cancer was the most common cancer in women in the region in 2012 and the fourth-ranked cause of cancer death. Rates stayed highest in Australia and New Zealand, but rose fast in several Asian countries. Death rates climbed in many places, notably Malaysia and Thailand, while falling in Australia and New Zealand. Trends were kinder for women under fifty. Early detection and good treatment access, the authors say, are key, though money and culture still block them.
europmc-pmc4158905:
Max A. Schlager, Simon L. Bullock, Andrew P. Carter, and colleagues rebuilt the human dynein transport complex from scratch and watched it move. Their study appeared in The EMBO Journal in 2014. Dynein hauls cargo toward one end of the cell's microtubule tracks, yet single mammalian motors had seemed poor walkers in dishes.

The fully recombinant complex, produced from one engineered virus in insect cells, rarely moved directionally alone. Adding its partner dynactin plus the cargo adaptor piece BICD2N produced steady one-way travel over remarkably long distances. Single-molecule imaging showed the partners switch each motor into a persistent mode rather than bundling motors together. Electron images showed an ordered assembly, dynactin lying along the dynein tail. The work links cargo binding to long-distance movement.
europmc-pmc4177405:
Hod Dana, Karel Svoboda, and seven co-authors built a new kind of imaging mouse and reported it in PLoS ONE in 2014. Brain researchers watch nerve cells fire by using proteins that glow when calcium rises. Getting those proteins into the brain usually means injecting a virus, which gives uneven and short-lived results.

The team bred mice that carry the sensor protein GCaMP6 in their own genes, switched on in nerve cells by the Thy1 promoter. Three mouse lines were tested for imaging in the visual cortex of living animals, and their signals matched or beat virus-injected mice. Because every cell carries the sensor from birth, the same cells can be watched for long stretches, even while the mice move and behave.
europmc-pmc4212005:
Limei Wang, Elke H. Heiss, and ten co-authors reviewed natural compounds that switch on a metabolic receptor in Biochemical Pharmacology in 2014. The receptor, PPAR gamma, helps control fat storage and insulin sensitivity, and drugs that activate it treat type 2 diabetes, though with side effects. Plants make many compounds that touch the same switch more gently.

The review gathers natural activators reported in the literature, among them magnolol and honokiol from magnolia bark, resveratrol, quercetin, and the amorfrutins. Many act as partial activators, which may keep the blood sugar benefit while trimming the weight gain and fluid retention of full-strength drugs. The authors compare binding and cell data for each compound and weigh which are plausible leads for safer metabolic medicines.
europmc-pmc4214605:
Gleb Kichaev, Bogdan Pasaniuc, and seven co-authors sharpened the hunt for causal DNA variants in PLoS Genetics in 2014. Gene scans flag neighbourhoods linked to a trait, but each neighbourhood holds many near-identical variants, and only lab tests can prove which one matters. Picking the right few to test is the bottleneck.

Their method folds in functional clues, such as whether a variant sits in a gene's start region or in a stretch of DNA that is switched off. It learns each clue's weight from the scan data itself. In simulations it cut the list needed to catch 90 percent of causal variants from 13.3 to 10.4 per site, beating rival tools. A check on four blood fat traits in real data backed the approach.
europmc-pmc4297605:
Yi Wang and Tian Liu review quantitative susceptibility mapping, a way to turn MRI phase data into a measure of tissue magnetism. Their review appeared in Magnetic Resonance in Medicine in 2015. Tissues differ in how they respond to a magnetic field, largely through iron and myelin content, but older MRI contrasts mix those sources in confusing ways.

Working back from the measured field to the tissue property is mathematically tricky, with gaps where the scanner picks up no signal. The review covers new fixes, including Bayesian methods, that make the maps stable and physically meaningful. Reliable susceptibility maps could serve as a biomarker for brain and body diseases where iron balance goes wrong.
europmc-pmc4306305:
Alexander F. Palazzo and Eliza S. Lee ask how much of the RNA copied from non-coding DNA does anything at all. Their essay appeared in Frontiers in Genetics in 2015. Most of the genome in large organisms does not code for proteins, yet cells transcribe much of it at low levels, and these transcripts have collected many names and much hype.

The authors push back on the view that existence proves function. Drawing on evolution and on how the gene reading machinery works, they argue much low level transcription is noise the cell tolerates. They set out criteria a transcript should meet before being called functional. The piece is a skeptical counterweight in a fast moving debate.
europmc-pmc4362205:
Kazuhiro Nitta and colleagues compared how gene switches bind DNA across flies and mammals, in eLife in 2015. Transcription factors are proteins that bind DNA and turn genes on or off. Species differ in body form, and one possible cause is change in what these factors bind. Earlier comparisons used different methods in each species, so the team measured binding for 242 fruit fly factors with one shared approach and compared the results with human and mouse data.

Binding tastes proved highly conserved between flies and mammals, split by about 600 million years of evolution. For matched factor pairs, likeness held down to fine details of DNA letter pairs. The few human factors that did differ work in cell types flies lack. That hints that new binding tastes help create new kinds of cells.
europmc-pmc4405705:
Zhenjiang Xu and Rob Knight reviewed how diet shapes the diversity of the human gut microbiome, in the British Journal of Nutrition in 2015. The gut hosts a complex microbial ecosystem that interacts with host and environment. Studies across Western and non-Western populations, and across ages, show how widely that ecosystem varies. Of all outside factors, the review concludes, long-term diet has the largest effect found so far on gut community makeup.

Short diet interventions can shift the microbiome dramatically within days, yet the community usually bounces back, and brief interventions have not succeeded in treating obesity or malnutrition. That resilience cuts both ways: it resists harm but also resists therapy. Xu and Knight argue that learning the dynamics of these shifts, in health and disease, is the route to using diet as reliable medicine.
europmc-pmc4408605:
Sonia Dalkin, Joanne Greenhalgh, Diana Jones, Bill Cunningham, and Monique Lhussier clarified a key concept in realist evaluation, in Implementation Science in 2015. Realist evaluation judges complex social programs by asking what works, how, in which conditions, and for whom, using linked context, mechanism, and outcome patterns. Its central term, mechanism, is often confused in practice, which makes studies hard to compare and repeat. The authors set out to develop the concept further.

They argue for splitting a mechanism into two parts: the resources a program offers, and the change in participants' reasoning that those resources trigger. That split also sharpens the line between context and mechanism. Mechanisms, they stress, act on a continuum, not as an on-off switch that simply fires. The paper is a teaching piece, aimed at evaluators learning the method.
europmc-pmc4489005:
Ritesh Maharaj, Ivan Raffaele, and Julia Wendon pooled studies of rapid response systems in Critical Care in 2015. Many hospitals have adopted teams that rush to ward patients who are deteriorating, hoping to prevent cardiac arrest and death. Adoption ran ahead of proof, and whether these systems actually cut hospital mortality was uncertain.

Searching four databases for studies from 1990 to 2013, the team found twenty-nine eligible reports, split into adult and child studies and by study design; most were simple before-and-after comparisons. Introducing a rapid response system was associated with lower hospital mortality in both adults and children, and with fewer cardiopulmonary arrests in adults. Results varied a lot between hospitals, though, and few studies used strong designs with a comparison group. The authors present the benefit as real but its size as unsettled.
europmc-pmc4551905:
Ruijie Liu leads a ten-author team improving statistics for gene expression studies, in Nucleic Acids Research in 2015. RNA sequencing compares gene activity between groups, but small studies often include samples of uneven quality. Dropping noisy samples wastes data and power; keeping them flat can bury real changes in static.

Their approach keeps every sample but weights each observation by its trustworthiness. A variance model estimates how noisy each sample runs across all genes, and those factors merge with per-measurement weights from the count data itself. Trials on simulated and real data showed more power to detect true differences than dropping or flatly keeping poor samples. The method slots into standard expression analysis pipelines.
europmc-pmc4596905:
Natarajan Jain and three colleagues published a 2015 review of linker chemistry in antibody-drug conjugates, or ADCs. These drugs join a cancer-seeking antibody to a toxic payload through a chemical linker. Two ADCs were already on the market, and many more were in trials. The review appeared in Pharmaceutical Research.

The authors report that 40 ADCs were in clinical development, with structures published for 34 of them. Most attach the linker to cysteine sites on the antibody, while the rest use lysine sites. Because attachment points vary, each batch is a mixture, so research now pushes toward site-specific attachment at engineered spots. More uniform products should allow better linker design and more predictable drug behaviour in patients.
europmc-pmc4612505:
A 2015 review from Norbert Müller and colleagues centres on the role of inflammation in schizophrenia. Patients often show raised levels of inflammatory substances in blood and spinal fluid. The review pulls together evidence from genetics, brain imaging, and studies of infection and stress. It appeared in Frontiers in Cellular Neuroscience.

Severe infections and autoimmune disorders raise schizophrenia risk, and a strong genetic signal sits in an immune-related region of chromosome 6. Chronic stress can also keep inflammation switched on. Active immune signals disturb several brain chemical systems and switch on an enzyme that alters serotonin and glutamate pathways. Brain scans showing volume loss and active microglia fit a slow inflammatory process. The authors present a model joining vulnerability, stress, and inflammation.
europmc-pmc4631205:
A 2015 mouse study from Adil Mardinoglu and colleagues centres on how gut microbes reshape the body's handling of amino acids and glutathione. Germ-free mice, raised with no microbes, were compared with normal mice. The team combined gene activity data with computer models of metabolism in twenty-eight tissues. The work appeared in Molecular Systems Biology.

The models predicted that microbes shift amino acid use across gut, liver, and fat tissues, with knock-on effects on glutathione, a key protective molecule. Blood measurements from the vein draining the gut confirmed changed amino acid levels. Simulations of the small intestine matched the pattern when diet content was included. The study shows gut microbes act as a body-wide metabolic organ.
europmc-pmc4667405:
In 2015, a review of exercise trials for frail older adults was published by Carmen de Labra and colleagues. Low activity sits at the heart of frailty, and exercise might halt or undo it. They searched three databases for trials from 2003 to 2015 that took in people classed as frail and put them on an exercise plan.

Nine trials passed the screen, most of them testing mixed programs, and their quality was scored on a set scale. Five trials counted falls, and three found that exercise cut them. Six counted how well people moved, and four showed gains on more than one measure. The control groups mostly kept their old habits. The sum of the work backs exercise as a real tool against frailty, and shows which gains come most often.
europmc-pmc4677105:
A 2015 review by Netalie Shloim and colleagues deals with how parenting style, feeding style, and feeding habits link to the weight of children aged four to twelve. Eating ways set in childhood tend to last for life, so the part played by parents counts from the start. The review used PRISMA rules and searched four databases for work from 2010 to early 2015.

Thirty-one papers fit the rules, most of them one-off surveys. In studies that tracked children over time, hands-off, lax, or over-guarding parenting went with higher child weight, while firm but warm parenting went with healthy weight. Lax feeding also tied to obesity risk in the surveys. Habits such as limiting food or pressing a child to eat tied to weight too, though parents may act in reply to the child's size.
europmc-pmc4678205:
Claudia Knief wrote a solo 2015 review of methane-eating bacteria, cultivated and uncultivated, judged by a marker gene called pmoA. These bacteria live on methane as their only food and energy source and curb a potent greenhouse gas. Culture-free surveys have found thousands of sequences from unknown members. The review appeared in Frontiers in Microbiology.

Knief organises the known diversity and summarises what each major group does and where it lives. Some genera, such as Methylocystis and Methylocaldum, are generalists, yet hold habitat-specific species inside them. She warns that related enzymes in non-methane bacteria and duplicate marker genes in true methanotrophs can mislead surveys. Habitat loyalty appears at several taxonomic levels, which helps predict where methane consumption happens.
europmc-pmc4702805:
Chunlei Wu, Xuefeng Jin, Ginger Tsueng, Cyrus Afrasiabi, and Andrew I. Su updated BioGPS in Nucleic Acids Research in 2016. BioGPS is a web portal where researchers open a gene's page and find links out to hundreds of annotation and expression resources. Its special design lets users, not just the core team, extend and rearrange it. Each outside resource arrives as a plugin that the community contributes.

Since the 2013 report, 162 plugins were added, a rise of about a third, and users built 488 new custom page layouts. The most popular plugin, a gene activity chart, now draws on roughly six thousand datasets, triple the earlier count. A new gene list feature lets users save query results for later. The update shows a portal growing by the hands of its own users, shaped to many different kinds of gene questions.
europmc-pmc4706605:
Jacinto López-Sagaseta, Enrico Malito, Rino Rappuoli, and Matthew J. Bottomley reviewed self-assembling protein nanoparticles for vaccine design in the Computational and Structural Biotechnology Journal in 2016. Modern subunit vaccines are safe but often weak, since a lone protein does not alarm the immune system. A fix is to mount many copies of the protein on a nanoparticle, arranged in ordered arrays that mimic a virus surface. The review gathers the early proof for that strategy.

Ordered repeats grip immune cells more strongly and keep the antigen stable longer. Preclinical results point toward vaccines against flu, HIV, and RSV built this way. The authors pair the approach with structural vaccinology, the craft of shaping antigens atom by atom for the best immune view. Together, they argue, design can replace luck in much of vaccine making. The field's promise is strong, safer shots for diseases that still lack any.
europmc-pmc4708105:
Konstantin Okonechnikov, Ana Conesa, and Fernando García-Alcalde presented Qualimap 2 in Bioinformatics in 2016. High-throughput sequencing data carries random errors and systematic biases that can sink an analysis if missed. Quality-control tools exist, but most chew through one sample at a time, a poor fit for modern projects with dozens or hundreds of samples. Qualimap 2 keeps the first version's full single-sample checks and adds modes that process and compare many samples together.

Side-by-side comparison exposes clustering patterns and outlier samples at a glance. Both a graphical interface and a command line expose the same features, and many upgrades came straight from user requests. The software and documentation are free online. For sequencing centers and big cohort studies, the update turns quality control from a per-file chore into an experiment-wide view, which is where batch-wide problems actually show.
europmc-pmc4754705:
Bryce T. Bajar and eight co-authors report brighter glow tags for live-cell work in Scientific Reports in 2016. The tags are fluorescent proteins, which shine under light and let scientists watch cell events as they happen. Green and red pairs suit energy-transfer sensors, a trick that reports cell activity through shifts in glow.

Their new pair, mClover3 and mRuby3, beats the older set on both counts that matter. The green tag resists fading far better, and the red tag is both brighter and much harder to bleach out. In mammal cells the pair gave the strongest signals of their color classes. The team also fit the tags into a sensor for a key cell enzyme and got a wider swing in its readout.
europmc-pmc4803805:
Renate Kunert and David Reinhart review antibody manufacturing in Applied Microbiology and Biotechnology in 2016. Most therapeutic antibodies are brewed in Chinese hamster ovary cells, a cell line adopted decades ago and improved ever since. The review marks the milestones of that climb and the numbers that govern it: how fast cells grow, how long a run lasts, and how much antibody each cell makes per day.

The authors compare rival host systems on those numbers, then turn to quality. A host stamps sugars and other finishes on its product, and those finishes affect how a drug acts in the body; the review sets cell-line output beside natural human antibody mixes. Despite many challengers, hamster cells remain the industry workhorse, and the review shows why.
europmc-pmc4837405:
Jian Ji and eleven co-authors reported in Scientific Reports in 2016 that butyrate, a product of gut microbes, helps macrophages take the M2 form. M2 macrophages calm inflammation and aid repair. Gut microbe products were known to shape T cells, but their effect on macrophages was unclear. The group tested butyrate on macrophages in dishes and in mice with colitis, an inflamed bowel disease.

Butyrate-treated M2 cells helped lung cells move and close wounds faster in lab tests. In mice, butyrate eased bowel inflammation and raised a marker protein of M2 cells in the colon. A signal path inside the cells grew more active, pointing to how the effect may work.
europmc-pmc4934905:
Nathan R. Hill and six co-authors estimate how common chronic kidney disease is worldwide. Their systematic review and meta-analysis appeared in PLoS ONE in 2016. Kidney disease raises the risk of heart disease and early death, yet it often causes no symptoms until late. Solid counts of cases were lacking, above all by stage and region. The team searched eight databases for studies of general populations.

From about fifty-eight hundred candidate papers they kept one hundred studies, covering near seven million patients. The pooled share with any of the five stages of disease was just over thirteen percent. The more advanced stages made up about eleven percent. Rates varied by age, gender, and place. Weighting studies by quality did not move the numbers. The authors present kidney disease as a large, quiet global health burden.
europmc-pmc4949005:
Virginia A. Fonner and eight co-authors pool the evidence on oral preexposure prophylaxis, or PrEP, against HIV. Their systematic review and meta-analysis appeared in AIDS in 2016. PrEP means taking a daily pill with the drug tenofovir before exposure, to block infection. The team searched databases and conference reports through April 2015 for trials and studies of safety, resistance, behavior, and pregnancy outcomes.

Eighteen studies qualified. Across groups and dosing plans, PrEP cut the risk of HIV infection versus placebo. Trials where use topped seventy percent showed the strongest effect. Trials with low use showed no clear benefit. Side effects matched placebo rates, and there was no sign that users took more sexual risks. The authors conclude PrEP works when taken, and they call for best practices that help people start and stay on it.
europmc-pmc4967105:
Agnieszka Loboda and four co-authors review the Nrf2 and HO-1 system across species, from worms to people. Their review appeared in Cellular and Molecular Life Sciences in 2016. Nrf2 is a transcription factor that switches on antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, and detoxifying genes. One of its key targets, heme oxygenase-1, breaks down toxic heme and yields products that protect tissue, calm inflammation, and aid blood vessel growth. Cousins of Nrf2 run the same program in the worm C. elegans and the fly Drosophila.

The review traces the system through development, stress response, and aging. Faulty HO-1 levels are tied to nerve degeneration, cancer, and macular degeneration. The authors present the pair as an evolutionarily conserved defense module. Its long history, they argue, makes simple model animals a sound way to study it. They also flag microRNAs as a newer layer of control worth closer study.
europmc-pmc5081405:
Konstantinos Tzelepis and a large co-author group hunt for drug targets in acute myeloid leukemia using CRISPR screening, in Cell Reports in 2016. This aggressive blood cancer still relies on decades-old treatments. The team tuned a genome-wide CRISPR dropout screen, cutting genes one by one and watching which losses leukemia cells cannot survive, to map the cancer's genetic weak points.

The screen found 492 genes the leukemia cells specifically need, including known targets such as DOT1L, BCL2, and MEN1 and many fresh candidates. The group checked selected genes with genetic and drug inhibition, then pursued one, KAT2A. Blocking KAT2A pushed leukemia cells to mature and die, shrank primary human leukemias of varied genetic types, and spared normal blood stem cells. The authors propose KAT2A inhibition as a treatment strategy worth developing, and they offer the full vulnerability list as a resource for other teams.
europmc-pmc5140605:
H. E. Drake-Brockman wrote about traditional Indian eye practitioners in The Indian Medical Gazette in June 1910. Responding to an earlier article on coucheurs, the itinerant cataract operators of India, he adds his own long study of their methods, first presented to the Ophthalmological Society in 1896.

Drake-Brockman describes tracking down many of these operators, called Suttiahs, across the United Provinces and Rajputana. He bought complete sets of their instruments. Three of those sets went to museums in London and Edinburgh. The craft passed from father to son, mostly among men of the Kayasth caste, with no written literature. He states plainly that he saw many eyes destroyed by their operations, and he questions whether charlatan is too strong a word for them.
europmc-pmc5142605:
Gregory D. M. Potter, Debra J. Skene, Josephine Arendt, Janet E. Cade, Peter J. Grant, and Laura J. Hardie reviewed body clocks and sleep in Endocrine Reviews in 2016. Near-24-hour rhythms time nearly all body processes, and modern life, above all artificial light, increasingly knocks them out of step with the solar day.

The review explains the clock system from its brain pacemaker and clock genes down to single cells. Then it surveys the fallout of disruption. Short sleep, light at night, and shift work all feature, as do inherited clock differences. Consequences run heavily through metabolism, including weight and blood sugar control, and are worsened by poor food choices made when tired or mistimed. The closing sections catalog countermeasures, from light and sleep habits to medicines, that can realign the clock.
europmc-pmc5143405:
J. Xiao and eight co-authors studied protective vesicles from heart stem cells in Cell Death and Disease in 2016. Cardiac progenitor cells from adult hearts are a promising repair cell type, and their secreted exosomes carry small RNAs between cells. The team asked how those vesicles shield heart muscle under oxidative stress.

Stressed progenitor cells released more exosomes, and one cargo RNA, miR-21, rose sharply in them. In heart cells, miR-21 held down a death-promoting gene called PDCD4; vesicle treatment restored miR-21, lowered PDCD4, and made the cells resist stress-driven death. Blocking pieces of the chain removed the protection, confirming the route. The authors propose progenitor exosomes as a cell-free therapy vehicle for ischemic heart disease.
europmc-pmc5154505:
H. Raza Ali, Leon Chlon, Paul D. P. Pharoah, Florian Markowetz, and Carlos Caldas mapped immune patterns in breast cancer in PLoS Medicine in 2016, with Marc Ladanyi also named in the text's byline. Immune cells inside a tumor affect outcome, but earlier work lumped very different cell types together.

Using a computational method on gene profiles from almost 11,000 tumors, they estimated 22 immune cell types in each. Tumors with little immune entry fared worst in estrogen-receptor-negative disease but middling in positive disease. Regulatory T cells and two macrophage states tracked with poor outcomes across the board, while killer T cells favored survival in receptor-negative tumors. Certain B cell and helper T cell patterns predicted full response to chemotherapy given before surgery. Eight immune-defined tumor groups emerged, largely set by macrophage balance.
europmc-pmc5177805:
Hyunsuk Jeong and six co-authors studied the mental health of people isolated during the 2015 MERS outbreak in Korea, reporting in Epidemiology and Health in 2016. Of 14,992 people quarantined for two weeks after contact with MERS patients, 1,692 took part in the study, answering surveys during isolation and again four to six months after release.

During isolation, 7.6 percent reported anxiety symptoms and 16.6 percent feelings of anger among those never diagnosed with MERS. Months later, anxiety had fallen to 3.0 percent and anger to 6.4 percent. Lingering problems were likelier in people who had felt MERS-like symptoms, lacked adequate food, clothing, or housing, had a psychiatric history, or lost money. The authors urge mental health support and reliable supplies and information during isolation.
europmc-pmc5241505:
Nazem Ghasemi, Shahnaz Razavi, and Elham Nikzad reviewed multiple sclerosis in Cell Journal in 2017, covering its causes, symptoms, diagnosis, and cell-based therapy. Multiple sclerosis is a long-lasting inflammatory disease in which the immune system attacks the central nervous system, stripping the insulation from nerve fibers. It can bring severe physical and mental disability, yet its exact cause remains unknown.

The review lays out a many-sided origin: inherited risk combined with triggers such as infections, vitamin shortfalls, and smoking sets off immune attacks that kill insulation-making cells. It describes the disease's subtypes, from relapsing-remitting to progressive forms, and the symptoms that follow from faulty nerve signals. Standard drugs calm inflammation and tune the immune system but cannot stop tissue loss. The authors therefore examine stem cell transplantation, including fat-derived stem cells, as a strategy that might repair what drugs cannot.
europmc-pmc5253905:
D. Berry Hart, lecturer on midwifery at Edinburgh's School of Medicine of the Royal Colleges, examined a rare vaginal condition in the Edinburgh Medical Journal in 1911. Diffuse adenoma of the vagina, newly described by Bowley and Glendinning, gives the vaginal walls a red, granular, honeycombed look, with small cysts and a steady mucus discharge like egg white.

Under the microscope, removed tissue showed a thinned surface layer and gland spaces lined by tall cells, running through muscle-rich tissue. In one earlier case recorded by Haultain the condition later turned malignant. To explain how gland tissue could spread so widely in the vagina, Hart turns to development. He traces how the Müllerian and Wolffian ducts unfold in the embryo, how the vagina forms, and how the hymen arises. He tests current theories against embryo sections and against marsupial anatomy, and disputes several accepted accounts.
europmc-pmc5296605:
Yue Shan, Autumn Brown Gandt, Sarah E. Rowe, Julia P. Deisinger, Brian P. Conlon, and Kim Lewis challenged the standard model of bacterial persisters in mBio in 2017. Persisters are dormant cells that shrug off antibiotics and drive chronic infections that will not clear. The accepted story blamed a stress signal, ppGpp, switching on toxin-antitoxin systems that halt protein production and put cells to sleep.

The team found holes in that story: stresses switched the toxin systems on without raising persister numbers. A reporter gene long used as a persister marker turned out to answer to ATP, the cell's energy currency, as well as to ppGpp. It still marked persisters in cells lacking the ppGpp machinery. Draining ATP with arsenate made cells drug-tolerant directly: low energy slows protein production and shields DNA from fluoroquinolone damage. Persisters, the authors conclude, form when ATP levels vary and antibiotic targets go quiet.
europmc-pmc5300905:
Patricia Gomez-Suaga, Sebastien Paillusson, Radu Stoica, Wendy Noble, Diane P. Hanger, and Christopher C. J. Miller showed that a tether between two cell organelles controls autophagy, in Current Biology in 2017. The endoplasmic reticulum and mitochondria touch at points where the ER protein VAPB grips the mitochondrial protein PTPIP51, and these contacts pass signals and materials between the two.

The experiments pushed the contacts both ways. Forcing extra VAPB or PTPIP51, tightening the embrace, reduced the formation of autophagosomes, the sacs that carry cell waste to destruction. Knocking the proteins down loosened contacts and increased autophagosome formation, and a synthetic linker that clamps the organelles together reproduced the suppression, proving the tether itself is the lever. Tight contacts blocked drug-induced autophagy, though not starvation-induced, and the mechanism runs through calcium delivery from ER stores into mitochondria. A new control point for the cell's recycling system is thereby exposed.
europmc-pmc5320705:
Silvia Argimón and co-authors presented a web tool called Microreact in Microbial Genomics in 2016. Microbe gene studies often end as a family tree of strains, linked to place, time, and case data. Still images in papers freeze that rich data and hide most of it. Front-line health staff need a way to explore the full set and share views with ease.

Microreact lets users upload trees plus linked data, or point to files held online. It then shows the data as linked trees, maps, timelines, and tables that answer clicks and searches. A view can be shared as a lasting web link, or placed inside a paper so readers can explore the data themselves. The team aimed the tool at users from skilled gene analysts to field staff tracking outbreaks.
europmc-pmc5379105:
Lorenzo Errichelli and co-authors tied a nerve-linked protein to ring RNAs in mouse cells, in Nature Communications in 2017. The protein, FUS, binds RNA and helps run many RNA steps. Its flaws drive two nerve diseases, ALS and a form of dementia. Ring RNAs, closed loops made when a gene message splices backward, are rich in nerve tissue and still little understood.

The team grew mouse motor nerve cells in dishes and listed their ring RNAs. A large share of the rings leaned on FUS for their birth. Cutting FUS down, or piling it up, moved ring counts in step, and disease-form FUS did the same by a toxic gain. FUS grips the spacer parts that flank the ring joint, which steers the backward splice. Human nerve cells that bear an ALS-linked FUS flaw showed the same ring upset.
europmc-pmc5591905:
Phillips reviews the link between a brain growth factor, depression, and exercise in Neural Plasticity. The factor is BDNF, short for brain-derived neurotrophic factor. It keeps neurons alive and helps them grow and connect. Those circuits govern mood and thought.

Stress and major depression go with lower BDNF and weaker plasticity. The review gathers clinical and animal evidence for that pattern. Treatments that lift mood also restore BDNF in key brain regions. Antidepressant drugs do this, and so does physical activity. Better BDNF supports neuronal health and stronger drug response. The author argues this chain should guide new treatments. Readers get a clear map from molecules to recovery.
europmc-pmc5663905:
Lorent and co-authors report a membrane study in Nature Communications. It asks what draws proteins into lipid rafts. Rafts are ordered domains within cell membranes. They recruit select proteins for many membrane tasks. The team directly measured raft affinity for dozens of protein segments. Only the transmembrane parts were tested. Three physical traits shaped the results.

Surface area of the segment mattered on its own. Length mattered too, as did palmitoylation. The authors built a physical model from these rules. The model predicts raft affinity from protein sequence alone. Applied to the human proteome, it showed a clear pattern. Plasma membrane proteins held higher raft affinity than inner membrane ones.
