europmc-pmc5708005:
Cooksey-Stowers and co-authors test whether food swamps predict obesity better than food deserts. Food swamps are areas dense with fast food and junk food outlets. Food deserts lack full-service grocery stores. The team merged data on food outlets, income, and obesity across the United States.

They used several versions of a retail food index to define each area type. A statistical method corrected for people choosing where to live. Food swamps showed a clear link to higher adult obesity rates. That link held even after food desert effects were counted. The effect grew stronger where income gaps were wide. It also grew where residents were less mobile. Zoning and store incentives are floated as policy tools.
europmc-pmc5717805:
Jakobsen and co-authors give a practical guide for handling missing data in clinical trials. Their guide focuses on randomised trials, where gaps can bias results. The risk depends on why data went missing and how analysts respond. Poor handling can break the fair balance that randomisation creates.

The authors drew on meetings, literature searches, and prior studies. They weigh methods such as multiple imputation and full information maximum likelihood. Best-worst and worst-best sensitivity checks also get attention. Flowcharts show when and how to use multiple imputation. Steps for the planning stage aim to cut missing data at the source. A checklist covers what every trial analysis should consider.
europmc-pmc5724505:
Grimm and Eckert review brain aging and nerve cell loss from a mitochondrial point of view. Mitochondria make most cell energy, but they also form reactive oxygen species that can harm cells. The brain uses much energy, so it may be hit hard when these organelles fail.

The review asks three main questions. What happens to brain mitochondria, their energy output, and their motion as age grows? Why is the brain so open to such age linked faults? And do men and women differ in this decline? The authors trace the free radical theory of aging and its brain effects. They close by seeking treatment targets that could guard nerve cells.
europmc-pmc5796205:
Luo, Zhou, and Zhang review the Aux/IAA gene family, early responders to the plant hormone auxin. Auxin steers growth across the plant's whole life. These proteins are short lived and sit in the nucleus. They bind partner factors called ARFs and block the genes those factors switch on.

Pairs of the two families form in many mixes, tuning replies in varied ways. Family members shape root growth, shoot growth, and fruit ripening. The review gathers fresh detail on their structure and control. It also covers how the partners interact, giving a base for work on plant form.
europmc-pmc5808205:
Gao and co-authors review how gut microbes shape gut immunity via tryptophan. Tryptophan is a nutrient building block from food. Microbes and the body both break it down. Its products help set the gut's immune tone.

The review sorts products from the body and from bacteria. Many act through a sensor called the aryl hydrocarbon receptor. That signal helps keep peace between microbes and gut tissue. Stress, aging, and gut diseases shift the balance. The authors suggest tryptophan support could calm gut inflammation. Readers get a clear route from diet to immune control.
europmc-pmc5820305:
Kers and co-authors review what shapes the gut microbes of chickens. A chick's gut community forms in its first weeks. That community affects growth, health, and infection resistance. Study results vary a lot between farms and labs.

The review sorts the noise into host traits and surroundings. Age, sex, and breed shift the microbes most. Litter, housing, feed access, and climate matter too. Lab steps like storage and DNA methods add their own skew. The authors urge full reporting of all these factors. Readers get a checklist for cleaner poultry microbe studies.
europmc-pmc5875005:
Tamborero and co-authors present the Cancer Genome Interpreter platform. Their article appeared in Genome Medicine. Tumour sequencing is now common in clinics and labs. Reading what the found changes mean remains a bottleneck. The platform automates that reading for new cancer genomes. It flags changes that may drive the tumour. It also notes effects on likely treatment response.

Results are sorted by levels of supporting evidence. That structure suits many uses in oncology care and research. Judging driver changes is slow and unsolved by hand, they note. Many variants, even in known cancer genes, stay uncertain. Therapy data tied to drivers is also scattered. The resource is public online for any user.
europmc-pmc5880805:
Kojima and co-authors build designer exosomes that deliver RNA cargo. Their article appeared in Nature Communications. Exosomes are tiny vesicles that cells use to message each other. Their natural message transfer is weak and hard to steer. The team encoded a set of devices in producer cells. These devices boost exosome output and load chosen mRNA. Cargo then reaches the cytosol of target cells efficiently.

Implanted producer cells delivered cargo to mouse brains steadily. No need arose to gather or concentrate the vesicles. A therapeutic catalase mRNA eased toxicity in Parkinson's models. It also calmed brain inflammation in those models. The system points toward implant-based RNA therapies.
europmc-pmc5912505:
Wright and co-authors show that reanalysing old genome data yields new diagnoses. Their article appeared in Genetics in Medicine. They revisited 1,133 families with severe developmental disorders. An earlier round had diagnosed 27 percent of children. Gene knowledge and tools had since advanced fast. The team reran the data with updated methods.

They diagnosed 182 more individuals, they report. Total yield rose to 40 percent of families. Most new answers came from genes found since the first round. Another 43 cases got uncertain but notable findings. First-line family sequencing could diagnose over half, they estimate. Clinics are urged to plan recontact from the start.
europmc-pmc5924105:
Middleton and Teacher reported spinal cord injury from a ruptured disc during muscular effort. The case was read in Glasgow in March 1911. It appeared in the Glasgow Medical Journal that year. A labourer aged 38 lifted a heavy plate at work. He felt a crack in the small of his back. Intense pain left him unable to straighten up.

Paralysis of the legs soon followed, they report. The man died sixteen days later. Bedsores and bladder infection drove that decline. Post-mortem found bleeding and softening in the cord. Disc pulp had been pushed into the vertebral canal. No similar case was found in prior records. The report links heavy strain to disc rupture.
europmc-pmc5938605:
Ingala and co-authors compare two ways of sampling the gut microbiome in wild bats. Their study appeared in Frontiers in Microbiology. Wildlife microbiome work has no standard sampling method yet. Most studies use faeces, rectal swabs, or gut contents. The team asked whether these sample types tell the same story. They worked with free-ranging bats at Lamanai, Belize.

They sequenced 16S rRNA from guano and from distal intestinal mucosa. The bats came from 19 species. Diversity and composition differed a lot between sample types, they report. Mucosal samples kept signs of host evolution, while faecal ones did not. Faecal samples instead held more signal of host diet. The two methods are not interchangeable, the authors conclude.
europmc-pmc5951805:
Deng and co-authors review RNA N6-methyladenosine modification in cancers. Their review appeared in Cell Research. This mark, called m6A, is the most common internal change in messenger RNA. Writer enzymes place it, and eraser enzymes can remove it. Reader proteins then decide the fate of marked messages. They can alter stability, splicing, or translation.

When this machinery goes wrong, it can feed cancer, the authors report. It affects how cancers start, grow, and answer drugs. The review covers recent work on these mechanisms across cancer types. It also discusses drugs that might target the faulty machinery. Such treatment is a growing hope in the field.
europmc-pmc5971205:
Peskett and co-authors show a change from liquid to solid at the root of harmful huntingtin clumping. Their study was published in Molecular Cell. The disease stems from a too-long repeat tract in the huntingtin protein. Bits of that protein gather into clumps in cells. The team paired two kinds of scopes to watch the clumps form. They worked in mammal cells, yeast, and test tubes.

The protein bits first form soft, liquid-like drops, they report. The repeat tract and a proline-rich stretch drive that step. The drops then turn solid and string-like in form. Such shifts in cells may start clumps that cannot be undone. That step could seed the disease.
europmc-pmc5971805:
Thomson examines how sepsis and endocrine disturbance affect carbohydrate metabolism. Her study appeared in the Glasgow Medical Journal. Sepsis in diabetic patients almost always worsens their symptoms. Sugar in the urine also commonly accompanies septic infections. Older writers disagreed on the direction of these effects. Some claimed acute infection could improve diabetes.

Thomson reviews views from Naunyn, von Noorden, Stengel, and others. Glycosuria often rose as boils or gangrene developed, they found. It fell again when the septic focus was removed. Cases included facial erysipelas, influenza, and bronchopneumonia. The paper sets infection and hormone effects side by side.
europmc-pmc5975705:
Wang and co-authors review how loneliness and felt social support link to mental health over time. Their review was published in BMC Psychiatry. Harm from loneliness to body health is well known. No past work summed up the mental health side across time. The team searched six data banks for studies that tracked people. They found 34 papers that fit the rules. A story-style sum-up handled the mixed groups and tests.

People with low mood who felt poorly backed fared worse, they report. Symptoms, healing, and social life all suffered. Loneliness was studied less, but more of it meant worse low mood. Early signs also link backing to two more brain ills. More proof is needed for those.
europmc-pmc5984805:
Hayes and co-authors overview climate change risks to mental health and set priority actions. Their discussion paper appeared in the International Journal of Mental Health Systems. Climate harms to physical health are well documented. Its mental health effects are lesser known and often missed. Pinning outcomes to single climate risks is hard, the authors admit. Yet the impacts are already growing fast.

Effects arrive directly, indirectly, and through wider social strain. They fall hardest on people who are already marginalised, the authors argue. Responses must be coordinated across climate and health work. They should rest on active hope, not despair. The paper closes with priority actions for the field.
europmc-pmc6036605:
Baptista and co-authors review nano-based ways to fight drug-resistant bacteria. Their review appeared in Frontiers in Microbiology. Multidrug resistance keeps rising while new antibiotics stay scarce. Bacteria defeat drugs by pumping them out or changing targets. Some hide inside biofilms instead.

Tiny structured materials offer another route of attack. Nanoparticles can carry antibiotics to infection sites. Some kill bacteria on their own. Others block efflux pumps, biofilms, or cell signals. Pairing them with plant compounds may cut toxicity. The review sums up each approach and its limits. Readers get a field map of a young strategy. Much lab work, the authors stress, still lies ahead.
europmc-pmc6039505:
Marras and co-authors estimate Parkinson's disease prevalence across North America. Their study appeared in NPJ Parkinson's Disease. Earlier estimates varied widely and rested on small samples. Planners need firmer numbers as populations age. The disease burden will grow with age structure.

The project combined five cohort studies. Sites covered California, Minnesota, Hawaii, and Ontario. Medicare data gave matching regional estimates for comparison. Prevalence among adults aged 45 and over was 572 per 100,000. That implied about 680,000 cases in the United States in 2010. Projections reach about 1,238,000 cases by 2030. Rates rose with age and were higher in men. Hawaii estimates ran lower than other regions. The authors call their figures minimum estimates for planning.
europmc-pmc6061505:
Jamróz and co-authors review 3D printing in pharmacy and medicine. Their review appeared in Pharmaceutical Research. Printing builds objects layer by layer from a model. Demand for custom drugs and devices drives the interest. The review focuses on work published since 2015.

Printed products now include fast-release drug systems. Doses can be shaped for a single patient. Implants and body models can match a patient's anatomy. Cell-based materials serve regenerative medicine. Extrusion methods get the deepest coverage. Rules and quality limits get a critical look too. Readers get both the gains and the open challenges of the field.
europmc-pmc6085705:
Murali and co-authors present IDTAXA, a classifier for microbiome sequences. Their article appeared in Microbiome. Marker-gene studies name microbes by matching sequences to references. Old tools often forced a label even for unknown groups. That over-classification distorts results.

IDTAXA learns from reference sets and withholds labels when unsure. It beat popular rivals on accuracy in tests. It held steady across varied read lengths. It also rejected random and repeat sequences outright. Mock community tests confirmed fewer false labels. The tool can also flag mislabeled reference entries. Readers get a safer way to name microbes in samples.
europmc-pmc6095905:
Chelakkot and co-authors review what keeps the intestinal barrier tight, and what loosens it. Their review appeared in Experimental and Molecular Medicine. One cell layer separates gut contents from the body. Tight junction proteins seal the gaps between cells. Mucus and immune cells back the seal up.

Signals from cytokines and small GTPases tune the junctions. Chemical tags on the proteins adjust them too. When balance fails, harmful matter leaks through. Leaks link to bowel inflammation, obesity, and metabolic disease. The review walks through each control mechanism. It also weighs barrier repair as therapy. Readers get a guide to the gut's front line and its failure modes.
europmc-pmc6115505:
Wang and Dreesen wrote a review in Frontiers in Genetics on markers of cell aging, with a focus on skin. Cells that stop dividing for good are called senescent. They build up in aged skin and may drive many age-linked skin changes. Finding them in tissue has been hard, since no single marker fits all cells.

The review checks the markers now in use. It asks how well each one spots aged cells in each skin layer and cell type. Clearing such cells can delay tissue decline in lab work. The authors weigh what each marker can and cannot prove. Readers get a guide to a key tool problem in aging research.
europmc-pmc6127005:
Köbel and co-authors wrote a review in International Journal of Gynecological Pathology on reading p53 stains in endometrial cancer. Staining for the p53 protein mirrors the mutation status of the TP53 gene in a tumor. That makes it a useful test in working up these cancers. Labs have not always read the stains the same way.

The review describes four main staining patterns. One looks normal, while three abnormal patterns strongly predict a TP53 mutation. The authors give practical advice on lab methods to improve staining. They also warn about pitfalls that can mislead the reader. The goal is results that different pathologists reproduce in the same way.
europmc-pmc6133005:
Patterson and co-authors offer a systematic review and dose-response meta-analysis in European Journal of Epidemiology on sedentary behavior and health. Sitting for long stretches is now a normal part of daily life. The question is how each added hour of sitting changes risk. The team also asked whether being active offsets that risk.

They pooled prospective studies found in six databases through September 2016. The studies tracked total sitting and TV viewing time. Outcomes were death from all causes, heart disease, and cancer, plus new type 2 diabetes. Results account for how active people were. The work maps the shape of risk as sitting time rises, giving public health a clearer dose picture.
europmc-pmc6141705:
Lee and Ashkar wrote a review in Frontiers in Immunology on the dual nature of interferons, key signaling proteins of the immune system. Type I and type II interferons are central to fighting virus infection. Without them, people and animals face worse infections and lower survival.

The review shows that these proteins do more than attack viruses. They also tune the immune response up and down. That tuning limits virus growth and starts the right defense. It then reins the response in to spare healthy tissue. The authors argue both jobs are vital during infection. Readers get a balanced view of molecules often cast as purely protective.
europmc-pmc6185905:
Wang and co-authors present a research article in Nature Communications on the body clock and colon inflammation. A clock protein called REV-ERB alpha helps run circadian rhythms. Its role in gut inflammation was unclear. The team studied mice with chemically induced colitis, a model of inflammatory bowel disease.

Clock genes in the colon were thrown off in sick mice, and breaking the clock made colitis worse. Mice lacking REV-ERB alpha suffered more severe disease. The protein normally represses the NLRP3 inflammasome, partly by blocking its gene directly. It also damps the NF-kappaB pathway. A drug that activates REV-ERB alpha eased colitis in normal mice. The work links daily rhythms to gut immune control.
europmc-pmc6199205:
Pesapane and co-authors wrote an article in European Radiology Experimental asking whether artificial intelligence in medical imaging is a threat or an opportunity. AI is among the most promising areas of health innovation, above all in imaging. Papers on it rose from roughly 100 to 150 a year in 2007-2008 to 700 to 800 a year a decade later.

The authors define terms such as machine learning and deep learning in plain language. MRI and CT together account for over half the studies, with neuroradiology the largest subspecialty. They also cover radiomics, which mines image features to predict treatment response and tumor type. Their verdict places radiologists at the forefront of this change, not replaced by it.
europmc-pmc6227505:
Foreman and co-authors forecast life expectancy and deaths to 2040. Long-term health planning needs robust future scenarios. Past forecasts gave an incomplete picture. The team modelled 250 causes of death. The study appeared in The Lancet. It covers 195 countries and territories.

Models drew on Global Burden of Disease data from 1990 to 2016. The team built a reference forecast for each cause. They also built better and worse health scenarios. Drivers such as income, education, and risk factors shaped the paths. Results show likely gains in life expectancy. They also show causes set to grow, such as dementia. The authors say the scenarios can guide investment. Policy choices can shift countries between paths.
europmc-pmc6251205:
Donati, Lorenzini, and Ciarrocchi review a gene reading protein called BRD4 in cancer. Their review appeared in Molecular Cancer. BRD4 helps switch on cancer genes at strong control regions. Drugs that block its family are in trials for several cancers. Blocking BRD4 cuts the signal between those regions and their target genes. Cancer cells that depend on those genes then die.

Newer work gives BRD4 a second job outside gene reading. It helps guard genome stability. Roles in damage checks, repair, and chromosome end care have been reported. Those jobs may explain part of how the blocking drugs kill cells. The authors build a shared model that joins both roles. The wider view suggests new uses for the drugs in the clinic. It also warns that effects may reach beyond gene control.
europmc-pmc6265305:
Feng, Ao, and Peng review how herbal medicines interact with gut microbes and their fatty acid products. Their short review appeared in Frontiers in Pharmacology. Herbal medicines anchor systems such as Ayurvedic and Chinese medicine. Most people worldwide still rely on them for basic care. Gut microbes turn parts of those herbs into short-chain fatty acids. Those fats help keep the body in balance.

Herbs can shift which microbes thrive in the gut. Changed microbe mixes then change fatty acid output. The review gathers what is known about that two way traffic. It covers where the fatty acids come from and what they do in health and disease. Mechanisms behind herb effects on the pathway are also laid out. The authors close with plans for sharper studies. The topic joins two old fields in a new way.
europmc-pmc6332205:
Tan and co-authors review melatonin as a built-in antioxidant. Their review appeared in Molecules in 2015. Melatonin is a small molecule made from tryptophan. It occurs in nearly all living organisms. It is best known for timing sleep in animals. Its oldest job was likely mopping up free radicals.

How melatonin is made differs between plants and animals. Its breakdown is complex and still partly unclear. Enzymes handle some of it inside cells. Free radical reactions handle another share, more so under stress. The breakdown products overlap between the routes. Under strain, the radical route may dominate. The authors expect new metabolites to be found. They frame melatonin as an inducible shield the body raises itself.
europmc-pmc6378305:
Cheung and co-authors present a systematic review in Frontiers in Psychiatry on gut microbes and major depression. New work links the gut microbiome to the brain. Transplants from depressed patients can even cause depression-like behavior in rodents.

The team searched for human studies that compared gut microbes in depressed and healthy people. They focused on which bacterial groups differed between the two. Results varied, but some taxa stood out across studies. The review weighs how strong that proof is. It points to diet and microbe-based care as lines worth testing in larger studies.
europmc-pmc6378405:
Hawkins and co-authors review the evolution of pesticide resistance in Biological Reviews. Pesticides protect crops, yet weeds, insects, and crop diseases often resist a new product soon after launch. That fast change makes resistance a sharp test case for evolution.

The authors ask where the needed traits come from. Some may wait in a population as standing variation. Others may arise as fresh mutations, or serve another use first. Similar tricks also recur across species. Knowing the source of resistance could help design sprays that last longer and protect food supplies.
europmc-pmc6471505:
Fattorusso and co-authors review the gut's possible role in autism, where gut complaints and atypical behavior often arrive together. An off-balance gut in autism is widely shown, and the gut-brain axis offers a plausible channel. No single germ profile marks autistic children, though, and profiles vary between studies.

This off-balance state may feed the low-grade, body-wide inflammation reported in patients with gut symptoms. Live-culture mixtures, mostly Bifidobacteria, Streptococci, and Lactobacilli, are rated the most hopeful non-drug approach for both bowel and behavior problems, but the trials stay small and uneven. The authors call for proper randomized, placebo-controlled studies that pin down strain, dose, and timing.
europmc-pmc6515705:
Zhou, Zuo and Jiang review astrocyte shape, diversity and plasticity. Their review appeared in CNS Neuroscience & Therapeutics. Astrocytes are the most abundant glial cells in the brain. Their fine processes touch synapses, blood vessels and other glial cells. One human astrocyte can cover about two million synapses.

Older views treated astrocytes as uniform across the brain. New work shows region and circuit differences in shape. Their fine structure also shifts with activity. Such plasticity may shape synaptic and circuit function. Shape loss was long read as a late sign of reactive astrogliosis. The authors note evidence that fine structural deficits come first. Those early deficits may drive disease progression.
europmc-pmc6555805:
Cui and co-authors report a chlorinated light-absorbing molecule that pushes organic solar cells past 16% efficiency, writing in Nature Communications. Swapping fluorine for chlorine in such acceptor molecules normally buys broader light absorption at the cost of lower voltage. Their new acceptor, BTP-4Cl, breaks that trade-off.

Built from the fluorinated acceptor Y6, BTP-4Cl absorbed light about 20 nanometers further into the red, as expected. Yet cells using it produced a higher open-circuit voltage than the fluorine version. The team traced the surprise to lower non-radiative energy losses in the blend film. With current and voltage rising together, the cells reached over 16% efficiency, and about 15% even at the larger one-square-centimeter size — among the best single-junction organic results then reported.
europmc-pmc6584505:
Wagner and co-authors present crYOLO, a deep learning particle picker for cryo-electron microscopy, writing in Communications Biology. Building a 3D structure from cryo-EM images starts with selecting over a hundred thousand tiny particle images from noisy micrographs. Template matching stumbles on messy data, and hand picking is drudgery.

CrYOLO adapts the YOLO object-detection network, which judges a whole image in one pass instead of scanning window by window. After training on as few as a few hundred example particles, it picks with high recall and precision at up to five micrographs per second. A pre-trained general network even handles datasets it has never seen, enabling fully automated processing while data are still being collected. It ships within the SPHIRE package.
europmc-pmc6614205:
Lidani and co-authors trace Chagas disease from its discovery to a global problem. Their review appears in Frontiers in Public Health. Carlos Chagas found the disease just over a century ago. He named its parasite, Trypanosoma cruzi, and its insect vector. The disease then stayed a quiet Latin American burden for decades.

About 6 to 8 million people now live with the infection. Roughly 50,000 die from it each year. Migration has carried cases to Canada, the United States, Europe, and Japan. There, spread runs through transfusion, transplants, and birth. Many carriers never show symptoms. Others reach a chronic phase with heart or gut damage. The authors review transmission routes, parasite diversity, and control efforts. A cure and full eradication, they note, remain out of reach.
europmc-pmc6688105:
Monteran and Erez review cancer-associated fibroblasts as drivers of immune suppression in tumours. Their review appears in Frontiers in Immunology. Fibroblasts dominate the stroma of many solid tumours. They support growth, remodel matrix, and promote blood vessels. Newer work casts them as immune players too. They secrete cytokines and chemokines that recruit immune cells. Those signals steer cells toward suppressive fates. Fibroblasts can also disable killer lymphocytes directly. Tumour killing then fails despite infiltration.

High stromal signatures track therapy resistance. Relapse follows the same pattern. The review details how immune cells are recruited and reshaped. Combined strategies targeting fibroblasts are the outlook. Blocking their support may unlock immunotherapy. Lab findings await clinical testing.
europmc-pmc6862505:
Ul Haq and co-authors review heat shock proteins in plants, in the International Journal of Molecular Sciences. Climate change exposes crops to more heat, drought, and disease at once. Stressed cells risk their proteins losing shape and clumping, which jams metabolism. Heat shock proteins act as chaperones, holding other proteins in working form. Plants lean on them heavily under stress.

The review explains how these chaperones protect membranes and mop up reactive oxygen by boosting antioxidant enzymes. They also help stabilise immune proteins, aiding defence against germs. Reactive oxygen itself acts as a signal that raises chaperone output. The authors present the family as a breeding and engineering target for tougher crops.
europmc-pmc6965005:
Song and co-authors sequence eight rapeseed genomes to chart the species' full gene set. Their study appeared in Nature Plants. Rapeseed, or Brassica napus, is the world's second most important oilseed crop. Huge variety in its traits rests on genetic diversity that stayed largely unexplored.

Comparing the eight genomes revealed millions of small variations. Long stretches of DNA were present in some lines and absent in others. More than nine percent of genes carried large-effect changes or structural rearrangements. Hunting trait links through those presence-absence stretches found causes for seed weight, pod length, and flowering time that standard methods missed. Three flowering genes tied the variation to how rapeseed types split by climate. Breeders, the authors say, gain a rich new resource.
europmc-pmc7049905:
The GBD Chronic Kidney Disease Collaboration measures chronic kidney disease worldwide in The Lancet. Health systems need solid figures on this disease to plan care, yet morbidity and mortality data are scarce or missing in many countries. The collaboration estimated the burden for the Global Burden of Disease Study 2017, including heart disease and gout caused by impaired kidney function.

Estimates drew on published literature, vital registration, kidney failure registries, and household surveys, modelled with ensemble and Bayesian methods. In 2017, 1.2 million people died from chronic kidney disease. The global all-age mortality rate rose 41.5 percent between 1990 and 2017. The report counts cases, deaths, years lived with disability, and disability-adjusted life-years by region. It also shows how much cardiovascular disease and gout burden traces back to failing kidneys, a hidden load many planners overlook.
europmc-pmc7075805:
Park and co-authors review the calcium-calcineurin-NFAT pathway in Frontiers in Immunology. Calcium is a universal signal inside cells, and in the immune system it steers growth, differentiation, death, and gene switching. When a T or B cell's antigen receptor fires, internal calcium stores empty and channels open to refill them, a process called store-operated entry. Two regulators of that channel, STIM and Orai1, transformed understanding of the system.

Sustained calcium elevation activates the enzyme calcineurin, which frees the transcription factor NFAT to enter the nucleus and switch on genes. Versions 1 to 4 of this pathway go wrong in autoimmune diseases. That is why calcineurin blockers, cyclosporine and tacrolimus, already treat conditions such as lupus and rheumatoid arthritis. The review explains the pathway in health, details its derangement in autoimmunity, and discusses where interference might help next.
europmc-pmc7084905:
Ali Syeda and co-authors review how microRNA expression goes wrong in cancer, in the International Journal of Molecular Sciences. MicroRNAs are small molecules that dial down gene activity after a gene is read. When their levels shift, cancer-promoting or cancer-suppressing genes can escape control.

Many microRNAs are raised or lowered in human cancers. Causes include deleted or copied gene regions, chemical marks on the DNA, and faulty control by transcription factors. Errors in the steps that trim microRNAs into their mature form also matter. Knowing these control points helps explain cancer biology and may guide new treatments that restore healthy microRNA patterns.
europmc-pmc7108005:
Zhou and co-authors describe the immune cells that drive inflammatory storms in severe COVID-19, in National Science Review. Why some patients die quickly from lung damage was unknown when the outbreak began. The team studied immune cells in patients' blood, including those in intensive care.

After infection, CD4 T cells quickly switched into a harmful helper type that releases GM-CSF. That signal produced inflammatory monocytes carrying CD14 and CD16 markers, which poured out IL-6, a key inflammation messenger. These cells likely flood the lungs and cause the damage behind severe cases. The authors propose that antibodies blocking GM-CSF or IL-6 could calm the storm and deserve testing as treatment.
europmc-pmc7141005:
Miao and co-authors introduce ImmuCellAI, a method that estimates the mix of immune cells in a tumor from gene expression data, in Advanced Science. T cell subsets shape how cancers behave and respond to immunotherapy, but counting them precisely has been hard. Their tool predicts 24 immune cell types, including 18 T cell subsets.

Tests against flow cytometry data and public datasets showed better accuracy than rival methods, especially for T cell subsets. Applied to immunotherapy trial data, the tool found dendritic cells, cytotoxic T cells, and gamma delta T cells enriched in patients who responded. A model built on its output predicted treatment response with high accuracy. The software is offered for tumor immunity research.
europmc-pmc7145605:
Papatheodorou and co-authors update Expression Atlas, the EMBL-EBI resource for gene and protein expression, in Nucleic Acids Research. The atlas gathers measurements of how active each gene is across species, tissues, cells, diseases, and experimental conditions, and serves them openly. Its newest branch covers single-cell data.

Single Cell Expression Atlas launched in 2018 and already held 123 studies from 12 species at the time of writing. Users can search a gene across species to find where it is expressed or where it marks a cell type. Each study offers visual maps of cells coloured by cluster or feature, plus downloadable count tables and metadata. The update marks the atlas's move from tissue averages to single-cell resolution.
europmc-pmc7158905:
Prem and co-authors model how reducing social mixing affected the COVID-19 epidemic in Wuhan, in The Lancet Public Health. Wuhan closed schools and workplaces for an extended period. The team fed location-specific contact patterns into an age-structured epidemic model and simulated different distancing and reopening plans.

A staggered return to work at the beginning of April worked best in their projections. It cut the median number of infections by more than 92% by mid-2020 and 24% by the end of 2020, compared with the alternatives tried. Returning in March performed worse. The authors offered the results as guidance for other places weighing how long to hold distancing and how to phase reopening.
europmc-pmc7190605:
Lugano and co-authors review how tumors build their own blood supply. Their article appeared in Cellular and Molecular Life Sciences. Tumors use several vessel-forming processes at once. These vary by tumor type and body location. Signals and cell types beyond the vessel lining can take part.

Drugs that block vessel growth are approved for several cancers. Yet the benefit so far has been modest, the authors note. Some patients never respond, and others develop resistance. Tumor vessels differ from normal ones in shape and gene activity. That difference complicates any attempt to cut tumors off from circulation. The review weighs these challenges against new openings. It maps where anti-vessel therapy might still improve.
europmc-pmc7200005:
Guest and co-authors offer a simple method for judging when qualitative research has reached thematic saturation. Their article appeared in PLoS ONE. Saturation means new interviews stop adding new themes. Researchers invoke it to justify sample sizes. Yet checking it during a study has lacked an easy, reliable tool.

The method uses a base set of interviews to count themes. Later interviews, taken in runs, add their new themes to the tally. When the share of new information falls below a set threshold, saturation is declared. In their worked example, the cutoff was 5 percent, reached after the eighth interview. The authors validate the approach and give reporting steps. Qualitative teams gain a transparent way to defend their sample size.
europmc-pmc7226105:
Alhmoud and co-authors review how DNA damage and repair shape cancer and its treatment. Their article appeared in Cancers. DNA lesions break one or both strands of the molecule. Unrepaired damage raises the chance of mutations. The resulting genomic instability is a core driver of cancer.

Cells run several repair pathways, each fixing a different kind of lesion. Base excision repair, for instance, handles damage from oxidation and alkylating agents. It works in short and long repair patches. When repair fails or falters, cancers start and evolve more easily. The same pathways help tumors survive chemotherapy and radiation. The authors discuss how understanding repair can improve therapy. Blocking repair in cancer cells is one strategy they survey.
europmc-pmc7278705:
Pandian and co-authors review cytochrome P450 enzymes and their part in how plants handle stress. Their review appeared in Antioxidants. These enzymes form one of the largest enzyme families in living things. In plants they help detoxify foreign chemicals and build protective compounds, antioxidants, and plant hormones.

New sequencing tools have shown that many P450 genes switch on or off under environmental stress. The enzymes sit at crossing points between responses to living threats, such as pests, and non-living stresses, such as drought or heat. Because of that central place, they are strong candidates for breeding or engineering crops that withstand harsher conditions. The review gathers the latest work on which family members matter most for stress response.
europmc-pmc7292505:
Premkumar and co-authors show that antibodies from COVID-19 patients aim mainly at one part of the virus: the receptor binding domain of the spike protein. Their study appeared in Science Immunology. The binding domain is the spike's tip, which locks onto human cells. Antibody tests were urgently needed to find past infections and map spread.

Blood levels of antibodies against this domain tracked closely with how well a patient's serum neutralized the virus. The target was also highly specific, meaning tests built on it should rarely confuse SARS-CoV-2 with other coronaviruses. That makes the domain a strong base for population surveillance, the authors argue, letting health agencies count infections, including silent ones, and judge when communities can safely reopen.
europmc-pmc7326705:
Davis and co-authors set out a consensus statement in Nature Reviews Neurology on biomarkers for pain drugs. A biomarker is a measurable body sign that can show how a drug is working. The statement grew out of a 2018 workshop under the NIH HEAL Initiative, which seeks non-addictive pain treatments.

Objective measures, the authors argue, could sort pain into subgroups, confirm that a drug hits its target, and predict who will benefit. They review the hard parts too, from validation standards to trial design. Industry, academic, government, and patient voices all took part in the workshop. Readers get a roadmap for making pain trials rest on evidence rather than self-report alone.
europmc-pmc7365905:
Bhaskar and co-authors present a consortium position paper in Frontiers in Immunology on cytokine storm in COVID-19. A cytokine storm is an acute flood of immune signals that can turn critical. The REPROGRAM consortium argues it sits behind many severe outcomes of the infection.

The manifestations they list include acute respiratory distress, blood clots causing strokes and heart attacks, brain inflammation, kidney injury, and vessel inflammation resembling Kawasaki disease in children. Patients in storm are thought to face worse odds and higher death rates. The paper lays out the immune pathways involved, the clinical signs to watch, and treatment approaches that calm the response. Readers get a coordinated expert view of a feared complication.
europmc-pmc7369905:
He and co-authors review NRF2 in the International Journal of Molecular Sciences, a transcription factor that runs the cell's stress defenses. NRF2 switches on genes that fight oxidative damage and detoxify harmful chemicals. Switching it on makes cells resistant to carcinogens and inflammation.

The factor reaches far beyond antioxidant defense, into metabolism, protein quality control, self-digestion of cell parts, and mitochondrial function. Its activity is tuned by a dense network of controls at several levels. Too much or too little NRF2, shifted by drugs or gene changes, shows up in many metabolic and inflammatory diseases. The authors place NRF2 at the center of a wide regulatory web. Readers get a portrait of a single protein with system-wide reach.
europmc-pmc7372105:
Harapan and co-authors ask Indonesians whether they would take a COVID-19 vaccine, in Frontiers in Public Health. No vaccine existed yet, so the online survey, run from 25 March to 6 April 2020, posed two hypothetical products. In total, 1,359 people answered.

Acceptance was high for a strong vaccine: 93.3 percent would take one that was 95 percent effective and free. For a vaccine only 50 percent effective, acceptance fell to 67.0 percent. Health care workers and people who felt at higher risk of infection were more willing. Effectiveness, the results warn, will decide uptake as much as availability. Planners in Southeast Asia get an early read on public sentiment.
europmc-pmc7405905:
Bu and co-authors ask who is lonely in lockdown, in Public Health. Two large United Kingdom datasets let them compare predictors of loneliness before and during the pandemic: 31,064 adults from a household study before, and 60,341 from a COVID-19 social study during.

The risk profile barely changed. Young adults, women, people with less education or income, the economically inactive, people living alone, and city dwellers were lonelier in both periods. Lockdown did not invent new loneliness so much as deepen old patterns: groups already at risk, such as adults aged 18 to 30 and those living alone, saw their risk heighten further. Support, the authors imply, should target the familiar map.
europmc-pmc7453005:
Aldridge and Teichmann review a decade of single cell transcriptomics and what it has revealed. The field reads the full gene activity of one cell at a time. Early methods handled only a handful of cells.

New tools changed the scale fast. Fluidic chips, robots, droplets, and barcoding pushed counts to tens of thousands of cells at once. Multi-way methods now join RNA with DNA and protein reads from the same cell. These gains let teams dissect cell identity and cell-to-cell talks in fine detail. The review highlights finds in health and disease made with these tools. It also looks ahead to where the field may go next. The authors frame the past decade as a coming of age.
europmc-pmc7472405:
Dunton, Do, and Wang study early pandemic effects on activity and sitting in United States children. School and park closures and canceled sports could cut movement. Parents of children aged 5-13 years filled an online survey.

The survey ran from April 25 to May 16, 2020, and covered 211 children in 35 states and the District of Columbia. Free play was the most common activity, at 90% of children, and walks came next at 55% in the parent reports. Children sat about 90 minutes a day for school and over 8 hours for leisure. Parents of older children saw bigger drops in activity and bigger rises in sitting. Activity moved home and onto neighborhood streets. The authors warn that habits set now may stick.
europmc-pmc7503605:
Tiotiu and co-authors review how air pollution affects asthma outcomes in adults and children. Asthma brings variable airflow block, airway over-response, and inflammation. Proof ties pollution to worse results across age groups.

Traffic fumes, nitrogen dioxide, and second-hand smoke raise the risk of asthma starting in children. A clear causal link for adult-onset asthma is not settled. Outdoor pollution can trigger symptoms, attacks, and drops in lung function. Active smoking worsens asthma control, and second-hand smoke raises attacks and care use. Indoor sources such as heating and molds add harm. The authors call for global steps to cut exposure. Cleaner air, they argue, should join standard asthma guidance in clinics.
europmc-pmc7538905:
Zhang and co-authors run a trial of berberine and probiotics for type 2 diabetes in China. The gut microbiome is a promising target for diabetes care and control. Both treatments can shift gut bacteria in ways that may help blood sugar.

The PREMOTE trial enrolled 409 newly diagnosed patients at twenty centres in China for twelve weeks. Groups got berberine alone, probiotics alone, both together, or a placebo pill each day. Combined use cut glycated haemoglobin by one point zero four points on the trial scale. Berberine alone cut it by zero point nine nine points, and placebo cut it by zero point five nine points. Berberine caused more gut side effects than the other study treatments used. Further tests tied its effect to one gut species and to a change in bile acid handling.
europmc-pmc7564605:
Yoshida and Delafontaine review how IGF-1 controls skeletal muscle growth and wasting. IGF-1 is a key growth factor in muscle tissue. It regulates both building and breakdown pathways there.

IGF-1 raises protein synthesis through PI3K and Akt signals. The mTOR and GSK3β pathways take part in that effect. IGF-1 can also block FoxO driven protein breakdown. It likely restrains autophagy through the same signals. Small RNAs that tune IGF-1 signaling are discussed. IGF-1 also activates satellite cells for muscle repair. Levels fall in many chronic diseases over time. That fall likely drives muscle wasting through combined effects. The review links each pathway to atrophy risk.
europmc-pmc7587605:
Hafeez, Parakh, Gan and Scott review antibody-drug conjugates for cancer therapy. These drugs pair an antibody with a toxic payload. The antibody seeks antigens on cancer cells.

That targeting spares much healthy tissue from harm. It can widen the usable treatment window for drugs. Nine such drugs had FDA approval at review time. More than 80 were in clinical development worldwide. The review covers design of each ADC component. Biology and chemistry of linkers and payloads are explained. Clinical results for approved drugs are summarized. Resistance pathways and future designs are also covered. Molecular imaging roles in drug work are discussed.
europmc-pmc7614605:
Abbosh and co-authors track early lung cancer spread in the TRACERx study using blood tumor DNA. Tumor DNA in blood can reveal leftover cancer after surgery. Large cohorts with long follow-up were needed for proof.

The team tracked a median of 200 mutations per patient. Mutations came from each patient removed tumor tissue. They tested 1069 plasma samples from 197 patients. No pre-surgery DNA signal marked slow, low-risk tumors. Within 120 days after surgery, 25% showed DNA signal. That group held 49% of all patients who later relapsed. Regular testing caught more impending relapses over time. A tool called ECLIPSE tracked subclone patterns in blood. Widespread subclone spread linked to poor outcomes.
europmc-pmc7677305:
Forrester and co-authors review the role of inflammation in diabetic eye disease. The disease, diabetic retinopathy, damages the retina's vessels and nerves after years of diabetes. It was long seen as a late event. The authors argue it starts much earlier, with quiet immune activity.

Low-grade white blood cell activation blocks tiny retinal vessels again and again. This starves the retina and brings on the late signs doctors see. Faulty sugar and fat handling may switch these cells on. The authors trace the signals involved and discuss steps that might block this early process before vision is lost.
europmc-pmc7694805:
Moraru and co-authors present a tool for comparing virus genomes to each other. The tool, VIRIDIC, computes how alike two virus genomes are at the letter level. Such scores guide virus classification. The tool follows the classic method used by the world virus taxonomy body.

In tests, VIRIDIC matched the classic method better than rival software. It also judged distant phage kinship more soundly, where others overstate links. Alongside scores, it gives the share of each genome that aligns and the length ratio. Its main output is a heat map, and it can cluster viruses by set thresholds. A web and stand-alone version are both free.
europmc-pmc7941305:
Manalastas-Cantos and co-authors present a software paper on ATSAS 3.0, a suite for small-angle scattering data. Such data reveal the rough shapes of molecules in solution. The ATSAS suite handles the full chain: processing, display, analysis, and modelling. This paper describes what the 3.0 release adds to a long-running and widely used package.

New programs in the release simulate scattering data from known structures. Others model lipids, nucleic acids, and mixed systems that older tools handled poorly. The authors walk through the expanded functions in turn. Each tool is placed in the workflow a typical user follows. The suite aims to serve both new users and experts in the method. The paper is a reference for what the current version can do. It also signals where this kind of structural analysis is heading.
europmc-pmc8190405:
Khalaf and co-authors examine how the tumour microenvironment drives immune and drug resistance. They call it a rogue organ with its own blood supply and nerves. Its mix of cells nurtures harsh, low-food conditions for tumours.

Signals between tumour cells and their setting release factors that hide the tumour. Matrix remodelling adds to therapy resistance. Exosomes from both tumour and normal cells spread messages through the mass. The review sorts these parts and their crosstalk. It shows why drugs fail even when they hit cancer cells. Fixing the setting may be as key as the drug itself.
europmc-pmc8227405:
Bai and co-authors review the nucleocapsid protein of SARS-CoV-2 and its uses as a target. The protein is a core building block of the virus. It shares 90% homology with the SARS virus nucleocapsid protein.

That likeness hints at a conserved, vital role. The review covers the protein's structure and its jobs in the viral life cycle. It packages the genome and helps the virus assemble. Clinical uses get a full section. The protein could serve drug design or vaccine work. Its stability across coronaviruses strengthens that case. Its many jobs make it a rich source of test markers too.
europmc-pmc8363505:
Spiegel and co-authors test dual-target CAR T cells in adults with B cell cancers that returned. CD19-targeting cells help many patients at first. Yet over half later progress.

Loss or thinning of CD19 drives much of that relapse. Ten of 16 lymphoma patients who progressed had low or absent CD19. The new cells target CD19 and CD22 together. This phase 1 trial enrolled adults with leukaemia or large B cell lymphoma. Main goals were making the cells feasibly and safely. Tumour response served as a secondary goal. Two targets aim to close the escape hatch.
europmc-pmc8371605:
Jumper and co-authors present AlphaFold, a neural network model that predicts protein shapes with high accuracy. Protein shapes help explain how proteins work. Yet lab methods take months or years for a single structure, and most known proteins still lack one.

The redesigned AlphaFold was tested in the 14th Critical Assessment of Protein Structure Prediction. The authors report that it can often predict structures with atomic accuracy. It does this even when no similar structure is known. Older methods fell well short of that level. The work offers a way to close the large gap between known protein sequences and known structures.
europmc-pmc8419805:
Billings and co-authors gather what frontline health workers say about working through pandemics. Staff worldwide took on COVID-19 care at real cost to their own health. Calls grew for mental health support, yet workers' own views got little attention.

The review searched major databases and grey sources up to September 28, 2020. It found 46 qualitative studies on worker experience and views of support. The studies spanned COVID-19 and earlier pandemics and epidemics. A meta-synthesis drew the findings into themes and sub-themes. The authors aim to show what support workers actually want. Their account comes from the frontline's own words, not from managers alone.
europmc-pmc8618305:
Habanjar and co-authors review three-dimensional cell culture systems and their use in tumor research. Flat, two-dimensional cultures have served labs for years. They cannot copy the true setting of a tumor in the body. Cells in flat layers lack the contacts and signals of real tissue.

Three-dimensional systems grow cells in matrices or as round clusters called spheroids. These setups copy tissue shape and cell talk more closely. The review compares flat and 3D methods side by side. It covers matrix types, both natural and synthetic, plus matrix-free options. Strengths and limits of each get a clear look. The field now treats 3D culture as a core tool for cancer work.
europmc-pmc8629105:
Patone and co-authors weigh nerve-related risks after a first COVID-19 vaccine dose and after infection itself. Rare reports of such problems had raised public concern. The team used a self-controlled case series design. It covered over 20 million people who got the ChAdOx1 vaccine and over 12 million who got BNT162b2.

Risk of Guillain-Barré syndrome rose in the weeks after ChAdOx1. Bell palsy risk also rose slightly with that vaccine. A Scottish group backed the Guillain-Barré finding. The BNT162b2 vaccine linked to a small rise in hemorrhagic stroke. Risks after a positive virus test were far higher for every outcome. The authors give counts to put the vaccine risks in context.
europmc-pmc8657205:
Di Tommaso, Gasbarrini, and Ponziani review the intestinal barrier and its role in health and disease. The gut lining lets nutrients pass while it blocks harmful factors. It is built from epithelial cells, immune cells, and their secretions. Gut microbes help keep this barrier in balance.

Germs, foreign chemicals, and food can break the barrier down. Genes and immune factors raise the risk for some people. Changes in gut microbes sit at the center of the process. A leaky barrier links to metabolic disease and autoimmunity. The review covers the gut-brain and gut-liver links as well. It frames barrier care as a path to new treatments.
europmc-pmc8683505:
Kürten and co-authors use single-cell RNA sequencing to study cell interactions in head and neck tumors. These cancers mix stromal, epithelial, and immune cells in complex ways. The team profiled tumors and matched blood from 18 patients. Six tumors were linked to human papillomavirus, and twelve were not.

The dataset held 134,606 cells in total. Cell signatures varied with inflammation and virus status. One fibroblast type predicted poor outcomes in virus-linked tumors. The team also mapped drug-targetable contacts between checkpoint proteins. Tumor macrophages supplied most PD-L1 and other checkpoint signals in the tissue. The work gives a cell-level view for new therapy design.
europmc-pmc8857305:
Wang and co-authors review how mechanical forces govern bone remodeling. Bone is rebuilt all life long. Builder cells add bone while eater cells remove it. The balance adapts bone mass to the loads it bears. Without load, bone weakens fast. Astronauts and bedridden patients lose bone for this reason. The review asks how bone senses force at all.

The authors describe which bone cells feel mechanical strain. They detail the structures that act as sensors. They then trace the signals sent once force is felt. The YAP/TAZ pathway gets its own section. A section on microgravity shows remodeling gone wrong. The authors close with open questions. Their aim is new strategies to restore bone. Force sensing, they argue, is the key lever.
europmc-pmc8885505:
Stenberg and co-authors update care guidelines for bariatric surgery under the ERAS approach. ERAS, or Enhanced Recovery After Surgery, trims stress around an operation. The goal is faster, safer recovery. Bariatric surgery demand keeps climbing worldwide. This document is the society's second update. It gives consensus advice for each step of care. The team searched major databases through December 2020.

Studies were graded with the GRADE system. Meta-analyses and randomized trials got the closest look. The panel then agreed on recommendations item by item. Many rest on modest evidence in bariatric patients. Some practices are borrowed from other surgery types. The authors say so plainly. Even so, the consensus is comprehensive. It covers care before, during, and after surgery. Hospitals can use it as a ready protocol.
europmc-pmc8909305:
Li, Li, and Wu review the cell's two main machines for destroying proteins. Stressed cells fill with unfolded and misfolded proteins. Clumped proteins can poison the cell. Ubiquitin tags mark the doomed proteins. The proteasome chews up tagged proteins one by one. Autophagy swallows larger loads, including whole clumps. If both systems fail, the cell may die. Their breakdown feeds many diseases.

The review explains the shared ubiquitin pool first. It then details each machine on its own. Crosstalk between the two systems gets a full section. They back each other up under stress. Disease links follow, from nerve degeneration to cancer. The authors stress the pair as one network. Drugs may need to tune both arms at once. Protein quality control is the unifying theme.
europmc-pmc8954705:
Jebari-Benslaiman and co-authors review the pathophysiology of atherosclerosis stage by stage. This artery disease underlies most cardiovascular deaths. It begins when the vessel lining activates. Lipids, fibers, and calcium then build up in the wall. The vessel narrows as plaque grows. Inflammation runs through the whole process. A ruptured plaque can trigger a fatal clot. The review follows that arc in order.

Sections move from the endothelium to the fatty streak. Fibrous plaque growth comes next. Stability and rupture close the main arc. Inflammation gets its own deep section. Gene regulation by microRNAs and long noncoding RNAs follows. The gut microbiota enters as a newer driver. Sex differences and smoking each earn coverage. The authors aim for a global view. Old and new risk factors share the frame.
europmc-pmc9168805:
GBD 2019 Human Resources for Health Collaborators measure the world's health workforce and its link to universal health coverage. Health workers span many jobs that promote or improve health. Comparable counts across countries were lacking, which blocked firm planning. The team built standard estimates for 204 countries and territories from 1990 to 2019.

They estimate the world had 104.0 million health workers in 2019. That total includes 12.8 million physicians and 29.8 million nurses and midwives. Sub-Saharan Africa, south Asia, and north Africa and the Middle East had the lowest densities. To reach a set coverage target, millions more staff would be needed in each main cadre. The authors call for more funding to train and keep health workers.
europmc-pmc9525705:
Lin and co-authors trace how mitochondrial damage signals amplify neuroinflammation in degenerative brain diseases. Faulty mitochondria and brain inflammation both mark these diseases. Signals spilled from damaged mitochondria act as alarms. Immune receptors on microglia read those alarms and react.

The review details each damage signal in turn. Mitochondrial DNA and reactive oxygen species lead the list. ATP, cardiolipin, and cytochrome c are covered too. Calcium and iron shifts join the account. Inflammation then feeds back on the mitochondria themselves. Released factors disturb their metabolism and function. Strong signs suggest mitochondrial faults come first in disease course. That order makes the signals prime drug targets. The authors map each signal to the diseases where it acts.
europmc-pmc9737905:
Naeem and co-authors review natural products as anticancer agents and their future prospects. Compounds from nature have fed cancer drug work for decades. Chemists tweak their structures or use them as build blocks. Modern cancer care stays costly with mixed gains in survival.

The review traces how natural products rose in cancer care. It sorts their roles across common cancer types. Some act as sensitizers that boost standard drug effects. Others feed immune therapy or pair well in drug mixes. New formulations aim to deliver them more precisely. The compounds' wide shapes give them fresh biological actions. Early lab results show a positive trend for many agents. The authors also map how these compounds kill cancer cells. They close with the trials and design work still needed. Safety plus strength is their case for more study.
farnell-evolution-of-religion-1905:
Lewis Richard Farnell was an Oxford scholar of Greek cults who gave the Hibbert Lectures printed in 1905 as The Evolution of Religion. The lectures compare how religions grow and change across peoples and ages. Farnell writes as a morphologist, a student of forms, of faith.

He traces prayer, sacrifice, priesthood, and the idea of God from simple beginnings toward higher unity. His method weighs Greek evidence he knew deeply against reports from Africa, Asia, and the Pacific. The book gives English readers a calm, learned map of comparative religion before the field hardened into schools.
fbi-vault-amerithrax-amerithrax-part-05:
Part 5 of the Amerithrax file holds late case work by the Federal Bureau of Investigation into the 2001 anthrax mail attacks. The sampled pages date to the spring and summer of 2008. By then the probe was years old, and its work had turned to small, exact checks.

Agents knocked on doors on April 21, 2008, under cover of a postal probe into reshipping. One home they reached was a halfway house for men in recovery from drink. Days later, a man was shown a motor vehicle photo and asked what he knew. The summer brought paper steps: a preservation order went to Yahoo for a set of email accounts, among them one named jimmyflathead. The part shows a cold case kept warm by door knocks and record holds.
fogazzaro-the-saint-1905:
Fogazzaro gives Italy a reformer in The Saint, dated 1905. Antonio Fogazzaro tells of Benedetto, a layman whose holiness draws followers and suspicion alike. The text here is the English version of the Italian novel. Its hero's words, spoken in private, carry farther than he knows.

The sampled pages catch that spread. A woman begs Benedetto to repeat a word he had spoken to the parish priest, the Arciprete, while she listened from the next room. He had said that a man may deny the existence of God without being an atheist. The God set before him might wear a shape his mind rejects. What counts is that he loves truth, virtue, and his fellow men. A word from you, she says, has given me life, and your going will kill me. Fogazzaro's novel asks what a saint may say in a church that fears him.
forster-where-angels-fear-1905:
Where Angels Fear to Tread, published in 1905, was E. M. Forster's first novel. Forster was twenty-six and writing from his own travels in Italy. The title quotes a line about fools rushing in where angels fear to tread.

A young English widow, Lilia Herriton, shocks her late husband's family by marrying a poor Italian in the town of Monteriano. Her in-laws send rescuers to fix the scandal, first to stop the marriage, then to claim her baby. Comedy turns to grief as English manners meet Italian warmth and pride. Forster's comedy of manners already shows his lifelong theme: feeling versus respectability.
freeman-debtor-1905:
Banbridge, the town in Freeman's 1905 novel The Debtor, sits close enough to the great City to see its glow. Trains speed between them, and half the men commute to wrestle for daily bread. Harper issued the book with pictures by W. D. Stevens.

Banbridge keeps its own season of luncheons, teas, dances, and clubs through the winter. Women there run a whist club and a strong club for study and fitness. Against that bright surface, a family slides into debt. Freeman tracks what owing money does to pride, marriage, and standing, in a shrewd study that refuses easy blame.
frus-1861-d105:
On 11 November 1861, William H. Seward wrote to Charles Francis Adams as the Trent storm gathered. The letter is document 105 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

Three days before, a Union captain had seized two Confederate envoys from the British ship Trent. Seward's November letter to London went out as that storm gathered. The whole tie with Britain now hung on the words men like Seward and Adams chose in the weeks ahead. The envoys, Mason and Slidell, were bound for London and Paris when their ship was stopped. Their names, Mason and Slidell, would soon be on every tongue in two capitals.
frus-1861-d205:
On 1 May 1861, William H. Seward wrote to Bradford Wood, his new minister to Denmark. Wood was the new American minister to Denmark. The letter is document 205 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

Denmark was a small post, but its straits guarded the Baltic sea road. Seward filled even minor posts with care that spring. His May letter to Wood shows the whole map of the service being set in order at once. Even minor posts closed the gaps through which Southern agents might have slipped. Gaps closed at small posts kept the whole fence sound around the South.
frus-1861-d305:
Writing home was Mr. Bigler's duty, and his letter of 2 August 1861 went to Seward. Congress received it as Document 305 in the papers printed with the President's message that year. The date falls in the first summer of the Civil War, when the Union fought to keep foreign powers from backing the South.

Readers get the field report side of the exchange, sent home for Seward to weigh and answer. Its worth grows in context, as one link in a chain of letters that kept the peace with Europe. Foreign Relations of the United States, the official record series, is where the full exchange can be traced.
frus-1862-d105:
Seward heard from Charles Francis Adams on 11 July 1862, in a dispatch sent from abroad. Congress received it as Document 105 in the foreign affairs volume that went with the President's message. It belongs to the summer of 1862, the war's second year, when keeping Europe out of the war was a core task for Washington.

Readers get the field report side of the exchange, sent home for Seward to weigh and answer. For students of the war, the value lies in the sequence: one dated step in a long exchange. The Foreign Relations series, kept by the State Department's Office of the Historian, preserves the full run.
frus-1862-d205:
On 14 January 1862 Lord Lyons sent Secretary of State William H. Seward a note printed as Document 205 in the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. It answered into a stream of notes the two men traded through that month.

Lyons prided himself on plain, even dealings with Seward, whom he found changeable but workable. Their written exchanges in January 1862 rebuilt a working tie strained by the Trent crisis weeks before. A single note may treat a small matter; the run of them shows two governments learning to live with a war neither could ignore. The British legation stood a short walk from the State Department, and messengers passed between them daily.
frus-1862-d305:
Three Seward dispatches to Paris are dated 23 August 1862, and the first is Document 305 in the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. All three went to William L. Dayton, the American minister to France.

A three-letter day at the Department usually meant a steamer sailing and a full desk. The topics across such a set could span the whole Paris brief, from the war to Mexico to trade. For the reader, the trio of 23 August is a snapshot of everything Washington wanted in front of its Paris envoy. It was taken as the summer campaign peaked. A steamer's sailing day set the legation's week, and Dayton wrote against that clock.
frus-1862-d405:
At the height of a hard summer for the Union, on 31 July 1862, Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote to Horace J. Perry in Madrid. The dispatch is Document 405 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs.

July 1862 brought the Army of the Potomac's retreat from Richmond and fresh fears that Europe might step in. Seward worked to keep foreign courts from reading Union setbacks as collapse. His orders to Madrid in this season carried the government's case to Spain. That court's Cuban ports and Mexican venture made it one the Union could not afford to lose or to provoke.
frus-1862-d505:
On 11 June 1862 James Shepherd Pike wrote from The Hague to Secretary of State William H. Seward. His report is Document 505 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, printed for Congress.

Pike's June report reached Washington in July, by which time the news it answered was history. That delay shaped all Civil War diplomacy: ministers had to be trusted with wide discretion. Pike used his to keep the Dutch ministry well disposed and well informed, and to report frankly when they were neither. His letters from The Hague, plain and sometimes tart, were among the files Seward could read for Dutch opinion without discounting the writer. The dispatch sustains that run into the summer.
frus-1862-d605:
Dated 21 March 1862, this letter comes from the Spanish commander in Mexico. It is addressed to Admiral Jurien de la Gravière. It answers the French admiral's note of the day before. It is Document 605 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs.

The catalog heading prints the Spanish general's name as Trim. He is evidently the Prim of the companion papers. Prim's despatch carried the admiral's letter as an annex. The exchange between the two commanders belongs to the allied quarrel that ended with Spain's withdrawal from Mexico within weeks. Read as a pair, Documents 604 and 605 show coalition diplomacy failing in the field. The failure is written in polite, exact language. It is the language officers used when they were parting company.
frus-1862-d705:
Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote to Charles N. Riotte on 6 October 1862. Riotte was the American minister in Costa Rica, and the letter is document 705 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1862. A second letter to Riotte followed three days later.

Outward letters in a pair often split one post's business into two short notes. Seward's October letters kept Riotte stocked with word from Washington as the war news turned. They show the State Department's habit of close guidance. It was kept up even for a small legation in Central America, while the Union's fate hung in the balance at home.
frus-1863p1-d105:
Charles Francis Adams received this letter from Secretary of State William H. Seward under date of 2 March 1863. It is the ninth of twelve Seward letters to Adams dated that day in the volume. Adams was the American minister in London; the letter is document 105 in part one of the 1863 volume.

By the ninth sheet, Seward had covered the great heads of the London brief and was at its finer points. The batch shows a secretary who knew his file cold and meant his envoy to know it too. This letter is a late piece of that day's work. Its worth is in the set: twelve sheets that reset the brief for spring.
frus-1863p1-d205:
The State Department's mail for London dated 23 May 1863 carried this instruction from Secretary of State William H. Seward to Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London. It is document 205 in the 1863 Foreign Relations volume. It survives in the 1863 volume of Foreign Relations of the United States, the State Department's official record of its work abroad.

After emancipation became official policy in January 1863, Seward could argue that aiding the South meant aiding slavery. That argument runs under much of the year's diplomacy. For a modern reader, it offers the war as working diplomats saw it: slow mail, sharp words, and constant risk.
frus-1863p1-d305: Secretary of State William H. Seward sent this instruction to Charles Francis Adams, his minister in London, on 5 October 1863. It is document 305 in the 1863 Foreign Relations volume, within the orders that steered American policy toward Britain during the Civil War. Through such letters Washington told its man in London what to press, protest, or let pass.
frus-1863p1-d405:
From the British legation in Washington on 1 March 1863, Lord Lyons sent this note to Secretary of State William H. Seward. It stands as document 405 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1863. It appears in the Foreign Relations series, where the State Department printed the papers it sent with the President's yearly message to Congress.

London watched for any sign that Washington meant to widen the war. Lyons's job was to read American intentions and report them home faithfully. For a modern reader, it offers the war as working diplomats saw it: slow mail, sharp words, and constant risk.
frus-1863p1-d505:
A letter of 9 May 1863, from Lord Lyons to William H. Seward, stands as document 505 in the printed record. Lyons was Britain's minister in Washington, and Seward was the American Secretary of State. The letter is one piece of the steady stream of notes that passed between the two governments in the spring of 1863. The State Department later published the letter in its 1863 foreign affairs volume, laid before Congress with the President's message.

British subjects caught up in the war filled many pages: men arrested, goods seized, and claims for losses that London took up with Washington. The letter also shows the craft of the period: a few stiff phrases could carry a warning, and both sides knew how to read them. The volume's editors printed it without comment; its meaning comes from the company it keeps in the file.
frus-1863p1-d605:
On 8 August 1863, William H. Seward, the Secretary of State wrote to Lord Lyons, Britain's envoy in Washington. It forms part of Foreign Relations of the United States, the official printed record of American diplomacy. America was then in the third year of its Civil War, and every letter to or from London carried weight.

The formal tone can hide the tension, but the pace gives it away. Notes this frequent mean both capitals were watching each other closely. The stakes behind this routine mail were high. If Britain had backed the Confederacy, the war could have changed course, so each note helped hold the line of British neutrality. The volume's editors printed it without comment; its meaning comes from the company it keeps in the file.
frus-1905:
Hay's death fills the front of this volume. John Hay had served as Secretary of State for years. Papers of sympathy run for dozens of files. Elihu Root then takes the post in his place. The first notes pledge that China will keep its land whole. One note pulls the American legation out of Korea. One short head names a planned talk on Morocco. Argentina reports a revolt at home in its own file.

The middle text is treaty talk on customs posts. Each side vows to weigh new posts or wider powers for old ones. Even closing a post needs a joint accord between the two states. Such dry clauses show how the daily work gets done. Korea's fate and China's pledge hang over the whole year. Japan has won its war and changed the Far East map. Root takes charge of that new map.
frus-1919Parisv05:
The Council of Four dominates Volume V of the Paris papers. Its minutes run from March 20 to May 24, 1919. Wilson, Lloyd George, Clemenceau, and Orlando decide in small rooms. Meetings crowd April, sometimes three in a day. A note explains the minutes' keeping at the front. The mid-volume debate turns to mandates. Italy claims a share if mandates bring gain. If they burden, Italy stands ready too, its spokesman says.

He cites the Treaty of London for support. Africa's map, he argues, owes Italy fair compensation. France and Britain gained colonies there in view. Such bargains underlie the public principles. The volume shows power at its plainest. Four men divide a world in conversation.
frus-1932v05:
The American republics fill Volume V of 1932. Their continental conference is put off at the start. The Chaco war then takes the largest space. Neutral commissioners offer good offices in vain. The ABC powers and the League are drawn in. Argentina proposes a pact against war. Leticia pits Colombia against Peru in its file. Brazil's São Paulo rising fills a long run. Chile's revolutions fill a longer one. Cuba and Costa Rica shake in smaller files. El Salvador's new regime wins no recognition. Its Communist rising is crushed in the same papers.

A mid-volume wire reports Santiago's June coup. Merino takes the Interior ministry in the new junta. Socialism had seized Chile days before. The volume is a hemisphere in upheaval. Washington watches, warns, and withholds its blessing.
frus-1933v05:
Bolivia's war taxes open Volume V of 1933. The Chaco levy hits foreign firms in 1932's law. Consuls win free imports by a swap of notes. Brazil then takes the volume's long middle. Trade talks open with Washington in earnest. Exchange curbs squeeze American firms and bondholders. Federal and state debts need fair servicing. Chile's exchange rules draw the same campaign. The nitrate trust Cosach is wound up in files. Its industry's rebuild fills a longer run. Colombia signs a trade deal in December, unperfected.

Debt halts in Bogotá draw a warning to its president. Cuba's revolution closes the contents. A mid-volume wire finds Welles cabling from Habana in October. The island's new rulers face his daily reports. The volume is creditors versus crisis.
frus-1934v05:
Chile's exchange curbs open Volume V of 1934. A sales tax on diplomats draws protest too. Colombia negotiates a fresh trade deal. Costa Rica opens its own trade talks. Cuba then takes the volume's center. Its provisional government wins recognition in files. A trade pact signs on August 24. Mendieta begs Roosevelt's help on sugar. A relations treaty signs in May that year. It ends the old Platt protectorate terms. Arms shipments to Cuba are curbed by rule.

Santo Domingo settles with its bondholders. A murdered American's claim is paid without blame owned. El Salvador's Martínez regime wins recognition at last. A mid-volume plea recalls Haiti's coffee glory. America once drank almost only Haitian coffee, it says. The volume is the Good Neighbor in practice.
frus-1936v05:
Buenos Aires hosts the peace conference in Volume V. It sits through December 1936 in these papers. Lima's next conference is prepared at the front. The Chaco peace talks grind on in theirs. Ecuador and Peru restate their border quarrel. A recognition rule then changes quietly. The 1923 treaty's test no longer guides Washington. Central America's coups gain a freer hand thereby. Defaulted bonds win one policy paper. The inter-American highway advances in files. Argentina talks trade and oil fairness. Bolivia's revolution fills a long run.
