Tin exports and an embargo court case follow there. A mid-volume claim letter warns of deadlines. Late claims, it hints, may lose the plan's shelter. Frankness, the writer says, compels the warning. The volume is neighborliness with conditions.
frus-1937v05:
The republics' Lima meeting is prepared in Volume V. The Chaco peace conference grinds toward its end. Borders fill the next files in line. Ecuador and Peru restate their old quarrel. Honduras and Nicaragua take a longer run. Guatemala asks help pressing its Belize claim. Three republics offer peace work to Haiti and Santo Domingo. Argentina drafts a pact on asylum rights. America offers old destroyers for lease as trainers. That proposal fills a curious file. Highway building and an air conference follow.

Radio rules sign at Habana in December. Argentina's exchange and trade talks close in. A mid-volume Chilean note weighs exchange pacts. Santiago cannot scrap its compensation deals at once. Its simpler offer still guards more than before. The volume is inter-American routine, steadily thickening.
frus-1938v05:
Lima hosts the republics in December 1938. Their eighth conference fills Volume V's front. Preliminaries stress that it must not be put off. The Chaco peace conference then closes its long war. Three neighbors offer peace to Haiti and Santo Domingo. Guatemala and Britain dispute Belize briefly. Borders take three files in a row. Argentina and Chile, Ecuador and Peru, Honduras and Nicaragua follow. Trade talks with Buenos Aires grind on. American air officers teach in Argentina meanwhile. Brazil objects to that mission in its file.

Bolivia seizes Standard Oil's fields; Washington helps informally. Brazil's exchange and debt fights fill long runs. A mid-volume note parses Ecuador's trade offer. Quotas on unscheduled goods stay free, it explains. The volume is the Good Neighbor at work.
frus-1939v05:
War in Europe summons the republics in Volume V. Their views on a joint arms resolution are canvassed. Foreign ministers then meet at Panama in September. Their declaration draws a safety zone at sea. Its map gets an explanatory note of care. Finance and neutrality committees are founded there. Patrols guard the zone by joint effort. German ships hiding in hemisphere ports pose puzzles. Belligerents breach the zone in a long file. A joint protest at Russia's Finland invasion is weighed.

Borders and trade close the contents. Argentina bargains and wins air instructors by pact. Bolivia's revolving regimes keep normal ties. A mid-volume talk delays Chile's money hopes. The bank's charter must settle first, Santiago is told. The sums asked were judged very high. The volume is neutrality organized.
frus-1940v05:
Hemisphere defense organizes the 1940 fifth volume. Arms policy toward sister republics is stated first. Consultations then run country by country. Twenty files map who would fight, and how. Foreign ministers meet at Habana in July. Their sessions fill a long central run. A neutrality committee works in the tail files. Europe's colonies in America gain a caretaker board. It stands ready if empires fall. An inter-American bank is drafted but unperfected. Joint economic plans follow in shorter papers. A coffee pact signs in November that year.

A mid-volume plea frees a detained Brazilian ship. London asks Rio for a swift answer. Passengers of the Siqueira Campos suffered enough delay. Such incidents tested the patrol's courtesy. The volume is solidarity being built.
frus-1941v05:
Japan's southern advance fills the 1941 fifth volume. Chapters run from January to December's end. Thailand and Indochina feel the pressure in turn. Americans sail home from the Far East in files. The undeclared war in China grinds on meanwhile. Marines and sailors are ordered out of China. Their leaving stays unfinished when war erupts. Aid and arms for China take the longest run. Foreign courts in China would end by agreement. That policy is stated in a short file. Customs funds and Shanghai's zone follow.

Fur seals end the contents oddly. Japan kills the old four-power seal pact. Tampered American mail draws a last protest. A mid-volume report catches secret talks in Shanghai. New Fourth Army officers confer with the Japanese there. China's allies were also its rivals. The volume is an empire expanding.
frus-1942v05:
Rio's January meeting opens the 1942 fifth volume. Foreign ministers gather days after Pearl Harbor. A caretaker board for Europe's colonies follows. Police chiefs confer at Buenos Aires in May. Money control experts meet in Washington in June. A political defense board sits at Montevideo. Axis voices must be cut off the airwaves. That campaign fills a long file. Spies are hunted in the next long run. Uruguay resumes ties with Russia by good offices. Blacklists unite London and Washington in files.

Argentina bargains over metals, exports, and arms. A mid-volume talk finds American patience thin. Home politics, the envoy warns, must rank second now. The war had reached that point, he says. The volume is the hemisphere closing ranks. Its machinery is lists, patrols, and pressure.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d105: Roosevelt replied to Winant on November 8, 1943, the same day the ambassador's letter in this series was written. The reply is Document 105 of the Cairo and Tehran volume. Guidance to London mattered in those days, with two conferences to staff and steer. The record names the parties and the date only. The letter is printed in the Foreign Relations volume beside its companion dispatch.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d205:
Admiral William Leahy, the President's chief of staff, sent President Roosevelt a memorandum on 10 November 1943. It reports the Joint Chiefs of Staff's view on the Soviet request for Italian naval and merchant ships, which Secretary of State Hull had raised in a message of 3 November.

The chiefs draw a careful line. Since the Soviet Union had accepted Italy as a co-belligerent, no Italian ships should change ownership or registry. But Soviet use of the ships to help the war effort is acceptable, so long as title stays Italian. Leahy recommends that the vessels Moscow asked for be made available on exactly those terms.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d305:
Mike Reilly, supervising agent of the United States Secret Service, telegraphed the agent at Cairo from Tehran on 24 November 1943 with travel and security findings for the President's journey. The message was to be shown to Roosevelt himself, along with Hopkins, Watson, and Admirals Brown and McIntire.

Reilly reports the American legation is adequate and a mile from the adjoining British and Russian missions, with no security problems on the route between. He lays out a slow option by air to Abadan and then by rail, crossing the Karun river by small boat, and warns the railroad holds many dangerous security problems. His urgent advice is to fly direct, leaving Cairo at half past seven and reaching Tehran the same afternoon. He asks for the President's decision that night.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d405:
President Roosevelt sent Ambassador Steinhardt a secret instruction from Tehran on 1 December 1943, carrying the invitation to Turkey's president. Having met Marshal Stalin, Roosevelt and Churchill will be in Cairo on Saturday and Sunday, 4 and 5 December, with a Soviet representative, and they greatly value a meeting with Inönü.

Steinhardt is to pass the message to Inönü at once, hand it over in person if possible, and impress its extreme secrecy on him. The British and Soviet ambassadors are being told to deliver matching invitations, and the three are to concert a simultaneous presentation. Inönü may consult his parliament in secret session about leaving the country if he feels he must. Roosevelt adds that it would be useful if Steinhardt could accompany the Turkish president to Cairo.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d505:
President Roosevelt messaged Secretary of State Cordell Hull on December 7, 1943, the day after the Second Cairo Conference closed. Roosevelt was beginning the long journey home while Hull held the State Department in Washington. The State Department printed the message in its Cairo-Tehran volume.

Post-conference cables carried the results home: what had been decided, what remained open, and what Washington should do next. This message sits in that homeward traffic, between the summit and the return to routine government. For readers, it shows the conference's work being handed back to the permanent departments that had to carry it out in the months ahead.
frus-1943v05:
Volume V of the 1943 Diplomatic Papers turns to the American Republics, with a regional opening on defense talks at Montevideo and Vice President Wallace's tour. Country sections follow for states from Bolivia to Venezuela. Export controls and blocked Axis funds recur across the region.

Argentina takes the largest share, as Washington pressed it to break with the Axis and cut trade and wireless links. Bolivia's new regime and its entry into the war also draw long treatment. Embassy reports and policy notes show the Good Neighbor policy under wartime strain. Hemisphere unity was the goal, and the papers show its limits.
frus-1944-quebec-d105:
Officials in the British Treasury prepared a memorandum dated September 4, 1944. The paper reached the files printed in the Quebec 1944 volume. It was written eight days before the conference opened. Britain's Treasury managed a strained wartime economy.

British finance papers stated what London could and could not bear. American aid had kept Britain fighting since 1941. The terms of that aid after Germany's defeat were uncertain. A Treasury memorandum put figures behind the British case. For readers, it shows money arguments prepared with care. Both sides knew the Quebec talks would test their partnership.
frus-1944-quebec-d205:
An editors' note follows the fight over three words: "or sold for profit," inserted into the lend-lease record of September 14, 1944. Morgenthau and Cherwell met over the phrase, and Morgenthau later recounted the meeting to Treasury colleagues. The British had cornered him on Friday evening at half past seven, wanting the words changed.

Morgenthau refused to go back to the president a third time. He explained his understanding with a gasoline example: goods sent over were booked at price plus transport, and could be sold back on that basis without profit. He would exchange letters instead of reopening the text. Cherwell's clarifying letter of September 16 is printed later in the volume.
frus-1944v05:
The Near East, South Asia, Africa, and the Far East meet in Volume V of the 1944 Diplomatic Papers. Saudi oil and a new American petroleum policy open the regional papers. Greece follows, with its post-liberation politics and relief needs.

India holds a long section, from the Phillips mission to aid and press questions. Ethiopia, Egypt, and Afghanistan appear in shorter country runs. Far East papers close the volume. Legation reports show American reach growing in lands long left to Britain. Oil, bases, and local politics shaped each contact. Local rulers bargained hard with both Allied camps.
frus-1945-50-intel-d105:
The Fortier Committee sent a memorandum to Director of Central Intelligence Sidney Souers on 14 March 1946. Committees of officers did much of the new group's early design work. The text comes from the Foreign Relations of the United States volume that looks back at American intelligence work from 1945 to 1950.

A committee paper to the director shows the CIG being built by study and report, the Washington way. The Fortier group's work fed the decisions by which the group took over the SSU's operations and set its own shape. Readers can use this memorandum to see the transfer from the receiving end. The remnant is not pleading to survive here. The new body is planning what to take and how to run it. The shift of viewpoint is the story of 1946 in one paper.
frus-1945-50-intel-d205: A text titled "Memorandum for the Record" bears the date 25 January 1947. Readers meet it as document 205 of the Foreign Relations series volume on intelligence from 1945 to 1950. The first peace-time setup paired the National Intelligence Authority at the top with the Central Intelligence Group below it. Notes to the file look minor, but they fix dates and facts that bigger papers leave vague.
frus-1945-50-intel-d305:
On 29 October 1948, the Director of the Policy Planning Staff (Kennan) sent a memorandum to the Under Secretary of State (Lovett). The Office of the Historian kept it as document 305 in the Foreign Relations intelligence volume for 1945 to 1950. An outside survey team led by Allen Dulles was then reviewing the CIA, and its findings would drive a round of reform debate.

The form is plain on purpose: a named sender, a named reader, and a short statement of the matter at hand. The reply, if any came, would build on the points laid out here. The FRUS editors kept it because the chain of choices is not whole without it.
frus-1945-50-intel-d405:
One entry in the 1949 record is a Central Intelligence Agency memo dated 21 December 1949. It stands as document 405 in the Foreign Relations volume on American intelligence from 1945 to 1950. The State Department's Office of the Historian published the volume.

Most papers in the volume name a writer and a reader, but an agency memo speaks for the CIA as a whole. Two years after its birth, the agency was setting its views down in formal papers for the rest of the government. The memo lets readers hear that new corporate voice. The paper's plain heading fits a season when the agency was still learning to speak with one voice.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d105:
Herbert Lehman, head of the United Nations Relief and Rehabilitation Administration, wrote to President Roosevelt on 19 January 1945. Hearing that a Big Three meeting is near, he asks the President to raise UNRRA's troubles with Stalin. His letter is printed in the Malta and Yalta volume.

Relief for Poland and Czechoslovakia, a prime UNRRA task, has been held up for want of Soviet leave to move staff and supplies across Soviet soil. Word has just come that supplies may enter through Rumanian ports, but lasting arrangements are needed. Lehman also cites a Council ruling to aid people driven from their homes in enemy lands for their race, faith, or work for the United Nations.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d205:
Roosevelt told Churchill on 6 December 1944 that their views on France matched, then parted from him on two points. His telegram number 670, sent from Warm Springs, is printed in the Malta and Yalta volume. Stalin's account of the de Gaulle talks lies behind it.

On keeping de Gaulle out of the Big Three meeting, Roosevelt holds firm: his presence would merely add a complicating and undesirable factor. He also resists sending France's frontiers to the European Advisory Commission, which is fully occupied with Germany's surrender. On Churchill's idea of a three-way pact, he is dubious. American opinion might read such a pact as a competitor to the future world organization, to which he attaches the very highest importance.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d305:
Foreign Secretary Anthony Eden wrote to Prime Minister Churchill on February 2, 1945. His heading named the subject: the future of Germany. Eden warned that the war's fast pace made it urgent for the major Allies to settle one shared policy on Germany. He pointed to the European Advisory Commission, set up in 1943 to draft joint advice on the war's end.

Eden lists what that commission had already produced. It had drafted surrender terms, a plan for zones of occupation, and control machinery for Germany. Only the surrender terms had won approval from all three governments. His letter shows London pressing for speed before the Yalta meeting made delay costly.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d405:
Unfinished business is the theme of Page's minutes for the foreign ministers on February 9, 1945. Stettinius, in the chair, proposed a general review of the items still open. The list ran long: Dumbarton Oaks matters, the subcommittee report on invitations to the United Nations conference, reparations, Poland, Iran, and the Yugoslav frontiers.

Poland, reparations, Dumbarton Oaks, Iran, and Yugoslavia each then came up in turn. The record reads like a stocktaking halfway through the endgame. With two days left at Yalta, the ministers could see exactly how much remained unsettled. Page's plain list gives the conference's agenda in its rawest form.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d505:
Why do later statements appear at the end of a conference volume? This editorial note explains. In compiling the volume, the editors found a few unpublished papers in which leading participants at Yalta had made authoritative statements on the proceedings. These statements filled out the contemporary record, so they are printed at this point.

The note also points readers to published accounts. Roosevelt's message to Congress of March 1, 1945, is cited, with its places in the State Department Bulletin and the Congressional Record. Churchill's report to the House of Commons of February 27 follows, with its column in the parliamentary debates. The note turns the volume's appendix into a reading list.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d105:
President Truman broke staffing news to Secretary of State Stettinius in a letter extract dated June 27, 1945. The extract is document 105 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference. Truman wrote from Independence, Missouri, about who would travel with him to meet Stalin and Churchill the next month.

Truman says he had wanted Stettinius to come with him. But congressional hearings on the United Nations Charter would run while he was away, and he had reluctantly agreed to Stettinius's own suggestion that he stay in Washington. The note printed here is drawn from the letter in which Truman accepted Stettinius's resignation as Secretary of State. Within days James Byrnes would take the post, and it was Byrnes who went to Potsdam.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d205:
Ambassador Winant passed on a British worry about Tangier in a telegram extract dated July 11, 1945. The extract is document 205 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference. The full message appears later in the volume. Foreign Office official Hoyer Millar had spoken to the embassy that day.

Now that the Russians have asked to take part, Millar said, he did not see how talks on Tangier could open unless the Russians were brought in. Bringing them in at once raises the question of how far they would share in any plan for the zone's future administration. That point has to be decided first, and it cannot be decided on the minute. It might best go to the Big Three meeting. Tangier, the international zone at the mouth of the Mediterranean, thus joined the summit's list of side questions.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d305:
An extract of Barnes's July 6, 1945 cable from Sofia describes the men in Bulgaria's cabinet who still resisted Communist control. The Socialist Cheshmedjieff, the independent Stoyanov, and Petkov's Agrarians all appear in his account. Their firmness, Barnes wrote, rested on one hope in particular.

That hope was that the end of the war in Europe would soon end sole Soviet rule over Bulgarian affairs. These ministers seized on any sign, however faint, that the West had not left Bulgaria to Russia. The extract also touches the fight over election candidates inside the Fatherland Front, the ruling bloc.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d405:
Occupation zones in Germany are the second topic in a summary report on the European Advisory Commission's work from January 1944 to July 1945. The extract, dated at London on July 12, 1945, comes from the American delegation to that Commission. It records how the zone map of Germany was built, step by step.

From March to September 1944 the Commission worked on the zones and on the joint occupation of Berlin. A protocol of September 12, 1944 set out three zones in Germany and three areas in Berlin. An agreement of November 14, 1944 then fixed the American and British zones. At Yalta it was agreed the French zone would be carved from those two.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d505: Polish property in London is settled in an extract of Winant's cable of July 5, 1945. A British official gave the news. The Foreign Office had concluded an agreement the day before, with the Polish government in London. Under it, all leases would be taken over by the British government. The lease on the Polish embassy property was among them. Most leases were short. Britain would either turn them over to the new Polish government, if it wished, or keep them on its own account.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d605:
A top secret briefing paper of July 5, 1945, maps the form Soviet forces might take in the war on Japan. It is document 605 in volume one of the Foreign Relations papers on the Potsdam Conference. It divides the fighting into zones by land and by task.

For the Japanese home islands, the paper keeps the lead with the United States. Landings there need special gear and skills that U.S. forces had honed most. Other states at war with Japan, Asian ones included, could still send units under the U.S. commander. Manchuria, Mongolia, and North China would be land warfare, a field the Soviets knew well. The paper urges that the Soviet commander invite Allied units there too, to head off suspicion. Korea, it adds, concerns many states, and none should gain the upper hand there.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d705:
British minister John Balfour sent Loy Henderson the Yalta record on the Straits in a letter of July 9, 1945. It is document 705 in volume one of the Foreign Relations papers on the Potsdam Conference. Henderson had asked that day what Stalin had in fact said at Yalta about Turkey and the Straits.

Balfour encloses London's telegraphic record of the plenary session of February 10. A few points arrived corrupt, he warns, but the tenor of Stalin's remarks is clear. Stalin called the Montreux Convention out of date. Japan, he noted, plays a larger part under it than the Soviet Union does. The pact was tied to the League of Nations, which no longer exists. Turkey, Stalin objected, could close the Straits not only in war but whenever she felt threatened. The enclosure was London's proof text in the argument over Stalin's Yalta assurances.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1005:
The Joint Chiefs of Staff sent President Truman this policy memorandum on July 17, 1945. Fleet Admiral William Leahy signed it for the chiefs. The subject is what to do with captured German merchant shipping, at a moment when the war against Japan still demanded troop transport.

Captured or surrendered ships fit for carrying troops should go to American military use at once, the chiefs urge. All such German vessels should be pooled and split among the Allied nations, first for use and later for final ownership. Only small coastal and inland craft vital to a minimum German economy would be exempt. No ocean-going ship built for foreign trade should stay in German hands.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1105:
Britain's team at Potsdam tabled this proposal on 30 July 1945, in the closing days of the talks. The British side had just changed leaders. Clement Attlee had taken over from Winston Churchill as prime minister after the election results came in on 26 July.

A formal proposal fixed a team's stand in writing for the other two to answer. This one shows the line London took as the final bargains were struck. It is among the last formal British papers of the summit. Set beside the final protocol, it shows what Britain asked for near the end and what the talks would bear.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1205:
Yost of the Central Secretariat wrote a fifth memorandum on 8 August 1945. The secretariat's chief kept writing after the leaders went home. Each note secured another piece of the conference's paper trail for the archive.

By now the pattern of his work is plain: no detail left unfiled, no paper left loose. A summit's record is only as good as this closing labor makes it. This note shows the record-keeping running well into August. It is a fitting mate to the volume itself, which exists because staff like Yost's treated paper as history in the making.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1305:
General Groves, who commanded the Manhattan District Project, wrote to Secretary of War Stimson on 18 July 1945. Groves had built the atomic bomb in secret, at sites across America. His message reached Stimson at Potsdam two days after the first test in New Mexico.

A report from Groves at that date could only carry one kind of news: how the new weapon had performed. Stimson waited on exactly that word to brief the president. This entry is the bomb entering the summit's record. Few papers in the volume carry more weight per line, or were read by fewer eyes at the time.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1405:
Another Caffery report to the acting secretary of state bears the date 7 August 1945. The volume prints pairs of Caffery cables for both 6 and 7 August. The text comes from the second Potsdam volume of Foreign Relations of the United States, the State Department's official history series.

Paired cables across two days give readers a short, dense window into the Paris embassy's work. France's leaders were digesting the Potsdam results and pressing their own claims for a zone and a voice in Germany. Caffery stood between that pressure and a Washington eager to move on. His reports from these days show the squeeze plainly. They close the volume's main run of French papers before the exchange turns to formal notes.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d710a-105:
Benjamin Cohen took these notes at Potsdam on July 25, 1945, as the Big Three talks moved through their second week. Cohen, a State Department counselor, recorded sessions where phrasing carried legal weight. His notes stand among the parallel American records printed in the second Potsdam volume.

A lawyer's ear shapes these pages. Cohen watched for what a word would commit each side to do. Readers get remarks in near-verbatim form, with the give and take intact. The notes reward slow reading: small shifts in wording at Potsdam later grew into large disputes about what the peace required.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d805:
The United States delegation tabled this proposal on July 21, 1945, as document 805. It dates from the conference's fifth day, in the thick of the first week's trading. American drafts flowed steadily from the delegation's staff. The proposal joined the second Potsdam volume.

A July 21 proposal shows the American side mid-adjustment. First positions had been tested; this text answers the test. Readers can trace the movement between drafts. The document also shows the delegation's confidence in paper. Where talk circled, a text forced the issue. Potsdam advanced by such forcing, one draft at a time.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d905:
Soviet delegates submitted this definition of restitution at Potsdam on July 21, 1945. It was one of the definitions offered to the Economic Sub-Committee. Restitution, in their draft, means giving back looted property to the country it came from.

The draft limits claims to property that can be identified. The goods must have existed when the enemy occupied the land, or have been made there during occupation. Destroyed property could be replaced only when it was unique, like art works or historic objects. Claims would be pressed by the owner's own state, even for goods found in a third country.
frus-1945v05:
Volume V of the 1945 Diplomatic Papers continues across Europe, from the Netherlands and Norway to Poland and Spain. Poland holds the center, with the making of its unity government and fights over its borders. Papers press Warsaw to honor the Yalta and Potsdam pledges.

Rumania's struggle for a broad government and Soviet removal of American oil gear follow. Portugal's Azores bases and Spain's Franco regime draw sharp sections. Relief for the Dutch and Norway's liberation round out the north. The record shows the wartime alliance splitting along the lines these cables trace.
frus-1946v05:
The British Commonwealth and Western and Central Europe share Volume V for 1946. Base rights in Commonwealth lands open the record. Britain follows, with the loan pact put into force, the Bermuda air accord, and mutual aid settlements.

Australia and Canada settle Lend-Lease accounts and plan joint defense. India draws a long section, on its politics, famine, and raised mission status. South Africa's bid to annex South West Africa also appears. The papers show wartime partners closing their war books and sorting out who owed what to whom. Tax and shipping accords fill out the legal record in detail.
frus-1948v02-d705:
Secretary of State Marshall cabled the Embassy in France on November 25, 1948, with Berlin policy for the UN talks. The cable went to Jessup and Bohlen on an eyes-only basis. Its first point is blunt: the United States will not be forced out of Berlin.

Twelve numbered points follow. They back a Soviet mark for all Berlin under four-power control, if the blockade ends. They set safeguards, neutral experts, and a deadline for the Western mark. The split of the city after the December vote runs through the plan.
frus-1949v05:
Volume V for 1949 covers Eastern Europe and the Soviet Union, and the tone is one of decay. Trade curbs and air policy set the regional frame. Human rights clauses in the peace treaties gave Washington a cause it pressed in vain.

Bulgaria moves toward a full break, and ties with Prague worsen month by month. Finland's freedom still draws care. Spy cases, the AMTORG listing, and ship returns fill the Soviet block. Yugoslavia, now aided by the West, closes the volume. The cables read as a ledger of lost ground.
frus-1950v05:
Volume V for 1950 covers the Near East, South Asia, and Africa, opening with a Cairo meeting of American officials. Oil growth leads the regional papers. Aid plans and joint talks with Britain on defense follow.

Israel takes the longest run, on the Palestine dispute after statehood. Iran's aid talks and oil concession fight come next. Egypt's canal curbs and Turkey's course also appear. Kashmir opens the South Asia block. The record shows oil, bases, and new nations drawing Washington deeper into three regions at once. Yemen and Jordan appear in brief closing sections.
frus-1951v05:
The Near East and Africa fill Volume V for 1951. Regional policy leads, with an Istanbul meeting of chiefs of mission and plans for a Middle East Command. Oil growth frames the talks that follow.

Egypt's move to scrap its 1936 treaty with Britain takes a long run. Israel fills the largest block, on ties and the Palestine question. Iran's oil row and Saudi airfield deals also appear. Jordan after King Abdullah's killing closes the Levant run. The papers show a region in revolt against old pacts, with Washington caught between allies and new national pride.
frus-1955-57v05:
Volume V of the 1955–1957 set joins the Austrian State Treaty with the summit year of 1955. Final treaty drafting leads, through the Vienna talks to the signing that May. Austria's freedom ends a decade of occupation in these papers.

The Geneva summit of July follows, told day by day. Groundwork in London and Paris fills the first files. A foreign ministers' meeting that fall closes the volume the same way. The record holds both the hope of that summer and its quick fade, in the words used at the table. Suez fallout reaches even these files by the volume's final block.
frus-1955-57v16-d505:
Soviet Premier Bulganin wrote to President Eisenhower on November 5, 1956, as British, French, and Israeli forces fought in Egypt. His letter calls the attack an aggressive war without cause. Bombing of cities and landings on Egyptian soil are described in harsh terms.

Bulganin urges joint action by the two great powers at the United Nations. Both fleets in the Mediterranean, used by UN decision, would end the war, he argues. He warns that the fight could grow into a third world war. Moscow stood ready, he closes, to talk at once on joint steps.
frus-1958-60v05:
The American Republics fill Volume V of the 1958–1960 set. General Latin America policy and hemisphere defense lead. Vice President Nixon's rough 1958 tour takes its own block, a turning point in the files.

Country runs follow, with Argentina and Brazil the longest. Mexico closes the main set. Most small states get a single paper each. The record shows a region long taken for granted. Castro's rise offstage shakes every page, and aid pledges grow as the tour reports come in. The Santiago foreign ministers' meeting also fills a block here. Cuba's shadow falls across the country files from 1959 onward.
frus-1964-68v05:
Vietnam, 1967 fills Volume V of the 1964–1968 set, the largest of the Johnson Vietnam volumes. Marigold and Sunflower peace probes lead the year. Debate over widening the war follows, through May.

Saigon's politics and the Thieu-Ky ticket take the middle block. The McNamara and Clifford-Taylor missions weigh the war's course in the summer. Pennsylvania's channel to Hanoi fills the fall. The Wise Men's November meeting closes the record. The volume shows doubt at the top in plain words, and a course held anyway, month by month. Troop ceilings and bombing limits fill the year's staff papers.
frus-1969-76v05:
Volume V of the 1969-1976 series covers the United Nations from 1969 to 1972. Chapters treat the UN headquarters, the Committee of 24 on colonial lands, and U.S. papers for each General Assembly. A long chapter covers UN finances and the U.S. drive to cut its share of the budget. The largest chapter, by far, covers Chinese representation. It follows the 1971 fight that seated Beijing and expelled Taipei.

Other chapters cover the choice of a Secretary-General and top UN staff posts. Cables from the U.S. mission in New York fill much of the volume. The records show vote counts, deals, and defeats. The China chapters form a full account of a turning point.
frus-1969-76v21-d305: An editorial note in Volume XXI of the 1969-1976 series sums up U.S. watching of Chile from July to September 1972. Officials tracked parties and business groups opposed to the Allende government. State Department aides feared that funding them would read as a green light for a coup. They judged that the army was not ready to move. One group, Patria y Libertad, had a 60-day timetable for a coup built on a national strike. The NSC staff concluded that the broad support a coup would need did not yet exist.
frus-1981-88v05:
Volume V of the 1981-1988 series covers the Soviet Union from March 1985 to October 1986. The first chapter covers Gorbachev's debut. Later chapters size up Shevardnadze and prepare the Geneva summit of November 1985. A chapter on new political thinking follows Gorbachev's proposal to abolish nuclear weapons. Arms control in the shadow of Chernobyl fills the next. The last covers the Daniloff arrest and the Reykjavik summit.

Talk records show both sides testing whether a shield against missiles could work. Each admits its own research while doubting the other's. The volume catches a relationship thawing fast, then stalling at Reykjavik's edge.
gao-gaoreports-b-296305:
SPAAN Tech protested an Energy Department award for office support work in GAO decision B-296305, dated July 14, 2005. The winner was Performance Results Corporation. The work backed the National Energy Technology Library. Sites were in West Virginia and Pennsylvania. The firm hit its marks and the final pick.

GAO denied the protest. The two bids were judged as near equal on merit. The winner cost less. GAO found no proof that tie call was wrong. With merit tied, low cost could rule. The firm had to show the tie was unsound. It did not. The award thus stood.
gao-gaoreports-b-299305:
Mathews Associates, Inc. protested the Army's refusal to score its proposal. The buy covered loudspeakers and battery boxes for a radio system. The Communications-Electronics Life Cycle Management Command ran the contest. GAO decided B-299305 on March 5, 2007.

The terms set firm limits on margins, font, and page count. They warned that pages past those limits would not be scored. The firm's bid broke the margin limit on each page. That fact was not in dispute. An agency may hold firms to clear format bars. A bid that flouts them on all pages can be set aside unread. The plea failed. GAO denied the protest.
gao-gaoreports-b-299705:
Metson Marine Services protested a Navy award to Seaward Services. The Military Sealift Command ran the buy. The contract covered port operations and vessel management for a high speed research vessel system. GAO ruled in B-299705 on July 20, 2007.

Long talks gave the firm a chance to cure its bid. Its last revised bid still missed a key staff post term. That post was core to the work at hand. GAO found the unfit call fair on that record. An agency need not hold more talks after such a full round. The winner's past-record review also stood up. No ground to upset the award was shown. GAO denied the protest.
gao-gaoreports-b-299805:
Midwest Metals protested an Army delivery order to Alpha Technologies. The buy covered 90 headless pins and 800 round nuts. The firm held the lower price in the contest. GAO ruled in B-299805 on July 17, 2007.

Price was not the sole test here. The terms let the agency trade price against performance risk. The winner's risk mark ran lower than the firm's. The agency judged that lower risk worth the higher price. GAO found that trade-off fair. It also backed the use of a past-record data system for the risk marks. A best-value call of that kind can stand. GAO denied the protest.
gao-gaoreports-b-311005:
Strong Environmental, Inc. lost its protest under GAO decision B-311005, dated March 10, 2008. The Library of Congress must shed old tape players for the blind. The gear plays talking books for those who can not see. The Library chose a pact with Federal Prison Industries for the shed work. Strong had bid in a past race for the same work. It said a deal, not a pact, was owed.

GAO denied the protest. The rules in play do not force a deal for this need. A pact path can serve when the rules leave the choice free. Form of the path is the agency's call here.
gao-gaoreports-b-311305:
Tip Top Construction Corporation lost its protest under GAO decision B-311305, dated May 2, 2008. The Highway Administration sought a firm to build a five-leg roundabout. The site sits on St. John in the U.S. Virgin Islands. Tip Top bid low for the job. Its bid was tossed for a bad bond. The bond drew on a man's stock of mined coal as its back.

GAO denied the protest. The coal wealth could not be held in escrow for the state. That gap made the bond's back unfit in the chief's eyes. The call was fair on these facts. A bond is just as strong as the wealth that backs it.
gao-gaoreports-b-400405:
Carahsoft Technologies Corporation and Avue Technologies Corporation jointly protested the same Transportation Security Administration human resources award at issue in a twin case. Their file was B-400405, closed on August 4, 2008. The award went to Lockheed Martin Integrated Systems, Inc. under request No. HSTS01-08-HRM010, sent out on October 18, 2007.

The pair faulted parts of the pick itself. GAO did not reach those points. Statute and rule bar GAO from hearing TSA protests tied to a request sent out before June 23, 2008. This request came well before that date. GAO dismissed the protest for lack of power to hear it.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-205:
Retiree Health Benefits, GAO-05-205 of February 14, 2005, asks what firms will do when a new Medicare drug plan starts. The Medicare Modernization Act of 2003 made a drug benefit that opens in January 2006. It pays a grant to firms that keep drug cover for retired staff who could use Medicare. Firms lose that grant for any retiree who joins the new plan.

GAO tracks how job-based retiree cover had moved before the law. It draws on surveys and the books of 50 large firms picked at random. It then asks plan chiefs which path they plan to take, and what each path means for retirees.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-305:
Combating Alien Smuggling, GAO-05-305 of May 27, 2005, asks if new tools can starve the gangs that sneak people across U.S. lines. World smuggling rings reap billions of dollars a year. They pose a threat to the land's safety too. The Department of Homeland Security, made in March 2003, joins border guards with sleuths skilled in cash crime. That join could let agents chase the gangs' cash.

In summer 2003, the sleuth arm vowed a national plan for the fight. GAO asks how far that plan has got. It counts wins in court and cash seized. Room to do more stands in clear view, it finds.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-405:
Information Management, GAO-05-405 of May 27, 2005, watches how the Energy Department charges for the facts it holds. The Freedom of Information Act lets any person ask for federal files. Agencies may charge some who ask for the hunt and copy work. They may waive the fee when set tests are met. Fees can aid or block the right the act grants.

GAO counts the asks the department took in fiscal year 2004, and their kinds. It tests how far fee work stuck to the act and to guides from the budget and justice arms. It tests how well each fee call was told to the one who asked.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-805:
An immigration tech program is judged in GAO-05-805, a report from September 7, 2005. The Atlas program aims to modernize the tech base of Immigration and Customs Enforcement. By law, its spending plan must meet set terms and face GAO review. GAO checked whether the fiscal year 2004 plan met those terms. It also offered views on the plan and on program management.

GAO found the plan met all the terms Congress set. But that rests more on plans and promises than on finished work. Much remains to be done before planning counts as effective, GAO said. The program's economic case does not reflect recent and planned shifts. GAO also called for tighter management practice. Measures should link to goals and gains, it said. The plan should state commitments clearly enough to hold leaders to account.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-905:
Base closure choices for 2005 are presented to the review commission in GAO-05-905, dated July 18, 2005. The Defense Department sent 222 recommendations, covering 837 actions. It projects net savings of nearly $50 billion over 20 years. Yearly savings would reach about $5.5 billion from fiscal year 2012. The cost to carry out the plan tops $24 billion. The statement sums up GAO's July 1 report.

GAO found the department built and mostly followed a logical, reasoned process. Data checks got special audit help, and military value drove the choices. GAO still flagged issues for the commission's eye. The size of the savings is one. About 47 percent of yearly savings, some $2.5 billion, comes from cutting jobs now held by military staff. GAO also named challenges in carrying out the plan, if approved.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-105:
Reserve force fitness tracking is faulted in GAO-06-105, a report dated October 27, 2005. War plans lean heavily on reserve members. By law, drilling members need a medical exam every 5 years and a yearly status certificate. Policy adds a yearly dental exam and fitness test. A 2004 law told GAO to study how the Defense Department manages this health picture for activated members.

GAO found the department cannot tell how far the force complies. Its data is incomplete and unreliable. Each component tracks exams, but only one has taken the quality steps to trust its data. The office in charge has no control framework or plan to oversee compliance. It has not even enforced its own rule that services report fitness status. After call-up, visibility over members' health is limited. Care for those deployed with prior conditions cannot be sized, GAO found.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-305:
Federal contracts with media and public relations firms are tallied in GAO-06-305, a report dated January 13, 2006. Agencies hire such firms to carry word of their programs to the public. No sound government-wide count of these deals existed before. GAO surveyed the seven departments behind nearly all such spending in fiscal 2003. It asked how many contracts each held and what they cost. It also asked how the deals were awarded and what work they bought.

The departments reported 343 media contracts worth $1.62 billion in all. Ad agencies took the bulk of both deals and dollars. Public relations firms came second by value. About 77 percent of the contracts were competed. Competed deals drew 92 percent of the money. The survey gives Congress its first firm ledger of the practice. It arrives amid charges that some spending crossed into covert promotion.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-405:
Rent aid for low-income families cost much more, and this study asks why. GAO decided GAO-06-405 on April 28, 2006, on the Section 8 rental housing programs. Federal spending on the programs climbed to nearly $21 billion in 2006. Section 8 has two parts. One gives vouchers to households. The other ties aid to specific projects.

GAO traced growth in outlays for each part. Rising average subsidies per household drove much of the growth. Market rent growth played a role. So did local choices on payment standards and slower growth in household incomes. Unit counts limited growth in project-based costs. Readers get a clear split of policy and market causes.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-705:
Federal oversight of Medicaid money is reviewed in GAO report GAO-06-705, issued on June 22, 2006. Medicaid covered over 56 million people at a cost of $295 billion in fiscal year 2004. The Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services oversees state programs and the claims they file for federal payment. Some state funding practices had raised federal costs in improper ways. GAO judged the agency's financial management drive.

GAO found that the agency had taken several steps to improve oversight. It hired about 90 funding specialists to examine high-risk state practices. Those staff worked with states to end practices that raised federal costs without cause. GAO said other actions were needed to sustain the effort. Staff turnover and shifting focus could erode the gains.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-805:
A new foreign aid agency is reviewed in GAO report GAO-06-805, issued on July 28, 2006. Congress created the Millennium Challenge Corporation in January 2004 to cut poverty through growth in well-governed nations. It had received more than $4.2 billion in appropriations. Partner nations propose compacts, multi-year aid plans they run themselves. GAO examined how the first compacts were vetted and set up, using Madagascar, Cape Verde, and Honduras as cases.

GAO found wide due diligence on the three proposals. At the same time, the agency was still writing guidance on key parts of the process. Implementation structures in the partner nations were being established. But GAO said the framework for measuring results needed improvement. Without it, the agency cannot prove that its grants reduce poverty.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-1005:
Rules that bar aid for moving jobs from one town to another are checked in GAO report GAO-07-1005, dated September 10, 2007. Congress fears state and local bodies could use federal funds to lure jobs, at a loss to the place left behind. Some aid programs carry bans on funding such moves.

GAO named the large aid programs towns can use as lures. It marked which ones hold legal bans on move funding. It tested if agencies have steps, in use, to enforce those bans. Formal watch steps are needed, the title states. The report shows a ban on paper is not a ban in practice.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-105:
Retirements will strain the nuclear regulator's workforce, GAO warns in report GAO-07-105, dated January 17, 2007. By 2010 about one third of staff with mission-key skills at the Nuclear Regulatory Commission can retire. At the same time the agency must grow.

From October 2007 it expects at least 20 bids for 29 new reactors. GAO asked if workforce planning fits the agency's mission and goals. It checked how the agency hires, trains, and keeps staff with key skills. It weighed future unknowns that could cut its capacity. The report is a warning to plan hiring before the wave hits, not after.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-1105:
Treasury cash investment has improved, but wider choices could cut risk and lift gains, GAO reports in GAO-07-1105, dated September 20, 2007. Lasting budget gaps drive debt and interest costs up. Each dollar the Treasury can invest well is a chance to trim those costs.

GAO traced trends in Treasury income, spending, and cash on hand. It set out the department's current plan for short-term investment. It named options to lift returns on that cash. The work drew on talks with Treasury staff and others, and on linked papers. The report treats a quiet task, cash care, as real money for the taxpayer.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-1205:
Special Counsel Patrick J. Fitzgerald ran his office with funds from a standing Justice Department account. This GAO financial audit is GAO-07-1205, issued September 28, 2007. It covers his office's spending for the six months ended March 31, 2007. Federal law requires GAO to audit such statements twice a year. No independent counsels were active in that period.

GAO's opinion was that the statement presented the spending fairly in all material respects. The statement was prepared mainly on a cash basis of accounting. GAO also reported that the office kept effective internal control over that reporting. The audit notes small payments made for a closed independent counsel office. Those payments included $26,922, mainly for severance pay, and $6,991 for printing a final report.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-205:
The full report behind GAO's Katrina contracting findings is GAO-07-205, dated March 1, 2007. Four agencies handled 94 percent of federal relief contract funds as of May 2006. They are Homeland Security, Defense, the General Services Administration, and the Army Corps of Engineers. GAO measured what small firms won directly. It also traced subcontracting and aid to disadvantaged business programs.

Small businesses won 28 percent of the $11 billion awarded directly, GAO found. Disadvantaged firms took 24 percent of the roughly $3 billion that went to small businesses. Local firms in the three hardest-hit states won 18 percent, or $1.9 billion. Small firms took about 66 percent of that local money. Subcontract records were far weaker, GAO said. For two agencies, plan data were missing on nearly three-fourths of contract dollars. One agency could not explain a gap covering $861 million.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-505:
Laptops and data keep vanishing at veterans' facilities, and GAO-07-505, issued July 16, 2007, blames loose controls. In July 2004, GAO had tested six Department of Veterans Affairs (VA) medical centers. Their property records were unreliable. Fewer than half the items GAO picked could be found, and most missing items were tech gear. Fresh thefts and data breaches raised the stakes.

GAO ran statistical tests at four case study sites this time. It rated the risk of theft and loss. It checked how sites guard gear marked for disposal, a known leak point. It then reviewed what VA leaders had done since 2004. Controls stayed weak, the tests showed. GAO urged the VA secretary to set one clear, detailed rule set for all sites rather than leave each site to improvise.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-705:
Cybercrime and the fight against it are the subject of GAO-07-705, dated June 22, 2007. Online crime spans fraud, identity theft, child exploitation, and terror funding. GAO set out to measure the harm to the economy and to security. It mapped which federal, state, and private bodies fight such crime. It also listed the blocks that slow their work. The report draws on past studies and talks with public and private officials.

One FBI survey put losses to U.S. groups at $67.2 billion a year. Identity theft losses hit $49.3 billion in 2006. Phishing scams cost about $1 billion a year. Foreign states and terror groups also use online attacks to steal data and fund acts. GAO found skill gaps in law enforcement labs and analysis teams. It urged the Attorney General and the Homeland Security chief to build those skills. The FBI and Secret Service noted steps they had begun.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-805:
The U.S. government's own financial statements are audited in GAO-07-805, dated July 23, 2007. For 10 years, flaws have stopped GAO from giving an opinion on those statements. In December 2006, it again issued a disclaimer for fiscal year 2006. This report details the flaws that persist and the new ones found. It makes 11 new recommendations. It also tracks action on GAO's past 143 recommendations in this area.

Treasury lacked sound steps to match receipts with agency records. Its method did not fully tie agency figures to the sums in the final statements. Cash balances and unused budget authority were also reported with flaws. Those gaps mean the statements may not balance or follow accounting rules. Treasury and the budget office mostly agreed with GAO's findings. Treasury disputed one point on social insurance totals. GAO held that a clear total aids openness.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-1005:
Overseas base plans and the buildup on Guam are assessed in GAO report GAO-08-1005, issued on September 17, 2008. The Defense Department has been cutting troops based abroad and merging overseas bases. Senate direction has required the department to file master plans and GAO to assess them each year. The Guam buildup joined that yearly review in 2007.

GAO weighed the fiscal year 2009 plans against its past advice. It found room to make future planning reports more timely. The report also takes stock of planning for more forces and facilities on Guam. GAO staff visited three combatant commands, bases abroad, and groups on Guam.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-105:
Women's retirement income is compared with men's in GAO report GAO-08-105 (October 11, 2007). Women aged 65 and over will form a growing share of the population in coming decades. Elderly women still face high rates of poverty. GAO set out to learn why their incomes lag and what changes could help.

GAO found that women draw less income from most major sources. Their median Social Security benefit is about 70 percent of men's. Fewer women have pensions, and the median pension is about half of men's. Lower earnings and weaker job attachment drive much of the gap. Divorce, widowhood, and time out of work deepen it. GAO modeled how some reforms would shift these results.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-305:
Hydrogen car research is graded in GAO report GAO-08-305 (January 11, 2008). The nation burns over 20 million barrels of oil a day, two-thirds of it imported. In January 2003, the government launched a 5-year, $1.2 billion drive for hydrogen fuel technology. The aim is bold: science ready by 2015 so industry can sell hydrogen cars by 2020. The Energy Department leads the push.

GAO measured progress against the drive's targets. It checked how well the department works with car and energy firms. It also reviewed joint work with other agencies. Real progress has been made, GAO reports. The 2015 expectations now need an honest update.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-405:
U.S. Trade Representative reporting on China's trade compliance is assessed in GAO report GAO-08-405, issued April 14, 2008. Congress requires a yearly report on how China keeps its trade pledges. GAO read the reports from 2002 to 2007 and checked the status of a February 2006 policy review.

The yearly reports kept a steady format but gave no summary counts, so readers could not track trends. GAO's own count found 180 separate compliance issues across nine trade areas. China had resolved about a quarter of them and made no progress on about one-third, with gains slowing since 2004. GAO urged the Trade Representative to count and sort issues in each report and to refresh its 2006 plans. The agency raised doubts about counting compliance in this way.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-705:
The Defense Department runs thousands of business systems for pay, supply, and records. Updating them has sat on GAO's high-risk list since 1995. GAO-08-705, dated May 15, 2008, checks the department's yearly report on its fix plans, as a 2005 law requires.

Top-level controls have grown stronger. The master blueprint for business systems keeps gaining needed content, and the plan to link service-level blueprints is clearer. But the blueprint still misses key rules and data flows, and the services lag far behind the central office. GAO made no new calls here, since past advice covers the gaps that remain.
haeckel-last-words-on-evolution-a-popula:
Haeckel called this 1905 book his Last Words on Evolution, a popular retrospect and summary of his long campaign. Joseph McCabe translated it from the second German edition. Haeckel was professor at Jena, and the most famed champion of evolution in Germany. The first chapter takes up the controversy about creation, evolution against dogma, with a plate of the genealogical tree of the vertebrates.

An old fighter sums up his case: the descent of man, the unity of nature, and the fate of the doctrines he opposed. Haeckel writes for the general reader, in a clear and fiery style. McCabe, a former priest turned rationalist lecturer, was his regular English voice. The book is a period monument of popular evolutionism, sure of itself and already facing new science it did not live to answer.
haitian-constitution-1805:
Haiti proclaimed its first constitution in 1805, a year after winning independence from France. Jean-Jacques Dessalines, leader of the slave revolt that freed the colony, now ruled as emperor of the new state. The charter was the freed people's answer to the world that had held them in chains.

The text declares Haiti free and indivisible, abolishes slavery forever, and bars white men from owning land or property in the country. In its boldest article, it declares all Haitians black by law, whatever their skin, making blackness a badge of citizenship rather than of bondage. The first founding law of a free Black nation stands as the most uncompromising claim of liberty ever written into a constitution. Its defiance shaped Haiti's hard, proud first century.
halevi-kuzari-1905:
Judah Halevi wrote the Kuzari in Arabic in the 1100s. Hartwig Hirschfeld turned it into English in 1905 from the source text. The form is a talk: the king of the Khazars seeks the true faith. A rabbi, a church man, and a Muslim each plead their case.

The rabbi wins the king not by proofs of the mind but by the tale of Israel. Halevi weighs faith and reason with rare grace and force. He defends the choice of Israel as a fact of the past, not a mere claim. The book is a peak of the faith thought of the Jews.
halima-and-the-scorpions-1905:
Robert Hichens published this long short story in 1905. Travelling about the world, the narrator says, one collects trifles named curiosities, worthless but for the memories they recall. Clearing a bureau drawer, he finds one: a hedgehog's foot, set in silver, on a tarnished chain, picked up in the Sahara. Its history is the tale. Mohammed El Aïd Ben Ali Tidjani, marabout of Tamacine, is a great man in the desert, famed for piety from Tunis to the land of the Touaregs.

The charm ties the narrator to Halima and to the scorpions of the title, in a sacred village of dried mud under the desert sun. Hichens, who wrote The Garden of Allah, renders the Sahara with a lover's exactness. The tale is brief, strange, and steeped in heat and holiness: a souvenir that turns, in the hand, into a story of faith and venom.
harold-the-last-of-the-saxon-kings-volum:
Book Five of Harold bears the title Death and Love. It opens with Harold gone to Dunwich, capital of his earldom, without waiting to see Edith or even to take leave of his father. At court, the King wholly forgot Algar and his suit, while Stigand, the grasping bishop, won the lordships at the King's disposal without an effort. Algar, in wrath, gathered loose men-at-arms and took his way into Wales with his young daughter Aldyth.

Rumour said Aldyth had long lost her heart to her father's foe, the fair Earl himself. Edith, after a long homily from the King, returned to her godmother Hilda. The part turns on the price of pride: suits lost, loves crossed, and feuds kindled that will burn into the great crisis of the reign. Lytton's Saxon world here narrows to its persons, and darkens.
history-of-friedrich-ii-of-prussia-volum:
Thomas Carlyle's fifth volume holds Book Five, the double-marriage project and what element it fell into, 1723 to 1726. George the First came to Berlin in October 1723 and watched his little grandson drilling the cadets; Carlyle now reveals the errand behind the visit. Two marriages would bind Prussia and Hanover: Friedrich to an English princess, Wilhelmine to an English prince.

The project swims into an element of court intrigue, French and Austrian counter-plots, and the Sergeant King's rages. Fassmann strolling show-booths in 1713, past a booth picture of a giant in Heyduc dress, gives Carlyle a characteristic street scene. By the volume's end the marriages hang fire and the storm of the sixth volume gathers.
homo-sum-volume-05:
Volume 5 of Homo Sum carries Georg Ebers and his Sinai novel toward its moral reckoning. Ebers gives this stretch to Paulus, the hermit who once took Hermas's sin and punishment onto his own shoulders. Now Paulus lies on hard stones through the night, certain that he has failed at the very point where his sacrifice should have made him strong.

Chapter XVIII stays inside his remorse over Sirona, the woman whose nearness shook his vow. He asks whether fleeing the world proves anything at all. A man who avoids every fight, he thinks, can hardly call himself a hero. Real worth, in his hard judgment, belongs to those who hold a heavenward road amid daily struggle. Desert faith here means self trial, not escape.
hyslop-science-future-life-1905:
James Hyslop made a tester's case for life past death in Science and a Future Life, his book of 1905. Hyslop taught thought at a great school in New York. He then built the chief band for such study in the United States. Grief for his own sire had drawn him to the theme in the first place, years ere this book.

He weighs the best cases with a strict hand. Fraud and flaw get no mercy in his sums. His claim stands on the rest that won't break. The book is his field's best brief from that land.
idle-ideas-in-1905:
Jerome K. Jerome published this set of twenty-one comic essays with Hurst and Blackett in 1905, a sequel in spirit to his Idle Thoughts of an Idle Fellow. Every chapter is a question. Are we as interesting as we think we are? Should married men play golf? Do we lie a-bed too late? The first opens at a dinner party where an introduction leaves him stranded.

Jerome's method is to worry a small question until it opens onto human nature. Should women be beautiful, are early marriages a mistake, and ought stories to be true get the same treatment as the servant problem and Chinese cheap labour. Two chapters, on hating the foreigner and on the white man's burden, take his comedy onto Edwardian politics. The laugh is the vehicle; the observation is the load.
jesuit-relations-thwaites-vol-05:
Quebec in 1632 and 1633 fills Volume 5, issued by Thwaites in 1897. The mission starts again after an English spell in control of Quebec. Paul Le Jeune's famed Relation stands at the heart of the book.

Le Jeune gives a classic account of Montagnais life in these years. He also sets out the Jesuit plan for winning converts, step by step. Hunting camps, winter cold, and sharp debates fill his long report. Many call his text the key document of early Canadian history. It opens the long St. Lawrence phase of the whole Relations series.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-aaron-ben-zion-:
Aaron ben-Zion ibn Alamani was a dayyan, or judge, and a prominent Jew of Alexandria in the twelfth century. His family name probably means the man of Oman. His father Joshua seems to have been a physician of some repute.

The poet Judah ha-Levi lived at Aaron's house while in Alexandria, and praised his friend warmly. Two of Ha-Levi's poems are addressed to Aaron. One came with a letter in rimed prose, kept in the "Diwan." Ha-Levi also mentions Aaron by name in a letter which he sent from Damietta to Samuel Nagid.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-aaron-of-jerusa:
Aaron of Jerusalem, also called Abu al-Faraj Harun, was a Karaite of the eleventh century. Rabbinite writers still ranked him a chief voice of Karaite learning and a great authority on grammar and exegesis. Abraham ibn Ezra quotes him as the sage of Jerusalem who wrote eight books on grammar.

Little was known of Aaron until Neubauer found Arabic fragments of his grammar, the "Mushtamil," among the Firkovitch manuscripts in St. Petersburg. Bacher then identified the lost author from those fragments. Aaron also wrote "Kitab al-Kafi," a commentary on the Pentateuch, and a word study, part of which is held in the British Museum.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-abdimi-mallaha-: Abdimi Mallaha, called the Sailmaker, was a scholar who worked at a trade. He was a man of the same age as R. Ḥiyya ben Abba and Jacob ben Aḥa. The entry places him in a large class of his time. Many scholars of that age, it notes, earned their bread by handicraft. His notice is very brief, and it cites two passages of the Jerusalem Talmud as its ground.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-abimelech-my-fa:
Abimelech is the name of four men in this entry, and the first takes the most room. He was a son of Gideon by a concubine, who claimed rule over Ephraim. Aided by his mother's kin, he killed all his half-brothers but the youngest, Jotham. He ruled three years in Shechem, till it rose against him. At Thebez a woman dropped a millstone on his head, and he had his armor-bearer run him through.

The second Abimelech was a king of Gath, the Achish of First Samuel. The third was king of Gerar, host to Abraham and to Isaac, in tales so alike that critics take them for one. Rabbinic lore counts him among the rare pious heathens, and gives him the gift of prophecy. The fourth was a priest, wrongly called a son of Abiathar, whose son he was.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-abraham-bernard:
Bernard Abraham was a French brigadier-general of artillery, born at Nancy on Jan. 12, 1824. His father sat on the Jewish Consistory of Nancy and was known as Moïse, though his name was Moïse Abraham. Bernard entered the École Polytechnique at nineteen, then trained at the School of Applied Sciences at Metz.

He served at Strasburg, then in Crimea on General Leboeuf's staff, winning the Legion of Honor after Sebastopol fell. He fought in Italy against Austria and in the Franco-Prussian war, serving with the army of the Rhine at Metz. At Metz he earned an officer's cross of the Legion of Honor after the battle of Gravelotte. He rose to colonel and then to general, and stayed in active service until he reached the age limit for retirement.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-abun-ben-saul-7: Abun ben Saul was a writer of elegies. He was most likely a pupil of Isaac Alfasi. He is most likely the man whose death Moses ibn Ezra laments in a poem. Two of his elegies sit in the Maḥzor of Avignon. The hosted text is short and its claims are hedged. It gives the art he worked in, the teacher he likely learned from, and the one book where his work can be found. It names no dates for his birth or death.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-adar-sheni-wead: Adar Sheni is the second Adar, an added month. It is the thirteenth month of a Jewish leap year. It has twenty-nine days. In such a year the first Adar has thirty. Purim is kept on the fourteenth of this later month in leap years. A death day that fell in Adar Sheni is kept in that month in a leap year. In a plain year it is kept in the first Adar. The hosted text gives those rules and points to the Calendar entry.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-adino-the-eznit: Adino the Eznite is a name that may not be a name at all. It stands in II Samuel xxiii. 8, in the list of David's heroes. Two odd words there came to be read as one hero's name. The entry says they are a garbled text. The true sense is brandishing his spear. A like verse in I Chronicles xi. 11 reads that way. The words paint Yosheb Bashshebet at work. Rabbinic lore takes the name for David himself. It reads it as a sign of his softness and his strength.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ahrweiler-1005:
Ahrweiler is a town of Rhenish Prussia, twenty-three miles northwest of Coblenz, on the river Ahr. It is mentioned in 1248 as holding a Jewish colony. Jews of Ahrweiler bought property at Cologne in 1255 and 1262. The community suffered in the Rhine persecutions of 1348, in the time of the Black Death.

Early in the fifteenth century, soldiers from Brabant and Holland attacked the town, and the community barely escaped destruction. Its learned names include Isaac of Ahrweiler, who wrote on the Pentateuch. Frommet, a rabbi's wife, was so learned that she copied a legal work in 1454 for her husband. After the old community vanished, a new one arose in the mid-nineteenth century. In 1899 it counted eighty-two Jewish families, and its new synagogue was built in 1895.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-aldubi-abraham-: Abraham ben Ismail Aldubi was a Talmudic scholar and author in Spain. He flourished in the first half of the fourteenth century. He studied under Solomon ben Adret, and he taught Jeroham ben Meshullam. He wrote many novellae and responsa. None of them survive on their own, though. They are known only from the many quotes in his pupil Jeroham's works. His chief work seems to have been an order of service for the Day of Atonement. A shortened form of it was printed inside Jeroham's "Toledot Adam wa-Hawwah."
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-amm-ammi-1405:
Amm is a word found in Semitic names for gods. It shows in Bible names like Amminadab and Ammiel. At root the word means a kinsman. In Arabic it means the uncle on the father's side. Semites used it for a god as a patron. Like words for father and brother served the same way.

Traces of that use run wide and deep. Babylonian kings bore names built on the word. A Canaanite ruler bore such a name as well. South Arabian names show the same build. No clear proof shows a god named Amm as such. The entry warns against that leap. Kin words in names do not make a god.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-antislavery-mov:
Antislavery movement in America traces how slavery took root in the New World and how American Jews stood toward it. The entry blames Las Casas, a pillar of the Church, for first proposing African slavery in place of enslaving Indians, who were dying fast under Spanish rule.

Jews, a people quick to take on the ways around them, held slaves too, the entry states plainly. It names Jewish slaveholders and even slave dealers in Brazil, Mexico, the West Indies, New York, and New England. Slavery faded in the North after 1800 but stayed common in the South. The entry then follows Jewish voices on both sides as the Civil War neared.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-arama-isaac-ben:
Isaac ben Moses Arama was a Spanish rabbi and author born about 1420 who died at Naples in 1494. He first headed a rabbinical academy at Zamora, likely his birthplace. Calls then took him to Tarragona and to Fraga in Aragon as rabbi and preacher. He ended as rabbi and academy head at Calatayud.

When the Jews were expelled in 1492, Arama settled in Naples, where he died. His chief work, Akedat Yitzhak, Offering of Isaac, is a long philosophical commentary on the Pentateuch in sermon style. It made him known as the Ba'al Akedah, the Akedah's author. He also wrote on the Five Rolls, on philosophy against theology, and a Proverbs commentary in memory of his dead son-in-law.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-asenath-in-gree:
A Greek apocryphal book tells the story of Asenath, wife of Joseph, in full. It carries the titles Life and Confession, or Prayer, of Asenath. The entry calls it a Greek Apocrypha of strong Jewish character with one small Christian addition. For long it was known only in a shortened Latin form inside Vincent of Beauvais. Batiffol printed the full text at Paris in 1889 to 1890 from four manuscripts.

Inside, a Midrash-like tale shows Asenath turning from idols to Joseph's God. She also shows mercy toward her enemies. Versions spread widely: a Syriac translation of the sixth century, an Armenian one, plus Slavonic and Ethiopic forms. Neither rabbinic nor church writing, the entry notes, kept any trace of the story on its own.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ashtoreth-2005:
Ashtoreth is the Old Testament name for the old Semitic mother goddess. In Phenicia she was Ashtarte, in Babylonia Ishtar, and in Arabia Athtar. The Hebrew form twists Ashtart after the pattern of Bosheth. At Sidon she was the chief goddess, worshiped on her own and also as Ashtarte of the name of Baal, a counterpart to Baal.

Phenician colonies carried her worship across the Mediterranean. She held great temples at Citium and Paphos in Cyprus and left her mark on Malta and Sicily. From Cyprus her cult reached Corinth and beyond. At Gebal, by Lucian's account, her rites included wailing for Tammuz, and women had to give up their hair or their chastity. Her shrine at Askelon held Saul's armor after Gilboa.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-aub-ludwig-2105:
Ludwig Aub was an author and poet. He was born on Aug. 4, 1862, in Munich, Germany. He was a grandson of Rabbi Hirsch Aub of Munich. From boyhood he loved books above all else. That love led him to work for booksellers in Vienna and Leipsic. In time he became a dealer in rare books himself.

Serious eye trouble forced Aub to give up his shop. It also hampered his writing for the rest of his career. His first book, an outline of German literary history, came out at Leipsic in 1888. His poems in the North-Bavarian dialect, printed in 1889, met with marked success. That same year he issued a book of aphorisms and epigrams with Thom. He founded the Orion Literary Association in Munich and led it as president. He also wrote for German papers and spoke up for Jewish interests against anti-Semitic attacks.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-azban-mordecai-:
Mordecai ben Isaac Azban was a cabalist and rabbi in Leghorn. He was born in the interior of Africa and died at Jerusalem in 1740. At Leghorn he quarreled with Abraham Ḥayyim Rodriguez, and the fight is printed in Rodriguez's book of rulings. Azban later served as rabbi at Aleppo, then settled in Jerusalem for the rest of his life.

His book "Zobeaḥ Todah," Thank-Offering, came out at Constantinople in 1733. It holds a long prayer of confession that goes through the parts of the body, noting how each can lead a man to sin. He wrote other works of a mystic cast as well.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-bacher-julius-2:
Julius Bacher was a German playwright and novelist, born in Ragnit, eastern Prussia, on Aug. 8, 1810. He studied medicine at Königsberg and settled there as a doctor in 1837. After ten years he gave up medical work to write full time. His first play was followed by a pause for the events of 1848, then a run of novels and dramas.

The entry lists his best known works in order. They include the novel "Sophie Charlotte" in three volumes, the drama of 1857 on Frederick the Great, and later romances such as "Ein Urteil Washington's" in 1864 and "Napoleon I. Letzte Liebe" in 1868. It also notes his move to Berlin and his travels in Switzerland and France.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-bali-moses-ben-: Moses ben Abraham Bali was a Karaite doctor and ḥakam at Cairo at the end of the fifteenth century and the start of the sixteenth. He is known here for verse. The entry credits him with 224 poems on the weekly lessons, finished in 1489 and called "Sefer Zeraḥ." A second set of 237 poems for Saturdays and feasts followed about 1500, under the title "Taḥkemoni." Both sets survive in manuscript in the Firkowitz collection at St. Petersburg. Many of his liturgical poems, it warns, are wrongly given to Moses Dari.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-baratz-herman-h: Herman (Hirsch) Baratz, a Russian lawyer, was born at Dubno in 1835. He graduated from the Rabbinical School of Jitomir in 1859 and from the University of Kiev in 1869. In 1871 the governor-general of Kiev appointed him censor of Hebrew books and consulting official on Jewish affairs. He wrote on the Jewish question in "Razsvyet," "Ha-Karmel," and "Syvernaya Pchela." The entry points to Censorship of Hebrew Books in Russia for more on his office.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-basch-raphael-2:
Raphael Basch was an Austrian writer and politician born at Prague in 1813. He knew Hebrew, the Talmud, classics, and philosophy well. He taught at a progressive school in Presburg before the Revolution of 1848 drew him to Vienna.

In Vienna Basch founded a paper on the assembly and later edited leading Austrian papers. He spoke for government ministers and, from 1875, wrote for the Neue Freie Presse in Paris. The entry also notes two political pamphlets from 1870, issued under a pen name, that caused a great sensation across Austria at the time.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-becher-wolf-270: Wolf Becher was a German physician and medical author born at Filehne, in Posen, on May 6, 1862. He studied at the town school and at the University of Berlin, earning his medical degree in 1889. He assisted at a Berlin clinic for inner diseases until 1892, then set up in private practice. His essays treat cholera and river shipping, the use of X-rays in medicine, and the form and place of the kidneys in the body.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-belial-2805:
Belial is a word found often in the Old Testament for men who defy rightful rule, civil or sacred. In weaker use it means simply wicked or worthless. One hard verse in Samuel speaks of rivers of Belial, which scholars read in rival ways.

The entry weighs four roots for the word, from a Talmud word play to a Babylonian goddess whose name was bent in scorn. Later sections show Belial grown into a demon prince in visionary books. There he is matched with Satan and with the angel of lawlessness. In the Sibylline books he drops down from heaven as a foe of the last days, the entry adds.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-bendavid-lazaru:
Lazarus Bendavid, a German philosopher and reformer, was born in Berlin on Oct. 18, 1762, and died there on March 28, 1832. He first earned a living polishing glasses while studying mathematics on his own. Lectures on Kant at Vienna in 1793 drew large audiences before foreign residents were forced out in 1797.

Back in Berlin he edited a newspaper and directed the Jewish Free School from 1806, raising it so high that many pupils were not Jewish. He stayed a Kantian for life and spread that philosophy widely. He also pled for abolition of ceremonial laws and wrote early radical criticism of the Bible.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-bennett-solomon: Solomon Bennett, an English theologian and engraver, was born in Russia before 1780 and died after 1841. He wrote many works on biblical themes, on sacrifice, and on the temple in Ezekiel. In 1841 he began to publish a revised rendering of the English Bible. Only two parts came out, covering Genesis up to chapter forty-one, and the plan was then dropped. He spent 1795 to 1799 in Berlin and his later years at Bristol. His book on Ezekiel's temple carries his own engraved portrait.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-bern-3105:
