Bern is the capital of the Swiss Confederation, and Jews lived in its lands as early as the sixth century. The first firm record of Jews in the city dates to 1259. They lived in their own street, under the city's guard, with the emperor as their true overlord.

All of them worked as bankers and pawnbrokers, at state-set rates of interest. Debt bred hatred, and in 1294 a charge that Jews had killed a boy named Rudolf sparked seizure and torture. The Jews were driven from the town, and their goods were seized at once by the Bernese.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-beth-gubrin-320: Beth Gubrin was a city named in the Talmud and Midrash. Ptolemy called it Betogaboa. It never appears in the Old Testament. Reland tied it to an Idumean fort taken by Vespasian. The city was also called Eleutheropolis. Under that name Eusebius mentions it often. It was then a provincial capital. Its site is the village Bêt Gibrûn. That lies in southwestern Judea. Ruins and enlarged caves surround it. The entry suggests the Greek name arose by confusion. Two similar Hebrew words meant "cave" and "free."
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-bina-ben-david-: Bina ben David was a Cabalist and rabbi. He served at Lockacze in Poland. His work fell in the mid-seventeenth century. His book "Zer Zahab" means Crown of Gold. It appeared at Cracow in 1647. It indexes and explains the Zohar and Midrash. Novellæ on Talmudic passages close the book. Knorr von Rosenroth translated much of it. His Latin version sits in "Cabbala Denudata." Steinschneider wrongly cited Bina as "Baruch."
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-blogg-or-bloch-: Solomon ben Ephraim Blogg was a German author. He came from Neuwägen in Hanover. He died on February 11, 1858, nearly eighty. He taught Hebrew and wrote on its grammar. In 1827 he founded Telgener's printing-press at Hanover. Its output won praise for scientific accuracy. His works span forty-five years of labor. They matter for Hebrew language history. His books include a Hebrew grammar introduction in 1810. A history of Hebrew language and literature came in 1826. His "Binyan Shelomoh" treats Hebrew and Talmud historically.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-bonaventura-for: Fortunato de S. Bonaventura was a member of the Royal Academy of Science of Lisbon. He worked about the beginning of the nineteenth century. The entry knows him for one attempt: a history of the literature of Jewish authors in Portugal. It appeared in the ninth volume of the Academy's memoirs. The entry judges that work to be of little value. No life dates or other writings are given for him here.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-bourges-3605:
Bourges is the capital of the department of Cher in France. Jews dwelt there from the beginning of the Middle Ages. Attempts to convert them are recorded in 568 and again in 624.

After five quiet centuries, a royal paper names the house of a Jew, Isaac Uradis, at Bourges. By the late thirteenth century local Jews were many and prosperous, tax lists show. A decree of Jan. 24, 1310, set rules for suits over debts owed to Jews. It barred suits on debts twenty years old unless steps had been taken earlier. It also shielded Christian debtors from prison if they mortgaged property. No learned Jews of Bourges are recorded, the entry says.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-bueno-bonus-380:
Bueno was a family of Spanish origin whose members settled across southern France, Italy, Holland, England, America, and the Orient. Many of them were physicians and scholars. The entry gives short notices for each person, arranged by first name. Abraham Bueno practiced medicine in Amsterdam and died there in 1633. Benjamin Bueno de Mesquita died in New York in 1683.

The fullest notice goes to Ephraim Hezekiah Bueno of Amsterdam, a noted physician painted by Rembrandt about 1647. He published liturgical works and helped found a scientific society in 1656. His father Joseph had treated Prince Maurice of Orange in 1625. Other notices cover editors in Venice and Cremona, a hakam in Jerusalem, and a mystic at Safed.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-caslari-joshua-: Joshua Caslari was a liturgical poet who lived at Avignon about 1540. He wrote four elegies placed in the manuscript prayer book of Avignon. His signature stands at the end of the last elegy. The entry identifies him, in all probability, with the Jozué du Cayslar named in a document of June 15, 1558. That record lists him, with Ferussol Pampelona, as a member-elect of the council of the Jewish community of Avignon. No other works or posts are named for him here.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-cherith-4305: Cherith is the name of a brook or wadi near the Jordan. There Elijah hid in a time of drought and famine, as I Kings xvii reports. God told him he would find water and food there. When the brook dried up, Elijah was sent on to Zarephath. The phrase before Jordan points to the eastern side. That rules out one proposed site west of the river. Other proposals link Cherith to Reḥoboth or to Wadi al-Ḥimar. None of the modern attempts satisfies, the entry concludes.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-clava-isaiah-44: Isaiah Clava was a Spanish poet of Amsterdam. The short entry records one work only. He rendered a Purim song from Hebrew into Spanish. Its long title begins Cancio de Purim and states that an unnamed author first set the song on the Purim story. Clava's version came out at Amsterdam in 1772. The poem runs to 110 strophes of nine lines each. A single source, Kayserling's bibliography of Spanish-Portuguese Jewish writers, supports the whole notice.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-cohen-shalom-be:
Shalom ben Jacob Cohen, a Polish Hebraist, was born at Meseritz, Poland, on Dec. 23, 1772, and died at Hamburg on Feb. 20, 1845. Hungry for learning Poland could not give him, he left for Berlin at seventeen. There the poet Wessely fired his love of Hebrew poetry. He revived the Hebrew review Meassef for two years with his own work.

A bid to found a Hebrew school in London failed in 1813, and he settled at Hamburg. In 1820 the printer Anton Schmid called him to Vienna to supply Hebrew material. There he launched Bikkure ha-Ittim, drawing the best scholars of the day. His own books range from verse fables in 1803 to an epic on David and a history of the Jews printed at Wilna in 1837.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-cup-4805:
Cup is the common Old Testament word for a drinking vessel, and the entry separates its forms. One term appears first for Joseph's divining cup in Genesis. It was larger than the standard cup, more a goblet or crater. Another word names the almond-shaped cups on the golden candlestick. Other renderings point to basins or bowls. Jewish cups likely matched those of Egypt, Assyria, and Phenicia in material and design.

Figurative uses fill the second half. A cup can mean good or ill fortune, as in my cup runneth over. It can stand for death, in the phrase to taste death. It can even stand for a man's wife, in Talmud passages. Ten cups, at one time fourteen, were set for a house of mourning. The cup of benediction at Passover ends the list.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-cyrene-1505:
Cyrene was a large city in Cyrenaica, on the north coast of Africa west of Egypt. It was one of the five cities that gave the region its name, Pentapolis. Jews went there from Egypt early. Ptolemy the First sent Jewish settlers to Cyrene and other Libyan cities. Under the Egyptian kings they held equal rights. Strabo lists the Jews as one of the city's four classes of inhabitants in the time of Sulla.

Cyrene became a Roman province in 74 B.C. Then the Greek citizens oppressed the Jews, the entry says. Jason of Cyrene stands behind the Second Book of Maccabees. Cyrene's Jews kept close ties with Palestine and sent offerings to Jerusalem. After the great war, the Sicarian Jonathan stirred a riot there, and Rome still met resistance in the city.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-darmesteter-ars:
Arsène Darmesteter was a French philologist, brother of James Darmesteter. He was born at Château-Salins on Jan. 5, 1846. He died at Paris on Nov. 16, 1888. His father, a bookbinder, kept a workshop full of books. The boy read widely there, then entered the Talmud Torah at twelve. He set himself a hard task: to explain the Old French words in Rashi's text. That task shaped his life's work.

He took his licentiate in 1864 and turned to Old French at the Ecole des Chartes. His dictionary of Old French won a grand prize at the Paris Exhibition of 1900. It also won the prix Jean Reynaud, of 10,000 francs. In 1874 he read the old elegy on thirteen Jewish martyrs burned at Troyes in 1288. That year he also studied fifty-five Rashi manuscripts at Parma and Turin.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-derenburg-deren:
Derenburg, or Derenbourg, was a Franco-German family of Orientalists. Their home town was Derenburg, near Halberstadt in Saxony. From there they moved through Offenbach and Frankfort to Mayence. The first known member, Jacob, left no record. His son Hartwig wrote a comedy printed at Offenbach in 1789.

Hartwig's play, "Yoshebe Tebel," puts eight speakers on stage, each standing for one of the deadly sins. A figure called the Prince of Peace rebukes them. Readers in Mayence could tell which local people were meant, though no names were used. The entry then follows Hartwig's sons, among them Jacob Derenburg, born at Mayence in 1794, and the family's turn toward Oriental scholarship.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-dinaites-septua: The Dinaites were a tribe named in Ezra iv. 9 among the peoples settled in Samaria. The entry says they opposed and denounced the Jews' efforts to rebuild Jerusalem. Beyond that short notice, the entry gives no history, homeland, or customs for the group. It closes by stating plainly that the Dinaites have not been positively identified. Readers get a name, a place, and one recorded act of opposition, and nothing more the entry can confirm.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-draguignan-hebr:
Draguignan, capital of the department of Var in France, held a Jewish community in the thirteenth century. The poet Isaac Gorni visited early in the fourteenth century. He mocked its rich Jews for failing to value his talent. He called the place a dragon's lair.

Jews from Draguignan turn up at Tarascon between 1350 and 1400, and one at Hyères. In 1427 the town's Jews were persecuted. They were forced to wear a wheel-shaped badge or pay twenty-five silver marks. Yet in 1475 they won leave to keep a synagogue. The price was four pounds of wax a year to the Bishop of Fréjus.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-eben-ezer-hebr-: Eben-ezer, the stone of help, names a battlefield and a monument in First Samuel. At that field Israel twice lost to the Philistines. The first defeat cost 4,000 men. The Ark was then fetched from Shiloh, but the second battle cost 30,000 men, the Ark itself, and Eli's two sons. The entry says the exact site is still unfixed, though it lay near Aphek. Samuel later set a stone of the same name between Mizpeh and Shen, to mark a victory there.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ela-hela-ilaa-i:
Ela was a Palestinian scholar of the third amoraic generation. He lived in the third and fourth centuries. His name appears in many spellings, among them Hela, Ilai, and Le'ia. Both Talmuds cite him often, mostly on Halakah, the body of Jewish law. His friend Zera praised his sharp mind in strong terms.

Ela lived what he taught, and his own house showed the rites in daily use. One Friday his work kept him late, and he found his gate barred for the night. Rather than break the Sabbath by knocking, he slept on his own steps. The entry gives his rules for reading Scripture. One rule says a reading must respect the context. Another says the words beware, lest, and not mark a ban. The entry also gives his eulogy for Simon ben Zebid, built from verses in Job.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-eliezer-eleazar: Eliezer ben Immanuel of Tarascon came of a family of scholars. That family had lived at Tarascon since the early thirteenth century. He wrote several works of his own. None of them can now be read, the entry says. Only his letters to Rabbi Samuel of Agde survive. He is also named as a teacher of note. The Dominican convert Pablo Christiani sat among his pupils. No dates for his birth or death are given here.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-elohist-5705:
Elohist is a name coined by Bible critics for a source text. It marks those parts of the first six books that call God Elohim. Jean Astruc first noted the two names in Genesis in 1753. He built on that fact a theory of mixed sources. Eichhorn took the thought further a few decades later. Ilgen then coined the term Elohist for the Elohim parts. He split those parts into two strands of their own.

Hupfeld's book of 1853 fixed the term in scholarly use. Near all later critics of that school took it up. The entry tracks how the word's sense shifted over time. At first its range was not set with any firm edge. The term names no man and no known book. It names a strand that critics tease out by style and word choice. The entry shows that work of source study step by step.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ephraim-safra-t: Ephraim Safra, whose name means the Scribe or Teacher, was a Palestinian scholar of the third century. He studied under Simeon ben Lakish. In his teacher's name he reports a civil law, cited at Baba Mezia 119a. The same report appears elsewhere without his byname. Some versions of the report read Ephraim Maksha'ah instead. If that reading is right, the entry says, the roles of author and reporter must be swapped. No other facts about his life are given.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-eupatoria-5905:
Eupatoria was a town in the government of Taurida, on the west coast of the Crimea. The Tatars called it Gezelew, and Russia renamed it on taking it in 1784. The entry presents it as the spiritual center of the Crimean Karaites. A Karaite community had stood there for many centuries.

About 1,500 Karaites lived there when the entry was written. Their court of three, a hakam, a hazzan, and a beadle, ruled on religion for all Crimean Karaites with state backing. The town held the Crimea's finest Karaite synagogue, a rich library, and a Karaite press founded in 1833. A small Rabbinite group also lived there, with a synagogue built in 1841. Most Jews worked as artisans and vine dressers.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-eve-15005:
Eve was the wife of Adam, named in Genesis as the mother of all living. The entry first retells the Bible account. God made her from Adam's rib after no animal proved a fit partner. In Eden the serpent talked her into eating the forbidden fruit, and she gave some to Adam. Both saw their nakedness and hid. Her punishment was pain in childbirth and rule by her husband.

Driven from Eden, she bore Cain, Abel, and later Seth. Rabbinic tales then take over. They say she was made from Adam's thirteenth rib on the right side, and that Satan was created with her. Ten bridal canopies were set for her, one tale claims. Arabic tradition, in a closing section, makes her from Adam's left rib instead.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-familianten-ges:
The Familianten Gesetz was a law capping Jewish families in the Bohemian crown lands: Bohemia, Moravia, and Silesia. No Jew there could marry without a state permit. The set policy was to keep the Jewish count from growing. When Maria Theresa withdrew her 1745 expulsion order, the cap was her price. Joseph II kept the condition in force.

A census of 1787 counted 8,541 Jewish families in Bohemia and 5,106 in Moravia. The caps were then set at 8,600 and 5,400, with 119 for Austrian Silesia. Permits opened only as permit holders died. A hopeful groom had to prove 300 florins, schooling, and an exam in religion, and be at least twenty-four. First-born sons, teachers, and veterans came first in line.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-fez-arabic-fas-:
Fez, capital of a province in the sultanate of Morocco, was built in the year 808 by Imam Idris II. A small stream splits the city into Old Fez and New Fez. Old Fez held the palace and the Mellah, the Jewish quarter. Idris settled Jews there from the start. They paid a special tax in place of army service.

Later rulers brought long spells of harsh rule for Fez Jews. The entry tells of forced conversion, flight, and attacks on the quarter. It also tells of refuge for Jews fleeing Spain in 1492. Near its close it gives varied counts of the Jewish population. It lists nineteen synagogues and schools run by the Alliance.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-fly-hebr-6205:
The fly here is the two-winged insect, above all the common house-fly. Ecclesiastes says dead flies make the apothecary's ointment stink. A fly in food raised questions of fitness and even of divorce. Wine with a fly in it, once the fly was removed, was still fit to drink. Yet fussy people would not drink it. The fly's habit of coming back makes it a picture of evil desire.

Other kinds are sorted out, among them the Egyptian fly and the gadfly. At times flies grew so bad in Palestine that public prayers were ordered. The Philistines at Ekron worshiped a fly god, Baal-zebub. Strange to say, there were no flies in the slaughter court of the Jerusalem sanctuary. A later part sorts out the insects of the plagues. Gnat lore and a poem on the fly by Abraham ibn Ezra close the entry.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-frankenthal-ado:
Adolph L. Frankenthal was the United States consul at Bern, Switzerland. He was born on July 1, 1851, at Lübeck, Germany. He was schooled in his home town and learned Hebrew from the local rabbi. At fifteen he entered business life in Hamburg. Five years later, in 1871, he emigrated to the United States.

He settled in Boston and worked there as a merchant. He soon took an active part in public life, above all in Jewish circles. He was prominent in various Jewish orders. In 1898 he was appointed consul at Bern. He still held that post in 1903.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-frosoloni-isaac: Isaac Hayyim Frosoloni was an Italian poet of the eighteenth century, born at Sienna and dead at Leghorn in 1794. After Hebrew and general studies at Sienna, he settled at Leghorn and joined its yeshibah. There he grew close to the family of the wealthy merchant Eliezer Shealtiel Recanati. He kept up Talmud study in a school that Recanati had founded. His poems appear in Piperno collection Kol Ugab.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-gerizim-mount-1:
Mount Gerizim stands south of the valley where Shechem lay, at 2,849 feet high. Its modern name is Jabal al-Tur. It drops steeply to the north and bears sparse shrubs at the top. After their split from the Jews, the Samaritans built a temple on it. John Hyrcanus destroyed that temple. Samaritans still hold the mount as their holy place.

They revere it as the scene of Isaac offering and keep Passover there still. Walls once ringed the temple, and Justinian walled a church on the top in 529. Rabbinic lore tells of six tribes on Gerizim for the blessing and six on Ebal for the curse. It charges Samaritans with changing a verse in Deuteronomy to favor their mount.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-gero-karl-6605: Karl Gero, a Hungarian dramatist born at Hevizgyork on October 18, 1856, studied law at Kaschau and Budapest. As a student he gave much time to letters and to the theater. His first play came out at the Budapest People Theater in 1883. He then took a post as playwright there. In 1886 he became secretary of that theater for a short time. His best plays treat Hungarian folk life, and two of them won Academy crowns.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-geshem-14205:
Geshem is one of the Hebrew words for rain, used mostly for the heavy rains of fall and winter in Palestine. The Mishnah calls that half of the year the days of rains. In German-Polish prayer Geshem also names the rain poems sung at the Eighth Festival Day. They lead into the first words that hail God as the one who makes wind blow and rain fall.

Those poems end with a sixfold plea. Each stanza closes by asking that water not be held back, for the sake of the patriarchs, Moses, Aaron, and the tribes at the Red Sea. The reader that day wears a white shroud and cap, as on the Day of Atonement. The plea asks for rain as a blessing, not a curse.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-grunfeld-alfred:
Alfred Grünfeld was an Austrian pianist. He was born at Prague on July 4, 1852. He studied at the Prague Conservatorium and at Berlin's Neue Akademie. In 1873 he settled at Vienna. There he received the title of Kammervirtuos. He toured Europe and the United States widely.

On a German visit he was named court pianist to Emperor William I. From 1897 he taught at the Vienna Conservatorium. His piano works named here are an Octave-study, a Minuet, and a Spanish Serenade. The entry is a compact career notice drawn from music journals.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-hadassah-lit-th: Hadassah, meaning "the myrtle," was the earlier name of Esther. The entry is very short. It says the name occurs only at Esther ii. 7, where Esther is called Mordecai's cousin. The Septuagint does not give the name at all. In the Vulgate the name takes the form "Edissa." The reader is sent to the Esther entry for more, and no further facts about Hadassah are given here.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-halizah-taking-:
Ḥaliẓah is the rite in which a childless widow takes off her brother-in-law's shoe. By that act he is freed from the duty of marrying her. She may then marry whom she will. Deuteronomy xxv. 5-10 sets the rite. It softens the older levirate custom. The brother may refuse, if he accepts the shame of the ceremony.

Over time rabbis came to prefer ḥaliẓah to the marriage itself, fearing mixed motives. Now the rite is the rule and the marriage the rare case. The entry walks through the rite in detail. A court of three is set the day before. The court sits in the synagogue at morning. Then come the loosened shoe, the spitting on the ground, and the fixed words. It closes with the rite's standing among reformers. It also covers the great body of Jews who still keep it in full.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-hanina-b-agul-7: Hanina b. Agul was a Palestinian scholar of the third century. A junior contemporary of Hiyya, son of Abba, he asked Hiyya why the words "that it may go well with thee" stand in the second Decalogue but not the first. Hiyya replied that he did not even know the words were in either version. He sent him to Tanhum b. Hanilai, a pupil of Joshua, son of Levi. Tanhum explained the omission. The promise was left out of the first tablets because those tablets were destined to be broken.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-hasdai-ben-samu: Hasdai ben Samuel ben Perahyah ha-Kohen was a Turkish rabbi born at Salonica. He studied there under Hayyim Shabbethai and later served as rabbi in the same city. He died there in September 1677. His answers to legal questions were printed after his death as "Torat Hesed" in 1722. That book also holds letters he wrote to Aaron ben Hayyim. His notes on the Hoshen Mishpat and on Talmud tracts were never printed. The entry traces his claimed descent from Joseph ben Gorion.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-heine-gustav-fr: Gustav Heine, born at Dusseldorf on June 18, 1812, was an Austrian publicist and a brother of Heinrich Heine. He tried farming and business, then joined the Austrian army and rose to first lieutenant. In 1847 he founded a Vienna paper that became the foreign office's official organ. Honors followed. He took the Order of the Iron Crown in 1867 and was knighted soon after. In 1870 he rose to the rank of Freiherr, taking his mother's family name, Geldern. He died at Vienna on Nov. 15, 1886.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-herodians-7605:
Herodians are described as a priestly party under King Herod and his successors. The Rabbis called them Boethusians, after the family of Boethus. Herod married into that family and made its sons high priests in turn. They sided with the Sadducees against the Pharisees.

Gospel passages place Herodians in plots against Jesus, sometimes beside Pharisees. Jesus is quoted warning against their leaven, explained as bad teaching. The entry notes that Luke leaves Herodians out in one passage. It also notes other passages where scribes and chief priests take their place. Sources cited include Gospel commentaries and Geiger.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-hillel-ben-samu:
Hillel ben Samuel, born about 1220, was an Italian physician, philosopher, and Talmudist. He was grandson of Eleazar ben Samuel of Verona. At Barcelona he studied Talmud under Jonah Gerondi. Gerondi's repentance in the Maimonides dispute turned him toward Maimonides' works.

Hillel studied medicine at Montpellier and practiced at Rome, Capua, and Ferrara. At Capua he lectured on philosophy from 1260 to 1271. In old age at Forli he fought a new anti-Maimonides move by letter. He proposed a council at Alexandria to settle the dispute for all Jewry. His chief work surveyed Greek, Arab, Jewish, and Christian philosophy. He died about 1295.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ibn-migas-josep: Joseph ibn Migas was a Spanish Jew of the eleventh century and founder of a line of scholars. Respected at Granada, he got caught in its politics. When King Habus died in 1037, his sons Badis and Balkin fought for the throne. Joseph and other Jews backed the younger Balkin. The crowd made Badis king in October 1037. Badis had his brother killed, and Joseph fled. The king of Seville, a foe of Badis, took him in and used him in public service.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-isaac-ben-moses:
Isaac ben Moses of Vienna, called Isaac Or Zarua', was a German halakist who lived about 1200 to 1270 and was probably born in Bohemia. Driven by a thirst for Talmudic learning, he traveled in his youth to the great yeshibot of Germany and France. At Paris, Judah ben Isaac Sir Leon was his chief teacher. He later studied at Worms and Speyer, and at Würzburg, around 1230, Meir Rothenburg was his pupil.

Toward the end of his life, about 1260, he composed the "Or Zarua'," a work that is both a ritual code and a Talmudic commentary. It follows the order of the Talmud's treatises while keeping each law's rulings together, and it quotes the law's sources rather than giving decisions alone. The book displaced the older ritual works. The entry also values it as a record of German Jewish life in the Middle Ages.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-israelitisch-th:
The Israelitisch-Theologische Lehranstalt was a rabbinical and teachers' seminary in Vienna, founded in 1893. Wilhelm and David von Guttmann proposed it, and Albert von Rothschild and Freiherr von Königswarter helped fund it. The doors opened on Oct. 15 of that year. The Austrian government and the Jewish communities of Vienna, Prague, and Lemberg all gave it money. A board of fifteen curators governed it.

Dr. Adolf Schwarz, who taught Talmud, halakic literature, and homiletics, served as rector. His colleagues covered Midrash, Bible study, history, and the languages of the crown lands. Each year the school issued a report together with a scholarly treatise. In 1902 it counted 26 students preparing for the rabbinate and 11 more preparing to teach religion.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-jacob-ben-ephra: Jacob ben Ephraim of Lublin was a Polish rabbi who died at Lublin in 1648. He taught first in Lublin's yeshibah, then was called as rabbi to Brest. There, in 1631, he hosted Yom-Tob Lipman Heller, who speaks of him with great respect. He returned to Lublin as rabbi and stayed until his death. Men called him the Gaon Rabbi Jacob of Lublin. The most eminent Polish rabbis of his time had studied under him. Only a few of his responsa survive, printed in another collection.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-jalomstein-mord: Mordecai ben David Jalomstein was an American journalist born in Suwalki, Russian Poland, in 1835. Well read in Talmudic and newer Hebrew writing, he moved to New York in 1871. There he edited the first Hebrew periodical issued in the United States. For about twenty years he was chief collaborator on the Yiddish Jewish Gazette of New York. His letters on American life, signed Yashan, drew wide notice, and his history of the United States ran as a serial for about two years. He died in New York on Aug. 18, 1897.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-joel-b-isaac-ha:
Joel ben Isaac ha-Levi was a German Talmud commentator of the twelfth century, probably born at Bonn. He studied at Ratisbon, Würzburg, and Mayence under noted masters, among them Eliezer ben Nathan, whose son-in-law he became. He taught chiefly at Bonn and Cologne and died at Cologne about 1200. His son Eliezer followed him as rabbi and teacher there.

Among the top Talmud authorities of his time, Joel wrote comments on many tractates. Those works are lost, but later books quote them, and his rulings live on in his son's writings. He broke with his old teacher Ephraim over how far later custom should bind, while still showing him respect. Six of his sacred poems survive, all dirges on attacks on German Jews.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-josephus-flaviu:
Flavius Josephus was a general and historian born in 37 or 38 who died after the year 100. On his mother's side he claimed descent from the Hasmonean line. As a boy he was known for a strong memory and quick learning. He passed through the schools of the Pharisees, Sadducees, and Essenes, then spent three years in the desert with Banus. At nineteen he joined the Pharisees for good.

When the great war with Rome broke out in 66, the Sanhedrin gave him the defense of Galilee. The entry follows his command, his capture, and his later life under Roman rule. It then surveys his writings and their sources at length. For the age of Alexander he used Greek accounts, for one stretch the first book of Maccabees, and Polybius where Jewish history touched its neighbors.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ka-b-al-ahbar-9:
Ka'b al-Ahbar was one of the chief fathers of Muslim tradition. He brought into that field both the method and much matter of the Jewish Haggadah. He died in the year 652 or 655 and came from Yemen, where he had been a Jew. He turned to Islam under the calif Abu Bakr, or by some accounts Omar.

For his learning he was called al-Hibr, from the Hebrew haber, a fellow scholar. He taught on the Koran and on Mohammed's life in a preaching, tale-telling way. His pupils Ibn Abbas and Abu Hurairah grew into great traditionists. The calif Omar prized him and asked his counsel often, chiefly on matters of faith. Late in life he withdrew to Emesa.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-kainan-3905: Kainan is named as the son of Arphaxad and the father of Salah. He shows up only in a few texts. The entry lists Genesis xi. 13 in the Greek version, the Book of Jubilees, and Luke iii. 36. Other versions leave him out and make Salah the son of Arphaxad. In Jubilees, Kainan finds an old stone carving. It holds the star lore taught by the Watchers, the rebel angels. Another book makes him a son of Seth instead.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-kapper-siegfrie:
Siegfried Kapper was an Austrian poet and physician. He was born at Smichow, near Prague, on March 21, 1821. He died at Pisa on June 7, 1879. He studied at Prague and at Vienna. He took his doctorate in 1847. He began life as a doctor. In time he turned to writing as his main work.

The entry lists Kapper's books across thirty years. Early volumes hold Slavic songs in German dress. Later ones tell of travels among the Southern Slavs. His tale "Geneda," printed in 1846, pictures early Jewish life in Prague. Some of his lyric poems were set to music. Solomon Sulzer and Josef Dessauer both composed settings for them. His Serbian songs fill two parts of one work.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-kibroth-hattaav: Kibroth-hattaavah was a stopping place of the Israelites in the wilderness. It lay on the road from Sinai to Kadesh. Its name means "the graves of lust." The name came from the crowds who died there. They had gorged on quail flesh and were buried on the spot. One passage seems to make it the same place as Taberah. Deuteronomy names the two as distinct places. Schwarz matches it with a modern spring in the heart of the desert.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-krauss-friedric: Friedrich Salomon Krauss, an Austrian folklorist born at Pozega in Slavonia on Oct. 7, 1859, studied classical philology at Vienna. He then turned to South Slav folk lore, which he was the first to study in a scientific way. Crown Prince Rudolph sent him through Bosnia, Herzegovina, Slavonia, Croatia, and Dalmatia. There he found a rich store of Muslim and Slav songs. For eight years he edited a folk lore monthly. His books include South Slav tales, witch tales, and custom studies dated from 1881 to 1900.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-lanczy-leo-9605: Leo Lánczy, a Hungarian deputy and financier born in 1852, worked first for the Anglo-Hungarian Bank and a land credit body. In 1881 he became director-general of the Hungarian Bank of Commerce. He pushed Hungarian trade hard and worked to free its finances from Vienna. Foreign credit for Hungary grew under his hand. Parliament took him in 1893 for Zsolna and in 1896 for Miskolcz. Orders came in 1891 and later, and a court title in 1902. The entry ends by noting that Lánczy is a convert to Christianity.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-lederer-joachim: Joachim K. Lederer, an Austrian playwright born at Prague on Aug. 28, 1808, died at Dresden on July 31, 1876. A private tutor gave him a thin schooling. He tried medicine for a year, then took a law degree. As a Jew he saw no path to a university chair, and law practice held no charm. Comedy writing became his life. His sharp, funny portraits of his countrymen won a sure place on the Austrian stage. Six hit comedies are named, the last written with a partner.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-levi-abraham-98:
Abraham Levi, a German traveler, was born at Horn in Lippe in 1702. He died at Amsterdam on Feb. 1, 1785. At five he was sent to Brog for study, and he stayed there until 1714. A love of travel seized him young. In 1719, at seventeen, he left home for good.

Levi crossed Germany, Bohemia, Moravia, Hungary, Austria, and all of Italy. He noted synagogues, customs, and counts of Jews in small places that other writers passed by. His Judaeo-German account, with a Hebrew poem on ten events of his trip, was later printed.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-levita-elijah-k:
Elijah Levita, a grammarian, Masorite, and poet, was born at Neustadt, near Nuremberg, in 1468. He died at Venice in December 1549. As a boy he showed a bent for Bible study and Hebrew grammar. He settled early in Venice, then taught Hebrew to Jewish children at Padua in 1504.

At his pupils' request Levita wrote a commentary on Kimhi's grammar. A copyist printed it at Pesaro under his own name, in a flawed form. Still, it became the favorite manual for Hebrew students, Jews and Christians alike. After Padua was sacked in 1509, Levita lost all he had and went to Rome. Cardinal Egidio of Viterbo housed him for thirteen years in trade for Hebrew lessons.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-levy-moritz-mar:
Moritz Marcus Levy, a Danish physician, was born in Copenhagen on Sept. 8, 1808. He died there on Dec. 30, 1865. He took his medical degree at Copenhagen in 1833. In 1830 he had won the university gold medal for a medical essay. He traveled abroad for three years to study obstetrics.

Back in Copenhagen, Levy became resident physician at the Nursery Institute. In 1838 he accepted baptism and took the name Carl Edvard Marius. That step removed a bar to a university chair. He rose to full professor in 1850 and served as the city's obstetrician. He wrote much on childbirth and coedited a journal of medicine and surgery.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-lipkin-10005:
Lipkin traces a Russo-Jewish family that began with Dob Bär Lipkin, rabbi of Plungian in the first half of the eighteenth century. Its best known member was Israel Lipkin, called Rabbi Israel Salanter. Born at Zhagory, he died at Königsberg on Feb. 2, 1883, after leading schools at Wilna and Kovno.

Israel stressed the daily use of moral teaching and the value of manual labor. He started groups for the study of ethics and published a monthly on law and ethics in 1861. His son Lipmann was a mathematician born in 1846. He devised a way to change straight motion into circular motion, shown at Vienna in 1873.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-lonzano-menahem:
Menahem ben Judah de Lonzano was a Palestinian scholar of the Masorah, midrash, and words, and a poet who died after 1608 in Jerusalem. His birthplace is not sure; it may have been Italy or Greece. Orphaned early, he lived with poverty, care, and sickness all his life.

Lonzano married at Jerusalem, was forced out by a friend's betrayal, and found shelter at Constantinople. He kept traveling to earn bread and spent about forty years in Jerusalem in all. Though lame in both feet and blind in one eye, he preached in Italy and won support to return home. His first book, printed about 1572, holds a moral poem and hymns.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-lydda-or-lod-10:
Lydda, also called Lod and later Diospolis, is surveyed in a Jewish Encyclopedia entry from 1906. The city in Palestine lay a day's journey west of Jerusalem. Tradition ties its founding to a descendant of Benjamin, and Benjamites settled it again after the Exile. The Talmud describes it as fortified already in Joshua's days.

The article moves through the city's changing rulers. A Roman commander burned Lydda under Nero, yet it later became capital of a district under Vespasian. Its name changed to Diospolis in Roman times, and it grew into a bishopric. Christians honored it as the burial place of Saint George. After Jerusalem fell, Lydda became famous instead as a seat of Jewish learning. Its academy is often named in the Talmud. The entry holds both pasts of one small city in a single frame.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-may-isaac-10505:
Isaac May was rabbi of Lublin in the second half of the sixteenth century. Herman Rosenthal and J. G. Lipman remember him in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906 for what he did with wet ground. He enjoyed the favor of Count Jenchinsky, the starost of Lublin. In 1556 May obtained a large parcel beside his house that had once been a mill-pond. He filled it, and the overcrowded Jewish quarter grew across it.

Most of the land filled with Jewish houses, but May kept a portion and gave it to the community for a yeshivah. It made him a founder of the first high-grade rabbinical school in Poland. The entry quotes the decree of August 23, 1567. In it King Sigismund August allowed the Jews to build their school and a synagogue on the land of May. The site lay near Lublin Castle, and the Jews paid the cost in common.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-mayence-10305:
Mayence is the Rhine city in the grand duchy of Hesse-Darmstadt. Gotthard Deutsch and Siegmund Salfeld tell its Jewish history in a Jewish Encyclopedia article from 1906, one of the oldest Jewish histories in Germany. Of 84,251 inhabitants, about 3,200 were Jews. Legend brought the scholar Kalonymus from Lucca at the call of Charlemagne. Documents begin only in the tenth century, and learning flowered under the Kalonymus family and Gershom ben Judah, the “light of the exile.”

Against that golden age the article sets the Crusades. In 1084 a fire was blamed on the Jews, and many fled to Speyer. On May 27, 1096, Crusaders under Emicho broke into Mayence. They massacred more than eleven hundred Jews, despite brave resistance and the protection of the archbishop. The community recovered under the king's peace of 1103, only to bleed again in the Second Crusade of 1147.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-melli-10605:
Melli is an Italian family of rabbis and scholars, named for the village of Melli in the province of Mantua. Gotthard Deutsch and M. Seligsohn trace the family in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. They carry it back to the fifteenth century. The earliest known member is Elijah ben Abraham Melli, rabbi of Parma. He survives through a responsum of 1470. It asked Joseph Colon about divorcing a baptized Jew. Colon approved.

The entry then moves through Mantua. Jehiel Melli was rabbi there in the early seventeenth century. In 1623 he published "Tappuhe Zahab," Golden Apples, shortening Elijah de Vidas' ethical classic. Phinehas Elijah Melli became chief rabbi on January 15, 1581. His son Zemah Elijah got the same degree that day. The article keeps that small dynastic moment. Eliezer Melli was a Venetian rabbi of the sixteenth century. He is known only from citations in the responsa of Moses Provençal.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-merzbacher-abra:
Abraham Merzbacher was a Munich banker remembered as a patron of Jewish learning. Isidore Singer profiles him in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born at Baiersdorf near Erlangen in 1812. He had meant to be a rabbi and applied, unsuccessfully, for the rabbinate of Ansbach before settling into banking at Munich. In communal politics he championed the moderate conservative party. He sat on the central committee of the Alliance Israélite Universelle.

His money built scholarship. At his own expense he published Raphael Nathan Rabbinovicz's monumental "Dikduke Soferim." It ran to sixteen volumes. For that friend and protégé he assembled one of the largest private Jewish libraries in the world. After his death, on June 4, 1885, it passed into the city library of Frankfort-on-the-Main. The entry is short. It fixes the name of the man behind a great edition and a great collection.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-midrash-from-th:
Midrash comes from a Hebrew root meaning to study or investigate. It is the rabbinic art of drawing more out of Scripture than its plain words say. Joseph Jacobs and S. Horovitz define it in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Against peshaṭ, the literal sense, midrash digs for the spirit of the text. It finds readings that are not obvious at first sight.

The Talmud compares such exposition to a hammer striking sparks out of a rock, the article notes. Yet the two kinds of reading never fully parted. Rab Kahana confessed that he knew the whole Talmud by eighteen. Only years later did he learn that a verse never loses its plain meaning. The entry traces the term back to the book of Chronicles.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-modena-10905:
Modena, the central Italian city, was capital of its own duchy. It had one of Italy's most important Jewish communities. Richard Gottheil and Ismar Elbogen write about it in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Jews lived in its territory by the year 1000. But the city record starts only in 1450, with bankers settling under the dukes of Ferrara.

Modena's luck was dynastic. When the Ferrara line died out in 1598, the duchy passed to a collateral branch of the Este, not to the Church. So its Jews suffered less than their neighbors under the ecclesiastical laws. The seventeenth century made the community a center of rabbis and study. Figures like Abraham Joseph Solomon Graziano rose there, and Cabalistic thought was in the ascendant.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-mordecai-nathan:
Mordecai Nathan, called Maestro, was a physician of Avignon in the middle fifteenth century. His identity must be assembled from four names. Richard Gottheil and S. Kahn do the assembling in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Joseph Colon corresponded with him and praised his medical skill highly. Colon addressed him by a title authorities read as master or as mere respect.

He is doubtless, the entry argues, the same man as the mathematician Mordecai Nadi. He is also the astronomer Mordecai Nathan. He is the Maestro Mordecai Todros Nathan for whom a scribe copied Alfasi at Arles in 1454. One error is fenced off: he is not Isaac Nathan of the famous concordance. He stands as a Provençal polymath — physician, mathematician, astronomer — recovered from footnotes.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-moses-ben-yom-t:
Moses ben Yom-Tob, known as Moses ha-Nakdan, was an English Masorite and grammarian of London. His Jewish Encyclopedia entry is by Crawford Howell Toy, Joseph Jacobs, and Jacob Zallel Lauterbach. He taught Moses ben Isaac, the author of the Sefer ha-Shoham. His own subject was the pointing and chanting of the Hebrew Bible.

His Darke ha-Nikkud weha-Neginot sets the rules of punctuation and accentuation for the Masorah. Jacob ben Hayyim first printed it in the Bomberg rabbinic Bible, and later rabbinic Bibles kept it. In time it became practically the standard work on Hebrew punctuation in the Middle Ages. The entry preserves a quiet craftsman of the biblical text.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-names-of-god-11:
Names of God, in the Jewish Encyclopedia, are treated as more than titles: each name carries Israel's idea of God's character. The article is by the editorial committee, J. F. McLaughlin, and Judah David Eisenstein. A name could stand for God's very presence, power, or glory. New experience of His care could give an old name new meaning.

Most of the space goes to the Tetragrammaton, which occurs over six thousand eight hundred times. The article shows that Jehovah is a mistaken form, born of reading the consonants with the vowels of Adonai. The name itself means He who is, or lives, and was spoken to Moses at Horeb. By the third century before Christ it was held too holy to pronounce.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-nebo-mount-1140:
Mount Nebo is where Moses viewed the promised land before death. The entry was written by the Editorial Board's Executive Committee and George A. Barton for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Deuteronomy ties that view to Moses' last days. The entry identifies Nebo with the peak called Pisgah. Pisgah stood among the Abarim mountains east of Jordan.

The name survives today in the peak Jabal Naba. It lies five miles southwest of Heshbon, near Madeba. A cairn there marks an ancient holy site. Its view covers Hermon, the Jordan valley, and the Dead Sea. Yet Deuteronomy seems to promise a still wider view. Scholars explain the gap as hyperbole or boundary language. The name itself echoes Babylon's god Nabu.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-newburger-josep:
Joseph E. Newburger was a New York judge and Jewish founder. Cyrus Adler and Frederick T. Haneman wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born in New York city in 1853. He was educated in its public schools. He took his law degree at Columbia.

Newburger was admitted to the bar in 1874. In 1891 voters elected him judge of the city court. He served on that bench until 1895. The next year he won a seat in General Sessions. He still held that office in 1904. Beyond the bench, he worked in Jewish societies. He was one of the founders of a seminary. The Jewish Theological Seminary of America counts him so.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-notovich-osip-k:
Osip Konstantinovich Notovich was a Russian journalist. Herman Rosenthal and A. S. Waldstein wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born in 1849 at Kertch. His father was rabbi of that town. Law was his study at St. Petersburg.

In 1873 he published and edited Novoe Vremya. The feuilleton kept him after the editor's chair. In 1876 he bought the small daily Novosti. Under him it won great political influence. It defended the Jews stoutly against anti-Semitic attack. His leading articles appeared as Osnovy Reform. He Englished Buckle's history into Russian dress. Censorship law drew a history from his pen. Plays from him reached the imperial theaters too. Early in life he joined the Greek Church.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ottensoser-laza: Lazarus Ottensoser was a German rabbi and teacher of boys. Isidore Singer and Schulim Ochser wrote his short entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born at Weimarsschmieden in the year 1798. He died at Hochstädt in August of the year 1878. He began life as a peddler with a pack on his back. He was called to teach at Scheinfeld, then at Aub in 1821. In 1828 he went to Hochstädt and founded a Talmud Torah school there.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-parashiyyot-the:
The Four Parashiyyot are four extra reads for the Sabbath. The board and M. Seligsohn wrote the entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Each week a lesson is read from the scroll of the Law. At times a fit, extra part is read after it. Four such parts fall near the feast of Purim.

Two of the four fall before Purim, and two fall after it. Their names are Shekalim, Zakor, Parah, and ha-Hodesh in turn. The Sabbaths that bear them take those same four names. Shekalim holds the law of the half shekel gift. It is read just before the first day of Adar. From that day, men of the court sent word out. Jews were told to bring or send their half shekels in.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-philippson-1210:
Philippson is a German family of scholars and public men. Four writers shared this article in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. The line traces back to Jacob Joshua of the 1700s. Its best known name is Ludwig Philippson. Its members filled chairs, schools, and banks.

Ludwig founded the Allgemeine Zeitung des Judenthums. That paper spoke for German Jews for decades. His son Alfred became a geographer of Greece and Asia Minor. Emil Philippson directed the Jacobson school at Seesen. Franz Philippson built a banking house at Brussels. The family joined learning, press, and finance.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-posner-carl-123:
Carl Posner was a German doctor and medical writer born at Berlin in 1854. Isidore Singer and Frederick T. Haneman wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was a son of the writer Louis Posner. He studied at five German universities in turn. He took a doctorate in 1875 and a medical degree in 1880.

Posner worked in a disease institute at Giessen for two years. He then helped a Berlin doctor for six years. In 1880 he settled in Berlin as a doctor himself. He began to teach at the university in 1890. The title of professor came to him in 1895. From 1889 he edited a Berlin medical weekly. From 1894 he edited Virchow's yearly report on medicine.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-prussia-12405:
Prussia was a kingdom and the largest state of the German empire. Gotthard Deutsch wrote its long article for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. The kingdom grew out of the march of Brandenburg. In 1415 that march was given to a Hohenzollern prince. One of his line ruled the Teutonic Order's lands in 1525.

That prince turned Protestant and made himself a worldly ruler. In 1618 his lands were joined with Brandenburg for good. New lands in west and north Germany came later. The Great Elector won them in the years 1640 to 1688. Upon that frame the article builds the tale of Prussia's Jews.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-rabina-i-12505:
Rabina the First was a Babylonian teacher of the fifth set of amoraim. Wilhelm Bacher and Jacob Zallel Lauterbach wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He died in about the year 420. He was a pupil of Raba ben Joseph ben Hama. He was so young then that Raba called him a child. Hama ben Bisa shared that name of dardeki with him.

Young as he was, Rabina put questions to his master. He cites Raba's sayings in the Talmud more than once. At an early age he was known as a teacher himself. He left the school at Mahoza to lead study elsewhere. The entry traces his questions and the men he taught.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-raziel-12605:
Raziel is an angel whose name means secret of God. Crawford Howell Toy and Ludwig Blau wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. He is first named in the Slavonic Book of Enoch. There he appears under the name Raguel or Rasuel.

The article says a Targum shows Raziel calling out daily on Mount Horeb. His voice carries the secrets of men across the world. The Book of Raziel makes him the angel of magic. He teaches astrology, divination, and the lore of amulets. The writers link his mysticism to practical Cabala. In Arab astrology he rules a lunar station. The entry sets his secret lore apart from other angel traditions.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-repentance-hebr:
Repentance, called teshubah in Hebrew, means a return to God. Kaufmann Kohler and Max Schlesinger wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. The noun appears only in post-Biblical literature. Its root, though, comes from Bible vocabulary.

The article says all the prophets preach repentance. Maimonides states that point in his code, they note. Repentance is the condition for Israel's redemption. It is also the condition for each person's salvation. Sin is pictured as straying away from God. Return means breaking resolutely away from sin. God's kindness waits for the sinner who turns back. Since no just person is free of sin, all need return. The entry gives repentance a central place in Jewish faith.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-reuben-ha-sefar:
Reuben ha-Sefardi is the reputed author of a work against Christianity. The Executive Committee of the Editorial Board and Peter Wiernik wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. That work is called Kelimmat ha-Goyim. Scholars link it to Profiat Duran's writing from 1349.

The article argues the names are likely invented. Zunz held that Reuben and his books are fictitious. Moses Botarel created many such names, they say. One supposed book is Sefer ha-Kelimmah. Another is Sefer ha-Shulhan, also ascribed to Reuben. The writers find no doubt in Zunz's verdict. A long source list backs that conclusion. The entry is a warning about fake authors in old books. It shows scholars testing a name and finding air.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-rofe-daniel-b-s:
Daniel Rofe was an Italian physician of the fourteenth and fifteenth centuries. Isidore Singer and Schulim Ochser wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. He lived at Pisa and at Perugia. His full name adds ben Samuel ben Daniel ha-Dayyan.

The article says he devoted much time to Arabic medical writers. Ibn Sina, or Avicenna, held his special attention. His work Eben Pinnah survives as a Paris manuscript. It was copied for him by Abraham ibn Karshef. That copyist praises Daniel and his father at its end. Four sources support the brief entry. They include Carmoly's history of Jewish physicians. Readers get only a sketch of this doctor's life. Still, his Arabic study and one book anchor the record.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-roth-wilhelm-12:
Wilhelm Roth was an Austrian rhinologist born at Kluckno, Hungary, on October 10, 1848. Isidore Singer and Frederick T. Haneman wrote his entry for the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. He took his medical degree at Vienna in 1873 and settled there.

Roth became a privat-docent at Vienna's university in 1885. He invented a drop-syringe for the larynx, for giving medicine drop by drop. For the nose he devised a mirror, an inhalation apparatus, and an electric lamp. He also built a carrier that placed medicine where it was needed. His book on chronic inflammation of the throat appeared in 1883.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-samuel-ben-hofn:
Samuel ben Hofni was the last gaon of Sura, and he died in 1034. Wilhelm Bacher and Max Schloessinger wrote his entry for the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. His father had been a Talmudic scholar and chief judge.

Samuel married into Hai Gaon's family, becoming that gaon's father-in-law in time. Hai reports that Samuel eagerly pursued non-Jewish literature, like many contemporaries. Yet Samuel composed few responsa, though gaonic writing is mostly responsa collections. Sura's academy had stood a century in Pumbedita's shadow by then. Seekers of rulings preferred to write to Pumbedita instead of Sura.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-sarko-zarko-zar:
Isidore Singer and M. Seligsohn wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia entry, published in 1906, on Joseph ben Judah Sarko. He was an Italian grammarian and Hebrew poet. He worked in the first half of the fifteenth century. Carmoly held that he was born at Naples. He may have taught Judah Messer Leon. His chief work is Rab Pe'alim, a Hebrew grammar in several sections.

Sarko says he finished Rab Pe'alim on the first day of Elul, 1429. Its section on numbers was printed at Paris in 1520. His Hebrew verses after the preface appeared in a German journal. Dukes also credited him with Ba'al ha-Lashon, a Hebrew dictionary. Zunz gave that book to a different Joseph instead. The entry closes on a namesake grandson who lived a century later. Later writers confused the two men.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-schor-naphtali-:
M. Seligsohn wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia entry, issued with the Executive Committee of the Editorial Board in 1906. It profiles Naphtali Hirsch ben Zalman Schor, also called Hirsch Elsasser. He was a Moravian Talmudist of the sixteenth century. Schor studied under Moses Isserles, the great Polish authority. Isserles sent him many of his responsa. Most of those letters explain the Sefer ha-Mordekai.

The letters suggest Schor lived at Posen for a time. He also spent long stretches away, hunting for a post in Germany. His finest pupil was Joel Sirkes, author of the Bayit Ḥadash. Fuenn tried to identify Schor with a rabbi of Brest-Litovsk. The entry notes that this match has been disproved. The Brest rabbi speaks as an elder authority, not as Isserles' pupil.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-seligmann-leopo:
Leopold Seligmann, an Austrian army surgeon, is profiled by Isidore Singer and Frederick T. Haneman in this Jewish Encyclopedia entry, published in 1906. Seligmann was born at Nikolsburg on January 18, 1815. He was a brother of Franz Romeo Seligmann. He studied at the gymnasium of his home town. At Vienna's Joseph Academy he took the medico-surgical course, graduating in 1843.

Leopold entered the army as assistant surgeon in 1843. He became a surgeon in 1855, after the Italian revolution. He served in the Italian wars of 1859 and 1866. From 1868 to 1876 he worked at the War Ministry in Vienna. He rose to surgeon-major in 1871. He resigned in 1876 with the rank of lieutenant-colonel. His one book gives reserve doctors handy extracts from the sanitary rules. It appeared in 1873.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-shapira-m-w-135:
M. W. Shapira was a Polish dealer in antiquities born about 1830. Isidore Singer and Joseph Jacobs wrote the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia entry on him. He converted to Christianity young and moved to Palestine. There he opened a shop selling local antiquities in Jerusalem.

After the Moabite Stone was found, Shapira sold Moabite pottery to Prussia. The pieces cost the government a large sum in thaler. Scholars soon proved the pottery had been faked for him. Debate over the fraud reached Prussia's parliament in 1876. Shapira still supplied real Yemenite manuscripts to great libraries. In 1883 he offered the British Museum a famed scroll. He killed himself at Rotterdam in 1884.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-shofet-kol-ha-a:
Shofet Kol ha-Arez, Judge of all the earth, is a major penitential hymn of six verses. Cyrus Adler and Francis L. Cohen wrote the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia entry on it. Each verse ends with a phrase drawn from Numbers. An acrostic signs the name Shelomoh in its lines.

Many credit the hymn to Solomon ibn Gabirol, the great poet. Zunz instead assigned it to Solomon bar Abun the younger. Hymn and tune hold honored places in northern and southern rites. Ashkenazim make it the chief poem before New Year. It returns on the morning of the Day of Atonement. Sephardim place it before Nishmat on New Year morning. The entry follows one solemn hymn through two traditions.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-siberia-11705:
Siberia, Russia's vast northern Asian territory, stretched from the Urals to the Pacific. Joseph Jacobs and J. G. Lipman wrote the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia entry on its Jews. In 1902 its people numbered over six million in all. About 31,380 of them were Jews, the census found.

As a land of banishment, Siberia gained Jewish settlers early. Exiled prisoners arrived there in the seventeenth century. Many had no crime beyond being Jews, the entry says. In 1829 officials proposed deporting unregistered Jews from Courland there. Families and friends followed the deported and settled freely at first. By the 1830s the Jewish question reached Siberia too. The entry opens a history of exile turned into community.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-simeon-of-kitro:
Simeon of Kitron was a tanna known from a single saying. Wilhelm Bacher and Jacob Zallel Lauterbach wrote this brief Jewish Encyclopedia entry, published in 1906. No other teaching of his has been kept. His one remark is a piece of haggadah, not law.

He taught that the sea split for Israel because of the bones of Joseph. The Israelites had carried those bones with them out of Egypt. The entry gives the source in the Mekilta and short book notes. It shows how one line can keep a minor sage in memory.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-slonimski-leoni:
Leonid Zinovyevich Slonimski was a Russian publicist born in 1852. Herman Rosenthal and S Hurwitz wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. He was the son of Hayyim Selig Slonimski. At age twenty he began writing on social and legal topics. Since 1882 he has contributed steadily to the Vyestnik Yevropy.

Some of his articles attacked fiscal policy in Russia. He said it enriched capitalists by artificial means. It did so, he argued, at the cost of farmers and laborers. He also opposed the teachings of Karl Marx and his followers. His books covered mental disorder in law and land ownership. One full work examined Marx's economic teaching in detail.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-solomons-levy-1:
Levy Solomons was one of the founders of the Canadian Jewish community. Joseph Jacobs and Clarence I de Sola wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. He was born early in the eighteenth century. He settled in Montreal right after the British conquest. Before Canada he had lived and traded in Albany.

He traded widely with the Indians across a vast region. His ventures ran from Michilimackinac to the Gulf of St Lawrence. In 1775 General Montgomery made him purveyor to American hospitals. Montgomery's defeat brought disaster and heavy losses to Solomons. General Burgoyne expelled him and seized his property in 1776. He later recovered and returned to Montreal for good.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-stein-philipp-1:
Philipp Stein was a German author born at Königsberg in 1853. Isidore Singer wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. He was born there on December 3 of that year. In 1864 his parents moved with him to Berlin. His father's death ended his studies, and he became a bookseller.

He later worked on the Deutsches Montagsblatt in Berlin. In 1881 he became an editor of the Dresdener Zeitung. In 1884 he returned to Berlin to edit the Litterarische Merkur. By 1905 he was editor-in-chief of the Berlin Bazar. He was also dramatic critic of the Berliner Zeitung then. He edited letters of Goethe's mother and speeches of Bismarck.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-uriah-urijah-14:
Three men named Uriah share this entry from Bible history. Emil G. Hirsch and Schulim Ochser wrote it for the Jewish Encyclopedia, published in 1906. The first Uriah was a Hittite warrior of David's picked men. He was husband to Bath-sheba, whom David desired. Uriah's refusal to go home frustrated David's cover plan.

David then ordered him placed at the battle's hottest front. Uriah fell at the siege of Rabbah in consequence. Josephus adds that he held his ground heroically. The rabbis instead blamed Uriah for defying the king. The second Uriah was Ahaz's high priest and altar builder. Isaiah took him as a faithful witness. The third was a prophet from Kirjath-jearim. He fled Jehoiakim's anger into Egypt.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-vinnitsa-vinitz:
Vinnitsa is a Russian town in Podolia, on the Bug River. Herman Rosenthal and J. G. Lipman wrote this entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. The town was founded in the fourteenth century. Two castles once guarded it. Tatars and Cossacks raided it for centuries.

Jews likely lived there in the fourteen hundreds. Records first name them in 1532. They traded cattle on a large scale. In 1616 only fifty Jews paid house taxes there. During the Cossack rising, the town's Jews were massacred. Haidamak attacks followed in the seventeen hundreds. By 1878 most of the town's people were Jews.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-yizhak-ben-parn:
Yizhak ben Parnak was a scholar of Palestine of a date not fixed. Joseph Jacobs and Schulim Ochser wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. His name is tied to a strange book on death. That book tells what takes place as a man dies.

Three angels come to the bed of the man, it says. One is the angel of death with his dread task. One keeps the count of the life that has been lived. One stands as a guard for the soul of the man. If the man has been good, three more angels come. Four more come at the last clash with death. Each one speaks a verse to the cries of the man. The entry sees a link to a famed tale of three friends. That tale is told in the book Barlaam and Josaphat.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-zechariah-ibn-s:
Zechariah ibn Said al-Yamani made an Arabic form of the Yosippon. Isidore Singer and Max Schloessinger wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He worked in the tenth or the eleventh century. His work lives on in three forms to this day.

One form lies in draft books yet to be probed in full. One short form was bound in two great Bible sets of old. Those sets came out at Paris and London in old times. There it bore the false name of Second Maccabees in print. That book runs from the death of Alexander to the fall of Zion. One brief form came out at Beirut in the year 1873. A Leyden book shows a sage of 1063 knew the work. The entry says the man was an Egyptian Jew at base.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-zurita-15305:
Zurita was a fortified city of Castile, on the River Tajo in Spain. Joseph Jacobs and Meyer Kayserling wrote this entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. It had a Jewish community by 1137, when Alfonso VII took the city from the Moors. During the Almohade persecutions, many Jews found refuge there.

Zurita's charter of 1180 drew no line between Jews and Christians. In 1215 Henry I freed its aljama, the Jewish community, from all taxes. The grant rewarded money given for the war and faithful defense of the fort. By 1474 the community was rich enough to give the king a thousand gold doubloons.
jewish-encyclopedia-rothschild-1905:
The Jewish Encyclopedia gave this long piece on the Rothschild house in 1905. Joseph Jacobs, Isidore Singer, and a team of hands wrote and built it. The encyclopedia was the great English work on Jewish life and lore of its time.

The piece tells the tale of the Frankfurt house and its arms in five great towns. It lists the chief loans, the men of each age, and the sources a reader can trust. Its source list names Steinmann of 1857 and Reeves of 1887, the base works for the whole theme. It is still a sound place to start on the family's tale.
journal-of-discourses-vol-05:
The Move South dominates Volume Five, covering the tense year 1858. Salt Lake City stands empty as the Saints flee before the army. Then, the crisis past, the people return to find their homes intact.

Sermons manage an exodus of thirty thousand people with calm order. Young directs camps, herds, and hope from the pulpit week by week. Relief and thanks mark the return, yet warnings stay sharp too. The army camps nearby, and trust between foes stays thin here. Faith under pressure, at a whole people's scale, fills this striking volume. Later Saints told the Move South as a founding miracle of order.
kenelm-chillingly-volume-05:
Volume five of Kenelm Chillingly opens Book Five with Kenelm vanished from London. Nobody knows exactly when he disappeared. His servant went down to Exmundham carrying a check for the quarter's allowance. Following orders, Kenelm walks the Richmond fields toward Moleswich, one of England's quiet old county towns.

The chapter lingers on the town: its hotel by the church, the town hall, and Will Somers's shop. Somers deals in books and fishing tackle, a combination fitting the novel's mix of thought and sport. Kenelm's flight from London restarts his wandering on foot. This volume returns the hero to the road, where Lytton lets him meet England man by man.
kuprin-duel-1905:
Alexander Kuprin served as an officer in the Russian army, and The Duel, published in 1905, drew on that life. The English translation first appeared in 1916. Young sub-lieutenant Romashov endures the boredom and brutality of a dull garrison town, dreaming of glory and escape.

Around Romashov, officers drink, gamble, bully their men, and chase each other's wives. His love for a clever, ambitious officer's wife deepens his trouble. A petty quarrel at last forces him into a duel he cannot avoid. Kuprin's exposure of army life caused a sensation in Russia. The novel made him the most widely read Russian novelist of his year.
lazzarelli-crater-hermetis-1505:
Lodovico Lazzarelli staged a Hermetic dialogue in Crater Hermetis, printed at Paris in the landmark edition of 1505. Mercury instructs his student Tat on the Crater, the divine mixing-bowl in which souls are reborn. The little work rode in great company: Lefèvre's edition joined it with Ficino's Pimander and the Asclepius.

That 1505 volume fixed the Hermetic canon for the Renaissance, and Lazzarelli's dialogue shows the teaching turned toward poetry and vision. The Latin text sings of a second birth granted to those who plunge into the bowl of mind. Readers meet Hermetic thought here at its most ardent and strange.
le-loyer-discours-des-spectres-french-16:
Pierre Le Loyer, a French judge with a scholar's appetite, published his Discours et histoires des spectres in 1605. Eight French books treat specters, visions, and apparitions of every order. Spirits, angels, demons, and souls of the dead each receive their chapters, in the French classic of apparition lore.

Le Loyer arranges the unseen world like an encyclopedia. He gathers cases from Scripture, classical authors, and recent report. His learning is vast and his curiosity larger. The Discours became the standard French reference on apparitions for its century. Readers who want the whole spirit world in one set of covers still start with Le Loyer's eight books.
le-loyer-treatise-of-specters-english-16:
Le Loyer's discourse on specters crossed the Channel the year it appeared, in Zachary Jones's English Treatise of Specters of 1605. The French original's eight books on strange sights, visions, and apparitions thus reached English readers at once. Few Continental works on the spirit world traveled so fast.

Jones's translation keeps Le Loyer's range: angels, demons, souls, and phantoms in order. English readers could now test their own ghost lore against a French judge's vast collection. The book is a landmark of apparition literature in English. Its speed of translation shows the market's appetite. Ghosts, in 1605, were international news, and Le Loyer was their chief reporter.
lucretia-volume-05:
Volume 5 of Lucretia drops into low, comic company for a time. A chapter oddly called 'The Rape of the Mattress' opens it. Mr. Grabman wakes with heavy eyes beside an empty gin bottle. His man Beck opens shutters, lays breakfast, and hears his master's praise.

Grabman plans a trip into the country on some enterprise. He leaves his key in a hole in the wall for Beck. Lytton loved such rogues, and writes them with gusto. The comedy darkens the main tragedy by contrast. Even small knaves serve the plot's slow machinery. This volume mixes farce with the gathering storm.
margery-gred-a-tale-of-old-nuremberg-vol:
Volume five of Margery rings with news: the Imperial Diet meets in Nuremberg. Tomorrow the Emperor and Empress enter the town, and Hans comes with them. A messenger has brought the tidings to Margery's house. She and her friends must use all diligence to prepare.

Margery, now a wife in the Haller family, is chosen for honor. She joins twenty-one council daughters to greet their Majesties with flowers. Ursula, chiefest by birth, will speak the discourse. The Hallers' garden, unmatched in the city, supplies their posies. Ebers stages the pageant with a historian's loving care. Private joy and public splendor meet in this volume.
memoirs-of-napoleon-bonaparte-volume-05: Bourrienne, Napoleon's private secretary, stands as author of volume five. Gutenberg's head note marks it NB number five in its Napoleon series. A year, 1802, sits in that head note beside the title. Past that head note, the sample held here gives only license terms and a plea for gifts to the Gutenberg fund. No page of memoir prose is shown, so no account of its contents can be grounded here.
mungo-park-journal-mission-interior-afri:
Mungo Park's Journal of a Mission to the Interior of Africa records his second expedition of 1805, published after his death. The book is drawn from his own journal, sent home in stages. Park led a party of soldiers and workmen back to the Niger, meaning to follow it to the sea.

Rain, fever, and hostile attacks thinned the party as they built a boat at Sansanding and launched down the river. The journal stops before the end; Park drowned at the Bussa rapids when his boat was attacked, as later reports established. His calm record, kept as the expedition died around him, is one of exploration's most somber documents.
my-novel-volume-05:
Edward Bulwer-Lytton's fifth book opens with a father's blunt fear. Mr. Caxton hopes Pisistratus does not mean to be dull. The son swears any dullness would be innocent, not planned. A long discourse on knowledge is the point at stake.

Caxton would cut it out for stopping the action. Pisistratus calls the speech vital to his whole subject. He is stunned that a scholar father could say cut. Caxton yields with a joke on critics and authors. The scene skewers every writer who fights his editor, while the family tale rolls on beneath the talk.
ocean-of-story-kathasaritsagara-tawney-1:
With volume five, Penzer's Ocean of Story reaches the middle of its ten volumes, in Tawney's translation of Somadeva. The Kathasaritsagara's hero draws nearer his fated throne among the Vidyadharas, while the tales around him multiply. Vetala riddles, merchant voyages, and love won through dreams crowd these central books.

Penzer edits with a folklorist's hunger for variants, and his notes here are among the set's richest. Tawney had served as a librarian and educator in Calcutta, and his Sanskrit was exact. The combination gives English a story ocean with charts attached. Somadeva's eleventh-century Kashmir seems, in these pages, to have heard every tale the world owns. Volume five is a sound place to test that claim.
oliver-dweller-two-planets-1905:
Frederick S. Oliver, a young man in California, said this tale was told to him by a spirit named Phylos the Thibetan. The book came out in 1905, some years after Oliver's death. He wrote it down as a youth and kept it by him for years.

The tale ranges over Atlantis and Lemuria, lost lands said to have sunk beneath the sea. It tells of high science, air ships, and wise adepts in those lost worlds. The book stands as a key work of the theosophic tale in the United States.
openalex-w1966553905:
Mark Preston, David Conway, and co-authors built this genetic barcode. Their paper appeared in Nature Communications in June 2014. Malaria parasites cross borders with traveling people, they note. Imported parasites can restart spread in cleared areas. Drug-resistant strains also disperse through such travel.

The team used markers from the parasite's organellar genomes. Those small genomes vary by place of origin. A barcode of such variants can identify strain origins. Tracing sources helps guards watch the right routes. It also helps track resistant parasites as they spread. The tool supports the global malaria eradication campaign.
openalex-w2048126105:
Fernando Espirito-Santo, Manuel Gloor, Michael Keller and colleagues measured natural forest damage across Amazonia. Their paper appeared in Nature Communications in 2014. Field plots suggest the Amazon stores much carbon. But small plots may miss how trees die at large scales. The team asked how disturbance size affects carbon loss.

They combined field surveys, airborne laser data and satellite images. Disturbances ranged from tiny gaps to huge blow-downs. Small death events caused most biomass loss overall. Mid-size and very large events added far less. Growth simulations tested whether losses change the carbon balance. Even counting all disturbance losses, the sink picture held. Forest carbon budgets must count small events, they argue.
openalex-w2049204605:
Danika Hill, Emily Eriksson, Connie Li Wai Suen and colleagues tested a functional antibody measure in malaria. Their paper appeared in PLoS ONE in 2013. Natural immunity to falciparum malaria can protect people. Standard tests only count antibody levels. They do not show what antibodies actually do.

The team used a new assay with blood plasma samples. The samples came from a long study in Papua New Guinea. The assay measured how antibodies help cells engulf parasite forms. That engulfing activity rose with age. It also rose with current infection. Stronger activity was linked with protection from illness. High parasite loads were less likely too. It was the first such evidence for this immune route.
openalex-w2102213705:
Peter Fretwell, Hamish Pritchard, David Vaughan and colleagues produced new maps of Antarctica's ice and bedrock. Their dataset, Bedmap2, appeared in The Cryosphere in 2013. Knowing ice thickness is vital for sea-level forecasts. The bed beneath the ice shapes how glaciers flow. Earlier maps had large gaps and older data.

The team merged data from many sources. Satellite, airborne and ground surveys all contributed. The grids cover the continent south of sixty degrees. They give surface height and ice thickness. They also give the hidden bed elevation. Many new surveys filled past gaps. The maps improve models of ice loss. They became a standard reference for polar science.
openalex-w2112657305:
Claudia Allemani, Hannah Weir, Helena Carreira and the CONCORD group compared cancer survival worldwide. Their study appeared in The Lancet in 2014. World data on cancer survival were scarce. Survival rates reveal how well health systems work. The team launched global surveillance of this metric.

Registries in sixty-seven countries shared patient records. The data covered about twenty-five million adults. Children with leukaemia were included too. Ten major cancers were analysed. Five-year survival was estimated for each country. Strict quality checks were applied to all records. Wide gaps separated rich and poor countries. The results inform global cancer control policy.
openalex-w2134079305:
Luca Amendola, Stephen Appleby, Anastasios Avgoustidis, and colleagues wrote this review for Living Reviews in Relativity in 2018. They wrote for the Euclid Theory Working Group. Euclid is a European Space Agency satellite mission built to learn why the expansion of the universe is speeding up.

Euclid will measure the shapes and redshifts of galaxies across a large share of the sky. It will also map how galaxy clusters are spread out. The review focuses on cosmology and basic physics beyond the standard models. Its five broad topics are dark energy and modified gravity, dark matter, early universe conditions, basic assumptions, and data analysis methods.
openalex-w2146594405:
Philippe Rasoanaivo, Colin Wright, Merlin Willcox, and Ben Gilbert published this review in the Malaria Journal in 2011. They compare whole plant extracts with single purified compounds for treating malaria. Traditional medicine uses whole plants or mixtures, and crude extracts often beat isolated ingredients at the same dose.

The review sorts the positive interactions behind that edge. Some ingredients boost each other's direct killing power, as with the Cinchona alkaloids.
