Others speed absorption, as in Artemisia annua tea, or calm side effects, like ginger against nausea. Some extracts also help the immune system or block drug resistance pumps, though those remain untested in patients. The authors call for proper clinical trials of combinations.
openalex-w2534929505:
Peter Läderach, Julián Ramírez-Villegas, and Carlos E. Navarro Racines, with colleagues, wrote this paper for Climatic Change, published online in 2016. It studies how climate change will reshape coffee growing, using Nicaragua as the test case. Coffee supports about twenty-five million farmers across more than sixty tropical countries, most of them smallholders. The bean is highly sensitive to climate.

The team combined coffee location and cup quality data with crop suitability models and global climate projections. They sorted future areas into four impact levels, from coffee disappearing to conditions improving. The authors then built an adaptation framework covering both place and time. Roundtable talks with Nicaraguan coffee actors helped pick the most promising strategies. The framework is meant to guide adaptation planning for coffee regions facing similar pressures.
openalex-w2608640705:
The ALICE Collaboration published this letter in Nature Physics in 2017. It reports on strange particles produced in proton-proton collisions at the Large Hadron Collider. When heavy nuclei collide, they can melt into quark-gluon plasma, matter where quarks move freely. Extra production of strange hadrons has long been treated as a sign of that plasma.

Several plasma-like effects had already appeared in busy proton-proton collisions, but multi-strange particles had not been checked. This paper presents those measurements in high-multiplicity proton collisions. It reports enhanced production of particles carrying several strange quarks, as its title states. The pattern resembles what heavy-ion collisions show. That blurs the line between small and large collision systems. It also challenges physicists to explain such effects without a big droplet of plasma.
openalex-w2789857505:
Daniel Osorio, Paola Rondón-Villarreal, and Rodrigo Gonzalo Torres introduced an R software package in The R Journal in 2015. The package, called Peptides, serves research on antimicrobial peptides. These small proteins kill bacteria broadly and rarely provoke resistance, making them promising antibiotic sources. Whether a peptide works depends on physical traits computable from its amino acid sequence.

The package quickly computes ten such structural characteristics for any sequence a user supplies. Those numbers feed data-mining work to classify known peptides and design new ones. The tool also reads and plots output files from the GROMACS molecular dynamics package. Freely available inside the R environment, it lowers the entry barrier for peptide researchers. Faster property calculation means larger candidate sets can be screened in silico. That speeds the hunt for new antimicrobial compounds.
openalex-w2936500105:
Kimberly Lackey, Janet Williams, Courtney Meehan, and colleagues published the INSPIRE study in Frontiers in Nutrition in 2019. It asks what counts as a normal mix of microbes in human milk and in infant stools. Earlier small studies in different countries had reported quite different microbe mixes in milk.

It was unclear whether those contrasts were real or came from unlike collection and testing methods. The INSPIRE team therefore ran a tightly controlled study with women from diverse populations, using standard milk collection methods. They report that the microbe mixes in milk and in infant feces are related to each other. They also find that these mixes vary by geographic place.
openalex-w2979655805:
Roberto Casadio, E. Contreras, Jorge Ovalle, and colleagues published this theoretical physics paper in The European Physical Journal C in 2019. It uses a method called gravitational decoupling to build new solutions of Einstein's field equations. Those equations describe how mass and energy shape space and time in general relativity.

The authors work with still, ball-shaped systems such as dense stars. They show their method can steadily turn any uneven, or anisotropic, solution into an even one. It can also generate fresh solutions whose complexity factor stays the same or drops to zero. They give a few worked examples to show the method in action. The result is a simple, powerful tool for theorists modeling self-gravitating matter.
openalex-w4280504305:
Olaf Erenstein, Moti Jaleta, Kai Sonder, and colleagues review world maize production, use, and trade in Food Security in 2022. Maize, or corn, was domesticated about nine thousand years ago in Mexico. It is now the world's leading cereal by volume and is set to become the most widely grown and traded crop. Most maize feeds animals, though it is a key food in sub-Saharan Africa and Latin America.

Production has surged over twenty-five years through new technology, higher yields, and more land. The review follows those shifts in supply and demand, with an eye on the Global South. It calls for more research spending that lifts food security while keeping farming within planetary limits. Fairness and sustainability, the authors warn, cannot be afterthoughts.
openalex-w4311665405:
João Botelho, Paulo Mascarenhas, João Viana, and colleagues reviewed the evidence linking oral health to body-wide chronic diseases, in Nature Communications in 2022. Theirs is an umbrella review: it re-examines hundreds of earlier pooled analyses rather than single studies. Links between gum disease and conditions such as diabetes and heart disease are often claimed. The question is how strong the proof behind those claims really is.

The authors graded eight hundred fifty-five pooled comparisons from the literature. About seven in ten reached nominal significance, yet only about eight in a hundred counted as strong evidence. Most comparisons also varied widely between studies, a sign of shaky ground. The review urges caution: association is common, proof of cause is rare.
openalex-w7207646205:
Tiara Rodrigues da Cunha, Claudia Ferreira Batista Fernandes, and Isabel Lopes Rodrigues study the pedagogical coordinator, the staff member who links school leadership with classroom teaching. Their 2026 research mixes published sources, documents, and fieldwork in public schools in Santa Maria da Vitoria, Bahia, using observation, questionnaires, and interviews with coordinators themselves. The aim was to understand the role's duties, its difficulties, and its effect on teaching and learning.

Coordinators, they find, play a central part in joining up teaching actions, training teachers on the job, and following classroom practice. Yet the role is often squeezed by piles of administrative work and tasks that belong elsewhere, which weakens its teaching leadership. The authors conclude that coordinators can genuinely change a school, provided the institution protects time and conditions for the pedagogical work itself.
openalex-w7212427205:
Fillipe Barreiros de Souza and Vilma Alves de Souza argue that a city's master plan can shield land and water, not just shape streets. In Brazil, that plan is the law that steers how a town grows. The pair read the plan's law base: the main law, the City Statute, and four green laws. Their lens was the green patch and the soil's thirst.

Poor growth, they hold, seals the soil and strips the green. Floods then hit the poor first and worst. The plan can fight back with set tools: a floor share of ground left open to rain, green banks kept in reserve, and tax breaks for green works. So used, the plan stops being a map of lots. It turns into a shield set up ahead of the flood.
openalex-w7213336005:
João Acyr Chueiry Filho and colleagues at a Brazilian hospital propose a new way to study mediumship. Their 2026 essay in Research, Society and Development treats mediumship as a question for cognitive psychiatry and brain science. It sets aside both religious claims and the idea that mediumship is simply illness.

The team suggests that mediums may show stronger links between the two halves of the brain and less separation between thought and feeling networks. They review gene, brain scan, and psychology studies, and note that the evidence is still mixed. A detailed plan for a case-control study is offered so the idea can be tested.
openalex-w7213356405:
Leandro Oliveira dos Reis and co-authors describe building ONcoCare, a web app for people living with cancer. Their 2026 article reports on a digital tool meant to support safe aesthetic care and self-care during cancer treatment. The project follows national cancer policy and a contextual design method.

A review of earlier work found few teaching materials on aesthetic care in oncology. ONcoCare therefore gathers trusted guidance on handling skin and appearance side effects, self-care, and safe product use. Separate areas serve patients and health workers. The authors say the tool could improve teaching and care, though early validation is still under way.
openalex-w7213367805:
Alva Valéria Moro Labs and co-authors write about intellectual disability from a social and historical angle. Their 2026 article follows the move from segregation toward full school inclusion in Brazil. It questions teaching methods that treat all learners with intellectual disability in the same standard way.

Disability, the authors argue, does not sit inside the person alone. It grows from the meeting point between a person's limits and a restrictive setting. They call for leaving the medical model behind in favour of respect for difference. Special support and universal design for learning, they say, should protect autonomy and full citizenship.
openalex-w7213747105:
Lais Tailla Cardoso Regis and Everton Regis de Santana map the new skills expected of nurses in digital health. Their 2026 documentary study reviews national and international normative and technical documents from 2021 to 2026. Seventeen documents from health bodies and nursing councils formed the corpus.

Six domains of competence emerged from thematic analysis. They cover governing and judging technology, ethics and professional responsibility, and data protection, among others named in the study. Artificial intelligence is widening nursing duties fast, the authors note. Whether undergraduate training keeps pace is left as an open worry. The mapping gives educators and regulators a checklist for updating what nurses are expected to know.
openalex-w7213869205:
Beatriz Baltazar Clivati leads a team profiling surgically treated meningiomas at a teaching hospital in western Paraná. Their 2026 quantitative, retrospective study reviews electronic records for 110 operated patients from 2020 to 2025. Clinical, imaging, and tissue features were all recorded.

Women were more than three quarters of patients, and the mean age was the mid-fifties. Headache was the most common first symptom. Most tumours were the lowest World Health Organization grade, led by two tissue subtypes. Complete removal was achieved in under half of cases. Recurrence and death rates were low, and most patients had no serious complications. Tumour grade and removal extent decided prognosis.
openalex-w7214062705:
Sulamita dos Santos Felix leads a cross-sectional study of medical graduates from a school in inland São Paulo state. Their 2026 article profiles the graduates and records how they perceive themselves as doctors.

Graduate profile and self-perception are the two objects named in the study design. Such follow-up tells a school who its doctors became and how ready they judge themselves to be. Inland schools carry a particular stake in that question, since their graduates often serve regions far from major centres. The article adds one school's evidence to that wider debate on medical formation outside the capitals.
openalex-w7214159805:
Alana Hellen Batista de Almeida leads a report on interactive simulations in a high school chemistry class in Pau dos Ferros, Rio Grande do Norte. Their 2026 intervention came through a federal teaching initiation scholarship programme. Thirty second-year pupils at a state school took part, working on balancing chemical equations.

A dialogued lesson was followed by a gamified group dynamic with challenges of rising difficulty. The PhET virtual simulator served as the teaching bridge, cutting the abstraction of the topic. Every pupil said the activity helped fix the content, and most reported an instant rise in motivation. The simulation linked symbolic, microscopic, and macroscopic levels, grounding the law of conservation of mass.
openalex-w7214243605:
Juliana Nogueira de Paiva led a 2026 narrative review on a veterinary surgery for male cats: penectomy, removal of the penis, paired with a new urinary opening. The operation is used when a cat's urethra, the tube that carries urine, is blocked and cannot be cleared. Such blockages are common emergencies in male cats and can quickly become life threatening.

Reviewing recent studies, the authors explain that blockages have many causes, from anatomy and inflammation to diet and surroundings. Surgery suits repeated or stubborn cases, narrowed passages, and injuries. Careful preparation, good technique, and aftercare decide success, though bleeding, infection, and narrowing of the new opening can occur. Done well, the operation usually restores urine flow and prevents new blockages.
openalex-w7215101505:
Lais Lopes Melo Kummer Tonet and Maria Claudia Freire Bezerra ran a 2026 systematic review on problematic social media use and mental disorders in adolescents. Under standard review guidelines, they searched five databases for observational studies from 2010 to 2025 on young people aged ten to nineteen, covering both problem use and mental symptoms or diagnoses. Only five studies met all their criteria.

Those studies found a clear association between such use and higher rates or severity of mental symptoms in adolescents, varying by sex, platform type, and region. The science is not yet settled, the authors caution. Even so, understanding this link can help design prevention strategies and mental health interventions aimed at digital-age youth, a practical stake that earns attention before the evidence base is complete.
openalex-w7218734105:
Amanda Tebaldi dos Reis led a 2026 field study on preventing type 2 diabetes in primary care in Cachoeiro de Itapemirim, Brazil. Type 2 diabetes often runs silently for long periods, delaying diagnosis, so routine exams are the central early-detection strategy. During an educational action at a basic health unit, sixteen users answered an anonymous structured questionnaire about their knowledge and their routine exam habits.

Half the participants had not had exams in the last year, and a large share only tested when symptoms appeared, citing lack of time and the belief that exams were unnecessary. Most still recognized the exams' importance, and testing identified several chronic conditions, with diabetes and prediabetes present in about a third of participants. Health education and stronger screening in primary care are fundamental, the authors conclude, to widen early diagnosis and cut complications.
openalex-w7220747305:
Plinyo Paccioly Rodrigues Santos wrote a 2026 article setting the Ten Commandments and other biblical sayings on justice beside contemporary criminal law and criminal procedure. It does not turn sin into crime or the Bible into a state code, he states plainly. Starting from the prohibitions on killing, stealing, and false witness, and from biblical images of the just person's path, guilt, judgment, and mercy, he dialogues with several legal ideas. They are legality, culpability, punishment prevention, proportionality, presumption of innocence, and due process.

Fear of sanction can work as an initial containment mechanism in both religious and penal life, he argues, but it is not a sufficient foundation for a just community. Normative maturity means passing from external obedience to inward-held values, without letting the state confuse morality, religion, and crime. His sources join texts of the Bible and Catholic teaching with Aquinas, Augustine, and Brazilian penal law thinkers.
original-short-stories-volume-05:
Monsieur Parent lends its name and its first place to volume five of Maupassant's Original Short Stories, a set of twelve tales in English translation. The contents also list Queen Hortense, Mademoiselle Pearl, Clair de Lune, and A Queer Night in Paris — stories of obsession, vanity, and the strange turns of ordinary evenings.

Monsieur Parent himself is first seen in a Paris park, oblivious to everyone but his little son George, who piles sand into heaps and crowns them with a chestnut leaf. The setting sun gilds the chestnut trees and turns the fountains to liquid silver. Then the church clock shows Parent five minutes late, and the devoted father hurries the child home, dreading arrival after his wife — tenderness already tightening into anxiety.
paul-clifford-volume-05:
Volume 5 of Paul Clifford opens at chapter twenty-two, with Clifford riding back to Bath in a brown study. His horse stops by habit at the suburban tavern where the gang takes its news. There he learns that Tomlinson and Pepper are out on an expedition that night, taking advantage of the moon's nap.

The talk runs in cant, which the narrator translates for respectable readers. Clifford goes home to arrange the gang's departure. As the net tightens in these middle chapters, the novel moves between tavern plotting and Paul's growing wish for a different life.
pelham-volume-05:
Volume 5 of Pelham opens with the hero's pamphlet taking prodigiously, its authorship credited to a leading Opposition talent. Chapter fifty-eight then finds Pelham at Almack's, London's most exclusive assembly rooms. At the door, Lord Guloseton rages because his young companion has forgotten his ticket.

Pelham procures a pencilled note from a patroness and gets the pair admitted. Gratitude wins him a dinner invitation from the epicure lord. These chapters run on such small currencies of favour. Lytton shows how a reputation in society is built, ticket by ticket and dinner by dinner.
perry-approach-philosophy-1905:
The Approach to Philosophy, published in 1905, is Ralph Barton Perry's introduction to philosophy from the standpoint of the new realism. Perry, a Harvard philosopher and James's student and biographer, wrote it to clear the ground for beginners crowded by systems.

He distinguishes philosophy from science, religion, and common sense, and sets out the problems each method can and cannot solve. His manner is patient, exact, and quietly argumentative for the realist cause. The book served as a doorway for students in Perry's generation. It remains a clean specimen of Harvard philosophy in the age of James and Royce.
phrenology-practically-explained-illustr:
J. Millott Severn's Phrenology Practically Explained, Illustrated and Applied comes from his Brighton institution at 68 West Street. The title page lists his credentials: president for 1905 and 1906 and holder of the qualifying diplomas of the Incorporated British Phrenological Society. A table of his wares promises phrenology applied to business, education, occupations, counsel to parents, and love, courtship, and marriage.

The book opens with Phrenology Up to Date, arguing the science has advanced and shaken off its charlatan reputation. Severn defines the mental faculties and the harmony of skull, brain, and organs. It is practical head-reading for paying customers, sold with confidence.
plaw-109-1-2005: Tsunami donors get a tax timing gift from Public Law 109-1, the first law of the 109th Congress, approved on January 7, 2005. The law speeds up the income tax benefit for charitable cash gifts made for relief of victims of the Indian Ocean tsunami. A taxpayer may treat a covered cash gift made in January 2005 as if made on December 31, 2004, gaining the deduction a year sooner. The gift must aid victims of the December 26, 2004, tsunami and qualify under section 170 of the tax code.
plaw-109-10-2005: Robert T Matsui is honored by Public Law 109-10, a naming law of the 109th Congress enacted in April 2005. The United States courthouse at 501 I Street in Sacramento, California, is designated the Robert T Matsui United States Courthouse. Any reference to that courthouse in a federal law, map, regulation, document, or other record is deemed a reference to the Robert T Matsui United States Courthouse.
plaw-109-100-2005: A charity stamp stays on sale under Public Law 109-100, passed by the 109th Congress in November 2005. The law extends the special postage stamp for breast cancer research by two years. It amends section 414(h) of title 39 of the United States Code with a single swap. The year 2005 is struck and 2007 is inserted, keeping the fundraising stamp alive through the later date.
plaw-109-101-2005: Two federal buildings are named by Public Law 109-101, passed by the 109th Congress in November 2005. The federal building at 333 Mt Elliott Street in Detroit, Michigan, is designated the Rosa Parks Federal Building. The same law names a second structure. The annex on the 200 block of 3rd Street Northwest in the District of Columbia becomes the William B Bryant Annex. It is attached to the E Barrett Prettyman Federal Building and United States Courthouse. References to either building in federal records are read under its new name.
plaw-109-102-2005:
American aid and trade abroad are funded by the Foreign Operations, Export Financing, and Related Programs Appropriations Act, 2006, Public Law 109-102 of the 109th Congress. The act provides spending money for the fiscal year ending September 30, 2006. Title I covers export and investment assistance, led by the Export-Import Bank of the United States.

The bank's inspector general receives one million dollars, available until September 30, 2007. The bank's program account is then authorized to spend within its funds and borrowing power, without regard to fiscal year limits. A firm ban is attached. None of the year's money may support the export of nuclear equipment, fuel, or technology to a country outside the named class of nuclear-weapon states. The ban applies if that country has set off a nuclear explosive after the act passed.
plaw-109-103-2005:
Rivers, dams, and energy programs are funded by the Energy and Water Development Appropriations Act, 2006, Public Law 109-103 of the 109th Congress, enacted in November 2005. The act provides money for the fiscal year ending September 30, 2006. Title I funds the civil works of the Army Corps of Engineers.

Corps money runs under the Secretary of the Army and the Chief of Engineers for rivers and harbors, flood control, shore protection, storm damage cuts, and restoring water ecosystems. Investigations receive one hundred sixty-four million dollars for gathering basic information, restudying old projects, and preparing plans before building. Two directions stand out. One million dollars is set aside for planning help to Stark County, Ohio, for a watershed study. Eight million dollars must fund a full federal study of hurricane protection.
plaw-109-104-2005: An aircraft carrier's midlife overhaul is authorized by Public Law 109-104, passed by the 109th Congress in November 2005. The Secretary of the Navy may sign a contract for the nuclear refueling and complex overhaul of the USS Carl Vinson, hull number CVN-70. A limit in title 31 is set aside to do it. Work may begin in fiscal year 2006, but obligations that year may not pass eighty-nine million dollars unless a later law allows and funds more. Later payments depend on Congress providing the money each year.
plaw-109-105-2005: Stopgap funding is extended by Public Law 109-105, a joint resolution of the 109th Congress approved on November 19, 2005. It makes further continuing appropriations for fiscal year 2006, keeping the government funded while final spending bills are finished. The resolution amends the earlier stopgap, Public Law 109-77, by striking the date in its section 106(3) and inserting December 17, 2005.
plaw-109-106-2005: Flood insurance borrowing jumps under the National Flood Insurance Program Further Enhanced Borrowing Authority Act of 2005, Public Law 109-106 of the 109th Congress. The law briefly raises how much the Federal Emergency Management Agency may borrow to run the National Flood Insurance Program. In section 1309 of the National Flood Insurance Act of 1968, the ceiling moves from three and a half billion dollars to eighteen and a half billion dollars. The increase is designated as emergency spending under the budget resolution.
plaw-109-107-2005: Mayor Joseph S Daddona is remembered by Public Law 109-107, passed by the 109th Congress in November 2005. The Postal Service facility at 442 West Hamilton Street in Allentown, Pennsylvania, is designated the Mayor Joseph S Daddona Memorial Post Office. Any reference to that facility in a federal law, map, regulation, or other record is deemed a reference to the memorial post office.
plaw-109-108-2005:
Public Law 109-108, the Science, State, Justice, Commerce, and Related Agencies Appropriations Act, 2006, passed by the 109th Congress, supplies the money for the fiscal year ending September 30, 2006. It funds science programs and the Departments of State, Justice, and Commerce, together with related agencies, drawing the sums from money in the Treasury not otherwise appropriated.

Title I, the Department of Justice Appropriations Act, opens the spending. General administration receives one hundred twenty-four million, four hundred fifty-six thousand dollars, with limits written in for the Department Leadership Program, the Office of Legislative Affairs, and the Office of Public Affairs. At least five hundred thousand dollars must go to an independent privacy assessment, and a separate account covers justice information sharing technology. Later titles carry the other departments and agencies through the year.
plaw-109-109-2005: Public Law 109-109, enacted by the 109th Congress in 2005, names one postal building in Buffalo, New York. The United States Postal Service facility at 2061 South Park Avenue becomes the James T Molloy Post Office Building. Every reference to that facility in a federal law, map, regulation, document, or other record is treated as a reference to the new name. The measure is a two-section designation act and makes no other change.
plaw-109-11-2005: Public Law 109-11 is a joint resolution of the 109th Congress, approved in May 2005, that fills one seat on the Board of Regents of the Smithsonian Institution. Acting under the Revised Statutes, it appoints Shirley Ann Jackson of New York as a citizen regent, in the class other than Members of Congress. She succeeds Hanna H Gray of Illinois, whose term expired on April 13, 2005. The appointment runs six years, beginning on the later of April 14, 2005, or the resolution's enactment.
plaw-109-110-2005:
Land in northern Arizona changes hands under Public Law 109-110, the Northern Arizona Land Exchange and Verde River Basin Partnership Act of 2005. The act, passed by the 109th Congress, also creates a river partnership. Title I orders a land exchange between the Secretary of Agriculture and Yavapai Ranch Limited Partnership, defining the federal and non-federal parcels and setting how the land is managed afterward.

Title II establishes the Verde River Basin Partnership. Its sections cover the partnership's purpose, Verde River Basin studies, a final report, and a memorandum of understanding, with a closing section on the title's effect. The act pairs the single exchange with a standing framework for studying and coordinating work across the Verde River basin in Arizona.
plaw-109-111-2005:
Public Law 109-111, the Veterans' Compensation Cost-of-Living Adjustment Act of 2005, raises the monthly checks of disabled veterans and their survivors. Passed by the 109th Congress, it increases the rates of compensation for veterans with service-connected disabilities, effective December 1, 2005. It also raises the rates of dependency and indemnity compensation for survivors of certain disabled veterans.

Section 2 rewrites the dollar figures in section 1114 of title 38, step by step across the disability schedule. The lowest listed rate rises from one hundred six dollars to one hundred twelve dollars. The top listed rate in the sample rises from two thousand two hundred thirty-nine dollars to two thousand three hundred ninety-three dollars. The adjustment keeps veterans' compensation aligned with rising living costs for another year.
plaw-109-112-2005:
Public Law 109-112, the Iran Nonproliferation Amendments Act of 2005, passed by the 109th Congress, amends the Iran Nonproliferation Act of 2000 on matters tied to International Space Station payments. Its findings open the act. Congress records that the Director of Central Intelligence reported Russian entities still supplying ballistic missile goods and technical know-how to countries such as Iran, India, and China.

The findings add that Russian help sped Iran's Shahab-3 missile and Tehran's drive for self-sufficiency in missile production. They quote Defense Intelligence Agency testimony that Tehran probably could produce nuclear weapons early in the next decade. They also note Iran's failure to act under its safeguards agreement with the International Atomic Energy Agency. Those findings frame the amendments that follow on the station payments.
plaw-109-113-2005: A two-word deletion carries Public Law 109-113, the Fair Access Foster Care Act of 2005, passed by the 109th Congress. The act amends part E of title IV of the Social Security Act so that foster care maintenance payments can be made to private for-profit agencies. Section 472(b) of the act is amended by striking the word nonprofit each place it appears. With that word gone, the payment rules no longer limit the agencies to nonprofit organizations, opening foster care maintenance payments to qualifying private for-profit providers.
plaw-109-114-2005:
Public Law 109-114, the Military Quality of Life and Veterans Affairs Appropriations Act, 2006, was passed by the 109th Congress. It funds military construction, Defense Department quality of life functions, and the Department of Veterans Affairs for the fiscal year ending September 30, 2006. Title I covers the Defense Department side, starting with the Army's building program.

Military Construction, Army receives one billion, seven hundred seventy-five million, two hundred sixty thousand dollars, available until September 30, 2010. Of that, fifty million dollars is set aside for overhead cover systems supporting force protection in Iraq. The title also rescinds earlier Army construction money, including three million, forty-six thousand dollars from a 2002 law. The remaining titles fund the other services, military family housing, and veterans programs.
plaw-109-115-2005:
Public Law 109-115 was passed by the 109th Congress in November 2005. It is the appropriations act for the fiscal year ending September 30, 2006. It covers the Departments of Transportation, Treasury, and Housing and Urban Development, the Judiciary, the District of Columbia, and independent agencies. Division A carries the main spending, organized department by department.

Title I funds the Department of Transportation. The Office of the Secretary receives eighty-four million, nine hundred thousand dollars. Caps are written in for the immediate offices of the Secretary and Deputy Secretary, the General Counsel, the Under Secretary for Policy, and the Assistant Secretary for Budget and Programs. Later titles work through Treasury, housing, the courts, the District of Columbia, and the independent agencies, setting each account's amount and conditions for the year.
plaw-109-116-2005: Public Law 109-116, passed by the 109th Congress in 2005, puts a statue of Rosa Parks in the United States Capitol. The Joint Committee on the Library must, within two years, enter an agreement to obtain the statue and place it in National Statuary Hall. It also sets a general rule. No statue of an individual may be placed in the hall until ten years after that person's death. Exceptions cover the Parks statue and statues furnished by the states. Such sums as necessary are authorized.
plaw-109-117-2005: Public Law 109-117, passed by the 109th Congress in 2005, adjusts the number of free roaming horses allowed in Cape Lookout National Seashore, North Carolina. Amending Public Law 89-366, it replaces the figure of one hundred horses with a floor of not less than one hundred ten. The target population is between one hundred twenty and one hundred thirty. Removals may be carried out as part of a plan to maintain the viability of the herd. It also repeals a duplicate subsection that had crept into the older statute's text.
plaw-109-118-2005:
About ten thousand acres of Puerto Rican forest become wilderness under Public Law 109-118, the Caribbean National Forest Act of 2005, passed by the 109th Congress. The land sits in the Caribbean National Forest and Luquillo Experimental Forest. It is designated as a component of the National Wilderness Preservation System under the Wilderness Act, and is named the El Toro Wilderness.

The boundaries follow a map dated April 13, 2004, titled El Toro Proposed Wilderness Area. After enactment, the Secretary of Agriculture must prepare a boundary description and submit the map and description to the Senate Committee on Energy and Natural Resources. The naming gives the tract the Wilderness Act's protections, under which such federal land is kept free of roads and development.
plaw-109-119-2005:
Public Law 109-119 is the Angel Island Immigration Station Restoration and Preservation Act, passed by the 109th Congress in 2005. It authorizes appropriations to the Secretary of the Interior to restore the Angel Island Immigration Station in California. Its findings tell the station's story. Called the Ellis Island of the West, the National Historic Landmark processed more than one million immigrants and emigrants between 1910 and 1940.

Congress records that the station was built to enforce the Chinese Exclusion Act of 1882 and later laws that unfairly and severely restricted Asian immigration. Chinese detainees carved poems into the detention barracks walls, and more than one hundred forty poems survive. Over fifty thousand people, including thirty thousand schoolchildren, visit each year, and the act's funding aims to preserve the writings and the site for future generations.
plaw-109-12-2005: Public Law 109-12, a resolution of the 109th Congress, fills a seat on the Smithsonian Institution's Board of Regents. The seat opened when the term of Wesley S Williams Jr of the District of Columbia expired on April 13, 2005. Acting under section 5581 of the Revised Statutes, the resolution appoints Robert P Kogod, of the District of Columbia, as a citizen regent in the class other than Members of Congress. His term runs six years from the later of April 14, 2005, or the date of enactment.
plaw-109-120-2005: Public Law 109-120, the Franklin National Battlefield Study Act, passed by the 109th Congress in 2005, orders a study rather than a park. The Secretary of the Interior must conduct a special resource study of sites tied to the Battle of Franklin in Williamson County, Tennessee, covering Brentwood, Franklin, Triune, Thompson's Station, and Spring Hill. The study weighs their national significance, and whether adding them to the National Park System is suitable and feasible. It also weighs the effect on the area, and whether they could join a federal unit in Tennessee.
plaw-109-121-2005:
Public Law 109-121 is the Senator Paul Simon Water for the Poor Act of 2005, passed by the 109th Congress. It makes safe water a stated goal of American foreign aid. The act makes access to safe water and sanitation for developing countries a specific policy objective of United States foreign assistance programs.

Its findings are stark. Water-related diseases kill up to five million people a year. A child dies about every fifteen seconds for lack of safe water and sanitation. One in five children in the poorest countries dies of a preventable water-related disease. More than one billion people lack safe drinking water and nearly two billion six hundred million lack basic sanitation. The act turns those findings into a standing objective that aid programs must serve.
plaw-109-122-2005: Public Law 109-122, enacted by the 109th Congress in 2005, names one postal building in Newville, Pennsylvania. The United States Postal Service facility at 57 West Street becomes the Randall D Shughart Post Office Building. Every reference to that facility in a federal law, map, regulation, document, or other record is treated as a reference to the new name. The measure is a two-section designation act and makes no other change to postal operations or to the building itself.
plaw-109-123-2005: Public Law 109-123, enacted by the 109th Congress in 2005, names one postal building in Staten Island, New York. The United States Postal Service facility at 567 Tompkins Avenue becomes the Vincent Palladino Post Office. Every reference to that facility in a federal law, map, regulation, document, or other record is treated as a reference to the new name. The measure is a two-section designation act and changes nothing else about the facility or the service it houses.
plaw-109-124-2005: Public Law 109-124, enacted by the 109th Congress in 2005, names one postal building in Parkdale, Arkansas. The United States Postal Service facility at 208 South Main Street becomes the Willie Vaughn Post Office. Every reference to that facility in a federal law, map, regulation, document, or other record is treated as a reference to the new name. The measure is a two-section designation act; it honors its namesake on the building and leaves postal operations unchanged.
plaw-109-125-2005:
Public Law 109-125, the Department of the Interior Volunteer Recruitment Act of 2005, passed by the 109th Congress, lets the Interior Department bring in unpaid help. Its purpose is to authorize the Secretary of the Interior to recruit volunteers to assist with, or facilitate, the activities of the department's agencies and offices.

The authority covers the Bureau of Indian Affairs, the United States Geological Survey, the Bureau of Reclamation, and the Office of the Secretary. The Secretary may recruit, train, and accept volunteers without regard to the civil service classification laws, for services given without compensation. Limits apply. Volunteers may not do law enforcement, regulatory, or enforcement work. They may not take part in policymaking, and may not displace any employee. Work on private property needs the owner's consent.
plaw-109-126-2005: Public Law 109-126 was passed by the 109th Congress in 2005. It directs the Secretary of the Interior to convey land held in trust for the Paiute Indian Tribe of Utah to the City of Richfield, Utah. When both request it, the Secretary must remove the property from trust and convey it within ninety days. The sale needs a tribal resolution, the price must meet the appraised fair market value, the City pays all costs, and the proceeds go to the Tribe. If it falls through, the land returns to trust.
plaw-109-127-2005: Public Law 109-127, passed by the 109th Congress in 2005, corrects a boundary mistake at the Cibola National Wildlife Refuge in California. It revokes Public Land Order 3442 of August 21, 1964, as it applies to about one hundred forty acres in Imperial County that had been erroneously included in the refuge. Within six months, the Secretary of the Interior must resurvey the refuge's boundaries as modified. The Secretary must also publish notice, post signs marking the boundaries, and prepare and publish a map of the refuge as corrected.
plaw-109-128-2005: Public Law 109-128 is a joint resolution of the 109th Congress, approved December 18, 2005, making further continuing appropriations for fiscal year 2006. It works by amending Public Law 109-77, the earlier continuing resolution: the date in its section 106 is struck and replaced with December 31, 2005, extending stopgap funding to that date. A second section adjusts the dates in section 114(b) of the same law, adding January 1, 2006. The resolution keeps the government funded past the earlier deadline while regular appropriations remained unfinished.
plaw-109-129-2005:
Public Law 109-129, the Stem Cell Therapeutic and Research Act of 2005, passed by the 109th Congress, builds a national supply of cord blood stem cells. It provides for collecting and maintaining human cord blood stem cells for treating patients and for research, and it amends the Public Health Service Act to authorize the C.W. Bill Young Cell Transplantation Program.

Under section 2, the Secretary of Health and Human Services must enter one-time contracts with qualified cord blood banks. The contracts cover collecting and maintaining one hundred fifty thousand new units of high-quality cord blood for transplantation through the program. Banks must tissue-type, test, and freeze donated units taken with the donor's informed consent. They must encourage donation from a genetically diverse population, supply transplant centers, and release units unfit for clinical use to peer-reviewed research.
plaw-109-13-2005:
Public Law 109-13 is the Emergency Supplemental Appropriations Act for Defense, the Global War on Terror, and Tsunami Relief, 2005. Passed by the 109th Congress and approved May 11, 2005, it sends emergency money for the fiscal year ending September 30, 2005. Division A carries the spending in six titles.

Those titles fund defense-related needs, and international programs and reconstruction tied to the war on terror. They also fund domestic appropriations for the war on terror, relief for the Indian Ocean tsunami, and other emergency appropriations. A final title holds general provisions with technical corrections. Division B is a separate measure riding in the same law: the REAL ID Act of 2005. References to the act inside each division are read as pointing only to that division's provisions.
plaw-109-130-2005: Enacted on December 20, 2005, Public Law 109-130 directs the Secretary of the Interior to give Beaver County, Utah, about 200 acres of land. The acres are shown as Minersville State Park on a map dated April 30, 2004. The transfer is free, subject to existing rights, for public recreation. The county may sell part of it for at least fair market value only if the money maintains recreation facilities on the rest. If it breaks that rule, proceeds go to the United States and the rest may revert.
plaw-109-131-2005:
Three California park matters are joined in Public Law 109-131, approved December 20, 2005, in the 109th Congress. One part concerns schools serving students inside Yosemite National Park. The others adjust the Golden Gate National Recreation Area and Redwood National Park.

Title I authorizes the Secretary of the Interior to provide added funding and services to certain local school districts for students attending schools in Yosemite. It also allows park facilities outside the park boundary. Title II adds the Rancho Corral de Tierra area to Golden Gate, and Title III changes the Redwood boundary. Together the titles pair school support with two boundary changes on the California coast and in its redwood country.
plaw-109-132-2005:
The Valles Caldera Preservation Act of 2005, Public Law 109-132, amends the earlier law governing the Valles Caldera in New Mexico. Congress approved it on December 20, 2005, to improve preservation of that volcanic valley, which the federal government had bought as a special preserve.

Most of the sample deals with buying outstanding mineral interests under the land. The amendments remove the willing-seller wording, say such interests shall be bought with available funds, and set a deadline. If talks fail within 60 days, the Secretary is to acquire the interests through a declaration of taking, with any extra compensation paid from the permanent judgment appropriation.
plaw-109-133-2005: Public Law 109-133, approved December 20, 2005, adds a criminal jurisdiction section to the Act of June 7, 1924, concerning Pueblo Indian tribes in New Mexico. It covers offenses inside a grant from a prior sovereign that Congress or the Court of Private Land Claims confirmed to a Pueblo tribe. The Pueblo has jurisdiction over offenses by its members and other Indians. The United States handles major offenses by or against Indians and cases involving Indian property. New Mexico handles offenses by non-Indians outside federal jurisdiction.
plaw-109-134-2005:
Under the Naval Vessels Transfer Act of 2005, Public Law 109-134, the President may hand surplus United States naval ships to named foreign governments. Congress approved the transfers on December 20, 2005, using two routes already in law: grants under the Foreign Assistance Act and sales under the Arms Export Control Act.

By grant, Greece would receive the minehunter Pelican, Egypt the Cardinal and Raven, Pakistan the destroyer Fletcher, and Turkey the destroyer Cushing. By sale, India would receive the amphibious transport dock Trenton, Greece the Heron, and Turkey the destroyer O'Bannon. The act also says grant transfers do not count against the yearly total for excess defense articles.
plaw-109-135-2005:
Hurricane recovery through the tax code is the subject of the Gulf Opportunity Zone Act of 2005, Public Law 109-135, approved December 21, 2005. It amends the Internal Revenue Code to give tax benefits to the Gulf Opportunity Zone. It also reaches areas hit by Hurricanes Rita and Wilma, after Katrina had devastated the Gulf Coast that year.

Title I sets up benefits for the zone, expands the Hope Scholarship and Lifetime Learning credits for students there. It gives housing relief to people affected by Katrina, and extends special rules for mortgage revenue bonds. It also extends bonus depreciation dates for taxpayers hit by all three storms. Title II extends Katrina emergency tax relief to Rita and Wilma.
plaw-109-136-2005:
Congress opened the Native American Housing Enhancement Act of 2005, Public Law 109-136, with stark findings about housing on tribal lands. More than three in ten Native homes were overcrowded, a third lacked adequate solid waste systems, and about 90,000 Native families were homeless or underhoused. The poverty rate was twice the national rate.

Approved December 22, 2005, the act amends the Native American Housing Assistance and Self-Determination Act of 1996 and other laws to improve housing programs for Indians. Its findings stress the federal trust duty to tribes and the 1996 law's aim. That aim is tribal preference in housing programs. Tribes may also combine federal money with other federal and private funds.
plaw-109-137-2005: Public Law 109-137 does one short job. Approved December 22, 2005, it amends the Federal Water Pollution Control Act to keep funding authorized for Long Island Sound. In section 119(f) of that act, the year 2005 is struck wherever it appears and 2010 is inserted instead. That five-year extension kept the federal program for cleaning up and protecting Long Island Sound. The sound is the estuary between Connecticut and Long Island, New York. The extension kept the program authorized through the end of the decade. It did not let its funding authority lapse in 2005.
plaw-109-138-2005:
Landowners in two southern Oregon irrigation districts gain an early-payoff right under Public Law 109-138, the Southern Oregon Bureau of Reclamation Repayment Act of 2005, approved December 22, 2005. A landowner in the Rogue River Valley or Medford Irrigation District may repay, at any time, the construction costs assigned to that land.

Once all such costs for the owner's land are paid in full, the land leaves the ownership and full-cost pricing limits of federal reclamation law. The act leaves existing district contracts and Oregon state law rights untouched, and the Secretary must certify a full repayment when asked.
plaw-109-139-2005:
Public Law 109-139, the Predisaster Mitigation Program Reauthorization Act of 2005, keeps a federal hazard program alive for almost three more years. Approved December 22, 2005, it amends the Robert T. Stafford Disaster Relief and Emergency Assistance Act by replacing December 31, 2005 with September 30, 2008 as the end date in the predisaster hazard mitigation section.

That program helps communities reduce damage before a disaster strikes. The act also moves a deadline in the Disaster Mitigation Act of 2000, changing a study provision about cost reduction to September 30, 2007. The act is a short reauthorization, not a redesign of the program.
plaw-109-14-2005:
Highway and transit programs got a one-month bridge from Public Law 109-14, the Surface Transportation Extension Act of 2005, approved May 31, 2005. Congress had not yet finished reauthorizing the Transportation Equity Act for the 21st Century, so this act extends programs paid from the Highway Trust Fund in the meantime.

The text raises the special minimum guarantee figure to two billion one hundred million dollars and extends the off-system bridge set-aside to June 30. It sets contract authority at twenty-five billion five hundred twenty-one million dollars for October 1, 2004 through June 30, 2005. Highway safety, motor carrier safety, and transit programs are all covered by the short extension.
plaw-109-140-2005:
Several separate State Department powers are gathered in Public Law 109-140, approved December 22, 2005, under the plain heading of authorities for the department. The sample opens with a health security project in Singapore and then turns to how the department handles money paid for medical care overseas.

Section 1 authorizes United States participation in the Regional Emerging Diseases Intervention Center, known as the REDI Center, in Singapore, under a November 22, 2005 agreement between the two governments. Before a formal review, the Secretary must consult two congressional committees and report on work there concerning bioterrorism. Section 2 lets the department keep reimbursements for medical care abroad for employees and eligible family members, crediting them to the current appropriation account.
plaw-109-141-2005:
Praise and practical relief for the Coast Guard after Hurricane Katrina make up Public Law 109-141, the Coast Guard Hurricane Relief Act of 2005, approved December 22, 2005. Congress found that Katrina, which struck the Gulf Coast on August 29, 2005, was the worst natural disaster in United States history to that point.

The findings say the Coast Guard positioned aircraft, vessels, and people the day before landfall and launched rescue teams within hours. It rescued more than 33,000 people by air and water, evacuated hospitals, cleared shipping channels, replaced aids to navigation, and secured uprooted oil rigs. Beyond the thanks, the act gives temporary relief to some people affected by the storm under laws the Coast Guard administers.
plaw-109-142-2005:
Commodore John Barry is recognized as the first flag officer of the United States Navy in Public Law 109-142, a joint resolution approved December 22, 2005. Its long list of findings traces Barry, a merchant captain born in County Wexford, Ireland, from his 1776 command of the Lexington in the Continental Navy through the Trenton campaign.

Barry refused a British offer to desert, carried French gold to America on the frigate Alliance, supervised building the flagship United States, and received Commission Number 1 from President Washington. He served as senior naval officer under Washington, Adams, and Jefferson.
plaw-109-143-2005: Public Law 109-143 simply reauthorizes the Congressional Award Act. Approved December 22, 2005, it extends the act's financial operation requirements through the years 2004 to 2009. It also moves the termination date in section 108. The date goes from October 1, 2004 to October 1, 2009. A savings provision says board actions taken during the lapse after October 2004 count as if no lapse had occurred. The rest is technical: fixing doubled words, changing section to subsection in one place, and adding a comma.
plaw-109-144-2005:
Federal backing for terrorism insurance continued under Public Law 109-144, the Terrorism Risk Insurance Extension Act of 2005, approved December 22, 2005. The act extends the Terrorism Risk Insurance Act of 2002, which was due to end in 2005, through 2007.

The extension defines Program Year 4 as calendar 2006 and Program Year 5 as calendar 2007. It also rewrites the rule on mandatory availability, so that during each program year insurers must make terrorism coverage available under the program's terms. Later sections amend other defined terms, including exclusions from covered lines. The law kept a post-2001 safety net in place while Congress debated its future.
plaw-109-145-2005:
A rotating parade of presidents on dollar coins is created by Public Law 109-145, the Presidential $1 Coin Act of 2005, approved December 22, 2005. It directs the Treasury to mint coins honoring each past president and, separately, their spouses, to improve circulation of the dollar coin, and to create a new bullion coin.

Congress found that dollar coins are useful for transit, parking meters, vending machines, and small purchases, but the dollar coin introduced in 2000 was not widely wanted. Drawing on the success of the state quarters program, lawmakers expected changing, educational designs to pull the coins into daily use. A government survey cited in the findings suggested many Americans would seek a dollar coin with an attractive rotating design.
plaw-109-146-2005:
Fifty years after nine Black students entered Little Rock Central High School, Congress ordered a coin in their honor through Public Law 109-146, approved December 22, 2005. The act requires the Treasury to mint coins marking the 50th anniversary, in September 2007, of the school's desegregation in Little Rock, Arkansas.

The findings call 1957 the first major national test of the Supreme Court's Brown v. Board of Education ruling. They name the Little Rock Nine, from Ernest Green to Minnijean Brown, and note that Martin Luther King Jr. attended the first Black student's graduation there in May 1958. Congress expected the coin to draw national and international attention to that legacy.
plaw-109-147-2005: One narrow contract rule changes in Public Law 109-147, approved December 22, 2005, for land inside the Gila River Indian Community Reservation in Arizona. The act amends a 1955 law so binding arbitration clauses may be included in all contracts affecting that land, not only in leases. The wording swaps contract for lease language throughout the subsection. The change takes effect as if it had been included in Public Law 107-159. Arbitration terms agreed in such a contract can now be enforced there.
plaw-109-148-2005:
Military spending for fiscal 2006 is funded by Public Law 109-148, approved December 30, 2005. Its long title names the Department of Defense, Emergency Supplemental Appropriations to Address Hurricanes in the Gulf of Mexico, and Pandemic Influenza Act, 2006. Division A is the regular Department of Defense Appropriations Act for the year ending September 30, 2006.

Title I pays the people of the services. The sample gives twenty-eight billion one hundred ninety-one million dollars for Army military personnel, covering pay, allowances, clothing, food, travel, and cadets, plus payments to the military retirement fund. Navy personnel funding follows in the same pattern. The wider act also carries emergency money tied to the Gulf hurricanes and pandemic influenza, as its heading states.
plaw-109-149-2005:
Jobs, health, and schools share one large spending bill in Public Law 109-149, the Departments of Labor, Health and Human Services, and Education, and Related Agencies Appropriations Act, 2006. Approved December 30, 2005, it funds those departments and related agencies for the fiscal year ending September 30, 2006.

Title I covers the Department of Labor. For training and employment services under the Workforce Investment Act and related laws, the sample provides two billion six hundred fifty-two million dollars plus reimbursements. Much of that money is tied to set periods in 2006 and 2007, and eight million dollars is set aside through 2009 for building, fixing, and acquiring Job Corps centers. Later titles carry the health and education accounts in the same detailed style.
plaw-109-15-2005:
Madison's post office at 215 Martin Luther King, Jr. Boulevard in Wisconsin receives a new name from Public Law 109-15, approved June 17, 2005. The facility is designated the Robert M. La Follette, Sr. Post Office Building, honoring the Wisconsin leader whose name the building now bears.

From then on, any mention of that facility in a federal law, map, regulation, document, or other record is treated as a reference to the Robert M. La Follette, Sr. Post Office Building. Facility-naming laws like this one change no postal service or funding; they attach a person's name to a public building.
plaw-109-150-2005: College programs were kept running for three more months by Public Law 109-150, the Second Higher Education Extension Act of 2005, approved December 30, 2005. It moves the general extension date for programs under the Higher Education Act of 1965 from December 31, 2005 to March 31, 2006. Related dates move too: a special allowance limit for loans from tax-exempt issues goes to April 1, 2006. A limit tied to higher teacher loan forgiveness benefits goes to June 30, 2007. A final section protects one school's eligibility.
plaw-109-151-2005: Mental health benefits keep an equal-limits rule for one more year under Public Law 109-151, approved December 30, 2005. The law extends provisions that require parity in applying certain limits to mental health benefits. It makes the same date change in three places: the Employee Retirement Income Security Act, the Public Health Service Act, and the Internal Revenue Code. In each, December 31, 2005 becomes December 31, 2006. Without the extension, the parity provisions would have expired at the end of 2005.
plaw-109-152-2005:
Public Law 109-152, the Buffalo Soldiers Commemoration Act of 2005, authorizes a memorial in Louisiana to the Buffalo Soldiers, the Black soldiers honored by that name. Approved December 30, 2005, it lets the American Battle Monuments Commission build the memorial in or around New Orleans, on donated land or on federal land with the land manager's consent.

The commission must raise contributions, may make fundraising agreements, and must arrange permanent maintenance and have enough funds assured before building starts. An escrow account holds the money and pays construction costs, then passes what remains to the group maintaining the memorial.
plaw-109-153-2005: Philadelphia's Benjamin Franklin National Memorial gets federal help from Public Law 109-153, approved December 30, 2005, ahead of the 300th anniversary of Franklin's birth. The Secretary of the Interior may grant money to the Franklin Institute to rehabilitate the memorial, including the Franklin statue. The money may also develop an exhibit about Franklin for a museum next to the memorial. Ten million dollars is authorized, in plain terms, and the Institute must match whatever federal money it receives. The law is a single grant program, not a broader Franklin program.
plaw-109-154-2005:
Young conservation workers are aimed at forest health work by Public Law 109-154, the Public Lands Corps Healthy Forests Restoration Act of 2005, approved December 30, 2005. It amends the Public Lands Corps Act of 1993 so corps projects can serve the purposes of the Healthy Forests Restoration Act of 2003.

The key new term is priority project. Such a project, done on eligible service lands, can cut wildfire risk to a town, a water supply, or at-risk federal land. It can also protect a watershed, fight insect and disease damage, or help threatened species, diversity, and forest growth. Carbon storage is named among the gains such work should support.
plaw-109-155-2005:
Space policy and spending directions for NASA fill Public Law 109-155, the National Aeronautics and Space Administration Authorization Act of 2005, approved December 30, 2005. An authorization act does not itself spend money; it sets the programs and amounts Congress allows for later funding bills.

Title I covers responsibilities, reports, cost controls, prize authority, safety, lessons learned, and whistleblower protection. Title II authorizes money for fiscal years 2007 and 2008, treats research on the International Space Station, and sets a station cost cap. A science title follows in the table of contents. The structure shows Congress steering the agency's plans, budgets, and safety culture in one package.
plaw-109-156-2005: Three unrelated items ride together in Public Law 109-156, the Delaware Water Gap National Recreation Area Improvement Act, approved December 30, 2005. First, the Secretary of the Interior may give Columbia Gas Transmission an easement to widen its natural gas pipeline number 1278. The line runs inside the recreation area in Pennsylvania. It may grow from 14 inches to no more than 20 inches across. Second, certain commercial vehicles may keep using Route 209 within the recreation area. Third, the National Park System Advisory Board gets a new end date of January 1, 2007.
plaw-109-157-2005:
Fractionated Indian land, split among many owners over generations, is the problem behind Public Law 109-157, the Indian Land Probate Reform Technical Corrections Act of 2005, approved December 30, 2005. It amends the Indian Land Consolidation Act on probate reform. 

Under the rewritten section, a tribe may buy part or all interests in trust or restricted land inside its reservation, or land under its jurisdiction, at not less than fair market value. Buying every interest in a tract needs consent from owners of at least half the undivided interest, counting interests the tribe itself owns.
plaw-109-158-2005: A single date moves in Public Law 109-158, approved December 30, 2005, under a section headed Settlement of Tribal Claims. It amends Public Law 107-153 by striking December 31, 1999 and inserting December 31, 2000. That one-year shift is the whole law. The sample gives no reason for the change and names no tribe, claim, or amount. Readers should treat the entry as exactly what it is. It is a one-line correction to a deadline or cutoff date in an earlier tribal claims law. The change extends whatever that date governed by one year.
plaw-109-159-2005:
Surplus American military gear stored for a Korean war reserve may go to South Korea under Public Law 109-159, approved December 30, 2005. It authorizes the President to transfer items from the War Reserves Stockpile for Allies, Korea, on terms the President sets, despite a general rule in the Foreign Assistance Act.

Covered items must be obsolete or surplus Defense Department stock meant as reserve stocks for the Republic of Korea and located in Korea or Japan. The list includes tanks, trucks, artillery, mortars, bombs, repair parts, and barrier material. Korea must give concessions worth at least fair market value, reduced by American savings from avoiding removal or disposal costs. No transfer may occur after three years.
plaw-109-16-2005: Brownsville, Texas, has its federal courthouse named by Public Law 109-16, approved June 29, 2005. The courthouse at the corner of Seventh Street and East Jackson Street is designated the Reynaldo G. Garza and Filemon B. Vela United States Courthouse, joining two names on one building. After the naming, any reference to that courthouse in a federal law, map, regulation, document, or other record counts as a reference to the building under its full new name. The act does nothing else; it neither builds nor funds the courthouse.
plaw-109-160-2005:
Expiring surveillance powers got a short reprieve from Public Law 109-160, approved December 30, 2005, the day before they were to lapse. It amends section 224(a) of the USA PATRIOT Act, striking December 31, 2005 and inserting February 3, 2006 as the sunset date. 

The act's stated subject also covers the lone wolf provision of the Intelligence Reform and Terrorism Prevention Act of 2004. Readers should note the enrolled text in the sample sets February 3, 2006, even though the catalog title describes a longer extension. The law bought Congress about five more weeks to debate renewal. It was one of several short extensions passed that winter.
plaw-109-17-2005: Farm credit mediation in the states is renewed by Public Law 109-17, approved June 29, 2005, in a single sentence. It amends the Agricultural Credit Act of 1987 to reauthorize state mediation programs, the services that help farmers and lenders work out credit disputes without going straight to court or foreclosure. The whole change is one date: in section 506 of the 1987 act, the year 2005 is struck and 2010 is inserted. That kept the federal support for state farm mediation programs authorized for five more years.
plaw-109-18-2005:
Getting lost in the health care system is the problem addressed by Public Law 109-18, the Patient Navigator Outreach and Chronic Disease Prevention Act of 2005, approved June 29, 2005. It amends the Public Health Service Act to authorize a demonstration grant program for patient navigator services, meant to cut barriers and improve health outcomes.

Grants, run through the Health Resources and Services Administration, pay eligible groups to recruit, train, and employ navigators who know their own communities well. Navigators act as contacts for patients, coordinate care and referrals, and help people seeking prevention or early detection services, or dealing with a symptom or abnormal finding after screening. The Indian Health Service, National Cancer Institute, and rural health office help design and judge the programs.
plaw-109-19-2005: Welfare aid was continued, briefly, by Public Law 109-19, the TANF Extension Act of 2005, approved July 1, 2005. It reauthorizes the Temporary Assistance for Needy Families block grant only through September 30, 2005. Activities under the Social Security Act continue as authorized for fiscal 2004, with payments through the fourth quarter at fiscal 2004 levels. A conforming change moves a June 30 date to September 30. The national random sample study of child welfare and child welfare waiver authority are extended on the same terms.
plaw-109-2-2005:
Big lawsuits brought for many people at once are reshaped by Public Law 109-2, the Class Action Fairness Act of 2005, approved February 18, 2005. It changes the procedures for interstate class actions, saying its aim is fairer outcomes for both class members and defendants.

Congress found class actions valuable when they fairly combine many similar claims into one case. The act then adds a consumer class action bill of rights and better procedures, gives federal district courts jurisdiction over interstate class actions, and allows removal of such cases into federal court. It also orders a report on class action settlements and enacts Judicial Conference recommendations, with rulemaking power for the Supreme Court and the Judicial Conference.
plaw-109-20-2005: Part II of the 2005 surface transportation extensions is Public Law 109-20, approved July 1, 2005, after Part I in this slice ran out. It again extends highway, safety, transit, and other Highway Trust Fund programs while a full reauthorization of the Transportation Equity Act for the 21st Century was pending. The minimum guarantee figure rises to two billion two hundred forty million dollars. The bridge set-aside runs to July 19. Contract authority reaches twenty-seven billion two hundred twenty-three million dollars for the period through July 19, 2005.
plaw-109-21-2005:
Unsolicited advertising faxes are the target of Public Law 109-21, the Junk Fax Prevention Act of 2005, approved July 9, 2005. It rewrites section 227 of the Communications Act of 1934, the federal law against junk faxes.

The ban bars sending an unsolicited advertisement to a fax machine unless the sender has an established business relationship with the recipient. The sender must also have gotten the fax number in allowed ways. The recipient may have given it voluntarily within that relationship. Or it may be listed in a directory, advertisement, or website for public distribution. Special wording covers relationships that already existed before this act, where the sender already held the number.
plaw-109-22-2005: Temecula, California, is the town in Public Law 109-22, approved July 12, 2005, an early naming act in this slice. The Postal Service facility at 30777 Rancho California Road is designated the Dalip Singh Saund Post Office Building. Section 2 then provides the usual rule for such laws. A reference in a United States law, map, regulation, document, paper, or other record to that facility is deemed a reference to the Dalip Singh Saund Post Office Building. The text names the honoree and address, without findings.
plaw-109-23-2005:
Los Angeles is the city in Public Law 109-23, approved July 12, 2005, which names a post office building for a soldier by rank and name. The facility at 8200 South Vermont Avenue is designated the Sergeant First Class John Marshall Post Office Building. 

The references section then applies the standard rule. Any mention of that facility in a federal law, map, regulation, document, paper, or other record counts as a reference to the Sergeant First Class John Marshall Post Office Building. The text contains the designation alone, with no service record for Marshall.
plaw-109-24-2005: Altamonte Springs, Florida, appears in Public Law 109-24, approved July 12, 2005, the same day as several other naming acts in this slice. The facility at 321 Montgomery Road is designated the Arthur Stacey Mastrapa Post Office Building. Under section 2, any reference in a United States law, map, regulation, document, paper, or other record to that facility is deemed a reference to the Arthur Stacey Mastrapa Post Office Building. The act is honorary, states no facts about Mastrapa, and changes no postal services in Altamonte Springs.
plaw-109-25-2005: West Washington Boulevard in Los Angeles is the address in Public Law 109-25, approved July 12, 2005. The Postal Service facility at 4960 West Washington Boulevard is designated the Ray Charles Post Office Building. Section 2 applies the standing rule for naming acts. References to that facility in federal laws, maps, regulations, documents, papers, or other records are deemed references to the Ray Charles Post Office Building. The enrolled text names Charles and the building only; it offers no account of his music or life.
plaw-109-26-2005: Hamden, Connecticut, receives its designation in Public Law 109-26, approved July 12, 2005, an early entry in this slice's long naming series. The Postal Service facility at 40 Putnam Avenue shall be known as the Linda White-Epps Post Office, using the plain post office form. Its references section deems mentions of the facility in United States laws, maps, regulations, documents, papers, or other records to be references to the Linda White-Epps Post Office. No findings or biography accompany the honor.
plaw-109-27-2005: Goliad, Texas, is the town in Public Law 109-27, approved July 12, 2005. The Postal Service facility at 151 West End Street is designated the Judge Emilio Vargas Post Office Building, with the title Judge carried in the official name. References to that facility in any United States law, map, regulation, document, paper, or other record are then deemed references to the Judge Emilio Vargas Post Office Building. The act is a standard naming law; the sample gives no account of Vargas's time on the bench.
plaw-109-28-2005: Vinita, Oklahoma, is the place in Public Law 109-28, approved July 12, 2005, in the first big naming batch of this slice. The facility at 120 East Illinois Avenue is designated the Francis C. Goodpaster Post Office Building. Section 2 then provides the rule. Any reference in a law, map, regulation, document, paper, or other record of the United States to that facility shall be deemed a reference to the Francis C. Goodpaster Post Office Building. The act does nothing beyond the naming and that rule.
plaw-109-29-2005: Sparks, Nevada, honors its mayor in the name set by Public Law 109-29, approved July 12, 2005. The facility at 750 4th Street is designated the Mayor Tony Armstrong Memorial Post Office, with both the office and the word Memorial in the official name. References to that facility in United States laws, maps, regulations, documents, papers, or other records are deemed references to the Mayor Tony Armstrong Memorial Post Office. The two-section act states the honor and the reference rule, and nothing else.
plaw-109-3-2005:
One family's court fight became a federal law in Public Law 109-3, approved March 21, 2005, for the relief of the parents of Theresa Marie Schiavo. It gives the federal district court for the Middle District of Florida power to hear a suit. The suit concerns alleged violations of Schiavo's federal rights. Those rights involve withholding or withdrawing food, fluids, or medical treatment needed to sustain her life.

Either parent has standing to sue anyone who was a party to the state court case, or who might act under a state order allowing that withholding. The federal court must decide the claim fresh, ignoring earlier state rulings, without delay or waiting for state remedies to end. After deciding, it may grant declaratory and injunctive relief to protect the rights at issue.
plaw-109-30-2005: Springfield, Virginia, is the town in Public Law 109-30, approved July 12, 2005. The Postal Service facility at 6200 Rolling Road is designated the Captain Mark Stubenhofer Post Office Building, rank included at the front of the name. References in federal laws, maps, regulations, documents, papers, or other records to that facility are deemed references to the Captain Mark Stubenhofer Post Office Building. The act passed the House in April 2005 and the Senate in June, and its text is limited to the designation and references sections.
plaw-109-31-2005: Overland Park, Kansas, appears in Public Law 109-31, approved July 12, 2005, designating the facility at 12433 Antioch Road as the Ed Eilert Post Office Building. The name is one of the shortest in this slice's naming run. Section 2 deems any reference in a United States law, map, regulation, document, paper, or other record to that Antioch Road facility a reference to the Ed Eilert Post Office Building. The enrolled text gives the designation and that rule only.
plaw-109-32-2005: New Bedford, Massachusetts, is the city in Public Law 109-32, approved July 12, 2005. Its facility at 695 Pleasant Street is designated the Honorable Judge George N. Leighton Post Office Building, one of the longest honorific names in this batch, with Honorable and Judge both included. References to the facility in federal laws, maps, regulations, documents, papers, or other records are deemed references to the building by that full name. The act is the usual designation and references pair.
plaw-109-33-2005: Belhaven, North Carolina, a coastal town, is named in Public Law 109-33, approved July 12, 2005. The Postal Service facility at 614 West Old County Road is designated the Floyd Lupton Post Office, in the short plain form without Building. Section 2 deems any reference to that facility in a federal law, map, regulation, document, paper, or other record a reference to the Floyd Lupton Post Office. The act passed the House in June 2005 and the Senate later that month.
plaw-109-34-2005: Rules for satellite firms are eased by Public Law 109-34, approved July 12, 2005. It amends the Communications Satellite Act of 1962 on INTELSAT, the former satellite body. It strikes section 623, the criteria for INTELSAT separated entities, and edits the interest rules for officers, managers, or directors of such firms. One rewritten section pledges that the United States shall preserve the space segment capacity of the GMDSS. That system is the maritime distress and safety system. The pledge changes neither its legal status nor competition for its services. A report on satellite service follows.
plaw-109-35-2005: Part III of the 2005 highway extensions, Public Law 109-35, approved July 20, 2005, may be the shortest bridge in this slice: it moves several dates by just two days. It again extends highway, safety, transit, and Highway Trust Fund programs pending a full reauthorization law. The minimum guarantee rises slightly, to two billion two hundred sixty-eight million dollars. The bridge set-aside and other dates move from July 19 to July 21, 2005, and contract authority becomes twenty-seven billion five hundred sixty-three million dollars through July 21.
plaw-109-36-2005: Public Law 109-36, passed by the 109th Congress in 2005, gives a new name to one post office in Texas. It names the post office at 301 South Heatherwilde Boulevard in Pflugerville as the Sergeant Byron W. Norwood Post Office Building. Any mention of that site in a federal law, map, rule, or record is to use the new name.
plaw-109-37-2005:
Highway and transit programs get a short new lease on life in Public Law 109-37 of 2005. The 109th Congress called it the Surface Transportation Extension Act of 2005, Part IV. It keeps the programs going while a full new transport law is still pending.

The act extends highway, highway safety, truck safety, and transit programs paid from the Highway Trust Fund. It adjusts the sums states are sure to get and raises the off-system bridge set-aside date to July 27. It also sets contract authority at about 27.97 billion dollars for the span from October 1, 2004, through July 27, 2005. The sample cuts off partway through the limits on spending.
plaw-109-38-2005: Four top staff of one Capitol office gain a chance at one more term under Public Law 109-38 of 2005. That body is the Office of Compliance, which serves Congress. The act sets aside the term limits in the Congressional Accountability Act of 1995 for the people then in post. The Executive Director, the Deputy Executive Directors, and the General Counsel may each serve one added term.
plaw-109-39-2005: Trade curbs on Burma are kept alive by Public Law 109-39, a joint resolution of the 109th Congress from 2005. In it, Congress approves the renewal of the import limits set in section 3(a)(1) of the Burmese Freedom and Democracy Act of 2003. That one approval is the whole act. It was signed into law on July 27, 2005.
plaw-109-4-2005:
Welfare aid gets a few more months under Public Law 109-4, the Welfare Reform Extension Act of 2005. The 109th Congress kept the Temporary Assistance for Needy Families block grant alive through June 30, 2005.

Under the act, aid work runs in the way set for fiscal year 2004, at the same payment levels. Funds are drawn from the Treasury for that end. The act also shifts a date in the Social Security Act from March 31 to June 30. It likewise extends a national study of child welfare and the waiver power tied to it, again through June 30, 2005.
plaw-109-40-2005:
Road and transit programs gain three more days in Public Law 109-40 of 2005. Called the Surface Transportation Extension Act of 2005, Part V, it follows Part IV in a chain of short extensions.
