The three games used their special points very differently. Save and travel points shifted from spread-out support toward late-game travel efficiency, while bosses stayed off to the side everywhere. Bao suggests network measures give designers a concrete way to judge and tune map layouts.
plos-pone-0354805:
Usama and colleagues, in a 2026 computer study, test whether chemicals made by a salt-loving bacterium could help maize grow under drought. Maize feeds much of the world, and dry spells cut its growth badly. Some soil bacteria help plants cope, but how their chemicals act inside the plant is poorly mapped.

The team docked bacterial chemicals, in simulation, into a maize enzyme that helps manage plant growth signals. Two bacterial compounds gripped the enzyme more tightly than two well-known plant hormones used as yardsticks. A long motion simulation, lasting two hundred nanoseconds of model time, showed the pairings stayed stable, held together by steady bonds. The authors are clear that this is all in silico, meaning done on a computer. The results nominate these bacterial chemicals for greenhouse and field tests, which alone can show whether they truly help crops in dry soil.
plos-pone-0354905:
Kyla Lee, Anna Gagliardi, and colleagues present in 2026 a study plan on how Korean immigrants in Canada share health decisions with family doctors. Earlier work on East Asian patients gave mixed results and rarely sampled with this group in mind. The planned interviews will be held in Korean or English, as each person prefers.

Twelve adults who moved under the economic stream and who see one doctor regularly will take part. Analysis will look for shared themes about care and about sharing choices, reported only in grouped, unnamed form. Recruitment was still open, so the document describes aims and methods rather than findings.
plos-pone-0355105:
Duyen Nguyen, Taehyeong Kim, and Junyoung Park combine in 2026 live experiments and computer simulation on how groups of mice escape under stress. Electric stimulus strength, an obstacle near the exit, guide walls at several angles, and group size were all varied. Escape time, speed, and spacing between mice were measured, and a validated agent model replayed and widened the conditions.

Obstacles and walls helped when groups were dense and stimulus was moderate, smoothing flow and cutting escape time, but hindered when groups were sparse or stimulus was extreme. Wide enough spacing between mice kept flow stable and prevented clogging at the narrow exit. The joined method validates well.
plos-pone-0355205:
Zhoujun Zhu and co-authors study in 2026 the pollen of a woody oil tree valued in Guizhou, China, building reliable tests for whether its pollen is alive and can sprout. Fruit yield and oil quality depend on good pollination, yet pollen testing for this tree lagged. Microscope work described pollen shape across family lines, and nine staining methods plus sprouting recipes were compared across two breeding lines.

Pollen kept a shared genus shape with clear variety between lines. Two stains separated living from dead grains best, and each line had its own best sprouting recipe in a growth mix. A two tier plan is proposed: one stain for precise lab work, another for quick field checks.
plos-pone-0355305:
Yinda Long and co-authors build in 2026 a physics based model that forecasts how long a phone battery will last. They used an open source phone as their test case and built the model in parts, covering the screen, chip, radio, and other uses. Heat effects on the battery were built in as well.

Across six common patterns of use, predicted run time ranged from about an hour under heavy load to more than a day when light. Chip use and room temperature drove fast drain most. Simple steps such as easing workload and screen use stretched heavy use time a lot in the model.
plos-pone-0355405:
Emily Zabor, Yağmur Seda Yeşiltaş, and Arun Singh ask how often doctors should scan the livers of patients treated for melanoma inside the eye, in this 2026 study. This cancer, uveal melanoma, tends to spread first to the liver, and catching spread early matters. At their center, a gene test sorts patients into low and high risk, with higher-risk patients scanned more often or with stronger imaging. The team modeled schedules from monthly to yearly against real outcomes.

Among roughly three hundred fifty patients, about one in five developed spread during follow-up. The analysis found yearly scans optimal for low-risk patients and scans every nine months optimal for high-risk patients, balancing detection delay against scan burden. Longer gaps were tied to larger lesions at detection. The authors offer the risk-tailored schedule as a framework for designing surveillance that is neither lax nor wasteful.
plos-pone-0355505:
Tahir Hussain and colleagues derive new exact solutions of Einstein's equations for cylinder-shaped universes filled with an imperfect, uneven fluid. Exact solutions are rare treasures in relativity because the equations resist direct solving. The team uses scaling symmetries of different sizes to organize the search. Then it reads off the matter content each geometry demands. It checks which solutions are empty. It checks which carry flowing matter, and which ripple like waves.

The family they build connects to classic models, including cylindrical waves, older static cylinders, and expanding models of Kasner type. Hussain and colleagues present the catalog as raw material for testing ideas about cosmic strings, gravitational waves, and how lopsided matter shapes spacetime over time.
plos-pone-0355605:
Ali Yalçın and co-authors address in 2026 how shoulder motion should be reported for children born with brachial plexus injury. Clinicians use a set of standard arm movements, yet labs describe the joint angles in different ways. The team rechecked motion sensor data from the uninjured arms of ten children.

Three common ways of ordering angle calculations were compared for jumps and for match with expected clinical values. One order caused locking problems in several movements, and no single order suited every movement best. The authors argue for movement specific reporting rules, so results from different studies can be compared with more trust.
plos-pone-0356005:
Yi Li and colleagues tested a simple blood-count score for predicting outcomes in advanced throat cancer behind the nose. Chemoradiation often suppresses blood cell production, but the combined effect across cell types was unclear. Their 2026 study scored several hundred patients by how many of three blood lines fell below normal.

Higher scores tracked with clearly worse survival and more spread of disease during about six years of follow-up. Patients with all three lines low faced far higher risks of death and distant spread than those with none low. The score added modest sorting power on its own. Li and colleagues suggest it can sit beside standard staging when judging a patient's risk.
plos-pone-0356105:
Saba Desta Tessema and six colleagues test a color-coded early warning chart for mothers in Ethiopian hospitals, in this 2026 quasi-experimental study. Most maternal deaths in Ethiopia are preventable if deterioration is caught early, yet warning charts are used inconsistently. More than eleven hundred obstetric inpatients at four public hospitals were split between two kinds of monitoring. One group used the chart, which grades vital signs, consciousness, bleeding, and other signs green, yellow, or red. The other received standard monitoring.

Charted patients triggered alerts nearly five hours sooner on average, were seen by a physician faster, and received interventions faster. They needed fewer ultrasound scans, left hospital about half a day earlier, and faced a meaningfully lower risk of severe maternal outcomes. The authors support wider use while calling for larger multi-cluster trials to confirm the effect across settings and risk groups.
plos-pone-0356205:
Ai Cui and colleagues lay out a trial plan, published in 2026, for testing whether a lung-scarring drug can prevent radiation harm in lung cancer care. Patients with advanced lung tumors that cannot be removed often receive combined drug treatment and radiation, and the radiation itself can inflame and scar the lungs. The drug nintedanib already treats one scarring lung disease, so the team asks whether it can also protect these patients.

Under the plan, a small group of patients at three centers in China will be split by chance. Half will take the drug around their radiation course. Half will receive standard care alone. Doctors will track lung injury, safety, and quality of life. Because no results exist yet, the value here is the careful design future findings will rest on.
plos-pone-0356305: Fielder and six co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE review on vaping during pregnancy. As a scoping review, it maps studies in both people and animals. The outcomes cover the mother, the unborn child, and the infant after birth. Pregnant people get mixed messages about vaping, so a clear map of what is known and unknown can guide honest advice.
plos-pone-0356505:
Likai Wu, Meina Zhang, and Wenzhe Wang combined two control ideas to make a cheap four-legged robot walk well. The first idea is biological rhythm generators that set each leg's beat. The second is a team of learning agents, one per leg, that nudge the rhythm to fit the ground. Their 2026 framework deliberately keeps the robot's onboard brain tiny. All four legs share one small policy network, run from simple body sensors.

In simulation and on a real low-cost robot, the system crossed obstacles, ramps, stairs, and rough ground. It did so more stably and efficiently than baseline controllers. Cameras, torque sensors, and motion capture stayed in the lab, not on the robot. The design points toward inspection and rescue robots that schools and small firms can actually afford.
plos-pone-0356605:
Jason Johnson-Peretz and a large team report what patients and clinic staff thought of a flexible HIV care model in rural Kenya and Uganda. Their 2026 paper draws on the SEARCH trial, which served people whose work and travel make regular clinic visits hard to keep. The model let patients choose longer refill gaps, community pickup, and help when moving between clinics.

Interviews with patients and providers found every option welcome, with a discreet travel pack of medicine and supplies liked most. Longer gaps freed patients to focus on taking doses rather than chasing appointments. Poverty and hunger still blocked steady treatment, so participants asked for wider services, food or job help, and stronger supply chains.
plos-pone-0356905:
You Tang and coauthors published a 2026 proteomics study in PLOS ONE on a tobacco relative used to manufacture proteins in leaves, called plant molecular farming. Yields often disappoint because the plant's own protein-cutting enzymes chew up the product. Using deep protein measurement, they separated three stresses leaves face: infiltration, the bacteria delivering genes, and the burden of making a foreign protein.

Even plain buffer infiltration, usually treated as a neutral control, triggered cell-wall remodeling and oxidative stress on its own. Filtering that background out revealed a core bacterial response marked by a growth-versus-defense trade-off. Making a virus capsid precursor provoked a stronger, distinct wave of protein-cutting enzymes than making a simple glowing marker protein did. They also expanded the plant's known enzyme catalog to about fifteen hundred entries The cargo itself shapes the plant's defenses, they conclude, so strategies should be tuned per product.
plos-pone-0357005:
Md Ahosanul Haque Shahid and colleagues isolate and sequence the bacterium behind fowl cholera, a major killer of poultry, from layer birds. Knowing the local strain's resistance pattern and danger genes guides control. From dozens of suspect field samples the team confirmed a small set of type A isolates. Culture and gene tests did the confirming. The isolates then faced a panel of common antibiotics. One representative genome was sequenced in full.

The sequenced genome held the usual two thousand or so genes. It also held a set tied to sticking to hosts and dodging immunity. A predictor flagged possible risk to people. Isolates resisted several front-line drugs yet stayed sensitive to a handful of others, including common fluoroquinolones. Shahid and colleagues offer the profile for surveillance and vaccine planning.
plos-pone-0357205:
Irtaza Tahir and colleagues publish the plan for a systematic review asking whether adding immune therapy to radiation before surgery raises danger for patients with removable solid tumors. The combination is spreading fast in cancer care, and harm data are scattered across small studies. Their protocol searches major databases, trial registries, and conference records from the past decade for studies reporting severe side effects, treatment stops, deaths, and surgical complications.

Where studies allow, results will be pooled with random-effects models and split by tumor site and radiation style. The entry here is the protocol itself: no results yet, but a fixed, public recipe meant to keep the later review honest. Tahir and colleagues aim to give surgical teams a clear harm ledger for a popular new combination.
plos-pone-0357405:
Md Sadiq Iqbal and Mohammod Abul Kashem published a 2026 paper in PLOS ONE arguing that asking whether a text is human or machine-written is the wrong question. Forensics wants to know which model wrote it; universities want to know whether a human collaborated. Their system, SiBot, treats detection as source attribution across many classes. They built and released two benchmark corpora. One spans more than twenty AI sources; another models pure and human-AI hybrid writing.

On the harder many-source corpus, the best classical combination reached only middling accuracy, showing how tough attribution is. On the ten-class corpus, their hybrid design, blending word-frequency features with a transformer's contextual embeddings, scored above ninety percent, beating the strongest transformer alone by a wide margin. The framework is publicly deployed. Detectors, they say, must move from binary verdicts to graded, source-aware answers among hybrid drafts.
plos-pone-0357605: Danilovich and six co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE trial on walking as a cure for frailty in older adults. One group walked at a brisk pace; the other walked at a casual pace. Whole clusters of people were assigned together in this randomized trial. If brisk walking reverses frailty better, a cheap daily habit could help older adults stay strong and independent longer.
plos-pone-0357805:
Jessica Chen and colleagues published a 2026 qualitative study in PLOS ONE on what happened to people displaced by the huge 2022 floods in Lismore, in regional Australia. The study draws on online news coverage over the following two years. Rather than interviewing survivors, the team analyzed seventy-one news articles and then checked how closely the coverage matched the wider research literature on flood displacement and health.

The reporting tied displacement to trauma, distress, and a gnawing feeling of being in limbo while housing stayed unresolved. Articles traced families through emergency shelters, short-term fixes, and the hunt for long-term homes, including informal arrangements that official systems never record, and showed how each stage shaped health. Yet the most severely affected groups received little attention. The authors conclude the media captured the broad harm accurately but underplayed the worst cases, which matters because coverage steers where help and sympathy flow.
plos-pone-0357905:
Vigneswaran Ravi and three colleagues describe a computer model of the Hall effect in a 2026 PLOS ONE article. The Hall effect is the small voltage that appears across a conductor in a magnetic field, and it sits at the heart of many magnetic sensors. Exact formulas struggle once a device's shape, material, and metal contacts all matter at once, which is where their model comes in.

Working in the free program FreeFEM++, they simulate the effect with the finite element method and check the output against known analytical solutions. They then show how physical defects, which formulas cannot handle, change the readings, using a cross shaped graphene sensor as the worked example. The shared script doubles as a teaching aid and a research tool.
plos-pone-0358705:
Tekle Gebremeskel Ygzaw leads a team of eight following children treated for severe pneumonia in Tigray, Ethiopia, reported in PLOS ONE in 2026. Pneumonia remains one of the biggest killers of young children, and Ethiopia carries a heavy share of that burden. Knowing how long recovery takes, and what slows it, helps hospitals plan beds and follow up care. Prospective local data from Tigray's public hospitals were lacking.

The team tracked just over three hundred admitted children across two months, recording when each recovered. About eighty-five percent recovered, with the typical child well again in five days. Statistical models then separated the factors tied to faster or slower recovery from background noise. Findings like these let regional clinicians counsel families realistically and flag the children who need closer watching during admission.
plos-pone-0359105: Heron and seven co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE study on a urine test tied to a risky pregnancy condition. Preeclampsia raises blood pressure and can harm mother and baby. The team analyzed bits of DNA in urine that come from kidney cells. If kidney DNA in urine flags the condition early, a simple sample could help doctors watch high-risk pregnancies more closely.
plos-pone-0359205: Islam and six co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE study on what people eat in Bangladesh at each stage of life. They mapped food consumption patterns from childhood to old age. They also checked whether diets at each stage supply enough nutrients. Gaps found at a given age can guide food aid and advice aimed at that stage rather than at everyone at once.
plos-pone-0359405:
Zihui Liu and eight colleagues wrote this 2026 PLOS ONE research article on esophageal cancer. The cancer studied is squamous cell carcinoma of the food pipe, tested in cell cultures and in TE-1 xenografts, tumors grown in animals. The treatment under study is Shenling Qige Granules, a traditional Chinese medicine preparation.

As the title states, the granules inhibit the cancer's progression in these models by acting on a chain of molecular signals that runs from DCN through TGF-β to Smad. Showing a mechanism, not just an effect, helps judge whether a traditional remedy deserves clinical testing. Researchers working where traditional and modern cancer medicine meet are the audience.
plos-pone-0360005:
Tharun Tom Oommen and a large clinical team studied in 2026 a blood signal that may help predict outcomes for patients hospitalized with cirrhosis, advanced scarring of the liver. The signal is interleukin-6, a messenger of inflammation, measured on admission. The authors describe it as a time limited and cause dependent prognostic signal: it carries information about the near future, and its meaning shifts with what caused the liver disease.

Their cohort study analyzes the data two ways, with standard frequentist statistics and with Bayesian methods that weigh prior knowledge openly. A cheap admission blood test that sharpens prognosis could help doctors triage scarce intensive care and speak more honestly with families about what lies ahead.
pmc-10652705:
A European Food Safety Authority panel reviews whether a smoke flavoring product, marketed as SmokEz C-10, should keep its authorization. The opinion came out in 2023. The product is made by burning a mix of hardwoods, including maple, oak, and hickory, and collecting the smoke compounds.

The panel examined the product's chemistry, how much people would eat, and its genetic toxicity. Five components raised a potential concern for damaging DNA. Two named compounds showed this concern in living animals after oral intake, at exposures above the safety threshold for such substances. The unidentified part of the mixture raised a further concern. The panel concluded that the product raises concern with respect to genotoxicity, which weighs against renewal of its authorization.
pmc-10655305:
Dongqing Yan and co-authors measure the heart disease burden from meat-heavy diets in a 2023 paper. Red and processed meat intake has been tied to ischemic heart disease. The team used Global Burden of Disease 2019 data for 204 countries and territories.

They counted deaths and lost healthy years tied to high meat intake from 1990 to 2019. In 2019, high red meat intake accounted for about 351,200 deaths, and processed meat for about 171,700. Death counts rose over time even as age-adjusted rates fell. China recorded the highest number of red meat-linked deaths. Results are split by age, sex, and development level.
pmc-10656805:
Adam Anz and colleagues wrap knee ligament grafts in birth-membrane collagen and inject them with the patient's marrow concentrate, testing whether biology can speed graft maturation, in this trial from twenty twenty-three. Forty patients aged eighteen to thirty-five, half with tendon-bone grafts and half with hamstring grafts, were split between standard reconstruction and the augmented version.

Over twelve months of MRI tracking and two years of follow-up, the honest answer was no difference. Graft signal and volume, the maturation readouts, matched controls at every time point for both graft types. Patient-reported pain and function scores matched too. The one clear finding was safety: no adverse events in either group. The authors report the augmentation as a safe dead end, sparing future trials a detour, at least at this dose and design.
pmc-10670105:
Yang Jiang, Wei Zhang, Shihao Huang, and a wider team wrote this research paper, published in 2023. It builds a prediction tool, from MRI scans, for warning which patients will suffer a fresh spine fracture after a procedure that props up a collapsed vertebra.

New fractures after vertebral augmentation are common and costly for patients with brittle bones. The team mined image features from MRI scans of patients at two centers and built a score for each vertebra. The score beat ordinary clinical clues at ranking risk. Combined into a chart with two clinical facts, a cleft inside the vertebra and the count of past fractures, the tool predicted well in training and both check sets. It also split patients into high and low risk groups. The authors offer the chart as a noninvasive way to plan care before surgery.
pmc-10671505:
Cristian Lieneck, Matthew McLauchlan, and Sean Phillips wrote a 2023 rapid review on the ethics of cyber safety in health care during the COVID-19 pandemic. Clinics leaned hard on telehealth and new digital tools to keep care going. That shift opened fresh risks for patient data and fair treatment.

The review searched studies from the pandemic years for ethical concerns tied to cyber safety in health groups. It used standard review rules to pick and sort the work. Concerns spanned privacy, consent, and unequal access to secure care. The authors pull the themes together so leaders can plan ahead. Their aim is care that stays both safe and fair when the next crisis hits.
pmc-10684305:
Vashisht, Gutman, and Kaur explore physicians' perspectives on advance care planning with Chinese and South Asian patients, in a study from twenty twenty-three. Planning talks are rare overall and rarer among minorities. Forty-one physicians serving older Chinese or South Asian patients are interviewed. Initiation patterns, topics, barriers, and facilitators are compared across groups.

Both groups share initiation patterns and a need for standardized routines. South Asian contexts involve family members more heavily in talks. Chinese contexts show more communication barriers and family hiding of diagnosis. Death taboos strongly influence Chinese families in the accounts. Unfamiliarity with planning explains limited South Asian engagement more.
pmc-10691405:
Jonathan Locqueville and others put out a 2023 ecology study of a picked mountain flower. Arnica is gathered for herbal remedies. Its mountain meadows are shaped by grazing and mowing. Harvesters care about plant size and flower traits. The team checked plants across twenty-seven French sites.

How land is run shaped the flower's working traits. The height of plants around it carried much of the effect. Grazing and mowing removed biomass in unlike ways. Harvesting then responds to the plants that result. That response feeds back into management choices. The loop links people and plant differences tightly. Seeing the loop helps design harvesting rules that last.
pmc-10693605:
Naomi Nota, James Trujillo, Vere Jacobs, and Judith Holler test eyebrow movements in avatar conversations. Their study from twenty twenty-three asks whether brows help spot questions fast. In face-to-face talk, listeners must recognise questions early. Quick recognition keeps conversation turns flowing smoothly.

Earlier work used exaggerated brow movements for the effect. This study uses natural movement strengths instead. Participants watched avatar videos and judged question or statement. Brow raises and frowns were varied against still faces. Accuracy rose for questions carrying brow movement. Specific intensities helped more than others in the task. Avatar designers should animate brows for clearer social signals.
pmc-10694905:
Chung and colleagues ask in twenty twenty-three whether dirty air after a severe chest infection in infancy raises the risk of asthma by preschool age. Both the infection and dirty air are known asthma risks on their own. The team used hospital records over a decade to compare later asthma in infected infants with different air exposures after the illness.

Exposure to six common air pollutants in the months after the infection all linked to higher asthma risk. The fine dust types showed some of the strongest links. In the subgroup of infants who had been hospitalised, four pollutants kept their link at all time windows checked. The authors urge cleaner air for infants after such infections.
pmc-10699005:
Carneiro and six co-authors profile the chemistry of drug-resistant breast cancer cells in a study from 2023. They compared a triple-negative breast cancer cell line that responds to the drug cisplatin with a daughter line bred to resist it. Nuclear magnetic resonance tracked small molecules in cell extracts over forty-eight hours, alongside standard cell tests.

Resistant cells burned less sugar and less glutamine and shifted how they fed their core energy cycle over time. Several molecule ratios stood out as candidate markers of resistance, including creatine-related and taurine-related pairs. Nucleotide levels fell broadly. The authors offer the signature as a lead for new markers and therapies.
pmc-10699805:
Megan Cullinan and colleagues mapped moving parts of an acid-sensing channel in two thousand twenty-three. The channel sits in cell membranes and opens in acid. Long acid exposure links it to cell death after stroke. Its inner tails may control a death-signaling partner. The leading idea said the tails bind together at rest. That binding would hide the partner site.

Sensitive distance measurements tested the idea directly. The tails were not close enough to bind at rest. Acid moved them only slightly closer. One tail end swung away from the membrane after acid. The old blocking model now looks wrong. Stroke researchers need a fresh explanation.
pmc-10704005:
Lin and six co-authors described a peer mentoring program in twenty twenty-three built to help academic hospital doctors climb the career ladder. Senior mentors are scarce in hospital medicine, and few training plans teach the scholarly skills promotion demands, so these doctors stall below senior ranks.

The program placed twenty-nine hospitalists into five small groups, each guided by a senior faculty member. Over nine months, large and small sessions alternated, covering topics tied to academic advancement. Attendance at the large sessions was strong, though small-group turnout varied more. Before and after surveys showed real gains in knowledge on nearly every topic. The authors offer the design as a template other hospital programs can copy. They note the model needs no rare superstar mentor, since peers carry much of the teaching.
pmc-10707005: Skorik opens a fresh set of works on plant- and life-based chains as drug and gene trucks in this twenty twenty-three note. Such chains can be shaped to haul drugs or gene loads to set spots in the body. The note frames the theme set as a next round in a fast field.
pmc-10708005:
Chaoyue Zhao and ten co-authors link the flow heat of ash slag to a charge based gauge, for gas making from coal mixed with phosphorus rich plant waste. Ash can coat, slag, and rust the burners in flow gas makers. The study came out in twenty twenty-three.

Plant ash holds many alkali metals, while phosphorus in slag binds them into calm minerals, most of all with calcium. The team made dozens of fake ashes with varied lime to phosphorus ratios and grain mixes, and read their melt heats. Computer heat models traced how the ratio shifts flow heat. A forecast model built on the charge gauge then fit both their data and past mixed ash data.
pmc-10712305:
Zhou and seven co-authors checked painkiller interactions in rats in this study from twenty twenty-three. Oxycodone is cleared by liver enzymes that cancer drugs can block. The team dosed rats with oxycodone alone and beside two targeted cancer drugs, icotinib and apatinib. A sensitive assay tracked the painkiller and its breakdown product.

Icotinib raised total oxycodone exposure while slowing its clearance. Apatinib mainly lifted the peak concentration. In liver preparations from rats and humans, both drugs inhibited oxycodone breakdown. The inhibition patterns differed by species and drug. The authors advise reconsidering oxycodone doses when the drugs are combined. The work is preclinical, in animals and lab tissue.
pmc-10713605:
Sigrid Bakke, Monica Ionita, and Lena Tallaksen link Europe's recent drying trend to shifts in the air pressure patterns that steer its weather. The brutal droughts of 2018 and 2022 were part of a longer dry spell. The team matched a standard dryness index with high-altitude pressure maps across four climate zones, from 1979 to 2021.

Spring in the west and summer in the center-east show the clearest joint move: higher pressure and drier ground. Dry spells and high-pressure spells have matched up most of the time since 1900. Looking ahead, climate models say high pressure will be the new norm, worse under high emissions. But the models blur the local detail of past shifts, so the authors warn the outlook is far from sure.
pmc-10714505:
Ioannis Mouratidis and seven co-workers bring in frequentmers, a new way to mine DNA scan data for ill signs. Many ills are caught late, past first signs, when cures work less well. Frequentmers are short code bits found time and time again in patients or in sound controls, but not in both. The team showed the idea on stool scan data for liver scar ill. Models learned from the frequentmer maps.

The models caught liver scar ill with a score of 0.91 in swap checks. Just 200 frequentmers hit near the same grade. The team also traced the best signs back to the germs that made them. The 2023 study hints that tiny code bits that recur could serve as cheap, early marks of ill. They could be found prior to when the ill shows in a clear way.
pmc-10716605:
Chapple and six co-authors review the skinks, a diverse lizard lineage, in work from twenty twenty-three. Success in animals can be measured by species count, geographic range, habitat breadth, and trait diversity. Skinks score high on all of them, hence their title.

The review covers distribution, morphology, ecology, and life history across the world skinks. Key traits were compared between the three skink subfamilies, and between skinks and other lizards. Understanding why one lineage thrives while others stay narrow can reveal general rules of evolution, from body shape to reproductive strategy.
pmc-10717605:
Zhong and a large team show a GABA-producing probiotic eases essential tremor in mice by restoring gut-derived GABA, in a study from twenty twenty-three. Essential tremor may involve deficiency of the calming signal GABA. Gut microbes are a major GABA source feeding brain signals. Patient stool sequencing compares tremor patients with healthy controls.

Patients' gut microbes show impaired GABA production and lower stool GABA. Transplanting patient microbes worsens tremor in model mice. A high-GABA Lactobacillus strain, L5, is identified and fed to mice. Tremor severity falls while movement and grip improve. Brain inflammation drops as cerebellar GABA rises.
pmc-10718305:
HongYu Lu and co-authors test in 2023 whether cobra venom can protect kidneys from diabetes. Earlier work showed the venom of the Chinese cobra improved kidney function in diabetic rats. The team split the question between human kidney cells bathed in sugar and diabetic rats given a venom toxin.

In cells, high sugar pushed kidney cells toward a scar-forming state; the venom blocked that shift and lowered a key scarring signal. In rats, the toxin cut protein leaking into urine and steadied two proteins that keep the kidney filter intact. The venom also eased oxidative stress. The authors suggest the venom's parts as candidate drugs for diabetic kidney disease.
pmc-10720205:
Bagade, Mersha, and Majeed review how social conditions shape mental health in women with infertility in this two thousand twenty-three paper. Infertility is tied to depression and anxiety, even when treatment later succeeds. What social factors drive that risk was less clear. The team searched major health databases for observational studies. They kept studies of women of reproductive age that linked social determinants to mental health outcomes.

The review sorts the determinants that studies found, from income and education to support and stigma. Knowing which women face the highest risk can target screening and services. The authors argue mental health care should be woven into fertility care. Clinicians and policy makers in reproductive health are the audience.
pmc-10725705:
Ismail Abuallut and seven colleagues asked what parents in Saudi Arabia's Jazan region know about amblyopia, or lazy eye. The condition is a brain development problem: the visual system fails to process one eye's input properly, reducing acuity without structural damage. Early treatment works, but only if parents recognize the problem. The cross-sectional study used an electronic questionnaire with five sections. It drew 572 parents, sixty-nine percent of them mothers.

Awareness levels were tested against age, gender, and education using chi-square statistics. Knowing which parent groups know least tells health educators where campaigns should aim. Amblyopia is common and treatable, yet invisible to a casual look at the child's eyes. The twenty twenty-three survey measures the knowledge gap that screening programs in the region must close.
pmc-10733905:
Douma and Bowser test how much sample sticks to the walls of plastic microfluidic chips during separations. Their study appeared in twenty twenty-three, under the byline Cecilia Douma and Michael Bowser. Sticking slows and blurs measurements in tiny channels.

The chips are molded from a clear cyclic olefin plastic. A two-stage separation fed short plugs of test molecules through the chip. Three small dyes barely stuck; their peaks stayed three to seven seconds wide. Two labeled proteins stuck moderately, with peaks near twenty seconds. Glass devices, by contrast, smear peaks over minutes. With easy making and solid durability added, the authors call the plastic a practical choice for timed detection work.
pmc-10734005:
Muhammad Irfan and seven colleagues make a magnetic powder designed to strip heavy metals from wastewater, then test it with statistics. The material coats a copper-magnesium ferrite core with silica, made by a sol-gel route. Checks confirmed the crystal structure. They showed the coating shrinks particles, roughens surfaces, and reduces clumping.

Tests of how it soaks up zinc and lead ions fit chemical-adsorption kinetics and a monolayer isotherm model best. The powder removed ninety-two percent of zinc and ninety-seven percent of lead ions. Being magnetic, it can be pulled back out of treated water with a magnet. The authors highlight that as the practical advantage for wastewater plants.
pmc-10736005:
Palgi and four colleagues present a new survey tool for measuring good time spent alone in twenty twenty-three. Time alone is often linked with loneliness, but many people seek it and gain from it. The team calls that gain positive solitude and built a nine item survey to score it. They set out the ideas behind the tool and early tests of its worth.

Scores on the tool linked in sane ways with measures of well being and mental health. A study of Holocaust survivors showed the trait played a role in stress symptoms after trauma. The authors sketch next steps for study and use of the tool. The work helps split chosen solitude from forced isolation.
pmc-10736805:
Amber Gum and co-authors describe a randomized trial of lay delivered therapy for depressed older adults in this 2023 paper. One treatment is behavioral activation delivered by clinicians. The other is a related program delivered by trained older adult volunteer coaches. Whether peers can match professionals is the key question.

The trial runs at three university sites in the United States. It will enroll 288 depressed older adults in total. Each person gets nine sessions of one of the two programs. Depression scales are measured at baseline and at five follow up points out to 36 weeks. Coaches train longer than clinicians, with more practice and role play. Weekly supervision and recorded sessions guard quality in both arms.
pmc-10737205:
Loriena Yancura studies grandparents who raise or help raise their grandchildren. Her paper, from twenty twenty-three, asks what drives their stress and low mood. She argues that the tie with the child's parents may matter a lot. That tie sits across three generations of one family.

Three hundred twelve grandparents who gave at least twenty hours of care a week took surveys online. Stress and low mood rose with strained ties to the parents. Child behavior also played a role. Race, income, and grandparent age mattered too. The study says support for grandparents should look at the whole family, not the grandparent alone.
pmc-10737705:
Hansol Kim and co-authors study how childcare, work, and care load affect family caregivers of older adults, in this 2023 paper. Data came from a national health survey that sampled over fifty-four thousand caregivers in 2015 to 2017. The team focused on 17,271 people caring for older adults. They modeled poor mental and physical health days for women and men separately.

Heavy care load hurt both sexes. Holding a job, though, was linked to better health for both. Children at home strained women's minds but not their bodies; for men the strain was physical. The worst mental health for women came with no job, children at home, and heavy care together. For men, no job plus children at home was the riskiest mix. The authors want finer study of how families split these loads.
pmc-10739405:
Lijuan Wang and colleagues published a 2023 study of blood fats in Guillain-Barré syndrome. The syndrome is a sudden immune attack on peripheral nerves. It can leave patients weak or paralyzed. The team measured blood lipids in eighty-five patients. Healthy volunteers of matching age and sex served as controls.

Several fat-carrying proteins ran higher in patients. Protective cholesterol particles ran lower. Sicker patients showed some lipids higher still. Lipid levels also tracked infections before onset and later outcomes. The patterns may help doctors judge severity. They hint that fat metabolism plays a role in the disease.
pmc-10740205:
Maaike Esselaar, Johnny V V Parr, Greg Wood, and Emma Hodson-Tole present a two thousand twenty-three study of muscle control in children with developmental coordination disorder. The condition affects movement skill, and muscle activity patterns may differ from typical children. Fine details of motor unit firing had not been studied in this group.

Eighteen children did gentle handgrip tasks at a small share of their strongest squeeze. Dense surface sensors recorded a small hand muscle, and signals were split into single motor unit trains. Children with the disorder showed less variation in firing patterns across squeezes. The finding hints at a distinct muscle control strategy.
pmc-10740405:
Lozano-Bilbao and co-authors compare metal buildup in a parrotfish around the Canary Islands, in a study from 2023. The fish, Sparisoma cretense, feeds in shallow reefs and ends up on local tables, so its tissue metals matter for both ecology and food safety. Samples spanned the years 2022 and 2023 and both cool and warm seasons.

Levels of six metals, from aluminum to copper, varied a lot by island. Values rose in 2023, above all in the warm season, when warmer water lifts marine life activity. Island geology, currents, sediment flow, water quality, and human pressure all shaped the pattern. The authors call for steady monitoring to guide conservation and fisheries advice in the archipelago.
pmc-10741605:
Aya Abou Hammoud and co-authors present a 2023 study of a simple test that reads what cancer stem cells secrete. Such cells drive tumor growth and shrug off chemo and radiation. The test feeds the wash from cancer cells to mouse stem cells that need a growth signal to stay young. How the stem cells fare then reports what the cancer cells sent out.

Wash from adult brain tumor stem cells kept the mouse cells young, in step with the signal they secrete. Wash from child brain tumor cells did not. Stomach cancer wash pushed the stem cells in other ways that did not need that signal. The test is cheap, gentle, and easy to read. Labs could use it to sort tumor lines by their hidden signals.
pmc-10742805:
Yaping Zheng and a team including Kailin Yang and Xiaonan Lu studied how a Chinese herbal tea interacts with gut microbes, in a paper from twenty twenty-three. The tea comes from a plant used in the north of China, and recent work hints it may ease gut swelling and tumors. Which parts of the tea do the work was unclear.

Lab tests tracked the tea's main active compounds as gut microbes changed them over two days. The microbes stripped sugar parts from the compounds, and the compounds in turn shifted the microbe mix. Helpful types grew while a harmful type was held back. The authors link these shifts to pathways tied to swelling and tumor disease.
pmc-10743605: Hiroaki Taniguchi, writing alone in two thousand twenty-three, gives a short piece on liver cancer, with the main form of it named in the text. That form is a major health care in the world, from its high spread in many lands. The piece, headed as a new-era take on the theme, sets the disease forth as a grave, wide ill. Its scope, as kept in this form, is the weight of the disease and why it claims care.
pmc-10747105:
Paulo Vieira Damasco and colleagues track infective endocarditis trends over twelve years at two teaching hospitals in Rio de Janeiro, Brazil. Their 2023 retrospective cohort study includes two hundred forty patients diagnosed by standard criteria.

Median age was fifty-five, and most patients were male. Healthcare-associated infection predominated, as did left-sided native valve disease and staphylococcal infection. Overall hospital mortality reached nearly forty-six percent, higher still in older patients and those with heavy comorbidity. Mortality showed no yearly trend across the study period. Age sixty or above emerged as an independent risk factor for hospital death in adjusted analysis.
pmc-10748405:
Luyi Huang and colleagues evaluated a urine test for tuberculosis in two thousand twenty-three. The test detects a bacterial wall component in urine. A light-based method measured it in this study. Hospital patients and healthy controls provided samples. Standard sputum tests supplied comparisons. Several disease groups were separated carefully.

The TB group tested positive far more often. Sensitivity reached about half of cases. Specificity was very high overall. The urine test beat DNA testing on sensitivity. It also led for lung TB detection rates. For disease outside the lungs, it beat another standard test. Immune cell counts and diabetes affected accuracy. Urine testing suits patients unable to produce sputum.
pmc-10753705:
Samwang and four co-authors tune conductive polypyrrole synthesis with a soap-like template, in a study from twenty twenty-three. Polypyrrole conducts electricity and suits biomedical uses due to easy synthesis. The template forms micelles that guide polymer shape during chemical growth. The team varies monomer dose, template dose, and oxidant ratio systematically.

With template present, sheets form instead of spheres in many conditions. Raising monomer dose enlarges sheets, narrows the band gap, and raises conductivity. Raising oxidant ratio also favors sheets with better electrical traits. Without template, only spheres form with wide gaps and low conductivity. Spectra link band gap and shape to charge carrier ratios. Size, shape, and electrical traits move together tightly.
pmc-10756905:
Huimin Chen and colleagues published a 2023 combined analysis of a drug for nosebleeds. The drug treats a hereditary vessel disorder. Patients with the disorder suffer frequent, heavy nosebleeds. The drug blocks growth of abnormal blood vessels. The team pooled results from published studies.

Seven studies with several hundred patients qualified. Bleeding severity scores improved with treatment. Bleed duration and frequency did not clearly change. Side effects showed no clear increase. Study quality was rated moderate overall. The authors call the benefit real but limited. Patients should weigh a severity gain against modest expectations.
pmc-10811605:
Fernanda Fortes de Araujo and a team of co-authors validate a blood test that tells whether Chagas disease treatment has cured mice. Their study was published in twenty twenty-three. The disease comes from a parasite and is common in Latin America, and new drugs need a fast way to prove they work.

The test hunts for bits of the parasite floating in blood, using short DNA-like strands called aptamers. Mice treated with one drug, fexinidazole, tested clear in about seven of ten cases across two parasite strains. The test also showed that drug beating the standard drug before a final check. The authors say the method is sensitive and easy to use, which could speed the search for better cures.
pmc-10825005:
Jhonathan Bazalar-Gonzales and co-authors published a study that the text dates to 2023; the catalog lists 2024. They hunted drug-resistant gut germs in monkeys of the Peruvian Amazon. Germs that defeat a key drug class sit on a world priority list. Wild primates near people can pick up such germs.

The team took 119 stool samples from seven monkey species in two regions. About seven percent of the gut germ strains made the drug-blocking enzyme. Gene reads showed two high-risk lineages also found in people and farm animals. The strains carried wide sets of resistance and attack genes. They are the first such finds in Amazon primates, the authors say. Human activity near the forest is the likely driver.
pmc-10839005:
Alireza Tajik, Hamid Reza Samadlouie, Amir Salek Farrokhi, and Amir Ghasemi tune the growing conditions of a medicinal mushroom to boost its useful compounds. Their study was published in twenty twenty-three. The mushroom, Ganoderma lucidum, makes substances that can fight germs and may act against cancer.

The team first screened single factors, then used a statistical design to fine-tune the mix. Mineral nanoparticles, a B vitamin, and sugars ranked high for making one key compound, while wheat starch and whey protein favored sugar-chain compounds. Two tuned recipes came out of the surface modeling, one for each product type. Extracts were then tested for germ-fighting and cancer-fighting action. The work gives producers a recipe-level guide to stronger mushroom extracts.
pmc-10903305:
Mahsa Mohammadkhani, Navid Abdi, and Khojasteh Sharifi-Sarasiabi report, in a 2023 case study, a worm infection found in an unusual place: a young woman's forehead. The disease, dirofilariasis, comes from dog heartworm relatives carried by mosquitoes, and humans are accidental hosts. The warm climate of Bandar Abbas in southern Iran suits the mosquitoes that spread it.

The twenty-year-old patient came to a surgeon with a lump on her forehead. Under the microscope, slices of the removed tissue showed cross-sections of a worm ringed by dead tissue, matching the Dirofilaria genus. The authors believe this is the first human case in Iran reported in the forehead. They publish the case so that doctors in similar climates will add this infection to their list of suspects when a puzzling lump appears.
pmc-11548805:
Arnold and a team including Spertus reported in twenty twenty-four on heart ultrasound measures and health status in obstructive hypertrophic cardiomyopathy. In this disease, heart muscle grows too thick and can block blood flow. The drug mavacamten can ease strain on the heart and help patients feel better.

The team drew on the EXPLORER-HCM trial, which tested the drug against placebo for thirty weeks in adults. They compared ultrasound measures of heart shape and function with scores from a health questionnaire. They looked at links both at the start and as measures changed over time. The aim was to learn which heart changes track most closely with how patients actually feel.
pmc-11575205:
Erik K R Hanko and colleagues present a two thousand twenty-four study engineering gut bacteria to make plant flavonoids. Flavonoids include many compounds valued in medicine. A molecule called pinocembrin is the branch point for a wide range of them.

Making these molecules in microbes had yielded only modest amounts. The team combined genome edits with enzyme screening in Escherichia coli. Edits boosted supplies of two key building blocks. The tuned strain produced a strong amount of pinocembrin from glycerol alone. It then served as a base for making four related flavonoids, showing a route to factory-style production.
pmc-11577105:
Ramin Lotfi and five colleagues screened wheat types for light based signs that predict strength under future climates. Climate change threatens dryland wheat, a staple for food security. Ten genotypes faced combined stresses: higher heat, doubled carbon dioxide, and limited water. The team measured the faint light leaves give off after taking light in. That glow, called chlorophyll fluorescence, opens a window on how leaves turn light into food. The types met the combined stress in different ways.

One old type, Sardari, and one new dryland line, Ivan, proved strong. Their scores for leaf light use in fact rose under combined stress. They also kept leaf pores and electron flow in better check than rivals. Stats tied set glow measures to how well each type did. Those measures could serve as fast signs, letting breeders screen hundreds of lines for climate readiness, no harvest wait needed.
pmc-11585505:
Jelena Jotanovic led a large team profiling DNA methylation in pituitary tumors in a 2024 paper. A small share of these tumors grow aggressively despite all standard treatment, and some spread to distant sites. Markers to spot them early are scarce because the tumors are rare. The team analyzed tumor tissue from dozens of aggressive and metastatic cases plus a small benign comparison group.

Unsupervised grouping separated aggressive and spreading tumors from benign ones by their methylation patterns. Copy-number changes riddled the aggressive genomes while benign tumors stayed mostly clean. The authors say methylation profiling could help flag dangerous tumors sooner.
pmc-11586105:
Shannon Brandt, Robin Lyle, and Catherine Sole trace the history of trapdoor spiders found only in South Africa's Karoo. Their study was published in twenty twenty-four. The genus had never had its geographic history reviewed as a whole.

The team built a family tree from three gene regions, dated with a fossil anchor. Fifteen species live in the Karoo, and the group's spread there began in the early Palaeocene. Most splits came between the late Eocene and the Miocene, matching big climate shifts. Gene maps showed how populations link across the land, and some species carry signs of past growth. Distance tests checked whether far-apart spiders differ more. The work grounds conservation of a little-known desert group.
pmc-11586405:
Youwei Yao and Xuesong Niu build a fitness model for elite skiers in a paper from two thousand twenty-four. The sport is freestyle skiing aerials, where athletes launch into flips and twists. The work began during training for the Beijing Winter Olympics and aims to guide future training.

The team reviewed past work, spoke with experts, and tested twenty-nine elite athletes. Their model covers body shape, body function, and athletic quality through eleven measures, from lean mass to sprint and squat tests. Each measure carries a weight based on its importance. A second model predicts performance from training years and a few key power measures. The authors offer it as a guide for coaches ahead of future Games.
pmc-11590205:
Kansal and Patel published in twenty twenty-four a letter from two medical students about question banks as a study tool. Question banks offer personalized, convenient practice and are hugely popular. The writers warn that over-reliance on them carries overlooked pitfalls. A prior article suggested students write their own exam questions. The pair doubt students can match proper exam complexity without training. They propose teaching question-writing inside tutorials instead.

They also worry school-specific banks train students only for local exams. A new national licensing exam aims to standardize knowledge across schools. Pandemic-era study habits pushed peers toward pattern recognition over deep thinking. Curricula are also shifting toward broader, discussion-based clinical knowledge. Independent banks may lag behind those reforms, they argue. The letter asks educators to guide bank use more deliberately.
pmc-11590805:
Robyn Tamblyn and co-authors set out, in a 2024 protocol, a trial of a phone app that helps patients manage drug changes after leaving hospital. Nearly half of discharged patients return to emergency care or hospital within ninety days. Missed drug changes and risky drugs drive many of those returns, and the app targets both problems.

The trial will enroll 3,250 adults leaving hospital, split evenly between the app and usual care. The app adds pharmacist oversight and warns patients about risky drugs to discuss with their doctor. The main outcome blends emergency visits, readmissions, and death over ninety days. Drug taking, patient confidence, and quality of life are also tracked.
pmc-11603305:
Teo and three co-authors hunt traits that flag head moves in brain scans in this twenty twenty-four study. Head moves blur scan grades for both care and lab work alike. A heads-up on who will move could shape how a study is built and run.

Inside, near forty-one thousand bank folks gave scan and trait data for the checks. Weight grade and root group tied most strongly to head move in the set. A ten-point weight jump matched a half-rise in move scores in the math. Mind ills, bone ills, and sugar ills did not raise move scores in the set. High blood push did raise them, though by a mild share. Brain game scores and past scan time also tied to moves.
pmc-11603905:
Mehmet Bulduk, Veysel Can, and Eda Muhafiz study nursing students and child liking. Their study from twenty twenty-four deals with paediatric drug giving. Drug errors are common in child patients, they note.

Students in later study years at a Turkish state university joined. Scales measured liking of children and drug giving confidence. Tests linked scores with student traits and each other. The aim was to see how feelings shape skill. Support for feelings may matter as much as technique. Such links can guide how nursing schools teach drug safety. Mean student age was among the traits logged.
pmc-11604805:
Davis, McDonald, and Yao wrote an opening essay in twenty twenty-four for a set of papers on Yao syndrome and kin illnesses. These illnesses link to a sensor protein in cells called NOD2, which helps fight germs and control swelling. Gene changes in NOD2 raise the risk of bowel illness and of rare swelling diseases. Two of those diseases are Blau syndrome in children and Yao syndrome.

The essay sums up what the new papers add on causes and care. One study finds a drug that calms swelling by lowering NOD2 in cells. A case report tells of a child who did well on two older drugs. The set aims to sharpen how doctors define and treat these rare diseases.
pmc-11605605:
Miyake and colleagues report a study from twenty twenty-four on brain function in patients with glioblastoma. Cancer care can harm clear thought, which hurts daily life and social life. The team used a scan tracer that sticks to a protein called tau in the brain. They scanned twenty-four patients before and after drug and radiation care. They also gave five short tests of memory, speed, and planning at entry and at discharge.

When scan buildup shrank, memory scores often rose for the better. When buildup spread to deep brain parts, thought scores often fell. The team names brain spots where buildup seems to matter most for thought. The work may help teams guard brain function while they treat the tumor.
pmc-11607305: Amano and co-authors study a blood marker that may help choose biologic drugs for inflammatory bowel disease. The marker is leucine-rich alpha-2 glycoprotein, measured in serum before treatment starts. Anti-cytokine biologics are strong drugs, and picking the right one for each patient remains hard. Pretreatment levels of this marker are tested as a guide for that choice.
pmc-11607805:
Marina Arkkukangas and co-authors test a fall-prevention exercise program for older adults led by trained peers, in work published in 2024. Falls are a major health risk in old age, and strength and balance training can cut that risk. Reaching a wide population with such training is hard, so the team tried a train-the-trainer model.

Older trainers were taught to lead weekly group sessions covering strength, balance, and safe falling methods over eight weeks. The trial enrolled 101 participants from groups for retired people in Sweden. Outcomes included physical performance, activity level, grip strength, quality of life, and fear of falling. Results were compared with a control group at eight weeks. The study tests whether peer-led delivery can spread proven training at low cost.
pmc-11608005:
Yi Zheng and co-authors test whether packets secreted by fat-derived stem cells can prevent a jawbone death linked to certain drugs. Their 2024 study uses a rat model where a bone drug plus tooth extraction triggers the condition. The packets, called exosomes, were mixed into a gel and placed in the socket right after extraction.

Treated sockets healed faster at the gum and rebuilt more bone on scans and tissue study. The team traced the mechanism to macrophages, the immune cells that set the socket's inflammatory tone. The drug pushed them toward an inflammatory state and a fiery cell death that spreads damage. Exosomes damped both shifts. A cell-free packet therapy would be easier to store and dose than live stem cells.
pmc-11610005:
Ganesh Acharya bids farewell after ten years as chief editor of Acta Obstetricia et Gynecologica Scandinavica, in this 2024 editorial. He hands the journal to Amarnath Bhide, the first chief editor appointed from outside Scandinavia in its century-long history. Acharya looks back on a decade spent pushing quality, visibility, and ethical conduct.

He argues that a journal's worth lies not only in citations but in the values of the society that owns it. For this journal those are Nordic values: openness, trust, equality, and respect. Steps taken under his watch included close work with sister journals on integrity and a strong international board. He leaves, he writes, with the journal in good health and good hands.
pmc-11610605:
Kamal Hossain, Mohammad Tanvir Ahmed, and two co-authors test a doped boron nitride sheet as a toxic gas sensor. Their study, from twenty twenty-four, uses quantum calculations. Two sheets are compared: plain boron nitride and an arsenic-doped version. Three gases are the targets: carbon dioxide, hydrogen sulfide, and sulfur trioxide.

Both sheets prove stable on energy grounds. All three gases stick, with warped shapes marking the contact. Doping multiplies the sticking strength many times over. The doped sheet's energy gap shifts by about a third on gas contact. That shift changes conductivity, the readable signal. Peak sensitivity shows near room temperature in their results.
pmc-11613805:
Lili Fan and six colleagues study what happens to bamboo shoot quality when a bamboo species spreads into tea plantations. Mixed tea-bamboo stands create new growing conditions. The team measured shoot size, nutrition, and taste across zones of the mixed forest, using structural equation modeling to identify the drivers.

Expansion made shoots larger and heavier and raised protein, fat, starch, and vitamin C, improving nutritional scores, especially at the mixed forest's center. Yet taste suffered there: more acids, oxalic acid, tannins, and cellulose dulled palatability despite extra sugars and flavor amino acids. Soil changes drove both the gains and the loss. The framework helps managers balance nutrition against eating quality in these agroforestry systems.
pmc-11615305:
Ligia Bastea and a large team of co-authors show how a virus doorway on early pancreatic lesions helps cancer take hold. Their study appeared in twenty twenty-four. Pancreatic cancer needs both a faulty KRAS gene and an inflammatory push, and the usual sources of that push were vague.

Lesion cells carrying the faulty gene raise a receptor that gut viruses use to enter cells. One such virus was found in about half of pancreatic cancer patients. In mice, a single infection faded in normal animals. With the faulty gene present, it sparked lasting inflammation and fast cancer growth. Removing the receptor from lesion cells blocked the effect. The work ties a common infection to a deadly cancer's spark.
pmc-11618305:
Wengui Mao and co-authors present a 2024 method for finding the true settings of electric motors when measures are noisy. Motor traits vary in ways that blur test results, and past methods were slow or broke down on ill-shaped data. The team pairs a fourth-order moment method with a trust region scheme that keeps the search in safe zones.

The inner layer works out how likely each motor output is under the spread of traits. The outer layer turns the hunt into a plain tuning task: shrink the gap between the worked-out spread and the measured one. Local stand-in models fill each trust zone and update as gaps shrink. The pairing cuts the load on the stand-in models and speeds the search. Motor makers gain a surer way to read traits from messy tests.
pmc-11618505:
Heyu Li, Zhangmeizhi Li, Shuyan Zhang, and Xiao Pu combine two neural network types to spot malicious web domains, in a paper from twenty twenty-four. The domain name system is core internet plumbing and a frequent attack target. Rule-based detectors need constant manual updates and lag behind new tricks.

Their model first upgrades a Transformer with tweaks to its attention heads and encoding. That output feeds a convolutional network, and a block ensemble makes the final call. In their scoring, the method rated high on accuracy, speed, and feature extraction, beating classic approaches overall. The authors offer it as a fresh tool for guarding the naming layer of the internet.
pmc-11624205:
Siyao Qin and six co-authors built a pressure sensor with a vast linear range. Their paper, from twenty twenty-four, deals with triboelectric sensors, which make signals from touch charge. Such sensors face a clash: high sensitivity fights a wide straight range. Their sensor rests on a rubber that holds water, with tiny channels lined by an ion rich face. A small dose of liquid sits in the rubber.

When pressed, water bridges shift the built in field and keep the signal straight near the squeeze limit. Ion moves at the wet face boost the touch charge, which lifts sensitivity. The range runs from low to very high pressure on one scale. Readers who build wearables get both reach and fineness in one sensor.
pmc-11626205:
Yifu Zhao and three co-authors test if work pay softens the tie tween work push and ward harm in China. Their survey appeared in twenty twenty-four. More than three thousand care staff in twelve Shandong wards filled forms on hours, night shifts, pay, rank feel, and past harm. Past half told of work harm met.

Long hours, night counts, and rank feel all tied to harm. Month pay softened the pay-harm and word-harm ties. Rank feel softened the night shift tie. The team read the marks through a push-pay gap frame and draw ward paths from them.
pmc-11627405:
Hefeng Zhang and three co-authors study a do-not-eat-me signal in lung cancer in a 2024 paper. The signal, found on cell surfaces, helps tumors hide from immune cells that would eat them. The team read its levels in tumor and nearby tissue from fifty patients treated at one hospital. They also tracked immune cells inside the tumors and patient survival.

The signal appeared in about half of tumors, far more often than in nearby tissue. High levels went with spread to lymph nodes, later stage, and poorer cell maturity. Patients with high levels also had more immune eater cells in their tumors and shorter survival. The authors name the signal a risk marker and possible drug target.
pmc-11628605:
Sini Huuskonen and co-authors build a shared knowledge base on how Covid virus variants hijack human cells, in a study from two thousand twenty-four. Cells infected with five variants were tracked from one hour to thirty-six hours for protein change. A tagging method also mapped which human proteins each viral protein touches.

Each variant left a distinct time pattern of protein shifts. Shared hot paths covered cell shape control, RNA splicing, and waste clearing in the cell. Contact maps differed by variant, showing how single mutations rewire viral grip. The open resource aims to guide antiviral design against new variants. Readers get a variant-by-variant playbook of cell hijack.
pmc-11630005:
Jesse Rijks, Justin Luermans, and Kevin Vernooy report a heart patient whose electrical delays shrank a year after a new pacing treatment, in a 2024 case report. The 77-year-old woman had weak heart muscle, a blocked left conduction branch, and stubborn atrial fibrillation. She received pacing aimed at the left bundle branch area plus ablation of the relay node. The implant captured the branch, but the paced signal stayed wide, hinting at disease further downstream.

A year later her pumping fraction had risen and her symptoms eased a class. More striking, the paced signal had narrowed on its own, and the delay to a key landmark fell. The authors read this as reverse electrical remodelling, the mirror of the known muscle recovery. They say pacing strategy choice now needs more study.
pmc-11631505:
Amaya-Ramirez and seven co-authors present a computer method to predict immune targets, in work from twenty twenty-four. The targets sit on HLA proteins, which shape how the body sees a transplanted organ. Antibodies against donor HLA are the main cause of organ loss.

Current maps of these targets rely on single spots in the protein chain, and on still, fixed structures. The new method uses moving simulations of the protein and patches of its surface in three dimensions. Machine learning then predicts which patches act as antibody targets. A fuller map could help match organs to patients with more care and cut the risk of rejection.
pmc-11632505:
Uluman Şişman, Mehmet Eren, and Emel Gönen (2024) report a rare bone variation found by chance in a child's feet. A ten-year-old boy came to the emergency department with a glass cut on the sole of his right foot. X-rays for the injury showed something unrelated: the middle bone of the third toe was split in two on both feet. Bipartite bones form when a young bone's centers fail to merge. The kneecap and sesamoid bones show this most often.

Middle toe bones had never been reported with it, the authors say. This mattered because a split bone can be mistaken for a fracture. Treating a normal variant as a break leads to needless casts and worry. The authors urge weighing bipartition when a clean split appears without matching trauma. Their case extends the map of where it can hide.
pmc-11635605:
Andreas Küttel, Louise Storm, Natalia Stambulova, and Kristoffer Henriksen explore mental health among Danish elite athletes in a 2024 study. Most research stresses risk factors, so the team asked athletes themselves what threatens and what nurtures their mental health. Seven international level athletes from varied sports were interviewed twice, once about their careers and again two months later about recent events.

Four themes formed a map. Elite sport felt like a relentless performance context full of demands. Athletes reacted with high self expectations, self blame, and anxiety. Over time they built coping resources: self reflection, recovery habits, planning skills, and passion for their sport. Supportive coaching and surroundings formed a nurturing environment. Many coping skills grew out of hard periods in adolescence.
pmc-11637405:
Schneider, Buchan, and Couch test in twenty twenty-four whether fasting after a stroke-like injury helps rats recover. Swelling harms the brain early after stroke but helps later, and fasting is known to calm swelling fast. The team created a small lesion in a deep brain area of rats, then fed them normally or gave water only for one day.

After one day, fasted rats had smaller damaged areas and less leakage across the brain's protective barrier. They also had fewer inflammatory white cells in both blood and brain. The authors suggest fasting could be a simple, drug-free add-on for stroke care. They stress the study is preliminary and small.
pmc-11638305:
Spinocerebellar ataxia type 3 is an inherited disease that wastes the cerebellum, yet its damage reaches the subthalamic nucleus, a deep-brain hub. In a research letter, Martina Minnerop and co-authors explore a puzzle. Post-mortem studies found severe neuron loss in that nucleus in nearly all patients, except one who had shown parkinsonian symptoms. They reason that losing the nucleus may mask parkinsonism, much as stimulating it treats Parkinson's disease.

To test the idea, they measured the nucleus's volume by MRI in eleven patients, against matched controls and a reference sample of 235 older adults. The series includes the patient with parkinsonian symptoms, whose bilateral deep brain stimulation of the nucleus worked well for three years. The authors hypothesize that this patient kept a larger nucleus than most patients without symptoms. If volume predicts who can respond, it could guide stimulation decisions in this rare disease.
pmc-11642305:
Chin-Yu Lin and co-authors test whether fragments of wheat protein can slow a key step in Alzheimer's disease, in a 2024 paper. The disease involves clumps of a protein piece called amyloid-beta building in the brain. An enzyme named BACE1 makes the first cut that creates those pieces, so blocking it is a favored strategy. The team broke down gliadin, whey, and casein proteins with three enzymes and screened the fragments.

Fragments of gliadin cut by bromelain, a pineapple enzyme, blocked BACE1 most strongly in test-tube assays. In mouse brain cells grown in dishes, those fragments lowered BACE1 and cut the processing of the parent protein that yields amyloid-beta. The authors credit the fragment mix, rich in building blocks that disrupt clumping. They suggest food-derived fragments merit study as a dietary route against the disease, while noting more work is needed.
pmc-11642405:
Paolo Bellavite, Alberto Donzelli, and Ciro Isidoro critique the World Health Organization algorithm for judging whether a health problem was caused by a vaccine. Their paper appeared in 2024. The algorithm walks reviewers through questions and sorts each case into a few classes. The authors say it fits the new genetic COVID-19 vaccines poorly. That is above all true for rare and unexpected events.

They name four weak points. Other causes are weighed too heavily. The time window and biological plausibility are set narrowly. Early literature is thin and disputed. And the final classes leave too much in a vague middle bin. Poor sorting, they warn, distorts safety reporting and skews judgments of benefit and harm. They propose fixes so novel vaccines get a fairer hearing.
pmc-11642705:
Ruth Phypers and three colleagues published a case series in two thousand twenty-four on light therapy for unexplained infertility. Red and near-infrared light applied through the skin is proposed to support cell energy. Three women with long unexplained fertility problems received a course of treatments.

Each woman had failed to conceive for over two years, with histories including miscarriages and failed IVF transfers. Light sessions ran weekly or fortnightly. All three achieved full-term pregnancies and healthy babies during nine months of follow-up. No adverse effects were reported in the series. The authors present the cases as grounds for a proper controlled trial, not proof. The series is tiny and uncontrolled by design.
pmc-11643005:
Zarate-Osuna and co-authors track child weight shifts around COVID-19 in Spain. The PESCA school program began in 2018 to cut youth overweight. The study held 207 children and teens from Madrid schools. Ages ran from about 3 to 16 years. Three checks were done, two before COVID and one after onset.

Overweight rates held steady before COVID, near 18 to 20 percent. After onset, the rate jumped to 26.57 percent. Body fat, activity, rest, and screen time were tracked as well. The authors split program gains from lockdown harm. School health work, they argue, needs shielding in crises.
pmc-11643805:
Angelika Wojtys and co-authors dry Japanese quince fruit in erythritol solutions in this 2024 paper. Osmotic dehydration pulls water from fruit into a strong solution before further drying. Erythritol is a low calorie sweetener that could replace sucrose in that step. The team compared solution strengths and measured both drying speed and fruit quality.

A 40 percent erythritol solution dried the fruit fastest of all agents tested. It also changed the fruit chemistry the most from fresh fruit. Fruit dried in a 30 percent solution kept higher levels of healthy phenolic compounds. Measures included acidity, sugar profile, color, vitamin C, and antioxidant activity. A statistical summary separated the effects of each condition. The work guides a sugar free route to dried quince.
pmc-11644305:
Keelan Jagaran, Saffiya Habib, and Moganavelli Singh present a 2024 lab study of fat-based carriers for gene-silencing cargo. Current care for brain diseases such as Parkinson's mostly eases symptoms. A carrier that ferries silencing RNA into cells could treat causes instead. The team built carriers from natural fats, added a ginkgo leaf extract, and coated them so the cargo binds tight.

The coated carriers held the cargo and shielded it from enzymes that chew RNA. In two human cell lines, harm stayed low, under 15 percent. A cell death signal even fell in treated cells. The carriers entered cells well in both lines. The work is a first proof step toward RNA care for brain disease, well short of patient use.
pmc-11644505:
Diego Gomez, Pablo Salvador, Juan Fernando Rodrigo, and Jorge Gil wrote a farm study in two thousand twenty-four on judging potato yield from light readings. They used a handheld device that measures how the leaf canopy reflects light. Such readings can support precision farming without harming the crop.

Over two growing seasons, the team measured sixty plants per plot across six potato varieties. They asked two things: when in the season readings link best to yield, and which light bands link most strongly. From a wide measured range, they picked out twenty-three features tied to tuber yield. They then built a math model that links those features to the harvest.
pmc-11648805:
Rohini Jadhav and co-authors share a photo data set of a medicinal plant in this 2024 paper. Centella asiatica is an herb used in traditional medicine across Asia. Its leaves hold compounds thought to drive its healing effects. Leaf quality matters for safe, strong herbal products. The team built the data set so computers can learn to grade the leaves.

The set holds just over nine thousand phone photos of leaves. Leaves are sorted as dried, healthy, or unhealthy, and shown singly or in groups. Single leaves appear from the front and the back. All images were resized to one standard frame. Researchers can use the set to train and test image-sorting tools for herbal quality checks.
pmc-11649605:
Amr Setouhi and colleagues report a two thousand twenty-four study predicting coronary artery disease severity in stable angina patients. A blood marker called sST2 is better known for heart failure. Its link to complex artery narrowing on angiography was unsettled.

Ninety participants were grouped by their angiogram scores into normal, simple, and complex disease. Blood marker levels were measured alongside advanced ultrasound strain imaging. Both the marker and several strain measures predicted severity strongly. Combining a blood test with detailed heart imaging may help doctors judge which chest pain patients hide the worst disease.
pmc-11649905:
Juan Carlos Baldermann and a large team of co-authors map the brain networks that matter in Tourette syndrome. Their study appeared in 2024. The syndrome brings unwanted movements and sounds called tics. Deep brain stimulation can ease severe tics, but the best networks to target were unclear. The team combined data from two stimulation cohorts and one group of patients whose tics came from brain lesions.

They mapped every stimulation site and lesion onto a wiring map built from a thousand healthy brains. Stronger tic relief came when stimulation sites connected well to networks for action control. One network, the cingulo-opercular, matched best. The pattern held in the second cohort. The authors say aiming at these networks could make stimulation therapy more reliable.
pmc-11651905:
Woojoo Kim and nine co-authors study how water striders glide across ponds in a 2024 physics paper. These insects row with their middle legs and then slide on the surface.
