The rowing stroke is well understood, but the slide that follows it had not been studied, so the team asked how body size shapes that glide.

They built a model of floating and drag during the slide and checked it against insects of many sizes. The model says heavy striders cannot hold their front body up on their front legs alone while both middle legs recover. Large species cope with longer front legs or an uneven gait. Mid-sized ones switch gaits in ways that cut drag.
pmc-11652505:
Geoffrey Dover opens an editorial from two thousand twenty-four with a memory from a rural sports camp in northern Ontario. Two boys aged twelve fell the same way while playing basketball, a week apart. Both broke the same wrist bone in what looked like an identical pattern.

Yet their pain could not have differed more. One boy sat calm and said he was fine though his wrist hurt a lot. The other screamed, turned pale, and nearly fainted. Dover uses the contrast to question the simple biomedical view of pain he was taught as a student. The editorial frames a wider look at non-drug treatment of pain, where the person's experience matters as much as the injury.
pmc-11653305:
Essi Honkonen leads a team that measures thigh bone twist in kneecap patients. Their study from twenty twenty-four deals with recurrent patellar dislocations. After a first dislocation, many patients dislocate again.

A twisted thigh bone may push the kneecap sideways. Whether both sided cases show more twist was unknown. Mature patients with repeat dislocations had rotation scans. A trauma control group gave the compare values. Each leg was measured on its own terms. A share of the study group had both sided history. Twist values were set against the control legs.
pmc-11654005:
Alex Griffiths and a team of co-authors review diet and vascular dementia risk, in a paper dated twenty twenty-four. Vascular dementia is the second most common dementia, and diet may be one risk factor people can change. The team searched five databases for long-term studies on foods, eating patterns, and new cases.

Sixteen studies made the cut. More fruit and vegetables, tea and coffee, and plant-based eating linked to lower risk. Fried fish, processed meat, and ultra-processed foods linked to higher risk. Results for other foods were mixed. The authors call diet a promising lever but note the thin evidence per food.
pmc-11654305:
Gary Mitchell leads a large all-Ireland team asking healthcare students what it is actually like to care for a patient with delirium. The acute confusion syndrome is common, harmful, and underdiagnosed, partly because professionals barely recognize it. Forty nursing, pharmacy, and medical students from two universities joined focus groups about their placements.

Reflexive thematic analysis produced three themes covering their experiences, what their pre-registration education had given them, and how interprofessional teamwork felt on the ground. The study's vivid title hints at disorientation mirroring the patients' own. Findings are aimed at curriculum designers: students meet delirium early and often, and their training should treat it as a core skill rather than a footnote.
pmc-11655905:
Guanghui Shen, Haoran Chen, Xinwu Ye, Xiaodong Xue, and Shusi Tang shrink a thirty-two-item mania screen to eight items for teens with learning methods, in a study from two thousand twenty-four. Near three thousand teens who took the full screen supplied the data. Two tree-based methods picked the items that carry the signal.

The eight-item form kept very high accuracy in the checks. Picked items cover core teen mania marks like high energy, risk taking, and short temper. Two cut scores are offered, one strict and one balanced, both with strong marks. A shorter screen eases clinic use where time and focus are scarce. Readers get a teen-tuned bipolar screen with proof behind it.
pmc-11656405:
Wei Luo and colleagues show that a gut-derived plant compound reduces inflammation and fat build-up in macrophages through a small RNA pathway. Their 2024 study explains how the tryptophan breakdown product protects against artery hardening.

In fat-laden macrophage cells, the compound raised a small regulatory RNA and two cholesterol-export proteins while lowering a gene-silencing enzyme. It also shifted macrophages toward a calming type and eased inflammation, cutting one inflammatory signal and raising a soothing one. The silencing enzyme proved a direct target of the small RNA. Overproducing the enzyme or blocking the RNA undid the compound's benefits. The pathway explains part of the compound's artery protection.
pmc-11656905:
Lewei Liu and a team of co-authors study the links between internet addiction, poor sleep, and suicidal thoughts in depressed teens. Their twenty twenty-four cross-sectional study enrolled five hundred two adolescents with major depression and one hundred twenty-three healthy controls. Half the patients met the bar for internet addiction and over a third for insomnia.

Standard scales measured depression severity, internet use, sleep, and suicidal ideation. Scores on all three problem scales rose together, and the links were stronger in girls. A mediation analysis showed insomnia carried part of the path from internet addiction to suicidal thoughts. The authors urge sleep care as one lever in this group's treatment.
pmc-11657105:
Nurses Güzel Nur Yildiz, Meltem Şirin Gök, and Bahar Çiftçi built and tested a short scale that measures how comfortable patients feel during an injection. No sound tool for this job existed before. They drafted questions, checked them with experts, and tried the scale on patients at two hospitals, first in a small pilot and then in a larger group.

The final scale has ten items in two parts: comfort during the shot itself, and comfort from the room and setting. Scores matched a simple comfort rating scale well, and the tool proved steady and reliable. The authors suggest routine use, and tests in other languages and cultures.
pmc-11659005:
Zilong Fu and co-authors build a lightweight AI detector for diseases on grape leaves, designed to run in real time on modest hardware, in a 2024 paper. Fast, accurate diagnosis in the vineyard guides spraying and saves crops, but strong detectors are usually heavy. Their model, MHDI-DETR, trims a known detection design in three ways.

A mobile-grade backbone cuts the computing load. A rebuilt feature pyramid blends fine and coarse detail better, with an attention step that lingers on the regions that matter. A reshaped scoring rule for box overlap sharpens small-target detection and speeds learning. Against its parent design, the model shed over half its parameters and nearly half its arithmetic, while scoring a little higher on accuracy and on both grades of overlap quality. The authors pitch it for field devices.
pmc-11665305:
Peter and coauthors make bread wrap films from beeswax and a plastic base. The base film lets too much water vapor pass for food use. Beeswax and glycerin were added to fix that flaw. Heat treatment was also used to firm the film.

Tests showed new cross-links formed in the mixed film. Glycerin cut water loss on heating in the tests. Beeswax lifted heat stability of the film as well. The best film let far less vapor pass than the base. Its vapor rate sat much closer to standard wrap. Models linked vapor flow to swell and decay traits.
pmc-11665405:
The authors search saliva samples for molecular signs of obstructive sleep apnea in Black girls, a group where the condition often goes undiagnosed. Sleep apnea blocks the airway during sleep, and diagnosis in children is hard, above all in underrepresented populations. The team sequences the full genome's methylation marks and the RNA from saliva of healthy controls and children with the disorder.

Children with sleep apnea show disturbed pathways for inflammation and metabolism. Chromosomes 19 and 22 carry stronger methylation signatures in these patients. Joining the two data types points to specific candidate markers, including the genes NAP1L4, CCR1, and LIF. The authors stress that genes and environment both shape the disease. They present the markers as leads for fairer diagnostic tools.
pmc-11666505:
Li-Na Meng and Gang Li published a case report in twenty twenty-four on two severe bloodstream infections caught outside hospital. Such community-acquired infections kill readily, especially in older or immune-weakened people. Both patients arrived with hidden onset and rapid decline.

One infection followed unhygienic eating; the other followed repeated enemas that injured the gut. Blood gene sequencing named the culprits: Klebsiella pneumoniae in one case and Staphylococcus aureus in the other, both traced to the gastrointestinal tract. Targeted antibiotics, fluids, organ support, and surgery saved both patients. One developed dry gangrene in the limbs, possibly from blood-pressure drugs. The authors stress early source hunting and precise identification.
pmc-11667005:
Jia Wang and colleagues published a 2024 genetics study searching for causal asthma genes. Asthma treatments often fail to control symptoms fully. New drug targets are badly needed. The team combined gene activity with DNA methylation data. Genetic instruments tested cause rather than correlation.

Hundreds of genes differed in patients' blood. Several passed stricter causal tests. Some protective genes lowered asthma risk when more active. Methylation sites linked genes to disease in chains. Results were cross-checked against large genetic studies. Candidate genes were screened for drug potential. The multi-layer approach narrows a crowded field of suspects.
pmc-11672505:
Natalia Roson-Calero and co-authors shared a study in twenty twenty-four on a peptide called MV6. MV6 is a synthetic cyclic peptide. It helps a class of drugs called aminoglycosides work better. The target germ is Acinetobacter baumannii. This germ resists many drugs, in part through efflux pumps. Few new cures exist. A booster that brings old drugs back is thus a good path to try.

On its own, MV6 barely killed the germ. With the drugs, it beat a reference pump blocker. The gain was largest with netilmicin. Checkerboard assays showed strong synergy. The team grew spontaneous mutants too. They read the genomes of those mutants. That showed how resistance might emerge. The work presents MV6 as a candidate booster for drugs that fail.
pmc-11672705:
Hosam Safaa and a team of co-authors map simple sequence repeats across the rabbit genome. Their twenty twenty-four article studies microsatellites, short DNA motifs repeated in a row, which serve as markers for genetic diversity and breeding. The work is mostly computational, with lab checks on two rabbit breeds.

Software scanned all chromosomes and found over a million such loci. Two-letter repeats made up the vast share, and none were found in mitochondrial DNA. Twelve primer pairs were tested on Baladi and New Zealand White rabbits. The local Baladi breed showed higher diversity than the commercial breed, in both marker variety and population measures. The catalog can guide rabbit genetics work.
pmc-11674905:
Nergis Özlem Kılıç and co-authors look for gene signals in used embryo culture fluid that mark whether an embryo is developing, in a study from 2024. Reading the fluid is a gentle way to judge embryos, since the embryo itself is not touched. Three genes tied to growth and cell survival were tested.

The fluid came from twenty patients at a fertility center in Türkiye. Samples from developing and non-developing embryos were compared. One gene, linked to a cell maintenance enzyme, was higher in fluid from developing embryos. A second gene, tied to low oxygen response, was lower. A third gene, tied to cell division, showed no clear difference. The authors suggest the pattern reflects steady growth with less cell death.
pmc-11675205:
Jordi Maggi and co-authors present a 2024 study of a hidden gene flaw behind Stargardt disease, an inherited loss of central vision. Standard gene reads found one bad copy in a patient, but the disease needs two. Deeper reads of the whole gene and genome found the second flaw: a complex change deep inside a non-coding stretch, paired against the first.

Lab mini-gene tests showed the deep flaw forces extra gene pieces, called pseudoexons, into the message. Those pieces sit in normal messages too, but at trace levels. The flaw pushed their share far up. Two blocker strands were then tested as a rescue. The case shows why whole-gene hunts matter when one flaw hides, and it opens a path to splice-fixing drugs.
pmc-11675705:
Qin and coauthors model nerve spikes sparked by acupuncture at one leg point. Needling that point sends signals to spine nerve groups. Each needling style may spark a distinct spike pattern. The team sought a math model that captures those patterns.

Their model uses each nerve cell spike past as a base. It adds pull from the stimulus and from peer cells. Fit checks on fake data proved the method works well. Real data came from two needling styles at the point. The model split which factor drove spikes most. Their aim is a clear code for acupuncture signals.
pmc-11676105:
Obinna Anike leads a team on membrane removal of antibiotics from water. Their study from twenty twenty-four deals with nanofiltration membranes. Wide drug use leaves trace contaminants in the environment.

Two commercial membranes from one family were tested. Targets were two antibiotics and one diabetes drug. Membrane traits came from a neutral solute test. Varied run conditions shifted how much was retained. A lab scale unit and liquid analysis gave the data. Models were fit to the measured results. Such filters suit wastewater treatment at scale.  Rejection rates were the headline measures taken.
pmc-11676905:
Dania Martínez-Alarcón and co-authors test which parts of a bean protein kill colon cancer cells in a 2024 study. The protein is a lectin from tepary bean, rebuilt in the lab. It triggers suicide in colon cancer cells by reading sugar chains on their surface. Two arginine units in its binding pocket looked decisive.

The team swapped each arginine for a neutral stand-in and grew the mutants in yeast. Both swaps cut the killing power, one by about half and the other to a third. Docking models showed the mutants gripping certain cancer-linked sugars more weakly. The authors conclude both arginines anchor the lectin's hold on tumor cell sugars. That hold is what makes the protein toxic to those cells. The work refines a candidate anticancer agent at the level of single building blocks.
pmc-11677005:
Balázs Vida and seven co-authors lay out a plan to compare ways of finding a key lymph node in vulvar cancer care. This twenty twenty-four paper is a protocol, a plan written before the review runs. The cancer is rare and mostly strikes older women.

Doctors check the first lymph node the cancer would reach, which spares many women a full node removal and its harms. Tracers used to find that node include a faint radioactive dye, a glowing green dye, and iron-based particles. The planned review will search five databases under set rules and pool the results. The goal is a fair ranking of how well each tracer finds the node.
pmc-11677405:
Sretko Lukovic and co-authors measure how active people with rheumatoid arthritis are and what holds them back, in a study from 2024. Regular activity eases joint pain and stiffness and builds strength and fitness in this disease. Yet many patients move far less than advised.

Just over one hundred and thirty patients took part, most of them women. They filled in standard surveys on activity, fatigue, fear of movement, muscle loss risk, and depression. Disease activity and treatment data came from their records. A class analysis searched for hidden subgroups. About one in eight patients had low activity, just over half were in the middle, and about a third were highly active. Strong fatigue stood out in the results. The study maps who needs the most support to move.
pmc-11679005:
Hao Wang and co-authors published a 2024 study of fine dust particles in the air, PM2.5, and early harm to the kidneys of mice. The dust is one of the most common air pollutants in the world. It raises risk in many body systems, the urinary system included. The team exposed male and female mice to the dust for eight weeks.

Kidney tests showed early harm in the females alone: their glomeruli, the filtering units, took in too much, a state of over-filtration marking strain. The glomeruli grew until they filled their capsules. Gene readings pointed to two drivers. A pressure tug-of-war between two cell systems fell out of balance, which raised pressure inside the glomeruli. Blood sugar also rose, which dulled a feedback brake on the inflow vessels. Both fed the strain. The study is a sex-specific warning about a pollutant people breathe.
pmc-11679205:
Woori Ko and co-authors build, in a 2024 study, test cases for judging the driving safety of automated vehicles from real driving paths. Buyer trust needs proof that such cars were tested on sound, repeatable scenes. The team turned drone footage of highway ramp lane changes into a ladder of scenes, from broad sketches to exact cases.

Representative lane-change paths were pulled from the footage to anchor the scenes in real behavior. Simulations using a time-to-steer measure then picked the final test cases from the concrete set. The authors show the path-based cases work for safety grading. They also give a step-by-step recipe that other teams can apply to other driving patterns.
pmc-11679505:
Ali and five co-authors traced in twenty twenty-four how the Omicron strain of the Covid virus spread and changed in Florida. Omicron was first found in late twenty twenty-one and soon took over from the Delta strain world-wide. In Florida it drove a surge that topped all prior waves there.

They read more than one thousand viral gene sets from the state. New cases flowed in most from three large states, and spread out to far lands. Each sub-strain had its own path, and one could re-infect folks who had a prior one. By late twenty twenty-two, broad defense from shots and past ills slowed the wave.
pmc-11679605:
Dmitriy Viderman, Diyara Mukazhan, Kamilla Kapessova, Meiram Tungushpayev, and Rafael Badenes gather the best proof on ketamine for sharp, short-term pain. Their work is a review of reviews: they searched major databases and kept twenty systematic reviews on the drug. Most of those reviews scored low on quality checks, which the authors flag with care.

Across the proof, ketamine given by vein around surgery cut pain soon after treatment. It also cut the need for opioid pain drugs in the first two days by a wide margin, and lowered nausea. The paper weighs the drug as a helpful add-on in care around surgery, while calling for stronger studies.
pmc-11679805:
Xiang An and colleagues built a tiny heart-rhythm classifier that can run on a wearable device with a single chest lead. Full hospital systems read many leads with big models that small gadgets cannot carry. The team used a teaching trick: a large model trained a small one to copy its skill.

The small model scored over ninety-six percent accuracy, near its teacher, while shrinking to a sliver of the size. It beat other small models in their tests. The team then built a working wearable monitor around cheap chips. It sorts rhythms live, a step toward round-the-clock heart checks outside hospitals.
pmc-11680005:
Jing Wang and colleagues watch adverse events after the shingles vaccine in older adults in Hangzhou. Their surveillance study from twenty twenty-four covers the first years after launch in China. The recombinant vaccine protects against painful shingles. Post-marketing data confirm safety in real local populations.

Two hundred seventy-five event reports followed vaccination in the city. The reporting rate was well under one per thousand doses. Only one case was classed as serious overall. Women and the youngest eligible age group reported more events. First doses drew more reports than second doses. Nearly all events were ordinary vaccine reactions. Local data reassure older adults considering the shot.
pmc-11680105:
Megan Neary and co-authors wrote a 2024 paper on pairing two antiviral drugs against the virus that causes COVID-19. Each drug, favipiravir and remdesivir, can slow the virus on its own. The team tested whether giving both together works better in Syrian golden hamsters, a standard animal model for this infection.

Hamsters were infected with an early variant and treated by injection. Four days later, the team measured virus in the nose and lungs. All three treatments lowered virus levels in the lungs against a sham treatment. The pair did best overall, cutting virus in more places than either drug alone. Results like this guide which drug pairs deserve trials in people.
pmc-11685005:
Sangyub Kim and Kichun Nam study how the two brain halves work together in word recognition. They use familiarity as a mark of proficiency. Word processing is split unevenly across the halves. The team held a clear hypothesis: the primary half chiefly guides how the two interact. They used a primed lateralized lexical decision task. Primes and targets went to left or right visual fields, with a brief gap.

A clear familiarity effect across the halves showed in response times, when the right half got the prime and the left got the target. A clear effect within one half also showed, in the right half. As a set, results point to a strong role for the right half in visual-perceptual processing as skill grows. The effect thus tracks more than skill: a shift in how labor is split, and a sign of expertise in routing across the halves.
pmc-11688405:
Diego Esperante and eight colleagues pool the evidence on whether mutations in the TP53 gene predict how long glioblastoma patients live, in a systematic review and meta-analysis published in two thousand twenty-four. Glioblastoma is the most aggressive common brain tumor, and any reliable prognostic marker would help doctors plan and counsel.

The review searched multiple databases for longitudinal studies and trials with at least forty adults whose tumors sat in the upper brain and whose TP53 status was known. Twenty-three papers covering over two and a half thousand patients met the bar. The authors rated the risk of bias with a prognosis-specific tool and graded the certainty of evidence. They then combined overall survival and progression-free survival results across studies. Whether its variants carry weight in this tumor is a narrower question, and this synthesis answers it with the full literature.
pmc-11689205:
Yuan and nine colleagues catalogue the kinesin gene family in pea in twenty twenty-four. Kinesins are motor proteins that move cargo inside cells. Pea is a key model for plant development and stress research. Its kinesin family had not been mapped before.

They found one hundred five kinesin genes in seven subfamilies. Comparisons with Arabidopsis and soybean showed uneven spread across groups. Duplication of genome segments drove the family's growth, under purifying selection. Thirty-eight genes showed tissue specific activity in roots, stems, petals, or seeds. Some switched on under drought, others under salt stress. The authors nominate those genes as candidates for breeding tougher peas.
pmc-11689405:
Jennifer Severance and Sara Murphy describe a federally funded program that trains the health workforce for age-friendly care in rural Texas. The state faces many rural hospital closures and severe shortages of primary care staff. Writing in twenty twenty-four, they outline a geriatrics workforce enhancement program built on partnerships among universities, primary care practices, long-term care providers, and community groups. The symposium report walks through the overall strategy first, with local partners treated as the experts on rural needs, then presents individual training projects.

Learners range from medical students and residents to practicing care teams and older adults with their caregivers, who act as change agents rather than passive recipients. Technology is used to stretch training across distance. Goals include stronger local capacity for quality elder care and wider spread of proven age-friendly practices at personal, community, and population levels.
pmc-11691405:
Jessica Maras and Kate Leger tested, in a 2024 study, whether cognitive reappraisal can soften stress reactivity, and whether age changes the effect. Cognitive reappraisal means reframing a stressful task in a more positive way. The study included 139 adults, with 89 younger and 50 older participants. Of these, 71 received the reappraisal prompt before a stress-inducing task, and 68 served as controls.

Reactivity was measured through negative affect, somatic symptoms such as stomach ache, and blood pressure after the task, with baseline levels taken into account. The one clear result ran against the authors' hopes. Older adults who received no prompt showed smaller blood pressure responses than older adults who used reappraisal. No other clear effects appeared. The authors caution that reappraisal may not help every age group, and that such strategies should be matched to the person.
pmc-11691805:
Hannah Friedland, Ashley Stripling, and Jillian Crocker published a review in 2024 of prolonged grief disorder in adults over sixty-five. The condition received formal diagnostic criteria in a major mental health manual in 2022. The COVID-19 pandemic affected this age group heavily and disrupted the traditional rituals that help people mourn.

The reviewers searched two sources for studies from 2013 to 2023 and kept fifteen that met their criteria. Prevalence rates ranged from under one percent to twenty-one percent. Participants were predominantly white women recruited from community and hospice samples. Preexisting depression raised the risk of the disorder. The death of a partner or a child brought the highest rates. Associated features included sleep disturbances, lower quality of life, and stress hormones out of balance. The authors urge accurate identification and sound treatment, along with further research.
pmc-11692105:
Elizabeth Anquillare and co-authors report a small pilot study from 2024 on how older adults who use cannabis judge their own thinking. The group had seventeen people aged sixty to seventy-nine. Each person filled in forms about their memory, focus, and planning, and then took short tests of the same skills online.

The team compared the self-ratings with test scores in each area. Weak scores on tasks that call for switching and holding back a response went with self-ratings across all three areas. Scores for memory and focus showed a weaker pattern in the same direction. The authors say these adults tend to describe their thinking in broad terms. They urge care staff to ask more pointed questions.
pmc-11692305:
Bennett Van Camp and Sean Curran report in twenty twenty-four on stress defense in the small worm Caenorhabditis elegans. A gene switch named SKN-1 helps the worm fight stress, but if it stays on, it can harm health late in life. The team bred worms by picking late young over many rounds to see how parent age shapes the health of the young.

Worms bred this way lost ground on many health marks. They fought stress less well, moved less, grew at odd rates, and lived for less time. When the age pick was lifted, some health marks shifted at once in the next brood. The authors say this points to a set point in parents that marks the span of their breeding years and sets stress strength in their young.
pmc-11692705:
Alfred Boakye and Jennifer Morgan published a study in 2024 on how direct care workers in nursing homes cope with persistent challenges through team functioning. Nursing homes face staffing shortages, heavy workloads, and residents with high care needs. Strong teams therefore matter for delivering good, person-centered care.

The researchers held extended interviews with twenty-five nursing assistants at two nursing centers known for high-quality care. Most participants were Black women in their forties. The assistants named strategies that helped their teams work well. These included defined team structures, breaking up cliques, and working side by side more often. They also supported check-ins tailored to each worker, by email, by phone, or in daily group huddles. The authors argue that nursing home leaders could benefit from supporting these practices, to improve care for residents and reduce strain on staff.
pmc-11709505:
Flavia Pereira and five co-authors compare gene changes across small animal models of Alzheimer's disease and mice. Their study came out in 2025. Worms, flies, and zebrafish are cheaper and simpler than rodents, but researchers must know whether they mirror the same disease biology.

The team mined a public repository of gene expression studies in all four species. Zebrafish shared the most changed genes with mice. Flies shared the most biological processes with mice, even where the exact genes differed. Shared processes were classic features of the disease: misfolded protein responses, inflammation, nerve signaling, and metabolism. Worms overlapped least with the vertebrates. The authors conclude these small models can speed the search for new treatments, if their limits are respected.
pmc-11719105:
Upasana Mukherjee and three co-authors sum how lost sleep plays with dementia and its mate ills. Their review appeared in twenty twenty-four. Heart ill, sugar ill, fat state, low mood, and gland ills oft ride with dementia and cloud its care. Sleep loss is both common in such folks and a driver of fast thought fall and kin load.

Paths by which mate ills mar sleep and thought are traced, with fix-able risks marked. Joint care that meets thought and sleep needs at once is urged. The team call for work on set cures for sleep loss in dementia to lift life for folks and kin.
pmc-11728105:
Venkateshvaran and three co-authors test a new heart check that uses leg lifts, in a study from twenty twenty-four. Some people with weak hearts look fine at rest but strain when blood flow rises fast. Lifting the legs sends more blood to the heart at once. The team pairs sound scans of the heart with a thin tube test that reads pressure.

They studied thirty-five patients and twenty healthy adults of the same age. They plot how the top left heart chamber stretches as it fills. The slope of that plot was much lower in patients than in healthy adults. A low slope flagged high pressure with strong skill. It beat two older scan scores by a clear margin.
pmc-11758505:
A team led by Chen Huang compared two ways to locate small lung spots that cannot be felt, before surgery to remove them. One way guides a needle through the skin using CT scans. The new way maps the drainage basin of the vein near the spot and marks tissue from inside. Records covered fifty patients with spots under two centimeters.

The vein method found the spot in ninety-four percent of cases, against ninety percent for the needle method, a gap too small to call real. Surgery time, blood loss, drainage, and hospital stay also matched. The authors judge the vein method a safe, painless equal that merits wider use.
pmc-11786005:
AbdelRahman Abdelhameed and two colleagues published a dental materials study in two thousand twenty-four on colour change in a glass ceramic. The material mixes zirconia into lithium disilicate for strong, natural-looking crowns. Dentists need to know whether light exposure ages its colour.

Seventy-two samples of the new material and a standard rival were made in four thicknesses. All sat under ultraviolet light for a period mimicking a year of service. The new material stayed more translucent than the rival before and after aging, at every thickness. Thicker pieces were less translucent in both. However, the new material shifted colour more. The authors conclude the standard material holds colour better.
pmc-11805305:
Abhishek Sinha and co-authors report a trial from two thousand twenty-four comparing toothbrush designs for people with disabilities. Physical, cognitive, and sensory limits make oral care hard in this group, and gum disease is common. The team asked whether a modified manual brush or a powered brush protects gum health better when users are trained well.

One hundred sixty-two adults with gingivitis and varied disabilities joined the trial. Each group received training tailored to its brush. Gum and plaque scores were checked at the start and at four, eight, and twelve weeks. Both groups improved a lot. The powered brush edged ahead on gum inflammation, and its users reported higher satisfaction and ease of use, with comfort about equal.
pmc-11816105:
Sumit Aggarwal and colleagues test drone delivery of medicines in the Himalayas. Their feasibility study from twenty twenty-four runs around Keylong in Himachal Pradesh. Heavy winter snow cuts off remote villages for months. Healthcare delivery fails exactly when roads close.

Fifteen drone flights carried medicines and clinical samples successfully. Health workers described local facilities and winter challenges. The mixed study design joined flight data with worker insight. Drones crossed terrain that ambulances cannot reach in snow. Sample transport back to labs also proved workable. Cold, altitude, and wind remain real operating limits. Mountain health systems gain a proven backup supply route.
pmc-12661705:
Léa Fieschi-Méric and co-authors asked why some ribbed newts fall badly ill from a fungal skin disease while others resist. The fungus, Bsal, is one of two chytrid fungi devastating amphibians worldwide. Skin bacteria are known to interact with the other fungus, so the team checked whether a newt's skin microbes predict its fate with Bsal. Captive newts from different source groups carried distinct skin communities even under identical care. Yet neither the diversity nor the makeup of those communities before exposure predicted infection strength or severity.

What did predict the outcome was the newt's source group, pointing to factors in the host itself rather than its microbes. Infection also failed to shake the skin community in proportion to its severity. The authors conclude the microbiota plays a limited role in this species' response to Bsal. They say other mechanisms behind individual resistance need study.
pmc-12662205:
Vicente-Muñoz and six co-authors studied how the body uses fuel in Fanconi anemia in twenty twenty-five. Fanconi anemia is a rare inherited disorder marked by birth defects, bone marrow failure, and higher cancer risk. About eighty percent of patients also show metabolic problems, such as poor growth and diabetes risk.

The team tracked a labeled form of glucose through the body after a meal. Unlike healthy controls, patients showed no rise in energy use after eating. Blood sugar stayed high, sugar breakdown rose, and the body made far more ketones, signs of a shift toward burning fat. Hormone patterns also differed. The authors say the findings reveal rigid, altered fuel use that could guide food and treatment choices.
pmc-12663405:
Wei Zheng and co-authors map, in a 2025 study, protein building inside human cells at near-atomic detail, using a cryo-imaging method that works in place. Past maps came from purified parts, which lose the cell's true setting. The team froze cells, milled them thin with an ion beam, and imaged the ribosomes where they sat.

They resolved the full human ribosome and twenty-three working states, most at very fine detail. Helper proteins and ion sites appeared that purification usually strips away. Chains of ribosomes wound in spirals along one message, as in living cells. Two blocking drugs froze distinct states, and a natural cell compound was caught sharing a drug's pocket. The native view redraws the textbook picture.
pmc-12695905:
Xi Chen and co-authors isolate, in a 2025 study, two new viruses that attack a hospital germ which resists many drugs. Such viruses, called phages, are being eyed as a backup therapy when antibiotics fail. The team tested the pair against drug-resistant strains of the germ and mapped their traits in detail.

One phage stayed active after heat, strong alkali, and three months of storage, and made modest bursts of new copies per cell. The other was less hardy but made huge bursts. Microscope images and genome reads showed both are new types, with no resistance or toxin genes found. The pair joins the pool of candidates for phage therapy trials.
pmc-12699805:
Dan Xu and a team of co-authors mine gene data for drug targets in polycystic ovary syndrome, in a paper dated twenty twenty-five. The common hormone disorder lacks targeted therapies. Their computer-only workflow screened 2,888 druggable genes with genetic causal tests.

Seven genes passed strict checks: four raised risk and three lowered it. One gene, NRBP1, showed the strongest confirmed link. Tissue checks spanned ovary, uterus, and blood, and cell maps charted the ovarian setting. Docking tests then matched candidate drugs to the gene products, setting up lab work to follow.
pmc-12707005:
Bianca Vitória dos Santos Barbosa and co-authors present a 2025 study on gentler dialysis schedules for kidney failure. Standard hemodialysis runs three long sessions a week and often wipes out the patient's remaining kidney function fast. Incremental dialysis starts smaller, with fewer or shorter sessions, and grows only as needed.

The case-control study covered eighty patients who began treatment between January 2021 and January 2023. Groups were matched on age, sex, disease, and lab values. After two years, forty-five percent of the incremental group still had working residual kidney function. None of the standard group did. The gentler group also had fewer infections and a longer time before losing that function. Diabetes and high blood pressure were the main causes of kidney failure.
pmc-12715205:
Ali and five colleagues tune a manganite material by adding calcium in twenty twenty-five. Lanthanum calcium manganite nanoparticles are used in energy conversion devices. Changing the calcium share may adjust their optical and electrical behaviour. The team made samples with three calcium levels.

All samples shared the same crystal structure, with grains tens of nanometres wide. Microscopy showed clumped spherical particles of similar size. Chemical checks confirmed the intended ingredients. The optical band gap shrank as calcium rose, from three point nine five to three point seven four electron volts. Dielectric loss fell as frequency and calcium increased. Electrical conductivity also grew with calcium content. The authors link the changes to refractive index shifts.
pmc-12718505:
Beate Vesterskov and Louise Schlosser Mose listen, in a study whose journal version is dated 2025, to patients who graduated from a headache school. Chronic headache erodes work, social life, and self-trust. The Danish clinic's answer is an eleven-session group program informed by acceptance and commitment therapy. It trains people to live by their values alongside pain, rather than waiting for pain to leave. Thirty-six completers, in nine focus groups, described what the course changed.

Three themes emerged. Recognition: learning the illness is real, with a name and mechanisms. Acceptance: making peace with its permanence without surrendering to it. Belonging: a room where nothing needed explaining, apologizing for, or defending. Patients reported clearer communication of their limits and choices steered by values, not symptoms. The authors argue the group itself, often treated as a delivery detail, was half the medicine.
pmc-12724105:
Ruxandra Ioana Toma, Lauren Blunstone, Mario Juruena, and Susannah Pick listen to people who live with atypical depression. Their study, from twenty twenty-five, asks how sufferers explain their own illness. This form of depression differs from the classic kind in mood and body signs. It also strikes women more often, for reasons that are unclear.

Sixteen people took part in one-to-one online interviews. Themes cover other illnesses that ride along and blur the picture. Trauma stood out as both cause and trigger in their accounts. Gender roles and identity shaped how the illness felt and showed. Daily swings in symptoms made life hard to plan. Coping habits close out the themes.
pmc-12729105:
Huimin Ding, Liqun Jiang, Hyun Seo, and Buongo Chun set sport types and doses side by side for gains in risky blood fats in metabolic syndrome. Sport is a key cure, but which type and how much stayed dim. The 2025 review searched four data banks for trials picked at random in adults with the syndrome. A set of 49 trials with 4,144 people met the bar. The work joined pair tests, web tests, and dose curve tests.

A set of 88 sport arms took in hard burst drills, plain aerobic sport, weight work, and mixed plans. Trial grade was scored with stock bias and trust tools. To rank sport types next to each other, and next to dose, gives staff a firm base for plans they write. People with this syndrome face high heart risk. So plain fat gains from the right sport plan still count a lot.
pmc-12731905:
Jiawei Ren and co-authors build a more robust way to pull guidance data from noisy sensor readings, in work from two thousand twenty-five. Real noise often breaks the neat bell shape that many filters assume. Noise can also shift in ways that are hard to pin down, which can throw a filter off course.

Their frame blends a robust scoring method with a learning-based filter. Extra math steps keep the sums stable, and a new kernel shape handles harsh noise from wide views and glare. Tests in clean and harsh noise both held high accuracy. The work aims at guidance design and filter research.
pmc-12732205:
Eleni Papamattheou and co-authors examine a growth pathway in a rare, harsh breast cancer, in a 2025 study. The cancer, metaplastic breast carcinoma, mixes several cell types, ignores hormone signals, and carries a poor outlook. The Hippo pathway, recently tied to cancer growth and drug resistance, was their focus.

Tissue from forty-four patients treated between 2003 and 2021 was stained and gene-tested for three pathway players. A strong signal from the pathway's effector pair appeared in about sixty-one percent of tumors. The team related each marker to the tumors' clinical traits. If the pathway helps drive this cancer, its parts could serve as both forecast markers and drug targets. The study is an early map in a cancer with few guides.
pmc-12732405:
Su and colleagues test a gut germ as a mood lift in sad mice in this twenty twenty-five study. Sad mood ills tie to gut germ shifts through the gut-brain line. One germ kind may calm the ill by that line's paths.

Inside, a germ sap shot set off sad acts in mice for the model. Fed germ then eased those sad acts at the top dose tried. Fire marks in blood and brain fell as the germ fed on. Gut germ bands re-set and fat sap goods rose in the mice. Mood sap marks in the brain also swung back toward sound.
pmc-12732605:
Arda Uzunoglu and co-authors pool trials of massage therapy for cancer symptoms in a review from two thousand twenty-five. Cancer and its treatment bring pain, anxiety, and low quality of life. Massage is proposed as a gentle add-on that calms stress systems.

Seven randomized trials met the rules across six databases. Massage beat control care on behavior symptom counts, quality-of-life scores, anxiety scores, and symptom intensity. All gaps were statistically clear. Yet the proof base was thin, with varied methods and bias risks. The authors say massage may ease symptoms in the short term as support care. Stronger trials with set protocols are needed.
pmc-12732805:
Anna Mikolajczuk-Szczyrba and co-authors set out the traits of antibiotic resistance in gut lactic acid bacteria from places where livestock are kept. Their 2025 study joins lab tests of how drugs act on the bacteria with whole-genome sequencing.

Four strains came from faeces of farm animals. Each was tested next to nine antibiotics. All showed resistance to at least one class of drug. That was most often the aminoglycosides. The genome did not at all times match what the lab tests showed. That hints at resistance built in, and tied to how drugs are taken up, in some cases. One strain held a gene for resistance, yet the drug tied to that gene still worked on it. Sequencing also placed the genes on chromosomes or on plasmids. Bacteria that live in the gut in peace can act as stores of resistance.
pmc-12733405:
Bogna Grygiel-Górniak and co-authors report a study from two thousand twenty-five on quality of life in people with long-standing rheumatoid arthritis. The disease brings pain, stiff movement, poor sleep, and higher risk of depression. Treatment helps, but the authors ask what else shapes daily life for these patients.

The team studied patients at one center whose disease was quiet at the time. They used standard surveys on quality of life, mood, and sleep, in people ill for a median of nineteen years. Only about a quarter slept well, and about a fifth showed signs of stronger depression. Younger age, being married, and good sleep linked to the best scores. The work points to sleep and mood care as extra support.
pmc-12733705:
Omar Abusedera and colleagues pooled trial evidence in 2025 on whether semaglutide restores the pancreas's own insulin-making cells in type 2 diabetes. The disease involves progressive failure of beta cells alongside insulin resistance. Semaglutide, a long-acting GLP-1 drug, clearly improves blood sugar and weight, but its direct effect on beta-cell function was uncertain. The reviewers searched three major databases for randomized trials through April 2025.

Following standard meta-analysis guidelines, two reviewers extracted data and judged bias independently. The main outcomes were established indices of beta-cell function and insulin resistance, including HOMA-B and the proinsulin-to-insulin ratio. Secondary outcomes covered insulin secretion measures and C-peptide. Pooling matters because single trials are small and their beta-cell results have pointed in different directions. A clear answer affects how doctors think about the drug: symptom control, or partial repair.
pmc-12733905:
Roberto Araya and Pablo González-Vicente measure trust in young schoolchildren, in a paper dated twenty twenty-five. Nearly three thousand fourth graders from 135 schools played a public goods game. Their choices showed how much they trusted classmates versus outsiders.

Trust ran much higher toward the in-group than the out-group. Boys trusted more than girls on the whole. Public school pupils trusted more than those in state-aided private schools. Kind and careful traits, drawn from a picture-based trait test, also predicted more trust. The study maps how trust grows in the classroom.
pmc-12735205:
Kübra Yıldız-Güler and colleagues report a 2025 trial in Turkey on how often diet advice should come, and whether phone-based follow-ups help. Their patients had metabolic syndrome, a cluster of risks that includes belly fat, high blood pressure, and poor blood sugar control. Diet care works, but busy clinics struggle to see patients often.

Ninety-three patients were split by chance into three groups. One group met a dietitian four times in person over twelve weeks. A second group got those visits plus weekly remote check-ins. The control group met only at the start and the end. More frequent contact went with better eating, body measures, blood results, and blood pressure. Adding remote calls strengthened the gains. The results support building regular follow-up into diet care.
pmc-12737205:
Andres Arana-Linares and co-authors review whether active packaging made from natural polymers, now common for food, could work for cosmetics, in a paper from 2025. Such packaging does more than hold a product: it can slow decay and fight germs. Buyers of cosmetics want greener packs with fewer added preservatives.

The team searched nine databases for work from 2000 to 2025. Four materials came up most often: chitosan, fish gelatin, zein, and kafirin. All break down in nature, form films well, and mix with natural additives. Their own germ-fighting and protective powers are weak but can be boosted by added plant compounds. Casting, coating, and fiber spinning were the best ways to shape them. Cost and feel remain barriers.
pmc-12738605:
Chisari and a large group of co-authors test whether rituximab works for people with relapsing multiple sclerosis who stop stronger therapies. Stopping such drugs can let the disease flare again. The study drew on an Italian registry and followed 362 patients after they switched.

Patients had come off five different earlier drugs for safety or effect reasons. After two years on rituximab, several groups showed less relapse-linked and silent disability worsening. Outcomes stayed stable in the group that had used natalizumab. Higher disability before treatment meant higher risk of later silent progression. The authors present rituximab as a workable option after highly active therapies end.
pmc-12742105:
Cara M Gill and colleagues offer a two thousand twenty-five protocol for a prospective study using home lung-function data to explain poorly controlled asthma. Many patients stay symptomatic despite inhalers, for mixed reasons: missed doses, poor technique, allergens, or look-alike conditions. Confirming asthma itself is the cause comes first.

Enrolled patients will be followed for twenty-six weeks across five visits. Digital records combine home breathing measurements with medication-use tracking. Inflammation markers join the dataset. The hypothesis is that dense home data beats usual guideline checks at pinning symptoms on asthma versus its imitators, sharpening treatment decisions.
pmc-12743405:
Graczyk and a team including Kurpisz study how sperm sorting changes sperm traits in twenty twenty-five. Sperm chromosomes sit in set positions inside the nucleus. That layout may affect early embryo growth after fertilization. Clinics sort sperm to pick cells with good movement and shape.

The team used semen samples from five men with normal sperm counts. Samples were sorted by swim up or by a density gradient method. A new staining sequence let them study the same single sperm cell in several ways. Sorted sperm showed better chromatin packing and higher levels of two DNA marks. They also showed much less DNA fragmentation of one type. Sex chromosomes shifted toward the edge of the nucleus in high quality sperm.
pmc-12747105:
Arad Iranmehr and five co-authors report a case of focused radiation treatment for cancer spread to the brain, in a paper from twenty twenty-five. Guidelines usually steer frail patients with many brain lesions toward comfort care alone. Whether targeted radiation can help such patients is debated.

Their patient had lung cancer that had spread widely in the brain, after earlier whole-brain radiation. The team gave two separate courses of split-dose targeted radiation to the lesions. The patient's nerve symptoms improved markedly afterward. Treating in two courses may also spare healthy brain by shortening each round. The authors argue such treatment deserves a place for frail patients, mainly to protect quality of life, even if survival gains are unsure.
pmc-12747405:
Brianna Jackson and co-authors listened to young Canadians who had aged out of foster care, to learn how the abrupt move to independence shapes mental health. Each year thousands leave care at nineteen, just as adult pressures and mental health risks climb. The study combined a survey of 203 young adults with in-depth interviews of 31, mixing statistics with personal accounts.

Survey modeling linked experiences of structural violence, before and after leaving care, with mental health struggles and with positive adaptation. Nine interview themes filled in the context of that transition, and combined displays merged the two strands. The authors argue the findings expose both the system's harms and the young people's capacity to adapt, and point to care designed around this group's specific needs.
pmc-12748005:
Soumya Patil and three co-authors cure a rare womb-wall pregnancy with drug doses in place of cuts. Their case study appeared in twenty twenty-five. Such growths sit in the tube's wall span, are hard to spot, and can bleed hard if they burst. A woman of thirty, first with child, came with low belly pain and spots at near six weeks.

Scans set the call. She was sound and fit drug care, so four drug doses ran with close blood and scan checks. The growth mark fell step by step and scans cleared. She stayed sound and her month flow came back in twenty-six days.
pmc-12748305:
Sekgotodi, Ng'ambi, Mabelebele, and Manyelo feed in twenty twenty-five varied levels of one amino acid to native Boschveld chickens to find the best dose. This hardy local breed matters for low-cost farming in South Africa. The team raised two hundred day-old chicks on five diets with rising levels of the amino acid, a building block for protein.

Dose shaped feed intake, weight gain, feed efficiency, and many gut measures, including gut part lengths and weights. Some traits, like several gut acid levels, did not respond to dose. Each trait peaked at a different dose, so no single level was best for all. One gut part's weight peaked at a mid dose. The authors say more work is needed to fix a firm feeding guide.
pmc-12748605:
Yi, Xie, Fan, Liu, Yang, and Liu probe in twenty twenty-five how faulty sugar handling develops in rats, as a step toward grasping early diabetes. Faulty sugar tolerance is the stage before full type two diabetes, yet its drivers are poorly known. The team created the condition in rats with a fatty diet plus a chemical dose, then read all active genes in liver tissue.

Over fifteen hundred genes shifted activity, split between genes switched up and genes switched down. One fat-sensing pathway stood at the centre of the change. Four genes emerged as key nodes, confirmed by protein tests, and blood levels of several swelling signals rose. The authors propose linked pathways that may drive the condition and offer targets for early care.
pmc-12750205:
Josip Jurković and four colleagues published a 2025 study of farm soil and crops after severe floods in central Bosnia and Herzegovina in the autumn of 2024. Floodwater can carry sewage, heavy metals, and germs onto fields. Plants may take these hazards into their roots, stems, and leaves.

The team took 21 samples of soil and sludge from flooded areas and prepared them to measure metals in two forms. They also sampled chard plants from flooded plots and from clean control plots, splitting each plant into roots, stems, and leaves. Their checks show what the flood left behind in soil and food plants, which matters for deciding when flooded land is safe to farm again.
pmc-12750705:
Hesnard and co-authors chart how a social amoeba rewires itself when oxygen runs low in this 2025 study. Most complex life uses oxygen to make energy. Mammals answer low oxygen through a master switch called HIF-1, but protists lack that network.

The team held Dictyostelium discoideum at 1 percent oxygen for 24 hours, then restored normal air. A striking 32 percent of measured gene transcripts changed level during the low-oxygen phase. The biggest shifts came early, at one hour, and late, at 24 hours. Protein levels followed the gene changes with a lag and matched them only modestly. Metabolic and chromosome pathways moved together across both layers. The atlas fills a gap in protist stress biology.
pmc-12751405:
Elisa Zanello, Adele Maggiore, Raffaella Dobrina, and a wider team wrote this research paper, published in 2025. It measures how continuous and coordinated care really is for children with special health needs in northeastern Italy, from both the system's records and parents' own ratings.

These children see many professionals across many settings, so their care frays easily. Over twenty-one months the team enrolled families at a university hospital and logged a year of care from family pediatricians, general practitioners, and community services. Nine to twelve months later, parents scored continuity on a twenty-item questionnaire. In 2020 the study also asked how the pandemic had bent their care. Most of the fifty-one children had cancer-related conditions. The authors use the findings to show where handoffs hold and where families are left stitching the system together themselves.
pmc-12752105:
Michael Jung and Craig Kuhns report two-year results for a back fusion implant in a 2025 study. The target is the sacroiliac joint, where the spine meets the pelvis, a common source of lasting low back pain. Their implant is a porous threaded device, printed in titanium, placed from the side through a lateral route. The team reviewed charts from two centers.

Forty-nine patients had surgery between early 2022 and mid 2023 and full two-year follow-up. The average age was about sixty-four, and most patients were women. No problems were tied to the device or the procedure itself. Average pain fell from about nine out of ten to under three, a large drop. Gains were alike across surgeons and held for patients who had past lower back fusion. No implant broke or moved.
pmc-12752905:
Khulood Ali Al-Taezi and co-authors chart the hidden hollow at the back of the lower jaw, a curve that can endanger dental implants. Using cone-beam scans from 406 adults, they sorted the jaw ridge into three shapes: undercut, parallel, and convex. They then measured the lingual concavity, the inward dip on the tongue side, against sex and tooth loss.

The undercut shape was by far the most common, at about sixty-four percent, and it clustered at the second molars. The convex shape grew more likely the longer a tooth had been gone. Men showed larger ridges and larger concavities across many measures. The dip most often sat at or above the level of the jaw's nerve canal. The authors say these patterns should guide implant planning tooth by tooth.
pmc-12755105:
Ashish Joshi and a large team of co-authors map how health diplomacy is taught around the world. Their scoping review appeared in twenty twenty-five. Health diplomacy, the negotiation side of global health, matters more each year, yet training for it lags behind.

The team gathered peer-reviewed articles, frameworks, and reports on courses and teaching models. They charted who is trained, in what formats, and toward which skills. Modern health work needs skill in negotiation, cross-cultural dealings, and policy influence. Competency-based teaching, which targets skills that can be seen and measured, frames much of the field. The review shows where programs cluster and where assessment of skills stays thin, guiding schools that plan new offerings.
pmc-12764105:
Yunxian Chen and five co-authors report a case of infection on a replaced heart valve that threw clots to the heart, brain, and leg. Their report came out in 2025. Infection of a prosthetic valve is a grave condition with a high risk of death.

A man in his early fifties came in with chest pain and short breath, years after valve surgery. Scans showed a blocked heart artery, which was opened with a balloon procedure. Ultrasound found growths on the valve, and a gene test of his blood named the infecting germ. During care, a clot blocked his right leg and small strokes appeared in his brain. After six weeks of antibiotics he went home improved, though the valve still worked poorly.
pmc-12771205:
Liping He and co-authors build a machine learning model that predicts which newborns will suffer kidney injury after surgery, in a 2025 study. Kidney injury is a serious complication in hospitalized newborns and is easy to miss early. The team gathered records for 2,025 neonates and split them into training and test sets.

Twenty-five variables fed the models, from age and operation length to fluids given and output after surgery. Six algorithms competed, and a classic logistic regression won, with the best balance of catching cases and not over-calling them. About 5.4 percent of the babies developed the injury. Age, operation duration, and urine output carried the most weight in the predictions. An explanation tool then showed, baby by baby, how the winning model reached each call.
pmc-12777405:
Yonghua Li, Qinchuan Ran, Hezhou Jiang, and Song Yao link environment traits to heart disease burden across China. Their study, from twenty twenty-five, uses twenty years of provincial data. Heart and vessel disease causes about forty percent of deaths in China. Five macro traits are tested: air quality, green space, public services, nature protection, and transport.

A structural model sorts direct from knock-on effects. City growth cuts burden through better transport links. Nature reserves give the strongest direct shield, with effects that lag in time. Green space and services reinforce each other strongly. Some provinces, named in the paper, carry high risk and need local plans.
pmc-12785805:
Setia and a large team of colleagues chart two kin immune ills in patients sent to one hub in India in this twenty twenty-five study. Both ills stem from a loss of self-tolerance in the body guard and share deep roots. That shared base makes their signs blur into each other at the bedside.

Inside, twenty-nine patients from across India were charted for signs, guard traits, and gene codes. Low blood counts, gland swell, and gut swelling led the signs in both ills. One ill showed more chest and ear catches and low guard stores than the other. Blood cell counts split the two ills on some T cell shares. Gene tests pinned the cause in case after case.
pmc-12787005:
Levi-Gofman, Atar, Grosbard, and Moady report a study from twenty twenty-five on heart tracings in a stress heart condition. The condition can mimic a heart attack, with like signs and raised blood markers. The team reviewed one hundred nineteen patients treated from twenty eighteen to twenty twenty-four. Half showed a raised segment pattern on their first heart tracing. The team compared heart pump strength and outcomes between the two tracing groups.

Patients with the raised pattern had weaker heart pumping and higher blood markers. They also had more heart failure and rhythm problems during care. After checks for other factors, weak pumping alone linked to more problems. Return visits to hospital were the same in both groups. The authors say the first tracing marks disease severity.
pmc-12788105:
Widartha and Kim present an anomaly detection model for indoor environment sensor data, in work from twenty twenty-five. Smart buildings stream temperature, humidity, and air quality data from many sensors at once. Subtle faults hide inside noisy, fluctuating readings.

Their hybrid model, HIPER-CHAD, separates two jobs: modeling normal behavior over time, and modeling the uncertainty of its own predictions. Anomaly scores then resist random noise yet stay sensitive to true abnormal events. Reliable detection supports ventilation control, energy savings, and early warning of equipment failure in buildings that run on sensor data.
pmc-12788205:
Qian Xu and four co-authors clean up the noisy renders produced by HumanNeRF, a system that rebuilds moving people in three dimensions. Its images suffer noise and lost detail from incomplete training data and rendering sampling. Their denoiser needs no labeled clean images.

Self-supervised contrastive learning first teaches the network to tell noise patterns from genuine human detail by comparing constructed sample pairs. A generative adversarial network then sharpens the result, its discriminator pushing the generator toward realism. Experiments showed effective noise removal with significantly better detail fidelity. Cleaner renders feed directly into more convincing three-dimensional human reconstruction for film, games, and telepresence.
pmc-12801605:
Sahar El-Kholy, Maher Helal, and Hossam Emam coat viscose fabric with palladium particles in a 2025 paper. Long UV exposure and microbe growth are growing health concerns, and treated textiles can help. Their method uses infrared light to seed tiny palladium particles inside the fabric.

They varied the salt strength, acidity, and a pre-treatment step to control particle size. Treated samples showed small, well-spread spherical particles under the best conditions. The fabric gained strong to excellent UV protection. It also cut microbe growth by over ninety percent against several pathogens. The authors present the fabric as a multi-use functional textile.
pmc-12812405:
Alkharashi and colleagues test how a common bug killer harms rat hearts and if a plant compound can protect them, in a study from twenty twenty-six. The killer is used widely and harms health with long exposure. Its long-term effects on the heart were still unclear. Rats got daily doses for thirty days, with or without the plant compound in tiny fat bubbles.

The killer raised heart damage markers and scarred heart tissue. It also raised oxygen stress and fired up several swelling pathways. A key defense protein fell at the same time. Rats that also got the plant compound showed far less damage. Their heart tissue and blood markers stayed much closer to normal. The compound looks promising as a heart guard.
pmc-12816305:
Haoyan Li and four colleagues compare two ways of replacing a narrowed aortic valve, in a study from two thousand twenty-six. Severe aortic stenosis can be treated with open surgery. It can also be treated with a valve put in by a catheter. How the heart's remodeling reverses after each may not be the same. The team sets the two side by side.

The retrospective study enrolled 175 patients at one institution. Ultrasound scans at baseline, thirty days, and one year tracked how the ventricle changed. The catheter group was older, at seventy-four years on mean, set against sixty-two. It also had more hypertension, coronary disease, and atrial fibrillation in its ranks. The team compares echocardiographic outcomes over time for the two groups. Data of this kind helps clinicians match the approach to the patient. That counts most of all for older patients with more than one condition.
pmc-12817705:
Austin Henderson and five co-authors gather pandemic lessons from isolated communities in a 2025 study. They studied three self-governing groups: a Tibetan monastic community in India, Alaska Native communities, and a Sioux tribe in South Dakota. Interviews with people in health care, schools, law enforcement, and governance covered policies, choices, and personal experience during the crisis.

All three groups restricted travel, and all leaned on internal resources when outside help was thin. Community members took new roles, such as enforcing quarantine, and shared culture helped shift health behavior. Stress ran high, above all from deaths. The authors urge ongoing support and tailored plans that respect each community's resilience.
pmc-12821905:
Macarena Aburto, Jael Escobar, Miguel Angel Munoz, and Issis Luque-Martinez published a dental study in 2025 on glue for fillings. Resin bonds to dentin weaken over years as water seeps in. The team tested a primer laced with a bioactive glass that releases helpful ions.

Tooth samples got one of two standard glue methods, with or without the new primer first. Bond strength right after gluing matched across groups. After twelve months in warm water, the primer groups held far stronger bonds. One primer group even grew stronger with age. Leak levels were alike across groups, and glass grains sat near the bond line, partly plugging tiny tubes. The authors say the primer can extend filling life.
pmc-12822005:
Tiffany Gooden and her twelve co-authors, publishing in 2025, survey psychological distress among people living with HIV in central Tanzania. The team interviewed 461 adults at two facilities in Dodoma, including some who had dropped out of care. A standard six-question scale measured distress. Questions also covered health, money, work, family, and stigma.

The burden was heavy: 59 percent reported mild to severe distress. Having a job, whether employed or self-employed, cut the odds of distress to about a third of the unemployed rate. Being in a relationship also protected. People diagnosed more than ten years earlier faced roughly double the odds of those diagnosed recently. Money, physical health, and family strain all fed distress, though the mix differed by site and subgroup. The authors call the level of suffering a concern that HIV services should address directly.
pmc-12824405:
Aida Gutiérrez and co-authors image germ erosion inside bones from hidden lime graves of the Spanish Civil War without cutting most samples, in a study from two thousand twenty-five. Four victims lay in two graves, buried with lime said to dissolve bodies and block germs. Ribs were checked by fine X-ray scans and electron views.

Germ attack ran the length of the ribs on scans, though cut sections missed it at times. Lime dried the bone but did not stop germs or fungi. The erosion pattern points to germs from the body itself. The team backs the trait as a forensic clue to post-mortem state. Readers get proof that lime graves preserve more than myth says.
pmc-12829005:
Yong Zhang and co-authors study a protein called TRIM2 that worsens scarring in the lungs, in work published in 2025. The disease, idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis, stiffens the lungs and has no clear cause. Stress in the cell's protein-folding compartment is known to play a role, but its controls were unclear.

The team found TRIM2 levels were high in lung tissue from patients and in a cell model of the disease. Lowering TRIM2 in the model slowed cell growth and movement. It also reversed changes that make cells act like scar-forming cells. Stress markers in the folding compartment fell as well. The protein acts in part through a growth signal called beta-catenin. The authors suggest TRIM2 as a possible drug target for this lung disease.
pmc-12830805:
Peng Jia and four co-authors watched the electrical resistivity of rock change as a crack grows, to warn of shear breaks, in a study published in 2025. Sound pops are the standard warning sign, but they can go quiet just before a break. The team sheared wet sandstone at mixed speeds while they logged both sound pops and electrical resistivity, with a camera on the surface strain.

The break ran in four stages, and resistivity tracked each one: a wobble, a steady fall, a sharp drop, then flat. At fast shear the sound pops dimmed and went quiet in the late stage. Resistivity kept falling through that quiet period, a clear lead sign. Damage scores built from each stream agreed on the break path. The authors present resistivity logs as a partner to sound monitoring.
pmc-12830905:
Zijian Liao and co-authors report a hybrid metasurface that works by light alone. It lets terahertz spectroscopy run at very high speed, and lets imaging be done with a single pixel. Their 2025 study deals with the bounds of standard terahertz spectrometers in size, in speed, and in cost.

The surface, made by design, gives many sharp resonances across a terahertz band. It modulates light through optical excitation of silicon patches. Surfaces modulated in time form the base of measures for detection with a single pixel. Spectral reconstruction hit a scale of nanoseconds. Its resolution was fine, across a bandwidth of a quarter of a terahertz. A form of the platform as an array of pixels showed imaging with a small grid of pixels. The plan needs no circuits and fits with chips. It gives a path to compact terahertz devices, for sensing and screening.
pmc-12831405:
Chunxiao Xu and a large team study whether poor sleep is linked to later diabetes in Chinese adults, in a paper published in twenty twenty-five. The data come from the China Kadoorie Biobank, a huge long-term health study.

The team followed four hundred and sixty-two thousand adults, aged thirty to seventy-nine, who had no diabetes at the start. They built a sleep quality score from seven self-reported sleep habits, where a lower score means better sleep. Over about eleven years of follow-up, more than eighteen thousand new diabetes cases appeared. People with worse sleep scores had a higher risk of diabetes, rising step by step with the score. The link held after accounting for body size and other risk factors. The study adds sleep to the list of habits tied to diabetes risk.
pmc-12837105:
Antoine Villa and a large team pool studies on immune proteins in blood and death from sepsis, in a twenty twenty-five review. These proteins include antibodies, complement parts, and germ-killing peptides. The team guessed that patients who die run lower on them, weakening germ clearance. Thirty-six studies with 6,330 patients were pooled, plus checks in a hospital database.

Survivors indeed held higher levels of two complement proteins, C3 and C4. A complement fragment tied to swelling ran higher in those who died. Antibody results were more mixed across studies. The authors say these proteins may flag risk and guide immune support in sepsis.
pmc-12838905:
Nishtha Singh and five colleagues review how chronic heavy drinking ages the brain through paths much like those of Alzheimer's disease. Heavy alcohol use harms the hippocampus, prefrontal cortex, amygdala, cerebellum, and hypothalamus. These are the regions that carry memory and judgment.

The shared paths include oxidative stress, microglial inflammation, tau protein hyperphosphorylation, changed amyloid turnover, and disrupted cholinergic signaling. That last one drives memory loss. Claims that light drinking helps stay murky, since studies define drinking in mixed ways and confounders abound. The authors conclude the link depends on dose. Heavy use raises the risk of Alzheimer's-type decline, so cutting harmful drinking is a practical lever for lowering long-term dementia risk.
pmc-12846105:
Noortje van de Weem and co-authors report poultry research from two thousand twenty-five on a vaccine against a chicken virus that harms the airways and egg laying. The virus keeps changing, and current vaccines often fail to cover new forms. The team tested a killed vaccine that mixes two strains of this virus with antigens against other poultry diseases.

The vaccine was given to both lab chickens and farm chickens, alone or after a priming dose. Birds were then exposed to the target strains and to other forms found in different parts of the world. The vaccine gave broad, strong protection, and antibody responses lasted at least to a late laying age. Egg production and clinical signs were tracked after each challenge.
pmc-12848005:
Barile and colleagues showed in twenty twenty-five that two dietary fuels together can rescue energy making in nerve cells lacking a key carrier protein. The missing carrier, AGC1, causes a rare childhood disorder with seizures, weak muscles, and poor brain insulation.

The team grew early nerve cells from reprogrammed patient skin cells. Without the carrier, the cells grew poorly, died more often, and burned sugar in a wasteful way because their power plants could not use a main fuel. Gene readings showed the entry gate for that fuel was turned down. Yet the power plants still worked when offered other fuels. Feeding the cells ketone bodies plus the amino acid glutamine fully restored their breathing-style energy making. The result helps explain why a ketone-rich diet helps these patients, and points to fuel choice as therapy.
pmc-12855905:
Subhankar Saha and co-authors report research from two thousand twenty-five on machining a nickel aluminium bronze alloy with a wire electrical discharge process. The process cuts metal with sparks, and its settings trade cutting speed against surface smoothness in complex ways. A good predictive model could help shops pick settings without endless trials.

The team built a tuned regression model that predicted both speed and roughness with very high accuracy. An evolutionary search then generated one hundred trade-off solutions that balance the two goals, beating twelve rival algorithms in ranked tests. Microscope images showed that high discharge energy left rough, cratered surfaces with thick melted layers, while low energy gave smoother cuts. Cracks appeared under all settings.
pmc-12881605:
Aryan Taheri and co-authors use cryo-electron microscopy to show how helper proteins build the tubulin pairs that make microtubules. Cells run on microtubule tracks, and each track is built from alpha-beta tubulin pairs. How the cofactor proteins TBCD, TBCE, and TBCC, with the small switch protein Arl2, join alpha and beta tubulins into pairs was unclear.

The structures show three of the helpers forming a cage round the tubulin pair. One helper hugs the beta unit while another stretches along the alpha unit. When TBCC joins, it grips the cage and the pair's inner seam at once. That grip twists one helper and primes the pair for release. The team reads this as a vise-like step, powered by GTP breakdown. The helpers act less like scaffolds and more like enzymes: they build the pair and can also take it apart.
pmc-12913905:
Thaw and nine co-authors mapped feline coronavirus in Thai cats in twenty twenty-five. The virus usually causes mild gut illness but can mutate into a fatal body-wide disease. It comes in two genotypes, and full genome data, especially for genotype II, were scarce in Thailand.

The team swabbed four hundred seventy-one cats at clinics around Bangkok during twenty twenty-two and twenty twenty-three. About twenty-two percent tested positive, with genotype I making up ninety-nine percent of cases. Four viruses were fully sequenced, including the country's first complete genotype II genomes. Thai strains clustered with Chinese and Dutch relatives, spike protein cut sites were conserved, and no mixing with other coronaviruses appeared. The authors urge genotype-aware monitoring and rethink vaccines aimed only at genotype II.
pmc-12920705:
Mohsen Zhaleh, Makan Moradi, and Maryam Ahookhash compare, in a 2025 rat study, how palm oil and sesame oil affect liver tissue under the microscope. Palm oil's saturated fat is tied to fatty liver disease, while sesame carries anti-inflammatory and antioxidant compounds. Eighteen rats ate one of the two oils or a control diet for ninety days.

Stains, vessel space measures, and liver weights told a split story. Palm oil brought liver damage, inflammation, and scarring. Sesame oil shielded the tissue instead. The authors suggest tissue study can aid diagnosis of oil-driven liver harm, and advise limiting palm oil in favor of healthier options like sesame.
pmc-12980105:
Rohan Magoon writes in praise, and in question, of a study on lactate levels after heart surgery. The study followed three hundred ninety-five patients who had bypass surgery on the heart. It linked lactate levels to kidney trouble after the operation. Magoon argues that lactate in this setting is more tangled than a simple sign of low oxygen.

Lactate can rise from more than one path, and nearly half of heart surgery patients show high levels. Magoon notes that pump time, poor blood flow, and certain drugs all play a part. He asks the study team to clarify their use of steroids. He also asks for drug doses, not just drug names, since a standard score ties dose to kidney risk. The letter pushes for care in reading lactate as a warning sign.
pmc-12993605:
