Jeffrey Bennetzen and six co-authors present MiPner analysis, a simple way to find bacterial partners by cell to cell binding. Most microbe pair interplay in nature stays unknown, since few bacteria are well studied. The study came out in twenty twenty-four.

A soil strain of Serratia served as bait, stuck to a wood stick. Bacteria that bound it tightly were then purified. The catch was rich in two genera, Sphingobium and Caulobacter. Two isolates could not grow apart from the bait on the plates used. The authors argue the trick can free bacteria long thought unculturable.
pmc-13086905:
Yuqi Zheng leads a large group of experts who wrote a consensus statement from twenty twenty-six on immune cells in gliomas. Gliomas are brain tumors. The statement sums up what is known about microglia and macrophages inside these tumors, called TAMs for short.

The group stresses that these cells vary a lot by type, place, and time. They can change roles and they interact with tumor stem cells and nerve cells nearby. The old split of these cells into just two classes is too simple, the authors say. The statement aims to clear up common errors and guide future care and research on brain tumors.
pmc-13120205:
Kitae Park and others modeled satellite antenna mesh in two thousand twenty-six. Deployable antennas use lightweight metal mesh reflectors. Their woven structure makes them hard to model. The team combined a classic impedance model with new fitting. One parameter, effective wire radius, was fitted for each band. Real tests used a waveguide contact setup.

Three gold-coated mesh samples underwent repeated trials. Fits matched the test data very closely in native bands. Effective radius varied with band and polarization. Even one sample changed with direction. The method gives satellite teams a compact model. Satellite designers can predict reflection without building the full mesh in software. Stowable antennas benefit from such shortcuts.
pmc-13135005:
Aizikovich and co-authors test if close care access erases ethnic gaps in thyroid cancer. Prior work shows split outcomes by ethnic group for this cancer. Their center serves a distinct minority group nearby. Records covered 316 patients treated from 2013 to 2024. One hundred patients formed the minority group.

Minority patients were younger at diagnosis by about 12 years. Their tumors were larger, with a median of 20 mm versus 15 mm. Tumors in more than one spot were also more common. Median follow-up ran about 4.4 years for the cohort. The paper weighs whether equal close access softened outcome gaps despite larger tumors.
pmc-13136505:
Muhammad Arshed and co-authors translate and validate a medication confidence scale into Urdu in this 2026 paper. The scale, called SEAMS, asks how sure patients feel about taking medicines correctly. It had not been validated in other languages. The study used patients with high blood pressure in Lahore, Pakistan.

Translation followed a forward and backward method with expert checks. Patients aged eighteen and older completed the Urdu version. Factor analysis tested whether the scale structure held in the new language. Consistency was checked with standard reliability measures, including a repeat test four weeks later. Convergent validity was also assessed. A validated Urdu tool lets clinics and researchers measure medication confidence in a large population.
pmc-13137405:
Daniel Ferreira and co-authors published this review in 2026 on the hidden complexity of Alzheimer's disease. The disease is officially defined by two protein deposits, amyloid-beta plaques and tau tangles. In real brains, though, other pathologies usually ride along. The review gathers evidence from clinical cohort studies on these co-pathologies and on the side processes that help drive decline.

The commonest companions are alpha-synuclein deposits, vascular brain injury, and a third protein pathology tied to TDP-43. Alongside them run inflammation, iron build-up, failure of the cholinergic signal system, and cell aging. Each person's mix differs, which helps explain why symptoms vary so much between patients. The authors stress the need for biomarkers that read the whole mix, not just the two headline proteins. Such tools would sharpen diagnosis, prognosis, and treatment matching.
pmc-13139905:
Elisa Tomita-Sudo and co-authors present a 2026 chemistry study on locked nucleic acids, building blocks for gene-silencing drugs. These blocks carry a bridge that locks their shape, which helps a drug strand grip its target RNA. Where the locked blocks sit in the strand may change the grip a lot. The team made strands with the blocks at set spots and measured each grip.

Strands with locked blocks near the ends gripped about 100 times more weakly than strands blocked near the center. The gap is large enough to shape how such drugs should be drawn. Center-heavy placement looks best for a tight hold on the target. The results give drug designers a clear rule for placing a costly but potent block type.
pmc-13146905:
Valerio Melas and nine colleagues compared two kinds of brain scans for stroke patients treated late. One scan, CT perfusion, helps doctors pick who can still get clot-opening care many hours after a stroke. A plain CT scan is faster and more widely at hand. The team asked whether the plain scan gives much the same picture.

One hundred fifty patients at a stroke center had both scans. Measures from the plain scan matched the perfusion scan's core damage volumes closely. Plain scan signs also tracked how severe the stroke was at arrival and at discharge. Both scan types linked to how patients fared after three months. Neither flagged a higher bleed risk. The results back plain CT as a useful guide when perfusion scans are not available.
pmc-13148705:
Laetitia Rater, Debra Marais, and Aisling Kelly explore postnatal depression in migrant mothers in the United Kingdom. Their 2026 study focuses on women who migrated by choice, for study, work, or family, a group little studied for mental health. Postnatal depression is more common among migrant women than others.

Seven mothers who had lived through the condition gave deep interviews. Analysis built four shared themes around layers of disconnection, isolation, despair, and grief. Their stories were shaped by being both mothers and migrants at once. The accounts also carried resilience and growth through a slow healing path. The authors argue that support services should grasp that double identity, rather than treating these mothers as generic new parents.
pmc-13150305:
Morgan and co-authors map the gene base of sap guard in loblolly pine. Sap guard shields pines from bugs and germs that breach bark. It also feeds green fuels and chem stock in trade terms. Yet the gene base of sap yield had stayed poor in grasp. Two clone herds of the pine gave the trait facts here. Traits span sap flow, duct counts, sap chem, and mix shares.

Gene counts, broad hunts, web learn, and gene pace reads join. Trait ties hint shared genes steer rest and woke sap flow. In sum, 236 marks tied to flow, ducts, and mix in hunts. Pick genes point to sap make, stem core shifts, and germ fight. Those picks may serve breed and build work on pines. Guard traits share much of their gene frame in the reads.
pmc-13155405:
Fan Xu, Ruoyu Wang, Zhenyang Cheng, Zhanxia Zhang, and Jianhui Tian review, in a 2026 paper, a class of designer crystals being groomed as cancer nanomedicines. Covalent organic frameworks are porous polymers built from light elements joined by strong bonds, with orderly backbones and tunable holes. A drug carrier wants exactly those traits: room to load, a shape that can be tuned, and gates that open on cue.

The review covers how the frameworks are made, how they differ from older nanomaterials, and how they can be built to release their cargo in answer to the tumor's own chemistry. Platforms that combine imaging with treatment on one frame get special attention. The authors are candid about the distance to the clinic: safety, scale, and consistency all lag the chemistry. They map the field's next steps for readers entering it.
pmc-13155505:
Julia Hunter-Schouela and a team of co-authors lay out a trial testing whether families entering data before clinic visits improves diabetes care for children. Their protocol appeared in twenty twenty-six. Type one diabetes visits drown in data transfer, crowding out the personal care families came for.

A children's hospital in eastern Ontario built a questionnaire inside its patient portal. Caregivers answer ahead of time, and answers flow straight into the doctor's notes. The randomized trial will judge care quality, visit efficiency, and unmet needs against usual practice. If pre-entered data frees real minutes, clinics everywhere could copy the model. The protocol registers outcomes and methods in advance, keeping the test honest.
pmc-13162005:
Kaustav Mukherjee, Tarun Prashanth, Dorai Kumar Raja, and Mohan Kumar study, in twenty twenty-six, a rare shoulder fracture in young adults where the ball of the upper arm bone splits. Such head-split breaks run along a flat plane, so standard X-rays often miss them. Missing the split in a complex break can ruin the repair. The team reviewed all such fractures fixed with hardware at their center. Scans sorted the breaks into three types by the direction the ball was displaced.

Twenty-four patients were included, with a mean age near thirty-five and most being men. Nine were fixed with screws alone, and fifteen with a plate plus screws. A control group held cases where the split was not properly addressed. Function and healing were tracked at follow-up visits.
pmc-13175705:
Giang Nguyen and Eun-Hee Cho reply to reader comments on their study of how lactate, a byproduct of sugar use, makes liver cells store fat. Critics had questioned whether the lactate levels and exposure times used match real body conditions. Writing in twenty twenty-six, the authors explain that brief lactate spikes after exercise differ from the high, sustained levels seen in severe sepsis, which their design targets. Mouse liver cells were exposed for days at levels that did not kill cells or cause open injury, yet fat still built up through a lactate sensor.

The authors agree that gentler, clamp-style or pulsed exposures would sharpen the picture. They report a failed attempt to raise blood lactate in live animals with pumps, then a zebrafish study that did sustain exposure and also produced fatty liver, supporting their central claim.
pmc-13175805:
YuanFeng Zhao, Jian Sun, and Shuai Lin compare two needle-free or minimally invasive ways to shrink benign breast lumps without surgery. Fibroadenomas are common and usually harmless, but patients often want them gone. High-intensity focused ultrasound cooks them with sound; cryoablation freezes them. Head-to-head trials do not exist.

Searching three databases through late twenty twenty-five yielded seventeen prospective single-arm studies. Focused ultrasound shrank tumors about fifty-four percent by six months and seventy percent by twelve, though results varied widely. Cryoablation's reporting was too incomplete to pool, but descriptively suggested greater shrinkage. Side effects were more frequent with ultrasound, about twenty-three percent versus seven, and none were severe in either group.
pmc-13178405:
Choi, Khan, and Kim review how three rice pests beat a common bug spray class in this twenty twenty-six paper. The three planthoppers rank among the worst rice pests in Asia, and heavy spray use bred strong shield in all three. How that shield formed and spread is the core theme here.

Inside, most shield comes from gut and liver-like enzymes that break the spray down, not from shifts at the spray target. One enzyme line does most of the work, with help from a few kin lines. Gene nets that switch those enzymes on are mapped across the three pests. The review ends with care plans that mix spray use with new tools like gene silencing.
pmc-13180205:
Nathan Dawthorne and colleagues describe a virtual peer support program called Coffee Chats, built by and for caregivers of neurodivergent adults who also face mental health concerns. Caregivers often find standard programs too focused on fixing problems, when some realities cannot be fixed. Writing in twenty twenty-six, the authors, writing from lived experience, explain how the program grew out of frustrations with earlier supports. Sessions meet online and are led by caregivers themselves, with a deliberate choice to hold space for feelings rather than hand out prescriptions.

Flexibility, honesty, and humility are named as the hallmarks that set the model apart from other peer support designs. The paper centers caregiver voices rather than surveying the wider literature. The authors argue that who designs a support program, and for whom, strongly shapes whether caregivers experience it as safe and relevant.
pmc-13183605:
Dustin Hammers and co-authors tested whether uneven performance within a single test session predicts decline in early-onset dementias. The measure, called cognitive dispersion, captures how much a person's scores scatter across tests taken the same day. The study followed 309 people for a year: patients with early-onset Alzheimer's, patients with other early dementias, and healthy volunteers. The Alzheimer's group scored higher on the measure than the other dementia group, and it tracked that disease's biomarkers.

The measure also predicted who would show reliable change over twelve months in several thinking domains. The authors suggest it, read alongside ordinary baseline scores, could sharpen clinical trials in early-onset Alzheimer's. It might flag who is likely to change, making treatment effects easier to monitor. They label the results preliminary. Still, the study gives a cheap paper-and-pencil statistic a possible second life as a trial-enrichment tool.
pmc-13185705:
Aarti Diwan and six colleagues study why thin silicon wires glow, in a paper dated twenty twenty-six. Two forces compete: quantum confinement, which widens the energy gap in tiny wires, and defects tied to oxygen, which can shift the glow. The team measured gap widening and disorder together. Disorder grew alongside the gap, yet the glow shifted rather than spreading wider.

They conclude the gap follows confinement, while the glow's color follows defect states. Both effects must be read together to explain the light. The work sharpens how engineers should design silicon wire light sources and sensors.
pmc-13194105:
Zhumei Zhan and five co-authors review, in a 2026 paper, why first-line treatment fails for a common adult lymphoma. Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma is the most frequent subtype of malignant lymphoma in adults. Sixty to seventy percent of patients reach remission on standard immunochemotherapy. The rest see the disease resist care or come back, and that group drives most deaths.

The review walks through the molecular mechanisms the cancer uses to resist each drug in the standard regimens. One point stands out: the components of the regimens do not boost each other much, but cross-resistance between the two main regimens is minimal. That leaves room to switch when one fails. The authors close with strategies for the rational management of resistant cases, drawn from the mechanisms mapped. The piece aims to guide both clinical decisions and new drug work.
pmc-13195305:
Zhao and eight co-authors test Eucommia extract plus soy isoflavones against weak bones after menopause in rats, in a study from twenty twenty-six. Loss of estrogen speeds bone breakdown, slows bone building, and keeps swelling alive once periods stop. Each one acts a bit like estrogen and calms swelling on its own. What the pair does as one dose was not clear before this work.

Rats with no ovaries got each agent on its own or the pair as one dose. The pair brought thigh bone strength and mineral stock back best of all. Signs of bone building rose in the blood, while signs of bone loss fell. The spongy inner bone, the trabecular web, looked far better, and cell stress eased. In dish tests, bone-building cells grew more, while bone-eating cells formed less. Key bone signals and immune signals shifted back toward balance.
pmc-13195405:
Mayasah Al-Nema is first author on a 2026 review of computer methods for finding drugs against flaviviruses. This virus family includes Zika, dengue, West Nile, and yellow fever. These viruses infect millions yearly, mostly in tropical regions. Good antiviral treatments remain limited despite vaccine and therapy progress.

The review maps the viruses' protein targets. Some are outer structural proteins, and seven are inner working proteins. It then surveys computer methods that predict a candidate's activity and toxicity from its chemical structure. Recent examples and new trends are highlighted. Frequent mutation breeds resistance, the authors note, so robust strategies matter. Challenges and future directions for faster, computer-guided drug discovery close the review.
pmc-13199805:
Tessa Rose Cornell and five co-authors review how far infectious disease is woven into climate policy in four Horn of Africa countries. Their document review was published in twenty twenty-six. The region faces growing climate extremes, and many of its diseases are climate-sensitive.

The team searched policy databases, agency sites, and reference chains for climate strategies and plans from Ethiopia, Kenya, Somalia, and Uganda. Ninety-eight documents were kept. Each was read for its aims, scope, and how fully it covered health and infectious disease, plus the reasons given for including them. Global agencies urge an end to split climate and health work. The review shows where these four countries stand and where the gaps in joining the two agendas remain.
pmc-13202205:
Sows pass protection against a deadly piglet diarrhea virus through colostrum, and a 2026 study from Ping Chen tracks those antibodies across many sample types. The research article follows responses to porcine epidemic diarrhea virus in infected pigs and in pregnant sows under different immunization strategies on commercial farms.

Antibody tests showed piglets seroconverted one week after infection, peaked within three weeks, and stayed detectable for up to thirty-one weeks afterward. In more than a thousand sow samples, blood antibody levels correlated strongly with colostrum levels, most tightly on the day of farrowing. Mouth and rectal swabs also tracked colostral antibody of one class, offering easier ways to judge maternal immunity.
pmc-13202305:
A childhood lung infection that destroys tissue nearly killed a five-year-old in a 2026 case report by Hani Abu-Hijleh from Palestine. The article describes a previously healthy girl whose illness first looked gastrointestinal before becoming necrotizing pneumonia linked to influenza, then sudden bleeding into the chest cavity.

Her course grew harder with drug-related kidney injury that required temporary dialysis, while bacterial cultures stayed puzzlingly negative throughout. Surgeons performed an urgent chest operation and removed the destroyed lung tissue, after which she recovered fully. The authors highlight how quickly this infection can escalate, and how timely surgery within multidisciplinary care can save a child's life.
pmc-13202905:
Heidi Szugye and co-authors study infant feeding after COVID-positive births in a 2026 paper. Parents who tested positive around delivery may face a different birth and feeding path. The study ran at a large US hospital system.

Records covered 72 parent-infant pairs from births between March 2020 and January 2022. Just over half of the infants were exclusively breastfed at discharge. A quarter more received mixed feeding. Two infants tested positive at one day old. A small survey named hurdles such as low milk supply, thin support, and conflicting advice. The authors chart both practice and experience in this group.
pmc-13203305:
Sobahi, Akpınar, Özçelik, and Sengur classified eye diseases in this study from twenty twenty-six. Their images are ultra-wide photos of the retina, which are hard to sort because disease classes look alike. Class sizes also skew, and some patterns stay ambiguous. The team built a student model taught by a larger teacher network.

Their twist is a logic that grades truth, falsehood, and uncertainty separately during teaching. An image-cleaning step evens out contrast before training. Heat maps showed the model looked at sensible retinal regions when deciding. Accuracy averaged about eighty-four percent across validation folds. The model beat classic feature-based methods and plainer student networks. The authors offer it as decision support for screening.
pmc-13204205:
Atsushi Koike and Ko Fujimori published this bone study in 2026. Osteoclasts are the cells that eat bone, and when they overwork, bone thins in diseases like osteoporosis. The pair tested a plant compound called CG-1, drawn from the seeds of a tropical tree. They asked if it could slow the making of osteoclasts from raw cells driven by a signal named RANKL.

CG-1 cut the count of mature bone-eating cells and muted the genes that build them. Dosing only in the first three days worked as well as dosing all five, so the early stage is key. The compound damped a growth path inside the cells and lowered the master switch gene for the change. The authors say CG-1 could seed drugs that curb bone loss, though animal tests come next.
pmc-13205405:
Vania Anagnostakou and colleagues tackle a tricky diagnosis problem in a 2026 imaging study. A patient arrives with a stroke, and scans also show an aneurysm, a ballooned weak spot in a brain artery, in the same territory. Did the aneurysm cause the stroke, or is it an innocent bystander? The answer decides whether to treat the aneurysm.

The team reviewed eight such patients, imaged with CT, MRI, and in some cases direct vessel imaging and vessel wall scans. Some patients had clots removed mechanically; others were managed with medicine alone. From the images, the authors built a framework that sorts an aneurysm as a possible, probable, or unlikely cause. Clot inside the aneurysm, wall inflammation signs, location, and other illnesses fed the judgment. The scheme aims to make a hard call more consistent.
pmc-13206905:
Allergy may shape how children fare long after COVID, and a 2026 questionnaire study by Giulia Brindisi explores that question in Rome. Families attending a pediatric allergy clinic at Umberto I Hospital noted infections, vaccination, lingering symptoms, and how allergic diseases changed once pandemic restrictions ended.

Two hundred fourteen surveys were analyzed for the study's comparisons. Allergy itself was not tied to catching the virus, but among infected children it came with clearly higher odds of Long COVID symptoms. Severe initial illness raised those odds further, while full vaccination lowered the odds of infection overall. After restrictions lifted, most allergic children reportedly had worse hay fever.
pmc-13207505:
Calin Pop and co-authors review infective endocarditis care at a regional hospital in Romania in this 2026 paper. The disease is an infection of the heart lining and valves. It still kills many patients. Real world patients often differ from those in trials, which can hide care gaps.

Records covered 206 adults with definite disease across two periods, 2011 to 2016 and 2017 to 2025. Blood cultures were positive in about two thirds of cases. Staphylococcus aureus was the top named cause. The team scored how well care followed guidelines in each period. They also compared patients who would fit trial rules with the rest. Models hunted for traits that predicted complications and death in hospital.
pmc-13207905:
Nguyen Quoc Chien, Keisuke Moriasa, Hiroshi Sugimoto, and Minoru Fujii report a 2026 study on boosting light capture in silicon disks at near-infrared wavelengths. Flat arrays of tiny disks can trap light through a pattern called a toroidal dipole resonance. The team wanted to sharpen that effect so the disks turn more light into electric current, within a narrow band of wavelengths.

They mixed germanium into the silicon disks to tune how much light the material absorbs while holding its bending of light nearly steady. Computer models showed the boost peaks at one set mix rather than rising steadily. Built samples matched the models: a small germanium share more than tripled the light absorbed and raised the current up to 3.4 times over plain silicon. The authors present alloy tuning as a practical route to stronger devices.
pmc-13209605:
Zoya Farmazyan leads a nine-author team developing silicone films that carry two medicinal salts, in a study published in two thousand twenty-six. The salts are thiamine bromide and sodium iodide, partners in a preparation called TIODIN. Both dissolve eagerly in water, yet the carrier film is water-repelling silicone.

This first part of the project characterizes the matrix itself. Films were cast from silicone polymers of different viscosities with a crosslinker and catalyst. Raman spectroscopy and X-ray diffraction mapped how the salts distribute and what crystal forms they take. Release behavior in laboratory tests was measured against that structure. The work is preformulation: groundwork for judging whether silicone films can deliver such unlikely cargo.
pmc-13211305:
Kento Suzuki and Takuma Ito refine a method for predicting where a cyclist will be at a blind intersection, in this study from twenty twenty-six. On Japan's narrow community roads, walls and hedges hide crossing cyclists until late. Their earlier system filled the blind spots with statistics: typical cyclist movements for each spot, used as virtual observations and virtual control inputs in position estimation.

The gap was classification. Real-time sensors see too little to sort a rider confidently into one behavior cluster. The new method keeps the classification soft, blending the statistics of every cluster by their probabilities, so uncertainty is priced in rather than ignored. Simulations and a real-world experiment beat the older, hard-classification approach. The authors aim the method at cooperative safety systems that warn drivers before the cyclist appears.
pmc-13212405:
Taiane Campos Braga de Assis and co-authors address, in 2026, gaps in hourly carbon monoxide readings from an air monitor in Salvador, Brazil. Missing stretches arise from power cuts, calibration, and transmission faults, and they weaken pollution records used for policy.

The team hid real data in artificial gaps lasting one to three days, then tested three models at filling them in. A boosted-tree model scored slightly best on error measures, though recurrent neural networks described more gaps consistently, and neither lead was statistically firm. Filled values showed no systematic bias and kept the series' daily and seasonal patterns, supporting model-based repair of monitoring records.
pmc-13212705:
Hongzhi Xiong and colleagues demonstrate in 2026 a chip that stretches a pulse of light into a rainbow spanning ultraviolet-C to mid-infrared wavelengths. Such broad spectra help probe molecules directly, but chip devices had never reached so deep into the ultraviolet.

The team built waveguides from lithium tantalate, a crystal prized for transparency and strong nonlinear response, with finely patterned domains that vary along their length. Their device reached below 270 nanometres at one end and 2400 nanometres at the other, using very low pulse energy. Covering more than three octaves on one chip opens paths toward compact ultraviolet light sources for spectroscopy and precision measurement.
pmc-13213105:
Bushra Elhusein and co-authors present in 2026 a woman in her fifties who heard voices for more than three years despite having no psychotic illness. Her hearing loss in both ears, from damaged inner-ear nerves, starved her brain of sound and likely generated the experiences.

Brain scans looked normal, she kept clear insight and functioned well, and several antipsychotic medicines barely helped. Hearing aids improved her sound input, yet the hallucinations continued, showing that such symptoms may not switch off once hearing is corrected. The authors warn that sensory causes are often missed, leading to needless psychiatric treatment, and they call for early hearing checks plus teamwork across specialties.
pmc-13213605:
Mohannad N. AbuHaweeleh and co-authors present in 2026 a case of brucellosis, an animal-borne infection, settling in one testicle of a camel and goat handler. The disease mimics many others, so genital involvement is easily missed or misread.

The 32-year-old man arrived with fever, aches, fatigue, and a lip ulcer, while early examination found little. Blood tests showed anaemia and inflammation, antibody tests pointed to brucella, and cultures confirmed the species. A scrotal scan showed an enlarged, overactive testicle and cord structures. Side effects first undermined his antibiotic course, yet after completing treatment his symptoms and laboratory values improved. He left hospital on two antibiotics with close follow-up planned.
pmc-13214805:
Hee Kyoung Chung, Lan Xiao, and Jian-Ying Wang wrote a review dated two thousand twenty-six on ring-shaped RNA molecules in the gut lining. The gut lining renews itself fast and forms the border between the body and the outside world. Keeping that border in balance takes tight control of cell growth, movement, and repair.

Unlike normal RNA strands, these molecules close into loops, which makes them stable and long-lived. The review describes how they steer growth of the lining, healing after injury, and the seal of the gut barrier. It also covers how their failure links to gut diseases such as inflammatory bowel disease and cancer.
pmc-13215205:
Jianyu Zhou and co-authors borrow in 2026 the armadillo's party trick for soft machines: a skeleton that curls into a protective ball when danger appears. Soft robots deform beautifully but usually stay fragile, the very softness that helps them move leaving them exposed.

Their module layers a segmented outer shell over an interlocking inner frame, echoing the animal's double skeleton. A muscle-like polymer skin drives curling, rolling, and grasping when a sensing layer detects a threat and heats it locally. The structure shrugs off impacts, punctures, and concentrated loads while carrying fragile cargo. Wireless control frees it for hazardous places. Morphing and armour, usually traded against each other, arrive together here.
pmc-13216105:
Hannah S Jesani and co-authors present a 2026 national survey of robotic chest surgery training across the United Kingdom and Republic of Ireland. Robotic operating is spreading fast, but nobody had mapped what trainees actually get to do.

Eighty-two trainees from all 14 training regions answered. Robotic surgery ran in 71 percent of their units, yet only 16 percent of those units had a structured training program. Over half of respondents had never fully performed a robotic procedure themselves. Most wanted more robotic training before finishing. Barriers included idle dual consoles, exposure limited to bedside assisting, and scarce simulator access. The authors call for national standards with staged, competency-based progression.
pmc-13216305:
Markus Mergen and co-authors present a 2026 study testing whether a general-purpose language model can sort cancer scan reports into standard tumour response categories by itself. The model ran entirely offline inside hospital infrastructure, which keeps patient data private.

The team fed 142 real CT reports, with their expert labels hidden, to a locally hosted LLaMA-3.3 model using three prompting styles. Simple zero-shot and example-based prompts already performed strongly. Asking the model to reason step by step worked best, reaching a micro F1 score of 0.81 against expert labels across the five RECIST categories. The authors see prompt-guided offline models as a scalable way to standardize response assessment without sending data outside the hospital.
pmc-13218105:
Emma Huijs and co-authors present the PEARL study in a 2026 protocol, a randomized trial of lifestyle treatment for endometriosis pain. Hormonal drugs for this condition often work only partly, cause burdensome side effects, and interfere with fertility, while surgery carries a real risk of complications. Many women are turning to lifestyle approaches, but solid evidence for them is thin.

The five-arm Dutch trial will enroll 250 premenopausal women, 200 with endometriosis and pain plus 50 healthy controls. Women with endometriosis are assigned to standard care alone, standard care with an anti-inflammatory diet, standard care with cognitive behavioral therapy, or both additions together. The diet is expected to calm immune activity and inflammation, while the therapy targets pain mechanisms and coping and should help dietary changes stick. Outcomes center on pain and health-related quality of life, measured around hospital visits at the start and end of the intervention period.
pmc-13220205:
Meera Madhu and four co-authors argue that skin pigment and the brown muck of soil and water owe their shared optical tricks to the same nanoscale architecture. Eumelanin and natural organic matter look alike, darken alike, and frustrate structural analysis alike, yet they are usually studied apart. Spectroscopy, steady and time-resolved, exposes their kinship.

By taking apart eumelanin particles layer by layer, the team identified the basic light-absorbing unit: small stacks of just a few molecular sheets. Ensembles of those stacks explain signature behaviors, including wavelength-dependent emission and transient hole burning, in both materials. Atom-level differences matter less than the couplings between stacked units. The framework unifies photoprotection chemistry with environmental carbon science.
pmc-13220905:
Mayank S. Kotadia and co-authors recount a 2026 case in which glue used to treat stomach varices later complicated a liver transplant. Their 62-year-old patient had cirrhosis, a shunt inside the liver, and clots spreading from that shunt toward the heart and into the splenic vein. Such clots once ruled out transplantation for many patients.

Surgeons removed the shunt, cleared the clots mechanically, and completed the transplant successfully. The report walks through the planning that balanced bleeding risk against clotting risk in a patient whose blood system was unstable. It shows that even extensive clots in this setting need not end transplant hopes when specialist teams coordinate care.
pmc-13221905:
Bijaya K Behera and co-authors study heart dysfunction in liver cirrhosis and its link to disease severity, in a 2026 hospital study from Cuttack, India. Between April 2023 and June 2024, 103 patients received heart ultrasounds, electrocardiograms, and laboratory tests. Cirrhosis severity was graded with the Child-Turcotte-Pugh scale, and alcohol caused most cases.

Diastolic dysfunction, a stiffening of the heart's filling phase, was the commonest abnormality and grew more frequent as liver severity worsened. Pumping function stayed preserved in most patients. Electrical changes such as a lengthened QT interval appeared in a subset. The authors note alcohol itself may contribute to the heart findings, so severity links need cautious reading.
pmc-13222605:
Dayong Xia and co-authors test a blended teaching method for neurosurgery residents, in a 2026 education study at Wannan Medical College. Sixty trainees in formal residency training were split evenly: one group learned through case-based lessons, scenario simulation, and flipped classrooms combined, while the other received traditional teaching. A varied scoring system compared the two.

The blended group reported higher approval of teaching arrangements. Their scores ran higher in surgical skills, theory examinations, and case analysis pass rates. Self-rated benefit also favored the blended group across all three measured dimensions. Given the field's speed and risk, the authors recommend wider adoption of the integrated approach in clinical teaching.
pmc-13223805:
Yukun Li and co-authors pair a KRAS-blocking drug with an autophagy inhibitor against pancreatic cancer carrying the G12C mutation, in a 2026 study spanning cell and animal experiments. Sotorasib was developed for this exact mutation, yet pancreatic tumors have rarely been its target. Pancreatic cancer still kills most patients within years, with five-year survival near ten percent.

The team reports that sotorasib switches on a protective self-eating process, autophagy, early in treatment, which blunts its killing power. Adding 3-methyladenine, a blocker of that early autophagy step, strengthened the antitumor effect in their models. The combination, they argue, deserves development as a strategy for this hard-to-treat mutation group.
pmc-13224005:
Shiyao Han and colleagues build a 2026 single-cell atlas of early ovary development in female cattle, then compare it with goats and pigs. Gene activity was measured cell by cell from the stage when sex is determined through the first formation of follicles. The comparison aims to separate shared mammalian programmes from traits specific to each livestock species.

Major germ cell and supporting cell groups emerged, and germ cells followed conserved stages involving retinoic acid response and the start of meiosis. Goats progressed through meiosis more slowly than cattle or pigs. Signalling between cells also differed, with certain retinoic-acid-linked pathways active in cattle and pigs but absent in pre-meiotic goat tissue.
pmc-13224705:
Shuaijie Pei and colleagues apply a 2026 data-mining approach to sepsis, hunting for genes tied to cellular senescence, the worn-out state cells enter under stress. Sepsis can push cells into that state and worsen organ damage, yet marker genes and matching drugs were unknown. Bioinformatics screening and machine learning narrowed the field to eight standout genes.

Those genes separated septic from healthy samples well, and six behaved consistently in validation data and laboratory samples. Immune-cell patterns tracked closely with the gene set. A drug database pointed to compounds acting on three of the genes, and one candidate, fenofibrate, reduced senescence and inflammation in cell and animal models of sepsis-related kidney injury.
pmc-13227005:
Rola Kwayess and co-authors compare a 2026 set of choices for hormone monitoring during parathyroid surgery at a Beirut hospital. Removing an overactive parathyroid gland cures the common disorder behind high blood calcium, and surgeons check hormone levels mid-operation to confirm success. Sixty-eight cured patients had samples drawn from both a central and a peripheral vein, each tested with two generations of assay.

Newer third-generation assays and central sampling each gave higher readings than their counterparts. Even so, the share of patients meeting the standard success rule, a hormone drop of at least half, did not differ by assay or sampling site. The newer assay fell more steeply and consistently, leading the authors to suggest assay-specific thresholds could sharpen decisions.
pmc-13227205:
Alejandro J Friedman and co-authors report a 2026 first published case of a finger pulley tearing without any injury, in a 27-year-old woman with ulcerative colitis. Pulleys are small bands that hold finger tendons against the bone, and climbers usually tear them through force. She presented with pain, loss of function, and a finger stuck bent at ninety degrees at the middle joint.

Imaging showed the A3 pulley of her right index finger had ruptured, letting the deep flexor tendon bowstring away from the bone. No trauma preceded it, implicating her inflammatory bowel disease, which is known to attack joints and tendons. Coordinated conservative care plus adjustment of her anti-rheumatic medication partly straightened the finger and restored pain-free use.
pmc-13229305:
Rodney N. Nagoshi, Ashley E. Tessnow, and Robert L. Meagher describe a 2026 pair of new genetic markers for telling apart the two host strains of the fall armyworm. This moth's caterpillars devastate corn and other crops across the Americas and, since 2016, Africa and beyond. The corn and rice strains look identical, and strain identification has rested on variants in a single gene, leaving population studies on shaky ground.

Their data support earlier conclusions that strain identity is anchored in the sex chromosome, which diverges as one unit, and they quantify how differently the two strains are evolving. Better strain tracking sharpens forecasts of this pest's global movements and host choices.
pmc-13229605:
Prachee Singh, writing alone, uses negative lab results as a sign of diagnostic gaps in a hospital study, in a paper dated twenty twenty-six. Four of five samples came back with no confirmed infection.

Blood-based tests made up most samples but confirmed least often. Culture tests confirmed about three in five. Older patients showed higher positive rates. Singh frames the high negative share as an exploratory flag for weak test use, not proof of waste, and calls for tighter test choices.
pmc-13233205:
Danilo Češljarac and colleagues published a 2026 narrative review of short screening tools that flag vulnerable older adults in emergency and acute hospital care. The authors favor a two-step model: quick screening at the door, then a fuller assessment on the ward, with results tied to actions like early mobilization and medication review.
pmc-13233905:
Chan-in Sio and colleagues published a 2026 study of MetaCourt, a virtual reality courtroom for training court interpreters. Twenty-one undergraduates in the field then tested it against conventional digital methods.

Students interpreting in virtual reality spoke more fluently, while accuracy stayed level with the traditional approach. Users reported strong feelings of autonomy, intuitive controls, and presence in the scene, plus lower mental workload than expected. The authors present MetaCourt as the first court interpreting trainer built on this motivation framework and a promising route to more engaging practice.
pmc-13234205:
Dhika Dharmansyah and colleagues published a 2026 mixed-methods systematic review on why older adults in Asian low- and middle-income countries accept or reject assistive health technology. The authors conclude that technology programs ignoring these forces will keep missing older Asian users.
pmc-13234405:
Isaac Allen and a large group of collaborators estimated in 2026 the risk of a second cancer in the opposite breast for women carrying inherited gene variants. Hazard ratios were clearly raised for BRCA1, BRCA2, and CHEK2 carriers in the pooled analysis. pmc-13234505:
Hongli Li and co-authors wrote a 2026 paper on how the placenta's cells decide their fate. It works by tagging a partner complex for disposal, which keeps key gene switches set correctly. The finding names a new suspect in unexplained pregnancy loss.
pmc-13235005:

Canada's huge distances, harsh weather, and varied regional systems complicate any single method. Talks covered when to start transfusion, which products to prioritize, logistics, and remote care.

Other concentrates can substitute when plasma is unavailable in the panel's view. Calcium replacement and preventing body cooling were stressed as vital companions. Twelve consensus statements resulted, plus a call for a standard national dataset and registry.
pmc-13235505:

Thirty-two genes linked to both smell status and disease status in the blood data. Groups of those genes overlapped with pathways central to Parkinson's biology in the analysis. Changes specific to monocytes, a blood immune cell type, added another link between smell loss and disease.
pmc-13236505:
Ximei Wang and colleagues study why young nurses stay in their jobs, in a 2026 survey from China. Early-career nurses face stress and shaky role changes, and many quit. The survey covered 337 nurses with at most three years of experience at four large hospitals in Henan Province. A stronger sense of a fair deal went with more confidence and hope, and with stronger ties to the job. Feeling stuck on a career plateau cut the other way. The paths worked in sequence: fair dealing built inner resources, which softened the sense of being stuck. Hospital managers, the authors suggest, can keep nurses by honoring the deal and easing plateaus.
pmc-13237305:
Tiffany Tavares and co-authors argued in 2026 that training for head and neck pathologists must change now that artificial intelligence shares diagnostic decisions. pmc-13238505:
Thakore and colleagues watch two notorious proteins misbehave together in a new mouse model of brain disease. The team built mice carrying the human forms of both proteins. They then tracked the earliest amyloid formation and the brain's inflammatory response that follows. Catching the partnership at its start could reveal which protein moves first, and where a future drug might break the chain before symptoms begin.
pmc-13239805:
Subadra Wanninayake and co-authors examine diagnostic delay in a rare inherited metabolic disorder in a 2026 British study. In a delayed subgroup the wait between first signs and diagnosis stretched to a median of seven years. A dislocated eye lens was the commonest first clue, and a third of symptomatic patients already had two or more complications.
pmc-13240005:
Julia Marchenko and colleagues ask why subarctic blue mussels remain scarce despite warming seas in a 2026 long-term study. Mussels returned to Spitsbergen after a thousand-year absence, heralding Arctic warming, so the team expected thriving populations along Russia's Murman Coast as well.

Recovery since has been partial and unrelated to temperature. The authors blame lasting effects of the crash, including sparse populations struggling to reproduce and competition with an invading sister species.
pmc-13240905:
Jo and Ahn in Seoul modeled what shapes job satisfaction and well-being among solo workers. Their data came from the Sixth Korean Working Life Survey of 2020. 12,703 people fed a path model. Digitalization, autonomy, work-life balance, engagement, and burnout were the five moving parts.

Work bleeding into life hurt both outcomes and tracked with burnout, while engagement and contentment supported well-being. Surprisingly, overtime work tracked with higher contentment and well-being in this group.
pmc-13241005:
Qiuju Yang and co-authors present a 2026 retrospective study of brucellosis in southwestern China across two decades. Cases rose steadily over the period, with most reported in Yunnan. Blood testing of tens of thousands of people found a notable share with signs of past or current infection. Sheep and goat results tracked the human pattern closely. Cases shifted from scattered to clustered, forming clear hot spots. One bacterial type dominated, carried by two widespread genetic lines. Coordinated regional control is the authors recommendation.
pmc-13241505:
Vulinovic's team at Lübeck probed why dopamine neurons die first in Parkinson's disease. Lab-grown cultures were sorted into pure dopamine-making and other neurons using a glowing tag. Two other Parkinson's genes shifted activity just in these neurons. The trio's interplay under stress may explain the selective death.
pmc-13241805:

Skill scores for laparoscopic technique and anatomy recognition were both high on a five-point scale. Most students said they were satisfied or strongly satisfied with the digital methods. The authors conclude that digital tools raised teaching efficiency and skill levels in their course. They propose the model as a path for practice-focused medical training.
pmc-13242005:

The team deleted the front four hundred building blocks of that protein. The mutant grew normally in lab cells. In young ducklings it caused no deaths and only mild signs, with far less virus in organs. Ducklings immunized with it were then protected against a strong wild virus challenge. The deletion mutant looks like a live vaccine lead.
pmc-13242105: Mohan and colleagues, writing across London, Karachi, Brazil, Calgary, and Boston, argue in an editorial that child and adolescent mental health training needs a shared global curriculum. Their proposed GC-CAMH framework answers a worldwide shortage of specialists equipped for young people's mental health. The piece contends the world cannot wait for piecemeal national efforts. It appears in Child and Adolescent Psychiatry and Mental Health in 2026.
pmc-13242205:
Amornrat Deeboonno and co-authors present a 2026 qualitative study of how pregnant women in Thailand use online health information. Twenty women, pregnant or recently delivered, from urban and suburban hospitals took part. Most searched through Google, YouTube, and Facebook. Participants could find information readily, yet they worried about source credibility, privacy, and hard medical wording. They asked for Thai-language resources that are simple to use and endorsed by trusted national health bodies. The authors urge providers and institutions to build and promote reliable digital materials rather than leaving women to navigate alone.
pmc-13242405:
Koray Özşeker and colleagues at Karadeniz Technical University studied toxic metals in reservoir sediments in northeastern Türkiye, publishing their findings in Environmental Geochemistry and Health in 2026. They argue that bulk testing can miss these fine-grain hotspots, so risk checks should treat each fraction separately.
pmc-13242505:
A. M. Al Sabagh and colleagues turned waste cooking oil into cleaning agents that help squeeze extra crude from rock. Their study appeared in Scientific Reports in 2026. Used cooking oil is both a disposal problem and a cheap renewable raw material. The team synthesized two surfactants from it, one aromatic and one oily in character, and blended them with a helper alcohol for tests in a sand-pack model of a reservoir.

The blends sharply lowered the tension between oil and water and turned rock surfaces from oil-loving to water-loving, as shown by contact angle drops. Flooding tests recovered the most oil at a mid-range salt level and moderate heat. The best blend, combining both surfactants with the co-surfactant, recovered close to four-fifths of the oil in place. The results tie the molecules' structure to their performance underground.
pmc-13242805:
Ruofan Wang and co-authors report a 2026 case of a severe burn wound infection caused by an uncommon environmental bacterium. A 71-year-old farmer with diabetes burned her lower leg badly with a home moxibustion patch, then treated the wound herself. Such patches are popular for home pain care, yet reduced feeling in diabetic legs makes deep burns easy to miss.

Culture of wound fluid identified Pseudomonas oryzihabitans, an opportunist common in soil and water. Antibiotics were chosen to match the laboratory sensitivity results. Surgery cleaned the wound, suction therapy prepared it, and a skin graft closed it. Infection markers fell sharply, healing was good, and no recurrence followed. The authors credit the combined microbe-guided and surgical approach.
pmc-13243205:
Ilaria Righi and co-authors compare three ways to remove the thymus gland in a 2026 surgical study. The gland sits in the chest, and surgeons now reach it through small cuts rather than opening the breastbone. Care can use a camera alone or one of two robot systems.

The study covers 90 patients treated at one large center between 2016 and 2025. Thirty had camera surgery, and sixty had robot help split across the Da Vinci and Versius systems. Robot patients left the hospital about a day sooner, while pain, tube time, and complications stayed similar. Surgeons also settled into the robot methods faster, though Versius felt more demanding to use.
pmc-13243505:
Jinyoung Jeong and co-authors weigh published findings on low-calorie sweeteners and health in a 2026 umbrella review. Sweeteners replace sugar in many drinks and foods, yet their long-term effects remain disputed. The review pools prior meta-analyses rather than single studies to see the whole field at once.

The team reanalyzed 29 meta-analyses covering more than 50 million people in total. In observational data, higher intake of non-sugar sweeteners tracked with more weight gain, diabetes, and high blood pressure. Trial data told a softer story and at times pointed the other way. Quality ratings varied widely across the pooled reviews. The authors urge care in reading pooled claims about sweeteners.
pmc-13243705:
Yiyang Shen, Xiaofei Jiao, and Yuanjia Wen reviewed how recent clinical trials are changing the treatment of gynecologic cancers. Their review appeared in Cancer Innovation in 2026. Care has shifted toward specialist-led combinations of surgery, drugs, and radiation, yet surgeons still face hard calls in the operating room, and drug resistance and toxicity limit medical therapy. In advanced ovarian cancer, upfront debulking surgery beat chemotherapy-first approaches in fit patients at expert centers. Immune therapy gains ground through paired checkpoint drugs and triple regimens, while antibody-drug conjugates aimed at two tissue targets produced lasting responses in selected patients. The review maps where precision is genuinely replacing routine.
pmc-13244505:
Ayuko Yamashita and colleagues checked whether two kidney risk scores, built in Europe, predict outcomes for Japanese patients with ANCA-associated kidney inflammation. Both scores worked: renal survival worsened step by step as risk band rose, with highly significant separation. The revised score discriminated slightly better, with an area under the curve of 0.82 against 0.76 for the original. Nine in ten patients carried the MPO form of the antibody, the dominant pattern in Japan. The authors conclude the newer score is a useful prognostic tool for Japanese practice. pmc-13246005:
Biswas, Moore, and Rogers showed that a worm's nervous system must give permission before its body mounts antioxidant defenses, in this 2026 eLife study. Using the nematode C. elegans under chronic oxidative stress, they found mutants unable to make the neurotransmitter acetylcholine were strikingly vulnerable. The broad gene program that healthy worms switch on against the stress depended heavily on cholinergic signaling through one muscarinic receptor, GAR-3.

Without that signal, worms failed to ramp up their proteasome, the machinery shredding damaged proteins. Extra copies of the receptor in motor neurons, conversely, prolonged survival under stress. The authors frame antioxidant defense as neuronally coordinated, not merely cell-autonomous, and point to fresh links between cholinergic signaling, oxidative damage, and neurodegenerative disease worth exploring in larger animals.
pmc-13246805:
Borlepawar, Neu, Ma, and co-authors review proteostasis, the cell's system for keeping its proteins correctly made, folded, moved, and destroyed, in this 2026 Signal Transduction and Targeted Therapy article. Chaperone proteins, the proteasome shredder, autophagy, and organelle quality-control programs all cooperate in that balance. When it collapses, misshapen proteins pile up and drive disease.

The authors link proteostasis failure across Alzheimer's-type neurodegeneration, cancer, heart and metabolic disease, and autoimmunity, hitting hardest in heart and brain tissue that barely regenerates. They frame the system's strength as proteostasis resilience, its capacity to absorb stress and restore balance. The review closes with emerging drug platforms that aim to restore that resilience rather than fix single broken parts.
pmc-13247105:
Romero-García and co-authors used machine learning to sort intensive-care patients with brain dysfunction in this 2026 Intensive Care Medicine Experimental pilot study. Delirium and coma in critically ill COVID-19 patients vary widely, making prognosis hard. Working from an international database of the pandemic's first wave, the team clustered more than sixteen hundred patients using only data from their first ICU day.

Four reproducible groups emerged with distinct profiles. One with mild respiratory failure woke fastest and spent the least time on ventilators; others, defined by moderate or early severe lung failure, endured longer delirium. Intriguingly, the clusters did not differ in twenty-eight-day survival. The authors offer the grouping as a pilot step toward tailoring delirium prevention, needing prospective testing in today's ICUs.
pmc-13247305:
Hammad and co-authors present a rare birth defect of the thigh bone, with a literature review, in this 2026 Case Reports in Pediatrics article. Proximal femoral focal deficiency means the upper femur fails to form properly, shortening the leg. It occurs in about one in one hundred thousand births and affects both sides in only a small minority. Their patient was a two-year-old girl with odd crawling and walking, short bulky thighs, and tight, bent knees.

Imaging told two different stories: the right hip lacked a femoral head entirely, while the left had a head detached from its shaft. Both sockets were severely malformed with dislocations. Because the two sides differed, the authors stress imaging-led, individualized planning and a multidisciplinary team, weighing options from conservative care to reconstruction.
pmc-13248905:
Akingbola and co-authors charted forty years of childhood vaccination in Nigeria, in a 2026 study. Using Global Burden of Disease estimates, they tracked five routine vaccines from 1980 to 2023, including BCG, the triple DTP shot, polio, measles, and hepatitis B. Nigeria's program is one of Africa's largest, and its progress has been uneven.

Coverage sat lowest in 1980, rose through the early nineteen nineties, stalled for a decade, then improved again after 2005. The best years came around 2019 to 2021, with BCG peaking near three quarters of children. No vaccine ever reached the World Health Organization's ninety percent goal, so the authors urge fairer, targeted delivery.
pmc-13249705:
Creangă-Murariu and co-authors pooled the evidence on cannabis compounds for cancer pain, in a 2026 meta-analysis. Fifteen studies asked whether adding cannabinoids lets patients cut their opioid doses, a hoped-for benefit given opioid side effects. The reviewers separated fair comparisons against placebo from weaker before-and-after reports, and graded the certainty of everything they found.

Against placebo, cannabinoids changed nothing: total, background, and rescue opioid use all stayed put. Before-and-after analyses hinted at modest savings with THC-heavy preparations, but single studies drove those hints and results clashed. With certainty rated low, the authors conclude cannabinoids cannot be relied on as an opioid-sparing strategy in cancer pain.
pmc-13249805:
Giannini and colleagues ask whether the Mediterranean will trap its own sea snails as the climate warms, in a 2026 Ecology and Evolution study. Four collectible species, three cowries and a frog shell, were modeled using more than a century of occurrence records. The team projected past, present, and future ranges for the northeastern Atlantic and Mediterranean under two climate paths.

Mid-century decades look like a squeeze point, with habitat shrinking and no new ground opening in compensation. The Mediterranean's circulation works against escape toward cooler water, especially for species whose young drift as larvae. Adding larval sensitivity to more acidic water erased still more Atlantic habitat. The authors urge range forecasts that include life history, not just adult tolerance.
pmc-13251205:
Wafaa Yahia Alghonemy and co-authors tested injectable treatments for gum disease in rats, reporting in 2026. Periodontitis destroys the tissues and bone that hold teeth, driven by bacteria and the body's inflammatory response. The team compared hyaluronic acid gel, platelet-rich plasma from the animals' own blood, and the two combined.

Forty male rats with wire-induced gum disease were divided into five groups, including healthy and untreated controls. After two weeks, treated animals showed less tissue damage under the microscope than untreated ones. Blood markers of inflammation, two signals known as TNF-alpha and IL-1beta, also fell with treatment. The combined gel and plasma group healed best, while each treatment alone gave partial recovery. The authors suggest the pairing strengthens both the calming of inflammation and the rebuilding of tissue, though they call for further study.
pmc-13252705:
Sheng Soh and colleagues count hidden COVID-19 infections in Singapore in this 2026 study. Official case counts miss people who never seek care, yet planners need the true spread of an epidemic in near real time.

A community cohort of 1,899 people answered eleven survey rounds from September 2021 to November 2022, across two variant waves. Of 2,284 illness episodes, 756 were COVID-19, and only about six in ten of those saw a doctor, a share that fell over time. By modelling symptoms plus wastewater and staff testing signals, the team estimated total infections at one to nearly three times the reported numbers, matching blood-test surveys.
pmc-13252805:
Katherine Tezanos and colleagues pilot a positivity skills group for young adults with depression in this 2026 trial. The programme, called STEP, trains people to build positive emotions, aiming to cut suicide risk alongside standard care.

Fifty-two adults aged 18 to 26 at a community mental health service were split by chance between group STEP and enhanced usual care. Attendance was high and feedback positive, so the group format passed its feasibility test. The small trial could not prove group differences, yet STEP members showed larger rises in positive emotions and larger drops in depression and suicidal thoughts by follow-up. The authors call for a bigger trial.
pmc-13252905:
Fazeela Bibi and a large team report removing a giant nerve tumour in this 2026 case report. A 44-year-old labourer had a swelling in his neck for four years, and over the last year it brought arm pain, hand weakness, and wasting of the thumb-side muscles.

Scans showed a dumbbell-shaped tumour about eleven centimetres long threading from his neck into his upper chest, without invading nearby parts. In one operation through the back of the neck, surgeons removed it fully, using an ultrasonic tool to hollow it out safely. His pain vanished and nerve function recovered markedly. Lab tests confirmed a benign nerve sheath tumour. Careful planning, the authors say, made a giant case manageable.
pmc-13253205:
Justin A Kaskow and colleagues deliver a piece of the STING protein directly into ovarian cancer cells using nanoparticles in a 2026 study. STING is an internal alarm that, when triggered, floods a tumor with immune-stimulating signals. Many cancers silence STING itself, which defeats drugs that work by switching it on, so the team delivered a working fragment of the protein instead.

Their carrier is a degradable polymer nanoparticle tuned to slip into cells and release its cargo in the cytosol, the cell's interior fluid. A pH-shift assembly method then produced smaller, negatively charged particles, and the choice of partner polymer steered activation toward ovarian cancer cells over other types. In a mouse model, particles gathered in tumors across the abdomen, slowed their growth, and extended survival. The authors see protein-fragment delivery as a route to immunotherapy for cancers that have disabled this alarm.
pmc-13253905:
Yaying Song and colleagues propose a new field name, onco-neurology, in a 2026 article. Cancer care now keeps more people alive longer, yet nerve problems in cancer patients are rising in importance. Many are not caused by tumors pressing on nerves, but by immune reactions, treatments, or body-wide effects of the disease.

Old labels for these problems overlap and split care between cancer and nerve specialists. The authors argue a shared name would cut that fragmentation and push joint review of patients. It would also spur research on how tumors, the immune system, and nerves interact, without replacing older terms.
pmc-13254405:
Iñaki Echeverría-Huarte and colleagues study why crowds swirl counterclockwise in a 2026 paper. Groups of roaming pedestrians have been seen to develop a shared counterclockwise motion, in both dense and sparse crowds. The team ran five experiments under varied conditions in Spain and Japan.

The counterclockwise bias proved robust and repeatable across settings. It traced back to individual walking tendencies, not to interactions between people. That finding challenges the usual view that social dynamics shape crowd motion, and points to a built-in locomotor bias in how people walk, the authors argue.
pmc-13255205:
Leeanne Nicholls and colleagues seek expert agreement on trauma therapy for bipolar disorder in a 2026 Delphi study. EMDR is a therapy that targets unprocessed trauma memories, but guidance for adapting it in bipolar disorder is thin. Practitioners worldwide took part in three survey rounds, starting with 34 and ending with 20.

The panel agreed on 71 adaptations, covering mood monitoring, safety planning, pacing, and coping skills, with phase-specific changes for preparation and other stages. Fifteen supervision elements were also endorsed. The authors say the standard eight-phase protocol can be used, with care fitted to each person's mood pattern.
pmc-13255705:
Gang Fu and colleagues report a 2026 study from a twelve-year nitrogen addition experiment in a boreal forest in China's Greater Khingan Mountains. Extra nitrogen has rained onto forests worldwide since industrialization, and soil protists, tiny predators of microbes, help drive nutrient cycling. Plots established in 2011 received zero to seventy-five kilograms of nitrogen per hectare yearly.

Protists that eat microbes and those that make their own food responded strongly, while parasitic types barely reacted. Soil nutrients together with fungal and plant diversity steered the community shifts. The authors describe a soil-plant-microbe pathway through which nitrogen deposition reorganizes the hidden food web under northern forests.
pmc-13256305:
Muhsin Doran authored a 2026 expert evaluation of a GPT-5.3-based chatbot answering patient questions about scoliosis, curvature of the spine. A panel of experts graded responses for appropriateness, accuracy, completeness, and clarity, and sorted them by clinical risk.

Every answer cleared the panel's acceptability threshold on agreement measures, and overall quality scores ran high. Clarity earned the best marks, while depth and scientific accuracy scored lowest. Most answers were judged harmless or low risk, and none were rated high risk. The commonest flaw was simply too little information. Doran concludes the tool could support patient education under professional oversight, but stresses that expert-perceived quality is not the same as proven correctness.
pmc-13256805:
Nurmuhammet Taş maps in a 2026 citation study how research on combined muscle and joint rehab has grown between 1989 and 2026. Care teams as a rule mix exercise with hands-on therapy, teaching, and mental-health methods, yet most studies test each part alone, leaving combined practice uncharted.

Online attention signals pointed to policy interest as well. pmc-13257205:
Changli Zhang and co-authors profile gene activity in human disc cells treated with a growth factor in a 2026 study. Low back pain links closely to disc degeneration, where inflammation in the outer ring helps generate pain. PDGF-BB is known for tissue repair, yet its disc effects were unclear.

pmc-13257705:
İlke Taşkırdı and co-authors grade a chatbot's answers on rare childhood immune disorders in a 2026 evaluation. pmc-13258005:

pmc-13258105:
Takeo Shibata and a Kanazawa Medical University team describe one patient's cancer that grew out of endometriosis. Endometriosis is common, but its tissue can rarely turn malignant in the abdomen. Their 2026 case report pairs genomic testing with close pathological study of the tumor.

pmc-13258505:
Zhiwei Liu and coauthors examine how antimony affects hot cracking behavior in corrosion resistant steel during a 2026 study. pmc-13258805:
Yapeng Zhu and colleagues link aortic arch curvature to later vessel widening after stent repair in a 2026 multicenter study. One hundred twenty patients with a torn inner aorta wall received a branched stent graft. A tortuosity index measured how twisted each arch was before repair.

pmc-13259205:

pmc-13259305:

pmc-13259505:
Qianting Ma and coauthors characterize a wild tea plant with naturally low caffeine from Guangxi in a 2026 study. The upright tree type plant bears narrow leaves and five petal flowers. Fresh leaves were compared chemically against three standard cultivars.

pmc-13260205:

pmc-13262105:

pmc-13262205:

pmc-13262805:

pmc-13263105:

pmc-13263305:
Ferdinando Frattina and co-authors report a 2026 journal article on vitamin injections around calving in Italian Mediterranean buffaloes, a dairy breed. At calving, cows received intramuscular alpha-tocopherol, a form of vitamin E, plus beta-carotene, or served as untreated controls.

pmc-13263605:
Xiufeng Wang, Luping Ji, Xi Wang, and Jinhui Zhou measure vitamin D in sixty adolescents with idiopathic scoliosis, in a two thousand twenty-six observational study. Whether the vitamin relates to curve severity in this unexplained spinal setting was unresolved.

The authors conclude deficiency may contribute to the setting's development and suggest adequate supplementation could slow curve progression.
pmc-13264105:
Sarah Gonzalez-Coffin and co-authors review social science for climate adaptation in Great Plains grasslands in a 2026 article. pmc-13264205:
Fabiënne van Puijfelik and colleagues refine profiling of a suspect T cell type in multiple sclerosis in a 2026 study. pmc-13264305:

Joined-up registries could turn scattered clinic experience into solid guidance for patients.
pmc-13264405:
Qindi Hou and colleagues profile problem-solving styles in coronary heart disease patients in a 2026 cross-sectional study. pmc-13264605:

Accuracy leveled off near 70 percent, much like speech-in-noise findings. Signs that were read right felt easier. pmc-13265005:

pmc-13265305:
Yusuke Matsuyama, Richard G Watt, and Jun Aida study tooth loss as a pathway in social inequalities in health among older Japanese adults, in a 2026 cohort study.
