The authors suggest tackling unequal tooth loss could narrow health gaps.
pmc-13265405:
Tingting Mai and colleagues compare two forms of wrist-ankle acupuncture for muscle pain in rats, in a 2026 laboratory study. One form uses needles, while the other uses skin electrical stimulation based on the same theory. Inflammation was induced in the calf muscle. Gene activity was examined for mechanism clues.

Both treatments raised pain thresholds two to three times above untreated levels. Inflammation and collagen build-up fell, and inflammatory signals dropped. Gene analysis highlighted body-clock genes. Electrical stimulation adjusted some clock genes, while needle treatment adjusted others. The electrical form may serve as an alternative for early treatment.
pmc-13266705:
Zak Marshall and the team present QuantGUV, an image-based tool measuring how much material gets trapped inside synthetic cell bubbles (2026). Giant vesicles mimic living compartments for bottom-up biology. Reaction behaviour depends on internal concentrations, which were hard to measure per vesicle. Three fluorescent test materials were quantified.

Plastic beads were trapped almost completely under most conditions. A dye and a fluorescent protein trapped variably, depending on lipid amounts and oil-water ratios during formation. The software reads concentrations from images at single-vesicle resolution. Accurate internal control should help build quantitative synthetic cell systems for research.
pmc-13266805:
Hanyue Zhang and co-authors design in 2026 a standard set of Chinese speech tasks for studying voice changes in heart failure. Voice recording is cheap and non-invasive, yet earlier work used tasks built for other languages. Their study enrolled 203 people, about half of them heart failure patients, at a hospital in Taizhou.

Twelve tasks covered vowels, sentences, numbers, and a paragraph. Only about half of the participants finished every task, with reading trouble the main barrier, and age and education shaped success. Trimming the set to six tasks lifted completion sharply, especially for older and less educated participants. Voice features from the kept tasks separated patients from healthy controls well, supporting a future Chinese voice database.
pmc-13266905:
Reiko Shiba and colleagues wrote a 2026 study linking motivation to later mental distress. They surveyed 268 people in Japan using a questionnaire they adapted to measure inner drive for study and for daily activities. Distress was scored with a short six-item scale at the start and again one year later.

Of the group, 135 people finished the one-year follow-up. Two motivation patterns predicted higher distress a year on. One was strong inner drive for study; the other was a lack of drive, called amotivation, for the activities people do most often. Starting distress also predicted later distress. The authors say looking at motivation in several life areas may help prevent depression.
pmc-13267005:
Yunjun Cao and co-authors show in 2026 that a copper surface can flip how a reactive carbon species called a carbene behaves toward water. Free carbenes normally act as bases toward water, grabbing a proton and forming a charged product. The team combined surface infrared readings, atom-level microscopy, and computer modeling to watch the reaction on copper.

On the metal, the carbene instead acted as an electrophile, meaning it accepted electron density from water and formed a surface-held ylide. That intermediate then lost a proton to give the final product. The pathway differs completely from the same reaction in solution or in frozen matrices. Surfaces, the authors argue, can unlock reaction routes that are otherwise out of reach.
pmc-13267505:
Satoru Kuriu and Soo Hyeon Kim present a 2026 study of gut cells grown on a liquid surface inside a tiny device. Gut lining cells form a barrier that controls what passes into the body. Lab models usually grow them on solid sheets, which limits how the setting can be tuned. The new platform grows them where two liquids meet.

The meeting surface, coated with collagen, formed between an oil-like fluid and cell food in a microfluidic chip. Caco-2 gut cells attached, spread, and formed a single layer. Staining showed tight junctions, the seals between cells, and tidy inner scaffolding, signs of early maturing. The authors offer the soft, adjustable surface as a fresh way to model gut barriers.
pmc-13267705:
Chao Song and a large team build in 2026 tiny gelatin beads that fight infected bone defects from inside the wound. Infected defects resist treatment because bacteria form biofilms and inflammation lingers, while body-wide antibiotics often fail. Made with microfluidic precision, the beads carry two drugs: vancomycin to kill bacteria and resveratrol, a plant compound that calms inflammation and supports bone growth.

The beads released both drugs steadily and broke down biofilms of resistant staph bacteria in dishes. In rats with infected bone defects, they lowered bacterial counts, eased inflammation, and raised new bone volume and density. Lab tests traced resveratrol's help to a TNF and HIF-1 signaling axis that reshapes the wound's immune setting.
pmc-13267805:
Memy Rizkiyah and colleagues wrote a 2026 study building a chatbot to help families care for mental health patients at home in Indonesia. Families carry much of the care after hospital discharge but often lack information and support. The team interviewed five professionals and three family caregivers. They also read 67 past chat consultations and five discharge teaching documents.

Nine need areas emerged, from understanding the illness and handling medicines to coping with caregiver strain. Families wanted steady teaching, clear steps to prevent relapse, and easy ways to ask for help. The team turned these needs into a rule-based chatbot prototype that answers by decision tree. It offers teaching, care guidance, relapse help, and referral directions. Six experts checked the design. Testing with real users comes next.
pmc-13269305:
Patrick Meybohm and co-authors review in 2026 patient blood management for people in general intensive care, where anemia is common and often fixable. Critically ill patients lose blood through bleeding, repeated sampling, and blunted red cell production, while clotting problems complicate every decision. Their narrative review sorts published findings on anemia treatment, sampling practice, and each blood product.

Intravenous iron safely raised hemoglobin by a meaningful amount, while the hormone erythropoietin helped more selectively because clot risk is uncertain. Small-volume sample tubes and closed conservation systems cut losses from testing itself. Holding red cells and platelets back until truly needed proved safe in most settings, especially gut bleeding. Preventive plasma for non-bleeding patients gained no support. The package aims at safer, more personal care.
pmc-13269505:
Anna L Olsavsky and co-authors published a journal article in 2026 on anxiety and overall health in children with cancer and their caregivers. Both members of each pair rated their own anxiety and the child's health. The study used a model that separates a person's effect on their own ratings from their effect on their partner's.

Seventy-six pairs from two children's hospitals in the Midwest took part. Children averaged 13.35 years old. Both children and caregivers rated the child's health below average, while caregivers reported above-average anxiety and children below-average anxiety. Higher anxiety in either person went with that same person rating the child's health lower. Cross-partner effects were weaker and borderline. The authors urge care for the whole family system.
pmc-13269705:
Rima Gnaim and co-authors published a journal article in 2026 on barriers to microbial proteins, foods grown from microbe biomass, becoming everyday fare. Growing microbes for protein uses little land and water and emits few greenhouse gases. Yet the shift from specialty item to mainstream food has stalled before.

The authors propose three phases of adoption: a novelty barrier, early trust building, and mainstream normal life. Cost, rules, and factory capacity barriers are sorted into that path. They trace how single-cell proteins rose, fell, and returned, and match engineering and policy tools to each phase. Practical levers are offered to move these proteins into sturdy food systems.
pmc-13270405:
Larissa Dangel and co-authors published a journal article in 2026 on past infection with Coxiella burnetii, the bacterium causing Q fever, among blood donors in two German states. Q fever is underreported in Europe, and no general population figures existed for Germany. Over 5,000 donors with no known past infection were screened for antibodies.

A total of 153 donors, 2.96 percent, tested positive for antibodies against the bacterium. Living place, animal contact, and animal-related jobs each raised risk. In high-risk jobs, younger age groups showed higher prevalence than older ones, a reversed age pattern. The authors present donors as a stand-in for a normal, non-risk population and call the hidden infection burden notable.
pmc-13271005:
Annika Ladwig is lead author of a 2026 journal article on how read depth and read length affect splicing analysis in RNA sequencing. Splicing is the cutting and rejoining of gene messages, and studies compare splicing between conditions using short sequenced fragments called reads.

Using two standard ENCODE data sets with wide splicing changes, the team varied read length and depth and ran a leading analysis tool called MAJIQ. Both longer reads and deeper sequencing improved how sensitively and precisely splicing events were found, measured, and classified. The authors offer the results as practical guidance for researchers choosing sequencing settings for splicing studies, where poor settings can miss real changes.
pmc-13271105:
Naser Alotaibi is lead author of a 2026 retrospective cohort study of aspiration pneumonia after stroke in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia. This lung infection, caused by food or fluid entering the airway, is a serious stroke complication with high death rates. The study counted how often it occurred and what predicted death.

Among 5,921 adults admitted with stroke between February 2016 and January 2024, 118 developed the pneumonia during the admission or within 90 days. Swallowing problems were found in 54.2 percent, intensive care was needed in 46.6 percent, and 22.0 percent died in hospital. A lower consciousness score was the only independent predictor of death in the adjusted analysis.
pmc-13271505:
Marek Blatný is lead author of a 2026 longitudinal study, one following the same students over time, on how well students and teachers agree when rating adolescents' personality traits and social skills. Ratings came from 296 early adolescents, average age about 12.4 at the start of a two-year period, and their 28 class teachers.

Agreement was highest for traits that are easy to observe from outside. Student and teacher ratings of social skills agreed more for girls than for boys. Both traits and skills were highly stable over time for both raters, and agreement itself did not change substantially across the study. The authors urge attention to hard-to-see student characteristics before problems develop.
pmc-13271905:
Zhixu Zhang and coauthors test in 2026 whether contrast CT scans can tell two testicular tumors apart before surgery. Embryonal rhabdomyosarcoma of the testis is rare, while seminoma is far more common. The two need different treatment paths, so telling them apart on imaging has real value.

The team reviewed 15 confirmed rhabdomyosarcoma cases and 30 seminoma cases treated between 2012 and 2024. Patient age, scan measurements across contrast phases, and blood markers such as alpha-fetoprotein all differed between the groups. Combined reading of scan features and lab values improved the separation, which may help surgeons plan the right operation sooner.
pmc-13272405:
Zhongmian Zhang and coauthors chart in 2026 what the stomach lining looks like through an endoscope as autoimmune gastritis advances. In this disease the immune system destroys the acid-making region of the stomach, and blood markers cannot show how far the shrinkage has gone. A stage-by-stage map of scope findings was lacking.

Fifty-two Chinese patients meeting blood and tissue criteria were classed as early or late stage by how much acid-making lining remained. Standard and magnified imaging catalogued surface features in detail. The team also examined the strikingly frequent overlap with Barrett's esophagus, a change in the food pipe lining that needs watching.
pmc-13272505:
Mohamed Ibrahim and co-authors report a 2026 case of a 72-year-old man whose skin T-cell lymphoma spread to his heart. He also had kidney cancer that had spread, and he had long taken nivolumab, a drug that lifts a brake on immune cells. Heart spread by this lymphoma is very rare.

A surgical heart biopsy showed T cells matching his earlier skin disease. Doctors stopped nivolumab, fearing it had helped the spread, and switched to avelumab, a related drug. The heart disease then cleared on scans, heart blood markers improved, and his skin lymphoma stayed controlled for more than three years of follow-up.
pmc-13272805:
Meike Shedden-Mora leads a 2026 study asking whether what women expect in early pregnancy predicts how many symptoms they later feel. Symptoms such as nausea and fatigue are common, but mental factors are poorly understood. Women up to the tenth week of pregnancy filled in online surveys, with follow-up at the start of the second trimester.

Of 347 women at baseline, 227 completed follow-up. Symptom burden was high and rose across the first trimester. Stronger expected symptoms at baseline predicted greater burden and disability later, and symptoms and expectations also influenced each other over time. Negative mindsets about pregnancy linked to higher burden too, suggesting expectations could be a target for support.
pmc-13272905:
Catherine Hong Huan Hor and Bor Luen Tang asked in a 2026 review whether faulty primary cilia help cause major brain diseases of aging. Primary cilia are tiny antenna like parts on cells that carry many signal receptors. Defects were long tied to early onset disorders, but links to later diseases have grown.

The review weighs evidence from models and patients with Alzheimer's disease, Parkinson's disease, and amyotrophic lateral sclerosis. For each disease, the authors ask whether cilia faults drive harm, follow from it, or merely appear alongside it. Neuronal cilia host receptors for serotonin and other signals, so damage could matter deeply. The paper maps what is known and where proof is still thin.
pmc-13273205:
Andrew J Del Gaizo, Jackson K Del Gaizo, and Troy A Shahoumian surveyed radiologists about an artificial intelligence tool for brain bleeding in a 2026 study. The tool, cleared by regulators, flags bleeding on head scans in a national teleradiology network. Real value depends on how readers judge its alerts in daily work.

Sixty-five radiologists answered, about a third of them brain imaging specialists. Only a small share agreed that false alerts were rare enough to accept. About a third agreed the tool caught most bleeds, and trust was strongly conditional: half trusted it when it matched their own reading, while almost none trusted it when it disagreed. The results show caution toward the tool despite its formal clearance.
pmc-13274005:
Theresa Holst and colleagues report a 2026 case report of stone heart syndrome, a rare disaster during heart surgery. In this condition the heart muscle locks into a hard, lasting spasm when blood flow returns, and it does not respond to drugs or machines. A heart surgeon first described it in 1972.

Their patient was a healthy twenty-two-year-old having planned mitral valve surgery who developed failure of both heart chambers after bypass. Support machines were stepped up over days, then a lasting heart pump was placed on day five. Nothing reversed the damage, so the patient received a heart transplant on day twenty-three. The later course was largely smooth, and discharge to rehabilitation came six weeks after transplant.
pmc-13274105:
Paul Köbler and co-authors present a 2026 pilot study on finding hidden mental illness in hospital medical wards. Many inpatients have depression or anxiety that staff miss when referrals depend only on a doctor's hunch. One ward instead screened every patient with the four-question PHQ-4 form, while two similar wards kept usual practice.

The screening ward logged 127 admissions against 267 on the usual-care wards. Referrals rose from about eight percent to about seventeen percent of admissions. Confirmed diagnoses were found in about nine percent of screened admissions versus three percent under usual care. Screening patients also reached a consultation faster, a median of one day instead of three and a half.
pmc-13274205:
Engin Korkmazer compares, in a study whose journal version is dated 2026, two operations for a dangerous pregnancy complication. In placenta accreta spectrum, the placenta grows too deeply into the womb wall, and delivery can bleed catastrophically. The standard rescue removes the womb; the alternative cuts out only the invaded segment and repairs the rest. Reviewing one hundred thirty cases from 2016 to 2019, thirty treated by segment removal and one hundred by womb removal, the study compared blood loss, complications, and baby outcomes.

The womb-removal group fared worse on nearly every measure: more blood loss, more transfusions, more bladder injuries, longer stays, and more intensive care. Babies did equally well either way. The author cautions that the sicker cases likely landed in the bigger operation, so the gap partly reflects who got what. Still, for carefully chosen patients, segment removal looks like a safe way to spare the womb.
pmc-13274505:
Binata Mukherjee and colleagues present a 2026 scoping review of coaching programs for medical students and residents. Coaching pairs learners with a trained guide for reflection and goal setting, and schools keep adding such programs without a shared blueprint. The team searched three databases through May 2024 for what makes these programs work.

Of 801 articles screened, 141 were included, with publication peaking in 2023. Most programs targeted clinical competence, then learner wellness. Graduate medical education was studied more than undergraduate training. Programs commonly used reflection, goal setting, and direct observation. Success hinged on institutional support and coach training, while time pressure, fuzzy coach roles, and learner readiness were the main barriers.
pmc-13274705:
Hemal B. Rathod and co-authors made a palladium catalyst with help from a fungus in a 2026 green chemistry study. Palladium nanoparticles are powerful catalysts, but they clump and leak metal, which shortens their life. A biological coating might hold them steady without harsh chemicals.

They grew a strain of Aspergillus fungus that reduced palladium ions and wrapped the particles in its own biomass, with no added surfactants or stabilizers. Tuning culture age, biomass amount, and soaking time gave even particles of about thirty-five nanometers. The coated catalyst fully converted nitrobenzene to aminobenzene within thirty minutes in water at room conditions, with high turnover counts. Metal leakage stayed very low, and the coating improved storage stability, which supports reuse.
pmc-13275205:
Natasha Pearson, Peter Baker, and Jill Bradshaw study families of folks with pica. Their study from twenty twenty-six deals with eating non food matter. Pica poses grave health risks for folks with intellectual disabilities.

It is under known, more so in home settings. Deep talks were held with a small set of primary carers. Five themes rose, from life on high alert to silence. Carers told of constant watch and deep tiredness. They got little pro input despite life threatening acts. Yet they showed craft and grit in many roles.
pmc-13275505:
Alec M Giakas and a large team report a 2026 retrospective cohort study on whether nicotine from vapes and pouches, not cigarettes, harms neck fusion surgery outcomes. Using a national database of patients who had posterior cervical fusion from 2012 to 2025, they matched non-tobacco nicotine users against tobacco users and non-users. In total, 7,102 patients were included.

At three years, non-tobacco nicotine users had more failed fusions, called pseudarthrosis, at 2.51 percent versus 1.84 percent in controls. They also suffered more most other complications, though not deep vein clots. Against tobacco users their profile was broadly similar, with more cervical fractures and early pneumonia, but less opioid misuse and fewer readmissions. The authors urge counseling patients that non-tobacco nicotine is not risk-free.
pmc-13275605:
Malina Suchon, Daniel M Weary, and Marina AG von Keyserlingk present a 2026 narrative review of how dairy calf housing shapes calves' emotional states. Farm calves are usually separated from their mothers at birth, kept alone, and denied pasture, a stark contrast with natural life. The authors sort housing features into physical, social, and time-related groups and weigh the evidence from behavior clues such as play and time use.

Generous milk, varied solid foods, and soft dry bedding consistently supported positive states, as did full physical contact with other calves. Timing factors such as predictability and the calf's own control over its day look influential but remain little studied. The review stresses that lasting mood, not just momentary feelings, is still poorly understood and needs targeted research.
pmc-13276005:
José Serrano-Mestre and co-authors report a 2026 journal article on how the tuberculosis bacterium releases tiny sacs called extracellular vesicles. These sacs carry molecules that can sway the immune system. Which genes control their release was unknown, since no one had screened the whole genome for it.

The team built a fast screening system using small wells and either a fat-loving dye or an antibody that binds the sacs. They then tested mutant bacteria missing one gene at a time. The screen pointed to genes that rebuild the cell's outer envelope and genes that handle fatty acids as the main regulators of sac release. The authors say this platform can now support deeper studies of how the sacs form.
pmc-13276305:
Linzhu Wang and co-authors report a 2026 journal article on a cell type that may drive osteoarthritis toward its end stage. Osteoarthritis wears down joints and has no approved drug that stops it. The synovium, the joint's inner lining, is packed with fibroblast cells whose changes were unclear.

Gene profiling showed a fibroblast group marked by a protein called MFAP5 flooding late-stage diseased joints. Staining confirmed the protein was far higher in late-stage human and rat tissue than in early disease or healthy joints. These cells also made large amounts of LOX, an enzyme that stiffens tissue. Silencing MFAP5 cut the LOX rise in rat cells, and adding MFAP5 boosted it. A drug blocking LOX eased joint damage in rats with the disease. The authors propose this pathway as a treatment target.
pmc-13276605:
Zhili Ji and colleagues test a plant gum in refrigerated precooked alkaline noodles, in a 2026 food study. Ready noodles lose their springy texture in cold storage as starch firms and water shifts. The gum comes from Artemisia sphaerocephala seeds and is used here at a low dose.

Noodles with the gum lost less material when recooked after four days of refrigeration. Hardness rose far less than in plain noodles, and tensile strength improved by about a third. Water stayed more tightly bound, and microscopy showed a reinforced gluten network wrapping the starch. After reheating, gum noodles recovered texture better and leaked less starch, which supports longer shelf life for convenience products.
pmc-13276805:
Aga Natalis and Abdul Jalil wrote a 2026 letter to the editor on medicine registration delays as a gender justice issue. A study of nine countries found that on average only seventy-two percent of tracer medicines for mothers, newborns, and children had any registered product. In weaker regulatory systems the share fell as low as twenty-eight percent.

The letter applies the findings to Indonesia, where the drug agency is still being strengthened. Delays can deny pregnant women oxytocin, misoprostol, and magnesium sulfate, standbys against bleeding and eclampsia. Through a feminist legal lens, the authors argue slow, complex registration systematically reproduces inequality for women. They back reforms the study highlights: priority legal pathways for essential medicines, recognition of World Health Organization prequalification, harmonized rules, and digital registration systems.
pmc-13277205:
Elsayed Abdelhalim leads a 2026 case report of a rare, life-threatening problem after kidney stone treatment. A 75-year-old man had flexible ureteroscopy, where a thin scope is passed to treat a kidney stone, at another hospital. He arrived a week later with septic shock, a severe infection response, and heavy bleeding around the kidney.

Scans showed a large blood collection pressing on the kidney. Despite fluids, strong antibiotics, and intensive care, his condition worsened. Surgeons removed the kidney as a life-saving step. Single cases cannot show how often such harm occurs. Still, the authors stress fast recognition and quick transfer to a specialist center when warning signs appear.
pmc-13277405:
Xiaojie Mei, Wenqing Wu, Ning Fang, Yali Guo, and Xiaohu Dai weigh sludge compost as both cure and risk for worn-out soil, in a study from two thousand twenty-six. Gene and chemical reads tracked soil, maize roots, and root-zone germs across compost doses. Mid doses at or below fifteen percent of soil weight form the safe zone in the results.

Mid doses raised soil food, root growth, and helpful germ types, plus plant stress compounds. Heavy doses past twenty percent brought salt stress, weak roots, and germ shifts. Drug and pesticide traces also piled up at high doses, tied to human-disease germ paths. Root health ruled the plant-germ loop. Readers get a dose line for safe reuse.
pmc-13278405:
Andreas Nielsen Hald leads a 2026 randomized trial of a digital support program for children and teens after their parents separate. Parental separation can harm mental health and daily well-being. The Danish trial gave 866 young people from 467 families access to the SES NXT program, or placed them on a waitlist. It tracked body complaints, trouble falling asleep, and body size perceptions.

At twelve weeks, waitlist youth had far higher odds of reporting body complaints and sleep-onset problems than program users. Extreme body size perceptions were also more common in the waitlist group. Gaps appeared by four weeks and held to twelve. A digital program may ease less obvious signs of strain after separation, not only mood measures.
pmc-13278905:
Michelle Gomes and co-authors review AI risk tools for cervical cancer in a 2026 perspective, adding a new angle: the vaginal microbiome. Current screening cannot tell which high-risk HPV infections will progress to cancer. The authors view risk as a web of virus, immunity, vaginal ecology, vaccination, and behaviour.

Communities rich in Lactobacillus crispatus look protective, while other community types track with persistent HPV and precancer. Existing AI tools lean on background, clinical data, or images, and none yet use such profiles in validated calculators. The article sketches how self-collected tampon samples could feed AI triage inside screening programmes. Long-term multi-omics cohorts and bias checks top the needs list.
pmc-13279205:
Christopher P Ouellette and colleagues published a 2026 case report of a teenager with acute myeloid leukemia who survived a dangerous double fungal infection thanks to an oral form of amphotericin B. The 15-year-old developed sinus and lung infection with two molds, Mucor nidicola and Aspergillus calidoustus, three weeks after intensive chemotherapy had left her white cell counts near zero. The Aspergillus strain had limited susceptibility to azole drugs, the usual oral option.

Standard intravenous liposomal amphotericin B caused toxicity, so the team switched to MAT2203, an encochleated form that wraps the drug in lipid layers so it can be swallowed. The infection, which had spared the eyes and brain, was successfully treated. The report matters because invasive mold infections in children with leukemia are often fatal. An effective oral salvage option could spare patients weeks of intravenous therapy and its side effects.
pmc-13279405:
Zijun Zhou and Jianping Zhou published a 2026 review arguing that artificial intelligence should do more for colorectal cancer immunotherapy than predict who responds. Immune checkpoint drugs help only the minority whose tumors carry a repair defect, and even they respond unevenly. The authors propose two roles: AI as a microscope that uncovers hidden tumor-immune interactions in combined data. The second makes it a digital twin simulating one patient's course.

The review surveys AI on tissue slides, imaging, and blood-based liquid biopsy for sorting patients before treatment and tracking response. Such tools could map how resistance develops, shape adaptive trial designs, and suggest ways to warm up unresponsive tumors so immunotherapy can work. Barriers include models that fail outside their home data and opaque reasoning. Their larger claim is that coupling data-hungry AI with mechanistic modeling could move care from group averages toward personal planning.
pmc-13279705:
Didi Monwabisi and colleagues published a 2026 assessment of infection control in primary care clinics in South Africa's O.R. Tambo District Municipality. Weak control lets care-linked infections spread, a danger at clinics that are first contact in low-resource systems. The team applied the World Health Organization's framework, which scores eight core components, to thirteen clinics that took part from eighteen approached.

Most sites, 69.2 percent, landed at an intermediate level, with a median score of 452.5 on the framework. Programs, written guidelines, and the physical environment scored highest. Tracking of care-linked infections scored lowest, and training plus staffing fell below half marks. Every site had a control program on paper, yet fewer than half had clear objectives and annual plans. Only 15.4 percent received dedicated budget support. The authors call for investment in tracking, training, staffing, and financing to lift patient safety.
pmc-13280805:
Marjanur Rahman Bhuiyan and colleagues tested a wild plant as a possible aid for Alzheimer's disease in a 2026 study. Alzheimer's harms memory and thinking and is growing worldwide. One known thread is a drop in a brain chemical that helps memory. The plant, Aeginetia indica, grows without green leaves and feeds on other plants. The team made an extract from the whole plant and tested it in dishes, animals, and computer models.

The extract fought cell damage from rust-like stress in lab tests. It blocked an enzyme that breaks down the memory chemical, doing so at least as well as a standard drug in the test. In animals it cut swelling. Chemical scans found dozens of active plant compounds, and computer fits named three as top leads. The authors call for more tests before any human use.
pmc-13280905:
Hao Wu and colleagues published a 2026 study improving how 1-octanol, a long-chain alcohol, is converted with ammonia into fatty amines, ingredients for surfactants, pharmaceuticals, and corrosion inhibitors. The gas-phase reaction borrows hydrogen: the alcohol is dehydrogenized, condenses with ammonia, and is rehydrogenized to the amine. Their catalyst pairs nickel with a small addition of rhenium on an alumina support. They mapped how the rhenium changes the metal's behavior and the support's surface acidity and basicity.

Rhenium sped up nickel's activation by spilling hydrogen across the surface, loosened nickel's grip on the support and rebalanced the surface sites into a mix of weak, moderate, and strong sites. Amine yield traced a volcano shape against rhenium content, peaking at the two-percent formulation, which converted 99.5 percent of the alcohol with 64 percent selectivity for the single amine. The authors offer this acid-base reconfiguration as a design strategy for cheap catalysts.
pmc-13281405:
Rana Abjar and colleagues ran a 2026 trial of finger pressure therapy for surgery staff. Operating room staff face heavy strain, poor sleep, and fatigue. The therapy, called acupressure, presses set points on the body by hand. Seventy staff with at least two of anxiety, fatigue, or poor sleep joined. Half got true acupressure for four weeks. Half got a sham form, a light touch near the points with no pressure. Checks ran at the start and at two and four weeks.

At the start the groups looked alike on anxiety and fatigue. After four weeks the true therapy group felt calmer and less tired. Their sleep also improved more over time than the sham group's. The authors present acupressure as a drug-free way to support staff health. They say such low-cost steps could help hospitals keep skilled teams rested and sharp.
pmc-13281505:
Coelho and four co-authors map what drives drink use in Brazil teens in this twenty twenty-six study. Teen years bring body, mind, and town shifts that can open risk paths. Kin, school, and street all feed a teen's pull to drink in that span.

Inside, a big school health poll from one past year feeds the four-tier checks. More than one in four teens told of drink use in the past month. Age, smoke, drug use, sweet food, and sad mood each raised the rate. Mom and dad drink use was the top kin-tier tie in the set. Home force, sex force, and class skip all tied to drink as well.
pmc-13281605:
Jordan Curry and colleagues wrote shared advice on public roles in doctoral research in a 2026 paper. Public involvement means research done with the public, not just about them. Doctoral students, early in their careers, rarely get advice shaped to their stage. The paper was built jointly by doctoral researchers, public partners, and a coordinator who links the two. They wrote through rounds of talk and revision. Their rule was to make room to talk and room to change.

The team found public input sharpened study aims and design. It also made findings easier to reach and use. Public partners gained skills and a sense of impact. Hard parts included heavy topics, tight timelines, and wishes that could not all be met. The coordinator proved key to holding the work together. The authors offer the advice as a base for new doctoral teams.
pmc-13281705:
Eakkapote Prompunt and colleagues built a fast test for a dangerous yeast in a 2026 study. The yeast, Candida albicans, can invade the blood of very sick patients and kill. Naming it fast guides the right drug choice. Their test copies a telltale gene stretch in a warm bath, with no cycling machine needed. They checked how little yeast DNA it could find and whether it mistook kin yeasts for the target. Six other fungi that enter blood were used as decoys.

The test found DNA in amounts a thousand times smaller than a standard gene test needs. It stayed silent for all six decoy fungi. In blood spiked with the yeast in the lab, it kept finding the target at very low levels. The authors call it a hopeful bedside aid for this infection. They stress that patient trials must come before clinic use.
pmc-13282005:
Gulhan Ayhan Albayrak wrote a 2026 journal article on blood markers in chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, a long-term lung illness that narrows airflow. The study asked whether signs of body-wide inflammation, measured while patients were stable, could predict flare-ups. Those flare-ups, called exacerbations, are sudden worsenings that can send patients to hospital.

Albayrak looked back at one hundred thirty-two patients followed for at least two years. Simple blood ratios and scores, plus a protein called C-reactive protein, were linked to more flare-ups and more hospital stays. One index, the systemic inflammation response index, showed no such link. The scores had only moderate power to pick out frequent flare-up patients. Still, the author argues these cheap blood tests may help flag higher-risk patients during routine care.
pmc-13282405:

pmc-13285205:

pmc-13296005:
Roy Fleischmann and co-authors report seven-year results in 2026 from SELECT-COMPARE, a large rheumatoid arthritis trial pitting daily upadacitinib tablets against adalimumab injections. Patients who had not responded enough to methotrexate could switch to the other drug if their first choice fell short.

Both drugs held their gains through seven years, with upadacitinib slightly ahead on remission rates among those staying on treatment. Its side-effect pattern matched earlier reports, with somewhat more shingles, skin cancers and liver issues noted. Switching helped initial non-responders too. The authors judge the long-term balance of benefit and risk acceptable.
pmc-13296105:
Zexu Li and colleagues compare, in 2026, back muscle from stallions and castrated Kazakh horses to see how castration changes meat. Samples from three-year-old animals were checked for eating quality, fibre structure and gene activity.

Colour and acidity stayed the same, but meat from castrated horses lost less water in cooking, needed less force to cut and had smaller fibres. Gene reading found 848 genes differing between groups, centred on the cell scaffolding system, with eleven core genes flagged. The authors say the results explain the tenderness gain and can guide breeding for better horse meat.
pmc-13296305:
Sofya Mishina and co-authors propose, in 2026, that pollution rather than infection may increasingly explain rising autoimmune disease. Infections are falling, yet autoimmunity climbs, and the classic trigger story relies on germs whose shapes resemble body proteins, fooling defences into attacking self tissue.

The authors suggest pollutants could mimic that invasion signal in people prone to autoimmunity. Their hypothesis paper lays out the mimicry idea, its history since the 1960s and why a non-infectious stand-in deserves study. If right, the account would redirect attention toward chemical exposures in prevention research.
pmc-13296505:
Yue Yu, Shuntian Wang, Livia Cabernard, and Stephan Pfister trace biodiversity damage hidden inside global mining supply chains in a 2026 study. Mining land destroys habitat where it sits, but the goods are usually consumed elsewhere. Their framework links local species loss at mine sites to a global trade model of who ultimately buys the output.

Estimated impacts came out nearly twice as high as earlier global figures. Five hotspot regions, led by Indonesia and Australia, accounted for well over half of the total. Most of the footprint fell outside the consuming country, with demand from China, Europe, Japan, and the United States driving much of it. The maps give conservation planners clearer targets along supply chains.
pmc-13296605:
Dong-Ho Shin and co-authors grow, in 2026, stacked layers of lead sulphide and tin disulphide one atomic layer at a time and show the stack squeezes charge carriers into quantum confinement. Thinning the lead sulphide layer below a key size widened its energy gap in steps the team could dial in.

Vibration tests showed the layers coupled strongly despite clean, strain-free boundaries, and computer models confirmed squeezing in both directions. An individually grown film sat far below the stack's tuned range. The authors say the method opens precise quantum engineering of layered materials for light-based devices.
pmc-13296705:
Frédéric Millot and co-authors report, in 2026, registry outcomes for adolescents with chronic myeloid leukaemia, a rare blood cancer in the young. Data on 132 patients aged fifteen to eighteen in the early phase are compared with younger children treated in the same era.

Adolescents showed enlarged spleens less often and lower white cell counts at diagnosis than younger children. Among those starting on imatinib, response depth, freedom from progression and survival matched the younger group. Five-year survival compared well with adult figures. The authors say teenagers fare like children on modern targeted pills.
pmc-13296905:
Neha Chaudhary and colleagues uncover how a signalling protein protects pancreatic cancer cells from radiation in a 2026 study. The protein Rac1 sits downstream of the KRAS signal that drives most pancreatic tumours. Blocking Rac1 weakened the cells' DNA-damage alarm system, the team found.

The reason was loss of claspin, a protein needed to activate the damage checkpoint. Rac1 blockade sped claspin's destruction through a named degradation route, without changing its gene message. Normal pancreatic cells lost claspin too, yet only the cancer cells were pushed into death by radiation. Exploiting that difference could make radiotherapy work harder against this resistant cancer, the authors propose.
pmc-13297205:
Xingyu Hou and co-authors probe, in 2026, how xylazole, a sedative used in Chinese veterinary practice, shifts brain chemistry in rats. Young cortical cells in dishes and adult brains sampled by microdialysis were exposed, tracking the messenger cAMP and mood-related chemicals.

In young cells the drug raised cAMP through a known receptor, briefly lifted dopamine and steadily raised serotonin and its breakdown product. In adult brains it mostly lowered cAMP, dopamine and noradrenaline while raising serotonin, with one region rebounding late. The authors caution the high test dose makes the brain patterns exploratory, not proof of one receptor route.
pmc-13298005:
After BCMA-targeted therapy stops working in multiple myeloma, what helps next? Nagham Youssef and a large multicenter team examined real-world records from US academic centers in a 2026 study to compare salvage strategies.

BCMA-directed CAR T-cell therapy gave responses that ran deeper, and survival that ran longer, than BCMA T-cell engagers given after earlier BCMA treatment. Teclistamab lost potency when it followed prior BCMA therapy, especially within six months. Talquetamab, which aims at a different target called GPRC5D, stayed active in many patients, supporting a switch of target after BCMA failure. The authors argue that timing and antigen choice should guide the next trials and guidelines.
pmc-13298505:
Plain clinical tables beat endoscopy images for predicting a painful ERCP complication, found Anum Jamil and colleagues in a 2026 single-center study. They compared machine learning on tabular data, deep learning on procedure images, and a fused multimodal system for forecasting pancreatitis after the bile duct procedure.

The gradient-boosted tabular model reached an AUC of 0.95, though it caught only half the cases, and cross-validation lowered that to 0.79. The best image model scored 0.76, and the combined system trailed at 0.57. Explanation analysis highlighted cannulation time, ampulla type, and age. The authors blame the rare outcome and small image supply, urging multicenter data collection.
pmc-13298605:
Garrison Thornton and a large team review whether ultrasound elastography stiffness reflects force and activation in foot and ankle muscles, in a 2026 systematic review. Shear wave elastography measures muscle stiffness inside the living body, yet its meaning for strength was untested as a body of evidence. Twenty studies covering 637 participants met their criteria.

Most studies found at least one significant link between stiffness and a force or activation outcome. Resting stiffness related weakly to maximal strength yet consistently to rapid torque development at stretched lengths. Stiffness during contraction tracked effort within a person. Joint angle, contraction state, and the specific muscle all shaped the relationship.
pmc-13300305:
N M A S Atan and co-authors report a 2026 ten-year comparison of pacing-induced cardiomyopathy between leadless and transvenous pacemakers at Malaysia's National Heart Institute. Frequent right ventricular pacing can weaken the heart over time, and this study asked whether the leadless design changes that risk in a Southeast Asian population. Records covered implants from 2013 to 2023, with cardiomyopathy defined by a clear drop in pumping function and no other cause.

Of 1,053 patients meeting the study criteria, 244 developed the condition. Rates were 22 percent with transvenous devices and 32 percent with leadless devices, and one leadless model fared worse than its sibling version. Male sex, a wide paced QRS pattern, and high pacing burden were the dominant predictors. The authors urge structured follow-up after implant and favor pacing strategies that keep the ventricles in sync.
pmc-13301005:
Masahiro Shirata and Michiko Tsuchiya report the first known case of pleural empyema caused by the gut bacterium Mediterraneibacter gnavus, in a 2026 case report. The patient was a seventy-eight-year-old Japanese man with diabetes, severe malnutrition, and kidney disease from his diabetes. He also had a pre-existing pocketed pleural effusion, and he arrived with fever after days of fatigue and appetite loss. Standard aerobic cultures of blood and pleural fluid grew nothing.

Only anaerobic culture of the pleural fluid yielded growth. The organism was first named by mass spectrometry fingerprinting and then confirmed by gene sequencing as this obligate anaerobe, a normal gut resident more often discussed in bowel inflammation. Beta-lactam antibiotics plus pleural drainage treated him successfully. The authors warn that lung infections from such organisms will be missed unless laboratories run oxygen-free cultures and reach for advanced testing when routine cultures stay silent.
pmc-13301405:
Body shape predicts court speed differently at thirteen than at fifteen, Sousana Symeonidou and colleagues find in a 2026 study of eighty-nine youth male basketball players. Under-13 and under-15 squads were measured for height, mass, body fat, and fat-free mass, then tested on jumps, short sprints, and change-of-direction and reactive agility drills.

Younger players showed a web of links: height and lean mass helped jumping and sprinting, while fat held most scores back. Models explained up to forty-four percent of sprint variation in that group. Older boys showed fewer ties, though body fat still dragged on jumps and agility and mass aided sprinting. No body measure predicted reactive agility at either age.
pmc-13301505:
Humam Siga and co-authors phase the mutations of colorectal tumors, asking which chromosome copy each variant sits on, in a 2026 proof of concept study. Standard sequencing lists a tumor's alterations but cannot say whether both copies of a gene are hit, and that distinction decides whether a protein fails. The team applied droplet barcode linked read sequencing to paired tumor and normal samples, tagging long DNA molecules so distant variants could be assigned to the same parental strand.

Several cancer genes carried multiple mutations, some stacked on one copy and others split across both. Large structural rearrangements and copy number changes were resolved and phased alongside the small variants, and nearly every known cancer pathway in the samples carried at least some of the cataloged mutations. The authors present linked read barcoding as a workable route to haplotype aware tumor profiles, information they argue personalized treatment planning will need.
pmc-13301805:
M Macgillivray and colleagues present a 2026 systematic review on how extra heartbeats arising in the lower chambers affect daily life and mental state. These early beats are common, and even people with few of them sometimes report strong symptoms. The review centres on psychological factors that shape how symptoms are noticed and felt.

Six studies with 408 patients met the criteria, most involving structurally normal hearts checked by ultrasound. Treatments across the studies included beta-blockers, other rhythm medicines, and a targeted ablation procedure for many patients. After treatment, depression, anxiety, and fear of bodily sensations generally eased, while activity levels and social functioning improved. The authors argue that care should address mood and lifestyle alongside the rhythm itself.
pmc-13301905:
P Jurak and colleagues examine, in a 2026 study, whether ultra-high-frequency ECG measures of left-heart timing match real gains in pumping pressure during resynchronization therapy. This treatment paces both sides of a failing heart to restore coordinated contraction. Standard trace width is a crude guide, so finer frequency-based measures might track benefit better.

Twenty-three patients had special fourteen-lead recordings while blood pressure was measured directly through an arterial line. Pressure rose under both biventricular pacing and left bundle branch area pacing compared with single-site pacing. Two measures of timing spread within the left wall matched pressure change perfectly across 46 paired comparisons. Ordinary trace width and between-chamber timing matched less well, supporting the finer measures for tuning therapy.
pmc-13302005:
Metal sheets that dissolve as bone regrows tempt dental surgeons, and Dragana Gabrić with colleagues map the evidence in a 2026 scoping review of magnesium-based membranes. Thirty-nine studies, from bench tests to small case series, covered membranes and screws used in ridge regeneration and guided bone growth. The search followed scoping review guidelines across several databases.

Cells tolerated the material and stuck to it, and moderate magnesium levels nudged bone-forming markers upward in the lab. Animal work showed orderly breakdown with the barrier intact through early healing. Human reports describe mostly smooth healing and kept bone volume, with minor troubles such as membrane exposure and small gas pockets. Controlled trials are still missing.
pmc-13303205:
Iron stores relate to anemia in Chinese schoolchildren through a curve, not a straight line, Yan Sun and colleagues show in a 2026 matched case-control study. National surveillance supplied 175 anemic children and adolescents plus 525 matched controls. Serum ferritin was modeled in quartiles and with flexible splines, adjusting for age, body mass, sex, and inflammation.

Children in the second and fourth ferritin quartiles carried about half or less the anemia risk of the lowest group, and the spline confirmed significant non-linearity. The protective pattern belonged to girls alone; boys showed no association. The authors urge sex-aware, non-linear thinking when ferritin guides anemia assessment in pediatric practice.
pmc-13303305:
A brain bleed with no aneurysm to blame still shadows most survivors years later, Wouter J Dronkers and colleagues find in a 2026 prospective study from Amsterdam and Zurich. Patients admitted with non-aneurysmal, non-traumatic subarachnoid hemorrhage between 2015 and 2021 answered questionnaires and interviews at a median of nearly five years afterward. One hundred eleven responded, split between perimesencephalic and other patterns.

Forty percent scored at least two on the disability scale, a worse picture than earlier reports suggested. Seventy percent of previously employed patients had fully returned to work, but fifteen percent had not returned at all. Only about a quarter reported no complaints; tiredness and trouble remembering new information led the residual list.
pmc-13303605:
Hannes Vermue and colleagues present a 2026 review asking whether knee looseness after total knee replacement should be measured with tools rather than surgeon feel. Robot help has grown in knee surgery, yet soft tissue balance is still often judged by hand.

Searches of two databases found 34 studies linking measured looseness in two planes to patient-reported outcomes, with follow-up from one month to over eight years. A middle range of front-to-back looseness tied to better function, while too much or too little did worse. Side-to-side looseness on the inner side mattered most. Routine objective checks may lift results for patients.
pmc-13304105:
Fahri Akgül and co-authors test, in a 2026 multicentre study, a combined blood index as a survival marker in stomach cancer that has already spread at diagnosis. The CALLY index blends an inflammation protein, a nutrition protein, and immune cell counts into one number. Its value in this specific, poor-prognosis group was undefined.

The study covered 234 patients treated between 2015 and 2025, split at a data-derived threshold into low and high index groups. Patients with high scores lived a median of nearly fourteen months against under nine months for the low group. The disadvantage of a low score persisted after adjustment for tumour features, treatment type, and diagnosis era. Time to progression, by contrast, showed no significant split.
pmc-13304305:
Aleksandra Arsić and co-authors compare, in a 2026 case-control study, chemical signs of oxidative damage across heart failure severity grades. Eighty-five patients and thirty-three healthy controls gave blood for a panel covering damage products, nitrogen-based stress markers, and antioxidant defences, plus the standard heart hormone.

Every marker differed clearly between patients and controls, and the pattern worsened with symptom class and weaker pumping. In combined models, a nitrogen marker stayed tied to symptom severity while a fat-damage marker stayed tied to pumping weakness. The heart hormone still separated severe from mild symptoms best of all. The authors propose the two oxidative markers as complementary windows onto different faces of the disease.
pmc-13305305:
Dmitry Medvedev and colleagues develop a way to pull hypericin, a light-activated red pigment, from St. John's wort and package it for medicine in a 2026 study. The compound fights disease under light but barely dissolves in water.

Fat was stripped first with a Soxhlet setup, then sound-assisted acetone extraction freed the pigment from plant tops. A thin-film method packed it into soap-like bubbles of a common polymer, giving steady particles about 30 nanometers wide with very high loading. Mouse brain tumor cells soaked up the bubbles over time and died under light, with no dark harm.
pmc-13306005:
Daniela Mirela Vîrtosu used a coronary care example in 2026 to question standard risk modelling when outcomes are rare. Infections picked up in hospital affected only 16 of 870 unit patients, a rate of 1.8% in the reported cohort.

With four candidate predictors, events per variable came to about four, a level the authors link to unstable coefficients and overfitted models. As an alternative, they explore a preset adding-up framework that combines baseline frailty and exposure factors without heavy fitting. The case argues for simpler, pre-planned scoring when rare events make complex models unreliable.
pmc-13306105:
Claude Lambré chaired an EFSA panel that judged a plastic recycling method for food packaging in a 2026 safety opinion. The Bandera Twin process, listed as RECYC341, starts with washed flakes from used PET bottles, with at most 5% from non-food uses.

Flakes pass through hot extrusion under vacuum, named as the key cleaning step in the assessment. Challenge testing checked temperature, pressure and one further controlled factor against movement of unknown contaminants into food. The panel found the output acceptable for stated uses, including a capped share for drinking water containers stored at room temperature.
pmc-13306205:
Olga Felip reviewed evidence on the edible green alga Chlorella for gut microbes and brain health in a 2026 systematic review. Searches covered three databases for English work from 2009 to 2026 under a registered protocol.

From 1333 records found, 47 passed first checks and 21 met full criteria for the final synthesis. Outcomes covered microbe mix, short-chain fatty acids, a brain growth factor, hippocampal cell counts, behaviour tests and mood questionnaires. The authors weigh whether nutrient-rich Chlorella can link bowel change to brain benefit, while noting uneven study quality across the field. The review asks for more work on dose, safety and long term brain gain.
pmc-13307205:
Daniel Vélez-Díaz and colleagues describe a surgical technique in 2026 for rebuilding a long-ruptured patellar tendon using the patient's own peroneus longus tendon. Chronic ruptures scar, retract, and leave the kneecap riding high, so simple repair often fails. Their method threads the graft in a figure-of-eight pattern.

Fixation uses suture anchors at the shin attachment and one crosswise tibial tunnel, avoiding tunnels through the kneecap that risk fracture. The graft offers consistent size and low harm at the donor site in the lower leg. Planning relied on X-ray measures of kneecap height and magnetic resonance confirmation of complete rupture. The authors report satisfactory short and mid-term results. Restoring the knee's extension mechanism with strong, simple fixation is the goal of the design.
pmc-13307405:
Fatemeh Sadat Gheibi and co-authors review in 2026 animal studies of AdipoRon, a drug that acts on adiponectin receptors, for memory loss, low mood, and anxiety. Their search covered four databases up to August 30, 2025, and they rated study quality with animal research checklists and bias tools.

Treated rodents spent less time still in a forced swim test and showed calmer behaviour in an open field, most clearly under long term stress. Memory of new objects also improved in models of Alzheimer and Parkinson disease, and levels of two synaptic proteins rose. Gains varied a lot between studies, so careful human trials must come first.
pmc-13307505:
Padmasri Sridharan and Mini Ghosh build in 2026 a shared digital twin to test why cytomegalovirus flare ups weaken CAR-T cell therapy for B-cell lymphoma. Their model frames the clash as a contest for IL-15, a scarce growth signal, between virus specific T cells and the engineered cells.

Training drew on 414 patients from five cancer centres without pooling raw records, and a sixth centre with 89 patients served for checks. The twin foresaw major flare ups well, and its runs linked flare ups to a 41.8 percent cut in peak CAR-T growth under the model rules. Guided virus prevention in the model cut projected disease advance while using less drug overall.
pmc-13307605:
Hao Zhang and co-authors test a plant saponin in 2026 as a possible antibiotic-free treatment for cow udder infection. Pulsatilla saponin B4 was applied to bovine mammary cells inflamed by bacterial toxin and to mice with mastitis. Inflammation signals, tissue damage, and pathway activity were measured in both settings.

The compound reduced the inflammatory response in cells and eased signs and tissue injury in the mouse model. Blocking experiments pointed to the IL-17RA receptor switch as its main route, feeding into MAPK and NF-kappa B signalling. When that route was blocked first, the compound lost its effect, which supports the proposed mechanism. Mastitis costs dairy farmers heavily and drives antibiotic use, so alternatives matter. The authors present the saponin as a candidate worth developing toward farm use.
pmc-13307905:
Priscila Guerra and colleagues field-test in 2026 a sow vaccine built from virus-like particles against a toxin-producing E. coli that causes post-weaning diarrhoea in piglets. Thirty-five sows received the new vaccine twice before farrowing, and thirty-five received the herd's usual commercial products. Piglets were followed to eight weeks after weaning.

Piglets from vaccinated sows carried higher antibody levels against the bacterial attachment factor throughout the post-weaning weeks. Pathogen detection rates were similar between groups, yet diarrhoea scores at week six were lower in the vaccine group. Those piglets also gained weight faster and finished significantly heavier, with a trend toward fewer treatments. Antibodies passed through colostrum and milk did the protective work, since piglets were never vaccinated themselves. The authors present sow immunisation as a practical lever on a stubborn production disease.
pmc-13308105:
Sanne Boetzkes, Leontine van Balveren, and Florence van Hunsel review in 2026 reports of floppy, unresponsive spells in infants after vaccination, logged at the Dutch centre Lareb from 2012 to 2025. Only cases that met the strict top level rule, with all three core signs clear, entered the count.

In all, 294 cases met that bar, most after combined six in one plus pneumococcal shots in young infants. Median onset age was 9 weeks, spells began about five hours after the shot, and most lasted near ten minutes. Every child recovered fully, yet more than a quarter of cases counted as serious due to hospital stays. Wider staff awareness could cut needless urgent care.
pmc-13308705:
Dazhen Liu and co-authors uncover in 2026 a damage-response job for Orc6, a DNA replication starter protein, at the sites where chromosomes are copied and repaired. Mapping showed Orc6 sitting at replication origins and at damage sites during the copying phase. Its partner there is SMARCA1, a chromatin remodeller that slides DNA packaging proteins.

When Orc6 is missing, the remodeller binds more widely and reshapes packaging at those sites. After oxidative damage, Orc6 instead grips the remodeller and blocks its activity, which halts copying progress near the injury. The authors cast Orc6 as a barrier factor that rations remodeller access during normal copying. Upon damage, the same grip becomes a brake that protects the genome. Their model links replication licensing proteins to repair decisions far beyond their textbook starting role.
pmc-13309605:
Maryam Saba models heat flow in a tiny channel filled with a three-metal nanofluid in a 2026 study. Small channels cool electronics, medical tools, and compact heat units. The fluid here is water carrying gold, copper, and silver particles, with a thick, memory-like flow under magnetic forces.

Equations using a fractional derivative capture the flow memory, and a grid-based computer scheme solves them. Results were checked against earlier published profiles and matched closely. A sensitivity scan ranks which factors move speed and heat profiles most, covering magnet strength and particle traits. The author aims to guide cooler design where space is tight and heat loads keep rising.
pmc-13310405:
Hongzhu Bao and co-authors build a prediction chart for breathing machine weaning in lung disease in a 2026 study. Patients with COPD and carbon dioxide buildup often need a breathing machine, and judging when to remove it is hard. A simple chart that sums risk points could guide that call at the bedside.

Records for 159 patients admitted between 2020 and 2024 were split into building and check groups. Screening methods narrowed predictors to anxiety, collapsed lung, blood-pressure drug use, and a heart strain marker as independent risks for weaning failure. The chart scored very high accuracy in the building group, near 0.942 on the standard curve measure reported. The authors propose the chart for everyday weaning rounds.
pmc-13310705:
Alessio Falasca Zamponi and colleagues compare two ways to confirm heart vein isolation during ablation for atrial fibrillation in a 2026 study. Standard care adds a round mapping catheter to check the result. The team asked whether the ablation catheter alone could do that check in first time cases done point by point.

One group of 81 people had the extra catheter, while a later group of 245 people did not. Cases without the extra tool were shorter and used less radiation, with no clear gap in rhythm control after 12 months of follow up. Extra checks found missed conduction in a small share of veins, so gains need care.
pmc-13310905:
Qionglan Li and colleagues survey knowledge of scar pregnancy among women who had cesarean births in a 2026 study. A pregnancy that implants in a cesarean scar is rare but dangerous, and rates rise as cesarean births grow. What women know after surgery shapes early care seeking.

A poll covered 325 women at two Fujian hospitals in late 2023. Knowledge scores sat near half of the top score, while attitude scores were more positive. Higher schooling linked strongly to both better knowledge and more positive views. Tailored teaching after surgery, with focus on women with less schooling, could close the gap.
pmc-13311005:
Dan Zhou and a large team arm a cancer killing virus with a cell cycle blocker for bowel cancer in a 2026 study. Virus care needs high repeat doses, which can tire killer immune cells through constant antigen contact. The team built a virus that makes the blocker inside the tumor to limit body wide exposure.

In mouse models the armed virus curbed tumors better, built strong immune memory, and depended mostly on killer T cells. Blocking the cycle freed a signal part that raised a T cell luring factor, which drew cells in and reversed their tired state. Pairing with other immune drugs boosted gains.
pmc-13311105:
Hongxun Ruan and co-authors trace a low oxygen gene chain that drives liver cancer growth in a 2026 study. In oxygen poor tumor zones, a methyl adding gene rises while a muscle protein gene fades. Data from three large cohorts plus mouse tests were used to map the chain and its value for outlook.

High chain scores marked far shorter survival and stood as a solo risk factor. A fusion protein that restores the faded gene shrank tumors in mice, cut vessel growth, and slowed invasion and spread. Blocking a mid chain step raised protective proteins further under low oxygen. The chain may guide drug picks.
pmc-13311305:
Bing Wang and colleagues, in 2026, share a study on heart strain measures taken soon after a heart attack and later heart shape change. Global longitudinal strain, a measure of heart squeeze, is the test under study.

The study followed 131 patients who had artery-opening treatment at one hospital from March 2023 to October 2024. Strain was measured within seven days, and heart shape and thickening were checked at six to twelve months. Weaker strain on its own tied to higher odds of later shape change. Patients in the weakest strain third faced far higher odds than those in the strongest third.
pmc-13312005:
Claudia Montoya and co-authors offer a 2026 multi-center study of a patch-free form of lichen planopilaris, a scarring hair loss disease. The classic form shows clear bald patches with red, scaly edges; this form stays local without patches.

The study pooled 74 patients from 20 trichology centers, all confirmed by scalp viewing and tissue study. Patients with other hair loss types were excluded to keep the picture clean. The team describes the group's age and sex pattern, clinical signs, scope findings, and tissue features. Naming this variant helps doctors spot scarring loss early, before follicles are destroyed for good.
pmc-13312105:
Ruan Spies and colleagues report a 2026 genomic study of rifampicin-resistant tuberculosis in Ho Chi Minh City, Viet Nam. The country sees nearly 10,000 new cases of this drug-resistant form each year. It was unclear how many come from spread of resistant strains versus resistance arising during a patient's own treatment.

The team sampled adults newly diagnosed across the city from March 2020 to April 2024 and sequenced isolates from 1,491 of the 2,319 cases found. Most isolates belonged to Lineage 2. After correcting for sampling gaps, the authors estimate that between 72 and 87 percent of cases came from transmission of already resistant strains. Dating analyses traced repeated emergence of resistance from the 1980s onward, feeding long-lived spread across the city.
pmc-13313205:
Ying Hei Kan, Lin Gao, and Danny Leung review, in a 2026 article, how epigenetic control of non-coding DNA shapes the placenta. The placenta grows fast, invades in a controlled way, and tolerates the mother's immune system, all under an unusual epigenetic regime of widespread low methylation that resembles a managed, cancer-like state. That flexibility helps trophoblast cells switch programs across pregnancy, but it also leaves the organ sensitive to maternal inflammation, low oxygen, toxins, and stress.

The review explains how promoters, enhancers, their looping networks, and non-coding RNAs are rewired in the placenta, with ancient retrotransposons supplying much of the regulatory novelty. Disturbing any layer can derail cell differentiation, invasion, hormone signaling, or immune balance, feeding growth restriction, preeclampsia, preterm birth, and pregnancy loss. The authors see non-coding epigenetic signatures as promising early biomarkers, while noting how hard cell-specific mapping remains.
pmc-13313705:
Jianqiao He and colleagues pool, in a 2026 systematic review and meta-analysis, the search for markers that predict benefit from immune therapy given before surgery. The setting is locally advanced head and neck cancer. Many patients gain little from this neoadjuvant treatment, and no validated predictor existed. Searching four databases through June 2024, the team gathered 26 studies covering 980 patients. They compared tissue response rates across candidate markers.

The combined positive score, a measure of PD-L1 staining, tracked response consistently. Patients above a cutoff of 5 responded at notably higher rates, with a relative risk of 1.852 in the pooled comparison. Higher cutoffs pointed the same way. Tumors positive for HPV achieved complete tissue responses more than twice as often. Counts of tumor-infiltrating CD4 T cells also correlated with response. The authors nominate all three as candidate predictors, while asking for prospective validation before clinical use.
pmc-13314505:
Anouk Geraets, Artur Rydosz, and Frank Snoek introduce a journal research topic on digital health tools for diabetes in an editorial published in 2026. Apps, glucose sensors worn on the body, and AI tools are reshaping diabetes care with live tracking and tailored advice.

Proof grows that such tools improve sugar control and patient engagement, at least in the short term, as the editors note. Open questions hang on long-term success, which needs tools woven into steady, patient-led, clinic-based care paths. The topic gathers eleven pieces: three reviews, four studies, a trial, a methods piece, an opinion, and a brief report, spread across four Frontiers journals, as counted in the editorial. The set weighs promise against the work of making digital care last.
pmc-13314605:
Fan Zhang and colleagues study how parks, water, and heat shape jogging in a dense Chinese city in a paper dated 2026. Blue-green spaces are praised in health-led city planning, but proof on how they steer daily use of public space under heat stress was thin.

Taking Fuzhou as the case, the team blended crowd-sourced jogging data with maps of green and water features, land surface heat, and built form. Nine machine learning models were run side by side, and a method called SHAP ranked which factors mattered and how. Distance to vegetation, the green view index, sky view, and surface heat stood out as key factors, as the authors report. Path models then traced direct and indirect routes. The work gives planners hard signs for making hot cities more run-friendly.
pmc-13314805:
Folkert H van Bruggen and Roger S McIntyre review PCSK9, a cholesterol-control protein, at the crossroads of metabolism and mental illness, in their 2026 paper. The protein is a proven heart risk factor, yet it also touches immune and metabolic paths that go awry in psychiatric disease.

The review pulls lab, gene, and clinical proof on fat handling and PCSK9 paths in mental disorders. It maps disorder-by-disorder patterns of blood fat quirks and shifts in brain fat makeup and turnover. Data on the protein inside the brain and on its blood levels against metabolic load, inflammation, and symptoms are summed up. The authors argue that a heart drug target may also matter for the body-wide metabolic strain that shadows severe mental illness.
pmc-13315105:
Viviane Fahrni leads a large team that shares survey data on what farmers would accept to join group nature schemes, in a paper from 2026. The data cover grassland farmers in six European case studies: Austria, Switzerland, Germany, Estonia, Ireland, and Norway, as listed in the report.

The survey ran from spring 2024 into 2025 in two parts. A choice experiment gave each farmer 10 tasks in a row. Each task held two draft designs for a collective biodiversity scheme plus an opt-out that kept the status quo, as the design states. The second part logged farm and farmer traits, attitudes, and likes. Because the schemes pay groups of farmers to guard nature at landscape scale, knowing the price and terms farmers accept can make or break such programs. The open data set lets others retest the drivers.
pmc-13315605:

They cleared an infection from treated mice much faster, with the difference reaching a strong level. Removing one gene also reduced the immune signal the vesicles triggered in blood cells. pmc-13315805:
Konstantina Tzimou and colleagues investigate, in a 2026 study, why Chinese hamster ovary cells struggle to produce AAV vectors for gene therapy. The authors map ovary cell responses to helper elements and flag both the promise and remaining barriers to a viable ovary-cell platform.
pmc-13316205:
Tamjid Imtiaz and colleagues used task-based brain scans in 2026 to map how the language network reorganizes in temporal lobe epilepsy. Left-sided epilepsy showed clearly more whole-brain language reorganization than right-sided disease, with regional patterns also differing. Age at seizure onset and years lived with epilepsy further shaped how far language had shifted. Knowing each patient's new language layout matters before surgery near language cortex. Regional checks inside standard language areas of interest completed the analysis.
pmc-13316305:
Tyler M Cook and co-authors report 2026 mouse work on low blood sugar attacks that can follow sleeve surgery for weight loss. Their question centers on glucagon, the hormone that should raise blood sugar, and whether its release and effect go wrong after the operation.

pmc-13316405:
Sarbjit Clare, Jane Ho, and Rachel Barlow describe a 2026 blueprint article on the Midland Metropolitan University Hospital. Even with fewer beds, early results showed better patient flow, lower occupancy strain, faster emergency access, a steadier workforce, and gains in death rates and infection control. The authors offer the model to the national hospital building program, while noting longer follow-up must prove the gains last.
pmc-13316605:
Ellen C. Francis and colleagues, in a 2026 cohort study, link heart health during pregnancy with later metabolic disease. Pregnancy strains the body and can reveal hidden risk. The pattern held even after people with diabetes or blood pressure disorders of pregnancy were removed. Follow-up lasted seven years. pmc-13316705:
Sydney T Puda and co-authors developed, in a 2026 methods study, silicone implants that release testosterone steadily in young castrated male pigs, a model for studying hormone action during early development. Swine work lacked a proven way to replace androgens at controlled levels.

Blood hormone levels peaked one to two weeks after surgery, matched or beat intact levels, then eased down yet stayed above controls through all 49 days of checks. Growth ran evenly across groups, so the implants did not distort body gain. The setup gives researchers a reliable dial for hormone exposure.
pmc-13317605:
Qun Ma and Yan Xu review, in 2026, biosensing built on nanofluidics, the control of fluids inside channels and pores only nanometres wide. Uses range from DNA and protein sequencing to single-molecule analysis, disease diagnosis and tailored care. The authors weigh current limits, including fabrication cost and reliability problems, and suggest routes forward. Their aim is to guide teams building sensors that read biology through fluid behaviour at tiny scales rather than bulk chemistry alone.
pmc-13318705:
James Florin Petri and Gerard Lacey survey, in 2026, legged robots fitted with passive wheels. Legs handle rough, human-built spaces well but waste energy. Wheels roll fast and cheaply on flat ground. Hybrids promise both strengths, yet most research uses powered wheels.

Unpowered wheels are simpler, lighter, and more efficient. New control methods and faster onboard computing now make them workable. The survey gathers designs that place skates or free wheels on robot feet. It compares implementations and the control problems they raise. Key factors deciding whether such systems are viable are laid out. The authors close with directions for future research in this niche.
pmc-13318805:
Ehsan Alam and colleagues present, in 2026, a planning approach for nature-based flood solutions in urban coastal areas of the Great Lakes. Changing rainfall is worsening flood risk across the basin. Green infrastructure can ease pressure on grey drainage systems and support wildlife, yet projects remain fragmented and hard to coordinate across a whole watershed.

Working in deindustrialising southeast Michigan, the team used research through design to build shared planning tools. The tools translate engineering models, historical records and ecological knowledge into objects that utilities, municipalities, watershed groups and communities can use together. They reveal links between surface flooding, buried water paths and storm sewers, and clarify who holds authority and resources. Fish and wildlife habitat is treated as a core aim, not an afterthought.
pmc-13318905:
Génesis Carolina Arévalo-Guadalupe and co-authors offer a 2026 scientometric map of digital epidemiology from 2000 to 2025. The field uses artificial intelligence, big data, connected devices, and social media mining for disease surveillance. The team analysed records in Scopus and Web of Science. Big gaps remain in digital fairness, system compatibility, and ethical oversight. Those gaps bite hardest where technology infrastructure is weak. The authors propose a future agenda centred on algorithm ethics, transparency, cooperation, and inclusion.
pmc-13319705:
Alessandro Villaschi and co-authors report a registry study from 2026 on drug care for heart failure in rehab wards across Italy. Whether wards use that stay to tune proven drug sets was the main question.

Among 263 people with a known pump score, three in four had a weak heart pump and most were men. At intake most already took core drug types, and by discharge use of one key type rose and overall drug scores improved. Kidney illness made tuning harder, while higher body weight linked to more tuning. Rehab stays offer a real chance to lift drug care.
pmc-13320105:
Jie Lan and co-authors issue expert agreement in 2026 on pairing beam care with new drug care for breast cancer in China. Beam tools and drug types have both leapt ahead, which opens gains but also raises safety and timing puzzles when they are used together.
