Advice covers pairings with immune drugs, aimed drugs, drug linked antibodies, and hormone drugs across all stages of the illness. The aim is safer, more even care in daily clinics and a clear map of what to test next. Breast cancer is among the most common cancers in women in China, so shared rules carry wide weight.
pmc-13320405:
Sidar Copur and colleagues pool, in 2026, five randomised trials of a once-weekly insulin for diabetes. Rates of low blood sugar events, including severe episodes and night-time episodes, did not differ significantly either. The authors conclude that weekly efsitora matches daily degludec on both control and hypoglycaemia in the trials reviewed, easing injection burden without obvious penalty.
pmc-13320505:
Nina Yu, Scott Levin and Granger Wong review, in 2026, patients who arrived at their institution with complications after cosmetic surgery in private settings. Such complications burden patients and the hospitals that rescue them, yet this population is poorly understood. Records covered cases from 2020 to 2023.

Thirty-six patients were included, averaging about 38 years old. Nearly half had their original procedure abroad, most often in Mexico or the Dominican Republic. Tobacco or cannabis use and obesity were common in the group. Hospital charges were large while insurance payments covered only a fraction, and costs rose sharply when another operation was needed. Smokers presented more often with infection. The authors call for measures that give patients safer, fairer access to aesthetic procedures.
pmc-13321205:
Olga Maria de Silvério Carvalho and co-authors write a 2026 letter welcoming a dog ageing project as a model for human ageing research. The OLD-DOG Project follows companion dogs for 30 months to find and validate markers of ageing. Dogs age in shared human homes yet live short enough lives for full ageing paths to be tracked.

Its mix of clinical checks, physical and thinking tests, inflammation markers, microbiome study, and stored samples is praised as a step forward. Within a One Health frame, such dog data could bridge lab animal work and human ageing science.
pmc-13321305:
Dominic Shiels, William W. Brennessel, and Ellen M. Matson report new uranium complexes in a 2026 chemistry study. The team built asymmetric sandwich type polyoxometalate complexes holding uranium in the IV state, with either phosphorus or silicon at the centre. Such actinide assemblies with lopsided builds are rare and hard to make cleanly.

pmc-13321805:
Naibijiang Abuliezi and co-authors reframe immunotherapy for glioblastoma in a 2026 review. This brain cancer resists immune treatment through a suppressive setting, few mutations, wide variety, weak antigen display, and the blood-brain barrier. Successes in other solid tumours have not carried over, and gains stay modest.

Checkpoint drugs, vaccines, virus therapy, and cell therapies are all mapped onto those pillars. Recent designs, including bispecific engagers and new CAR T forms from 2024 and 2025, are highlighted as convergence points.
pmc-13322005:
Abdul-Wahab Inusah and four co-authors chart anemia in Ghanaian women of child years from two thousand to twenty thirty. Their study appeared in twenty twenty-six. Low blood in such women harms health and purse, though food and malaria plans run on. Past counts from a WHO fair-health base were read for state and zone gaps, and a time model cast counts to twenty thirty.

Share fell a bit, from near forty-eight to near forty-four percent in two decades. The Ashanti zone fell most, while the Upper West rose. Zone gaps grew by most counts. The cast sees a flat line to twenty thirty at near forty-four percent, short of world goals.
pmc-13322505:
Scott L Nuismer and co-authors assess a self spreading vaccine idea against Lassa fever in a 2026 study. Lassa virus spills from rodents to people across West Africa each year, sickening tens of thousands, and blocking spillover has resisted decades of effort. A vaccine that spreads through the rodent reservoir itself could give wide immune cover.

pmc-13322805:
Young-Hyo Jeon and co-authors review ginkgo extract for dizziness from brain disorders in a 2026 systematic review and meta-analysis. Nine trials with 2394 people were included, drawn mostly from dementia groups at 71.6 percent of participants in the review. Smaller shares came from cerebral arteriosclerosis and rear circulation disorders. Planned subgroup and sensitivity checks probed differences by cause and treatment type. The review weighs whether ginkgo's blood flow and protective actions translate into real relief.
pmc-13323305:
Vivek Mahapatra and co-authors pool how well artificial intelligence reads baby X-rays for necrotising enterocolitis, in a 2026 meta-analysis drawing on a systematic search. This bowel disease is a leading threat to premature and very low birth weight babies, and early signs are vague.

Pooled sensitivity sat near 0.78 and specificity near 0.84 in their hierarchical model, giving moderate diagnostic value with wide variation between studies. pmc-13323405:
Thomas E Wessendorf reviews doping in chess in a 2026 article written in German, asking whether performance drugs matter in a mental sport. Health risks include strain on the heart and circulation, psychotic symptoms at high doses and a path toward dependence. Chess counts as an organised sport, so doping controls exist, but they cover only elite play and stay rare, with no major cases known so far. The author judges electronic cheating the larger threat to fair play, while suspecting higher hidden use among professionals and amateurs alike.
pmc-13324305:
Jiyoung Lee and co-authors grow human heart organoids with working electrical currents, in a 2026 stem cell study. Their culture recipe for embryonic stem cell derived organoids used concentrated laminin-entactin and growth factor FGF4, plus BMP4, BMP10 and a ROCK blocker to steer heart formation.

The authors offer the system for development studies and drug safety testing.
pmc-13326005:
Tian Zhou and co-authors study how spare walking capacity cushions the cost of thinking while walking in older adults in a 2026 study. Doing two things at once strains gait and raises fall risk as people age.

Costs on both walking and thinking were clear, and the memory task tangled with walking in an uneven way. Stopping to talk was rare, at 2.8 percent of participants, and marked a coping style rather than fall history.
pmc-13327105:
Haruka Harata and colleagues report a 2026 heart case tracked with repeated ultrasound scans from inside the food pipe. Brain scans showed several small strokes on both sides despite blood-thinning medicine, so doctors looked for a heart source.

During surgery the mass flattened, and lab study of the removed tissue confirmed a calcified amorphous tumor with a soft, caseous form. pmc-13327805:

pmc-13328005:

pmc-13328505:
Dengling Huang and colleagues report in 2026 on a new blood test for tuberculosis in captive cynomolgus monkeys. The test was checked in a learning group of 19 animals and a separate group of 21 animals. In the second group it found over 92 percent of cases with no false positives. The authors present it as a fast tool for routine colony checks.
pmc-13329905:
Weijia Shen and team built a ruthenium catalyst for highly enantioselective alkynylation of fluoral. pmc-13330305:

pmc-13330605:

pmc-13330805:

Common routes include ring-closing of thiosemicarbazides or diacylhydrazines, substitution, and C-H activation. pmc-13332105:

pmc-13332505:

pmc-13332705:

pmc-13333405:

pmc-13333505:

pmc-13334305:

Efficiency ratios were worse in both experimental groups. Breast muscle share rose in experimental birds. Meat characteristics were measured in detail. pmc-13335805:

pmc-13336405:

pmc-13336605:

pmc-13336905:

pmc-13337005:

pmc-13337205:

pmc-13337705:
Müzeyyen Soyer and Seçil Ömür Sünbül examine partner phubbing in a 2026 survey of adults in romantic relationships. Phubbing means ignoring a partner to look at a phone during face-to-face time. The study asks how that experience differs by gender, marital status, age, and time together.

Reports rose with age, and couples together 5 to 10 years scored highest. Statistical models flagged gender and that mid-length duration as predictors, suggesting daily phone habits weigh differently across stages of a relationship.
pmc-13337905:
Alex Zaharakis and Christian Bogner report a 2026 single case of light therapy and urine metals in a young child. Baseline aluminum sat near 10 units, then rose to 58 on day 3 and peaked at 98 on day 7 in the reported values. Levels stayed above the reference range at two-month follow-up. Mercury also ran high throughout, so results need cautious reading.
pmc-13338405:
Polina Tikhonova and five co-authors tracked gut microbes in Ethiopian children before and a year after deworming, in this 2026 study. Mass deworming is a standard defense against gut worms in low-income settings, but its long echo in the microbiome was unclear. Stool samples came from 132 children at baseline and sixty-seven a year after a single albendazole dose.

Children worm-free at baseline gained six favored groups, while infected children gained a partly different five. The authors call for animal studies to pin down cause and effect.
pmc-13340305:
Yani Hao and colleagues hunted root microbes in 2026 that free phosphorus in chalky soils, where locked phosphorus wastes plant food. Rapeseed roots give off organic matter that can free bound phosphorus, yet the microbe route in chalky soils was unclear. The team screened root zone soil for microbes that dissolve phosphate and mapped their key chemical routes.

pmc-13341005:
Umesh Pandwar and colleagues tested the Renal Angina Index in 2026 for predicting acute kidney injury in paediatric intensive care. The prospective study included 300 children aged one month to 13 years, treated at Gandhi Medical College in Bhopal between September 2022 and February 2024. The index was calculated 24 hours after admission and correlated with kidney injury after that point.

Mean age was 36.16 months and 50.7 percent were male, while acute kidney injury occurred in 5 percent. Death rates rose sharply across risk groups: 0 percent low risk, 7.5 percent moderate risk, and 68.8 percent high risk. pmc-13341305:
Forecasting a hard airway view in babies with Pierre Robin sequence is tackled by Danling Hu and colleagues in the 2026 machine learning study. These infants often have small jaws and displaced tongues, so laryngoscopy can be unexpectedly difficult during surgery.

Records covered 214 infants treated in 2023 and 2024, with airway anatomy measured from three-dimensional CT scans. Seven learning models were built and checked in a separate group of 80 infants from a later period. Tongue length emerged as one independent predictor among the scan measures. Objective imaging-based forecasts could help anesthesia teams prepare equipment and plans before the first attempt.
pmc-13341505:
A hybrid neural network sorts nine retinal diseases from fundus photos, in a 2026 study by Yaoyang Cheng and colleagues. RHT-Net fuses residual convolutional layers for local detail with transformer encoders that catch long-range patterns across the image.

pmc-13341605:
Banana varieties host partly distinct inner microbes, in a 2026 study by Shiva A. Aghdam and Amanda M. V. Brown. Six cultivars, three wild diploids and three domesticated triploids, grew side by side while their above- and below-ground endophytes were deep-sequenced.

pmc-13342205:
Qiuyu Mo and co-authors present a 2026 laboratory study of signaling proteins in bone marrow fluid from people with acute myeloid leukemia. The group measured a broad panel of interleukins and related immune signals and asked whether the mix shifts as the disease starts, clears, or returns.

Marrow samples came from 75 patients: 41 newly diagnosed, 19 in complete remission, and 15 with relapsed or stubborn disease. Several signals differed across the groups, and levels of IL-17 and TGF-β rose at diagnosis, fell in remission, and rose again at relapse. Tracking these proteins over time could help doctors judge disease activity and adjust treatment.
pmc-13342605:
Yu Wang and five colleagues study tungsten carbide reinforced iron-based coatings made by laser cladding, in a paper from twenty twenty-six. Iron-based coatings suffer uneven microstructure, segregation, and weak bonding under laser processing. Adding tungsten carbide particles aims to densify the coating and optimize several properties at once. Coatings were deposited on tool steel with a coaxial powder-fed laser.

Partially dissolved particles reacted with the iron matrix, forming dispersed strengthening phases and refining grains. Hardness rose about eighty percent above the substrate. Wear rate fell to a fraction of the substrate's, and corrosion current dropped by roughly two-thirds. The authors link microstructure directly to the performance gains.
pmc-13343005:
Ulrike Grote, Trung Thanh Nguyen, and Manh Hung Do describe the Thailand Vietnam Socio-Economic Panel in 2026, a long-running household dataset from rural Thailand and Vietnam. Farm families there face droughts, floods, price swings, and health shocks, and the panel tracks how welfare and coping change over many years.

Ten survey waves from 2007 to 2024 cover 2,200 households in 220 villages across three provinces in each country. Topics span income from land, crops, and livestock, spending, assets, housing, well-being, and personal traits, with a migrant tracking arm linking city workers to remittances sent home. The data let researchers and policymakers study long-term rural change with real household histories.
pmc-13344205:
Carrie J Ngongo and colleagues reviewed heat risks in pregnancy in 2026, urging clearer public messages to help mothers and babies in a warming climate. Extreme heat exposure raises pregnancy risks, and exposure is increasing worldwide, with low income countries hit hardest by high maternal and neonatal death plus marked climate vulnerability. Despite proof on heat linked risks, clear messages have not reached the public in usable form.

Heat exposure links to obstetric harms affecting mother and offspring, yet risk communication stays weak. Strengthening proof and improving messages are urgent needs to prevent heat linked deaths and illnesses. The review calls for heat guidance that pregnant people can actually act on during heatwaves.
pmc-13346005:
Agasthian Thirugnanam reported in 2026 the first known case of an isolated jugular vein clot caused by an abnormal thymoma pressing on the vein. Tumours of the thymus can invade nearby veins and cause superior vena cava syndrome, but blockage limited to one internal jugular vein had not been described.

A 51-year-old man noticed prominent left neck veins for a month, and ultrasound confirmed a clot in the left internal jugular vein. Scans found a five-centimetre thymoma growing from an anomalous thymus lobe behind the left innominate vein, compressing the junction with the subclavian vein. The clot cleared within a week of treatment, and the tumour was removed by keyhole chest surgery. The case widens the differential diagnosis for unexplained neck vein clots.
pmc-13347705:
Witness Mapanga, Chenai Mlandu, and Khuthala Mabetha map child health policy and its weak spots in South Africa, in a scoping review published in 2026. Sources from 2008 to 2023 spanned journals, health ministry reports, planning bodies. Grey material, charted by a standard scoping method to show where policy effort clusters and where delivery lags over fifteen years.

Effort clustered on food provision, mother and child health, growth, income support, and access to resources. Yet wording and delivery in those areas still rated poor to moderate in the synthesis. Caregiver support and related areas drew weak priority and vague plans, leaving uneven care despite a wide policy shelf, a gap the review urges planners to close.
pmc-13349905:
Wenbo Lv and co-authors reviewed lactylation, a newer chemical tagging of proteins, in atherosclerosis in 2026. Atherosclerosis narrows large and medium arteries and underlies much heart disease and stroke.

Lactylation attaches lactate-derived groups to proteins, changing how they behave. The review gathers evidence tying this process to inflammation, vessel wall cell ageing and identity shifts, new vessel growth, and disturbed metabolism inside plaques. Lactate was once seen as mere waste from oxygen-starved cells. Showing it actively rewrites protein function opens fresh drug targets, and the authors argue that blocking harmful lactylation might slow plaque growth and cut cardiovascular events.
pmc-13350005:
Chun-Rui Liu and co-authors weighed in 2026 deep learning, radiomics, and fusion models for telling parathyroid adenoma from carcinoma or atypical tumours on ultrasound. This split is vital for surgery planning. Yet ultrasound accuracy still leans heavily on the operator.

Looking back at 1,122 patients from two Chinese hospitals from 2016 to 2025, the team pooled multi-centre data to tackle the rarity of carcinoma and atypical cases, only 74 in total. Cases were split into training and validation sets by pathology. Radiomics, deep learning, and joined models were weighed head to head. The fusion path promises more steady, less operator-bound sorting, helping surgeons plan the right operation first time.
pmc-13350605:
Jakub Śmiechowicz and co-authors audited sepsis care in 55 Polish hospitals in a 2026 analysis drawn from a European survey. Sepsis kills quickly when missed, so hospitals are urged to screen and treat it in a standard way.

Only 44 percent of hospitals applied the current Sepsis-3 definition. Screening ran in just 27 percent, and standardised management in 38.2 percent, across emergency departments, wards, and intensive care. Quality improvement programmes were also patchy. A national baseline like this turns vague concern into specific gaps that training, staffing, and protocols can be aimed at closing.
pmc-13351905:
Zachary Hoglund and a large team compare costs and outcomes for two neck surgeries. Their analysis from twenty twenty-six covers three-level disc replacement against fusion. Fusion has long been the standard for worn cervical discs. Disc replacement preserves motion and may protect neighbouring segments.

Data came from one health system and matched small groups. Ten patients received three-level disc replacement surgery. Ten others received three-level fusion surgery instead. Admission costs and three-month outcomes were compared directly. No prior study had compared these three-level options head to head. The authors frame the work as early cost-effectiveness evidence. Larger samples will be needed before firm guidance is possible.
pmc-13352505:
Yang Ma and co-authors build a layered graphene and MXene material for charge storage in 2026. MXene sheets tend to restack during use, which blocks electrolyte access and caps storage. Vertical graphene nanowalls were grown on Ti3C2Tx MXene films to hold the layers apart, using acid etching, filtration assembly, and plasma vapour growth.

The upright walls widen sheet gaps and open multi-direction paths for ions, exposing more active sites. In sulphuric acid within a 0.7 V window, the hybrid reached an areal capacitance of 163.17 mF per square centimetre at a slow scan rate. That value is a 1.2-fold gain over the base material. The design offers a route to stronger supercapacitor electrodes.
pmc-13352605:
Noah Richter and co-authors report a nickel-catalysed route to fluorinated alcohol building blocks in 2026. Their catalyst forms in place from a stable nickel stilbene complex and a chiral VAPOL-based ligand, with triethylborane as promoter. Fluorinated sorbamides were coupled with aldehydes in a handedness-controlled way.

The ligand steered where the new bond formed and set excellent handedness control, creating a fluorinated carbon centre beside a fresh alcohol group. The motif mimics a common anti-configured unit in natural products with fluorine swapped in, enabling a fluorine scan of known active compounds. Mechanism checks showed the only visible nickel complex sits off the working cycle as a reservoir, backed by a negative nonlinear effect and computer modelling.
pmc-13352905:
Yasuyuki Arai, Timothy Bolt, Hikaru Onishi, and a wider team wrote this research paper, published in 2026. It surveys Japanese blood and cancer specialists on what they think lymphoma patients want: to decide treatment alone, together, or to leave it to the doctor.

Shared decision-making is central to modern cancer care, but doctors' guesses about patients are rarely checked. Two hundred twenty-seven specialists who had treated diffuse large B-cell lymphoma answered online. Most assumed patients want collaboration: about a third picked joint decisions, a third patient-led with doctor input, and a quarter doctor-led with patient input. Almost none imagined patients wanting total control or none. Doctors with more hard-to-treat cases leaned physician-led, as did older doctors. Female doctors more often assumed patients want the lead. The authors say assumptions vary with the doctor, not just the patient.
pmc-13353005:
Xue-Jiao Yang and co-authors model how blood sugar states shift over time in a Chinese health check-up population. Their study appeared in 2026. A multi-state Markov model then estimated the odds and timing of moving between states. Most visits, about seventy-three percent, stayed in the same state; about twenty percent progressed, and about seven percent improved from prediabetes back to normal.

pmc-13355005:
Naima Parveen and co-authors review in 2026 how the thyroid gland and the liver affect each other. The authors flag open questions on hormone measures, long-term drug safety, and when hormone replacement helps the liver.
pmc-13355405:
R van Pel and co-authors report a 2026 case series on using guided bronchoscopy to check lung spots in people being assessed for lung transplant. Most patients had severe COPD, and spots were small, at a median of twelve millimeters. The authors say the method can speed clear decisions on who can proceed to transplant.
pmc-13355805:
Emil Espinal and co-authors compared two repair methods in 2026 for a bone cut used in stemless shoulder replacement surgery. Both methods failed at much the same load and after much the same number of cycles, and gapping during loading did not differ. The tunnel method trended stiffer but also shifted more, though neither trend reached significance. The authors call this pilot work a base for larger studies of repair choice.
pmc-13356505:

pmc-13358505:
Abisiniya Kabtimer and co-authors tell the story of a tricky case in a 2026 report. A 21-year-old woman had a thigh lump that looked like a stubborn infection. pmc-13359005:
Vasileios T. Stavrou and co-authors test exercise at home for a scarring lung disease in a 2026 report. Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis makes travel to a rehab center hard for many patients. The report supports home programs as safe and workable, while showing that benefits need upkeep.
pmc-13359105:

pmc-13359605:

Two patients reached a fair response and three a poor one. As a pilot, the study mainly maps how the skin changes, to guide larger trials.
pmc-13359705:
Zoltán Kiss and co-authors chart cancer in Hungary across the COVID-19 years in a 2026 study. pmc-13361805:
Burak Manay and co-authors studied swallowing in brain-injured patients with tracheostomies in a 2026 paper. pmc-13361905:

pmc-13362405:

pmc-13365605:

pmc-13369205:

pmc-13369505:

pmc-13369605:

pmc-13371705:

pmc-13373305:
Smith and colleagues tested in 2026 whether oxidants made naturally in the body can switch off p16INK4a, a tumor guard protein that brakes cell division. pmc-13373605:
Sarah Cook and co-authors made a free kit for social media hiring into drug trials in a 2026 paper. Trials often miss their sign-up goals, and social feeds give a new way to reach people. Many teams lack clear steps for that work, though.

The kit was built by a hub for hiring craft, shaped by user views and years of team know-how. It gives best steps, tips for each feed type, and forms teams can adapt. Kit pages walk a team from plan to posts to checks on what worked. The aim is more fair and full sign-up, so trial results speak for all.
pmc-13373805:
Katherina Petrou and colleagues comment on new molecular signs of heat stress in coral symbionts in a 2026 commentary. The commentary frames assisted evolution, including selective breeding and genetic interventions, as a way to speed adaptation. New molecular signatures could help researchers spot tolerant symbionts early and choose breeding stock for reefs that must survive warmer seas.
pmc-13377005:
Irene Best and co-authors review qualitative research on the distress that accompanies delirium in hospitalised older adults. Fourteen studies with qualitative or mixed designs were included, covering patients, their care partners, and nurses, since distress extends to witnesses as well as patients. The reviewers found the experiences of care partners and nurses understudied, as were patients whose delirium sits on top of dementia. pmc-13377805:

The review traces melatonin action across gastrointestinal cancers, emphasising its power to boost chemo effect while reducing toxicity. Because melatonin is already well characterised, it could be used off-label as an adjunct to improve prognosis and quality of life. pmc-13379505:

The authors conclude that cutting delay needs coordinated public health effort, better diagnostic infrastructure, and more professional training, so patients reach earlier diagnosis, better outcomes, and timely genetic counseling for their families.
pmc-13380405:
Finian M O'Malley, Amelia Street, and Kush Deshpande describe a 2026 quality improvement project on handover notes when patients move from intensive care to a ward. That move carries risk, and local rules require the verbal handover to be documented with its time. In practice, recording was patchy.

Working in a large hospital in Sydney, Australia, the team first measured one week of discharges. It then introduced changes over two days: a visual prompt, a meeting reminder, and digital messages. The design drew on human factors ideas to cut mental load. A repeat check four weeks later measured whether documentation became more frequent and more complete.
pmc-13382005:

pmc-13382905:

pmc-13412605:

pmc-13418505:

pmc-13420705:

pmc-13422805:

pmc-13439605:
Ester Martínez-Renau and a large team compare microbes living on bird skin and in the preen gland across species, ages, and nest types, reporting in 2026. Feathers and skin form a first defence against infection, seeded partly by oily secretions from the uropygial gland near the tail. Birds spread those secretions while preening. The team sequenced bacterial DNA from gland secretions and gland skin of nestlings and adults in 26 species from southern Spain.

Bacterial communities differed clearly by species, and nestlings carried richer mixes than adults, mainly on gland skin. Birds nesting inside cavities held more varied and uneven communities than open-cup nesters, an effect strongest in adults and secretions. Cavity nesters also carried relatively larger glands, hinting at more preening effort. Nesting habits and age thus shape the microbial shield birds wear.
pmc-13440105:
Jie Wang's team traced a CA9-driven chain in 2026 that accelerates colorectal cancer through neutrophil traps. Carbonic anhydrase IX was flagged as a candidate cancer gene in single-cell data, but its immune role was undefined. Serum levels, mouse models, neutrophil recruitment, trap formation, and molecular binding were combined to test how CA9 shapes tumors.

CA9 ran high in patient serum and tracked poor prognosis, bound ITGB1, switched on NF-kB signaling, raised CXCL8, and drew neutrophils that cast DNA traps, fueling tumor growth. Blocking this CA9-ITGB1-CXCL8 axis emerges as a therapeutic idea. Colorectal teams get a complete immune mechanism with a druggable target, still preclinical.
pmc-13440505:
João Pedro Rocha Nogueira and colleagues describe the field investigation of a confirmed West Nile virus case in an infant in Mato Grosso, Brazil, reporting in 2026. The mosquito-borne virus circulates in birds and usually leaves people without symptoms, though rare cases invade the nervous system. The infant's illness began in mid-December 2025, and spinal fluid testing confirmed the virus days later. A three-day investigation in February 2026 combined case review with door-to-door searching.

Interviewers reached 112 residents near the case. Twenty-nine reported symptoms, and eight of them described neurological complaints. Surroundings favoured mosquito breeding, raising concern about local transmission. West Nile virus has been confirmed in Brazil since 2014, with about one hundred ten human cases logged in the following decade. The authors urge joined human, animal, and environmental surveillance with wider laboratory and insect investigation in the territory.
pmc-13440705:
Takuji Igarashi and colleagues report a fatal case where a gut bacterium seeded an abscess inside a recent brain bleed, publishing in 2026. Abscess forming at a haemorrhage site is exceedingly rare, and Bacteroides fragilis is an oxygen-hating gut resident seldom blamed. Their patient, an 86-year-old woman, arrived with bleeding in the right back of the brain plus body-wide inflammation signs. Abdominal scans suggested inflamed bowel pouches, a plausible entry point for the germ.

She first developed meningitis from the same bacterium under conservative care. Sixteen days after the stroke, swelling around the bleed ballooned and her condition crashed. Emergency surgery found pus inside the blood cavity, and cultures confirmed the organism. Despite surgery and targeted antibiotics, infection spread to brain tissue and the fluid channels, and she died. The authors advise contrast imaging whenever fever and decline persist after brain haemorrhage.
pmc-13441505:
Qiutong Lu and colleagues improvise a rescue tool from spare parts to extract a fragile foam object lodged in the rectum, reporting a 2026 case. Their patient, a 51-year-old man, arrived after the object had been retained for a day and a community hospital attempt had already failed. Scans showed bowel swelling but no dense object, matching foam's faint signature. Urgent scope examination found the large foam body at the rectosigmoid junction, where the colon bends.

A standard snare slid off the soft, slippery surface, and grasping forceps could not hold it either. The team folded a guidewire through the metal outer sheath of a stone-crushing device, building a homemade gripper. That improvised tool seized the friable object firmly and removed it whole. The authors offer the construction as a fallback when stock retrieval gear fails on soft, fragile foreign bodies.
pmc-13441905:
Kivian Obed Matamoros Padilla and colleagues profile stroke in young Honduran adults at a national referral hospital, reporting a 2026 case series. Stroke is rising in the twenty-to-fifty-four age band worldwide, and local Central American data are scarce. Seventy patients aged eighteen to fifty-five were studied with examinations, laboratory tests, brain imaging, and neck and brain vessel ultrasound, including a bubble test for heart shunts.

Young adults made up thirty percent of the stroke cases assessed. Women formed the majority, and average age sat in the early forties. High blood pressure history led the risk list, followed by diabetes and migraine. Most strokes were ischemic, with clots from the heart the top identified mechanism. A heart shunt turned up in a notable share of those tested. Death claimed about one case in six. The authors highlight modifiable risks that local prevention could target.
pmc-13442605:
Majlinda Naco and colleagues recount sleep-drug care for a 65-year-old woman with a giant belly tumor in a 2026 case report. The ovarian growth weighed about 21 kg and filled most of her belly, pressing on organs and chest parts. Surgery removed the growth along with her womb, belly fat apron, and appendix.

The mass squeezed her main belly vein, so body shifts on the table swung her blood pressure hard. Direct pressure checks inside the belly forced quick changes to both the drug plan and the cut plan mid-surgery. She came through the full course well in the end. The team stresses joint planning across surgery, sleep-drug, and watch teams, plus lung prep and close line checks, when a mass of this scale goes to the table.
pmc-13442705:
Xuejun Liu and colleagues study why time stress feeds reliance on AI text tools among graduate students in a 2026 survey. Replies came from 1,157 students, and the team traced paths from time stress to tool reliance through mind states. Profile sorting then split students into groups by how their reliance formed.

Time stress fed reliance through two side paths, worry about research and faith that tools boost output. The worry path held a 41.22 percent share of the total link in their model. Four profiles emerged, from an all-low group at 5.77 percent of students to a dual-high group near two-fifths. Sex, study year, and critical thought marked who fell where. The authors warn that stress care and thought training may cut heavy reliance more than bans can.
pmc-13443105:
Ronak Nikbazm and coauthors report a 2026 case-control study of premature ovarian insufficiency, the loss of ovarian activity before age 40, seeking blood markers that flag the illness early. The team compared 38 affected women with 38 controls on body measures, the protein chemerin, follicle stimulating hormone, blood fats, and cardiometabolic indices.

Chemerin, total cholesterol, and triglycerides each separated cases from controls only moderately, but a joint model reached strong discrimination, with 94.7 percent sensitivity and 76.3 percent specificity. Schooling, activity level, and several blood measures also linked to the illness. The joint panel looks promising as a screening aid, though larger and more diverse cohorts must confirm the cutoffs before clinical use.
pmc-13443505:
Rebekah Erin Strong and colleagues make primary amines from alcohols inside charged microdroplets in a 2026 paper. Amines serve as core building blocks, yet classic routes need guard groups or harsh reducers. Their spray rig makes ammonia from air nitrogen on the fly, right inside the droplets.

The fresh ammonia swaps the alcohol's oxygen group for a nitrogen group in one pass. Adding hydrazine as a twin ammonia source lifted yields more than tenfold in their runs. Three spray setups faced off, from twin spray with hydrazine to solo sprays at high and low flows. NMR reads confirmed the swap at the same carbon spot. The authors pitch droplet chemistry as a mild route that skips harsh goods and rare catalysts.
pmc-13443605:
Huacen Wang and colleagues build a paper-thin flexible robot for work on huge structures in a 2026 paper. Ships and planes need cutting and checks in place, yet stock robots are heavy and may harm weak skins. Their robot is 970 micrometers thick and weighs 19.7 g, driven by a two-way electric actuator on flex circuits.

Sticky electric feet let it climb flat, curved, and upright faces with path repeat marks near 21.7 micrometers of drift. Top speed hit 290 mm per second in their runs. Loads reached more than four times its own weight, and a 3 kg drop failed to kill it. Trials showed gap checks, curved grinding, and micro spark cutting. The authors pitch the platform for tight, delicate work zones.
pmc-13444105:
Aleksandra Ferenc-Mrozek and colleagues demonstrate a 2026 biophysics finding that the DcpS scavenger enzyme, known for stripping caps from decayed messenger RNA, can misfold into amyloid-like fibrils in the lab. The team tested human and worm versions of the protein, plus a mutant tied to Al-Raqad syndrome, tracking phase separation and fibril growth.

Both species' proteins formed fibrils, and the disease-linked mutant aggregated faster than the normal protein. Liquid-liquid phase separation appeared to precede fibril formation and may explain the odd kinetics, including a missing lag phase. The work links DcpS aggregation to possible loss of function in disease, though physiological relevance in living tissue remains to be shown.
pmc-13444305:
Moeza Zulfiqar and colleagues report a 2026 cross-sectional study of treatment adherence among 401 women with polycystic ovary syndrome treated at hospitals in Lahore, Pakistan. The team used structured questionnaires to grade adherence and test links with social and clinical factors.

Only 21.4 percent reported full adherence, while 50.6 percent were partial and 27.9 percent non-adherent. Socioeconomic status and body mass index predicted adherence, with upper-middle-class women less likely to adhere than upper-class women. Limited knowledge, side effects, and cost led the barriers, pointing to education, financial support, and system fixes as remedies.
pmc-13444505:
Denis Qirinxhi and colleagues track a giant liver hemangioma that shrank on its own over three years in a 2026 case paper. A 53-year-old woman had the lump found by chance during checks for vague belly discomfort. MRI scans across three years, from February 2022 to January 2025, charted its course.

Classic scan marks confirmed a cavernous hemangioma at each visit. The lump first grew, from 14.1 cm long to 15.9 cm at the mid scan, then fell to 8.0 cm by the last scan. Volume loss topped 80 percent across the full span, with no drugs, surgery, or needle work in between. She stayed well, with clean labs and no cancer signs. The authors back watchful care for stable giants with classic marks.
pmc-13445205:
Atsushi Musha and colleagues present a 2026 case report on carbon-ion radiation therapy for a rare jaw tumor, ameloblastic fibrosarcoma of the upper jaw, in a patient who declined radical surgery. The 68-year-old woman arrived with nasal congestion, tooth pain, and a watering eye, and biopsy confirmed the tumor in the left maxillary sinus.

With no standard treatment or guidelines for this rare tumor, the team planned a two-stage carbon-ion course totaling 70.4 gray in 16 fractions, shrinking margins midway to spare the eye, brain, and jaw muscles. The report offers a treatment path for inoperable cases, though the record shown covers planning rather than long-term outcome, so efficacy remains an open question.
pmc-13445505:
Jiaying Zhao and colleagues ask why some skull and face bones harden well while nearby zones lag, in a 2026 study of bone growth. Citrate, a small molecule in bone, shapes the crystals that give bone its strength. The team found citrate piling up in just the zones that harden most.

Gene readouts split hard and soft zones along two lines: a growth signal chain and the cell's primary cilium, a tiny antenna-like part. Citrate switched the signal chain on, and the chain in turn fed citrate build-up, a loop that raised bone cell activity. Working with the cilium, citrate steadied young mineral clusters. The pattern hands bone repair work a new metabolic lever to test.
pmc-13446005:
Bárbara Dieck-Gutiérrez and colleagues report a young woman found to carry three rare belly vessel squeeze conditions at once, published in 2026 with a review of past reports. One condition presses the gut's main artery under a chest ligament, causing pain after meals. The second narrows the gap where the gut passes between two vessels, blocking food and driving weight loss.

The third presses the left kidney vein between the aorta and a gut artery. Each condition is uncommon alone, so the triple match is a true rarity that tests diagnosis and care. Surgery treated her case with success. The report walks through scan choices and treatment paths, urging doctors to keep these squeezes in mind when belly pain defies easy answers.
pmc-13446105:
Haoming Huo and colleagues sharpen a sound-and-light imaging method by borrowing fine vessel maps from a sister technique, in a 2026 study. Photoacoustic imaging reads light absorbed in tissue as sound, giving depth and contrast, yet its detail is capped by sound spread, and partial views smear the picture. Ultrasound tracking of single bubbles can map vessels far more finely.

Their method folds those sharp vessel maps into the rebuild of photoacoustic data, weighting the smoothing by region. Tests ran on computer models, tissue-like phantoms, and the living mouse brain. The new rebuild cut blur, raised contrast, and kept blood oxygen maps tighter and truer than the standard rebuild. Vessels that once blurred into haze stood out, which widens the method's use in brain and tumor studies.
pmc-13446305:
Iovino and colleagues argue for combining two immunotherapies that each fail on their own. Their 2026 commentary discusses bispecific T-cell engagers, or BiTEs. These antibody-like drugs drag T cells onto tumour cells. The authors pair them with donor stem cell transplant, which can cure blood cancers through the graft-versus-tumour effect. Both approaches lose effectiveness over time in many patients.

The authors review why. BiTEs depend on the patient's own worn-down T cells, which heavy pretreatment leaves exhausted, while transplant relapse remains common, especially when disease is not fully cleared beforehand. Their proposal is to give BiTEs around the transplant window, redirecting fresh donor lymphocytes against the cancer instead. They frame donor cells as an immunologic dream team for the engagers: unexhausted, abundant, and already primed to attack. The piece maps the rationale and obstacles for trials of this combination.
pmc-13447105:
Xi Yang, Taras Gerya and Anna Gülcher model rifting on Venus in a 2026 study of long cracks and raised ground on the planet. Whether those rifts are still active has long been debated. Wide raised flanks beside a rift may be a clue, since raised ground can fade once stretching stops.

Three-dimensional computer models tested how Venus rock behaves under heat and stress, then let the land relax after stretching ended. Wide flank uplifts matched young or still active rifts best, not old inactive ones. Three named chasm regions on Venus show that same pattern. Their shapes also imply faster stretching than often assumed, possibly linked to hot rising rock deep below the surface.
pmc-13447305:
Lorena Bejarano-Hernández and co-authors review HPV vaccination in adults in 2026, asking whether programmes should reach beyond teenage girls. The virus causes several cancers and infects most sexually active people at some point. School programmes for girls have worked well, yet they leave large adult groups, especially men, unprotected under age-based rules.

Recent studies were sorted by outcome, from infection and viral persistence to precancerous neck-of-womb changes, recurrence after treatment, cancers and genital warts. Vaccination linked to lower infection and persistence in several reports, while estimates for high-grade cervical changes varied widely across studies. Adults aged eighteen to forty-five form the review's focus. The authors argue the findings support folding HPV vaccination into adult immunisation schedules, with gaps in consistency still to close.
pmc-13448805:
Wei Guo and coauthors screen a 2026 hope strain for a killed Coxsackie B4 vaccine, a virus behind hand, foot, and mouth disease, brain-lining swelling, and links to type 1 blood-sugar illness. Building on killed gut virus 71 and polio vaccine past wins, the team adapted the harmful strain 140/CHN/2019 to Vero cells through plaque cleaning and rounds.

The clone KM140-G01 grew above ten million live doses per ml, and its killed vaccine raised high blocking defense titers in mice and blocked varied medical samples. Mother defenses fully shielded pups against lethal challenge. The strain looks viable for CVB4 vaccine work, with a newborn mouse model aiding testing.
pmc-13451905:
Anmut Assemie and Beyene Bashu Haile test in 2026 whether garlic and ginger extracts kill mosquito young in water. Mosquitoes spread malaria and other ills, and plant brews could offer a cheap local weapon. The team gathered larvae from breeding sites, named them by shape keys, and brewed equal mixes of the two plants in water, ethanol, and methanol.

All brews held the same broad plant chemical classes. Kill rates climbed with dose, and the methanol brew did best, wiping out near all larvae at the top dose. Half-kill doses ran lower for the malaria mosquito than for a second kind. Bench success is clear, the authors note, while field and safety work still lie ahead.
pmc-13452105:
Ahmad Almadani and a large team measure in 2026 how often sexual trouble and distress ride along with depression at a Riyadh hospital. The study drew 258 adults with depression, aged up to 65, who filled Arabic forms on sexual function and distress plus background facts. Data came in over three months of 2025.

Near half the group met the bar for sexual dysfunction, and near three quarters met the bar for distress. Dysfunction tied to female sex, lower income, long-term illness, and body symptoms. Distress tied to marital state, extra mental ills, and smoking history. The authors say these hidden burdens deserve plain talk in depression care, since they weigh hard on daily life.
pmc-13452305:
Yuan and colleagues publish in 2026 a laboratory protocol for switching on a key growth signal inside cancer cells with light while the cells squeeze through narrow channels. Optogenetics, the use of light-sensitive proteins as switches, rarely meets the confined spaces that mimic real tissue.

The protocol uses a blue-light pairing system. Light of 488 nanometers drags a signaling piece to a chosen spot on the cell membrane. This enriches the enzyme PI3K at the leading edge and switches on the Akt pathway there. Detailed steps cover building the microfluidic channels, preparing triple-negative breast cancer cells carrying the light-sensitive parts, and stimulating them during confined migration. The authors note the workflow can be adapted to other cells, proteins, and channel designs, letting researchers watch signaling dynamics in real time as cells navigate tight spaces.
pmc-13453005:
Jhosy Canedo and five co-authors measure how late migrants in Spain got their first COVID-19 vaccine dose during 2021. Their 2026 study uses health records for more than 26 million people aged 12 and up who got at least one dose. Spain born people made up 86.1 percent of the group, and the rest were grouped by world region of birth.

Every migrant group waited longer than the Spain born group, whose median wait was 147 days. Waits ran from 160 days for South America born people to 185 days for Eastern Europe born people. The gap held after the team adjusted for sex, age, priority group, and region. The authors call the pattern a sign of real access barriers and urge stronger outreach so future vaccine drives reach migrants on time.
pmc-13453605:
Yukiyoshi Sumi and others set burnout cures for trainee doctors side by side in 2026, pooling trial data. Burnout in training harms doctors and patients, yet which cure helps most was not clear. The team trawled five data banks in Feb 2025 and logged the plan first.

Cures fell in six kinds: coaching, deep thought work, short intensive-care shifts, mind-body work, stress-skill drills, and plain news-giving. Scores covered worn-out feelings, cold detachment, weak efficacy, and whole burnout, ranked by network stats. The rank shows which cures merit first use in training plans. Hospitals gain head-to-head proof to shield trainees and, through them, patients.
pmc-13454205:
Guilherme Lepski and six co-authors report a compassionate use case of a patient's own bone marrow stem cells in long standing brain damage from oxygen loss. The patient, a young adult medical student, had lived with a disorder of consciousness after the injury. Their 2026 report works under national regulatory oversight, with cells grown under strict manufacturing and safety testing, then delivered into the spinal fluid.

Four months on, reviewers of video records scored the recovery scale at 11, up from 8 before treatment. Small gains showed in hearing, vision, and arousal, and the patient began a first repeatable yes no signal by blinking. Muscle stiffness eased a point in some groups, and no side effects appeared. Brain wave maps showed faster activity in front regions. The authors stress that one uncontrolled case cannot prove the cells worked.
pmc-13454505:
Ackermann, Reiner, and Kruss review new light-based sensors for brain signaling chemicals in this 2026 paper. The chemicals, catecholamines such as dopamine and norepinephrine, steer mood, movement, and many body processes, but they are hard to watch in action. Optical sensors can report them with fine detail in space and time, allowing live imaging in living tissue.

The review focuses on two families. One uses single-walled carbon nanotubes, tiny carbon tubes that change their glow near these chemicals. The other uses genetically encoded sensors that make cells themselves light up. Together they have mapped release dynamics at resolutions older methods could not reach. Remaining problems include telling similar chemicals apart, matching sensor speed to fast signals, and getting light deep into tissue, and the authors outline how the two approaches complement each other.
pmc-13455205:
Tereza Dousova and others characterized two ultra-rare CFTR variants in 2026, testing whether cystic fibrosis modulator drugs can help carriers. People with ultra-rare CFTR variants remain untreated with modulators due to missing functional and clinical data on variant-specific responsiveness. The team studied p.Glu1104Lys and p.Leu999del, each paired with the minimal function variant G542X.

Patient-derived intestinal organoids from rectal biopsies of two people with cystic fibrosis were tested by forskolin-induced swelling assays, with function quantified by area under the curve after sixty minutes. Human nasal epithelial cells from nasal brushing were tested in Ussing chambers, with CFTRinh-172-sensitive currents expressed as percentages of healthy controls. Both organoids showed visible swelling even untreated, and modulator responses were measured for triple combinations elexacaftor-tezacaftor-ivacaftor and vanzacaftor-tezacaftor-ivacaftor. The work provides theratyping data to guide treatment for ultra-rare variant carriers.
pmc-13455305:
Shabana, AlKoumi, and Abdeen tested mint sold in Hebron markets for E. coli carrying antibiotic resistance, the first such check on Palestinian fresh produce. Fourteen mint samples were taken across central, western, and southern districts of the city between January and March 2024, with identity proven by biochemistry and gene testing.

Thirteen proven E. coli isolates went through disc diffusion testing against a panel of antibiotics used in the study. Resistance hit 53.9 percent for tetracycline and 46.2 percent for chloramphenicol among the isolates, and 61.5 percent showed intermediate resistance to the oral drug cefuroxime in laboratory testing. Nearly a quarter, 23.1 percent, qualified as multidrug-resistant under standard criteria, and 15.4 percent showed possible heteroresistance to fluoroquinolones. The authors frame mint as a potential resistance reservoir needing wider surveillance of market produce.
pmc-13455405:
Tangfei Ran and colleagues build a visual risk chart for cement leakage during spine cementing in a 2026 study. Vertebroplasty steadies broken vertebrae by injecting bone cement, yet leaked cement can press nerves or reach the lungs, and surgeons still judge risk largely by eye. The team reviewed patients treated between January 2022 and June 2025, splitting them by whether leakage occurred and testing many bone, fracture and procedure factors.

Bone density, multiple fractures, a broken vertebral wall, degree of compression and cement volume each predicted leakage on their own in a multivariable model. Those five factors feed a nomogram, a points chart that turns a patient's profile into a leakage risk, which showed good discrimination and excellent calibration in validation. Surgeons gain a bedside aid for counselling and planning, though the model needs testing in other hospitals before routine use.
pmc-13457005:
Youdi Wei, Yujie Liu, and Yuling Yuan pool, in a 2026 meta-analysis, trials of mindfulness programs delivered by phone or computer for adults struggling with weight. Mindfulness training can steady eating habits, and apps widen its reach, yet proof on body weight stayed mixed. Ten studies with 902 participants survived the team's screening across three databases.

The programs clearly eased binge eating, with a moderate pooled effect. Emotional eating eased too, by a smaller margin. Two other habits, uncontrolled eating and deliberate restraint, did not move convincingly. Body mass index dipped slightly on average, but the change fell short of statistical confidence. The authors conclude that digital mindfulness helps the psychology of eating more than the scale, and they urge sharper protocols and sturdier trials to find whether weight effects can be made real.
pmc-13457105:
Susanne Kuprat leads a large team asking, in a 2026 secondary analysis, who sticks with exercise programs in schizophrenia, and why. Exercise eases symptoms and cuts early death in this population, yet attendance at structured programs fades fast. The team reworked data from two Munich trials covering one hundred patients on three months of supervised training, either endurance or flexibility and strength work.

Before training, patients were measured for motivation, personality, symptom load, past exercise, emotional support, fitness, and expectations. After correction for many comparisons, nothing predicted who adhered. Personality also failed to predict who got fitter. The authors treat the blank result as information, not failure: the usual suspects do not explain engagement here. They suggest support may need to be personal and practical rather than screened, and that programs should design for the many who drift, not the few who stay.
pmc-13457205:
ChenXing Cui and Kai Ma ask whether treating the parents of bariatric surgery patients improves the patients' own long-term results. Their 2026 retrospective study covers 200 people who had sleeve gastrectomy or gastric bypass at one institution between 2018 and 2024. The team had noticed that many patients' parents showed anxiety and overcontrol around eating, patterns that could quietly undermine recovery at home.

The first 100 patients received standard surgical care alone. The next 100 also had parents complete a structured program built on cognitive behavioral therapy and family systems therapy. At 24 months the second group had lost 78.2 percent of excess weight against 55.1 percent for controls, and weight regain was 4.2 percent versus 18.5 percent. Drops in parental control scores tracked closely with better patient eating adherence. Because treatment eras, not randomization, defined the groups, the authors call for a prospective trial to confirm the effect.
pmc-13457905:
Shalin S Bhatt and a large team searched donated human bodies for lymph vessels where the central and peripheral nervous systems meet in the neck. Lymph vessels drain fluid and carry immune cells, but their anatomy around the spinal cord was poorly documented. In their 2026 cadaver study, the team injected dye at low pressure through major lymph trunks in nine donors. They then tested harvested tissue with a stain for podoplanin, a marker on lymph vessel walls.

In four of the nine donors, they found thin walled, marker positive vessel structures. These ran with cervical spinal nerves at the skull base, through the openings where nerves exit the spine, and near the brachial plexus roots. The vessels sat outside the dura, the cord's tough covering, rather than inside it. The map is groundwork for studying how neck lymph networks drain brain and spinal fluid, the authors say.
pmc-13458005:
Dlkhwaz Hama and Karzan Mohammed Hawrami report a nutrition study, published in 2026. It measures iodine and selenium intake in 201 healthy adults. Thyroid function was also measured. The adults lived in Halabja City, in the Kurdistan Region of Iraq. Food questionnaires were combined with chemical analysis. Composite food samples were analysed. Blood and urine biomarkers were used too. This is a total diet study design.

Staple foods supplied roughly two thirds of both minerals. Biomarker results showed adequate-to-high status across the group. Most participants had thyroid function in the normal range. Dietary iodine was not independently linked to thyroid-stimulating hormone levels after adjustments. The authors urge monitoring of iodised salt use. This matters where staples dominate the diet.
pmc-13458605:
Yixuan Huang and colleagues present a graft source for rebuilding a narrowed ureter: the bladder's own lining. A 36-year-old woman arrived with a worsening blocked left kidney after endoscopic attempts failed, and imaging showed a stricture about five centimeters long in her mid-ureter. Because she was scheduled for dental implants, the cheek-mucosa graft was unattractive, so the team chose bladder mucosa, tissue at home in urine.

The robot-assisted operation ran in four steps: opening the strictured segment lengthwise, harvesting and thinning the graft, and sparing its inner layer. It ended with placing a stent with a ventral onlay join, and wrapping the repair in fat. Dye imaging confirmed the graft's blood supply. Surgery took 146 minutes with 10 milliliters of blood loss, and the hospital stay was five days. Six months on, the patient felt well, with stable kidney function and a draining kidney on scans.
pmc-13458705:
Ismet Hortu and colleagues test dental pulp stem cells against endometriosis in rats in a 2026 study. Endometriosis, an estrogen-driven inflammatory disease, persists through abnormal blood vessel growth and scarring, and current medical and surgical options leave many patients in pain or infertile. Twenty-eight female rats with surgically induced endometriosis were randomised to sham, untreated disease, one dose or two doses of human dental pulp stem cells given into the abdomen.

Untreated disease raised systemic and peritoneal inflammation, while stem cells cut peritoneal TNF-alpha and interleukin-6 in both regimens and lowered vessel growth factor more with double dosing. Histology and fibrosis improved most with double dosing, alongside lower CA-125, vessel, collagen and inflammation markers. The dose-dependent pattern supports a disease-modifying cell strategy, pending human safety and fertility trials.
pmc-13459205:
Yoshinobu Hyakuda and co-authors used artificial intelligence to reconstruct leg muscles in three dimensions from CT scans of patients with end-stage knee osteoarthritis. The scans came from 75 patients awaiting knee replacement surgery, divided into bow-legged varus deformity and knock-kneed valgus deformity by their leg angle. In their 2026 study, a validated AI model separated 23 muscle compartments and measured each one's volume and fat content, since fatty muscle is weaker muscle.

The valgus group, only 16 patients against 59 with varus knees, showed significantly smaller biceps femoris, tensor fasciae latae, and superficial back-thigh muscle volumes. Their tensor fasciae latae, a hip-stabilizing muscle on the outer thigh, also carried significantly more fat infiltration. The more knock-kneed the alignment, the smaller and fattier that muscle appeared. The authors suggest rehabilitation should be tailored to which deformity a patient has.
pmc-13459505:
Vahid Shamsabadi and co-authors tested whether selenium, a trace element that boosts plant antioxidant defenses, can protect peppermint crops from drought. In their 2026 greenhouse study, plants grew under full irrigation or half the crop's water requirement. Selenium was delivered four ways: not at all, mixed into irrigation water, sprayed on leaves before drought began, or sprayed after drought began, all at five milligrams per liter. Growth, leaf water status, pigments, water productivity, and the valuable essential oil were measured.

Drought significantly cut plant biomass, root weight, photosynthetic pigments, oil percentage, and leaf water content, while raising water productivity, phenol levels, membrane leakage, and antioxidant activity. Selenium blunted most of the damage, and spraying leaves before stress hit worked best. It raised shoot weight, oil yield, water productivity, pigment levels, and leaf water content together. Post drought spraying helped less. The authors recommend preventive low dose selenium sprays.
pmc-13460205:
Si-Qi Lyu and colleagues pooled in 2026 twenty-two studies to compare early surgery against initial medicine-only care for type A aortic intramural hematoma, a bleed inside the wall of the aorta. Management of this condition is genuinely controversial. Their meta-analysis covered 1,831 patients and tracked deaths in hospital and during later follow-up, with special attention to patients who crossed over to surgery after starting on medicine.

Early surgery showed a lower in-hospital death risk that fell short of significance, yet it clearly reduced deaths across follow-up. Patients who switched to timely surgery fared about as well in hospital as the early surgery group, though their later survival comparison flipped in surgery's favor. The authors suggest careful watch-and-wait may suit selected patients, pending prospective proof.
pmc-13460805:
Courtney T. A. Bonato, Greta Neethling, and Liska Budding examined in 2026 how the COVID-19 pandemic reshaped cytopathology work at an academic laboratory in central South Africa. Their retrospective analysis covered adult non-gynecological specimens received from March 2018 to April 2024. Records were divided into before, during, and after pandemic eras, and sorted by sampling method, body site, and whether the diagnosis was benign or malignant.

Specimen volumes fell during the pandemic and, notably, never recovered afterward. The share of fine needle aspirates held steady, yet breast aspirates and benign diagnoses dropped sharply while malignant and suspicious results grew as a share. Respiratory samples rose during the pandemic years. The authors read the pattern as delayed arrival building a testing backlog, and they argue for resilient laboratory services in future crises.
pmc-13461605:

Gene control regions carried many stress and hormone response signals. The team then tracked gene activity in leaves and roots under drought, added nitrogen, both, or neither. Different genes switched on under each stress, matching the idea that the family helps the tree adapt.
pmc-13488205:
Emmanuel Chilanga studies soybean porridge for young children in rural Malawi in a 2026 community experiment in Dowa District. Removing the hull gave the highest measured protein, while soaking gave the lowest in the reported tests. Caregivers liked the dehulled-and-roasted porridge best overall, with plain dehulled close behind. Combining nutrition and taste, the author favors dehulling, with roasting added, as a practical home method families will actually use.
pmc-13489705:

A cutoff split patients into low- and high-risk groups with clearly different survival. pmc-13491605:
Saullo Queiroz Silveira leads a ten-author team reporting a 2026 randomized trial on ventilator settings during weight-loss surgery performed through small incisions. Patients with obesity face lung stress under anesthesia when air pressure is poorly set. The trial tested whether a lung recruitment maneuver plus pressure-guided adjustment of PEEP, the pressure kept in the lungs between breaths, would prevent high driving pressure.

During the gas-inflated phase of surgery, high driving pressure struck far fewer patients in the guided group before and after recruitment. pmc-13491705:

pmc-13491805:
Fang Wang and Ling Zhou model in 2026 why boredom-prone teenagers' minds wander so often, surveying 3,736 adolescents at seventeen schools in Guangdong Province, China. The average participant was about fifteen years old. Questionnaires measured proneness to boredom, mobile phone addiction, sensation seeking, and everyday mind wandering, and structural modeling tested how the traits connect.

Sensation seeking strengthened the link between boredom and phone addiction, so thrill-hungry students showed the pattern most clearly. Because all measures came from one moment in time, the authors avoid causal claims and suggest interventions that teach boredom regulation and healthier phone habits.
pmc-13493505:
Naghmeh Nademi and five colleagues build in 2026 a wound dressing that fights bacteria, conducts electricity, and releases antibiotic on schedule. The film blends gellan and agar gels with chopped electrospun fibers carrying a conductive polymer-graphene mix, plus particles loaded with ciprofloxacin. Conductivity matters because gentle electrical cues are thought to help tissue repair.

The best fiber recipe, using one and a half percent of the conductive blend, delivered the highest conductivity and noticeably strengthened the film's stretch resistance and stiffness. Drug release followed a steady first-order pattern rather than dumping its payload at once. Growth halos in culture dishes confirmed killing power against both Staphylococcus aureus and Escherichia coli, stronger against the latter. Swelling and breakdown behavior also suited wound contact, and the authors propose trials in living tissue.
pmc-13493705:
Antonio Martorell and two colleagues argue in 2026 that hidradenitis suppurativa staging misses much of the disease because it counts a tunnel as active only when it drains pus. Their prospective study paired clinical examination with high-frequency ultrasound and Doppler flow imaging across 312 tunnels in eighty-four patients at three centers. Each tunnel was classed by depth and shape before its clinical signs were matched against blood flow inside its walls.

Doppler found active blood flow in ninety-one percent of tunnels, including most that never drained. Draining tunnels always showed flow, yet two bedside patterns predicted flow nearly as well in dry tunnels: pain combined with redness, or pain combined with firmness. Shallow dermal tunnels, though never draining, were inflamed in most cases and often painful and red. The authors propose widening the definition of an active tunnel to catch a treatable early window.
pmc-13493805:
Zhong and colleagues modelled a 2026 land use study for Sichuan Province in China, tracking how land change moves the carbon stored in soils and vegetation. Balancing growth with ecological protection is central to China's dual carbon goals. Their coupled model links land simulation, carbon accounting, and a driver analysis tool.

Between 2000 and 2020 Sichuan lost a large amount of stored carbon, with declines centred on the middle and south of the Sichuan Basin. Zhong found vegetation greenness was the strongest single driver of carbon patterns, and its effect grew stronger when combined with elevation. Looking ahead, natural trend and economy first scenarios kept losing carbon through 2060. Only the ecological conservation scenario reversed the trend, gaining a substantial amount by 2060.
pmc-13493905:
Kocabıyık, in a single-author 2026 study, builds a mathematical model of chikungunya, the mosquito-spread virus that causes fever and long-lasting joint pain. Standard epidemic models treat time as uniform and forget the past, but real outbreaks show memory, where earlier conditions shape later spread, and bursts at many timescales. The new model combines fractional derivatives, a calculus that weights history, with fractal time, which stretches and compresses the clock.

The author proves the model's solutions stay positive and bounded, works out its resting states, and computes the basic reproduction number, the threshold deciding whether an outbreak grows or fades. Analysis shows the system switches stability exactly at that threshold, as theory expects. Simulations then show the memory and fractal settings bending the epidemic curves away from classical predictions, lingering longer in some regimes. The author argues such models fit real outbreak shapes better.
pmc-13494205:
Maureen M Black and Chessa K Lutter set out, in a 2026 article, a plan for programs that join nutrition with early child development in poor settings. Millions of young children in low- and middle-income countries grow and learn below their potential, held back by poor diets and few chances to learn. Few big efforts support food, growth, learning, and caregiving together.

Goals should rest on theory and proven methods, and the program should reach the children most at risk with content that fits their age and culture. Staff need training and support, with checks on quality. Families, communities, and officials should hold active roles, and outcomes should be tracked with simple tools. Lasting funding and updated policy round out the list. A joint partner team, guided by steady data feedback, would steer the system.
pmc-13494605:
Kaori Koga and colleagues report a 2026 phase 3 trial in Japan of a flexible hormone pill routine for painful periods, known as dysmenorrhea. The pill pairs desogestrel with a low dose of ethinylestradiol. Rather than fixed monthly cycles, users take the pill for 24 to 80 days in a row, then pause for four days, choosing the rhythm themselves. The trial ran at 21 centers with a blinded phase and an open follow-up.

The study enrolled 211 women with regular cycles and period pain, giving most the drug and the rest a placebo. Pain scores fell far more on the drug through day 84, and days of strong pain shrank. Over eighty percent on the drug reported feeling better, against under thirty percent on placebo, and satisfaction scores ran higher. Bleeding between periods, colds, and nausea were the most common side effects, and no deaths occurred.
pmc-13495305:
LiLi Deng and a large team review, in a 2026 article, how fat-based nano carriers could carry Chinese herbal compounds into the brain against Alzheimer's disease. The disease tangles memory through amyloid plaques, tau tangles, inflammation, and oxidative stress, and current drugs ease symptoms only. Several plant compounds from traditional Chinese medicine guard nerve cells on many fronts, yet they break down fast and cross the blood-brain barrier poorly.

The review weighs carrier types, from liposomes and cell-shed exosomes to solid and mixed fat particles, for stability, barrier crossing, and brain build-up. Fresh tactics add guided targeting and disguise, such as coating particles in cell membrane so the body treats them as its own. The authors also face the blocks ahead: mass production, quality checks, rules, and long-term safety. They frame the platforms as a promising scaffold needing hard proof before clinic use.
pmc-13495405:
Enyu Xu and a large team track, in a 2026 study, six years of malaria mosquito ecology across city and country sites in eastern China. China has ended local malaria, yet the vector Anopheles sinensis remains, and how weather, farming, and city growth steer it was a knowledge gap. Nets and light traps logged biting and density from 2016 to 2021 under a One Health frame joining human, animal, and land factors.

Nearly fifty thousand mosquitoes were counted, confirming the species' dominance. Heat ruled: rural biting peaked near twenty-eight to thirty degrees a month later, and rain showed threshold effects. Crops raised risk slightly, while cattle and buffalo nearby shielded people by drawing bites. Dense city living, oddly, suppressed the mosquito. Male-skewed local populations raised rural biting. The authors say control must be tuned separately for city and country, since the drivers diverge.
pmc-13498505:
Martino Azzi and others follow cardiometabolic risk over ten years of testosterone-based gender-affirming hormone therapy in transmasculine adults. In 2026, the single-center long-term cohort tracks fifty-seven people who completed a decade of yearly examinations, blood tests, and body composition tests. Long-term energy effects of prolonged male hormone were earlier poorly documented.

Blood protein rose early then stabilized, while glucose, insulin, and blood pressure changed little. Lipids worsened throughout, with higher LDL, total blood fat, and blood fats and lower HDL, with rising weight, waist tests, lean mass, and trunk fat. No major heart and vessel events occurred, and one participant developed atrial fibrillation. The authors recommend ongoing tracking, risk treatment, and lifestyle support.
pmc-13499205:
Shuang Guan and co-authors review how artificial intelligence is reshaping wildlife conservation work, in this 2026 paper. Species loss is outpacing old survey methods. The authors organize the new tools in three layers. At the data layer, environmental DNA, sound recorders, and satellites feed fused streams of evidence. At the algorithm layer, image networks, transformers, and learning agents name species and judge habitat.

At the system layer, privacy-safe shared learning, digital twins, and field-side computing tie the stack together. Practice shifts from reacting to predicting: tracking animals live, grading habitat finely, flagging threats early, and ranking where money helps most. The authors also flag data bias, opaque models, and social tensions. They argue governed, cross-field development is the path to global targets.
pmc-13499705:
Walsh and colleagues forecast demand for community-based health and publicly funded social care tied to frailty, in a 2026 modeling study. The forecast covers people aged fifty and over in England from 2025 to 2040. Evidence on hospital and primary care demand was good, but community services were unquantified. The team derived contact rates by age and frailty index from North-West London cohort data, then ran a system dynamics simulation nationally.

Walsh projects use rising over the sixteen years, with mental health contacts up about a sixth and community health and social care contacts up about thirty percent each. Preventing frailty could save hundreds of thousands of social care contacts. Slowing progression could save tens of thousands of health contacts, yet both gains are partly swallowed by population ageing. Because so many people already live with mild frailty, the authors conclude demand will grow regardless and planning must assume it.
pmc-13499805:
Ki Hong Lee and a team of co-authors present a study from twenty twenty-six on how blood flow tells the liver what work to do where. The liver's tasks are zoned: cells near the center vein do unlike work from those at the rim. Vessel lining cells hand the orders through a signal family named Wnt. What sets those orders was not known.

The team ties the orders to the push of blood flow on the lining cells. Gene maps at single cell level and space protein maps chart the talk between lining and liver cells. Wnt receivers and senders both pile up near the center vein. Wnt also feeds back on the lining's own genes and shape. The lining reads as a decoder of force into orders.
pmc-13500505:
Huimin Hou and colleagues trace in 2026 how the conservation capacity of Lanzhou, a dry northwestern Chinese city, changed between 2000 and 2023 and what drives it. This ecosystem service, the landscape's ability to hold and regulate water, buffers scarcity and climate stress. Scenarios were then projected to 2050.

Capacity fluctuated strongly year to year without a significant long-term trend, sitting highest in northwestern and southern mountains and lowest in central river valleys and the southeast in their maps. Soil water content, rainfall, and vegetation greenness pushed capacity up, while human activity intensity was the dominant drag, with drivers interacting in nonlinear ways. Future patterns stayed spatially similar, though total volume depended heavily on the climate and development path chosen.
pmc-13500805:

Artificial intelligence runs at the network edge, close to users, so decisions stay fast. Deep reinforcement learning adjusts spectrum and power settings as conditions change, while successive interference cancellation separates overlapping signals from different users.

The system was implemented in MATLAB and compared with plain MC-CDMA, MIMO-OFDM, and hybrid precoding designs. Simulations reached a spectral efficiency near 32.7 bits per second per hertz and an energy efficiency near 14.8 bits per joule. pmc-13501605:

pmc-13503805:
Haixia Zhai and four colleagues present a tool that finds loops in folded DNA inside the cell core, in a 2026 paper. Loops bring far-apart gene switches next to the genes they control. Broken loops can cause birth defects and cancer, yet spotting them in noisy map data is hard.

In tests it beat older tools on overlap scores, protein enrichment, and match with known 3D shapes. The code is posted in public for other labs to use.
pmc-13503905:
Armin Behfrouz and Maryam Tahmasebpoor improve a natural mineral so it pulls more ammonia from wastewater, in a 2026 study. The mineral, clinoptilolite, is common and cheap, yet in raw form it takes up ammonia poorly. Chemical treatment can sharpen its appetite.

Standard uptake curves fit the data well. The beads held up over repeat cycles, which suits plant-scale trials.
pmc-13504005:
Francisco Rodrigues dos Santos leads a team explaining a heart tracing that points to poisoning by an old drug, in a 2026 case answer. The tracing showed a junctional rhythm with the upper and lower heart chambers beating apart, a short QT span, and a scooped dip in the ST segment, a classic digoxin mark. pmc-13504805:

The authors prescribe curriculum reform and clear professional guidance as the fix.
pmc-13505105:

pmc-13507105:

pmc-13507205:

pmc-13508005:

pmc-13508205:

pmc-13508305:

pmc-13508505:
Amira Othman and a team of co-authors surveyed university students in Egypt about misuse of antibiotics, in two thousand twenty-six. The survey ran at Suez University in early two thousand twenty-five. It asked what students know, how they feel, and what they do with these drugs.

Feelings about the drugs explained most of the link between knowing and doing. Past use of the drugs and reliance on social media raised the odds of that gap, while doctors as a source lowered it.
pmc-13508805:
Dadashpour and colleagues compared five machine learning methods in 2026 for identifying type 2 diabetes and the factors tied to it. They used a public dataset of health records for nearly 100,000 people, testing models that included logistic regression, a neural network, and a random forest.

pmc-13509805:

pmc-13510105:

pmc-13510705:

Among the face injury cases, a few thousand involved alcohol only, and fewer involved drugs or medicine only. The drug group's share rose over time, while the alcohol share stayed flat. Drug-group patients were older on average and were admitted to hospital far more often. Keeping the groups apart, the authors argue, gives a clearer picture.
pmc-13511005:

The authors present it as an effective option for endometriosis pain, grounded in those paired mechanisms.
pmc-13511305:
Hu and colleagues reviewed the mixed evidence on isoflurane, a used anesthetic gas, and thinking ability, in their 2026 article. pmc-13513705:

pmc-13513905:

pmc-13516005:

pmc-13516805:

pmc-13517405:
