The authors suggest the toxin's benefit partly reflects fascial remodelling, a structural effect beyond nerve blocking, and propose ultrasound fascial measurement as a monitoring biomarker.
pmc-13517505:
Muhammad Farid leads a nine-author review of measles and rubella across the WHO Eastern Mediterranean Region in a 2026 analysis. The two diseases serve as tracers of how well vaccine systems work, and pandemic disruption tore gaps in coverage. The team examined surveillance, coverage estimates, and elimination status for all twenty-two countries and territories over 2023 and 2024.

Regional measles incidence crept up, and rubella more than doubled per million people. Big outbreaks in Yemen, Iraq, and Afghanistan drove much of the rise. First-dose coverage held near eighty percent, second-dose near seventy-five, and only nine countries cleared ninety-five percent on both. Zero-dose children and dropout between doses kept transmission alive. Farid's team judges the region off track for 2030 elimination and urges equity-first catch-up, stronger surveillance, and faster outbreak response, above all in fragile, conflict-hit settings.
pmc-13517705:
Krisztián Németh leads a nine-author review, the second of two parts, tracing collagen fragments from the gut through the whole body in a 2026 article. Collagen supplements are usually sold for joints and skin, but digested fragments travel widely. In the gut they help seal the lining, nudge the resident microbes, and change bile, the liver's digestive fluid, which in turn talks to appetite, blood sugar, fat, liver, and brain.

The authors grade the findings honestly. Firmest ground: joint disease in dogs and horses, plus taurine, a separate nutrient working through bile, for a reversible heart condition in some dog breeds. Lab hints about fat burning, memory, and clotting remain unconfirmed in animals. Németh's team frames diet as a shared gut-bile signalling system that collagen and taurine each tune differently, relevant across pets, horses, and livestock.
pmc-13518805:
Yujie Chen and six colleagues unveil CAPO in 2026, a yeast platform that makes gene activity tunable and predictable. Engineers often combine promoters, DNA switches that set gene output, only to find behavior changes in new combinations. Output reached levels matching strong natural yeast promoters with little background leak, and strength order held across genes. The team programmed broad fluorescence colors and quickly optimized production of lycopene and 3-hydroxypropionic acid, showing practical range.
pmc-13520305:
Ava Safaroghli-azar leads a 2026 laboratory study of AU2-94, a drug designed to block only the CDK4 protein in prostate cancer. Earlier drugs block CDK4 together with CDK6, so the team tests whether a narrower drug keeps its strength while working in cancers that resist standard care.

Readers get a detailed early case for selective CDK4 blockade before any human use.
pmc-13520705:
Sadaf Khursheed Baba and colleagues outline in 2026 a term-long course in cancer biology for undergraduates. Students run a real lab project on HPV-linked cervical cancer. They also learn science writing in a structured way. The class silenced a candidate gene in cancer cells and tracked gene activity.

That step links bench work with scholarly output. The group was small. The design is still offered as a model that other schools can scale.
pmc-13521805:
Xiao Chen and colleagues linked climate exposures to a pregnancy liver disease in 2026. The disease causes itching and fetal risk. Its cause remains unclear in general. Climate may trigger onset in some women. Shanghai and Sanya records were compared. Two centres supplied the cohort data.

One city kept higher rates under steady warmth. Thalassemia was also commoner in cases. Both regions showed that gene pattern. Climate planning may inform pregnancy care.
pmc-13522005:
Ling-Gen Xiong and colleagues derive in 2026 breast cancer subtypes from microscope image features, then trace a key gene's spatial pattern with single-cell and spatial gene data. Image traits from tumour slides numbered 1,406, narrowed to 25 core features for clustering.

Two subtypes emerged, with one tied to advanced disease and poorer outlook. A splicing-related gene called ESRP1 stood out as raised in that harsher subtype. Spatial maps placed the gene inside tumour zones alongside epithelial and support cells. Communication analysis cast support cells as hubs in a growth-factor network in gene-rich regions, suggesting a microenvironment role worth targeted study.
pmc-13523205:
Peerapen and co-authors test chlorogenic acid, a coffee bean compound, against the kidney scarring that kidney stones set in motion. The crystals duly triggered the transition, raising the spindle index and a mesenchymal marker while the electrical resistance across the cell sheet, a seal quality measure, fell. Chlorogenic acid prevented every one of those changes when given before or with the crystals. The authors suggest a dietary compound might interrupt stone-driven fibrosis early.
pmc-13523305:
Mingjie Xu, Hao Cheng, and Lijian Xu report a rare gut cancer that mimics another cancer type in a 2026 case report. An eighty-two-year-old man had persistent black stools and severe anemia. Imaging found multiple lesions in the stomach and small intestine, and surgery removed several bowel segments. Gene sequencing found amplification of the MYC gene, usually associated with radiation-linked cases, although this patient had no prior radiotherapy. He died three months after surgery. The authors propose MYC amplification as a possible driver and marker of aggressive behavior in primary cases.
pmc-13523405:
Margaret Kurop, Hekmat B Khoukaz, and William P Fay present an electrocardiogram puzzle in an eighteen-year-old woman in a 2026 case report. She arrived at the emergency department with nausea, fatigue, and tremor, and her heart tracing showed inverted T waves in the chest leads. In adults such changes often suggest reduced blood flow to the heart, yet in a young patient other causes move up the list. Her history included depression treated with medication.

The teaching point centers on lithium toxicity. Because lithium resembles sodium and potassium chemically, it interferes with the channels and pumps that set heart cell electrical activity, in both slow nodal tissue and fast conducting tissue. The resulting tracing changes most often include T-wave inversion and lengthening of the QT interval, a pattern clinicians should recognize in patients taking lithium.
pmc-13524605:
Alfaro Hudak and colleagues examined whether the time adults spend on responsibilities squeezes out home food preparation, a question sharpened by new dietary guidelines urging whole, minimally processed foods. Their 2026 study first surveyed United States adults about which daily activities count as responsibilities. They then linked national time-use data from 2014 to 2016 and 2022 to 2023 to examine cooking time across household types.

Alfaro Hudak found households with children spent the most time on both responsibilities and food preparation, while single parents cooked less than two-parent households. More responsibility time was linked to slightly less cooking in every household group, a small per-hour effect that households seem to resist by protecting cooking time. Accumulated across realistic differences, though, the loss reached a meaningful share of average preparation time. That suggests many households already cook near their feasible minimum and need time relief, not just dietary advice.
pmc-13524705:
Eric Xu and seven co-authors tell, in a 2026 case report, of a kidney transplant patient whose new organ was infected by a virus. Viral infection of a graft poses a hard diagnostic call, since its tissue marks can look like rejection. The treatments for the two pull in opposite ways, one calming the immune system and one freeing it. A blood test for donor-derived cell-free DNA is validated for rejection, but its role in infection was open.

Soon after the transplant, the man's kidney function slipped and the donor DNA marker ran high. A biopsy showed marks of adenovirus, a less common graft virus. The team walk through how graft viruses are told apart. They weigh where the DNA test fits: it flags graft injury but not its cause. The case adds a rare virus to the list the test has faced.
pmc-13526205:
Parissa J Ballard and colleagues examined how civic life relates to health among United States school students. Published in 2026, the study surveyed 1,286 students in grades six through twelve, average age near fifteen, between fall 2021 and spring 2025. Civic engagement covered actions, attitudes, and skills, while health covered physical, mental, and overall well-being, split by race and gender groups.

Whole-sample averages hid distinct subgroup patterns. Girls, transgender, and gender-diverse students showed more positive links between civic engagement and health than boys did. Political participation and civic discussion, by contrast, linked more negatively to health for students of color than for White students. pmc-13527905:
Jian Wang and eleven colleagues report a 2026 experiment on whether melatonin can protect cotton seeds from cadmium, a toxic heavy metal that builds up in farm soils. Working with the cultivar Nongda 601, the team compared plain seeds with seeds given melatonin, cadmium, or both together, then sequenced gene activity to see how the hormone changed the response.

Adding melatonin restored enzyme activity that breaks down stored starch, lowered the harmful byproducts, and shifted hormone levels back toward growth. Gene data pointed to antioxidant defenses and a plant chemical pathway called phenylpropanoid biosynthesis. The findings may guide cotton growing on polluted land.
pmc-13528005:
Cagri Ates and Onur Karaaslan report a 2026 prospective study of fetal heart function in growth-restricted pregnancies. Telling a naturally small fetus from a truly restricted one is hard. Standard Doppler blood-flow tests can look normal until late. The team used a modified heart performance index on 157 pregnancies at or past 32 weeks. Fetuses were grouped by belly size percentile.

Usual Doppler measures and fluid levels did not differ among groups. Heart timing measures did. Fetuses below the tenth percentile showed longer contraction and relaxation phases and higher index values. That pattern signals early heart strain. Borderline fetuses between the third and tenth percentiles looked much like those below the third. The authors suggest the index adds useful warning where Doppler stays silent.
pmc-13528105:
Qianqian Wu and seven colleagues delete a gene in a pig and human pathogen to see what it does in a 2026 study. The germ is Streptococcus suis serotype 2. The gene makes a small enzyme that strips phosphate tags from proteins. Such enzymes help build capsules in related germs. The team built a mutant missing the gene and compared it with the normal strain.

The mutant grew a bit slowly in mid-phase. Its capsule ran thinner, with about twelve percent less capsule sugar. Colony looks, cell sticking, and dodging of immune eating stayed normal. Mouse infections were no milder than with the normal germ. Lab tests showed the enzyme cannot strip the expected partner protein. The authors conclude the enzyme trims the capsule but is not vital for disease. They warn against copying mechanisms between cousin species.
pmc-13529805:
Sina Ghanbari and eight colleagues hunt durum wheat lines that yield steadily under rain-fed farming in a 2026 study. They grew 118 inbred lines from a cross between a drought-fit Iranian cultivar and a protein-rich landrace. Four sites in Italy and Iran hosted the trials. Both grain yield and grain protein were scored. Several stability methods ranked the lines.

One line, ZD-050, gave the top yield at about 3.9 tonnes per hectare. Another, ZD-032, led protein at about 14.3 percent. Rankings shifted by method, as expected. Yield-focused and dynamic methods still put ZD-050 near the top. It kept moderate protein while adapting widely. Gene, place, and their interplay all shaped both traits strongly. The authors nominate ZD-050 for breeding programs chasing steady harvests without rain insurance.
pmc-13529905:
Simran K Chandawarkar and Ibrahim Amjad review lasting harm from dermal fillers in a 2026 synthesis of published evidence. Fillers lift and reshape facial tissue, and most side effects stay minor. Their search followed PRISMA guidance across PubMed reports from 2000 to 2024. Blindness, stroke, lasting inflammation, and tissue death emerged as the gravest outcomes, tied mainly to injection site, technique, and product choice. Hyaluronic acid products stayed favored because their effects can be reversed.
pmc-13530105:
Sathish Kumar Gunasekaran and four co-authors review the sugar trehalose as a candidate Alzheimer's treatment, in a two thousand twenty-six review. Trehalose is known for switching on autophagy, the cell's cleanup system, to clear amyloid and tau proteins.

The authors argue its protective reach is wider. Evidence from cell and animal studies links trehalose to stabilizing neuronal membrane domains, managing stress granules, mimicking metabolic stress through nutrient-sensing pathways, and calming microglia and astrocytes. The gut-brain axis features too, through microbiota and barrier effects. Translational hurdles remain: poor oral bioavailability, limited brain penetration, and long-term safety in elderly patients.
pmc-13531705:
Davide Ninarello and Luigi La Barbera ask whether ceramic cages could serve in lower back fusion surgery, in a computer-based study published in twenty twenty-six. In this surgery a cage is placed in a worn disc space, with screws and rods to hold the spine steady while bone grows.

Common cage stuff, titanium alloy and a plastic called PEEK, does not break down in the body, which can raise the risk of the cage shifting or sinking over time. The pair first checked a model of one spine joint against known loads. They then modeled the full surgery in two ways, from the back and from the side, and compared a ceramic cage with titanium ones under daily loads. The study is an early test of whether a ceramic that can break down is strong enough for the job.
pmc-13534405:
Mehedi Hasan Meraj and colleagues present in 2026 CAE-BrainNet, a model that sorts brain tumours from MRI scans into four classes. Past models often covered few classes, lacked clear explanations, and skipped firm statistical checks. pmc-13536705:
Souhaib Atri and colleagues recount an unusual trauma recovery in a 2026 case report involving a complete cut through the common bile duct. A 29-year-old man arrived with a stab wound through the chest and abdomen, severe liver injury, and active bleeding. Scans two months later showed a new natural channel between the bile duct and the small intestine that allowed bile to drain inside the body. Because liver tests stayed normal and no blockage appeared, surgeons chose close follow-up instead of reconstruction. One year later the patient remained well without symptoms. The authors present careful staged care plus watchful follow-up as a workable path in rare cases like this one.
pmc-13538305:
Myriam V. Thoma and colleagues test two accounts of how early-life hardship shapes mental health in old age in a 2026 study. One account predicts steady harm with each added hardship, while the other predicts a curved pattern where moderate hardship toughens people. A total of 211 older adults with an average age near seventy years took part, split between a high-hardship group and a lower-risk comparison group. Past-year mental disorders were counted.

About six in ten participants qualified for at least one past-year disorder diagnosis, with higher shares in the high-hardship group. Disorder counts rose steadily with hardship level, fitting the straight dose pattern. No curved toughening pattern appeared. The authors conclude that early stress casts a long shadow and stress prevention across life deserves priority.
pmc-13538405:
Yaan-Kit Ng and colleagues map protein interaction changes in muscle insulin resistance in a 2026 study combining two mass measurement methods. pmc-13538605:
Mengmeng Zhu and co-authors review how diabetes shapes calcium buildup in artery plaques, in work from two thousand twenty-six. People with diabetes tend to carry more of this buildup, and its forms vary. The buildup can affect how stable a plaque is and how much risk it poses.

High blood sugar and other body shifts drive the process, the review says. Paths named include swelling, cell death, tiny mineral packets, and cells that turn bone-like. Scans should judge more than the total amount of buildup. Current care has clear limits, and the authors point to open lines for new work.
pmc-13538705:
D Gavars and colleagues probe single tiny wires of mixed copper and zinc oxides for infrared harvesting in a 2026 scope study. The cheap, common oxides form junction wires mostly studied for visible light, leaving infrared response untested. The wires acted like diodes, confirming a working junction between the oxide types. A strong current appeared under infrared light with no applied voltage, traced to a heat-driven effect. Voltage per degree, power factor, and response speed all reached solid levels. The authors see promise for tiny power units running on small heat gaps in wearable gear and sensors.
pmc-13539805:
Yomna Khallaf, Olfat Hassanein, Aya Adly, and Dina Kamal test a way to make tooth sealants last in this two thousand twenty-six trial. The trial weighs a short extra step at placement against the main cause of sealant failure, loss of the coating itself.
pmc-13539905:

pmc-13540905:

The team reprogrammed her blood cells into stem cells. The cells kept a normal chromosome set. They also showed the standard markers of stemness. They could form all three early tissue layers. The team then turned them into neural stem cells. Those cells offer a base for drug screening work.
pmc-13542205:

pmc-13546705:
Md. pmc-13547305:
Dominika Zaremba and a cross-national team ran a preregistered experiment in 2026 on whether stirring climate emotions moves people to act. The authors suggest future work needs more natural or immersive emotional material, longer exposure, and tasks matched more closely to the feelings raised.
pmc-13548705:

pmc-13550605:

pmc-13550805:

pmc-13550905:

pmc-13551305:

New fat chemistries can hitch a ride past that wall. Others cloak the dose from immune watch or aim it at set brain cells, with the liver spared. Readers get a map of what stands between a fast shot tech and the old brain.
pmc-13551705:

pmc-13551805:
V P Ansar Ahamed, Abhay Mudey, Abhishek Joshi, and T Athila Jasmine published a 2026 case report from rural India. A 75-year-old farmer had lived with a swollen leg and scrotum for about seven years. A blood smear showed young worms, the offspring of a filarial parasite. An ultrasound showed the classic dance sign of the worms. Care combined sugar control, drugs for the infestation, and limb hygiene advice. Staff also counseled him on mosquito control and follow-up. The team argues for joining worm disease checks with chronic disease care in rural programs.
pmc-13553005:

pmc-13553705:

pmc-13556005:

pmc-13556105:

Scores rose with depression, anxiety, and symptom burden, and fell as quality of life and spiritual wellbeing rose. Family and social wellbeing showed no such link. pmc-13558605:

The authors present interpretability as the method's chief prize.
pmc-13559105:

pmc-13559205:
