pmc-13559805:
Manuela Araque and colleagues examine how social conditions track with metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease in the All of Us research database. Their 2026 cross-sectional analysis identified cases by diagnosis codes, excluded other liver diseases and heavy alcohol use, then matched cases to controls by age and race or ethnicity. The matched sample held 57,895 participants, with full survey data for 16,666.

People with the liver disease were more likely to report incomes at or below $35,000 and schooling below high school level. They also scored higher on social isolation, neighborhood disorder, perceived stress, food insecurity, and transportation insecurity, each gap statistically significant. The authors note the disease already affects roughly a third of the world's adults by current estimates. They call for research on how these social factors combine to drive risk and progression, rather than treating each factor in isolation.
pmc-13560305:
Young Sun Hwang and three colleagues explore why lab-grown human primordial germ cell-like cells split into distinct states. Their 2026 study centers on DND1, a protein whose production from its message varies between cells. Dual fluorescent reporters, single-cell sequencing, and functional assays tracked what the DND1-positive state means for these early germline cells.

DND1-producing cells were rich in RNA regulation machinery, including genes tied to processing bodies and translation control. They divided slowly, exited the cell cycle, and raised the brake protein P27 in their nuclei. At the same time they kept stable expression of genes the germline needs for later differentiation. Adding the signal BMP2 steadied DND1 production without changing its message level or growth rate. The authors conclude that control after transcription coordinates cell cycle behavior with germ cell identity during development.
pmc-13560405:
Ömer Faruk Turan and three colleagues analyze emergency care at a Turkish national hospital deployed for the 2025 Hajj pilgrimage in Makkah. Their 2026 retrospective study covers a mission serving 84,942 Turkish pilgrims between April and July 2025. Operational data from such independent national missions are rarely published.

Nearly ten thousand pilgrims, 11.7 percent of those served, made 13,360 emergency visits. Respiratory illness dominated at about half of presentations. Referrals to higher care stayed low overall, yet heart and neurological problems, small shares of visits, supplied outsized shares of referrals. Age was the strongest referral predictor, with pilgrims seventy-five and older referred at roughly fourteen times the adjusted odds of younger groups. Repeat visitors also faced higher referral risk. Mortality ran at thirty-four per hundred thousand pilgrims. The authors recommend age-based planning and stronger advanced life support.
pmc-13561005:
Xueying Lin and co-authors pair a cancer-killing virus with an immune drug, in work published in 2026. The virus, OVM18, kills tumor cells and carries a tweaked gene that fires up a local immune pathway. Response varied a lot, so the team hunted for the immune traits that drive gains.

One T cell type inside tumors, marked by a receptor for that pathway, tracked with success. Those cells were grown, tumor-focused killers seeded by a dendritic cell type in lymph nodes. A second drug that lifts a brake on immunity boosted those cells and broke resistance. The pair slowed tumors and stretched life in weak-response models.
pmc-13561105:
Yu Sakamoto and colleagues measure the thermal strain of recreational runners racing in tropical heat. Their 2026 study follows 162 runners through ten- or twenty-one-kilometer events in warm, humid conditions near twenty-seven degrees with humidity in the high eighties. Core temperature, heart rate, skin temperature, and fluid balance were tracked in real time for subsets of the field.

Peak core temperatures averaged about 39.4 degrees in both races, with some runners crossing forty-one. Heart rates peaked near maximal values, and half-marathoners lost about two and a half percent of body mass. Four factors independently fed peak core temperature: the temperature a runner started at, mean heart rate, body surface area, and average speed, together explaining about half the variance in the reported model. Age and finishing time did not matter. The authors aim the findings at safer mass-participation racing in the heat.
pmc-13561205:
Sumet Kumar and colleagues pooled trial evidence on lorundrostat, a new drug for high blood pressure that stays high despite several medicines. Lorundrostat blocks the making of aldosterone, a salt-holding hormone, while leaving related hormones alone.

Three trials with 1,568 patients compared the drug against placebo, a dummy treatment with no active drug. On average, systolic pressure fell about 8.4 points more on lorundrostat, and diastolic pressure fell about 3.8 points more. Side effects came more often on the drug, notably low pressure and high potassium, though serious harms were not clearly higher. Kumar says the drug looks promising but larger, longer trials must confirm its safety.
pmc-13562205:
Marie Linderup Funck and six colleagues measured frailty in older adults booked for planned bone and joint surgery in Denmark. Frailty means a body with little reserve, so stress such as surgery hits harder. Their 2026 study covered 519 people aged 65 and older, most booked for hip or knee replacement, and graded each person's health from medical records before surgery.

About one in four patients was pre-frail, and a small share was moderately frail, while none was severely frail. Both groups spent more days in hospital during the 90 days after surgery than patients who were not frail. Spotting this weakness before surgery, the authors argue, lets care teams plan support across clinics and wards and head off complications.
pmc-13562505:
Haohao Wang and six colleagues tackle a deep coal mine problem: the floor of a kept roadway bulging upward unevenly under shifting pressure. The roadway runs beside a mined-out area, and cutting the roof to relieve stress makes the load lopsided. Floor heave then warps the passage and raises upkeep costs. The 2026 study combines a scaled physical model, a mathematical failure model built on earth-pressure theory, and measurements underground at the Zhaogu No. 1 Mine.

Model tests traced how floor strain spread from shallow layers downward after roof cutting. The team proposed a pressure-balancing support scheme: pre-split the roof, fit yielding supports that give under load in roof and walls, and brace the floor with an inverted beam. In the field, the scheme cut floor heave by 46.1 percent against an uncontrolled section. Theory, model, and mine data agreed.
pmc-13562905:
Wang and colleagues review in twenty twenty-six tiny bubbles shed by plants as a new material for skin care and repair. These nanovesicles carry proteins, small regulatory RNAs, and active plant compounds inside a fatty skin, are plentiful, and rarely provoke immunity. The review traces how plants build and load them by two routes, then maps how their cargo defends skin.

Claimed actions include switching on antioxidant defences, slowing the enzymes that chew collagen, calming pigment overproduction, and speeding wound closure through growth signals. The authors compare the bubbles with synthetic carriers and animal vesicles, favouring the plant ones for safety and uptake. Scaling, quality checks, and storage remain hurdles, with engineering fixes proposed.
pmc-13563705:
Lukas Sigmund and co-authors present BONAFIDE, a Python package that computes local features of atoms and bonds in molecules. Data-driven chemistry needs clean, repeatable ways to turn molecules into numbers. Tools for whole-molecule descriptors are common. Local features, per atom and per bond, were scattered across many tools with clashing interfaces. BONAFIDE gathers them under one roof.

The package links 11 outside tools, from RDKit and MORFEUS to quantum engines like xtb and Psi4. It now computes 590 distinct atom and bond features, from 2D or 3D structures and from electronic structure data. Inputs are flexible, outputs can be shaped, and every setting is logged so runs can be repeated. Users can add their own featurizers inside the same frame. A case study on amines shows the workflow end to end.
pmc-13563805:
Mohammed Azhar Hussain and two colleagues pair continuous glucose monitors with meal records to see how diet mix and meal spacing move blood sugar in Indian adults with type 2 diabetes. Swings in glucose, beyond the average marker, drive complications on their own. Their 2026 study kept 47 adults who wore a sensor for ten to fourteen days. Food diaries supplied carbohydrate, protein, and fat shares, plus meal gaps. Sensor metrics captured time in range, time above it, and variability.

Carbohydrates dominated the story. Eating more tracked with higher variability, more time above range, higher average glucose, and less time in range. Longer gaps between lunch and dinner, and between breakfast and dinner, linked to more time in range in simple looks. Those timing links faded once total intake and body weight entered the models. The authors advise cutting carbohydrate share first, and call for trials to test meal timing.
pmc-13563905:
Yinchun Huang and seven colleagues ask whether the chromosome pattern in Turner syndrome predicts heart and metabolic trouble in girls and young women. Turner syndrome follows the loss of one sex chromosome, fully in some patients and in mosaic or structural patterns in others. Their 2026 review covered 289 patients assessed at one centre between 2016 and 2023, split into 149 with the single-X pattern and 140 with mosaic or structural variants. Ultrasound scans and blood tests supplied the comparison.

Heart disease appeared in 32.9 percent of the single-X group against 18.6 percent of the others, and the gap survived adjustment for age, weight, cholesterol, and insulin resistance, at odds of 1.88. Aortic widening by the size index was equally common in both groups. Cholesterol clustered in the single-X patients, and LDL cholesterol tracked with structural disease. The authors advise karyotype-aware surveillance, while conceding that scan differences were small and need multicentre confirmation.
pmc-13564005:
Taşkın Mumcu and co-authors build a green, low-cost method for measuring lead and cadmium in rice and paddy soil. The pair of toxic metals can pass from soil into the food chain, so both must be watched. The method concentrates the metals on a new sorbent before reading them with flame atomic absorption. The sorbent carries a molecule chosen with quantum chemistry calculations.

Three new anthraquinone-based ligands were synthesized, and computer analysis picked the one with the best binding profile. Loaded onto silica, it became the working sorbent. A six-factor statistical design tuned the extraction. The method detects lead and cadmium at fractions of a microgram per liter, with tight precision and tolerance for other ions. Green chemistry scores were high thanks to low reagent use and no solvent. The authors offer the platform for checks of soil-to-rice metal transfer.
pmc-13568005:
Zan Liu and co-authors build a bendable fiber sensor array that reads heat up to one thousand degrees in tight curved spaces, in a study from two thousand twenty-six. Flight and power gear need exact heat reads where stiff probes cannot fit. Quartz wool inside and a nickel alloy tube outside form the dual wrap.

Against a standard reference probe the top error was about two degrees and the mean error near one degree. A heat-set step steadied the sensors before the checks. The array bent to a small radius without loss, suiting curved paths. Readers in harsh-setting sensing get a flexible heat tool with probe-grade accuracy.
pmc-13568205:
Jinsha Tian, Junyu Guo, Bingbin Feng, Hongjin Zhu, and Yang Luo design a lean network that upscales single images. Their paper, from twenty twenty-six, revisits plain convolutional design. Transformer models lead on quality but cost too much for many devices. The team finds a subtle flaw in classic residual learning for this task.

Residual signals carry a bias from mapping errors, and that bias stacks up layer by layer. Their network corrects the residual on the fly, tuned per input. A weighted join replaces the plain shortcut for fusing features. The whole model stays a simple convolutional stack, fast to run in parallel. Tests confirm gains from both fixes.
pmc-13569505:
Lauren Fernandes and co-authors map, in a 2026 scoping review, interventions that fix inappropriate prescribing for older adults in emergency departments and acute geriatric units, where many medicines and frailty raise risk. Searches across major databases and grey sources from 1991 to 2025 found twenty-one studies, only four of them randomized trials.

Eighteen interventions fell into pharmacist-led medication reviews, computer decision support, staff education, or combinations of those. Inappropriate prescribing was often the main measure, yet few studies reported whether patients actually fared better. The map exposes a field rich in process checks and poor in outcome proof, guiding where future trials should aim.
pmc-13569605:
Lin and a large team of colleagues test if urine traits can sharpen life-span forecasts in bowel cancer in this twenty twenty-six study. Stage of spread is the main guide now, yet tumors of like stage can act in unlike ways. Urine holds small traits that may catch body-wide signs stage alone misses.

Inside, the team used urine data from seventy-six patients in a German study, all checked before surgery. Four math routes that add urine traits beat a plain route based on stage and age. The best route picked out three urine traits that showed up in all four routes. The authors call for checks in fresh groups before the tool is used in care.
pmc-13572405:
Abhijit Bhowmik, with eight colleagues, reports a 2026 study of fly ash mixed into an aluminium alloy to cut wear. Fly ash is a fine waste from coal plants. The alloy, AA8011, gains a harder filler when ash is stirred into the melt, which may save energy and raw stock in parts that rub.

The team cast mixes with 0, 4, 8, and 12 percent ash by weight and rubbed pins against a disc under dry conditions. A Taguchi test plan and a grey relation method weighed wear rate, friction force, and friction level together. The best run used 8 percent ash, a 30 newton load, a slide speed of 3 metres per second, and a 3,200 metre slide path. Load shaped the outcome most, at near 49 percent of the effect in the variance checks.
pmc-13572505:
Udomporn Manupibul, with four colleagues, reports a 2026 pilot test of a wearable system that reads how people walk. Lab gait rigs are costly and fixed in place, so the team built SMART F-IMU, which joins motion sensors with flexible foot force pads. The test asked whether it can spot gait shifts tied to body weight outside a lab.

The system estimates ground force, joint angles, and step timing as a person walks. The overweight and obese group took longer strides and spent more time in stance, swing, and double support than the normal-weight group. Their step rate fell, and many joint angles at key gait moments differed with large effect sizes. The authors say the kit can track joint motion in daily life over time. That opens a path to low-cost checks in real settings.
pmc-13572905:
Dorothea Mhina and colleagues survey tetanus vaccine knowledge and uptake among women in Ifakara Town, Tanzania. Their community study from twenty twenty-six covers women of reproductive age. Tetanus shots protect both mothers and newborn babies. Uptake can fade as the required number of doses rises.

Nearly four hundred women answered an interviewer-led questionnaire. Almost all had heard of tetanus vaccination. Almost all also reported receiving it at least once. Reported uptake fell steadily at higher dose counts. Two thirds reported at least three doses, the main outcome studied. Statistical models explored which factors tracked with reaching that level. Local planners gain a clear picture of the drop-off.
pmc-13573105:
Trofimova and colleagues investigate in 2026 why certain boron bonds survive in molecules where they should quickly fall apart in water. They work with MIDA boronates, compounds in which a protective ligand grips the boron atom loosely enough to let go when needed.

That loose grip, called hemilability, has already let chemists isolate boron species once thought too fragile to exist. The study shows that under acid, the group attached to boron can migrate, leaving boron bound to nitrogen across different oxidation states. Most strikingly, a boron-nitrogen compound with an azide group formed in preference to the aminoboronate that energy arguments favored. That defied the expected easy escape route of releasing nitrogen gas. The authors present these stabilized boron bonds as versatile building blocks for wider use in chemistry.
pmc-13574505:
Seo writes in this 2026 editorial about two menopausal burdens that hormone therapy handles poorly: broken sleep and urinary incontinence. He comments on a systematic review and meta-analysis by Martins and colleagues, published in the same issue, on exercise as treatment for both.

Seo summarizes the review's findings: for sleep, exercise outperformed the comparison interventions. Mind-body practices like yoga and Pilates matched conventional aerobic and strength training, with the largest effects in programs running at least three times weekly. For incontinence, the pooled estimate missed statistical significance, yet pelvic floor strengthening showed a distinct effect. Seo reads this as proof that matching the exercise to the symptom matters more than simply exercising more. He also praises the review for treating the two symptoms as an interacting pair, since night-time urination fragments sleep and embarrassment deepens isolation.
pmc-13575005:
Rajiv Yeravdekar and Alaka Chandak report screening results for Indian university students in a 2026 study. Young adults are often seen as low risk, yet these years are when food and health habits set in. The pair reviewed records from a campus health screening programme.

The records covered 13,628 students aged 18 to 30 screened between June 2023 and May 2024. Close to half were overweight or had obesity, and 53 percent met World Health Organization cut-offs for anaemia. High blood pressure readings were common too, more so in men than women. Being male linked with both anaemia and high readings in adjusted models. The authors urge universities to run routine screening with follow-up care.
pmc-13576305:
Takashi Watanabe leads a 2026 study of immune side effects from checkpoint inhibitor therapy in lung cancer. These drugs free the immune system to attack non-small cell lung cancer, yet they can also trigger inflammation in healthy organs. The team reviewed five years of cases at a Japanese university hospital to find what shapes that risk.

Among 203 patients, 92 had at least one immune side effect, with lung inflammation the most common, followed by thyroid problems. One factor stood out in reverse: patients with heart failure developed side effects far less often, with a risk near one third of others. The link held under a second method that accounts for competing risks. A related model swapping in use of certain heart drugs also showed a link. The authors suggest heart history belongs in monitoring plans.
pmc-13576805:
Luxi Yu, Antonio del Rio Chanona, and Cleo Kontoravdi present a method for carrying a cell culture model from one setup to another without rebuilding it, in a 2026 bioprocess paper. Mechanistic models of CHO cell culture are usually tuned to one cell line, scale, or set of conditions, which limits their reach. Their tool is the ensemble Kalman filter, borrowed from weather forecasting.

The filter folds live process measurements into the model step by step, updating uncertain rate constants and predicting the culture state together. A model tuned on one system could then adapt to a new one from a single experiment. The shifting parameter sets double as a sensitivity map, showing which rates matter under new conditions and when. Tests on six datasets across scales, cell lines, temperatures, and feeding plans reconstructed behaviour well, with forecasts improving as data grew.
pmc-13577805:
Upendra Bhattarai and co-authors published this study in 2026. It digs into a famous case of parasite control: worms that drive their insect hosts to seek water. The team used European earwigs infected with a nematode worm. They read gene activity in both animals across stages of infection and manipulation. Over twelve thousand earwig genes and nearly ten thousand worm genes were active.

Hundreds of host genes shifted up or down, and thousands shifted in the worm. In the host, signaling and sensing pathways rose. In the worm, transport and secretion genes rose during the manipulation stage. One shared gene-switch motif turned up enriched in both animals at that stage. The authors say host and parasite change in concert. Their candidate genes give the next studies a concrete place to start.
pmc-13577905:
Zhong Cao leads a 2026 study pricing the global economic cost of depression from 2025 to 2050 across 154 countries. Depression already ranks among the largest causes of disability worldwide. The team built a macroeconomic model from World Bank and Global Burden of Disease 2021 data, tracking how the illness cuts labour force participation, schooling, and work experience by age and sex.

The projected bill comes to 12 trillion US dollars over the period, equal to 0.460 percent of world output each year. Counting deaths by suicide attributed to depression at an assumed upper rate lifts the total to 14 trillion dollars in the same accounting. The United States and China carry the largest absolute burdens, while North America loses the most relative to its economy. Lost work and productivity drive most of the cost. The authors argue treatment pays for itself in output.
pmc-13578005:
Tsz-Lung Choi and co-authors compare three ways of performing knee replacement: the classic manual technique, a robotic arm's guidance, and pressure sensors that report joint loads live. Their study appeared in 2026. The cohort covered 173 knees in 139 patients at one center, split unevenly among the three methods. Pain, motion range, and function scores were compared after adjusting for starting state, age, sex, and body size.

After strict correction for multiple testing, no outcome separated the three groups convincingly. The authors also probed whether starting severity changed the ranking, and found no firm pattern. They counsel that, on patient-felt outcomes at least, the expensive guidance tools have yet to prove they beat a good surgeon's hands.
pmc-13578305:
Bo Zhang and a large team uncover how liver cancer resists a key drug in this two thousand twenty-six paper. The drug, sorafenib, is a mainstay for advanced liver cancer. Tumors survive it in part by fending off reactive oxygen, a toxic byproduct of stress. The usual defense pathway was thought to do most of that work. This team found a second route: the cancer switches on hemoglobin, the blood's oxygen carrier, inside its own cells.

A low-oxygen sensor and a partner factor drive that switch. The hemoglobin then mops up reactive oxygen and keeps the cells alive. Tumors with more hemoglobin also fare worse in patients. Blocking this odd defense could restore the drug's power. The finding opens a fresh target in liver cancer.
pmc-13579905:
Chasapis and Touloupis study non-consensual sexting among minority teens in Greece. The sample held 293 students with a mean age of 14.9. Most came from Albanian or Bulgarian backgrounds. Roles covered sending, receiving, and forwarding sexual content. Peer pressure, self-control, and sexual preoccupation were tested as drivers.

Teens were mostly senders and receivers in the data. Forwarding without consent ran far lower than the other roles. Albanian and Bulgarian teens showed the highest direct involvement. Native peer pressure meant pressure from Greek majority peers. The authors call this digital aggression under-studied worldwide.
pmc-13581005:
Carleigh Cowling and colleagues return to Naoero a year after mass antibiotics to see how far the blinding eye disease trachoma has retreated, in this study from twenty twenty-six. The island nation gave azithromycin to its whole population twice, reaching an estimated eighty-seven and then ninety-three percent coverage. Trachoma is driven by repeated infection with an eye strain of chlamydia.

Surveyors examined over two thousand residents. Among children aged one to nine, active inflammatory trachoma sat at six percent, still above the World Health Organization's elimination line. Actual infection had collapsed, from nearly forty percent before treatment to under three percent. The late blinding stage was rare enough to pass its threshold, and nearly all households had improved water and latrines. The verdict: the drugs worked powerfully, but one more push is likely needed.
pmc-13581605:
Morawetz and co-authors light the thorium-229 core with a smooth-wave laser for a clock. That core shift sits at low force, a rare trait for cores. Past work lit it in doped gems with pulse lasers. Pulse tools waste most shots, since few match the thin shift. Their tool is a smooth, thin-band, solid laser at low force. It works at sub-nanowatt force in the core tests.

The core signal is read in soak, not in glow, in the work. That swap drops the slow glow wait from the read path. Fast reads thus suit clock work with the core in gems. Two thorium hubs in a lime gem got read in the work. The shift gap twixt those hubs was gauged in the runs. One hub shows a near-nil still field slope in the gem.
pmc-13582305:
Kartik Akkihal and eight co-authors published a surgical cohort study in twenty twenty-six comparing meshes for ventral hernia repair. Poly-4-hydroxybutyrate mesh slowly dissolves in the body, unlike permanent synthetic mesh. Surgeons tend to choose it for the hardest, contaminated cases, which skews simple comparisons.

The single-center study covered four hundred three repairs from twenty fourteen to twenty twenty-five. Patients with the absorbable mesh had bigger defects, worse hernia grades, and dirtier wounds at the outset. To compare fairly, the team matched those patients one-to-one with synthetic mesh patients on age, weight, diabetes, wound class, and hernia size. Recurrence and infection outcomes in the matched groups are the study's core result.
pmc-13582405:
Hesham Salah El-Din Taha and colleagues report a high-stakes rescue of a man whose lung arteries were chronically blocked. A 55-year-old West African man first showed up with a large saddle embolus. It fully blocked the left lung artery and nearly blocked the right. He later came back in shock, with oxygen at 81 percent. Surgery to strip the clots was judged unsuitable at that stage. This 2026 case report describes the catheter-based alternative.

With veno-arterial ECMO, a heart-lung support circuit, backing two sessions, operators reopened both arteries with aspiration, wires, balloons, and a stent. Mean pulmonary artery pressure fell from 89 to 59 millimetres of mercury by the second session. The authors present ECMO-supported intervention as a viable path when chronic central blockage and shock rule out surgery.
pmc-13582505:
Fangyuan Wang and co-authors compare two large language models on Chinese-language questions about a childhood hip condition, developmental dysplasia of the hip. Caregivers increasingly turn to such models for health advice, but reliability in pediatric orthopedics is unproven. The team poses 53 questions: 31 common caregiver questions and 22 drawn from guidelines. Each model answers once, in five sentences, under a standard prompt.

Six blinded pediatric orthopedic surgeons rate the answers for accuracy and agreement with Chinese guidance. DeepSeek-R1 scores clearly higher than ChatGPT-4o on both counts. Rater agreement is good for accuracy and moderate for guideline agreement. Readability measures give mixed results, with some favoring ChatGPT before adjustment. The authors caution that findings on surgery questions are exploratory. They frame the study as a check on how safe these tools are for caregiver education.
pmc-13582705:
Regina Molnár and colleagues studied how foreign med students in Hungary settle into local life. They used Berry's model of four paths: blending with both cultures, keeping one's own culture apart, dropping one's own culture, or drifting from both. Of 326 students, near half took the blend path and just over half kept apart, while the other two paths were rare. The work thus sets the two big groups side by side.

Men, early-year students, non-drinkers, and students with less stress blended in more. Non-smokers and students who shunned shrink visits, oddly, blended in less. Schools can use these trends to shape help that lets foreign students fit in well and stay well in mind and body.
pmc-13582805:
Shamaila Zafar and Jay S. Schneider propose that Parkinson's disease is, at root, a failure of the brain's sleep-driven clearance system. Parkinson's involves alpha-synuclein build-up and steady nerve loss, and sleep and body-clock disruption are common long before motor symptoms dominate. This 2026 review unites two clearance routes: autophagy, the cell's internal recycling, and glymphatic transport, the brain's external wash, across neurons, glia, and the blood-brain barrier.

When sleep architecture and circadian timing fall out of sync, both routes falter, proteins pile up, and pathology spreads. The authors frame sleep-circadian trouble as an upstream driver rather than a side effect, and suggest that restoring healthy sleep rhythms could improve clearance and support disease-modifying strategies.
pmc-13583105:
Shuhao Wang and co-authors offer a 2026 review of flat metamaterials for steering electromagnetic waves. Stealth and signal tools now demand thin, broadband, and flexible surfaces. Older materials respond in fixed ways and hit hard limits.

Flat patterned surfaces can shape waves through resonance and spatial effects. The review spans stealth uses across wave, heat, light, and sound domains. Active tuning by electric, light, heat, magnetic, or motion triggers is a major theme. Programmable and data-designed surfaces point toward smart control. Engineers get a cross-scale tour from materials to structures.
pmc-13583205:
Ahmed Abdelmaksoud and colleagues ask in a 2026 study whether people with trisomy 21, the condition also known as Down syndrome, face a higher risk of gout. Gout is a painful joint illness caused by uric acid buildup, and high uric acid had already been noted in this group. Proof of a gout link, though, rested on a handful of case reports.

Using health records from a large United States network, the team compared more than 30,000 people with trisomy 21 against matched people without it. Gout showed up in close to three in a hundred patients with the condition, about triple the rate in the comparison group. The higher risk held across age, sex, and racial groups, and the authors urge more work on why it happens and how to screen for it.
pmc-13583305:
Yuki Inoue Nakata and co-authors (2026) tested whether people can see motion and stillness in the same display at once. Philosophers had suggested that motion illusions might carry both contents together. The claim had never been tested in the lab. The authors showed participants displays with illusory motion or real physical motion. For each display, people rated how much motion they saw and how much stillness they saw.

For real motion, the two ratings moved in opposite directions, as expected. More motion meant less stillness. For illusory motion the link was much weaker. A single display could score high on both at once. The authors read this as the first direct evidence that one visual experience can hold two contents that seem to contradict each other. The result speaks to both vision science and philosophy of mind.
pmc-13583705:
Xin Ou and her six co-authors, publishing in 2026, grade the efficiency of China's public infectious disease hospitals across all 31 provinces. These hospitals anchor the national public health system. The team surveyed 133 of them and ran a three-stage efficiency analysis that first scores raw performance, then strips out regional conditions beyond a hospital's control, then scores again fairly.

After adjustment, the average score sat at 0.61, dragged down by management and technology rather than scale. Hospitals in Beijing, Hainan, Tianjin, Sichuan, and Tibet ran at full marks. Scores ran highest in the east and lowest in the northeast, while scale scores showed the reverse pattern. Richer provinces scored better; higher urbanization scored worse. The authors advise sizing hospitals to local need and investing in management quality and medical technology.
pmc-13583805:
Wang and eight co-authors lay out the Alzheimer's disease burden in China study protocol, in a protocol paper from twenty twenty-six. Alzheimer's costs fall mainly on long-term informal care by families. China's rapid aging sharply raises the burden nationally. Prior Chinese evidence lacks full cost frameworks and caregiver costs.

The nationwide study measures patient and caregiver economic burden and quality of life. It is the first to include mild cognitive impairment nationally. Costs are estimated per person and weighted to national totals. Future burden is projected from statistical yearbooks and UN data. Results will support early-intervention health technology assessment.
pmc-13584505:
Jamaal Ibrahim, Sahardiid Abdilahi, and Mohamed Osman measure anemia among people with HIV in Jigjiga, Ethiopia, in this 2026 paper. Anemia, a lack of healthy red blood cells, drains energy and shortens life for people on HIV treatment. Their clinic-based study covered 392 patients on antiretroviral therapy at public facilities, surveyed over one month in 2023 with blood tests and a set questionnaire.

Close to four in ten patients had anemia, and nearly all of those cases sat in the moderate band. Being female, carrying another infection on top of HIV, and eating a narrow range of foods each raised the odds clearly. The authors call anemia a moderate public health problem at these sites and urge targeted help for women, faster treatment of extra infections, and food advice for patients with poor diets.
pmc-13585305:
Silin Kuang and co-authors interview primary care doctors about an AI tool that triages chest X-rays in a 2026 study. The program was piloted in a public clinic in Singapore, where it sorted scans to speed reporting. Whether doctors trust and keep using such tools depends on more than accuracy, yet real-world views from front-line doctors were scarce.

Twenty doctors took part in interviews and group talks. Use varied and hinged on three themes: whether the tool seemed valid and fit the workflow, whether doctors felt confident, and whether the clinic backed it. Endorsement by the institution, a phased rollout, and the safety net of radiologist reports built trust. Worries about overcalling findings, missing clinical context, and legal duty held some back. The authors urge rollout plans shaped by user experience.
pmc-13585505:
Anna Pokrzywa and four co-authors examine a special MRI method after brain tumor surgery, in a paper dated 2026. The surgery removes cancer that has spread to the brain from elsewhere. Later scans must tell leftover tumor from normal healing tissue, which can look alike. The method studied builds maps from how fast dye clears from the tissue.

The team reviewed four patients whose post-surgery scans showed the varied patterns known from earlier work on a focused radiation treatment. All had proven spread of cancer and regular follow-up scans. The paper pairs the case images with a review of past studies. It discusses how these maps might guide choices about further treatment. The work is early and descriptive, meant to build careful use of the tool.
pmc-13586505: Mark Mewissen and Safoora Choudry report a salvage operation in a 2026 paper. A sixty-nine-year-old man had a branched graft placed for a chest-and-abdomen aneurysm. Ten days later, scans showed a leak because the bridging stent to his left kidney had slipped fully out of place. Working through an arm artery, the team inflated a balloon inside the stray stent to shorten it, restoring alignment with the kidney artery. Scans six months later showed the rebuilt stent open with no leak.
pmc-13586705:
Meunier and a large team set out a feasibility study for a decision support tool that guides screening in French primary care, in a protocol from twenty twenty-six. French adults face forty-two screening recommendations with complex eligibility rules. Short visits and rival priorities block systematic delivery. Their tool, Lianeli, builds a personal screening plan from a patient questionnaire.

The study will recruit two hundred ten patients across seventeen sites. Patients answer digitally, then discuss benefits and harms with their doctor within sixty days. The team measures completion, usability, and workflow changes. Interviews with patients and clinicians add depth on acceptability. Links to health literacy and deprivation are also explored.
pmc-13587305:
Haimanot Andualem Ayalsew and colleagues compare balance in schoolchildren with and without hearing loss in Addis Ababa. The inner ear houses both hearing and the balance organs, so children who cannot hear well may also wobble more, yet balance is rarely checked in this group. Their study tested 148 children aged 7 to 18, half with hearing impairment and half matched peers with normal hearing, on standing, reaching, and a child balance scale.

Children with hearing loss scored lower on every test, in still standing with eyes open or shut, in reaching, and on the full scale. The gap held for boys and girls alike. The authors argue that balance checks belong in the routine care of children with hearing impairment, so that training and support can start before falls and missed play shape their school years.
pmc-13587705:
Sima Namin and five co-authors mapped access to colonoscopy across the United States. Their study, from twenty twenty-six, starts from a gap: colon cancer rates and deaths run high in rural and Appalachian areas. Long trips and few specialists may block screening there. The team ran a geospatial read of all census tracts in the mainland states. They found providers through national ID records and procedure marks.

A four band catchment method scored how easy each tract is to reach care. Small area estimates gave screening rates for each tract. The team set access scores side by side for rural, town, and Appalachian tracts. Readers who plan cancer screening learn where distance most cuts people off from a key test.
pmc-13588105:
Liguang Wang and co-authors identify a driver of drug resistance in breast cancer in this 2026 paper. Everolimus is approved for hormone receptor positive, HER2 negative breast cancer. Many tumors stop responding to it, for reasons that were unclear. The team grew patient derived organoids, small tumor models, in sensitive and resistant forms.

Gene reading showed the gene LRRC32 was turned up sharply in resistant organoids. Forcing the gene on in sensitive cells cut cell death and raised survival. Turning it down in resistant cells did the opposite. It also stalled the cell cycle at the first growth phase. The findings mark LRRC32 as both a resistance driver and a possible drug target.
pmc-13591305:
Prabhu Manickam Natarajan and colleagues published a 2026 review of new ways to attack the slimy bacterial communities, called biofilms, behind stubborn mouth infections. Biofilms shield bacteria from antibiotics and cleaning, which is why gum and tooth infections return so often. The review covers five non-antibiotic strategies that each strike a different weakness in the biofilm's defenses.

The strategies include enzymes that digest the slime, chemicals that break it apart, viruses and gene tools that kill bacteria, light-activated treatment, and cold plasma. The team graded study quality across laboratory, animal, and clinical work, mapping which approaches are ready for patients and which remain experimental.
pmc-13592305:
Florian Maurer leads a 2026 team watching single platinum particles dissolve into lone atoms on ceria supports, then tying that decay to catalyst performance. Platinum on ceria anchors many clean air and chemical catalysts, yet under oxygen the particles can scatter into single atoms and lose punch. Using an electron microscope that works inside gas, the team timed the shrinking of individual particles on shaped ceria cubes.

Neighboring particles and flaws in the support slowed the scatter, while each particle lost volume at a steady rate regardless of starting size. Those atomic scale rates matched the fall in whole catalyst activity closely enough to forecast it. Maurer and the team call this a first step toward predicting catalyst life from particle kinetics.
pmc-13592605:
Chung-Fen Tsai leads a team comparing brain bleeds in 202 Taiwanese patients by where the bleed sits and what caused it. East Asians face higher rates of this stroke type, yet most past data come from Western patients. The group recruited acute cases at two large hospitals, recording risk factors, gene variants, scans, and early thinking tests. They then contrasted bleeds near the brain's surface with deeper ones, and amyloid linked bleeds with others.

Surface bleeds came with older age, larger volume, worse awareness, higher one month death rates, and weaker early cognition. Deep bleeds tracked far more often with high blood pressure. Early thinking scores tied to age, schooling, awareness, stroke severity, bleed size, and small bleed burden near the surface. Tsai and the team urge location aware care and study.
pmc-13592705:
Denise Fuchten and four colleagues check how much tinnitus distress questionnaires overlap in content with depression questionnaires. The two states correlate strongly, and shared items can blur what a score really measures. Six tinnitus scales and seven depression scales were taken apart item by item. Each item's concepts were linked to categories in a global functioning classification, and overlaps were counted at the shared category level.

Depression scales covered fourteen categories, tinnitus scales twenty three. Seven categories appeared in both families, spanning energy, sleep, attention, emotion, thought, social life, and leisure. Overlap ran from about a tenth between the least similar pair to near total for one depression subscale. Fuchten and the team advise picking scales with the study question, not habit, in mind.
pmc-13593705:
D. Pamei and co-authors measured how broken teeth from accidents affect daily life for young patients at a large hospital. Their 2026 study enrolled 266 children and teenagers aged eight to sixteen. All had injured their teeth within the previous year. The team scored the impact with a standard questionnaire on oral effects on daily performance.

Front upper teeth took the most damage, usually as uncomplicated crown fractures, and about a third of injuries were severe. Hardly anyone arrived quickly: only a small minority got emergency care within a day. Nearly all the children were aware of the broken teeth, most reported sensitivity, and two thirds disliked how their teeth looked. Eating, cleaning the mouth, smiling freely, and mixing with friends all suffered. Severe overall impairment, seen in about a quarter, tracked with worse injuries, repeated trauma, soft tissue wounds, and appearance concerns.
pmc-13594405:
Ida Steiro leads a ten-author team asking whether bispecific antibody therapy for multiple myeloma weakens the T cells' memory of past infections, helping explain why treated patients suffer more infections. The therapy joins T cells to a target called BCMA on myeloma cells. The team tested T cells from healthy donors. The cells were grown with the engager drug pavurutamab and with myeloma cells.

Those T cells still killed myeloma cells well, yet their responses to common pathogen fragments dropped compared with untreated cells. A small exploratory check of blood from four patients responding to the same class of therapy pointed the same way, with reduced pathogen-specific memory responses. The authors are careful to call the observation preliminary, urging a larger study to confirm whether this immune dulling truly drives the infection burden.
pmc-13597505:
Ahren Hart and co-authors publish an open dataset of real-world 5G performance across Glasgow, gathering 720 outdoor measurements in fifteen neighborhoods over three days in April 2025. All four major British operators and two flagship phones were used, giving the 2026 release a neighborhood-level view that operator maps rarely supply.

Citywide averages came to roughly six hundred seventy megabits per second down and one hundred sixty-five up, with a ping near twenty-two milliseconds. Individual readings swung from under fifty to over twelve hundred megabits, a variability the authors stress is the honest face of shared urban spectrum. One operator posted the highest median download, suburbs beat the city core, and signal strength barely predicted speed at all. The openly licensed dataset is offered for coverage modeling, smart city planning, and as a 2025 baseline against which future 6G claims can be judged.
pmc-13597705:
Lorea Jordana-Urriza and co-authors build, in a 2026 lab study, a three-dimensional bone marrow niche to test engineered T-cell therapy against a blood cancer of plasma cells. The therapy wins early but relapse is common, and the marrow shelter is a suspect. Flat dish cultures cannot copy that shelter, so the team grew bone-like scaffolds with marrow support cells in a flow system.

Cancer cells settled and clustered in the niche as hoped. The niche also mimicked the tumor's brake on bone building. Therapy cells wiped out free-floating cancer but faltered inside the niche. The block was not a failure of the cells to arrive, hinting at deeper protection the model can now probe.
pmc-13597905:
Beate Standal and four co-authors study how health staff in Norway see guided online therapy fitting their clinics. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-six. The therapy is cognitive behavioural care over the web, with a therapist's help. It works for common ills and could widen access, yet its place in routine care stays small.

They talk with staff at three specialist clinics and watch the work in place. Views of fit shift by level. The tool's tech feels out of step with current care. Staff norms and values pull in unlike ways. Clinics doubt their readiness, and the complexity of their patients adds doubt. Face-to-face care still holds sway in the wider system.
pmc-13598105:
Alice Vivien Barchet and colleagues recorded brain signals from sixty-three adults aged nineteen to seventy-one as they picked a target voice out of competing talkers, asking why comprehension frays with age. Their study combined fine-grained behavior with models of how the brain tracks each speech stream.

Older listeners' weaker performance came with stronger brain tracking of the distractor voice, hard evidence for a filtering failure: the aging auditory system lets the wrong speaker in. Yet older adults also leaned harder on word-level linguistic knowledge, at both the behavioral and neural levels, and that reliance paid off, offsetting the leakier filter and supporting comprehension. The authors frame successful aging listening as a trade. Degraded bottom-up selection is compensated by richer top-down prediction. Hearing support might aim to restore that balance. Merely amplifying sound is not the goal.
pmc-13600905:
Jocelyn Bélanger and ten co-authors ran a worldwide contest of risk markers for radical intentions, in a study published in 2026. Radical intentions, the will to use force for a creed, are a core worry of the field. Their pool held more than 10,000 people from 40 countries, plus 80 jailed jihadists. Twelve known markers, the best from an earlier pooled review, were set head to head in one mathematical framework.

Three markers kept a firm independent link in each country and creed: moral neutralization of force, rigid creed commitment, and felt group bias. The first two held in the jailed group as well; the third ran weak there. The authors frame the trio as a test-ready base for prevention work. Each maps to a known theory of the path to force.
pmc-13601105:
Anne Kristin Fischer and three colleagues present a 2026 German-language case report on a liver change that mimics a tumor. The condition, massive ductular reaction, is extensive liver remodeling triggered when local blood flow through liver veins and sinusoids is blocked, starving the area. A cancer growing into vessels is often the cause, though cirrhosis or widespread liver cell death can also produce it.

Their patient was a 68-year-old man followed for fatty liver cirrhosis, in whom imaging found a large mass in liver segment VIII. Scans suggested an atypical liver cancer possibly spreading into small vessels, and the tumor board advised surgical removal. The report walks through the imaging in detail, from ultrasound to contrast MRI and CT. Because imaging cannot always separate this reaction from cancer, the authors stress that a biopsy may be needed before treatment decisions.
pmc-13601605:
Virginia Panara and co-authors map how the 3D folding of DNA helps shape lymphatic vessels, in a 2026 study. Genes switch on and off as an embryo builds tissues, and folding controls which control switches can reach which genes. The team compared lymphatic vessel cells with blood vessel cells, pairing maps of DNA contacts with maps of open regions. They worked in a model system where vessels can be watched as they form.

The two cell types showed distinct folding domains, with changed borders near genes tied to lymphatic fate. Enhancers, the switches that boost genes, also sorted differently between the types. Tests in living tissue confirmed that several predicted switches work in lymphatic cells. The team rebuilt control networks for one gene and found a partner gene that limits stray vessel growth when both act together.
pmc-13601905:
Weizhen Yang and colleagues ask whether depression can inflame the pancreas, in this cohort study from twenty twenty-six. Over two hundred seventy-three thousand UK Biobank participants were followed a median of nearly fourteen years. Four hundred eleven developed chronic pancreatitis, a scarring, painful disease of digestion.

Depression came first and carried weight: a diagnosis of major depression raised pancreatitis risk by about half. Blood metabolite profiling suggested part of the pathway is fat chemistry. Triglycerides riding in HDL and LDL particles and the saturation of fatty acids each mediated a few percent of the link, and a fifty-one-metabolite signature mediated about a fifth. The link ran stronger in those sixty and under. The authors frame metabolic dysregulation as a plausible bridge between mind and pancreas, worth mechanistic follow-up.
pmc-13602005:
Donghyeong Koo and co-authors study heart resuscitation in hospital during a mass resignation of junior doctors in South Korea, in work from two thousand twenty-six. Records covered nearly four hundred patients and more events over two years at one large hospital. Care before the crisis was compared with care during it.

Arrest rates and revival rates were much the same in both periods. Long resuscitation attempts past thirty-five minutes grew rarer during the crisis. Stopping efforts without revival became more likely in adjusted checks. Survival and brain outcomes did not clearly differ. The authors call for standard rules on when to stop.
pmc-13602505:
Hbibi and a team including Kadri survey Moroccan dentists on gum checks during orthodontic care in twenty twenty-six. Gum disease can affect how safe and how well tooth straightening works. This risk is higher in adults and in patients with weak gum support. Good care needs a gum diagnosis and stable disease before treatment starts.

The online survey drew three hundred dentists from eleven regions. Few could define the main gum disease correctly on the survey. Most did report some gum screening before orthodontic care. Far fewer did full mouth probing at six sites per tooth. Less than half confirmed that gum disease was stable before they began. Most said they need more training in this area. The authors see clear gaps in routine practice.
pmc-13604205:
Gokhan Ozkocak and Rocco Salvatore Calabrò present a study dated 2026 on robot-assisted walking training in Parkinson's disease. Parkinson's stiffens gait, harms balance, and can freeze steps mid-walk. A treadmill robot called Walkbot guides the legs through stepping while supporting the patient.

The study looked back at sixty patients with moderate disease. Half trained with the robot and half with standard rehabilitation, each for thirty sessions over six weeks. The team compared leg torque in the stance and swing phases for both legs. Balance, freezing questionnaires, and quality of life scores were also tracked. After adjusting for starting values, the robot group showed higher phase-specific torque after treatment.
pmc-13605805:
Zhang and co-authors test how five rootstocks change Cabernet Sauvignon wine made in dry regions. Vines grafted onto their own roots served as the control. All wines were made the same way and checked for basic traits, color, taste, and aroma.

All wines met national dry red wine standards. Grapes on SO4 roots gave the best overall quality score, ranked first at 4.167. That wine held more dry extract, sugar, and resveratrol than the control. Vines on 5BB roots gave the most aroma compounds, with esters at 42.85 percent. Ninety-four aroma compounds were found in total.
pmc-13606005:
Ian Li, Cristina Correia, and Choong-Yong Ung test whether stacked MRI channels plus transfer learning can tell true tumor return from treatment effects that mimic it, in work from twenty twenty-six. After surgery and chemoradiation, glioblastoma scans often look alike in both cases. Wrong calls steer care badly.

Seven image types from one hundred twenty-four patients fed a three dimensional network first trained on a larger glioma set. Careful cross validation kept each patient's scans in one fold. The recurrence call scored strongly, with high marks across accuracy measures. Three other targets, a gene marker, survival, and radiation choice, landed near chance. The authors frame the work as proof of concept at one center.
pmc-13607205:
Robert Mîndreanu leads an eight-author systematic review asking whether the epilepsy drug levetiracetam changes oxidative stress markers in people. Oxidative stress is tied to epilepsy, but seizures, diet, illness, and treatment all move the same markers, making drug effects hard to isolate. The team searched four databases and sorted human studies three ways: change within a person, patients versus healthy controls, and levetiracetam versus other seizure medicines.

Eleven non-randomized studies contributed 297 participants with usable data. Where effect sizes could be calculated, they came out wide, pointed in inconsistent directions, or rested on designs unable to credit the drug. Definitions, matrices, assays, and reporting varied so much that pooling was ruled out. Certainty rated very low throughout. Dropping one study that failed a source check changed nothing. The message is negative: current literature can neither support nor refute a redox effect for this widely used medicine.
pmc-13608105:
Jianxin Cao, Xin Song, Ning Han, and Huiping Qi present a two thousand twenty-six simulation study of damage during thread rolling of a titanium alloy. Rolling threads into TC16 alloy parts can crack the metal. Predicting where damage starts helps set safer processes.

A combined material and damage model was tuned with tension tests at varied speeds and temperatures. A full rolling simulation was then built in engineering software. Predicted fracture points matched experiments closely. Damage concentrated at the thread root and its flank transition. High strain and stress concentration together explained the pattern.
pmc-13608405:
Anna Paspala and a large team review rare growths of the liver made of a mixed cell kind, from first find to care. Their review, from two thousand twenty-six, pulls the proof into one place.

The growths carry marks of both dark-skin cells and smooth muscle. They are a hard test for scan readers, tissue readers, and surgeons alike. Most grow at a slow pace, but a small set turns fierce. The team joins fresh work on finds: scans, tissue reads, the small-scale build, chance sorts, surgery, drug care, and long watch. The aim is a clear, clinic-ready map of a rare ill.
pmc-13608605:
Fajrianti and co-authors compare two ways to build maps for indoor AR guides. Hand-built 3D models take long and can drift from real halls. The rival method scans space to the cloud with the Immersal SDK. Forty-eight people did build tasks with both methods in one campus hall. Task order was balanced across the group.

The scan method cut total build time by about 38 percent. The biggest cuts came in capture and model build stages. Workload scores fell by about 31 percent overall. Mental demand and effort dropped, though physical demand rose a bit. A spot check also found the scan map matched real space more closely.
pmc-13609905:
Peng Shi and co-authors test a cheaper feed protein for farmed catfish in a 2026 study. Fish meal is the classic protein in fish feed, but it is costly and strains wild fish stocks. Poultry by-product meal, made from processing leftovers, could take its place. The fish here is a hybrid yellow catfish bred from two species.

The team made six diets that swapped fish meal for the poultry meal at rising shares, up to three fifths. Young fish ate the diets for eight weeks. Growth peaked and feed use was most efficient at a mid-level swap, and a fitted curve put the best replacement near one quarter of the fish meal. The team also tracked body status, disease resistance, and gene activity in the liver. The results mark how far the swap can go before it costs the fish.
pmc-13610105:
Sandoval-Caballero and coauthors review human trials of a plant compound for aging illness. The compound, called fisetin, calms swelling and clears worn cells in lab work. Most proof so far comes from animal and cell studies. Human proof has lagged well behind that base.

The team searched two trial lists for all fisetin trials. They found 34 trials across a wide span of illness. Frailty, sugar illness, cancer, and heart illness all appear. Brain and immune illness trials also made the list. The review logs each trial phase and main goal. It maps where human proof stands and where gaps stay.
pmc-13610305:
Pu and coauthors seek crop plans that save water in a dry river basin. The Shiyang River basin in China faces tight water supply. River flow swings change how much water farms can use. Crop choice must fit wet years and dry years alike.

The team studied five counties in the mid and low basin. Flow records from 1995 to 2024 set four flow cases. Those cases ran from wet to very dry years. Crop yields fed into water use counts for each plan. A search method weighed yield, water, and soil goals at once. Top plans were ranked for use in each flow case.
pmc-13611105:
Fernando Valero and co-authors test whether merely expecting caffeine lifts cycling endurance, in a study from two thousand twenty-six. Nineteen trained male cyclists rode to exhaustion at a hard set power twice. In one trial they swallowed a dummy capsule they believed held caffeine; in the other they took nothing.

Total work, heart rate, and effort ratings matched closely between the trials. Some riders reported mild effects like extra activeness after the dummy capsule. The authors caution that such feelings cannot be firmly tied to expectation alone. Belief in caffeine, at least here, bought no extra endurance.
pmc-13611405:
Hatice Aylin Karahan Toprakci and colleagues develop flexible textile sensors that monitor human movement through pressure-related resistance changes. Their 2026 study combines two carbon fillers with different shapes inside a stretchy polymer layer on knitted fabric.

Three coatings were blade-coated onto elastic textile: carbon black alone, carbon nanofibers alone, and a hybrid of both. All coatings were uniform and adhered well through mechanical cycling checks. Every sensor tracked strain, but the hybrid formulation showed the highest sensitivity among those tested. Responses depended on both strain size and speed. The hybrid sensor successfully monitored knee, wrist, and elbow movements during exercise, showing clothing-integrated sensing potential.
pmc-13611505:

Their interface, PIR-SBFR, routes each scale's features by two separate judgments. One asks how much detail the scene demands, which a visual branch estimates. The other asks how reliable the observation is, which a fixed analytic rule derives from sampling, sharpness, and noise, with no sensor-specific calibration.

Average precision rose from 62.98 to 65.52 percent on the DIOR benchmark and from 29.58 to 32.10 percent on an AI-TOD-v2 split. Three rival tiny-object detectors landed between those endpoints. The interface also lifted three host detectors by about two points, won under all 27 controlled quality conditions, and ran at a median 19.55 milliseconds on a Jetson board. The authors claim acquisition-aware routing as a practical upgrade.
pmc-13612305:
Sujogya Kumar Panda leads an eight-author team prospecting the leaves of Limonia acidissima, the wood apple tree of South Asian folk medicine. With drug resistance rising, the team extracted leaf compounds in acetone, ethanol, and water, screened them against microbes, and followed the strongest extract. Four compounds emerged, including kaempferol, luteolin, and a biphenanthrene reported from this plant for the first time.

All four isolates killed Gram-positive bacteria, with weaker action against Gram-negative bacteria and yeast. The four also showed moderate worm-killing activity and selective toxicity toward some cells. Computer docking ranked the kaempferol derivative afzelin as the strongest, most consistent binder across microbial targets, with luteolin close behind. The authors present the leaves as a source worth developing, and the two lead compounds as candidates for deeper testing. The study supports the plant's traditional uses, now tied to named molecules.
pmc-13614805:
Nitin Peters and eight co-authors assess keyhole surgery for Wilms tumor, the most common childhood kidney cancer. Their report was published in twenty twenty-six. Surgery anchors treatment, and doing it through small incisions is demanding when cancer rules apply.

Seventeen children had the laparoscopic kidney removal after chemotherapy. Just under half finished fully by keyhole; the rest converted to open surgery, mainly over bleeding or rupture risk. Completed keyhole cases lost less blood, left hospital sooner, and hurt less afterward. Lymph node counts and rupture rates matched the open group. The authors conclude the approach is safe in chosen cases, in expert hands.
pmc-13616005:
André O. Fatty liver tied to metabolism is now called metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease, replacing the older non-alcoholic label. From 2,099 papers found across four databases, twenty long-term studies in adults free of kidney disease at the start qualified.

The pooled work asks how often new kidney disease appeared in people with fatty liver against those without, under each naming scheme. Incidence studies through June 2025 fed the analysis. A firm link would mean liver clinics should watch kidney numbers as a matter of routine, and kidney clinics should ask about the liver. The naming comparison guards the answer against a change in labels rather than biology.
pmc-13616605:
Ami Aoyama leads a team studying in 2026 two sugar-processing proteins as possible forecast markers in lung adenocarcinoma of dogs, a rare and aggressive cancer with no settled molecular predictors. The proteins, MCT4 and GLUT1, help tumours feed on sugar under low oxygen and spell poor outlook in the human form of the disease. The team stained tumour samples from 61 affected dogs and compared them with normal lung tissue.

Both proteins ran higher in the tumours, and high levels of either tracked with spread to lymph nodes. Surprisingly, dogs with high MCT4 lived longer overall, the reverse of the human pattern, while GLUT1 carried no survival signal. On fuller modelling MCT4 dropped out as an independent factor. Dog lung cancer, the results warn, does not simply mirror the human disease, so markers must be proven in dogs themselves.
pmc-13617105:
Andreas Hinz and co-authors test, in twenty twenty-six, whether single questionnaire items can usefully measure sleep disturbance in cancer patients. Sleep problems are frequent in cancer. Multi-item scales exist, but ultra-short items are cheaper to use. The analysis reuses a multicenter study of nine hundred seventy patients with newly diagnosed cancer, mean age about sixty. Three single items were compared: sleep questions from a cancer quality-of-life scale, from a depression scale, and a yes-no item on a distress problem list. General population samples served as comparisons.

Patients slept markedly worse than the general population on all three items. The items correlated strongly with each other. They told similar stories across demographic and clinical groups. The authors weigh when one item is enough.
pmc-13617305:
Simran Jawanda and five colleagues examine what helps and what hinders members of an integrated knowledge translation panel. On the panel, patients and other knowledge users partner with researchers throughout a consensus-building study. The team interviewed panel members, including youth, caregivers, healthcare providers, and health system leaders. A standard engagement scale measured how meaningful taking part felt.

Eleven panel members took part, and most who completed the scale rated their engagement as very meaningful. Five themes emerged. Clear communication, trust in the team, a welcoming atmosphere, flexible options for taking part, and feeling valued all helped. Communication overload, power imbalances, competing commitments, technology problems, and mismatched expectations worked against it. The authors say success depends on trust, needing careful structure and steady effort.
pmc-13617405:
Zhang and colleagues published in twenty twenty-six a review of gut microbes and immune crosstalk in autoimmune encephalitis. In this disease family, the immune system attacks the brain. Gut microbes may regulate that process through metabolites and immune signals. Signals also flow backward, with brain immune states reshaping gut communities. The review gathers evidence on disease-linked microbial changes. It proposes a phase-based frame covering onset, progression, and chronic stages.

Possible treatments include diet changes, probiotics, and fecal transplantation. Precision microbiome engineering is discussed as a future option. The authors caution that direct evidence in this disease remains limited. Much support comes from related disorders and animal models instead. They call for long-term patient cohorts with multi-omics profiling. Such work could ground microbiota-based diagnosis and therapy, they argue.
pmc-13618405:
Renee Veldkamp and seven colleagues chart physical therapy after COVID-19 in Dutch primary care across the pandemic's first two and a half years. Using routine records from therapy practices, they followed seventy-one thousand one hundred fifty-two treatment trajectories started between March 2020 and December 2022. They asked how much care patients received, who the patients were, and whether advised outcome measures were actually used.

Completed courses averaged twenty-four weeks and twenty-eight consultations, with therapy shrinking steadily over time. Care peaked for patients aged sixty to seventy-nine, tapering for both younger and older groups, and women's courses ran about a week and a half longer than men's without more visits. A baseline score on at least one advised measure, such as the six-minute walk test, was recorded in eighty-three percent of trajectories. The authors provide the descriptive baseline that post-pandemic rehabilitation policy lacked.
pmc-13619605:
Yang Li and his twelve co-authors, publishing in 2026, turn liquefied wood into carbon materials with shapes they can dial in. Wood is messy and uneven, which usually defeats precise self-assembly. The team dissolves it and lets it organize inside a reactive emulsion. A phosphate additive swells the building blocks and changes their preferred curvature, steering how they pack together.

By tuning that push, the team walks the product through a family of forms. Ordered fibers with neat pores come first. Hollow fibers and then bowl-like shells follow as the ordered channels thin out. One hollow fiber version powers a heat-to-electricity device with a strong output. The authors present the method as a flexible route to designer carbon materials from biomass, with uses in energy devices and beyond.
pmc-13619705:
Elchanan Quint and four colleagues compared what blast injuries and blunt injuries demand from a level one trauma center. Blast wounds combine pressure damage, fragments, falls, and burns, so the team suspected they strain hospitals more than ordinary blunt trauma. Their records covered 321 blast patients and more than nine thousand blunt patients, with a matched comparison group built to balance age, sex, and injury severity.

Blast patients hit the study's high-burden mark far more often, a composite of long stays, intensive care, or urgent surgery. They also went to the shock room more, needed surgery within hours more often, and far more often needed three or more operations, massive transfusion, or intensive care. The gap held for both milder and severe injury groups. The authors warn planners that even a modest blast caseload can swallow resources built for everyday trauma.
pmc-13619805:
Marilena Panarelli examines how a medieval Italian physician used plant life to think about animal reproduction. Dino del Garbo, a Florentine doctor, wrote his commentary on a Hippocratic treatise about the nature of the fetus in the early fourteenth century. His text is the only known Latin commentary on that work, and it greatly expands the short original.

Dino leaned on analogies between seeds and embryos, asking how plant generation mirrors animal generation. Panarelli follows his treatment of seed anatomy, sex differences in plants, and the vegetative soul, the life principle medieval thinkers assigned to plants. Background influences include a pseudo-Aristotelian book on plants and Albert the Great's work on vegetation, even where Dino never names it. The study presents the commentary as a rare meeting point of medicine, botany, and philosophy in the Bologna medical tradition.
pmc-13621405:
Angela F Journell and four colleagues reviewed their center's experience using the blood thinner rivaroxaban in children with short bowel syndrome. These children live on intravenous nutrition through a central line, which raises clot risk, and standard prevention means daily injections families dislike. An oral drug is attractive, yet rivaroxaban absorbs mainly in the stomach, a real question for a shortened gut. Three patients with earlier line-related clots tried it.

Outcomes split three ways. One child developed a new clot while the drug was paused, one suffered a gut bleed, and one finished therapy with no event at all. The authors judge the drug possibly workable in carefully picked patients, provided blood levels are monitored closely. Three cases cannot settle safety or dosing, so they call for larger studies before the practice spreads.
pmc-13621705:
Christopher Herz and colleagues describe a 2026 laboratory study that designs and tests a reusable funnel for cytospin work, the method labs use to fix cells from body fluids onto microscope slides. Commercial funnels are mostly single use, costly, and limited to a small slide area. The team set out to print a cheaper funnel that covers a larger area.

Working with design software and a printer that builds parts from a medical resin, they shaped prototypes to fit a standard cytocentrifuge. Tests used two human pleural fluid samples, meaning fluid taken from around the lungs, across a wide range of cell counts. The printed funnel roughly tripled the cytospin area, raised how many cells could be loaded, and survived repeated cleaning with two common disinfectants. Because the design file is published, other labs can print and adapt it, which may help places with tight budgets.
pmc-13623405:
Kaeun Bae, Fraser Hugh Simpson, and Michael Hatzifotis report a case of transient intussusception after a weight-loss operation called SADI bypass. Intussusception means one stretch of bowel telescopes into the next, which can block the gut. The complication is known after the gastric bypass operation but had never been described after this variant.

The patient, a forty-seven-year-old man, came in with cramping pain that came and went, several years after his bypass. A CT scan showed the pattern of telescoped bowel. When surgeons looked inside with a camera through small cuts, the problem had undone itself, so no bowel needed repair. The authors review why this may happen after bariatric surgery: changed bowel movement patterns, lost fat padding after weight loss, and staple lines that give the bowel a starting point. They advise keeping the diagnosis in mind for episodic pain after this operation.
pmc-13623505:
Mychal Machado and co-authors ask what cats actually want, and whether the favorites work as training rewards, in a 2026 study. Four house cats chose freely among foods, toys, and social time in their own homes. First the team ranked items inside each category, then pitted the category winners against each other. A final test paid out the best and worst prizes for nose pokes.

Three of the four cats worked harder when the top prize was on offer. The workflow, from free choice to reward check, is the first of its kind for cats. It runs in ordinary homes and shelters without special gear. The authors offer it as a practical route to better training and enrichment.
pmc-13623805:
Stefan Uddenberg, Jun Kwak, and Brian J Scholl test whether visual memory quietly edits the physical world toward stability. Block towers are a test object in the study of intuitive physics, since viewers instantly sense whether a stack will stand or topple. Earlier work asked people questions about falling; this study instead asked them to rebuild towers from memory.

Volunteers viewed generated towers on a three-dimensional drag-and-drop screen, then reconstructed them without any mention of physics. The team ran both the original towers and the rebuilt versions through a physics simulator. Reconstructions were accurate in most respects, yet they drifted in one direction: remembered towers were more stable than the real ones. The authors say the finding shows memory is shaped not only by which objects a scene contains. It is shaped by how those objects relate, even when nobody is thinking about physics at all.
pmc-13624005:
Sarah Beierle and eight colleagues published a mixed-methods study in two thousand twenty-six on local support services for families in Germany. Help for children's mental health is scattered across health, school, and social services. No one had mapped how that patchwork looks in a city.

The team studied three disadvantaged neighbourhoods in large German cities. They interviewed nineteen professionals and mapped services visible online. The map found one hundred twenty-two facilities offering three hundred sixty services. Professionals called the landscape fragmented and hard to navigate, above all for poor and migrant families. Gaps appeared in specialist child care and outreach. The authors propose a standard tool for mapping such landscapes.
pmc-13625905:
Eric R. Wengert and Roshan A. Jain describe a semester-long undergraduate course at Haverford College that turns students into comparative neurophysiologists, a 2026 teaching paper. Course-based research experiences are known to build inquiry skills and belonging in science, yet few let undergraduates run modern recording methods and analyze the results with code. The course, Advanced Laboratory in Neurobiology, had students compare escape behavior in crickets and zebrafish through drug treatments, electrical recordings, and live calcium imaging.

Students mastered both recording approaches, wrote their own MATLAB scripts for analysis, kept digital lab notebooks, drafted fellowship-style proposals, joined a journal club, and gave final talks. End-of-term surveys showed clear growth in conceptual grasp and in skills with rigorous, computational analysis. Teachers get a tested, portable design for bringing real comparative physiology and coding into the undergraduate lab, with student work that mirrors professional practice.
pmc-13627305:
Abdessalam Cherkaoui, Patrice François, and five co-authors characterize a stealthy drug-resistant bacterium found in Switzerland. Their report, from twenty twenty-six, concerns vancomycin-variable Enterococcus faecium. The isolate carries the vanA resistance gene yet tests as drug-sensitive. Such hidden carriers can seed silent spread in hospitals.

A full lab workup follows: drug tests, gene PCR, population profiling, and whole-genome sequencing. Survivors persist at low rates even under drug pressure. The genome is compared with resistant isolates from the same patient. Outbreak strains from Geneva hospitals join the comparison. The authors flag the variant as a reservoir worth hunting.
pmc-13627805:
Deepshikha Kataria, Madhuri Hegde, and Gurmeet Singh test whether an old Ayurvedic step called murchana makes ghee last longer before it spoils. Their study was published in twenty twenty-six. In murchana, ghee is infused with a mix of herbs before herbs are cooked into it to make a medicated ghee.

The team made four batches: plain ghee, herb-treated ghee, and each kind cooked with Centella asiatica, a healing herb. They stored the batches in hot, damp air for one hundred and sixty days and checked signs of spoilage and decay over time. The herb-treated batch with Centella held up best, staying under the safe spoilage limit with a longer time before decay set in. The results back the old practice as a way to extend shelf life.
pmc-13629405:
Ramon Peres Brexó and six colleagues ask if heat and ultraviolet light spoil the antimicrobial power of essential oils, in a study from two thousand twenty-six. Essential oils serve agriculture, food preservation, and health products of many kinds. What the conditions of storage do to them once they are out was underexplored till now. The team put four oils to the test.
