The four oils were oregano, lemongrass, clove, and a Brazilian pepper-rosmarin. Samples stood for forty-eight hours at seventy degrees, or sat under UV radiation. Gas chromatography tracked the changes in their chemistry as they went. Antimicrobial tests targeted two bacteria and two fungi of food and crop concern. Both forms of treatment altered the chemistry of the oils. The team gauges how much biological activity is left after the kind of abuse that real supply chains inflict on goods as a matter of course.
pmc-13629705:
Yuliya Dzyazko and co-authors review how adding inorganic materials to polymer filter membranes fights fouling and boosts performance. Such membranes strain out particles and large molecules, but they clog with organic matter and bacteria. Water-loving inorganic additives are chemically stable and can help on several fronts at once.

The review sorts additives into three families: harmless ones that resist fouling, bacteria-killing ones such as silver particles and advanced carbons, and photocatalysts that destroy bacteria and organics alike. It compares ways of building the additives in, weighs gains in flow and retention, and notes each family's limits. The authors call for a universal design theory and for tests on real water, not just lab solutions.
pmc-13630405:
Woo and colleagues reported in 2026 on a better way to make porous silicon-carbon anode material for lithium batteries. Silicon can store far more charge than graphite, but tiny silicon particles pack poorly and large ones swell and crack. The standard route uses magnesium to strip oxygen from silica, yet poor balance between magnesium supply and surface reaction causes impurities and collapse of the shape.

Woo built a heat-and-rate model to keep magnesium supply matched with surface use during the reaction. With that balance, round silica particles became even, porous silicon spheres without clumping. A carbon shell added before acid cleaning held the fragile frame together. The final material still stored a high charge after 100 cycles, with first-cycle efficiency above seven in ten. The porous shape and carbon skin limited damage and spread current flow more evenly.
pmc-13630505:
Sung-Yoon Kang and nineteen colleagues followed patients whose chronic cough had a known cause. They worked with the Korean Chronic Cough Registry team. The question was who slides into refractory cough, the kind that resists cause-based treatment. Their 2026 letter analyses 245 patients. All had at least two follow-up visits.

About one in five moved to refractory cough over the follow-up span. The median time was roughly nine months. Starting traits of those who converted looked much like those who did not. Asthmatic cough was commonest in both groups. One thread set the groups apart: cough hypersensitivity, an exaggerated cough reflex. Its link to conversion depended on age. The authors argue for tracking sensitivity, not just causes. That helps judge which patients need stronger care.
pmc-13630705:
Antea Scrocco and colleagues try out a remotely driven humanoid robot as a quiet watcher in a children's clinic, in this usability study from twenty twenty-six. Waiting rooms offer a rare chance to watch how children behave in a natural setting. A robot that a clinician steers from afar could do that watching without looming over the child, but only if staff find it easy to run.

No children took part yet: thirteen clinicians and engineers tested the robot, called Alter-Ego, in a child neuropsychiatry waiting room. Standard questionnaires scored its ease of use in the acceptable range, and users rated it lively, likeable, safe, and smart. Mental demand and effort were the main costs, while frustration stayed low. Past gaming or virtual reality experience made no difference to the scores. The team takes the result as a green light to test the robot with real patients next.
pmc-13631305:
Le Blanc and co-authors study how bacteria grow when trapped in tight spaces. Crowded growth happens in biofilms, inside host cells, and at infection sites, where it builds mechanical pressure. As cells divide in confinement, their internal turgor pressure rises against the walls around them.

Using a microfluidic device that squeezes growing bacteria, the team watched how pressure changed cell physiology. Survival required transcriptional adaptation, a broad shift in which genes are switched on. The work shows bacteria sense and answer mechanical force, not just chemicals, a point that matters for infection control.
pmc-13633305:
A gentle electrical therapy for failing hearts is reviewed by Fudim and colleagues. Many people with heart failure and a weakened pumping chamber stay breathless and limited even on full guideline drug treatment, so new add-on options are sought. Cardiac microcurrent therapy delivers a continuous, very weak direct current that does not trigger heartbeats. It aims instead to reshape heart muscle biology by easing fibrosis, calming inflammation, and steadying calcium handling inside cells.

Laboratory work and animal studies support that mechanism. Early human experience, including a randomised trial in selected patients with non-ischaemic failure, shows feasibility with consistent hints of better pumping function, exercise capacity, and reported wellbeing. The evidence remains small, open-label, and without sham controls, and every clinical result so far comes from surgically implanted systems. Fudim and colleagues therefore call the therapy investigational, pending larger sham-controlled trials.
pmc-13634005:
Fabio Nocera leads a team that reviews learning curves in bowel surgery. Their review from twenty twenty-six compares robot and keyhole methods. Past reports use mixed terms, which makes them hard to compare with each other.

The team searched three data sets by set guide rules. They kept trials and both past and planned case studies. Main check was how many cases it takes to learn. They also note how curves and phases are defined. Colon and rectal work are split in the checks. A shared frame for reports is proposed.
pmc-13635405:
A large team of co-authors reports a study dated two thousand twenty-six naming a new antibody linked to brain inflammation. The condition is autoimmune encephalitis, where the immune system attacks the brain, sometimes alongside a cancer elsewhere in the body. Labs keep finding patient antibodies that match no known target.

From eight hundred forty-four such samples, three patients shared a distinct staining pattern in the brain. Protein screening named the target as copine-4. All three patients had encephalitis, two during immune therapy for lung cancer and one with a second known antibody syndrome. The authors argue the antibody marks a cancer-linked brain disorder.
pmc-13636605:
Nabeeha Haque, Alexander G. de Dios, and Angel C. de Dios published this 2026 study modeling an oxygen signal that nuclear magnetic resonance can measure in water. The signal, a quadrupole coupling constant for the rare oxygen-17 isotope, reports on the electric environment around each oxygen atom. Hydrogen bonds reshape that environment, so the signal could expose water's bonding patterns. Full quantum calculations are slow, so the team built a simpler additive scheme.

Quantum calculations on pairs, clusters, and ice-like arrangements showed bond distance doing most of the work. Each nearest neighbor's contribution could be added up under a donor-acceptor scheme, with accuracy improving once distance was counted. Second neighbors added small, systematic corrections tied to lopsided bonding networks. With those refinements, the cheap model matched full calculations closely. The authors offer it as a fast, interpretable bridge between molecular simulations and measured oxygen signals in watery settings.
pmc-13639505:
Removing coverslips from old cytology slides so their cells can be reused for extra tests is examined by Htun and three colleagues. Archival aspirate smears increasingly support lab and molecular assays, but the coverslip must come off first. The usual solvent soak takes hours to days while exposing staff to hazardous fumes. The team reviewed published removal methods and tested freezer-based removal at a major cancer centre, using eighty slides from forty cases across several freezing times and temperatures.

Thick xylene-based mounting medium with rigid glass coverslips resisted cold removal. Complete removal came on only about a third of slides, with the best result at ten minutes. Slide-to-slide variation within the same case mattered more than temperature or time. Htun and colleagues conclude that mounting choices made at preparation time strongly shape later reuse, so coverslipping workflows should anticipate future testing.
pmc-13643305:
Nidhi V Banavar and Kirk Bansak present a model that sorts out which choice rules people use in conjoint tasks. In these tasks, people pick between options set out by a few traits. Standard work lumps all people together and assumes full, careful thought.

They used the model on two tests with 3,762 people. The topics were migrants, candidates, and climate plans. The simplest shortcut rule came out most common in all three. Roughly two thirds to three quarters of people switched rules between topics. Making a task harder also shifted the rules people used. The authors say split results by rule type give a sharper read on what surveys truly show.
pmc-13645505:
Rohini Roopnarine and two colleagues wrote an opening piece for a research set on One Health and joint training across health jobs. One Health gives the why for teamwork across doctors, vets, and public health staff. Joint training gives the how.

The editors praise courses where students solve real problems in their own towns. One class built a plan for a real One Health issue near home. One began with a cattle disease that hurt local farms. One used live cases on pollution and fair treatment. Such work teaches doubt and hard trade-offs in a way lectures cannot. The set aims to spread course plans that weave One Health through health training.
pmc-13645605:
Tong Wu and Ying Xie track blood inflammation markers in seventy people with type 2 diabetes to see which markers move as diabetic eye disease worsens. Diabetic retinopathy damages the retina and can threaten sight. Forty patients whose eye disease progressed were compared with thirty whose disease stayed stable. Eye scans sorted patients into the two groups, and white blood cell measures were compared across two time points.

In the progression group, neutrophil and lymphocyte counts fell over time, while a platelet-to-lymphocyte ratio rose. The stable group showed no clear changes in any marker. When the team tested links directly, only the drop in neutrophil count tied significantly to progression. The pair caution that the other markers changed within the group yet failed the direct test, so their value needs confirmation in larger work.
pmc-13645705:
Yang Zhao and three colleagues build a prediction chart for gallbladder stones in people with type 2 diabetes, using records from one hospital's surgery and hormone departments. Patients seen from September 2023 to December 2024 were split into an earlier group for building the model and a later group for checking it. A selection method first narrowed the candidate measures from routine clinical data. The chart type used is called a nomogram.

Six factors stayed in the final model: age, high blood pressure, fasting blood sugar, and three blood fat related measures. The model sorted patients with moderate accuracy in both groups, and its risk estimates lined up fairly with real outcomes. The authors say the chart may help flag higher-risk patients for earlier prevention work. They also stress that the model still needs testing at other hospitals before clinics rely on it.
pmc-13646105:
Ilaria Marcomini and six colleagues map how patient experience questionnaires are used outside hospitals across primary care and home and community services. Such questionnaires, called PREMs, ask patients how care felt rather than what it achieved. Their review searched five databases through July 2025 under standard scoping methods. A total of 168 studies qualified, mostly from wealthy countries.

Most studies used validated questionnaires, though many built their own, and a minority mixed both. Communication, access, relationships with staff, and continuity of care were the domains checked most often. Fairness-related topics appeared less, and children, older adults, and poorer countries were underrepresented. The authors say these tools hold real promise for person-centered improvement, provided measures become more standard and more sensitive to context and equity.
pmc-13649405:
Ameera Jaradat and six colleagues improved a vision model that draws the outline of the cheek sinuses on CT scans. Hand drawing is slow and error prone, since the sinus walls are thin and shapes vary a lot from person to person. Their model adds two tricks: one that tracks where things sit along each axis, and one that bends its sampling grid to fit odd shapes.

Trained on scans from 130 patients, the new model beat three close rivals on a held-out test set. Tests that removed one trick at a time showed both were needed for the gain. The authors call this a proof of concept for use in surgery planning and sinus disease checks.
pmc-13649505:
Danru Zheng and two colleagues report the first known case of a lung cancer switching type to dodge a targeted drug. A 55-year-old man who never smoked had advanced lung cancer with a HER2 gene fault. A new drug aimed at that fault shrank his disease at first.

After six months, blood markers of the small cell type rose and scans showed growth. A fresh biopsy found the tumour had turned mostly into small cell cancer, while keeping its old gene faults. Drugs for the new type lowered its markers, yet the gland-type part kept growing on its own track. He lived about five and a half months after the switch was found. The authors urge marker checks during such therapy.
pmc-13650005:
Chong Tian and three colleagues introduce a second collected volume on cognitive impairment, the broad decline in memory and thinking that ranges from mild complaints to dementia. Their editorial explains why the topic needs many fields at once, since aging populations face risks to independence, well-being, and daily life.

The overview previews studies on stroke, where one pooled analysis found impairment in close to half of people after a first stroke. It also previews work on children with attention difficulties using brain-wave measures. Other pieces cover a blood marker in a movement disorder, chemotherapy effects on the brain in rats, and new tools for testing and rehabilitation. The editors frame the volume as a step toward earlier detection, better prediction of decline, and care that protects daily function.
pmc-13651505:
Alfred Larsson and ten co-authors watch ions gather at a platinum electrode surface using X-ray fluorescence, finally measuring the electric double layer that steers nearly every electrocatalytic reaction. This charged boundary layer's strong fields and rearranged water shape reaction performance, yet its atomic picture stayed incomplete because interfacial ions are so hard to count.

A sponge-like porous platinum electrode boosted the interface signal in acidic solutions. Across ten electrolytes, the team found the surface charge behaving unevenly and overshooting as voltage changed, because adsorbed species rewrite the surface's free charge. With anions that do not adsorb, the classical theory of the layer held up as concentration varied. On negatively charged surfaces, dissolved cations and protons competed to do the screening, and ion charge mattered greatly in who won. The results give catalyst designers a hands-on handle on a layer they usually only model.
pmc-13659105:
Aizhan Oralbek and five colleagues grade the statistics lessons that students actually find on YouTube. Video platforms now serve as informal classrooms, yet popularity says nothing about accuracy. The team searched for common statistics terms, took the most relevant results. After exclusions reviewed well over a hundred videos with a global quality scale and a modified reliability tool.

Each video was classified by who made it, how it was presented, and how viewers engaged with it, so quality could be compared across sources and formats. The findings speak to teachers who assign videos, students who cram from them, and creators who want to teach well. Knowing which kinds of channels and formats tend to be reliable helps learners spend their study time on statistics instruction that deserves trust.
pmc-13662505:
Joao de Souza and a large team test whether adding adults can improve a child trauma prediction model. Their critical appraisal from twenty twenty-six uses a Tanzanian injury registry. The PRESTO score predicts short-term death in injured children. It uses bedside measures suited to low-resource hospitals.

Injuries kill many children and teenagers worldwide each year. The score had already performed well in several African settings. But child deaths were rare in the local data, which weakens prediction. The team added adult patients from the same hospital to enlarge the sample. Their report weighs whether that fix truly helps. The work warns readers about machine learning with rare outcomes.
pmc-13672905:
Alastair John Stewart Webb and colleagues review the role of impaired cerebral autoregulation in small vessel disease and vascular cognitive impairment, a 2026 synthesis. Autoregulation holds brain blood flow when pressure varies, using vessel muscle contraction driven by muscle and nerve signals. Small vessel disease, present in over half of people by age sixty and over eighty percent by eighty, brings wilder blood pressure swings and faulty small vessels. Autoregulation may fail as cause, consequence, or both.

The review covers autoregulation mechanisms, their overlap with vessel pathology, and measuring methods. It covers evidence across everyday disease, stroke, and genetic forms, plus how therapies affect autoregulation. It stresses that small vessel disease drives thirty percent of ischemic strokes, eighty percent of hemorrhagic strokes, and forty percent of dementia, yet autoregulation's role remains underexplored. Clinicians and researchers get a map of gaps and studies that could make autoregulation a target.
pmc-13677005:
Shuiyu Xu and a large team trace a driver of gut inflammation in this two thousand twenty-six paper. Their focus is Th17 cells, immune cells tied to bowel disease and colon cancer. How these cells set their sugar use was unclear. The team found that a protein called HECTD1 boosts the making of HIF-1 alpha, a master switch for sugar burning. That push speeds Th17 growth and activity.

Mice bred to lack HECTD1 in T cells had milder colitis and fewer tumors. Gene scans showed clear shifts in Th17 and sugar pathways. Without HECTD1, Th17 cells formed poorly both in dishes and in animals. Higher HECTD1 levels also track with human bowel disease. The work nominates this pathway as a drug target for gut inflammation and its cancers.
pmc-13678205:
Genevieve Kanter and Toni Mankowitz check in 2026 who speaks for the public at United States drug advisory meetings. Each FDA panel includes a patient and a consumer representative. Rules police the experts' industry ties, but little attention goes to the advocacy groups these public members belong to.

The authors traced the groups' funding for meetings held from 2013 to 2022. In nearly two of five meetings, a public representative had active ties to a group funded by drug companies. In more than one in ten, the group took money from the very company whose drug was under review. The authors say the pattern is common enough to deserve policy attention.
pmc-13679705:
Erin Seybold and a large team published a hydrology study in two thousand twenty-six on the smallest streams in the United States. Headwater streams shape water quality and connect whole river networks. Yet they are poorly mapped and rarely measured at large scales.

Using national spatial data, the team classified headwaters by climate, land shape, cover, and soil. Seven main types emerged, each with a distinct mix of traits. Headwaters also differed systematically from the watersheds below them, above all in how deep water likely flows. The classic picture of headwaters as steep, forested, and untouched needs updating, the authors say. Their types offer a shared frame for monitoring, research, and planning.
pmc-13684705:
Kesia Esther da Silva and a large team tested whether gene-guided dosing can even out a tuberculosis prevention drug. People break down the drug isoniazid at very different speeds. A gene called NAT2 sets much of that speed, and wrong exposure raises the risk of harm. The weekly preventive course pairs isoniazid with a second drug.

The trial ran in Brazil with two hundred twenty-eight adults starting the course. Each person got both a standard flat dose and a dose set by their gene type, on separate visits. Gene-guided dosing cut the spread of drug exposure about in half. Slow, middle, and fast breakdown groups landed much closer together. The team derived dose levels for each gene group. Such tailoring could make preventive therapy safer and more even.
pmc-2633005:
Bursac, Gauss, Williams, and co-authors discuss purposeful selection of variables in logistic regression. Logistic models predict a yes-or-no outcome from many possible factors. Builders must choose, from a large set of candidate factors, which ones belong in the best model.

Choices may rest on clinical sense or on statistical strength, and several selection methods compete. The authors argue for a purposeful approach that mixes both grounds and checks each step. Better variable choice yields models doctors can trust for risk prediction, rather than models that merely fit one dataset by chance.
pmc-3176805:
Song, Dong, Long, and co-authors present REST, a toolkit for processing resting-state brain scan data. Resting-state fMRI records brain activity while a person lies still and does nothing in particular. Interest in the method had grown fast, since resting patterns reveal how brain regions connect.

No publicly available, well-integrated, and easy-to-use tool for this data yet existed, the authors say. REST fills that gap with a systematic processing pipeline. Easy tools widened the resting-state field, letting smaller labs study brain networks in health, ageing, and mental illness.  Group studies of meditation and sleep adopted the toolkit for resting data.
pmc-3436805:
Rausch, Zichner, Schlattl, and co-authors present DELLY, a tool for discovering structural variants in genomes. Structural variants are large gains, losses, or rearrangements of DNA. Finding them with high sensitivity and specificity is essential for describing natural variation and disease-causing changes in personal genome sequencing.

DELLY integrates two kinds of evidence: paired reads spaced oddly along the genome, and split reads that cross a breakpoint. Combining both signals catches variants either signal alone would miss. The tool became a standard choice for genome studies of rare disease and cancer.  Clinical genome services use it when hunting the cause of rare disease.
pmc-3557905:
Jinek, East, Cheng, and co-authors show that CRISPR-Cas9 editing can be programmed with RNA inside human cells. In bacteria, type II CRISPR systems use a dual RNA guide to direct the Cas9 enzyme to cut foreign DNA at specific sites. The team asked whether that system could be rebuilt for human cells.

They show Cas9, assembled with hybrid guide RNAs, cutting DNA inside human cells at a chosen matching site. That result helped turn a bacterial defence system into a general genome editing tool, with wide effects across medicine and biology.
pmc-4708105:
Okonechnikov, Conesa, and García-Alcalde presented Qualimap two in 2016. Finding random errors and systematic bias is a crucial step in any sound pipeline for high-throughput sequencing data. Tools for this quality control task existed, but multi-sample work needed more.

Qualimap two gives advanced checks across many samples at once. Users can compare quality metrics side by side and spot a bad run before it poisons an analysis. That early warning saves costly re-sequencing and false findings. The tool covers both general sequencing data and targeted types, making it a standard checkpoint in genomics pipelines.
pmc-4934905:
Hill, Fatoba, Oke, and their colleagues estimated the global prevalence of chronic kidney disease in 2016. Kidney disease is a global health burden with high costs to health systems. It is also an independent risk factor for cardiovascular disease, the world's leading killer.

Their systematic review and meta-analysis pooled studies from around the world. All stages of kidney disease carry higher risks of heart problems, early death, and reduced quality of life. A single global estimate helps governments plan dialysis, transplant, and prevention services. It also underlines how often kidney disease goes undetected until late stages.
pmc-4967105:
Loboda, Damulewicz, Pyza, and their team reviewed the Nrf2 and HO-1 system in 2016. Nrf2 is a switch that turns on genes which guard cells. Those genes fight oxidants, calm inflammation, and clear toxins from the body.

The pair is found, in some form, in a wide range of species, from worms to humans. That long shared past points to a core role in how life deals with stress. The review also covers how this system shapes growth and how long a species lives, and its part in disease. The work helps labs see where drugs that boost this guard might help.
pmc-5717805:
Janus Jakobsen, Christian Gluud, Jorn Wetterslev, and coauthors wrote this practical guide in 2017. It covers missing data in randomized clinical trials, a problem that can bend results if handled badly. How much bias appears depends on why the data went missing.

The guide explains when filling in missing values by multiple imputation is a sound choice. Flowcharts walk readers through checks on the trial design and the pattern of missing values. Worked examples show the steps in real trials. Trial teams can use the guide to plan analyses that reviewers and readers can trust more.
pmc-6095905:
Chaithanya Chelakkot, Jaewang Ghim, and Sung Ho Ryu reviewed the gut barrier and its breakdown in 2018. The gut lining does far more than digest food. Together with mucus and immune cells, the cell layer keeps microbes and toxins out of the body.

The review explains the seals between gut cells and the signals that tighten or loosen them. Stress, alcohol, and disease can open gaps that let harmful material through. Such leaks are tied to bowel disease, liver trouble, and wider inflammation. Readers see why a quiet barrier failure can echo through the whole body.
pmc-6227505:
Kyle Foreman, Nicholas Marquez, Anne Dolgert, and coauthors forecast future health for many countries in 2018. Long-term planning needs a view of how life expectancy and causes of death may change. Earlier forecasts covered only part of that picture.

The team models future mortality for a large set of causes under a reference path and under better and worse paths. Rising incomes, education, and risk control drive most gains in the better path. Some causes, tied to obesity and mental health, worsen even then. Governments use such scenarios to test whether today's investments fit tomorrow's burdens.
pmc-7049905:
Boris Bikbov, Caroline Purcell, Andrew Levey, and coauthors estimated the global burden of chronic kidney disease in 2020. Planning care for kidney disease needs solid counts, yet many countries have none. The study fills that gap with modeled global estimates.

Coverage runs from 1990 to 2017 for nearly two hundred countries. Kidney disease proves common, affecting roughly one in ten adults in their global estimate. Deaths tied to it have risen as populations age and diabetes spreads. The authors press for screening of high-risk groups and cheaper access to dialysis and transplant where needs are unmet.
pmc-7190605:
Romano Lugano, Mohan Ramachandran, and Anna Dimberg reviewed tumor angiogenesis in 2019. Tumors grow new blood vessels through several distinct processes. These vary by tumor type and site and can run side by side in one tumor.

Secreted factors, above all VEGF, orchestrate the sprouting and remodeling of vessels. The resulting network is leaky and chaotic, which feeds resistance to therapy. Anti-vessel drugs help some patients but often lose effect. The review maps causes and consequences and points to combinations that might finally normalize tumor blood flow. Combination strategies that pair vessel drugs with immunotherapy are reviewed as the most hopeful direction.
pmc-7369905:
Fei He, Xiaoli Ru, and Tao Wen reviewed in 2020 the roles of NRF2, a protein that acts as a master switch for cell defense. When switched on, it raises the production of genes that help cells withstand poisons and oxidative stress, the chemical wear caused by reactive oxygen. It also helps cells clear drugs and ride out other kinds of damage.

The review ranges well beyond that core defense role, covering how this switch affects inflammation, metabolism, and diseases such as cancer. The authors explain the signals that turn it on and off, and why both too little and too much activity can cause harm. Their account frames a target that drug developers watch closely, since nudging it could protect tissue or, done wrong, shield tumors.
pmc-8371605:
John Jumper and a large team at DeepMind reported in 2021 that their AlphaFold system could predict protein structures with high accuracy. Proteins do the work of life, and knowing a protein's folded shape helps explain how it functions. Experiments had solved the shapes of roughly one hundred thousand proteins, a small share of those known to exist.

AlphaFold instead computes the shape from the protein's sequence alone, and the team shows it matching experimental results closely across many test cases. They describe how the system reasons about the sequence and its evolutionary relatives. The work reshaped structural biology almost at once, putting a reliable predicted shape within reach for nearly any protein a researcher cares about.
purchas-hakluytus-posthumus-maclehose-vo:
Samuel Purchas, an English clergyman, took up Richard Hakluyt's papers after Hakluyt's death and built them into Hakluytus Posthumus, or Purchas His Pilgrimes, in 1625. Volume one here opens the twenty-volume MacLehose reprint, Glasgow, 1905 to 1907. The Latin word posthumus in the title marks the book as Hakluyt's legacy, carried on by another hand.

Purchas printed voyage accounts from across the known world, many saved nowhere else. His set grew into the largest voyage collection of its age, a storehouse of first-hand travel. Sailors, traders, and missionaries all speak in its pages. The Pilgrimes became the great sequel to Hakluyt, and this volume starts it.

Volume two continues Purchas His Pilgrimes, Samuel Purchas's huge voyage collection of 1625, in the MacLehose reprint of 1905 to 1907. Purchas, a clergyman with a scholar's hunger, had gathered papers that Richard Hakluyt left behind. He added far more of his own finding, until the work outgrew its model.

The narratives bound here came from men who had sailed, traded, and wintered in strange lands. Dozens of such accounts survive only because Purchas printed them in time. His collection served readers of the 1600s as a window on the whole trading world. Volume two keeps that window open, dense with journeys told by those who made them.

Purchas His Pilgrimes reaches volume three in the twenty-volume MacLehose edition, Glasgow, 1905 to 1907. Samuel Purchas first published the work in 1625 as Hakluytus Posthumus, the posthumous Hakluyt. He meant it to stand beside Richard Hakluyt's Principal Navigations and carry the record of travel further.

It did more than that: it became the largest voyage collection of the seventeenth century. Purchas preserved dozens of narratives that would have been lost without his press. The voices range across the globe-trotting trades of the age, from sea captains to envoys. Volume three holds its full share of that rescue work, in the tellers' own words.

Volume four of Purchas His Pilgrimes comes from the MacLehose reprint, Glasgow, 1905 to 1907, of Samuel Purchas's collection of 1625. Purchas was a Church of England clergyman who never voyaged himself. His journeys were made in print, through the journals and letters of men who had crossed every sea his age knew.

Those journals fill this volume with first-hand reports of lands, peoples, and trade. Purchas printed much that Hakluyt had gathered and much that Hakluyt never saw. Because paper perishes, dozens of the narratives here exist in no other copy. The Pilgrimes earned its place as the seventeenth century's great sequel to Hakluyt, and volume four shows why.

Samuel Purchas issued Purchas His Pilgrimes in 1625, and volume five here follows the MacLehose edition of 1905 to 1907. The full title, Hakluytus Posthumus, ties the book to Richard Hakluyt, whose unpublished papers Purchas obtained. Around that core Purchas built the broadest travel archive of his century, in twenty modern volumes.

The accounts in this volume span the working world of sail: discovery, trade, embassy, and mission. Many were printed by Purchas alone, and survive through him alone. Readers in his day treated the set as a library of the whole earth. Volume five keeps faith with that scale, one hard-won narrative after another.

Volume six continues Samuel Purchas's Purchas His Pilgrimes in the twenty-volume MacLehose reprint, Glasgow, 1905 to 1907. The original work of 1625 dwarfed every rival: no age before it had printed so many voyage narratives under one name. Purchas, a quiet clergyman, assembled it from Hakluyt's leavings and his own wide gathering.

First-hand testimony is the set's strength, and this volume shares it fully. Captains explain their courses, merchants their markets, and travelers their wonders, each close to the day of the event. Scores of these texts live only in Purchas, rescued from single, fragile copies. That rescue is why historians still shelf the Pilgrimes beside Hakluyt himself.

Purchas His Pilgrimes, volume seven in the MacLehose edition of 1905 to 1907, carries on Samuel Purchas's life work. Published in 1625, the Pilgrimes took Richard Hakluyt's project past Hakluyt's death and doubled its reach. Purchas called his book Hakluytus Posthumus to honor the master whose papers he had inherited.

Within this volume, voyage follows voyage in the plain words of the men who sailed them. Purchas cut and arranged, but the voices stay rough, eager, and near the events. The collection preserved dozens of narratives otherwise lost to fire, damp, and neglect. No other English book of the 1620s holds so much of the world between its covers.

Volume eight of the MacLehose Purchas, Glasgow, 1905 to 1907, continues Purchas His Pilgrimes of 1625. Samuel Purchas built his collection over years of patient asking, buying, and copying. What Richard Hakluyt had begun for England, Purchas widened to the voyages of many nations and trades.

The result, in this volume as in the whole set, is a crowded harbor of texts. Sea journals, embassy reports, and travelers' tales ride side by side, many printed nowhere else. Purchas knew paper was frail and print was rescue, and he rescued at scale. His Pilgrimes became the largest voyage collection of its age, and volume eight adds its full cargo.

The ninth volume of Purchas His Pilgrimes appears in the MacLehose reprint, Glasgow, 1905 to 1907. Samuel Purchas published the original in 1625, working from papers left by Richard Hakluyt and from his own vast gathering. He was a clergyman at a desk, yet few sailors of his day saw as much of the world as his pages hold.

Narrative after narrative here reports discovery, commerce, and encounter in the first person. Purchas preserved dozens of accounts that survive in his book alone. Scholars of early travel treat the twenty volumes as a standard, complete edition of a classic set. Volume nine earns its place in that run without thinning the stock.

Volume ten brings the MacLehose Purchas, Glasgow, 1905 to 1907, to the midpoint of its twenty volumes. The source work, Purchas His Pilgrimes of 1625, was Samuel Purchas's answer to a simple problem: voyage papers were vanishing. Hakluyt had saved many; Purchas, holding Hakluyt's own leavings, saved many more.

This volume's narratives show the method at work, testimony printed before its only copy could perish. The tellers are sailors, merchants, and envoys of the early 1600s, speaking close to their journeys. Together they made the Pilgrimes the seventeenth century's great sequel to Hakluyt. Halfway through the modern set, the supply of such voices shows no sign of failing.

Volume eleven opens the second half of the MacLehose Purchas His Pilgrimes, Glasgow, 1905 to 1907. Samuel Purchas first published his collection in 1625, naming it Hakluytus Posthumus for Richard Hakluyt. From Hakluyt's papers and his own searches, Purchas raised the broadest archive of travel his century produced.

The narratives here keep the family character: first-hand, urgent, and close to salt water. Merchants price their goods, captains log their storms, and envoys describe strange courts. Dozens of the texts in the full set survive only in Purchas's print. Volume eleven carries that rescue forward, proof that his net caught what single copies could not hold.

Purchas His Pilgrimes, volume twelve in the twenty-volume MacLehose edition of 1905 to 1907, descends from Samuel Purchas's folio of 1625. Purchas was an Essex clergyman who made himself the heir of Richard Hakluyt. He bought Hakluyt's remaining papers and spent years turning them, with much more, into print.

Readers of this volume meet the same rich traffic as in the rest: voyages, embassies, and trades across the known world. The accounts speak in the words of the travelers, near the hour of their return. Many would be lost today if Purchas had not set them in type. The Pilgrimes still stands as the great sequel to Hakluyt.

Volume thirteen of the MacLehose reprint, Glasgow, 1905 to 1907, continues Samuel Purchas's Purchas His Pilgrimes. The work of 1625 grew from a desk piled with other men's adventures. Purchas, who stayed home, coaxed journals out of sailors and companies until he held the largest voyage hoard of the age.

Printed here, those journals keep the dust of the road and the roll of the deck. The set preserved dozens of narratives that single manuscripts could not have saved. Purchas meant the Pilgrimes as Hakluyt carried on past the grave, and the scale proves the claim. Volume thirteen adds its own voyages to that crowded, seaworthy shelf.

Samuel Purchas's Purchas His Pilgrimes reaches volume fourteen in the MacLehose edition, Glasgow, 1905 to 1907. The original collection of 1625 was a publishing event: four great folios of travel under one editor's name. Purchas had taken Richard Hakluyt's unpublished remains and built outward in every direction.

This volume's share follows the set's rule, testimony first and polish second. Sailors, factors, and missionaries report what they saw, in words set down near the time. Scores of accounts in the Pilgrimes live nowhere else in print or script. For students of the early modern world, that survival is the book's first claim on their shelves.

The fifteenth volume of the MacLehose Purchas, Glasgow, 1905 to 1907, keeps Purchas His Pilgrimes under full sail. Samuel Purchas published the work in 1625 as the heir and rival of Richard Hakluyt. Where Hakluyt had gathered England's voyages, Purchas ranged wider still, printing the travels of many peoples and trades.

Bound in this volume are narratives that Purchas alone preserved from loss. Their tellers write as participants, with a participant's pride, error, and wonder. The whole twenty-volume set forms the standard complete edition of the Pilgrimes. Volume fifteen is no appendix or afterthought: it is main cargo, first-hand and irreplaceable, from the great age of sail.

Volume sixteen continues Purchas His Pilgrimes in the MacLehose reprint of 1905 to 1907, from Samuel Purchas's original of 1625. Purchas edited at a distance, but his sources did not: they are journals and letters written on the spot. The book's full title, Hakluytus Posthumus, declares its descent from Richard Hakluyt's famous collection.

Here the descent shows in method as much as in matter. Purchas prints whole accounts where he can, trusting the traveler's words over his own summary. Dozens of narratives across the set owe their survival to that trust. The Pilgrimes became the largest voyage collection of the seventeenth century, and this volume keeps its decks crowded.

Purchas His Pilgrimes, volume seventeen in the MacLehose edition, Glasgow, 1905 to 1907, nears the end of a twenty-volume voyage. Samuel Purchas began the work with Richard Hakluyt's papers in hand and published it in 1625. He was a clergyman-editor of endless appetite, and the Pilgrimes fed a nation's hunger for news of the world.

The accounts in this volume share the set's plain virtue: they were written by men who were there. Their reports cover trade, discovery, and the meeting of peoples across great distances. Many such texts exist only because Purchas printed them before their copies perished. Volume seventeen keeps the rescue late, full, and seaworthy.

Volume eighteen of the MacLehose reprint, Glasgow, 1905 to 1907, carries Samuel Purchas's Purchas His Pilgrimes of 1625 toward its close. Purchas built the work as Hakluyt's posthumous heir, and said so in his title. The labor took years of gathering from sailors, merchants, and the families of dead travelers.

What that labor saved fills this volume: narratives in the first person, rough with real weather and real risk. The Pilgrimes grew into the largest voyage collection of its century because Purchas refused to let such papers die. Modern readers meet the early global age here without a middleman's polish. Volume eighteen delivers its share of that direct witness.

The nineteenth volume of Purchas His Pilgrimes, in the MacLehose edition of 1905 to 1907, stands one step from the end of the set. Samuel Purchas published the original in 1625, having inherited Richard Hakluyt's papers and Hakluyt's mission with them. That mission was rescue: print the voyages before time eats the manuscripts.

This volume's narratives show the mission still at work near the finish. Travelers tell their own tales of coasts, courts, markets, and storms, in words close to the events. The full set preserves dozens of accounts found in no other source. Volume nineteen holds its place in that archive with undiminished, first-hand weight.

Volume twenty completes the MacLehose reprint of Purchas His Pilgrimes, Glasgow, 1905 to 1907. Samuel Purchas's original work of 1625 closed with the bulk of a small library. In twenty modern volumes, the Pilgrimes stands as the standard complete edition of the seventeenth century's great sequel to Hakluyt.

The final volume keeps the set's character to the last page: voyage narratives told by the men who lived them. Purchas, a stay-at-home clergyman, gave those men a print afterlife that manuscripts could not promise. Dozens of their accounts survive through him alone. To close volume twenty is to finish the largest gathering of travel testimony its age ever made.
quadratum-alchymisticum-das-ist-vier-aus: Quadratum Alchymisticum is a German alchemy book whose title page, printed at Hamburg by Christian Liebezeit in 1705, is badly garbled in the scan. What can be made out promises the long-sought stone of the philosophers. The stone is newly found, the page claims. It is called the greatest secret and wonder-work of natural art. The book is set out for the use of lovers of wisdom. A motto from Seneca, on teaching others what one knows, closes it.
recollections-of-the-private-life-of-nap: The fifth volume of The Private Life of Napoleon Bonaparte opens, in the pages at hand, with a publisher's header rather than with Constant's own words. The header supplies the full title, the author's name, Constant, and the language, English. After it comes no preface, no chapter, and no contents list for this part of the memoir. So the honest report is a short one: a fifth part of Constant's life of Napoleon exists under that title, and its substance is not shown here.
richard-carvel-volume-05:
Winston Churchill's Richard Carvel opens its fifth volume with The Part Horatio Played, as Richard walks free of a sponging-house. The bailiff's business is quickly settled, he says, and he breathes deep of the open air. A coach in private arms waits, and a crowd stares at the young lady of queenly beauty beside him.

Dolly and Richard take the back seat while Comyn orders the coach to Mr. Manners's house. Richard cries out against entering Arlington Street in his present dress. Lord Comyn covers for him: he is still proud, and must plume himself first. The volume's chapters run on to a conspiracy, Lady Tankerville's drum-major, and Drury Lane.
russell-on-denoting-1905:
On Denoting, published in the journal Mind in 1905, is a paper of barely fifteen pages that founded modern philosophy of language. In it Russell presents his theory of descriptions, and analytic philosophy has lived off the idea ever since.

The puzzle: sentences about things that do not exist, like the present king of France, seem meaningful yet cannot point to anything. Russell shows such phrases are not names at all but structures that dissolve into quantifiers and predicates. The analysis cleared famous tangles in logic and metaphysics at a stroke. Philosophers still teach this paper as the model of their craft.
santayana-life-reason-vol-1-1905:
Reason in Common Sense, published in 1905, opens The Life of Reason, Santayana's five-volume account of how reason grows within human life. This first volume traces the birth of reason in common sense and the imagination.

Santayana describes how the mind, pressed by need and chance, builds a world of objects, selves, and causes out of flux. Common sense is honored as a hard-won achievement, not a naive error. Philosophy begins, for him, by understanding this natural achievement before judging it. The prose is lucid and quietly poetic. It introduces the most graceful philosophical system America produced.
santayana-life-reason-vol-2-1905:
Reason in Society, published in 1905, is the second volume of The Life of Reason. Santayana follows reason out of the single mind into the life men build together: love, the family, industry, government, and war.

Each of these is judged by one standard: how far it serves the harmony of human interests and the life of reason. Santayana praises and blames with an even hand, a Spaniard's eye on Anglo-Saxon pieties. His chapter on love and the family remains much quoted. The volume shows his method at its best, cool appraisal in beautiful sentences.
santayana-life-reason-vol-3-1905:
Reason in Religion, published in 1905, is the third volume of The Life of Reason and Santayana's most famous treatment of faith. He reads religion as poetry and myth: the imagination's picture of man's fate, true as poetry even where it fails as fact.

Trouble comes, he argues, when myth is taken literally, made literal at our peril. He treats prayer, piety, and dogma with sympathy and without belief, being himself an atheist who loved Catholic forms. The book offended the devout and charmed the skeptical. Its balance of reverence and detachment remains unmatched in the philosophy of religion.
santayana-life-reason-vol-4-1905:
Reason in Art, published in 1905, is the fourth volume of The Life of Reason. Santayana turns from religion to art, asking how the love of beauty fits the rational life he has been tracing through mind, society, and faith.

Art, for him, is reason in the realm of sense: the plastic arts, music, and poetry give feeling a formed and shareable shape. He treats fine art and useful craft on one scale, judging both by the harmony they achieve. The writing is measured, aphoristic, and quietly sensuous. The volume completes his survey of man's great pursuits before the final word on science.
scheible-das-kloster-vol05:
Band five of Das Kloster, cells seventeen through twenty, came from Johann Scheible's press in 1846. Scheible called his giant anthology a cloister, worldly and spiritual, and stocked it like one. Every band held complete reprints, a rule he kept from the first cell to the last.

Grimoires of folk practice stand here with Faust books and Höllenzwänge, the spell books that promise power over spirits. Folk charms and cheap chapbooks, the reading of fairs and kitchens, take equal room. No editor before him had treated such low print with such care. Band five keeps that promise deep into the set, without thinning the stock.
serapis-volume-05:
Georg Ebers wrote this historical novel of Alexandria; volume five opens at chapter twenty. Gorgo leaves her grandmother unable to rest, her usual calm broken. Music and song, her normal cure, only sharpen her pain. A hymn of longing by Sappho brings her own heart's hunger into full light.

Gorgo finds that each nerve yearns for the man she loves. She would trade her life for one hour of full joy with him. Her faith in the old gods, her art, and her scorn of the new faith all bend before that longing. This volume presses the tale's love and faith toward their crisis.
shaw-major-barbara-1905:
George Bernard Shaw wrote Major Barbara in 1905, and it was first staged in London that year. Shaw, an Irish playwright and critic, filled his plays with long debates about money, power, and morality. Major Barbara is one of his boldest arguments.

Barbara Undershaft has left her rich family to serve as a major in the Salvation Army. Her father, a maker of cannons and gunpowder, argues that money and power, not charity, truly rule the world. When the Army accepts his donation, Barbara's faith in her work collapses. Shaw forces his audience to weigh poverty, weapons, and good intentions against each other.
sketches-by-seymour-volume-05:
Robert Seymour's comic plates close with this fifth part, given to the autobiography of Andrew Mullins. Chapter one opens on how much modest assurance life writing demands. Mullins doubts that Lord Cherbury or Vidocq, masters of self-esteem, could deny that point.

Home's hero Norval, blowing his own trumpet in famed lines, supplies his model of the art. Mullins follows in that wake like a cock-boat behind first-rate ships, he jokes. Economy ruled his family, he confesses, because necessity parented the virtue. The editor of the full set guessed that Mullins may be the whole work's hidden pen name.
sma-n-and-safti-s-summer-day-1905:
Robert Hichens pairs two tales in Smaïn; and Safti's Summer Day, under a 1905 copyright, printed by Frederick A. Stokes Company. A Sahara saying heads the first tale: when the African is in love, he plays upon the pipe. Far off in the desert, the narrator hears a flute, pure sound in pure air, as he rides with Safti past a sandstorm into palm gardens.

The gardens lie in deep calm, with brown earth walls, slim water rills, and small pools of pale yellow water. Tall palms brood over the shade they make, and no man, hut, robe, or dog can be seen. Only the flute sounds on, wild and odd, from some hidden place. Hichens asks Safti where it comes from, and Safti blinks his one eye and names a gardener among the trees.
stapleton-1905-sal-ammoniac-1905: Stapleton 1905, on sal ammoniac, sits in the Memoirs of the Asiatic Society of Bengal. The Society printed those memoirs at Calcutta. The opening leaves are HathiTrust wrapper matter. They mark the work public domain in the United States. They note its Google digitizing as well. Copies serve to keep the work safe, the note says. Rights may differ in other lands, it adds. Past the wrapper, the scan breaks into stray marks. Broken letters fill the page. No clean lines of the work itself can be read there.
sudraka-little-clay-cart-ryder-1905:
Arthur W. Ryder translated The Little Clay Cart for the Harvard Oriental Series in 1905. The Sanskrit play, ascribed to King Shudraka, is the Mrcchakatika, named for a child's clay toy cart. Charudatta, a poor but noble merchant of Ujjain, loves the courtesan Vasantasena, who returns his love.

A stolen jewel casket, a false murder charge, and a rising against the king braid the private and public plots. Unlike most Sanskrit drama, the play crowds its stage with thieves, gamblers, and street life. Critics call it the most realistic surviving play of ancient India. Ryder's lively version kept its humor and bustle intact. The ten acts move like a novel in dialogue.
swanton-haida-texts-and-myths-1905:
Swanton's 1905 bulletin gathers texts and myths he recorded in the Skidegate dialect of Haida, spoken on Haida Gwaii off the British Columbia coast. Like his Tlingit volume, it prints the native words beside English versions, from the Bureau of American Ethnology.

Raven stands at the center of many stories, shaping the islands and outwitting gods and men. Other texts tell of the potlatch, the great feast of giving, and of shamans, spirits, and voyages to the world of the dead. Haida storytellers were famed for long, polished tales, and this book preserves that art in the original tongue.
tales-and-novels-of-j-de-la-fontaine-vol:
A single long tale fills the fifth volume of La Fontaine's Tales and Novels. It is The Princess Betrothed to the King of Garba. It retells the wanderings of Alaciel, the princess whose betrothal sets her on a road of captures and escapes.

The poet opens by weighing how tales are told: in stories, invention may be admitted, since no posterity demands the strict truth owed to history. Alaciel's story, he owns, is of another kind, and he has altered it a little, careless whether critics find faults or refuse belief, since Alaciel's memory cannot be harmed by his telling. The verse then follows the princess through a chain of masters and rescuers, in the manner of Boccaccio's original, with fortune turning at every stage.
teed-cellular-cosmogony-1905:
Cyrus R. Teed, who took the name Koresh, led a small faith group in the United States and set out this scheme in 1905. He held that men have the cosmos the wrong way round. His group built a town in Florida to live by his word.

Teed held that we live on the inside face of a hollow sphere, not the outside. The sun, stars, and sky all lie within the ball, and space ends at its shell. The book adds U. S. Morrow's land survey claims as proof, and stands as the sect's main text.
the-bride-of-the-nile-volume-05:
Volume 5 of The Bride of the Nile, by Georg Ebers, opens at Chapter XVII with Orion alone in his rooms. Next door lies little Mary, his father's grandchild, in a high fever. Orion has not seen her since he left his father's death-bed, and he can't bring himself to ask after her. His soul is shaken to its base.

He holds himself the most wretched man on earth, blighted by his father's curse. A cruel power, he feels, has turned his truest friend into a foe, with no hope of atonement or a word of pardon. He paces the long room, flings himself on his knees before the divan, and buries his burning face in the cushions. All he thirsts for is pardon, his father's pardon.
the-burgomaster-s-wife-volume-05:
Volume 5 of The Burgomaster's Wife, by Georg Ebers, opens at Chapter XXVIII in a starving city. Days and weeks have passed, and sultry August draws to a close. The Spaniards still surround Leyden, and the city resembles a prison. No message of hope comes from the Prince or the Estates. The plague, the terrible follower of war, has entered Leyden with the famine.

Discontent grows each week, and friends of liberty, watching their families sicken, join those who demand surrender. Junker Georg, long lodged in Burgomaster Van der Werff's house, comes home on the morning of August 29 with a cross-bow in his hand. In the kitchen Barbara asks what he brings today. Smiling, he shows a fat snipe and four larks. Then comes a headless, legless, plucked creature from his bag, and Barbara grows suspicious.
the-caxtons-a-family-picture-volume-05:
Pisistratus narrates Part V of The Caxtons, the family picture he has been painting from the start. The son's voice carries the tale, as before. His father the scholar and the quiet of home form the ground against which travel and ambition are measured.

Setting out the next morning, the narrator earns a kind tip from the Boots at his inn. A footpath through a gentleman's park can save a mile of the road and give a pleasant walk. The grounds are shown to visitors, the Boots adds. An old woman at the lodge will show the walks and the great cascade for a small coin. The gardener would charge far more.
the-confessions-of-jean-jacques-rousseau:
Book V of Jean Jacques Rousseau's Confessions stands here as volume V of the twelve-book set, privately printed for members of the Aldus Society at London in 1903. In 1732, by Rousseau's own dating, he arrived at Chambery and began work registering land for the king.

He was almost twenty-one, with a mind well formed in sense for his age but very deficient in judgment. A few years of experience had not cured his romantic ideas. He knew as little of the world and mankind, he admits, as if he had never paid for instruction. He slept at the house of Madam de Warens, though not as at Annecy. Here there were no gardens, no brook, no landscape, and the house was dark. Book V thus opens a settled, working chapter of the life, under the roof of his protectress.
the-count-s-millions-pg305:
Emile Gaboriau's The Count's Millions, translated from the French, is a novel in two parts; the second part stands in a companion volume, Baron Trigault's Vengeance. The first part, headed Pascal and Marguerite, opens on a Thursday evening, the fifteenth of October, dark by half-past six, with cold wind and rain falling in torrents.

The scene is the Hotel de Chalusse, a grand mansion in the Rue de Courcelles in Paris. Its servants gather in the porter's lodge, where the porter, M. Bourigeau, rules the staff through favors and silence about late returns. With the master out, the count's head valet serves coffee laced with cognac, and the staff unite in abusing their common enemy, the master of the house.
the-crisis-volume-05:
Volume 5 of Winston Churchill's The Crisis opens at Chapter XVI, The Guns of Sumter. Spring has come with a hush, and anxious eyes strain toward a little island in Charleston harbor. Was the flag still there? One sultry night in April, Stephen Brice's mother wakes with fear, sure she has heard the guns.

Stephen wakes too and remembers childhood nights in the great Boston house, when his mother came in the dark to feel whether he was covered. She tells him the war has come and that he will have to go. He protests that the family has nothing left but what he earns. She answers with a courage the narrator calls woman's alone: remember Wilton Brice; she can get along; she can sew.
the-disowned-volume-05:
Volume five of The Disowned opens at chapter forty-nine with the poor scholar Glendower. While Clarence's friend Talbot leaves him a legacy of hard-won wisdom, Glendower tries to live by the same rules. Since his bookseller died, no publisher will take his work, though some offer pay for base or flattering writing. He refuses each offer and sinks deeper into want.

His wife fades with illness while he clings to his secret, prized manuscript. Lytton draws a stark picture of honest talent starved by a trade that rewards flattery. Pride, hunger, and hope grind against each other.
the-divine-comedy-by-dante-illustrated-h:
Part five of Hell in Dante's Vision, in the Rev. H. F. Cary's rendering, spans cantos nine through twelve. Dante pales as his guide turns back at a hard passage, and both men wait, tense, for promised help. Dante asks if any soul from the first circle ever sinks to these depths, and the guide gives a rare reply.

Ahead lie the walls of a burning city and rings of violence. Fallen angels, a great bull-like beast, and rivers of blood mark this stretch. The part raises the scale of horror step by step.
the-emperor-volume-05:
Chapter nineteen opens volume five of Georg Ebers's The Emperor with a grand treat for Alexandria's women. Plutarch, the rich papyrus maker who employs Selene and Arsinoe, funds a show for the wives and daughters of the city, and with him, suitable means splendid. At the theatre door, boys in flower bowers hand each guest blooms and an ivory-and-gold ticket brooch.

Arsinoe finds the pomp past her hopes. Clara Bell renders Ebers's Alexandria in full dress: wealth, craft, and girls caught between work and wonder. The feast day sets new loves and risks in motion.
the-heir-of-redclyffe-pg2505:
Charlotte Yonge wrote The Heir of Redclyffe. Chapter one opens in the drawing-room of Hollywell House, a room with a bright fire, greenhouse plants, and a view of wintry fog and bare trees in November. Laura sits drawing at a round table while Charles lies on a couch near the fire, books and newspapers around him and crutches at his side.

Philip enters and is greeted by both. He brings a letter for his uncle bearing the Moorworth post-mark, the post-town for Redclyffe, Sir Guy Morville's place. Talk turns to guardianship: old Sir Guy had asked that Philip's father take charge of his grandson, with the uncle joined in the trust. A sibling record in the library shows only the title page and contents for the same title.
the-history-of-don-quixote-volume-1-part:
Part 5 of Don Quixote, Miguel de Cervantes' novel, appears in John Ormsby's translation. Chapter fourteen inserts the despairing verses of the dead shepherd. Other incidents not looked for stand with the verses. The Lay of Chrysostom fills the opening. It is a song of cruelty, suffering, and scorned love.

The singer calls on harsh sounds to aid his complaint. He names the lion's roar and the wolf's howl. He names the hiss of the snake and the moan of wild winds. He even names the wail of Hell's choir. All these sounds mix in one discord, he says. Pain like his demands new modes of song. Grief gets a full, wild voice before the prose resumes.
the-innocents-abroad-volume-05:
Part 5 of Mark Twain's Innocents Abroad opens in chapter XLI. The text comes from the 1869 first edition. The party camps in the mountains of Lebanon. A grievance from Ephesus still smarts. The travelers had gathered marble fragments there. They hauled their plunder five miles by mule. An officer with orders from Constantinople made them disgorge it all. Twain confesses his vanity in the affair. He never plundered a stranger's premises without pride.

The order's envelope bore a British Embassy seal. That sharpened the party's anger. Respectable ladies and gentlemen were treated as suspects. Twain still grants the excavation company its rights. Travelers are notorious scorners of honest behavior. From Smyrna the party sailed in wild expectancy. The Holy Land, the grand goal, lay near at hand. Trunks buried for months came up for packing.
the-inside-of-the-cup-volume-05:
Volume 5 of Winston Churchill's novel opens with chapter XVII, Reconstruction. Hodder faces a paradox he cannot dodge. He is still rector of St. John's. He has entered a restaurant of ill repute. He ordered champagne there for an abandoned woman. He woke with no sense of sin. Orthodox language blames the devil for the visit. Only that friendship gave him footing with Kate Marcy, though. She mixes good and evil in one person.

What surprises him is hope. A month of silence on the riddle has passed. A new energy stirs in him without cause. Something stable touches him again in the chaos. The scales have fallen from his eyes. He sees evil, injustice, and despair clearly now. He once mistook an orderly illusion for the world. The sorrow of it all has turned to meaning. He cannot yet say what the meaning is.
the-last-of-the-barons-volume-05:
Edward Bulwer Lytton labels the portion in this record Book Five of his Warwick novel. Spring 1468 opens on a rich cavalcade climbing toward Middleham Castle. Below them lies a wooden village where smoke escapes through roof holes and lattice stands in for glass.

Lytton pauses the plot to explain rural England in the middle ages. He notes old prejudice against chimneys, since smoke was thought to season timber and guard families from colds. The contrast between noble riders and poor homes shows the social gap that drives much of the novel unrest.
the-league-of-the-scarlet-pimpernel-pg58:
Baroness Orczy gathers eleven Scarlet Pimpernel episodes in this record, whose opening pages match the other record of the same title held here. A starving woman dances for alms in a Paris street while crowds watch with sullen contempt. Her fine features show sorrow and ruin under the lanthorn light.

Contents promise passports, patriots, a scarecrow, a traitor, and a battle of wits at the Cabaret de la Liberte. Sir Percy explains matters in the first piece, and his league rescues people from the guillotine. Each short rescue turns on disguise, timing, and nerve.
the-memoirs-of-count-grammont-volume-05:
Volume 5 of Anthony Hamilton's Memoirs of Count Grammont, edited with notes by Sir Walter Scott, opens at Chapter Ninth, various love intrigues at the English court. Hamilton begins with a general essay on jealous husbands. A man who stakes his honor on his wife's conduct, he argues, torments himself and drives her to despair. Spaniards rely on duennas, grates, and locks, while Italians add ingenious precautions or worse.

Against those savage customs Hamilton sets the courteous, indulgent nations that leave wives their liberty. Lord Chesterfield then breaks ranks with his patient countrymen. His jealousy advertises an adventure that might otherwise have stayed within the court's verge and been forgotten in a month. Once he marches off with his prisoner, the wits fall on him: Rochester, Middlesex, Sedley, and Etherege among them. Readers get Restoration court scandal framed by Hamilton's cool, amused moralizing about marriage.
the-mirror-of-literature-amusement-and-i:
The Mirror's number for Saturday, November 22, 1828, No. 342, moves from the Druids' temple at Avebury to the Council Office in Whitehall, a stride the editors joke about. The engraving shows the new range housing the Council Office and Board of Trade. Mr. Soane adapted its facade from Rome's Temple of Jupiter Stator. The adaptation, though, kept mainly the columns and entablature details.

An Athenaeum critic is quoted at length against the result. The site is among the metropolis's most favourable, no expense was spared, and the richest order of antiquity supplied the decoration. Yet the whole is called a failure: poor, or at best but pretty. Its want of elevation and of a prominent centre give it the character of a flank rather than a front. Readers watch the magazine hand its engraving over to a hostile review.

Volume 20, No. 560, dated August 4, 1832, shows elephants kept in the Zoological Gardens, Regent's Park. The engraving is offered as a fair picture of the roomy housing the society gave its animals. Earlier British menageries had kept elephants caged, with only the head free outside the bars.

The elephant stable stood at the far end of the northern garden. A small enclosure beside it and a much larger paddock opposite, fenced in light iron, gave the animal space to move. Lime trees inside lost their lower leaves to the elephant's trunk, twisted off as neatly as a gardener gathers fruit. His chief luxury was a deep bath pool. Comparisons with the Duke of Devonshire's Chiswick elephant and the Paris gardens fill the account.
the-parisians-volume-05:
Volume 5 of Edward Bulwer-Lytton's The Parisians opens with Book V. M. Louvier sits closeted with M. Gandrin and boasts of behaving handsomely to the young marquis. Besides easy terms for transferring mortgages, Louvier gave a free bonus of one thousand louis. The young man has already spent it on a fine apartment, a coupe and horses, and entry at the Jockey Club.

Louvier expects the money to run out fast. Then the marquis, having tasted Parisian life, will borrow no more, and Louvier, sole mortgagee, will buy his estates. A clerk interrupts with a visitor who declines to send in a card but claims Louvier's acquaintance.
the-phrenological-era-organ-of-the-tope-:
The Phrenological Era, a journal of phrenology, is headed in its record with the year 1905, yet the issue present prints Volume XXXV, Number 2, dated February 1939. The clash is stated plainly rather than smoothed over. The issue opens with an article, Structure of Mind, in numbered propositions. Phrenology teaches, it says, that the mind in each person is an organized, substantial entity made of primary elements called faculties.

Each faculty, in action, produces a distinct kind of mental operation. The article argues from simple syllogisms that the mind moves the body, so it must be a substance superior to the body. Its substance is unknown, perhaps of the nature of electricity. From this the writer draws the mind's indestructibility and inherent immortality. The scanned text is rough and garbled in places, but the argument can be followed.
the-principal-navigations-voyages-traffi: Volume XII of Hakluyt's Principal Navigations, edited by Edmund Goldsmid, covers America, Part I. The transcriber's notes describe Hakluyt's own sidenotes, kept and labelled, and footnotes added by the editor in modern spelling. Companion records hold other volumes of the same edition, from Northeastern Europe to Asia. For this volume the pages provided end at the title pages; the American voyage accounts themselves are not among them.
the-right-of-way-volume-05:
Gilbert Parker's fifth volume opens on Michaelmas Day under a cloudless sky, where Mrs. Flynn greets the post-office keeper Maximilian Cour by crying that it is the fun of the world to be alive. Rosalie, working behind the postal wicket, colors at words she herself spoke days before.

Contents promise a trial and verdict, a question about Kathleen, six months passing, a forgotten man, one taken and another left, and an open gate. Joy here feels painful and excessive, hinting at cost. The volume listing overlaps the combined contents given in the complete record in the set.
the-spinster-1905:
Robert Hichens published this story with Frederick A. Stokes Company in 1905. A narrator recalls arriving at Inley Abbey that afternoon. He dines with Inley and his pretty wife, unseen for five years since he stood as best man. Then a church bell begins tolling faintly from the grounds.

Lady Inley shudders and guesses the bell tolls for Miss Sarah Bassett, an elderly spinster taken ill with influenza and then pneumonia while Inley was in town. Inley, visibly moved, stops eating. His wife mocks spinsters as dry twigs whose only purpose seems to be loving cats. Her cruelty contrasts sharply with her husband's feeling.
the-story-of-my-life-volume-05:
Volume five of Georg Ebers's autobiography opens at chapter seventeen. It covers the gymnasium years and his first university period. Leaving Keilhau was hard. The trip to Rudolstadt with his dearest companions was merry, though. It ended in a banquet at a peasant tavern. Kreutzers paid for it. The boys had collected them as fines for offences against the school's table rules.

At one table only French was spoken and at another only the purest German, with a kreutzer fined for any slip, and teachers were welcome guests. Ebers remembers pranks too. One was a frozen snowman in a black cap. The boys planted it in a young teacher's room as a ghost. Then he turns to the part of his life he least wishes to describe.
the-thirty-years-war-volume-05:
Book Five of Frederick Schiller's History of the Thirty Years' War opens after Wallenstein's death, with a new generalissimo to appoint. The Emperor at last took Spanish advice and raised his son Ferdinand, King of Hungary, to the post, while Count Gallas did the real commanding. The Duke of Lorraine and the Cardinal Infante brought strong reinforcements, the latter with 10,000 men from Italy. Ferdinand pressed the siege of Ratisbon, which fell after obstinate resistance.

Donauwerth fell too, and Nordlingen was invested, losses the Swedish party felt keenly. Honour forbade deserting their confederates, so Horn and Bernard of Weimar advanced to relieve Nordlingen even at the cost of battle. Schiller shows Gustavus Horn urging caution in council, outvoted by men intoxicated with long success, heading toward one of the war's great disasters.
the-wandering-jew-volume-05:
Volume five of Eugene Sue's Wandering Jew holds book five. Its contents chapters promise a thug, two brothers of the good work, and a house in the Rue Saint-François. An heir, a testament, and a deed of gift follow. Chapter fourteen, The Eve of a Great Day, joins Rodin and the Abbé d'Aigrigny in the Rue du Milieu-des-Ursins.

Since the July Revolution, d'Aigrigny has moved his order's secret archives to this temporary lodging, fearing expulsion from the fathers' grand establishment. Rodin writes modestly at his desk, playing humble secretary. That role hides his real office of Socius: never leaving his superior, spying into his very thoughts, and reporting everything to Rome. Unease shows through Rodin's usual impassibility.
tob-0005:
James Legge's translation, under the older title Tao Teh King, presents eighty-one short chapters attributed to the ancient Chinese sage Laozi. Together they form the Tao Te Ching, a founding text of Taoist thought. Its subject is the Tao, the way things naturally are when they are not forced.

Chapter by chapter, often in paradox, the text praises softness, quiet, and action that does not strain, using water wearing down stone as a guiding image. Advice to rulers sits beside counsel for anyone seeking a simpler life. For over two thousand years, rulers and seekers have returned to these brief, puzzling sayings.
tob-0105:
Thirteen short lines, said to be cut on an emerald, carry the whole weight of Western alchemy. The Emerald Tablet credits Hermes Trismegistus as its author. Its most famous claim, that what is below mirrors what is above, gave alchemists their motto: as above, so below.

The lines speak of one thing from which all things come, of sun and moon as father and mother, and of a work that must be done with care. Commentaries on the tablet fill shelves, from Alexandria to Newton, who translated it himself. The evidence notes no public-domain text has yet been located for this entry.
tob-0143-68705:
H. P. Blavatsky burst onto the occult scene in 1877 with Isis Unveiled, a huge attack on the science and religion of her day. Volume one, the science half, argues that modern science has cut itself off from real knowledge. Blavatsky defends wonders that laboratories dismissed as fraud or error.

She marshals travelers' tales, old books, and reports of mesmerism and mediums as her witnesses. Floating bodies, healing magnets, and ancient feats of engineering all enter her case. The writing is fierce, learned, and digressive, often all at once. Few debut books have started a movement so fast.
tob-10264-68705:
Blavatsky aimed volume one of Isis Unveiled straight at materialist science. Mesmerism, mediumship, and reported wonders become her evidence that matter is not all there is. She writes as a prosecutor, summoning witnesses the laboratories preferred to ignore.

Ancient feats, Eastern adepts, and modern seance-room reports crowd her brief. The prose is dense, passionate, and stuffed with citations from every age. First published in 1877, the volume made its author famous and notorious at once. This Gutenberg copy gives the plain text of Theosophy's opening blast. Readers will argue with it, but few will call it dull.
tob-10508-68705:
Part of Blavatsky's Isis Unveiled, the science half, argues that the wonders spiritualists reported, floating bodies, mind-reading, and magnetic cures, expose the limits of 1800s materialism. Blavatsky summons scientists, travelers, and old texts as witnesses for phenomena official science dismissed. The volume appeared as half of the 1877 work that launched modern Theosophy.

Her method mixes genuine puzzles of her day's science with séance-room testimony a modern reader will weigh very differently. The polemic energy, though, is real: she writes as counsel prosecuting materialism before a jury of the curious. Read as part of the complete Isis Unveiled, this half supplies the scientific indictment matching the theological one.
tob-10805:
J. A. MacCulloch reconstructed the religion of the ancient Celts in a scholarly study still treated as a standard account a century later. The Celts left no scriptures of their own. MacCulloch therefore works from Roman reports, archaeology, and later Irish and Welsh myth that may preserve older material.

Gods and goddesses, the druids, sacred groves, human and animal sacrifice, and rites of war and harvest are pieced together region by region. He is candid about gaps and hostile Roman witnesses. Readers get the most careful available picture of a major European faith known mainly through its enemies and its echoes.
tob-10808-50205:
Baron Friedrich von Hügel's monumental study The Mystical Element of Religion centers, in volume one, on Saint Catherine of Genoa. Her life, her visions and treatise on purgatory, and her care of the sick in plague-stricken Genoa supply the case study. Von Hügel lays historical and biographical groundwork before any theory, letting one mystic's documented life anchor the inquiry.

Catherine's purgatory is a place of joyful, willing purification, a doctrine von Hügel examines against her experience. V1 evidence calls the completed study the most thorough Catholic account of mysticism written in English. Volume one rewards patience: its detail about a fifteenth-century saint becomes the evidence base for volume two's philosophy.
tob-12905:
Manly P. Hall published The Secret Teachings of All Ages in 1928, when he was twenty-seven. The huge, richly pictured volume surveys occult and symbolic lore from many cultures. Hall built it from his Los Angeles lectures and years of private study.

Chapters treat mystery schools, secret societies, gods and symbols, alchemy, the tarot, and the Kabbalah, among much else. Hall reads all of it as one hidden wisdom passed down through the ages. Fact and fancy mix freely, yet few books did more to spread occult learning in America, and its plates alone keep it in print.
tob-13330-68705:
Science stands trial in volume one of Isis Unveiled, presented again in its Gutenberg text. Blavatsky calls the seance room, the mesmerist's couch, and the records of ancient wonders as witnesses against dry materialism. Her 1877 debut argues that soul and spirit are facts, not dreams.

She writes as scholar and partisan at once, piling citation on citation. Learned readers of her day split sharply: some hailed a prophet, others cried fraud. The quarrel itself made the book. Anyone studying the roots of modern occultism will meet few texts more cited, more fought over, or more alive with conviction.
tob-13505:
