Ali al-Hujviri's Kashf al-Mahjub, here titled Revelation of the Veiled in Reynold Nicholson's translation, stands among the first Persian treatises on the Sufi path. Hujviri wrote in the eleventh century for readers confused by rival Sufi claims. Stations of the path and sayings of the saints organize his teaching.

Alongside doctrine, Hujviri mounts a defense of mysticism against orthodox critics, and criticizes false Sufis in the same breath. Nicholson's translation opened the treatise to the West and made it a fixture of Sufi studies. A thousand years after composition, teachers still assign it as Sufism's early textbook, a measure of how completely Hujviri mapped his subject.
tob-14405:
A Hermetic text from Nag Hammadi, the Discourse on the Eighth and the Ninth, records a teacher leading his son upward in prayer. Hermes speaks, not of spells, but of ascent through the spheres. Few Hermetic writings of this kind survive at all.

Beyond the seven planetary spheres lie the eighth and ninth, realms of pure praise where the soul sings with the powers above. The teacher prays, the son joins, and both reach a stillness words cannot report. The piece reads as an initiation script and shows the mystical side of the Hermetic tradition in late antique Egypt.
tob-4005:
Baldassare Castiglione set The Book of the Courtier at the court of Urbino, where gentlemen and ladies debate across several evenings what makes the perfect courtier. Published in 1528, the dialogue became Europe's handbook of aristocratic manners for two centuries. Grace under pressure stands at its center.

The ideal courtier must excel at arms and letters, music and conversation, while hiding all effort. Castiglione names that art sprezzatura: making difficulty look easy, as if excellence cost nothing. Beneath the polish sits a serious question about how people fashion themselves for public life. Renaissance courts took the answer as a standard, and its influence reached Shakespeare's England.
tob-4205:
Roy Merle Peterson surveyed the local gods and shrines of Campania, the region around the Bay of Naples, in a scholarly work of the 1919 edition. Greek settlers, native peoples, and Rome itself layered their cults on the same hills and harbors. Peterson works district by district through the evidence.

Temples, inscriptions, coins, and votive gifts tell which gods each town honored and how cults merged over time. Isis beside Apollo, Hercules beside local heroes: Campania's religious landscape was a true mixture. Verified public-domain text supports the entry. Students of Roman religion gain here a ground-level view, town by town, of ancient Italian worship.
todd-hydesville-1905:
Thomas Olman Todd tells the birth tale of a faith in Hydesville, his book of 1905. Hydesville is the small town in New York where the Fox girls heard their famed raps in 1848. Todd was a hand of the faith who knew its chief folk. He tells the tale whole: the house, the girls, the crowds, and the wave that swept the land from that one farm room.

His aim is to fix the tale ere its first hands are gone. The book is a home town tale of a world faith. Fans prize its close, plain notes.
treaty-of-portsmouth-1905:
Russia and Japan ended the Russo-Japanese War with the Treaty of Portsmouth in 1905. The talks met at Portsmouth, New Hampshire, where President Theodore Roosevelt had pressed both sides to negotiate. Japan's armies and navy had shocked the world by beating a great European power, but both nations were worn out and short of money.

Under the terms, Russia accepted Japan's leading position in Korea and gave up the southern half of Sakhalin Island. Russia also handed Japan its leases and rail rights in southern Manchuria, though it paid no money damages. Roosevelt won the Nobel Peace Prize for his part in the settlement, the first American to receive it.
uarda-a-romance-of-ancient-egypt-volume-:
Chapter twenty opens volume five of Uarda, with the dwarf Nemu trudging home from his visit to the Regent Ani. A boy stops him with a ring from his mother Hekt, who wants speech with him in the stranger's quarter. Nemu is footsore: his ass is dead, and Katuti cannot afford another.

He spent his last money on a garment and a new wig to appear worthily before Ani. The Regent laughed at his account of Paaker's wild passion, then turned earnest and met his demands halfway. Nemu feels like a duck hatched on dry land and put into water at last. Ebers gives the scheming dwarf his moment of triumph.
un-ga-res-505:
China's charge against the Soviet Union fills Resolution 505, adopted by the General Assembly on 1 February 1952. The Republic of China held that Moscow had broken the Sino-Soviet Treaty of Friendship and Alliance of 14 August 1945. That pact bound both sides to respect each other's land and rule, and to keep out of each other's home affairs. It also pledged Soviet moral backing and arms aid to China.

The Assembly frames the case as a threat to China's freedom and to peace in the Far East. Breaches of treaty pledges, it holds, strike at the trust world law must rest on. The charge came at a Cold War peak, with Chinese and UN forces at war in Korea.
un-ga-res-united-nations-general-assembl:
General Assembly Resolution 505 (VI), adopted on 1 February 1952, charged the Soviet Union with breaking its 1945 Treaty of Friendship and Alliance with China. The treaty had promised respect for each other's sovereignty and land. It promised no meddling in home affairs. It promised Soviet aid going only to China's National Government as the country's central authority.

The Assembly found that the Soviet Union had blocked the National Government's efforts to restore its authority in the three eastern provinces, Manchuria, after Japan's surrender. It had given military and economic aid to the Chinese Communists against it. On those findings it ruled that the Soviet Union had failed to carry out the treaty.
un-sc-res-105: Judge Sir Benegal Narsing Rau of India died in November 1953. His death left a vacancy on the International Court of Justice. On 28 July 1954 the Security Council set the election to fill it. The vote would take place during the General Assembly's ninth session. It had to come before the regular election for five other seats. Those terms expired in February 1955. The short text handles only this scheduling.
un-sc-res-1305:
Bosnia and Herzegovina prompted the Council to adopt Resolution 1305 on Bosnia and Herzegovina on 21 June 2000. The Dayton peace agreement was in place, but carrying it out still fell to local leaders. Refugee returns stayed central to lasting peace. Croatia had taken welcome steps to work with its neighbor and with the war crimes tribunal.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council lets the multinational stabilization force, SFOR, run for twelve more months. Member states may take all necessary measures to enforce the peace deal and guard the force. The text also extends the United Nations Mission in Bosnia and Herzegovina, including its police task force, until 21 June 2001. Parties must hand over indicted suspects and help refugees go home.
un-sc-res-1405:
Reports of many deaths in the Jenin refugee camp reached the Council in April 2002. Israeli forces had fought in the camp during a West Bank offensive. On 19 April 2002 the Council voiced concern at the plight of Palestinian civilians. It noted reports from Jenin of deaths and wide destruction. It called for limits on aid groups in Jenin to be lifted.

The resolution stresses urgent access for medical and aid teams. It welcomes the Secretary-General's plan to send a fact-finding team to Jenin. That team would build an accurate record of the recent events. The Secretary-General had to keep the Council informed. In the event, the team never deployed, after disputes over its terms.
un-sc-res-1505:
The Rwanda tribunal gained its own prosecutor in September 2003. Until then one prosecutor had served both war crimes courts. Resolution 1503 split the office in two. On 4 September 2003 the Security Council appointed Hassan Bubacar Jallow to the Rwanda post. The Secretary-General had nominated him. His term began on 15 September 2003 and ran for four years.

The appointment is a single sentence in the text. Its effect was large for the court in Arusha. A dedicated prosecutor could focus only on the Rwanda cases. Those cases concerned the leaders of the 1994 genocide. The split also let each tribunal chase its own completion strategy.
un-sc-res-1605:
The Golan force was renewed in June 2005 with the conduct clause in place. On 17 June 2005 the Security Council extended UNDOF until 31 December 2005. The Secretary-General had reported on the force a week earlier. The Council welcomed UNDOF's work on the zero-tolerance policy for abuse. Personnel had to follow the United Nations code of conduct. The Secretary-General had to keep taking steps on that front.

The parties had to carry out resolution 338 right away. A report was due at the end of the term. It would cover events and measures taken toward 338. UNDOF's observers continued their patrols of the separation zone. The frontier between Israel and Syria stayed calm.
un-sc-res-1705: A Rwanda tribunal judge was mid-trial when her elected term neared its end in 2006. Judge Solomy Balungi Bossa was hearing the Butare case, one of the court's largest. Her term as an ad litem judge would expire in June 2007. On 29 August 2006 the Security Council authorized her to keep serving in that case until it ends. The decision overrode the normal term limit in the tribunal's statute. Changing judges mid-trial would have wasted years of evidence.
un-sc-res-1905: Resolution 1905, adopted in 2009, survives here as a formal act of the Security Council in record form. English Wikisource made the copy this collection holds. Inside, the Council's well-known pattern turns once more: past decisions are named, the facts of the day are weighed, and new orders are set down in numbered form. The entry keeps one full turn of that pattern.
un-sc-res-2005:
On 14 September 2011, the Council adopted Resolution 2005 on Sierra Leone. The country was preparing national and local elections for 2012. Those polls would test how far peace had taken hold since the civil war. The peacebuilding office in Freetown, called UNIPSIL, was helping the government get ready.

The Council extends the office until 15 September 2012. Its top task is backing peaceful, free, and fair elections. It will also help calm party disputes and cut youth joblessness. Drug trafficking, graft, and small arms all need attention too. Success in 2012 should let the office wind down into a normal country team. Reports come to the Council every six months.
un-sc-res-205: Among the formal acts of the United Nations Security Council sits Resolution 205, which the catalog dates to 1965. The Council is the UN body charged with world peace and security, and it speaks formally through texts like this one. For students of the UN, the record offers the Council's language itself rather than a summary written later.
un-sc-res-305: Security Council Resolution 305 survives in the official record, and the catalog dates it to 1971. Resolutions are the way the Council states its decisions, and member states are expected to take them seriously. Preserving the text in this form keeps a small piece of diplomatic history open to any reader. Its place here reflects the library's aim of keeping primary records readable.
un-sc-res-405: From the Council's official record comes the text numbered 405, catalogued here at 1977. Behind each numbered text lies a meeting, a draft, and a vote, even when the final wording runs to a few lines. Read in sequence with its neighbours, it helps trace how Council practice grew across the postwar decades. No summary replaces it; the record itself is the content of the entry.
un-sc-res-united-nations-security-counci:
A seat on the world court fell empty in 1953. Judge Sir Benegal Narsing Rau of India died on 30 November that year. His term still had time to run. Resolution 105, passed without a vote on 28 July 1954, set the plan to fill the gap.

The Council fixed the vote for the ninth session of the General Assembly. The special poll would come first. Only then would the Assembly hold its routine ballot. Five more seats were due to open on 5 February 1955. Rau had been a key voice in India's founding debates. He helped shape its charter of rights. The text is dry and brief, but it kept the bench at full strength.

Bosnia's post-Dayton order is renewed by Resolution 1305, adopted on 21 June 2000. The Peace Implementation Conference had met in Brussels in May. A UN judicial system assessment programme for Bosnia was due to end by December 2000. Croatia's new steps toward better relations and cooperation were welcomed, and refugee return was called crucial to lasting peace.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council authorizes SFOR, the multinational stabilization force, for a further 12 months. SFOR is to enforce the military annexes of the Dayton Peace Agreement and control Bosnian airspace. The Council extends the UN Mission in Bosnia and Herzegovina, UNMIBH, including the International Police Task Force, to 21 June 2001. It reaffirms the High Representative's final authority on civilian implementation, including binding decisions. It warns that international support depends on the Bosnian authorities' compliance, above all cooperation with the Yugoslavia tribunal, stronger joint institutions, and refugee returns.

Reports of death and ruin in the Jenin camp drove this text of 2002. On 19 April, the Council adopted Resolution 1405 without dissent. Israeli forces were running a big West Bank offensive at the time. The Jenin refugee camp saw the fiercest fight of it. Aid groups were barred from the camp. The toll inside was still unknown.

The text stresses how urgent aid access had become. Medical and relief teams must reach Palestinian civilians now. Curbs on their work, above all in Jenin, must be lifted. The Secretary-General's plan for a fact-finding team is welcomed. The team would pin down what had happened in the camp. Israel refused to work with it in the end, and it was disbanded.

The tribunal trying the leaders of the 1994 genocide in Rwanda gained its own chief prosecutor through Resolution 1505, adopted unanimously on 4 September 2003. A week earlier the Council had split the job, creating a separate prosecutor for the Rwanda tribunal instead of sharing one with the Yugoslavia tribunal.

On the Secretary-General's nomination, the members appointed Hassan Bubacar Jallow of the Gambia to the new post. His four-year term was set to begin on 15 September 2003. Having a dedicated prosecutor was meant to let the Arusha-based court push its heavy caseload of genocide trials forward on its own schedule.

Mid-2005 saw the Golan force renewed once more. The chief's report of 10 June 2005 found the scene calm. UNDOF had kept the truce line since 1974. Its term was weeks from its end. Resolution 1605 passed on 17 June 2005.

Six more months were granted, to 31 December 2005. The old call went out again: act on the 1973 ceasefire text at once. The text takes time for a new sort of clause. The force's work on the UN's zero-tolerance rule won a warm note. Staff must live by the UN code. Troop states must probe abuse claims and punish guilt. A report was due at the close. By then, these conduct clauses were a fixed part of each Golan vote.

One judge, one trial, one fix. A stand-in judge at the Rwanda court had a term due to end on 24 June 2007. Her trial, the Butare case, would not end by then. Swapping judges mid-case could wreck years of work. The chief wrote to the Council on 25 August 2006. Resolution 1705 passed on 29 August 2006.

Judge Solomy Balungi Bossa could keep her seat. The grant ran from 28 August 2006. She would sit till the Butare case closed, term or no term. The rulebook bent for this one case, by name. Such bends were rare. They show a court near its end, keen to close big trials with the judges who had heard the proof from the start.

Iraq's oil money is the subject of Resolution 1905, adopted by the Security Council on 21 December 2009. Iraq's prime minister wrote to the Council asking for one more year of international oversight. His letter is attached to the text. Iraq still had to settle old debts and claims left over from the former regime.

The Council extended the existing rules until 31 December 2010. Under those rules, income from Iraq's oil and gas exports goes into the Development Fund for Iraq. An international board watches the fund and checks how the money is used. The Council ordered reviews during 2010. It also required Iraq to present a plan and a timetable for taking full control of the fund itself. The goal was an orderly handover, with outside auditing kept in place until then.

Sierra Leone's peacebuilding office is renewed ahead of elections in Resolution 2005, adopted on 14 September 2011. National and local elections were due in 2012, likely to raise tensions, and the Secretary-General recommended another year for UNIPSIL. The government was pushing its Agenda for Change. A Transnational Organized Crime Unit fought drug trafficking. The Special Court had finished all its cases except one contempt matter and the trial of Liberia's former president.

The Council extends the UN Integrated Peacebuilding Office in Sierra Leone, UNIPSIL, until 15 September 2012. UNIPSIL must help the government and electoral bodies prepare peaceful, credible 2012 elections. It must support conflict prevention and party dialogue and tackle youth unemployment. It must assist on governance, anti-corruption, drug trafficking, and human rights. The 2012 vote and acceptance of its result are called a milestone that should shape UNIPSIL's transition into a regular UN country team.

Santo Domingo was under a pause in fighting in May 1965. Resolution 205, adopted on 22 May 1965, tried to make that pause last. A week earlier, Resolution 203 had called for a strict cease-fire and sent a United Nations envoy. Resolution 205 asked that the suspension of hostilities be turned into a permanent cease-fire. The Secretary-General had to report to the Council on how the resolution was carried out. The short text does one thing: it presses both sides to stop fighting for good.

Cyprus's peacekeeping force came up for renewal again late in 1971. A report from the Secretary-General, dated 30 November, said the force was still needed to keep the peace. The government of Cyprus agreed it should remain beyond 15 December. Resolution 305 was adopted unanimously on 13 December 1971.

The Council reaffirmed its chain of Cyprus resolutions, beginning with Resolution 186 of 1964. The parties were urged to act with the utmost restraint. They were also pressed to keep working together toward a settlement. The force's stay was extended for a further period ending on 15 June 1972. The Council expected that progress by then might allow a withdrawal, or at least a cut in the size of the force.

Mercenaries attacked Benin on 16 January 1977, striking Cotonou, the country's main city. The invading force killed people and caused heavy damage before it withdrew. A special mission of the Council investigated the attack. Resolution 405 was adopted by consensus on 14 April 1977, after that mission reported.

The Council took note of the report and thanked the mission for its work. It strongly condemned the act of armed aggression against Benin. The text reaffirmed an older Council stand from 1967. States must not allow mercenaries to be recruited or helped in order to overthrow governments. All states were told to guard against such activity on their own territory. Training or moving mercenaries had to be prevented, and states were urged to consider banning it in law. Benin was offered help to assess the damage, and states were asked to aid its repairs.
uslaw-usc-t1-s205:
Section 205 of Title 1 of the United States Code deals with the print of the Code and its supplements. It sits in Chapter 3, on the Code of laws and its supplements. The works in view are those let through by two named sections of the title. They are to be printed at the Government Publishing Office. Their form and their style are to be as a named panel sets. That panel is the Committee on the Judiciary of the House.

The Librarian of Congress is told to work with that panel. The joint work is on the prep of the aids that go with the books. The books are to be made with thumb marks and with other marks to set their parts apart. They are also to be made with a way to put in new matter as it comes.
uslaw-usc-t2-s2105:
Section 2105 of Title 2 of the United States Code clears appropriations for a Senate commission on art. It sits in Chapter 30 of that title, on the Capitol complex, in the part on historic preservation and fine arts. Sums may be appropriated out of the contingent fund of the Senate for the costs of the Commission. The sum is such amount as may be needed in each fiscal year.

The sums are to be paid out by the Secretary of the Senate. Payment is made on vouchers signed by the Executive Secretary of the Commission. The Committee on Rules and Administration of the Senate must approve those vouchers, as the text goes on to state. The text is current through Public Law 119-134.
uslaw-usc-t2-s4105:
Section 4105 of Title 2 of the United States Code deals with the buy of paper goods for the stationery rooms. It sits in Chapter 41, on the officers of Congress, in a general part of the chapter. The goods in view are paper, envelopes, and blank books. They are the goods the stationery rooms of the Senate and of the House need for sale. The sale is to Senators and to Members, for use in public work.

The goods may be bought from the Director of the Government Publishing Office. The price is the true cost of the goods. Pay for the goods must be made before the goods are handed over. The rule is thus a short one on a set buy for two rooms of Congress. It names the seller, the price rule, and the time of pay in one clause.
uslaw-usc-t2-s505:
Section 505 of Title 2 of the United States Code deals with mass mailings by Senators under the frank. It sits in Chapter 16, on the marks for mail sent by Congress. In the year 1991 and in each year since, a Senator who sends out facts under the frank by a mass mailing must act. The Senator must sign up each three months with the Secretary of the Senate for such mailings. The term mass mailing is given its sense by a part of Title 39.

The sign-up is made in a set way. The Senator files a copy of the matter mailed with the Secretary. The Senator also gives, on a form the Secretary gives out, a note of the groups of men and women to whom the mailing was sent. The count of the pieces mailed must be given as well.
uslaw-usc-t2-s5105:
Section 5105 of Title 2 of the United States Code covers transfers of appropriations by House Leadership Offices. It sits in Chapter 51 of that title, on House leadership. Part (a) states the rule in general terms. Each office named under the heading House Leadership Offices in the legislative branch appropriations act may move sums.

The sums may be moved among the classes of allowances and expenses for that office under the same heading. Part (b) carves out one class from that power. The power does not reach sums appropriated for official expenses. Part (c) takes up how the section applies, as the text goes on to state. The text is current through Public Law 119-134.
warren-eolithic-flints-1905:
S. Hazzledine Warren, an English digger, gave this paper on the eolith row to a learned group in 1905. Eoliths were rough flints held by some to be the first tools of man in Britain. Warren had run trials of his own on how such stones can form with no hand at work.

He showed that shifts and crush in the drift can chip flints just like crude tools. Frost, weight, and the foundering of beds do the work that men had lent to a lost race. His trials shut the long row on man in the age before the ice in Britain.
wharton-house-of-mirth-1905:
Edith Wharton published The House of Mirth in 1905, her novel of Lily Bart society. The American novel at its sharpest, it tracks Lily's glittering, fatal navigation of New York high society. Serialized, the book made Wharton famous and fixed her subject, old New York's rich tribe.

Lily, twenty-nine and dowerless, must marry money to keep her place in the world she was bred for. Debts, a venal friend's errands, and Bertha Dorset's lies stain her name season by season in the social round. Lawrence Selden loves her but watches, and Lily's own scruples spoil each scheme that might have saved her fortune. She pays her debts with an inheritance, takes chloral, and dies alone as Selden comes too late to speak. Wharton's irony and pity make the tragedy of manners a judgment on her class.
what-will-he-do-with-it-volume-05:
Book five of Lord Lytton's What Will He Do With It? starts with a short, sharp line on envy and the microscope. The scene then shifts to Montfort Court in the season when great folk leave town. Lytton calls the place grand in size and grounds, yet void of charm. Sumptuous is the word for all of it, picturesque for none.

The house rose in the reign of George the First, in dull brown brick with two wings. Stone rails guard a flat front lawn, and miles of park roll out beyond. Deer graze in the wide, still turf. No cornfield, roof, or spire breaks the view. Wealth here looks vast and dull at once.
wilde-de-profundis-1905:
Oscar Wilde wrote De Profundis in Reading Gaol, and it first saw print in 1905. The long letter, to Lord Alfred Douglas, is the essential Wilde document of his fall. Wilde wrote it in 1897, in the last months of his two-year prison term there.

Wilde recounts his ruinous friendship with Douglas and the trials that jailed him for gross indecency. He weighs his fame, his folly, and his art with candor and flashes of wit. Sorrow, he writes, is the supreme emotion, and Christ his model of the artist. The letter turns blame outward at first, then inward, in a slow arc of reckoning. It stands as one of the great prison writings in the English tongue.
young-journal-of-discourses-vol05:
Volume V of the Journal of Discourses, issued at Liverpool in 1858, keeps the sermon record rolling. Brigham Young and his fellow speakers address a people still new to their mountain home. Their words, caught in shorthand and printed abroad, traveled back across the ocean to the very congregations that heard them.

Teaching here is practical as often as it is lofty: how to live, work, worship, and endure. The set's value lies in that closeness to the spoken moment. Volume V adds its year to the running doctrinal record of nineteenth-century Mormonism, one discourse at a time.
